reviewText:
I used to have Siouxsie's name inscribed on my pencil-case. But after seeing her live in 83 in the Wellington Town Hall, with Robert Smith on guitar, I moved the inscription to my heart. (Mainly for the music, but there was also the way she nearly dented some particularly obnoxious audience members, shaven-headed boot-wearers who admired Hitler, with a deft swing of the microphone stand, which in those primitive days had a base made of concrete. All without missing a note: ahhh, Siouxsie...)
I'm a fan. I still list "Spellbound" somewhere in my top 20 songs, and I still have moods where only the thunder of the Banshees and Siouxsie in full cry will really do. I've even tried to persuade people that the Cure were the second best band that Robert Smith played guitar in. (I usually lose that argument, but win the fall-back position that the Banshees' _Nocturne_ is the best album he ever played on.)
So I bought the "Seven Year Itch" concert DVD the moment I saw it, expecting a nice dark romantic energy transfusion. And I got a serious disappointment instead.
The first five or so songs are performed in a sort of monotone muttering, not only by Siouxsie herself, who seems to have spent the last 10 years smoking and coughing, but also by the Banshees. But those first songs were never my favourites anyway, so my expectations lifted again when Siouxsie announced "Happy House". "Happy House" always had a nice line in obsessive incantatory power. But as performed by the new Siouxsie, it doesn't even have a tune any more, let alone any power. After that, "Christine" came and went without even conjuring up a ghost, a faded wisp, of the glorious song that it ought to be. More muttering from Siouxsie, more off-hand rumbling from the Banshees. And then I took the DVD off, since this was too damn depressing for words.
A few days later I tried "Spellbound", on the theory that the song is damn near indestructible, and surely it would galvanise even this batch of Banshees into some sort of life.
Tester's report: "Spellbound" not indestructible. Banshees still shambolical. Siouxsie still lost her voice.
So. As an irrationally passionate Siouxsie and the Banshees fan, I'm here to warn you that this hideous travesty is not only awful in its own right, but it can have a sort of reverse halo effect, seriously tarnishing the memory of some great music. The cure, after hearing as much of this as you can stand, is to play _Nocturne_, the Banshees' 1983 live album, which is all the proof you need that the Banshees were a brilliant live band with an awe-inspiring catalogue of songs.
Buy _Nocturne_ instead, if you don't already have it; it's virtually a best-of, up to 1983, with versions that often improve on the studio originals. But whatever you do, don't succumb to _the Seven Year Itch_.

reviewText:
First off I have always like UFO and their past history. They have produced some of the best classic rock despite commercial radio stations ignoring their incredible past. The pinnacle of their career was of course the Live album "Strangers In The Night". The Visitor is another story.

As bands age and produce newer records they do leave proof as to whether or not they still possess musical integrity. There has been a string of past newer CD releases from UFO and they all suffer from the same problem.

First off, the playing and sound quality is superb on this CD. You cannot argue with that. The songwriting on the other hand is less than to be desired. Listen closely to the material, (and also the prior last releases) and you will find the verses of the songs are all in the same meter and the same "melody". In other words songwriting wise there are no interesting woven catchy melodies to stick in your ear like proper ear candy should.

Every single verse of each song is exactly the same. The vocal parts thereby kill any of the wonderful instrumentation. This is the main problem with this release. It's cookie cutter paint by numbers vocals which translate to a dull and uninteresting product. This happens to be one big problems with a majority of heavy metal acts. To prove my point listen to the verse of Black Sabbath's "Symptom of the Universe" and then listen to all the verses on this CD.  It's the same stock I, IV, V chord progression generic meter. It's just boring, dull and uninteresting.

Someone needs to tell whoever is writing the vocal parts (I am assuming Phil Moog) to cease writing and use well written songs by someone else in any future releases. A change like that will let them do what they do best and produce a release worthy of buying. He still has the pipes but he just needs to stop using the same lazy songwriting style. This is what will separate the cream from the dull and uninteresting.

reviewText:
SONY!  What in the world are you doing?  You were my champion of better sound.  And now, this!  Set after set of mediocrity.  This is what you did 25 years ago!  If it were fruit, it would be rotting.

It seems that Sony came out with SACD and it was a great improvement in sound - normal CD 26 bits per second, SACD 150 plus bits per second, so much more glorious sound.  BUT you had to be a SACD player, which I did, a nice Marantz model.  SACD player prices have since dropped and the technology has been put in many a player; my cheapo Blue Ray Panasonic plays them shockingly well.

Then Sony developed DSD, which plays on the regular CD players and for a while it seemed that all their new releases would be in DSD.  DSD is a clear improvement.  Look for it.  This was going to be the wave of the future until the market caught up.  I don't know if the DSD can be copied but I know of no recorders for SACD therefore the the music industry would buy some time and a new age of golden sound would arrive in the SACD.  All hail Sony!  (Blue Line, which I have not heard but have only read about has not topped SACD.  As for DVD audio, it died.  It was sick to begin with.)

DSD and SACD.  I anticipated.  I waited.  I grew jaded.  Sony is now putting out the oldest versions of their early CDs for, I guess, people who want smaller boxes since the disks are out there in used shops.  Sony has turned into the now bankrupt EMI, just repackage and release, repackage release and do it the cheapest way possible.  Sony US seems committed to providing low quality in a world of God-awful I don't know how you can stand it MP3!  But only in the US, and I guess, Europe.  Sony Japan seems committed to providing great sound.  Because the Japanese know and demand quality.  How anyone can listen to a symphony orchestra on MP3 is beyond me.  It is like peeing in a fine French feast.  I suppose you can eat it but oh God!

Look, these are wonderful performances.  Classics.  Benchmarks.  However, the new DSD remasters have much better sound.  Buy that version.  I did even though I had this older set.  I just picked up a "like new" complete Murray  Perahia Mozart piano concertos DSD for about 5 bucks more than this set.  The disks sound wonderful.

Sony, don't make us root for your demise.

reviewText:
None of the Simon & Garfunkel hits were live recordings.

So how does one get the actual hit recordings in keeping with the promise that is the title of the CD?

One buys more CDs in hope of getting the actual hit versions -- and in mono, as originally released, and as played on the radio.  And then one must deal with hit-or-miss mastering.

With the immense popularity of this rather overrated duo, and the immense amount of money made from their recordings, one would think Simon would get over the greed and put together an actual "Greatest Hits" CD with the actual hits.  But, no: countless re-releases of the legitimate material -- well, not so much -- mixed in with live versions as substitutes, alternate takes one listens to perhaps once, etc.  All sorts of manipulative compilations of this and that -- but no promise kept with a CD of the recordings that were actually the hits, on one CD.

If only their were one collection made with all the LPs, in both mono and stereo, and all the actual hit recordings, in mono.  Instead, the effort to arrive at that means buying numerous CDs with recordings that were rightly rejected the first time.  Instead, it's so blatantly obvious that it's all about the greed for more and more money.  The whole program reeks of contempt for the fans.

reviewText:
"Have you listened to the radio lately? Have you heard the canned, frozen, and processed product being dished up to the world as American popular music today?"---Billy Joel

How many of us are old enough to remember what American music was like when talented musicians who could actually play and write their own music ruled the pop/rock/country charts?? The nightmare we are currently facing in the modern music industry is a corporate mainstream music scene that has been hijacked by money-hungry record company executives who are killing off real talent and musicianship in the name of GREED. Never before has the music industry valued money over music to such a disturbing degree. The 21st century is now upon us and the music industry has made their stance loud and clear: the days of promoting musical integrity and originality for mass consumption are over.

American music in the 21st century has split in two---the diverse independent music that attracts fans on the internet and at small venues across the country, and the homogenized corporate product that is fed to consumers everyday by the media. Getting music from artists to the public today is now completely controlled by conglomerates and bottom-line analysts who are too blinded by dollar signs to care about the quality or integrity of modern music. Today's record companies are being run at the top by greedy corporate executives who care about one thing: making a profit by promoting what they want you to hear. These executives dictate which artists we are exposed to, and they determine how long today's Top 40 stars will remain relevant. Today's record labels seek pretty boys and prettier girls who appeal to the fickle 18-30 year old demographic---clueless music fans who ignorantly believe that any artist not shoved down their throats by radio or TV is simply not worth listening to. Radio stations are no longer an outlet for great talent to get airplay. The radio station monopoly in America is now a corporate marketing machine that has completely homogenized the mainstream music scene. The result is a sad reality where REAL artists who don't fit the crowd of cookie-cutter pop stars go tragically unnoticed by a brainwashed music-buying public that naturally assumes whatever music we hear on the radio must be the best music available to us.

Instead of promoting and supporting real artists who stand for musicianship and originality, today's record companies have created a contrived, superficial music scene where real talent, soul, and originality take a backseat to a pretty face and a hot body. Top 40 music has seen a dramatic decrease in musicianship in the last 15 years with manufactured record company clones who can do nothing more than sing, shake the booty, or look sexy for the camera. Musicians are being relegated to background roles, while entire crews of technicians and make-over people are used to turn tone-deaf, sexy young women into the latest contrived pop star {Britney, Miley, Katy, Taylor}. The great music legends from previous decades who paved the way for today's superstars (Ray Charles, Elton John, Billy Joel, Eric Clapton, Brian Wilson, Simon and Garfunkel, Waylon Jennings, Ronnie Milsap, John Fogerty, Stevie Ray Vaughan, to name just a few) would've never had a chance in today's market! These were "real deal artists" who stood for talent over sex appeal and surface value. These legendary performers proved that "real music" doesn't go out of style in six months. No matter how much great talent that modern radio programmers and music executives refuse to support or promote, a great piece of music will always be a great piece of music, regardless of age or era. True talent has no expiration date...

Meanwhile, televised "karaoke contests" {The Voice, American Idol, X-Factor} give no attention to aspiring musicians who actually write and play their own music. Many of the judges chosen for these shows are former pop stars or money-driven executives like Simon Cowell with no experience in creating music. Do the producers of these programs honestly feel there's something wrong with allowing young musicians who create their own music to be stars on Top 40 radio?? These ridiculous shows are spreading a false message to a young audience that a cookie-cutter singing voice and a pretty face is all it takes to be a music star in 21st century America! How many American Idol supporters care anything at all about a great guitar solo, a brilliant piece of songwriting, or anything else that has nothing to do with just singing or looking pretty?? The great John Fogerty recorded at least two albums in his career where every single instrument was played by John himself.  That, my fellow music lovers, is REAL TALENT. Let's count the number of American Idol contestants with any musical ability at all besides singing.  While there is nothing wrong with good looking music stars who only sing, there needs to be room in the Top 40 for music produced by real musicians---both young and old.

Truth be told, there are less than six corporations who control 90 percent of everything we see and hear on radio and television everyday. The media conditions us to believe that any artist not given radio airplay or media exposure is simply not as worthy as whoever is popular on the charts. This false idea has been sadly embraced by a large number of ignorant music fans for decades and it's time to wake up.  Knowledge is power and change begins with us. Music lovers everywhere all have a decision to make: do we blindly embrace the contrived, disposable, homogenized music that greedy executives put in front of us, or do we seek out the worthy overlooked talent that Top 40 radio stations don't allow us to hear? As music lovers, what can we do to tackle this ongoing issue and beat back at the corporate take-over of mainstream music?  First, we need a growing army of "informed" music fans to rise together and force narrow-minded radio programmers and record labels to embrace a new policy of talent over sex appeal, musicianship over gimmicks, and integrity over greed.

Here's what we all can do to achieve this....

Turn off your local corporate radio station and seek out the many great overlooked artists who are denied the radio airplay and media attention that the corporate stars are getting.  Do not allow greedy music executives and the media to do your thinking and choosing for you!  Do not assume that everything you hear on American Idol and Top 40 radio is the only music worth your time and attention. It's not! There is a wealth of great overlooked talent out there that can be found on Youtube, Pandora, Spotify, Sound Cloud, and internet radio stations. Open your ears to these artists! Spread the word about them to your friends and other music fans. Most importantly, we must speak with our money and buy the music these underexposed artists are putting out. By taking a stand for real talent, we can all send a loud message to the music industry that real music has nothing to do with youth, sex appeal, gimmicks, or copying the sound and style of every cookie-cutter clone on the charts. Instead, it has everything to do with the talent, soul, and originality that our legendary performers represent.

 The next time your teenager tells you how amazing the new Taylor Swift CD is, show them just how little of Taylor is truly inside the CD, and how much of it is make-up, computer technology, marketing, and music executive greed. Then buy them some real music, played by real musicians with real talent. Our children won't learn about America's greatest music makers unless WE expose them to it. Our corporate Top 40 radio stations are not going to do it for us. As music fans who care about the future of American music, we must join together in the fight to put real musicians and the music they create back into the mainstream where it belongs!

reviewText:
Diana Krall has stated in interviews that the selections on this "concept" album have nothing to do with jazz or with the "swing" associated with Sinatra--which is representative of a tradition, or lineage, emanating from the "black" music of Louis and Bessie Smith along with its symbiotic relation with the blues and a distinguished "Songbook" composed by by Berlin, Kern, Gershwin, Arlen, Ellington, Rodgers, Porter.  Instead, her purpose from the beginning was to produce an album (and subsequent world tour) representing the vaudeville, or burlesque, tradition of the "roaring 20s," along with songs by the favorites of her parents and grand parents: in short, the music of vaudeville and burlesque, a "white" tradition associated with the show-hall performers of the "roaring" 1920's, the era of the flappers,  and a "jazz" age which pronounced impresario Paul Whiteman as the "King of Jazz."

The result is an "alternative" program of songs that, for the most part, have vanished from public memory (the first track--"We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye," which was recorded by Sinatra, is the closest to a "standard").  As stated in my original review, the tunes frequently come alive--with sincere and unguarded melodramatic emotion, with theatrical and spirited flare--in their original versions from the '20s and '30s.  No one who has this albums should pass up the opportunity to hear the original "Glad Rag Doll" as performed by Ted Lewis (and slightly later by legendary, tragic torch singer Helen Morgan).  Another "must" is Georgie Jessel's original recording of "When the Curtain Comes Down," who makes clear the song's function as a "show opener"! By contrast, the Krall version--which employs the narrative voice of Elvis Costello--treats the song as a morose, funereal closer, implying that no one on the present recording has taken the trouble to listen to the lyrics of the song.

Listen to the Boswell Sisters' recording of "We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye" (and catch their breath-taking "Everybody Wants My Baby" while you're at it).  Then there are plaintive, affecting originals by Ruth Etting (played by Doris Day in "Love Me or Leave Me") and Jimmy Rogers, Gene Austin, Frank Crumit, Annette Hanshaw.  In each case, the original version is barely "hinted at" in Krall's low-register, unemotional, breathy delivery, which is simply unsuited to capture of the spirited originals.  Although the last century's most prolific, versatile and influential singer, Bing Crosby, is represented several times, Krall passes by the jazz-singing Crosby who was inspired by Louis Armstrong ("Shine," "St. Louis Blues," "Stardust") in favor of the melodramatic, more vaudeville-style Crosby of the late '20s and early '30s.  The problem again is that she can't begin to approach the near-operatic intensity and vocal artistry of Crosby's original performances, which he could effectively project even before sensitive microphones.

In short, there's an important vein of American music that Krall has opened up on "Glad Rag Doll," but a musician of her "cool jazz" stylistic qualities--pleasant and sultry vocals (rarely moving above middle C) and finely honed but stylized piano improvisations (she has yet to demonstrate she can sustain musical interest beyond two choruses of a tune)--is the least likely to approximate the spirit, passion and theatrical strengths of the original performers of vaudeville music.  Contrary to the hype of the producer-promoters of this album, it does not begin to recreate the energy off the age of the flappers, the roaring '20s, the "Jazz Age."  Rather than revisit the music of the Great Gatsby BEFORE the party, the listener is invited to the tragic "aftermath" of Jay Gatsby's party, leading to his death and desolate funeral.

Initially, I was seduced by the "concept" and gave the album a lonely (at the time) 5 stars.  But my feelings, along with circumstances surrounding the album, have changed.  From the beginning the album was: 1. panned by Krall fans, who found the music not only a totally different path for the popular jazz vocalist but dreary, dull and monotonous experience; 2. loudly hyped by rich promoters as an unqualified artistic success.  Soon, the big money won, with the album appearing in one publication after another (this week, the cover story of "Down Beat" magazine, the bible of the jazz world.  What we're witnessing with "Glad Rag Doll" is NOT a democratic, "middle-out" success but a "top-down" triumph that's been orchestrated by the "smart corporate money," tin-eared, opportunistic and relentless producers accustomed to putting their materialistic might behind a Taylor Swift or Justin Timberlake.  Certainly such promotion is better devoted to Krall than teen-pop but why not the best Diana Krall, the one growing out of the black jazz tradition of Nat Cole?  Or why the scandalously overlooked Roberta Gambarini (the new millennium's Ella)?  Even some of Sinatra's best albums with the Nelson Riddle Orchestra are out of print.  Why not preserve this cultural hallmark of the previous century rather than "force" this album of inferior music down consumers' throats.

Previously, I was seduced by the concept Diana was honoring in "Glad Rag Doll."  After listening to the album, observing the marketing tactics behind its "apparent" success, and re-discovering the musical tradition that the present weak representation claims it is paying tribute to, I must expose the same "Emperor's New Clothes," that initially had me fooled.

Original review:

Frank Sinatra was the first artist to grasp the significance and potential of the new long-playing 33 rpm vinyl record format.  Despite the rise of Ole Blue to "matinee idol," or "Elvis stature" in the 1940s, he still trailed by good measure the prolific Bing Crosby, who excelled in every genre of popular music--melodramatic movie music, Hawaiian melodies, Irish favorites, Broadway tunes, heated jazz (with scatting and whistling) and, of course, country-western.  It seemed there was no "fencing in" this seminal voice of American popular song.

In the early 1950s, however, Sinatra seized the long-playing format and, together with orchestrator Nelson Riddle, released a series of  artistically whole "concept" albums, each unified by a central theme, each composed of "old"songs from the '20s and '30s, each organized as a "narrative" capable of holding the listener's attention for the twelve songs--all ballads, or all swing tunes, or all songs about subjects normally considered inappropriate for popular entertainment.  Sinatra sang about loneliness, loss and aging--while taking on the persona of the character in the song and making you believe every word.

The commercial and artistic success of the "concept albums" raised Sinatra in public esteem, leading many to proclaim Ole Blue not only the best jazz singer but the most compelling and poetic voice of the 20th century--the "master storyteller," a nuanced interpreter of ballads, who slowed them down to "undanceable" tempos and conveyed their very essence with his legendary "breathless phrasing."

Diana Krall may not possess the vocal talent of Frank Sinatra, but in "Glad Rag Doll" she is, like Sinatra, taking a similar bold, conservative direction by mining the tunes of the past.  Moreover, she's centered the songs around a unifying theme, or a "narrative" and "persona"--that of a New Orleans "sporting house" lady, whose success depends on singing in a sultry, undeniably pleasing manner but with limited  opportunities for emotional engagement with this material (admittedly, our attention is necessarily directed to her pianistic skills as much as her voice}.  On the cover of the album she's dressed in black silk stockings and garters, and filmed on a couch or next to the parlor piano (perhaps meant to evoke the ragtime melodies of Jelly Roll Morton, the most colorful of all New Orleans Sportin' House pianists).

It's a daring concept (as were the Sinatra-Riddle albums, which ignored contemporary fluff in favor of songs from forgotten shows, revues, and movies). For Sinatra the approach not only worked but sparked one of the most storied comebacks in entertainment history. Perhaps "Glad Rag Doll" will enjoy some of the same success.  Still, much of the material seems at odds with Krall's strengths as a versatile jazz musician. The songs have a pre-Louis Armstrong mechanical beat and dispassionate elocution that does a disservice to the creativity of 1920s musicians such as Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Earl "Fatha" Hines and even Jelly Roll. Without swing, what's left is the dramatic interest of the featured performer's persona as a Sportin' House lady and the songs she's required to sing for patrons' pleasure. Or is that the point? Her persona is that of a victim, forced to perform for the pleasure of clientele who are too jaded to reward songs of heartfelt emotion.

Diana Krall has not as yet followed Nat Cole's (or Carmen McRae's) example of converting her image from "singer-pianist" (in Nat's case, one of the 3-4 best jazz pianists alive!) to a "stand-alone" singer (even the credits unfailingly bill her as responsible for "vocal and piano" for each selection).  Her voice hovers around middle C, often remaining comfortably beneath the note.  Even when piano is replaced by various guitars and "period piece" instruments, her elocution too often is overshadowed by accompaniment that occupies the foreground, requiring the listener to strain to catch all the words. The infectious personification of the opening lyrics--"The chair and then the sofa /  broke right down and cried /  the curtains started waving for him to come inside"--embraced whole-heartedly and sung with unapologetic openness and clarity by Crosby/Clooney or the Boswell Sisters--is reduced to a throwaway line in Krall's desultory approach, which appears to be aiming for an ironic displacement between sentimental lyrics and her low-key delivery of them. The result could be seen as a hip modernization of these "ancient" sentiments--or could easily lead to a sense of accumulative, enervating dreariness and monotony.

Albums (along with CD players) are continuing to slide in sales, and a piano-playing singer with a Julie London-like voice, however gifted, is arguably forced to try something different to attract and hold the public's attention.  Maybe Diana will score with a growing number of Sportin' House patrons who purchase the album and choose to revisit it frequently.  If so, she can be a "glad doll," but credit must be given to her producers as much as her vocal and pianistic skills.

When in 1982 Alan Wilder was recruited to be part of DM, the band was destined to be just another of hundreds of brit-pop new-romantic bands that were around. When, thirteen years after that point he left them, they were an icon. They've created a new musical style. They were one of the most influential bands standing in their time. Fourteen years after that, the remaining members, now in their 50's, have just returned to the point they were 27 years before. And they've done it with a terrible bad taste. Unbelievable.

The album, musically speaking, is a black hole. Not only it is a nullity, but also absorbs and destroys any idea you had on music before, while you're listening to it. Having it playing in the radio is obscene. Voices and chorus, simply horrendous. Only in "peace" they sound a bit coordinated. The impressions i had while listening to it was some sense of nervous irritability mixed with pity and shame. I just can't believe they've dared to make this. I would never have believed they could go so far. I feel ashamed of putting this mockery in public. Instrumentals, a nintendo sonnerie.

Total collapse.

reviewText:
The title of Timbaland & Magoo's latest effort is ironically the best way to describe it. "Under Construction (Part II)" seems more like a mixtape than an album. Timbaland's beats simply sound unfinished and the less that can be said about the incredibly sad hooks, the better.
As for the lyrics, Timbaland loads up every verse he spits with tons of braggadocio, while Magoo (who is oddly absent from a few of the tracks) shows a bit more restraint, only going as far to say that he's "numero uno". Timbo gets much more time on the mic than his partner, giving him plenty of time to explore the space of his massive ego on songs like "Naughty Eye (Parts 1 and 2)", "Don't Make Me Take It There", and especially "That S**t Ain't Gonna Work" in which he basically proclaims himself the god of beatmaking AND music altogether. Despite his claims, Timbaland seems to realize how much his music's sucked lately and shows his self-consciousness on the anti-bootlegging track "Cop That Disc". I guess he doesn't want people to know that he's releasing garbage before it even comes out.
Still, there are some brief moments of polish on "Under Construction (Part II)" that stand out over the others. "Cop That Disc", "Shenanigans", "Indian Flute", and the two R&B-ish tracks "N 2 Da Music" and "Insane" are definitely listenable, but most of the other songs sound either recycled and plain, or are ruined by Timbaland's subpar singing on the choruses.
Don't buy this album, and download it if you MUST have it. Maybe that'll teach Timothy to cut the crap.

reviewText:
When Charlotte Church first came onto the music stage at the young age of twelve, I noticed some things in her technique that were not quite correct, however, given the fact that she was only twelve, I just listened to it, thinking that she would improve with each new CD.
Then out came her second CD. While it was more of an opera album, because of all the arias, I was shocked that Miss Ryan (Miss Church's Voice Teacher) would allow Miss Church to sing such difficult repertoire. Those arias are for a soprano in her last years of college, not a soprano in her first years of junior high. Why? Well, if you have plans on becoming an opera singer, or if you want to sing those arias when you are older, you don't sing them when you are young. This is because when you are young, the voice is still in training and trying to get rid of bad habits.
If you sing the arias when you are on the bad habits, you will most likely not be able to break them when you are older. Wich is why you should wait it out--wait till your technique is supurb on the art songs--then--and only then--go onto arias. When you do go onto arias, the first ones should be light pieces, like Handel's As When The Dove, or Mozart's Vedri Carino, his Batti, Batti O Bel Masetto, and also, young classical artists should also sing Caro mio ben, even if it is the most common piece in the 24/26 Italian Song and Arias--it helps you along with some common used Italian words.
Instead of singing As When The Dove (Handel), or Vedri Carino (Don Giovanni, Mozart) Miss Church went for pieces such as La Pastorella (The Little Shepherdess). Before Church recorded this, the youngest singer I ever heard sing this piece was twenty one, and a junior in college, a opera/vocal major.
Why is it a good idea to wait until you are a little older to sing this piece? Because of all the high Cs and Bs, as well as trills that most young people can't tackle.
Soon after that, Miss Church came out with a recording of Christmas Carols. I don't think that the Ave Maria should be touched by a fourteen year old girl, in fact I think you should be sixteen before you attempt this. There are a great many reasons why--breath support, phrasing, and tone qualities are required that people under the age of sixteen can not master. It is by no means that they have bad voices, it is just that they are still trying to train their voices to tackle the breath control and phrased tones.
Soon after that, out came Enchantment. Again, the songs on this disc were not suited to a fifteen year old, such as The Flower Duet, and the Habañera. The Flower Duet is not a good idea to sing for a great many reasons--number one--the higher part is for a coloratura soprano and the lower part is for a coloratura mezzo-soprano. Number two--both parts being a touch on the heavy side for a fifteen year old to sing and bring out the tone required for the pieces.
Somewhere in there, came the soundtrack to "A Beautiful Mind." I can stand the wordless vocalises, but, All That Love Can Be was very raspy, and had to much air escaping in her tone. I think that Miss Celine Dion or Miss Sarah Brightman would have been better choices for the Beautiful Mind soundtrack.
Then we hear four new recordings, wich still has sound far back in the mouth, and not up frount in her mouth where it should be.
I hope Miss Church goes and trys to get a carreer in something else--because I believe that the music industry has had enough.
label: negative

reviewText:
I'll be honest --- I sat through about 45 minutes of this documentary [...].  It's not that the photos aren't interesting; but I'd rather have them in a coffee table book so I could look at them at my leisure.

What I saw of this film is mostly zooming in and out of Barry Feinstein's photographs.  Not only is there no footage of Dylan performing, but there are almost no photos of Dylan performing, either.  In fact, Feinstein states that he was only interested in photographing Bob's personal side, and that if you want to see performances, you should go to a show.  So you see a lot of pictures of Bob talking to kids in the street in England, and so on.

Interviewing is an art, and the director who interviews Feinstein doesn't have the talent.  His style is leaden and ponderous and Feinstein seems a very dull interview subject.  A skilled interviewer might have drawn out more interesting stories, but Feinstein talks about himself and his views on photography and has very little to say about Bob Dylan.

This disc is for hard, hard-core Dylan fans only.  In my opinion, you're better off buying one of the numerous biographies or checking out "Don't Look Back" or several of the other videos that actually have musical performances.

A book of these photographs would be much more interesting [...].

reviewText: I'm not usally a fan of mainstream music. Occasionally I'll like the mainstream but more often I'll like stuff that's  more off the beaten path. I have nothing against actresses trying their hand at music either: just in the past year Minnie Driver and Emmy Rossum released strong albums that weren't in keeping with the traditional pop music scene. But when I listened to this my opinion of Scarlett Johansson as a singer dropped significantly. I'd heard her rendition of "Summertime" on the "Unexpected Dreams" CD, and though she has a limited range, I thought she might be able to produce something worth listening to on an album. No such luck. I'm not a Tom Waitts fan to begin with, so I won't critique her choice of material. However her voice is raspy, frequently off key, with only a slight awareness of pitch. Her range encompasses is maybe an octave, and she sounds like she's falling asleep as she sings. For me that is the biggest problem. She doesn't seem to care about what she's singing. There's no sense of coloring her voice or phrasing in order to express any kind of feeling (she IS supposed to be an actress, you'd think she would at least um...act?) I'm a big fan of musical theater and I know Scarlett has expressed interest in doing that in the future. Based on this album I have to say I hope that never happens. I don't like writing bad reviews, but this kind of vanity project is what gives actresses who attempt music a bad name and make it harder for those who are actually musical to be taken seriously.

reviewText: This is perhaps the most annoying record I've heard. Whatever you might think are the merits of hip-hop, its aesthetic is the polar opposite of the light and cheery samba and bossa nova of Sergio Mendes, and trying to graft one on to the other only produces a mess. I think there may be some good songs in here, but they're buried beneath the dumbed-down bass-heavy layer of hip hop and rap, so who can tell? All the sophisticated and complex rhythms of Brazil are bludgeoned by the idiotic simplicity of New York street music. I can't imagine anyone, of either musical persuasion, finding this CD to work. But then maybe you think Justin Timberlake is a musician, in which case you'll probably love this travesty.

reviewText:
Somewhere around track 10, I stopped trying to count the clichs and references to back roads, fishing holes, boots, and good kissin.  Suffice to say, the number was high.

Kick the Dust Up has been renewed ad nauseum, yet it still feels like it would be appropriate to remark on how terrible this song is.

The albums title track, Kill the Lights, is the albums first requisite club-dance-EDM track.  Its every bit as bad as you might imagine, with Luke suggesting that they kill the lights, that they feel skin on skin, don't care where weve been.

This is where the album finds itself getting a little bit jumpy.  Strip It Down is a song similar to Aldeans Burnin It Down, though the song at least seems to be reaching for something a bit more suggesting that the couple is trying to recover from a period of distance.  There is some callbacks to a previous Dierks Bentley hit, Come a Little Closer.  Ill be honest, I don't completely hate this song.  It could be a whole lot worse, and the production isn't too bad, but its still pretty clich ridden, and Luke still cant get through even this song without mentioning back roads and summertime heat.

Home Alone Tonight finds the album right back on the wrong path.  And Razor Blade isn't a bad song; in fact, it feels like some effort was put in to the song.  Fast though finds itself right back into clich-ridden paradise with a song about how time goes by too quickly.  This is the kind of theme which can be done well, but nothing about the song is original.  Honestly, this one sounds like it was one that was rejected by Kenny Chesney.

Move.  I wonder what this song is going to be about.  Prediction: its going to be about wanting to move with a pretty girl out on a dancefloor and hoping to get with her.  Final verdict: its a song about watching a sexy girl dance and move underneath the southern sky and wanting to get with her so bad that he cant move when he watches her move.  OK, the prediction was close enough.  I won't even get in to how awful this song sounds.

As soon as the next song started, I was wishing it was [David Caruso flip of sunglasses] just over.

Love It Gone is yet another predictable song that can be telegraphed from the moment it starts to the second it ends.  Its predictable and boring.  Way Way Back feels like another Kenny Cheney reject.

To the Moon and Back and Scarecrows are the only true bright spots on the album.  To the Moon and Back is a throwback to what Luke was capable of before he hit it big and sold out.  Its a reminder of what he could still do if he was willing to put in the time and effort.  Its subtle, its toned back, its mostly clich-free, its well-produced. Scarecrows feels a little bit like We Rode in Trucks from his first album

I wouldnt venture to say that the album has more than two true bright spots; I will say that you can see a little bit of sun hiding behind the clouds, but its nowhere near enough to give this album any kind of positive light.  And unfortunately, the album waits until the very end to give anything worth the time, and by that point, I didn't feel like listening anymore.  When Bryan isn't in his EDM dance mode, its mostly pure pop, with a little Kenny Chesney-esque beat thrown in in a couple of different songs.  My opinion of Bryan may have actually worsened, due to the fact that the couple good songs show us that hes still capable of putting out something goodhes just not willing to take the time to do more of it.

Every generation or so, the successors to Buddy Holly's record company, Coral Records (Decca, MCA, Universal), releases a 'new' Buddy Holly disc. And almost everytime (1979 and 1983 are exceptions), the same old few tracks are put forth. "Peggy Sue," "That'll be The Day," "It Doesn't Matter Anymore"...the list is short. This time, we get ABSOLUTELY NOTHING that MCA didn't puke out in 1993 with their BUDDY HOLLY COLLECTION. Same tracks, same playing order. While good, this set did not go far enough.

In 1979, British MCA released THE COMPLETE BUDDY HOLLY, a six-LP set featuring everything that had been released by the legendary rocker, including interviews, TV appearances, some undubbed tapes and even early productions for artists like Lou Giordano and Waylon Jennings. Then in  1983 FOR THE FIRST TIME ANYWHERE, a set of containing more undubbed recordings, was released. Other than these epochal releases, all we've seen since are overpriced, undertracked crappy compilations.

When will Universal get on the ball and give us a complete box-set, remastered in 24-bit sound, comprised of all the material that they have sitting on the shelf?

reviewText:
Radiohead's Kid A has been critically lauded and all the critics think it is the cat's pajamas, but ultimately, for sheer entertainment value, it fails. The entire album is slow, muffled and just plain boring, such as the pervasive, synthesised drone of `Idioteque' or the weird instrumental misfire of `Kid A' (the song). Ultimately, Kid A is an album that may well be a triumph of art-house and avant-garde music - a revisiting of David Bowie's Berlin Trilogy days - but if you're in the market for something entertaining, Kid A is not the way to go.
  Radiohead's previous album, OK Computer, was excellent. They had wavered just enough from the contemporary musical scene to produce something unique, entertaining and melodic; however, with Kid A, they have bitten off a little more than they can chew. This is one of those `indulge me' albums that a band puts out to try something new and offbeat, like `Fear of Music' for the Talking Heads, or `Frank's Wild Years' for Tom Waits. The aforementioned albums, however, are both excellent: the artists succeeded in making their new sound not just unique and individual, but also compelling and entertaining for the listener. In contrast, Kid A does not succeed in achieving this. The album is just a series of droning, slow `pieces' (they can't really be called songs) that ostensibly have some hidden meaning, and probably do (the critics seem to love it), but it's just not something you can hum or tap along to. It doesn't even feel like music.
  Which is fine. All of this is my opinion, and nobody else's. All I'm saying is that it didn't entertain me - the majority of people out there seem to love it, just like some people love Finnegans Wake, and others don't. Therefore, Kid A is a very subjective album, like English Literature - it can mean a number of things to a number of people. Yet, like English Literature, if one doesn't look for the subtext and the hidden themes, it's just plain boring (see: Middlemarch). Listening to Kid A, I have searched for a subtext but I haven't found one, which probably just boils down to my fledgling perspicacity. As Beth Massa said: "The band's future-perfect musical grammar may be hard to decipher, and the melody is even more subliminal," but I, like many people, don't have the patience to sit and listen to something that fails to at least get my toes tapping or me singing along. So, many people may love subliminal melodies and indecipherable grammar, but not this cowboy.

reviewText:
Saw these girls poppin' up everywhere a few months ago.  I liked the look.  Down to Earth.  Innocent, but yet dangerous.  I had yet to hear their music, but assumed by their appearance that it would be some sweet ol garage rock girls rock revival.  A few months went by...

Heard them compared to Fleetwood Mac.  Saw them get BNMed.  Heard they opened for U2 (which made me a little skeptical.)  So I had to check em out.

I was shocked by what I heard.  First off by how terrible it sounded.  Second, by the crazy professional production behind their music.  This was not what their image had portrayed.  Were they trying to fool me?  Haim?  You naughty naughty girls!  They've got some muscle behind this record.  Not that I have anything wrong with the corporate sound.  I love it all.  But this is trying to pass itself off as something it ain't.

I could hear the similarities to the Mac only in that the lead singer sounded like Christine McVie.  To me it sounded more like Lisa Lisa and the Cult Jam on steroids.  Don't get me wrong.  Lost in Emotion was, and still is, my jam.  But holy production!  Maybe there are some good songs here, but I couldn't hear em with all the techniques involved.

They started to feel creepy to me.  I pictured all those studio executives around these girls...creepy!
It's kind like that girl who got all dressed up in the little kid beauty pageants and then was missing and they thought her parents did it and it was really big news.  And whenever I saw a picture of her, it creeped me out.  That's how I feel listening to Haim.

They are a lot like the band Rush.  There is a lot of promise in their music, but no delivery.  You hear that first note, and there is hope, but then they just go on to do something dumb and ruin it.  Or like when Lenny Kravits did his "American Woman" cover...people were like...Whao?  So hot!

Not at all.

I think sometimes people want to be accepted and that makes them weak.  And in that weak moment they listen to Haim.  And think they have to like it.  To be loved.

I can also see this band ruining a lot of chicks' highschool experience.  Like you think you gotta have fun your senior year.  Hiam looks like fun.  So you and your girls get all Haimed out and learn all the lyrics to the songs.  So you're in the car with your boyfriend.  Driving around.  Stinging along to stupid Hiam songs and he starts to get disgusted with you.  Starts to find you unattractive.  Looks at your mouth singing and never wants to kiss it again.  You tell him to shut up.  You pick up your girlfriend.  He has to sit in the back seat all night listening to two 17 year old girls sing Hiam songs.  You don't hear from him again.  No prom.  No smooching.  You're in your room.  With your thoughts.  Alone with Haim.

I'm not against Prom Rock in any way shape or form.  There is a great catalogue from the past to pull from.  As well as two great Prom Rock albums released this year by Wavves and Mickal Cronin.

I ain't sayin' they are as gawd awful a band as Pearl Jam or anything.  As far as awful goes, Pearl Jam always takes the cake. There is an audience for this band.  And it ain't for kids looking to get wasted and have a good time.  This is for kids driving to bible camp, trying to act all rebellious.  Actually, I don't even know who this was made for.  But it ain't me.

Beginning in 1983 I started buying cds.  Over time, I have accumulated well over a thousand.  So, I have come to encounter some great and some not-so-great sounding cds.
I already have the Kingston Trio Collector's Choice and Capitol Double Play series.  Each are different but excellent in their own way. The double play series was except for debut and hungry I (mono) remixed from the original 3 track master tapes, not run through Capitol's famous echo chambers. The collectors choice are from the original Capitol album masters as released.
However, the Real Gone nine album collection startled me.  The first cd, which is the Trio's first two albums, is OK.  The majority of the other discs are mediocre, taken from vinyl and lack ambiance.
But........the mastering of "The Last Month Of The Year" is by far the worst-sounding, atrocious, bizarre, unlistenable, excruciating  piece of music I have heard, including vinyl, 8-track, cassette or any other recording media. It requires listening to it just to comprehend how bad it is. The only way I can describe it-- taking a well-worn lp, transferring it to cassette, , putting it in a cheap boombox, dropping it down a well, then hanging a cheap microphone at the edge of the top of the well, recording it onto another cheap boombox.
There is absolutely no excuse for this.  How reviewers give it 3, 4, or five stars is beyond me.

Keep in mind that I know this is their 1st album and the band was still trying to find their sound and come into their own.  the only tune that I mildly enjoyed was Diamonds and Rust.  That tune was so much better though on Sin After Sin a few years later.  I am not against JP early material I think Sad Wings and Sin after Sin are awesome records but Rocka Rolla is anything but.

If I was one of the heads in the music business and in a position to sign these guys back in 1975 and could of offered them an extended record deal, I honestly would not have based on the strength of this album alone.  Thankfully I was not in charge of making that decision and Judas Priest made some of the best albums in metal history.  Sad Wings, Sin after Sin, Leather, Steel, Screaming, Defenders, Painkiller the band has a treasure trove of great songs and material but Rocka Rolla is just not in that category.

Judas Priest wrote the book on what a heavy metal band is and should be.  Black Sabbath may have started it but Judas Priest are the ones who carried the torch and really defined the music.  The guys put out a ton of high quality great heavy metal albums but this is definitely not one of them.  Seeing all the 4 and 5 star reviews for this album makes me think that people are basing the album on the bands later material or just because they like the band without even hearing the album. Which would be dishonest to a buyer.

The album is very dull overall no point in sugar coating it.  Now I loved their second album Sad Wings of Destiny is amazing and has all kinds of great songs on it but this debut Rocka Rolla just sucks.  lets be honest I own the album and rarely listen to it at all.  Outside of diehard fans who have every album this one rarely if ever gets played.  When I pickup and listen to a Priest album this one also gets skipped over every time.  Mediocre is a very correct term for the album.  There is no big hit single that jumps out at you saying that's a hit for sure.  I would rate this album 1 or 2 stars and would advise new fans of the band to start with Sad Wings of Destiny instead.

reviewText:
Oh, this album is terrible. Why? Let me count the ways. Actually, I don't want to do that. It'll take way too long. I will be as concise as I can.

Somewhere along the way I realized that U2 are just really annoying. I used to listen to them quite a bit. "Zooropa" was a personal favorite of mine. I spent lots of time listening to "Rattle & Hum" and "October," and I didn't grumble and pout over "Pop" the way other people did. But as I've grown older I've realized how much I can't stand these guys, even at their supposed "best." To me, U2 are like that irritating little kid who always wants you to watch him/her do handstands and won't shut up about it. I thought "Atomic Bomb" was their worst album.

Wrong. This one outdoes the last one. There are some decent moments, but no good songs. Tracks three through seven get on my nerves ("Get On Your Boots," as stated earlier, is not a song but just recording software patchwork). Lots of people seem to like "Magnificent," but to me it only means that U2 is content to beat a dead horse for the rest of their days. The rest of the album I merely tolerate, but that's the most I can say about it.

I also think it's misleading to trumpet this album as being so experimental. If sticking a lemon wedge in lieu of a lime one in your Corona bottle is your idea of experimental, then cool. But it's discouraging to hear Eno and/Lanois describe this album as redefining arena rock when all it does is maybe redefine Bono's stock portfolio.

Which leads me to another point; why keep bringing in guest producers? Why rely on them so, so much? U2 are big boys, they can produce their own album. All they need is access to a studio, an engineer, and an assistant engineer and they can knock out an album in no time. Too many cooks get invited into this kitchen nowadays (Eno, Lanois, Jackknife Lee, Howie B, Rick Rubin, Steve Lillywhite). Would U2 be better/less annoying without so many fingers in their pie? I dunno, I say let them give it a whirl.

Also, I'm pretty sure I see a line on the album's cover.
(I give U2 credit for not putting a picture of themselves on yet another album - that was getting old)

This important collection of unreleased Frank Sinatra songs was produced on the cheap.  There is no meta-data in the CD, and the meta-data is not available online.  If you play the songs on a smart player, they will be displayed as track 1, track 2, etc.  It is deplorable that such a special new collection of songs was manufactured on the cheap.  You will not be able to search for a song by its name.

The audio quality is very good.  Why did the family cut corners on the meta-data, the importance of which, is well known in this digital age?

Nancy Sinatra is listed as an Executive Producer.  Charles Granata and Michael Feinstein are listed as Producers.  Columbia Legacy is usually a reputable producer.  They all should be ashamed.  I call on them to make an explanation here, or better yet, offer a correction.

I am not a VERIFIED PURCHASE because I received this Frank Sinatra, A Voice On Air (1935-1955) as a gift.  I own just about every Sinatra CD that has ever been released, and I own around 50 vinyl records by Frank Sinatra.  It is so disappointing that Frank Sinatra, A Voice On Air (1935-1955) is a project half finished.

If you are a big Sinatra fan as I am, and you do NOT rely on the meta-data, you will love this CD.  If the meta-data is part of your listening experience, you will be disappointed.  I hope this review is helpful.

reviewText:
Dear lord, how many repackaged sets of Jackson can the public want? I've lost count. They're certainly desperate to get every last cent out of a ruinous deal they made with a mutilated freak like Jackson. After listening to the laughable remixes I can only hope someone thinks them better than barely passable. I also hope that number is in the low single digits.

The original record is one of the greatest jobs of production ever and Quincy Jones has to take a bow for ridding most of the excesses of Jackson. The musical credits are a lie as Eddie Van Halen only plays a few bars of "Beat It" and the rest is a studio musician.

The best songs on here are written by others, the horrid material by Jackson recalls some of the worst McCartney lyrics. The difference is that McCartney writes the words after the music and it works. Since Jackson has no musical talent (he's credited with hand clapping on several songs - <giggle!>) the music is forced to fit the words and ghastly things happen on Thriller, even with Quincy to patch it up.

If Quincy were dead, hearing the remixes would have him doing 60,000 RPM and I'm not sure any casket would hold up. Here's hoping he'll opt for cremation if anyone foolishly plays these remixed songs a year or more from now.

In short, don't encourage anyone to put out yet another repackaging of a sick human being like Jackson. What's next, a Gary Glitter box set on Blu-Ray?

reviewText: This is not a review of the songs. I like them, and purchased this hoping to upgrade my copy of A TRAMP SHINING, which is a much earlier released CD. It also includes his 2nd collaboration with Jimmy Webb, THE YARD WENT ON FOREVER. There is also a version from Australia's Raven Records featuring both albums as well, entitled WEBB SESSIONS: 1968-69, but it was more expensive. Knowing Raven's penchant for sound quality (I own a few of their CD's), I should have spent the difference. The sound on this CD is horrible, "brickwalled" to the max. For the uninitiated, "brickwalling" or compression, occurs when the record companies boost the bass and lower the highs to equal the mid-range. That way, if someone is listening with an iPod or similar device, the music will be loud enough to hear every detail. The problem is, that in music every detail is not supposed to be at the same volume, but with differing frequencies, not just one. When listening to these compressed CD's/mp3's your ears get tired from the all-at-once onslaught. This is also know as "ear fatique." That is why there is a growing market for earlier generation CD's, with the music transferred properly. If you are interested in both of the above albums, purchase the Raven version, if you only want A TRAMP SHINING, click my link above, and avoid this travesty...... If you are interested in the early music of Jimmy Webb, try GLEN CAMPBELL Sings the Best of Jimmy Webb 1967-1992,Someone Left the Cake Out In The Rain: The Classic Songs Of Jimmy Webb,The Moon's A Harsh Mistress: Jimmy Webb In The 70's

reviewText: I can review a Nels Cline solo album and use a word like "awful" and it would be applicable to all of them. Having said that, this album blows. In fact, I don't even know why good guitarists like Cline choose to play a "free" jazz style anyway? Could it be that his compositional skills aren't that great? Could it be that he just doesn't have any idea what good jazz music is? Chances are all the above. Random noises, vast amounts of feedback, and heavy distorted guitar doesn't constitute good music. This "music" goes against everything music stands for. No structure, no melody, no rhythm, and no harmony. Without these crucial components, then all you will have left is anarchy. Don't believe the hype about Nels Cline. Go ahead and explore the sonic worlds of Pat Metheny, Bill Frisell, John Abercrombie, Terje Rypdal, and Steve Tibbetts. You can't go wrong with any of these fantastic jazz guitarists.

reviewText: "Springtime Can Kill You" is a somnambulist's dream album.  Devoid of energy, it is the perfect set to put you to sleep or for those depressed people finally looking at the bottom of the bottle.  Holland is an  interesting lyricist.  For example on "Stubborn Beast" she sings, "When the flames rise around us & I can't see the door, this is still my home & it has never burned before."  However, the music is slow and the melody is unimaginative.  Similarly, "Ghostly Girl" is a pitiful drone that cannot end soon enough.  It's followed by "Nothing to do but Dream" that has plunky guitar that sounds like it's played by a student on their third guitar lesson.  "Adieu False Heart" is the title of the new collaboration set by Linda Ronstadt & Ann Savory.  Without the Holland twang, Ronstadt & Savory put the emphasis on the melody in a beautiful rendition.  Here again, the prosaic guitar strum weighs the track into boredom.  "Mexican Blue" has an interesting lyric but has Holland's two-finger piano sounding like a rehearsal.  It's not usual that I find a set that has no tracks that I enjoy, but Holland has pulled that off.  Listen to be sure that you're depressed enough to appreciate this music B4 U buy.  Taxi!

reviewText: The only wonderful song off Neon Ballroom is "Emotion Sickness". "Miss You Love", "Ana's Song", "Black Tangled Heart", "Point of View", and "Paint Pastel Princess" are all whiny, plodding schlock. Nearly everything off Neon Ballroom sounds like a cliche... and a whiny, pretentious one at that. Daniel Johns and the rest of his bandmates are too old to convincingly pull off angst anymore. All of the genuine edge and caginess that was found on Frogstomp and Freak Show is absent. And in the short bursts Johns tries to recapture what he once expressed on his first two albums, he comes off as whiny and pathetic (just take a listen to "Spawn Again", and have a good laugh at Johns once again trying to be thrashy for no reason). "Spawn Again" ranks right up there with "Minor Threat", "Trash", and "Lie to me" as some of the most stupid, pointless Silverchair songs ever. Frogstomp and Freak Show are great Silverchair buys because the guys were still teenagers trying to find their place in the world. They were young enough to get away with being moody and unsure of themselves. But when Ballroom was made they had been adults for quite some time, and any smart person should have been able realize that that Johns should have given himself a more mature portrayal than he does on this album.

reviewText:
For the love of music, do yourself a favor and pass up on shelling out your dollars on Paris Hilton's self-titled album. A CD that has been in gestation for two years, "Paris" is a smoldering smorgasbord of embarrassing, gimmicky pop schlock that could not be more painful to listen to. Why is that? This chick has no talent.

Sure, some of the songs are mildly flirtatious and fun in the lyrical department, but even with an assortment of cream of the crop songwriters in the pop music scene Hilton cannot obscure the fact that she is nothing but a quick buck for a record company cashing in on her pointless fame. She can sing without her voice cracking, but she is definitely unworthy of even the D-list of pop vocalists, and her persona and style certainly don't boost her over the artistic threshold. She is to Gwen Stefani what Jessica Simpson is to Mariah Carey, only even worse; the poorest imitation.

The sole glimpse of talent on the record is on the egotistical "Fightin' Over Me," but only because Fat Joe and Jadakiss give it a much-needed facelift. Nevertheless, just like all the rest of the tracks, it is pure, unadulterated product. Hearing her whisper "that's hot" and namedropping hot shot producer Scott Storch under her breath at the beginning of the mind-numbing "Turn It Up" is even less of a pleasure.

Some of the beats on "Screwed" create a cool cadence, but no one has ever sounded less like they knew what they were singing about. Also, "Stars Are Blind"? "Stars Are Deaf" is more like it. Or at the very least, "Stars Are Bland," for never has their been a more bland pop single. Lastly, her cover of Rod Stewart's "Do Ya Think I'm Sexy?" turns the classic into a lightweight roller disco confection, but she simply cannot deliver a decent voice and, most importantly, any grit or soul.

Do yourself a favor and refrain from buying "Paris." Don't support music that is 100% product and 0% genuine or a woman who inspires misogyny as she thrusts herself down the throats of Americans on a daily basis. For a pop album that actually sounds great in every aspect, opt instead for the latest releases from Madonna, Robbie Williams or any Kylie Minogue album this side of 2000.

Products like "Paris" are complete and utter atrocities, and spell death for art as we know it. Just wait - in late December you'll read the following obituary: "Art As We Know It passed away December 23, 2006 at 9:25 pm. It was 1097 years old. It passed away upon the realization that Paris Hilton's debut album was certified platinum."

reviewText:
I can only give it one star, and that's only because of the song "Spade". I really can't sit through this album. Lyrically, it's not Manson's best, and musically, it's not that good either. The album conversly though, is a waste of guitar riffs, lack of live drumming, lack of multi-dimensional instrument playing, all in a poppy commerically accessible formula that is at first appealing, but fades away because in the end the Golden Age of Grotesque marks Marilyn Manson's musical atrophy. Tim Skold is highly responsible for this, but Marilyn Manson hiring him is a testimony to his lack of an ear for exceptional music. Also, most of the inspiration for this album is from Manson's Yoko Ono- Dita Von Teese. Exceptions are scattered minutely throughout the album--but this is by far Manson's worst album. It doesn't have the musical integrity to elevate him anywhere, but just to demote him to a dishearteningly low level. The Golden Age of Grotesque is Marilyn Manson reminiscent of Linkin Park, because the formula in their music is now identical. The only good song in this album is Spade. The problem with Marilyn Manson now is that he is trying to hard to be Mr. Pop Star....literally. What happened to the Marilyn Manson we all use to love...the one who was brave enough to be different from other bands? Who was outspoken? Has Dita Von Teese completely brainwashed Manson into becoming "Mr Cabaret Burlesque man" and told him this album was great? Because this album is far from great. Buy instead "AntiChrist Superstar", "Holywood", or "Mechanical Animals". Those albums are brilliant. As for Manson, start doing music the way you want to. Not the way your girlfriend Dita wants you to. We already have a Yoko Ono.
This album also comes with a DVD of a movie Manson made called "Doppleherz". I really don't know what to say about the DVD. It's just plain weird. Manson repeats the same line over and over again and before you know it, your falling asleep watching the thing. I would have perferred to see some behind the scenes kinda documentary, then some bad B-movie of Manson's. Manson appears, with his band, the two Siamese twin girls, Aria Giovanni the porn star and of course Dita Von Teese- another porn star. The DVD's not any better then the actual music.

It's unreformed sophomoric "break stuff for the sake of breaking stuff" music, laced with goofy socialist and anarchist prattle.
Moreover, it's impossible to take Rage Against The Machine seriously knowing how many millions this band and its component members have raked in over the years.  Hey guys, cry me a river.  You live a rock and roll life far away from the every day world of work-a-day struggle.  All the fist-in-air rhetoric is just silly considering that none of you schmoes have any clue what it's like to work an honest job.
Impressionable and disaffected youth will eat this album up, as has been the case from the beginning.  Speaking as a formerly disaffected youth who grew the hell up and now holds a responsible position in the very society that Rage claims to hate so much, I am embarrassed that I ever gave this band any ear. reviewText:
Were I to judge this cd on technique, it would get five stars.  However, technique is practice...training...and though I would never derogate it  (that would be perilously close to criticizing Bird for technique and that would be  borderline insane), it no longer thrills the same way rich composition does.  It is probably true that there are many years ahead of new compositions, but I am afraid that it is much more difficult to find interesting intervals and arresting harmonies.  Metheny, from around 1978 to 1993, filled the universe with compositions and arrangements that were as tuneful as they were technical.  He was not alone in that universe--Brazilians, at that time, were good company--Tom Jobim, Joao Bosco. Chico Buarque de Hollanda, Djavan, Toninho Horta, and Guinga were rich inspiration for Metheny, though he never copied them; rather, he created his own derivations and they were stellar.

Though the Unity Band compositions are, occasionally, interesting, they are not warm and evocative in any way. This is not to suggest that Metheny has lost his passion or his penchant for musicality--rather, he is on a different road trip.  The terrain seems...well...dry and desolate.

okay, before i say anything else, please keep in mind that i am a huge mariah fan and own ALL of her albums.  after having said that, here goes:
anybody who knows even a LITTLE bit about music should know that this is not the one.  i have no idea what was going through her head, or what she's doing or what direction she believes she's trying take, but mariah's "glitter" is tremendously bad.  the cd's only redeeming qualities (outside of the really pretty glossy paper used on the insert and the highly innovative use of various forms of pink) are the songs "never too far" (or maybe it's "never too far away"...who cares?) and another one, i can't remember the name off the top.  it's a ballad, though, which she should stick to.  outside of that the cd is not good at all.  when i think of how much i love "emotions" (i belive that that is her best cd), i am so hurt.  for the most part, the album just seems like one big rap collaboration.  if i wanted to buy a rap album, i would have done so.  but, hey, that's just me.  also, the writing on the original tracks is awful.  what's up with "twister?"  basically the song is about her mother (in the movie i assume) and how she and her mother were finally getting close and how her mother was finally making something of her life or whatever.  you think for a minute that the tune might have some artistic value, but then she bawls out "[a] twister went and threw it all away."  what?!!?!?!?!?  what in the blue hell is she talking about?!?!??!?!  she wasn't playin' when she said she needed some time off...
in a nutshell, i have listened to this cd more than once trying with all of my might to give it a chance, and have come to one conclusion: this cd pretty much sucks eggs.  if you want to hear jarule, busta rhymes, and that other girl she likes kickin' it with, then buy their cds (or buy this one, i guess).  but basically, be forewarned, and buy at your own risk.

reviewText:
I don't understand how these remixes are getting such good reviews. Nick Davis used to do such amazing recordings. What happened? When did he become such a fan of over EQing everything? Can't everyone hear how overly EQ'd these mixes are? They simply aren't enjoyable to listen to. They're harsh and thin with a boomy low end and hollowed out midrange and clearly have inferior musical balances than the originals. I guess it's a case where people buy into believing remastered always means better even without volume matched comparisons. Remember, louder doesn't mean better.

I can take about ten minutes of these discs before my ears just start ringing and I have to shut it off. They've lost a lot of the punch and power the original mixes had. The sound of the SSL console EQ Nick used has a distinct tone. They will ring when overused. You can hear it all over this set. It should be annoying even to those whose ears haven't been trained. There's a lot of poorly chosen EQ that adds a nasal quality to the instruments. The cymbals are harsh and Phil's vocals are nasally and sound like a they're coming through a megaphone. Things sound small and jammed together.  Nick Davis has made everything sound like a small transistor radio, albeit a very loud transistor radio.

And what's with all the compression? These heavy mixes are ridiculously inappropriate for this beautiful, emotionally dynamic music. These songs used to have dynamics, loud and soft orchestrations that built the music. Now everything is LOUD! The LOUD! parts are LOUD! and the soft parts are LOUD! That's not detail you're hearing, it's just compression.

It makes me sick to my stomach that these loud, overly EQd, overly compressed remixes are going to replace the dynamic, fuller and more artful original mixes.

Welcome to the MP3 generation where sound quality just doesn't matter as long as it's loud. I guess I should get a cheap stereo that makes everything sound bad. That way these Genesis remixes won't upset me so much.

Genesis... the George Lucas of the music world. ICK!

This type of music sells not because it sounds good,  but because 'they' WANT and DESIRE it to sound good.  It doesn't.  It's futile to brainwash oneself.  This music sucks. Apparently the christian music industry cares not for unwritten rules.  I am embarassed for Jennifer Knapp, one of my favorite artists, that she would release an album like this. reviewText:
In 1994, the Meat Puppets released one of my favorite albums, Too High to Die. After the misstep of their next album, No Joke, and recovery from drug addiction, the Meat Puppets return. Unfortunately, it is not a reunion worth waiting for.

The first thing I notice is the horrible recording quality. In the days of affordable computer-based studios, it's shocking that a CD could be made of such horrible quality. Most demo CDs by unsigned bands sound better. It sounds like it was done over 2 days with a few mics set up in a warehouse studio.

Next, the album just meanders on and on through the midway point. There are no catchy hooks, no great guitar work or quirky charm. It's just terrible. By the middle, it sort of hits its stride and has a few pretty good songs. But, they are ruined by the sound quality. Songs like "New Leaf" and "Disappear" are probably excellent live. But, horrible EQ, reverb, and balance between the instruments suck all the life out of these songs.

Finally, the vocals and lyrics have always been a love it or hate it trademark of the band. Curt Kirkwood by all rights shouldn't sing but has the ability to somehow squeeze out some great performances. On Rise to Your Knees, he mostly fails to bring out the charm and hooks of previous work. Coupled with uninspired guitar-work in many songs, his vocals just don't cut it this time around.

Sad to say I'm very disappointed with this effort and hope for better material in the future.

That said, his solo career over the past few years with the upcoming anticipation and release of 'SMiLE' and the long-deserved praise for the well-packaged, well-presented live efforts of late has had me, well, excited for him. Normally, half of the material is either first rate or, has echoes of past glory to carry the day. Here, there is not much to recommend (remember, I WANT this CD to be great...), and all of the documented criticism in posted reviews; sloppy, careless, uninspired, writer's block, dated - all apply. My hope for Brian as 'SMiLE' is about to finally see the (`official') light of day is that he continues to focus on what makes him happy and GREAT as a singer/songwriter/producer - NOT trying to 'update' his sound to any modern standards, but to find creative joy in building sound bites that capture the very nature of God's gift to us in the form of glorious five-part harmonic music.

reviewText:
Not sure if it's apparent, but Diana Krall definitely works her blond mane on many of her (better) album covers.  I always thought it was a quick attention grabber, but now I know: a strange set of syllogistic rules apply to the music industry, so it should come as no surprise that good hair increases the probability of a good recording.

The people who brought you Quiet Nights skimmed on the hair stylist, and now we, the listeners have to pay.

Listening to Krall attempt to capture the indolent, fragile, enervated voice with which Astrud Gilberto (whom many of these songs presented here have come to be associated with) made her unforgettable imprint in bossa nova is as painful as listening to Sting trying to stretch a vowel in a Dowland or an English Tudor classic like it was an economic stimulus check.  The enchantment of Gilberto comes from the beaches of Rio, the certain sadness that comes at the end of a samba at Carnaval- when dancers have to return to the favelas, the dreams of cachaca, and the discrete charm of the wife singing leisurely in the kitchen when Stan Getz first heard her (and decided to use her on The Girl From Ipanema).

Krall's super high definition recording, on the other hand, is like all the gloss of a fancy stereo set...with Kenny G cued on the cd player: you can hear all the breathy nuances and inflections of her singing...but there's no backbone, no historical justification for the inertia in her voice, no emotional undertone to it. Unless you needed Ambien after a drugstore has closed, but Amazon mp3 was still open for a download.

In the present culture of recycling, the only saving grace from vacuous remakes of classics is a profound new insight in a contemporary reading (think the exiting line of Pet Shop Boys' extended version of Willie Nelson's "Always On My Mind" - "maybe I didn't love you."), to simply do something that's already been done before is purely ego needing to be stroked with the aid of modern electronics.

Anyway...my theory is that Krall's hairstylist went to work for Eliane Elias.  Check out the cover for Elias's 2009 Bossa Nova Stories.  Better hair = better renditions.

So better hair will lead to better covers.  Unless remake-happy musicians want to start re-making Midnight Oil's discography, let this be a lesson.  If you don't like what you see in the mirror when you wake up in the morning, avoid the hairclip, stay away from the scrunchie.

reviewText: In the past I have been an ardent defender of Celine Dion's. While working in a music shop on the eve of Dion's world domination, I heard many a not-so-nice comments about 'sell-out Celine'. Sure, she may lack the credo someone like Whitney Houston or even Streisand have with the genuine warmth of their instruments. But Dion is far from an insincere vocalist; she actually believes everything she sings and never sounds less than that. She may hit vocal heights, but not for the sheer purpose to impress. Against her also is the fact that it is too terribly easy for critics and audiophiles to dismiss interpreters of ballads these days as prosaic industry hack. However, often getting in her way, and leading her detractors to feel more than correct, has been for the most part her material: tired ballads that stretch the listener's attention of an entire CD way beyond its limits; uninspired David Foster productions; vocal deliveries devoid of any bite. So it was a fresh breath when all of these reasons seemed to be taken into account when she delivered her last studio outting, One Heart, an album that exuded spontinaity, daring, grit, and beauty--all Celine style and all within a tollerable span of time. "Have You Ever Been In Love?" was simply the best grande ballad Dion ever recorded. Its understated substance and beauty made it a real winner, and made Celine sound good on the radio again. Not to mention her muscled and convincing turn on AC/DC's "Shook Me All Night" at VH1's Diva Concert. But what happened? This live recording offers none of that and shouldn't really instigate anyone contemplating on seeing her Vegas spectacle to do so. Her spoken interaction with her adoring audience is stiff and any sentimentality felt is rehearsed and perfunctory at its very best. Her performances of this too-familiar material (certainly her catalog offers more interesting, entertaining, invigorating, and adventerous material) read like a fatigued actress reciting lines toward the end of a very extended and fatiguing theatre run--completely lacking that sincerity I've always insisted she's possessed. If this was Sony's attempt to keep Dion in the record buyer's conscience, then it failed in doing so while keeping it in good faith. As for the two studio tracks: "You & I" is a pop/dancer that evokes all of the best parts of her cover of "I Drove All Night", except its energy; "Ain't Gonna Look The Other Way" is another ballad, no better no worse. So unless you're a Dion completist, wait patiently for One Heart, Part Two...If Vegas hasn't gone to her head.
