reviewText:
UPDATE:  I used to agree with two stars, but now one.  The artwork, while an attempt to recreate the LP, is stretched.  So glad I jumped off the AF train!!
__________________________________________________________________________________________

I actually think the packaging is pretty cool as it recreates the style of the original LP.  However, I rip all of my CDs to FLAC, so I don't need to take the disc out every time I want to hear the music.  The packaging almost made me think AF was kicking it up a notch and starting to release some high quality products.  That was prior to discovering the clipped peaks on this disc.

I was a member on Steve Hoffman's forum (under the name Dream Operator) and I noticed posts from people wondering if this release sounded better than the Dennis Drake master.  I decided to put up some samples from this version so people could get an idea of the sound.  I opened the first track (True Blue) in a sound editing program and created a 30 second sample.  Then I opened the second track (Lost Paraguayos) to make a sample of that.  It was then that I noticed the end of the song had consistently leveled peaks.  I zoomed in and found the peaks are actually clipped (flat-topped).  Other songs on the album have clipped peaks as well, but Lost Paraguayos was the worst offender.

I sent Steve Hoffman a private message about this (after issues with other discs, he asked me to contact him about AF issues in the future)and he told me they don't have peak limiters at RTI.  He said he would have his copy in a week.

I then emailed Marshall Blonstein (President of Audio Fidelity), but I did not receive a reply.  After a few days, I posted on Steve Hoffman's forum about the clipped peaks.  The post was mild and did not make any accusations.  The post was removed in less than a minute and I was soft banned (my account appears active, but I cannot access anything on the site when I log in).

I sent another email to Marshall [...], but this time I received a reply from Heather.  She said he was out of the country and would be returning on Monday (11/16/2009).  I sent Marshall another email on 11/19 and asked if he had a chance to read my previous email and asked what his thoughts were.  I still have not received a reply.

I don't think the disc sounds bad and the dynamic range is quite good.  However, the disc does not live up to the promise on their website: "The original dynamic range of the recordings are not maximized, brickwalled, limited or compressed in any way during remastering." (also printed on all previous AF CDs, though slightly different).  Clipped peaks are the result of some type of compression.  Whether it was a peak limiter or perhaps the analog-to-digital converters were simply over-driven by accident, I do not know.

This is the third CD from Audio Fidelity's 2009 releases to reveal compression (The Doors - The Soft Parade and The Pretenders - The Pretenders being the other two discs).  Sad for that company that attempts to build their reputation on producing albums without additional compression.

For the record, Kevin Gray is credited for remastering this, not Steve Hoffman.  Steve was credited for the other two Audio Fidelity discs that have compression.  These guys appreciate dynamic music, so it's hard to say why these issues are happening.

reviewText: My infamous review of "Is This It" was probably not the apex of sound musical critique, and I am certainly not overly proud of it. Yet my feelings towards it and towards this sophomore effort are still those of unimpressed cynicism--I do not understand how a mediocre power-pop band that writes uncatchy songs consistently in the same key and with the same simple chord progressions can be elevated to the plateau of "rock saviours." Each of these 11 tunes mines the same ground of VU-Television-Cars regurgitation--and such overlying simplicity ought not to be excused with comparisons to the Ramones, since The Strokes are doing nothing as revolutionary as their punk predecessors. Fabrizio Moretti still sounds like he can't find a fill to save his life, Hammond and Valensi's guitars spit out the same stuttering riffs again and again, and Julian tries to make everyone forget the fact that he can't sing by recycling that grating noise-distortion vocal effect again and again (surely The Strokes have something more up their sleeve that this). The riff of "12:51" owes an unpayable debt to The Cars, and the song's mumbly vocals (more distortion) provide no distinction whatsoever. But, according to such magazines as Spin and Rolling Stone, it only matters how 'cool' a band is anymore--forget their actual songwriting or performance talents. While this diluted garage rock, falling somewhere between VU-Lite and Stooges-Lite, may have been appealing to some two years ago, I can't see how anyone could throw such praise upon The Strokes now that the far superior Interpol and White Stripes have taken center stage.

reviewText: In the vast spectrum of music, we have a good share of gold. However, gold isn't everything, and according to Newton's third law, "for every action there's a reaction", it's always countered by bad music. The 90's had lots of great music to come out from that era, but I definitely would be lying if everything from that decade was redeemable. For every Pearl Jam, there was a Creed. For every A Tribe Called Quest, there was an Insane Clown Posse. For every Nine Inch Nails, there was a Limp Bizkit. And the list goes on. For every album that was highly regarded, we're given a Cracked Rear View. Why is this album so bad? Why the one star rating? WHY? It's simple as this: Hootie and the Blowfish were nothing more than ear candy to the adult listener of the mid 90's. When the adults wanted something different from their Kenny G enema, they'd change the radio to what was hip at the time. Hootie and the Blowfish was perfect for every John and Jane Smith that were too cowardly to live outside the box, because the music was completely inoffensive, non-engaging and blended in perfectly with their everyday lives. The music is completely vapid of anything worthwhile. At best, the song structure is predictable, verse-chorus-verse style that bands could pull off if they did everything else right. Unfortunately, that is not the case. We're treated to dull guitar chord progressions without any hooks or feeling behind them, and Darius Rucker's vocals are completely monotone and soulless. Perhaps, if the band managed to broaden their horizons and explore music beyond typical pop song, along with playing with some passion and emotion, we could have had an unsung classic. It's too bad that any potential this band may have had is completely wasted on nothing more than dull, mindless and vacuous garbage like this. When it comes to music, the best music will provoke emotions, no matter what decade it hails from. For example, whenever I listen to Ten, I'm treated to some of the greatest rock of the 90's with its distinctive traits and powerful dynamics. Hootie and the Blowfish, on the other hand, can't do that because this is completely restrained and hackneyed. It would only be a matter of time before the followers in its wake would emerge, providing the rest of the 90's with flash-in-the-pan adult alternative rock that only grew worse with age. Thus, this is why Cracked Rear View is nothing more than an artifact of its time. It broke no rules, it provided nothing, and it was way too safe.

The fact is, this is worse that what I heard on the radio in the middle 1990s. There is little melody and most of the vocals show no power or passion - something I over my many changes in musical taste have always appreciated. Rather, it is just wishy-washy melody which is thinly produced and overtly simple, with no fluency in the rhythm or the slightest form of expression.

For those willing to look, there is plenty of good music in the rock and folk fields, such as late 1960s English folk-rock or early 1990s dream pop. I recommend you try and look there for musical listening (amongst many other possibilities).

I only enjoy the backgrounds on "When We Were Young" and the final track, "Sweetest Devotion." So many critics have acquiesced, giving this effort average to stellar reviews. Why? Are they under spineless mind control like the other 3 million people who rushed to buy this album the first week of release after a subpar delivery like "Hello" as it's first single? Back when people paid attention to first singles and not media hype, an album's first offering meant a hell of a lot. On a positive note, the album cover is striking and Adele does a great job at not being that quintessential, attention-seeking pop diva. However, the music is of the greatest importance. Much of the album lags and struggles to find a clear shining moment. In fact, I've given it three listens and I still can't find one. Both "19" & "21" were better than this album and I refuse to let someone tell me something is good when my ears protest in sincere defiance.

reviewText: I listened to the new album a few times on my computer and than once in my car.  I don't know what it is, but this is the most monotonous album U2 has ever released.  It's predictable, boring, has that sameness running through it, bland, and lacking any originality whatsoever. These guys need to forget EVERYTHING they have done in the past and make a fresh sounding album. Some of the songs sound like they were taken from older songs and sound EXACTLY the same in certain parts. I could swear for a few seconds I was hearing an old U2 song. They clearly are trying to draw upon old musical experiences and albums they made in the past. The great thing about Achtung Baby for example is how fresh and different it was. What a marvelous progression. Than later when they seemed to be losing some originality they stripped it all down and came out with the simple yet pure sounding lovely album All That You Can't Leave Behind. Of course I also loved Joshua Tree and even Rattle and Hum a very different kind of live album. U2 has had it's high points. But I don't see this album as much of an improvement over No Line On The Horizon, just bad for different reasons. One thing I have to admit I do like though is the take on all the songs on the Deluxe Edition during "The Acoustic Sessions".  But even still, the familiar hooks, melodies, harmonies, it's just too much of the same.  However, had the album been made this way in the first place, I would increase my rating to 3 stars. I like this style of music making compared to the full production on these boring songs. Next time I hope they dare to do something different, sound different, just make a new album and explore some unpredictable territory.  They certainly proved in the past they could sound different and explore new terrains, it's that time again. Look how bold and daring Pop was, love it or hate it? But at least they had the balls to make it. This latest album they had no intention of being daring in any way, shape, or form. And that's why I don't like it!

reviewText: My infamous review of "Is This It" was probably not the apex of sound musical critique, and I am certainly not overly proud of it.  Yet my feelings towards it and towards this sophomore effort are still those of unimpressed cynicism--I do not understand how a mediocre power-pop band that writes uncatchy songs consistently in the same key and with the same simple chord progressions can be elevated to the plateau of "rock saviours."  Each of these 11 tunes mines the same ground of VU-Television-Cars regurgitation--and such overlying simplicity ought not to be excused with comparisons to the Ramones, since The Strokes are doing nothing as revolutionary as their punk predecessors.  Fabrizio Moretti still sounds like he can't find a fill to save his life, Hammond and Valensi's guitars spit out the same stuttering riffs again and again, and Julian tries to make everyone forget the fact that he can't sing by recycling that grating noise-distortion vocal effect again and again (surely The Strokes have something more up their sleeve that this).  The riff of "12:51" owes an unpayable debt to The Cars, and the song's mumbly vocals (more distortion) provide no distinction whatsoever.  But, according to such magazines as Spin and Rolling Stone, it only matters how 'cool' a band is anymore--forget their actual songwriting or performance talents.  While this diluted garage rock, falling somewhere between VU-Lite and Stooges-Lite, may have been appealing to some two years ago, I can't see how anyone could throw such praise upon The Strokes now that the far superior Interpol and White Stripes have taken center stage.

reviewText:
So you know where I'm coming from, I'm a Peter Gabriel fan from way back. I was at his first-ever solo concert at the Capitol Theatre in NJ back in 1977 (Television was the opening act). I went to every tour after that for years.

Each song is slow and melancholy and one song from the album would serve well as a slow break during a live concert, where Gabriel might stop and play something on the piano.

Collectively, however, the album is painful to listen to. Gabriel takes other people's songs and sucks the life out of them, turning them into depressing funeral dirges. I understand the impetus for a musician to try something new, but I don't understand putting it onto CD and selling it when the experiment has clearly failed on such a grand scale.

reviewText:
No way to sugarcoat it: "Chicago 13" is one of the worst albums of the band's career.

From the obnoxious overplaying by the horn section to the unusually muddy rhythm parts to the execrable songwriting, "13" seems to be, indeed, a very unlucky album for the band.

The album is simply too forgettable and lame for a track by track analysis, but here are the (few) highs and some of the lows:

"Street Player," the title track composed by drummer Danny Seraphine and his buddy David "Hawk" Wolinski, keyboard player for Rufus, tries to discofy Chicago's sound with disastrous results. In addition to the Chicago horn section -- trumpeter Lee Loughnane, trombonist James Pankow, reeds player Walt Parazaider -- the late Maynard Ferguson plays on this song -- to no good effect: Just because a trumpeter CAN play in a very high register doesn't necessarily mean it's always a good idea.

Thanks to an apparent policy for this album of "everybody in the band gets a publishing credit," we are (mis)treated to "Life Is What It Is," composed by percussionist Laudir de Oliveira with Marcos Valle. It's insufferable.

Keyboardist Robert Lamm, once Chicago's finest composer, continues the awful slump he fell into after the death of his friend, guitarist Terry Kath, producing the wretched "Paradise Alley" and "Reruns."

Enough, already. I know I said there were some highs here, but I overpromised. Don't waste a nickel on this awful album.

Some very distinguished tenors started out as baritones.  Such was the case with the great Carlo Bergonzi who retained a warm Caruso like baritonal timbre in his voice while still hitting ringing, spinto high B-flats and singing in sweet head voice and mezza voce.  Ramn Vinay also began his career as a baritone, becoming a gifted heroic tenor before returning to the baritone repetoire as his voice darkened with age.

Unfortunately, Kaufmann is not cut from the same cloth.  With some effort, he could become a useful baritone.  But his premature and unjustified desire to enter the tenor range is quite ridiculous, producing a strained, constipated and thoroughly unpleasant sound.  And he should learn to shave.

reviewText:
Some music critic, I think Stephen Thompson is his name, came on NPR Radio and plugged this CD.  So I bought this and their other CD.  So now I need to confess to what is probably a very cynical understanding  and I need to realize something and take it to heart, and that is probably that in exchange for good interviews Music Critics probably get recognition and access friends in the Business.  Or music critics can be really tone-deft and beat-less no talent idiots, or they would have been musicians themselves.  Or Stephen Thompson was some lonely desperate nerd and those two young girls aren't so prudish as they sound on their CDs.  Or Stephen Thompson wanted to be gallant, and help discover these poor needy girls.  Or he had the delusional ambition  to find the next Joni Mitchell or something as though it is a matter of luck or percentages, and not a matter of whether or not these stiff and stodgy girls had any real talent as singers, musicians and entertainers.  Or maybe it has come to the point  where Music Critics now have to be investigated like the Radio Stations in the 50s were investigated for payola  accepting gifts and money for promoting records.  Yes, so many possibilities, but something needs to account for why the worst CDs I have heard in a long time have been plugged on a radio franchise, NPR, that is heard around the World.  It is so out of place that one cant help but to suspect unethical interests were somehow at play.  After all, there are Record Companies out there with huge resources, with the best Agents, Producers and Engineers and Editors, in cities where Talented Musicians flock because of their rich music culture, and these Record Companies have thousands of Acts to choose from, and they only sign the Best.  But, somehow, that NPR Reviewer, Stephen Thompson I think his name is, he picks an Act that was recorded by some unrecognizable Record Company (honestly, the print on the CD was so small I could not distinguish the name of the Record Company) in Bloomington, Indiana  which is too North for Country Music, and not on either the Left or the Right Coasts where cool Rock and Pop resides and not even near Chicago.  My guess is that these CDs were Vanity CDs  that the girls weren't signed by the Record Company, but that they walked through the door themselves with small bag of money, and out came these budget basement CDs, that is, produced very cheaply.  It doesnt seem quite fair, does it, that the Consumer has to pay full price for a CD that was produced for a fraction of a penny on the Dollar that a Quality Record would be produced for?  And all while NPR Music Critic Establishment was clamoring for us to buy buy buy it.  It all feels like a big rip-off, and I am sure that NPR will never ever get another pledge from me.

So, what is wrong with these CDs anyway.  Well, every song sounds the same.  Same instrumentation on every song.  Heck, it even sounds like all the Control Board and Effects setting never budged.  The CD covers give credit for Drums and Percussion, but I don't hear anything.  After all, the songs are so flat and without any lilt or rhythm , that I would believe that a drummer would have a difficult time trying to figure out exactly what to drum to.  It is obvious that there was not enough Budget available for the Producer to bring in Arrangers and Song Writing Consultants, to help punch up the dreary  and shapeless material that the girls walked through the door with.  So whatever the drummer did try, simply didn't work, and the Engineer earned his money by editing it out.  Oh, and I suppose the girls insisted on playing themselves  one on piano and the other on guitar.  Really, was the Budget so constrained that they could not get Real Musicians to play.  It really doesnt sound like these girls have been musicians for very long.  No smoothness or elegance, but just careful plodding along, making sure they were hitting the right basic chords  not very inspiring no flights of talent to sweep us away, but the impression we are standing outside the door of a Music Lesson in progress.  Oh, wait, the Production Team did reach out and hire a real good Cello Player, Shannon Heyden the only listenable music on both CD is Shannon Heydons Cello rising and falling with a sublimity that she must have brought to the game herself, because none of the other musical parts show  any such inspiration in their arrangement.  Everyone else plodded just behind the just learning how to play playing of the two beginner girls.
The Critic raves about the girls exquisite singing.  Well, how would anybody know?  In both CDs the singing is slid back behind a veritable fog bank of reverb and echo effects maybe some chorus to fatten up their thin and shrill voices if they are thin and shrill, but buried in so much and many Effects, who knows what they actually sound like.  But if so much work went into augmenting and disguising their voices, then isn't it highly probable that if they sang into a Clean Channel that it would sound very much as though their voices needed a lot of work.  Well, that should be nothing a discerning Music Critic should be raving about.  Oh, even a lot of the instrumentation was fogged over with effects as though the band is playing a quarter mile away between glass office buildings with sound bouncing in and about from everywhere.  It reminds me of those old Enya Records from the 90s  it was supposed to be some sort of a New Age sound, but really it was just twisting up the effects knobs  a lot of echo, reverb, chorus, tone stretch and overlap all to take off any natural edge and make everything sound , well, not warm and fuzzy, but round and fuzzy.  Maybe the girls were big Enya fans and thought that sounded neat.  Or the Production Team figured that the Enya Formula was their only chance to find a willing audience for this unique material.  You see, the girls aren't County, they aren't Rock, they're too dull  and un-catchy to be Pop, and too plain and basic to be Jazz, and so the Production Team turned up the  water-color and pastel Blur and let the Effects Fog roll in and the girls could be the next New Age Nebula.
But, back to the singing.  We also hear from the critic about the wonderful close harmonies.  Well, yes, there are close harmonies, but why are there never any far harmonies.  It always seems the same interval.  It is as though the two sisters started practicing singing together, and learned just one harmonic interval, and froze in place, never ever learning anything more, and decided that that would be their style and they would stick to it for the rest of their lives.  There is no back ground singing, no counterpoint, no framing, no weaving, no syncopation, no duets.  Nothing but their One Trick Pony  the Close Harmony.  One girl simply shadows the other girl exactly.  They both rise together.  They both fall together, keeping the same tonal interval.  It gets tedious very quickly.  It is especially bad that in both CDs there is not a single catchy musical phrase.. nothing to remember nothing to tap ones foot to.  You definitely will not have to worry about whistling while you work after sitting through either one of these girls CDs.

And there is a huge stylistic problem one concerning a very reasonable and practical musical convention.  You see, the lyrics and the singing squeeze out any opportunity for the Instrumentation to provide any Contrast, Framing or Texture.  The girls never seem to pause they never shut up!  They could have had the best studio musicians in the World, but the girls droning was endless and uninterrupted  the musicians would never have stood a chance.  It is as though these girls have never heard a song before, where  the Singer sings, then the instruments play.  It isn't rocket science!  Somebody needs to buy those girls a radio or something.
. Oh, I just had this terrible thought, that maybe these two girls ARE the most musically talented girls in the Midwest today, and it just goes to show how steep Americas artistic decline has been.  All the Rap Music and Video Gaming have taken their toll, wiping out the Culture of Music in young people today.  When I was growing up, kids only had the TV and the Radio, and both mediums were rich in presenting a wide variety of often times very good Popular Music  Rock, Soul, Country Western  even Classical and Jazz (even the Cartoons had the best and most sophisticated music of their times, because the Studios wanted to appeal to the Adult Market also, and the kids, well, seemed to like it too I know I did.  But then sometime during the 80s, they decided to start making special Baby Cartoons with special Baby Music  oversimplified to the point of stunting childrens musical development).  Anyway, with the Baby Boom Generation  kids, enveloped by a thriving and ubiquitous Musical Culture,  there developed musical taste and knowledge without anyone even having to think about it.  Well, obviously that is over.  Computers going beep beep beep and Rappers spitting and cussing in rhyme simply does not present the same depth of Musical Culture as Before.  The new crop of musicians and songwriters coming up, well, they all seem like they were all born yesterday  primitive, but not in a good way  no rich field of music in their Conscious or Subconscious Minds to harvest from and so they have no sophistication of ear or taste.  Well, I guess to such a Generation as that, Lily and Madeleine might actually be all that they can understand well, for a minute or two anyway.  People just discovering Music for the first time in their lives might find L & Ms close harmony appealing for a moment, but then soon enough richer, fuller, and better music will certainly begin to exert an attraction.  Maybe even the Music Critics of this modern Music-less Generation  will begin to develop some taste and perspective.
label: negative

reviewText:
I can't share the other reviewer's enthusiasm and, personally, I don't know why anyone would even want let alone buy this goofy CD...bleeding chunks of two Tristans shuffled together.  Why not just release the two performances complete.

Other than that, the vocal performances are far less than great; they range from mediocre to acceptable, the conducting is pretty routine like Barenboim.

If you're in the market for one Tristan, the old DGG Bohm recording with Nilsson and WIndgassen is still the overall best and may continue to be.  I've far prefer Nilsson to any other recorded Isolde even Flagstad.  Vocally she is nigh on ideal, and by the time of this recording, her understanding of the role is solid and secure.  Windgassen never sounded better and matches her voice better then usual.  Bohm's conducting is of the type that Wagner would have approved.  He keeps the work moving while projecting the work's depth and subtlety.

Beware of the "legendary" EMI Furtwangler recording.  I've long felt it's very overrated.  Suthaus is a very weak Tristan, Flagstad is clearly over the hill, Greindl sings well below par and is recorded in a way what accentuates his vocal deficiencies, Fisher-Dieskau sounds way too young for the part.  The only first class vocal performance is Thebom's Brangane.

The best Tristan that I know of is the one with Bohm and Nilsson and Vickers in the leads...Berry is the Kurvenal...from the Roman amphitheater at Orange that's a little rough around edges but very satisfactory.

reviewText:
Let me just say that I'm not too impressed with the series "Ken Burns' Jazz." It was a pretty hack job and really didn't cover all the bases in my opinion. To me, Burns is a very misguided figure and hasn't really done the research about jazz, but I'll save that argument for another time. The music on this box set, while most of it is indeed great and timeless, it fails to capture the true essence of this music I think. I think if anyone is interested in jazz music should start with Miles Davis' "Kind Of Blue" recording and go from there. Being interested in jazz has more to do with passion in my experience. Casual jazz listeners don't really understand the music, because if they did, then they wouldn't have done such a terrible job of putting together such a collection.  Jazz cannot be marketed and that's the problem with these record companies. Jazz doesn't need promotion, you either "get it" or you don't. I wouldn't waste my money or time on this box set.

Some obvious omissions: Bill Evans, Chet Baker, Stan Getz, Shelly Manne, Freddie Hubbard, Horace Silver, Stan Kenton, Gerry Mulligan, Jim Hall, Bobby Hutcherson, etc.

There is only one reason why I bought this album. When I tell you this reason, some of you will roll your eyes and click your tongue with disgust, but here it goes. The one reason I  bought this album? The pictures of Justin Hayward on the front and back cover (Swoon!)
OK, so now I've established the fact that I am pathetic, let's move on with the review.
If there is one  thing my beloved Moodies are guilty of, is creating music that is dated. For example, the sitar laden "In search of the lost chord" screams "THIS WAS MADE IN THE  SIXTIES." So,"The Other Side" screams "THIS WAS MADE IN THE EIGHTIES." The difference  is this: after I listen to "Chord" despite its groovy, love peace and joy feeling, I know I  have just listened to a quality album. I have listened to "Chord" many times since purchasing it. With "Other Side" I listened to it once, and have no desire whatsoever to  hear it again.  Yes, I like the title track, and of course the big 80s hit "Your Wildest Dreams" but after that, there is nothing enjoyable. We have an album filled with synthesized mush and all sorts of swooshing special effects.
One  song I particularly distain is my beloved Justin's "I Just Don't Care." This gorgeous man has written many love songs that are as beautiful as he is. This isn't one of them. With cloying lyrics like "The lovesick schoolboy turning up for school" it's one of the worst songs on the album. If you want to hear a GREAT Justin love song, check out the beautiful "All that is real is  you" from "Strange Times" or "In My World" from "Long Distance Voyager(an AWESOME album by the way.)
It's not like I have nothing to show for my 12.99. At least the pictures of Justin are good.

reviewText: This is not the Cure I know and love. Perhaps Robert Smith may have to, as he has often threatened, fold up the tent on this project and call it a day. They appear to have walked through this project half asleep.  The music is uninspired, and the lyrics are average.  It's a shame too, for the legacy that they have created cannot be questioned.  Their influence is heard on albums from groups like the Smashing Pumpkins to Interpol. Perhaps this has fueled their passion to create music all the more, or it may be that they recognize that the market they created is flourishing to such a degree they want a part of it. I'm thinking they should've pushed back the release date, that they hurried, and tweaked and touched up the material.  Your fans would've been a little ticked by the delay, but we would've understood if we heard this album as it is.  Whatever the case is, and I say this with great regret, either they have simply released a couple of bad albums, or they've become a poor imitation of themselves.

reviewText:
What is Black Metal? Cutting edge drumming + awesome guitar work (played classically at times)+ sweeping synth soundscapes + 'extreme' vocals. This is what black metal is all about.
If you cut out the synth, what are you  left with....any of the 1000's of the death metal bands out there. This is  not to say that IX is not a good Death Metal album, though I can't comment  on that.
Given the legacy of Emperor, from the awesome and majestic In  the Nightside Eclipse to Anthems, both voted as some of the most important  metal albums of the decade by Terrorizer, I would have expected Emperor to  come up with something much better than this....
The first two songs on  the album, correction the first one-and-a-half songs on the album, (the  second half of Decrystallizing Reason deteriorates into something else  which affects the rest of the album)are great. The album's production is  first rate and Ihsahn's vocal performance on these two songs is good.  Though, I must admit, when I heard the almost falsetto screaming yelling  intro of the first song, I was reminded of Manowar!
The reason why this  album does not work, is not because of the better production (as some  reviewers have suggested). I can identify three main reasons:
1) In 'in  the nightside' and 'Anthems' the synth was perfectly balanced with the rest  of the metal machinery (i.e. drums+guitars+vocals). In this album, guitars  have come to the forefront, with synth bits being added, almost as an  afterthought! There is far less variation in the drums, and a lot more  concentration on fast guitars.
2) The songs themselves are poorly  crafted, which is in contrast with Emperor's past two efforts. I can almost  not believe that this Emperor!
3) Ihsahn is a great black metal  singer, but his clean vocals....oh please....save us from the out of tune  singing!  Get someone like Simen of Borknagar/Dimmu Borgir to do the clean  bits, and stick to your strength- 'unclean' singing.
So that's my review.  I do not recommend this album, as it would spoil your vision of Emperor as  a leading Black Metal artist. One star for production, and one star for the  first 1 and 1/2 songs. Avoid at all costs.....

reviewText:
What do you think of when you think of Queensryche? Saxophones, rap beats, muddy guitars, and talk through vocals, well if these aspects are what come to mind then "Dedicated to Chaos" for you.

Amazingly enough this record is the straw that broke the camel's back. That's saying a lot for me because it means I continued with Queensryche through "Q2K", "Tribe", and "American Soldier". Yes I actually thought Mind crime 2 was decent. But this record makes all of those albums seem like epic masterpieces. I never thought it would actually get this bad for Queensryche. This album is pure trash. I'm sorry but there is not any redeeming qualities here at all.

"Got it bad" is without a doubt the worst Queensryche song ever recorded. The best way to describe the sound of this album is it sounds like a really bad modern U2 record. There is nothing on this album that would give the listener any indication that this is a Queensryche album. The core sound of anything that remotely resembles this once great band is gone here.

There really isn't anything more that can be said that hasn't already been said about this album. Something really needed to change for Queensryche to continue without them completely self destructing. Well it happened, that big change came, and it couldn't have came any quicker. Thank the Rock Gods. This is one album most Ryche fans try to pretend doesn't exist. Stay clear away from this abomination.

reviewText: Let's face it: Die For The Gov't, TSDWFY, and A New Kind of Army, as well as Underground Network are all amazing albums. The rest= all terrible. I really wanted to like Mobilize but couldn't due to it's cookie-cutter production, The Terror State is to AF what Train of Thought is to Dream Theater. And For Blood and Empire? Ugh, let's not even go there (although Emigre and I'd Tell You But... were cool songs). I've seen Anti-Flag twice (Both times opening for another band), the first time is what got me into them when they opened for Billy Talent (One of the best concerts ever). The second time was opening for Alexisonfire in December 2006 and they rocked the Shaw Conference Centre. However, all good things about Anti-Flag had to come to an end after that. Now this atrocity has wreaked havoc in the stores everywhere. I bought this thinking it would be good, but no. Every song is laden with crappy lyrics. All the songs sound the same, with the vocals becoming weaker every track. One good thing though, is that Justin doesn't perform solos on here, which is good, because while he's a good guitarist, he ain't no Adrian Smith. But hold that thought for a minute. Let's look at the lyrics. For the most part, they feel like they just wrote a chorus, came up with a song title, and then decided to copy and paste both the chorus and the title to fill the length of the song. But then there's the real lyrics. A Sample from "If You Wanna Steal (You Better Learn How To Die)": "The fine line between genius and insanity Is one he often treads so patiently While pigs and bulls will always try to lock the door..." Wait- did Justin just say what I think he did? No, wait, I'm gonna rewind that last line: "While Pigs and bulls will always try to lock the door." Three words: What the crap???? Doesn't Justin write clever lyrics, usually? If that ain't bad enough, here's another sample, this time, from "Tanzania", where the same line is literally repeated 4 times: "What will it take to end the massacre? What will it take to end the massacre? What will it take to end the massacre? What will it take to end the massacre?" Why are you asking ME this, Mr. Sane? You tell ME what it'll take to end this massacre. The music on this album is just as bad as, if worse than For Blood and Empire. The musicianship is bland and uninspired (as in unoriginal, people), as are the lyrics. And if that weren't bad enough, this is the most over-produced album I've ever heard. Child choirs, voice choirs, laughably awful keyboard orchestration, you name it. The keyboard orchestration on Iron Maiden's Dance of Death (AMAZING album- check it out, it's my 3rd favorite album of all time) worked because it made the album darker, and gave it a modern feel. Iron Maiden are metal (and my favorite band too!), Anti-Flag are punk. Keyboard orchestration works in metal, but not political punk. I know a few punk bands that use Keyboard orchestration and it works well, here it doesn't. So if anything, this album has to be one of the most disappointing albums since Dream Theater's Train of Thought. Everything sounds forced. Chris has too many singing parts like on FBAE. As one reviewer Mentioned, if this is what the future holds for these guys, then they have indeed sold out. (NOTE: The song "Tanzania" actually came with the online pre-order edition.)

reviewText: First, let me get this said: I love Rainbow.  I found out about Deep Purple because I was a Ritchie Blackmore's Rainbow fan first. I only recently began to appreciate On Stage (which is excellent!) and the first album with Man On the Silver Mountain.  I always liked things like "Jealous Lover" and "Stone Cold" with Joe Lynn Turner.  But this record is awful, horrible, and an embarrassment.  It doesn't do the band justice, and if it DOES, then it's no wonder Ritchie pulled the plug on it.  If this was the only post-Purple Blackmore ever heard, I'd think he was the weakest member of Deep Purple and you would be hard pressed to prove otherwise.  Joe Lynn Turner sounds ridiculous, even by 80s standards, and Graham Bonnet is no better.  (I saw Bonnet on the Down To Earth tour, and he was a major disappointment to the fans and to Ritchie on that show.)  Too bad...let sleeping dogs lie if this is the best the "archives" have to show us; let us remember these line-ups for their great records instead of these lame live performances.  Call it: FINAL NAIL IN THE COFFIN.

reviewText: I have reviewed 670 CDs on Amazon.com and I never have given a CD one star until now.  This CD richly deserves it.  It is a strong caution against putting too much faith in genetics.  I have seen Hank Williams Jr. and Roseanne Cash in concert.  Both of them inherited legitimate talent from their fathers.  All Shooter Jennings has inherited from Waylon and Jessi Colter is his name.  He can't write songs, although 4th of July has something to it.  He really can't sing, although he makes a good stab at it on Lonesome Blues and Living Proof.  His band would be best characterized as mediocre, and even that is being charitable.  The drummer in particular sounds lethargic.  Their live cut from Irving Plaza, really a test of their chops, is truly awful.  I suppose there is a market for this stuff and that I am offending some people.  But as a real country music fan I could find no redeeming merit in this album.

reviewText:
I was at work a few days ago, and I happened upon that new Blue Pepsi stuff that's out right now.  Me and my friend had never seen it advertised before, so it kind of took us by surprise, and, naturally, we felt obligated to give it a try.  On the first sip, I remember thinking, wow! This is great!  I could drink this stuff forever!  However, I proved to be jumping to conclusions, and after finishing roughly half the bottle, I began to reconsider my opinion on this blue stuff.  Every sip afterward that followed got progressively worse, and by the time I was on my last sip, it tasted like garbage.  What was wrong with it?  It tasted like carbonated gatorade.  Pepsi took two flavors that, while they work well by themselves, DO NOT work well together.  I was initially excited by the taste on my first sip, because it tasted so different, but by the end of the bottle, I realized that just because something is different doesn't always mean it's GOOD.
That got me thinking.  I realized that Limp Bizkit is a lot like Blue Pepsi, in many ways.  For one, they both..., but that's an unjust example.  For another example, they both combine two separate things, which could presumably work well together, but in the end don't, just because they're weren't matched very well.  In Limp Bizkit's case these two things are rap and metal, two things which COULD presumably go great together, but do they manage to pull it off?  No.  As experimentation has taught us, combining two different things together CAN sometimes work well, as there have been good, or at least decent rap-rock bands before.  However, Limp Bizkit cannot pull it off, and neither could Pepsi with their Blue nastiness.  Another important similarity is that Blue Pepsi is a drink which essentially hides behind its flashy logo, crazy color, and cool advertising to hide the fact that it tastes like junk.  It has no substance.  Limp Bizkit also has this same quality.  They hide behind their pizazz and in-your-face attitude, have good media coverage, advertising, and crazy and weird album covers, but yet, they have no substance beneath all of that.  They taste terrible.
So what else do Limp Bizkit and Blue Pepsi have in common?  Why, the same method to put an end to their existence: don't buy them.

reviewText:
Goodall's "interpretation" of Wagner consists of playing almost everything verrrryyyy slowwwwlllly. (Or should I say "vehwy swowy"?) That's it. Literally.

These performances are indescribable because there is nothing _to_ describe. There is no "insight" into the music -- either inspired or misguided. If you programmed a synthesizer to simply play the notes at a very slow tempo, without any sort of phrasing or inflection, you would have a "performance" indistinguishable from the Goodall.

If you have nothing better to do with your time than waste it listening to pointless, meaningless "music-making," or you enjoy staring at a blank wall, you will no doubt enjoy the Goodall Ring. If you believe your time should be more-profitably spent, there are more-entertaining, more-stimulating versions available.

As Gertrude Stein said about Oakland -- "There's no _there_ there."

reviewText:
I'm a huge Dream Theater fan, I love the Dixie Dregs (check them out, good stuff), and I'm even one of the few DT fans who absolutely loves Derek Sherinian.  I've heard some Kings X, some of which I loved, some of which I  disliked.  This album REPULSED me, I was VERY much angered by this album  just because these "progressive" musicians are all some of the  best at what they do and I was hoping for something at least about 100x as  good.  For one, all the sounds start to sound the same!  Only two songs  really stick out, and are by far the best tracks on the album, the heavily  keyboard driven "Plat-Opus" and the soothing ballad  "Chimes."  The rest I was very dissapointed with.  Not only is  there absolutely nothing "progressive" with it (certainly NOT a  measure of greatness) but there is hardly anything interesting lyrically,  musically, technically, or otherwise.  Even if you like lots of rock  grooves and catchiness, there is none here.  I'm told that this album  appeals most to heavy fans of Kings X, but if you are a "prog"  fan, KEEP AWAY.
I highly recommend getting the OTHER side project albums  including Dream Theater personelle: LTE and LTE2.  Another incredible album  that John Myung plays on is Gordian Knot featuring players of the chapman  stick and touch guitar, beautiful alum, absolutely brilliant. reviewText:
First the departure of the legendary Halford (and reason for decent lyrics), a 7 year lay-off between Painkiller and the awful Jugulator, handing lyric responsibility and production over to Glenn Tipton, and finally a loss of all focus. While Priest did not actually pick up the gun and shoot themselves in the head they dug the grave with this album. It is up to the fans to cover the hole up with dirt.
The album kicks off with "Machine Man" which sounds as ridiculous as the song title would leave you to believe. Finally 12 songs later and 70 minutes less left of your life you are left with only two or three worth repeating.  "Hell Is Home"  is the best track on the album with juvenile but tolerable lyrics and some great high screams from Owens. There is actually some melody discernible in this song. "In Between" is also a decent song which like "Hell is Home" has some clean passages mixed in with the heavy detuned nu metal guitar sound that permeates every single track on the album. "Close To You" shows signs of melody also but is not enough to salvage the album from the dung heap.
The rest of the album is characterized by inane lyrics, hopelessly pedantic guitar riffs and unispired chromatic nightmare examples of how not to play a guitar solo. Like Jugulator, Priest adapted to nu metal guitar trends of detuning while singing with a sort of menancing snarl somewhere between speaking and yelling. Expect no melody or brilliance in the guitar work and more of the same pathetic lyrics from Tipton as with Jugulator. Owens is also restrained not being allowed to carry the songs vocally or use the trademark Halford scream very often. Owens may be trying to claim his own identity but he could be in a much better band than Priest is now.
The problem here is not Owens, who has shown he can hit the high notes and deliver the ear-piercing scream. The problem is the the lyrics are awful and the guitar work simply thrown together with little harmony or focus on groove and structure. I would like to be able to blame it on these guys all approaching or in their 50's but Blue Oyster Cult just put out one of the best albums of their career and they are all over 50. Please save yourself the pain and keep the nostalgic memories of the former Priest intact and avoid this album.

reviewText: Like sheep to the slaughter, many 70's Yes fans continue to buy every new release since the dubious Drama album with the increasingly faint hope that the band has recovered its musical idealism.  The blade of disappointment  falls on us every time. One would be hard pressed to find a band that has  divided its fan base the way Yes has.  Newer fans will argue that there's  nothing wrong with a Yes that abides by the changing fashions and sounds of  the 80`s and 90's, and that change is good.  Is that a good enough reason  for change?  Wasn't classic Yes the product of integrity in search of  novelty and originality, of never forsaking  quality and ideas for trends?  "Open Your Eyes" is a slap in the face of those who hoped the  band for once would cut the bull and return to serious music-making instead  of MOR radio-catering.  Although Trevor Rabin doesn't play, ever since he  was allowed to stick his fingers in the pie the music has been perfectly  insipid, although some would say modern.  Amazingly, the rest of the band  are still under the spell or on equally daft trips of their own.  Anderson  is now a grating figure with his puerile lyrics and simplistic melodies  while the others, including the once respectable Howe, play music for  teens, technically challenging no doubt, but bereft of any inventiveness or  ambition.  How did so much damage ever take place?  As Lennon once said of  his band, the dream is over.

Those of you who already have a copy of this great album and especially if you have a truly remastered copy you have been warned!  Unless you want to pay a bomb in these tough economic times for what effectively amounts to well-designed cardboard you are no better off and indeed would be worse off given the price tag on this baby if you get this.

Other than "True", this is my favourite Spandau Ballet album as every track here just like in the previous album deserve to be on any best-of compilation of the band.  "Purist" fans usually despise this side of Spandau Ballet pointing instead to their earlier work as one of the pioneers of the "New Wave" movement but to be realistic once that great genre died off in the early 80s the band had to re-invent itself to remain relevant and as far as New Romantic smooth pop goes, few bands have even come close to the very high standards Spandau Ballet achieved.

This is why this mini-lp replica sleeve (mlps) version is such a disappointment; as far as mlps designs go, this version while not the best one I've seen is not the worst and is fairly well designed out of unfortunately very thin cardboard but at least looks as though the glue will hold for awhile and there is also a nifty A4-sized colour poster of the band and an insert with all the lyrics in both English and Japanese and so the mlps design in itself is not perfect but acceptable.

The sound quality, however, of the cd itself is horrible!  It certainly has not been remastered at all and to make things worse even sounds worse than the old cassette that I had all those years ago!  You would think that they could at least have gone through the trouble to remaster this album so as to justify the price that they are asking us to cough up to "upgrade" from our existing cds to this!  The Japanese "sound engineer" in charge of this project should be ashamed of himself for such a terrible standard of work.

Very, very disappointing for fans and if you don't already have this brilliant album, do yourself a favour and save yourself some cash and get the "normal" remastered version in the jewel-case format and if you already have the cd, don't even bother with this wasted opportunity to be a genuine upgrade worth getting.

As for me, I'm thinking of getting a properly remastered cheaper version out there and switching the discs so that this acceptable mlps design can house a cd that is more deserving of the format.

Very, very, very much NOT recommended!

reviewText:
Imagine, if you will, that Capitol Records chose years ago to put out the Beatles' "White Album" on compact disk when the format was in its infancy, and for whatever reason decided not to invest the funds to put out a double CD, instead choosing to cram the entire thing onto one CD, and advertising it as a "specially low-priced single disk." But in doing so, they found that the whole thing wouldn't fit onto a standard disk, so they hacked about a minute or so out of "Revolution #9" (thinking nobody would notice), eliminated or shortened the silence between songs (if any), and nickel-and-diming the album until it fit just under the time limitations of a single disk. Then pretend that Beatles fans were too blinded by their fanaticism for the album to objectively criticize, let alone realize, the absolute horror of this corporate hatchet job. If this fictitious story sounds too weird for you, then now you know how I feel seeing five-star review after review here, when Warner-Reprise has performed the ultimate sin right under all our noses.

I only recently started amassing a CD collection of Neil, preferring to stick to the vinyl. I figured there will eventually be a remaster job of these albums, although with Neil you never know, and I could wait until then. But I broke down and went ahead and bought "Live Rust" on CD, which is one of my absolute top 10 favorite albums of all time. Knowing the guitar majesty of "Cortez the Killer" on this album better than I know my own date of birth, and having heard it countless times note-for-note, I immediately fast-forwarded to that track and waited for my world to be sonically blown to bits by the digital clarity of the CD, which happened indeed. For about four minutes.

And then I stopped cold. I stared out the window. I was frozen, playing air guitar to notes that were no longer coming out of the speaker, singing guitar parts in my head that weren't happening. "Am I getting that progressed into Alzheimer's already?" I thought, or is this some sort of a defective joke? Well, my Neil fan faithful, I'm here to tell you: the actual track of "Cortez" is approximately a minute and a half shorter than not only the vinyl version, but a minute and a half shorter than THE TIME GUARANTEED TO ME ON THE CD INSERT by good ol' Warner-Reprise. And where did this extra 90 seconds come from? well, it was right there in the LEAD GUITAR parts of the song, right prior to the "hate was just a legend" lyric. They have AXED a huge section of Neil's guitar lead, digitized it out to save space, and done God-knows-what to the rest of the album to give us a low, low price.

I frantically fast-forwarded the track to the end and compared the ending times on my CD player to the one on the CD cover. I was right. And I was disgusted. Then I started REALLY losing it: who was responsible for this? And why in the living name of God could any self-respecting Neil fan put up with the absolute desecration of one of the greatest recorded versions of one of his most jaw-droppingly gnarly songs?

I for one took the CD back. It took me a while to explain to the clerk why, but he chalked it up to a bad mistake on WB's part. Personally, I think their strange urgency in reissuing four of his least-selling albums "remastered with the original cover art" on CD is unusually nice, but I would much rather have a full-blown remastered version of "Live Rust" than anything else in his catalog. Especially now that I know about this hatchet job that sits on the shelf indefinitely, with no plans to improve on it. And Reprise, while you're at the task of putting that 90 seconds of guitar bliss back into "Cortez" that you so thoughtfully took out, go ahead and put out some other songs from that tour that weren't on the original CD to restore my faith in corporate America, because this is more of a disgrace than Watergate, "read my lips", and Monica's dress put together. Get the President on the horn.

reviewText:
The original Columbia LP came out in 1974 and, with the advent of the CD, the suits at Columbia naturally thought that the buying public, in order to satisfy their curiosity about the new format, would rush out to purchase equally-skimpy CDs. And they were right. At least until faced with competition from the likes of Rhino, Ace of London, Bear Family, Eric Records, etc., and within a few short years we were able to get 20- to 30-track CDs and with substantial liner notes to provide background information on the artist or artists concerned, as well as discographies.

Having said that, at first glance at the sealed CD contents, when it came out as a CD in October 1990 a potential buyer probably thought it at least filled the bill insofar as their greatest hits were to 1974 by having these 5 charted singles and three B-sides: Jingo (Jin-Go-Lo-Ba on some pressings) - # 58 Billboard Pop Hot 100 Nov 1969 b/w Persuasion on Columbia 45010; Evil Ways - # 9 Hot 100 Feb-March 1970 (b/w Waiting which is missing from the set) on Columbia 45069; Black Magic Woman - # 4 Nov-Dec 1970 b/w Hope You're Feeling Better on Columbia 45270; Oye Come Va - # 13 Hot 100/# 32 R&B March-April 1971 b/w Samba Pa Ti on Columbia 45330; and Everybody's Everything - # 12 Hot 100/# 39 R&B Oct-Nov 1971 (b/w Guajira - another omitted B-side).

The same buyer might have wondered at the inclusion of tracks 8 and 9, which were not among their "greatest hits" but if long-time fans of the band would recognize that Everything's Coming Our Way was from their 1971 LP "Santana III" (Columbia KC-30595) while Se A Cabo was culled from their 1970 "Abraxas" (Columbia CA-30130). They might also have wondered why the original 1974 album compiler at CBS chose not to include instead the April 1972 # 36 Hot 100 No One To Depend On which came out on Columbia 45552 b/w Taboo, along with one of the missing B-sides, or even go to 12 tracks and include all 6 hits and their B-sides.

But even at the (then) steep price for 10 tracks, and figuring that beggars can't be choosers, they bought the CD, took it home ... and then were horrified at the pathetic sound reproduction which included abridged and often cut-off tracks. As most other reviewers point out, avoid this. No R&R Hall of Fame inductee (1998) should have this kind of junk still circulating.

The latter speaks for "Once More, With Feeling," a horrible episode of "Buffy The Vampire Slayer," which was part of Season Six, the show's ultimate downfall season. The season started out with a depressing episode, and the show never seemed to recover from it's depression. This episode tried and failed to do that. No matter how popular the episode gets (or how well this CD sells), this will always signify to me that this was the season that signified "Buffy's" demise. reviewText:
I have one moderately nice thing to say about this record.  See the "Quasar" note.  Otherwise it's gonna get rough so read on at your peril.  You've been forewarned!

Instead of "Oceania" this record should be titled "Bill Corgan's pathetic wimp and whine egofest 2012."  Well, OK -- if you're tiring of Justin Bieber because you just recently went through puberty and want something that you think will pad your pop culture ego as a little "edgier" or even (gasp) "retro," by all means waste your money on this record (newsflash: it won't work) .  Oceania is yet another irrelevant, straight-out-of-the-pop-vending-machine formulaic piece of crap, but plenty of people will buy it anyway -- which is the only reason I can think of for why Bill released this record.  I mean, he can't possibly need the money, so why tarnish his name and his legacy with this stinky unemptied colon of a project?  It would be much more appropriate if it just came free with a happy meal -- but I'd still rather have a cheap plastic Spiderman toy that broke the first time I took it out of the box.

To be a little more specific, you can just *tell* where the songs are going to go -- and despite how much you don't want the train to wreck it's inevitable.  I mean, you can just hear the stupid, standard sappy guitar solo around the corner and then BAM -- it happens.  You can anticipate the stupid keyboard and bass hooks (coupled with emo strings) coming up and then, just like turds in a litterbox, they appear (see The Celestials, 1:16 in).  Similarly, you start to think, "huh, I haven't heard Bill whine for awhile," and then, just like garbage on the beach, it rolls in predictably.  And man, what boring, standard drum work -- constant highhat/ride cymbals and hackneyed tom rolls pretty well covers it.  I've said it before and I'll say it again:  THIS is what passes for "creativity"?  Don't be fooled!  You don't have to accept anything that's meant for Applebee's background music, or as a soundtrack to a movie that no one wants to see.  There actually IS good music out there, but you've got to wade through so much cookie-cutter nonsense that sometimes you lose hope.

Some even more specific notes:

Quasar:  I didn't have high expectations for this record.  But between 0:20 and 0:58 the song actually, ahem, kind of rocks!  I like the guitar work in that 38 seconds, and I thought I might be pleasantly surprised by the whole record [end the one nice thing].  That's when the whole record collapses.  The bellwether of the descent into the toilet?  The mantra at 0:59 in, whatever it means.  I don't care, I just know that mantras and rock songs DON'T MIX!  You don't need to add anything to your resume of pretentious douchebaggery, Bill -- it's stuffed to the gills.  And 38 seconds of decent rock isn't worth the price of this turkey.

The Celestials:  "I will be special k."  That's a real lyric in this song -- look it up in the liner notes.  A question, Bill:  you don't want to be a better cereal?  I mean, you're so rich, you could sit around in a kiddie pool full of any cereal you want for the rest of your life, stuffing face and watching TV nonstop!  Might I suggest Lucky Charms, Fruity Pebbles, or even Frosted Cheerios at least?  I get it -- you're getting older and needed the extra fibre in Special K to address your creative constipation.  But don't forget -- despite what you think, not everyone likes the smell of your musical farts.

Violet Rays:  stupid keyboards introduce even stupider guitar.

My Love Is Winter:  Another predictable melody underneath boring, tired lyrics.  1:14 in cue the stupid keyboards.  Did he hire a toddler to write songs or something?  Can't you just see, say, Barney dancing with the letter "A" 1:14 in?  Did Bill write the soundtrack to a forthcoming Barney epic masterpiece?

One Diamond One Heart:  more stupid keyboards!  Did he use a preset pattern set to charmsichord?  Wimpy, predictable, boring drums.  LOVE the electronic pan flute, Bill.

Pinwheels:  wait, am I playing a video game?  Wait, 0:38 in -- am I listening to a bastardized ripoff of Spacemen 3?

Oceania:  6:38 in, perfect example of crappy, standard, wuss guitar.  8:20 in another terrible solo.  the only way to close a song this bad is to fade out.  and guess what?

Pale Horse:  the pop music machine suggested picking one word and repeating it over and over like a moron.  Bill obliged.  LOVE the melody, too:  dee dee dee dee dee dee, dee dee dee dee dee dee ... dee dee ... dee dee.  In case you're pining for another song structured around repeating one word in a failed attempt to be deep, don't worry -- you only have to wait until Wildflower.

The Chimera:  "if I'm wrong I'm right."  WOAH, deep!  I gotta catch my breath, my mind is blowing!!!

Glissandra:  more stupid guitar work right from the start, followed by another video game keyboard twiddle and the awesomely outrageous lyric "la-la-la-la-la."  I guess four la's wasn't enough, but 6 was too many.  Genius.

Inkless:  1:27 in, perfect example of a trite and idiotic guitar solo.  What software came up with that one, Bill?  The refrain:  "The stars are out tonight."  It's more like Bill's mooning us, but we can't tell if we're staring at his rear or his head.  That pretty well sums up this album for me.

Wildflower:  the last song on the record is a *real* gem.  In case you didn't get enough of Bill's nasal complaining, cue the wimpy whining Bill Corgatron-5000, masquerading as artistic!  3:25, splice in the stupid guitar solo!  And what an ending!  Did Bill just get tired, uninspired and say, "screw it -- let's just repeat the word 'wildflower' over and over.  People will eat it up and think it's deep and musical.  Let's pinch this loaf off once and for all and serve it up for all to smell!"  Cause that's what happens.  What I wonder is this:  how did Bill decide on 9 times to repeat the word?  Why not 8, why not 10?  Oh no, 8 wouldn't be enough -- we need at *least* one more "wildflower" to drive it home!  I GET IT BILL, WILDFLOWER.  Now gimme my $9 back!

Honestly *this* is the best Bill can do in 5 years?!  If I puked in a guitar and sent it to the monkey house for 5 years I'd get a better album.  Disappointing and embarrassing, Bill.

reviewText:
I love Whitney Houston. How could one not love someone with such an incredible gift? But that gift is no longer present in her current work, "I Look To You". I bought her last two albums "My Love Is Your Love" and "Just Whitney" when most gave it the thumbs down but I thought they were actually pretty decent. But this CD here is just the worst. This is a complete hot mess. The fact that Clive Davis and the media painted this as her comeback (her 3rd comeback if anyone has bothered to keep count) makes this that much sadder. Sure she looks beautiful on the cover and she's now free of Bobby (and the drugs?) but her voice is long long gone and the songs ALL sound dated. She struggles through most of the tracks and avoids all high notes whenever possible.

The first single "I Look To You" though the message behind it is beautiful is dreadful and when I played it at home for the first time my family wanted to know who was the old white male country singer I was listening to. I had to tell them it wasn't an old white male country singer, it was Whitney Houston!!! Now you know something is horribly wrong when your voice is so far gone people are now confusing it for that of an old white male country singer. It's a darn shame. "Million Dollar Bill" is suppose to be this big hit but it sounds like something Whitney stole from some long forgotten 1970's soul act and is trying to pass it off as new school. Songs like "Call You Tonight" are so elementary that I wonder how they even made it on the record. "A Song For You" would've been amazing had it been sung and not talked in a song-like way (if that makes any sense). And as other reviewers have stated there is no reason for this album to sound so dated like it does. Whoever was responsible for the writing and producing of this material must not have their ears to the street OR the radio because this stuff is so off the mark with today's popular music. This CD doesn't represent the present or future - it's the past and that is where it should have stayed, in the past. Even on a track like "Salute" which is the closest we get to a song sounding the least bit fresh and edgy, Whitney seems out of her element and can't pull off the youthful spirit sounding tired instead. The only reason I could see why this CD hit #1 was due to all the initial hype because it really lacks any kind of substance or genuine soul. I'm going to hope and pray that on her next album Whitney will finally get her comeback (which at that time would be her 4th attempt) because this comeback was a major flop. No one wants to see Whitney fail but releasing such a poor record is unacceptable.

Download: "I Didn't Know My Own Strength" - The lone exceptional, beautifully done track on this misguided, overly-hyped CD.

Listen To: "Like I Never Left" - This smooth jam reveals a calm, cool, and collected Whitney amongst the mess.

reviewText:
The Black Crowes impressed people because in the 90s they looked like a 70s rock band, and sounded like a 70s rock band, and they had the attitude of a 70s rock band. The boogied, they had anthemic choruses, they were a little bit country and a little bit blues and a lotta bit rock `n' roll, and when you listened to their music you could sorta see them drinking beer and playing some dingy bar and doing the whole sex drugs and rock `n' roll thing. It was all cool, but here's the problem- not all 70s rock bands were good. In fact, some of them, despite all of their country and blues and suds and heroin, were terrible. The Crowes ain't immune from that fact. Sounding like the Small Faces in the 90s can be cool, but that's only the case if you have good songs to justify the sound. Otherwise, it's just a gimmick. And that's exactly what Shake Your Money Maker is.

In fact, this album tends to remind me why 70s rock isn't that fondly remembered a genre in the first place. This is an album full of macho posturing, instantly forgettable riffs, boring ballads, go-nowhere guitar riffs, and so on. It wallows in bar rock's clichs without contributing anything new, and frankly, if I wanted that I'd listen to Bad Company. "Could I've Been So Blind" and "Jealous Again" are bland, joyless rockers with lame riffs and cheesy choruses, while "Seeing Things" and "Sister Luck" are equally uninspiring ballads that amble their way past the five minute mark in almost pitiful fashion. "Twice As Hard" is a badly misguided stab at a hard rock anthem, and "Thick n' Thin" is a joyless boogie with old-hat guitars and a quiet/loud dynamic that's only sort of cool. Even the big hit, a cover of Otis Redding's "Hard To Handle," has little more to recommend it than some funky rhythms. "She Talks To Angels" is another flat-on-its face country ballad.

Maybe I should just pass this off as mediocre, give it three stars because it isn't exactly offensively bad, but that would be too generous. These guys don't even get points for originality. Don't waste your time.

reviewText:
Let's do a little math. Over the course of their career, Aerosmith have released fourteen "proper" albums. There are also five official live albums (1. Live Bootleg, 2. Classics Live I, 3. Classics Live II, 4. A Little South of Sanity, 5. Rockin' the Joint.) Meanwhile, not including various repackaging schemes, re-releases, and international items, there are currently nine Aerosmith compilation albums on the market. (1. Greatest Hits, 2. Gems, 3. Pandora's Box, 4. Big Ones, 5. Box of Fire, 6. Young Lust, 7. O Yeah, 8. Gold, 9. Devil's Got a New Disguise.) Add those compilations to the live albums and you get fourteen "retrospective" releases. So Aerosmith and their record companies have managed to squeeze fourteen retrospectives out of fourteen original albums. A pretty impressive feat, if you think about it. But it's obvious what the true fan should really spend his or her money on, if you disdain market saturation and contractual fulfillments.

The recent compilations favor the overblown blues/soul orchestrations of the latter phase of the band's career (late 80s to present), while giving short shrift to the well-toned heavy rock of the classic years (up to the late 70s) and completely ignoring the lost years (late 70s to mid 80s). If you're partial to the hard rockin' classic years, then for a useful overview you still can't do any better than the short and snappy Greatest Hits from 1980. Or just buy all the proper albums from that period, which would be infinitely more rewarding than these useless modern compilations. As for this new Devil's Got a New Disguise release, the song selection is nearly identical to the O Yeah collection from just four years ago, with the obligatory so-called bonus tracks to supposedly make the purchase worthwhile. Here, "Sedona Sunrise" is actually rather unique for the band's recent history, but there's a reason the two bonus tracks were previously unreleased. One could certainly blame the record companies for regurgitating all these quickie compilations, but some fault also lies with the band, who have diluted their legacy by allowing these repetitive retrospectives to be released, as easy ways to fulfill contracts. If you're really into Aerosmith, just commit some money to all of those fourteen original albums. After all, there's as many of those as there are retrospectives, and the originals are where the action really is. [~doomsdayer520~]

reviewText:
I wasn't sure I wanted to write this review or not ... I've been thinking about it for a very long time, and decided that my words were as valid as those of Kelly Joe, and folks might just want to fully understand what they're getting themselves in for.

Phelps had an inquisitive mind and restless spirit that have always carried him forward and moved into new forms of expression, though experimentation [hed like you to believe] comes at a costs. When his album Western Bell baffled not only his record company but puzzled many of his fans, and failed to expand his audience, Phelps laid low, he withdrew from recording in search for a new direction, for something that may be more accessible. He claims that unexpectedly, inspiration came through a re-examination of his christian [small c] roots, and resulted in an unexpected flurry of creative activity that gave birth to a whole new set of songs and a reinvigorated approach to playing the guitar as Phelps opted to play bottleneck rather than his customary lap slide to achieve a sound that wouldnt have been out of place on a classic John Fahey record, though the message surely would.

Of course this is how Phelps likes to see things, when the truth of the matter is, the man found that drugs, drink, and an endless series of bad tattoos caused him to hit bottom and hit hard.  And like most all people who feel that they they can not be responsible for their own lives, Phelps turned to god, fell on his knees, and put the responsibility for his life in an imaginary being, and in short, became a christian musician, a shill for god, where he found a ready made flock willing to follow him.  Trouble is, he doesnt tell you that before you book a ticket to his show  so there you sit, youve paid your money intent on hearing some bluesy material, but instead you get preached to.  Yeah, this is called subversion, bait and switch, leaving you no choice but to up and leave not only the show, but your money at the ticket window.

With song titles like Talking to Jehovah, Ive been Converted and The Holy Spirit Flood, theres no escaping that something has gone sideways, something that thematically changed in Kelly Joes world. Phelps lyrics fuse poetry from the Book of Jonah and claims a kinship with the vintage gospel blues of Mississippi John Hurt [though there is no evidence to support Hurts christian beliefs] with aspects of the early gospel work of Bill and Charlie Monroe thrown in for good measure, professing that these songs must surely be the most literary gospel songs recorded since Bob Dylans adventure down the same road decades ago.

Phelps explains some of the motivation behind the new songs. Id arrived at a place where I was sinking. I had to do something or my head was going to blow up or my heart would stop. When I found a way to allow myself to open up to creative impulse, this is what was staring me in the face and I did not want to say no to anything.  This change was bewildering to those whove followed Kelly Joes music.  Hed like you to believe that this change isn't too surprising as it represents a natural growth from the rural routes his music has traveled until now. He goes on to say, This is going to be referred to as a gospel record, I suppose. The music is presented in an ancient form, but itll sound contemporary because of the way I play and write. But, thematically, Im basing my compositional approach on old styles like the old blues and folk guys played.

But it is a surprise Mr. Phelps  you had the choice of making time honored music that would last forever, or thinking that you could save your ragged bones by selling out to a higher power, thinking that wed all follow along.  But not me, I dropped Dylan when he failed to take responsibility for his own life.  What makes you think that Id follow you down that same path of irresponsibility?

Of course, on the other hand, if you're a christian, and you like to be endlessly reminded that you are nothing without a mystic magical being defining your life, then you just might enjoy this album.

reviewText:
I never reviewed this cast recording before?  Hmm, guess I didn't think it was worth my time.  Seriously.  Wicked does absolutely NOTHING for me.  There are like eight songs that I listened to it more than once (though Defying Gravity finds itself on my playlist quite often)

Wicked is basically a mess of mediocre and so-generic-it-hurts showtunes.  Every song in it reminds me of another (better) song from another musical.  The most obvious of these would be all of the Wizard's songs.  Every song he sing reminds me of Amos Hart from "Chicago."  I'm almost beginning to think that Amos IS the Wizard!  I can't even listen to the Wizard's songs because, not only are they boring and insipid (at least "Chicago" had the jazziness to get by), they are BLATANT RIPOFFS.

When it isn't stealing songs from other shows, "Wicked" is filling the obligatory song cues.  None of the songs feature any characterization whatsoever.  If you took out all of the crazy Oz references, you could insert the songs into any situation and it would be dandy.  There is one that tries its hardest, Dancing Through Life, but it is so dumb that it hurts.  The worst offender is the love song, As Long as You're Mine, which was completely random.

A lot of the songs just plain don't belong in the show.  I already mentioned the love song, but there is also "For Good" which I agree DOES seem to want to be like "Who Will Love Me As I Am?" from "Side Show."  A lot of Glinda's songs were really unnecessary too.  It's like Schwartz had a checklist of what types of songs he needed in the show, and just went down the line.  Here's the thing, Schwartz, you of all people should know that musicals have to show story and character through song.  "Wicked" doesn't do this.

Its songs aren't the only failure.  The whole storyline is absolutely awful. If you watch "The Wizard of Oz" and keep "Wicked" in mind, you will realize how little the plots go together.  Have they even seen the movie?  Another thing I found dumb was the whole romance with Fyero.  Umm... okay, Elphaba is an intelligent girl who has had difficulties from day one.  Why in the heck would she fall in love with a guy who has it incredibly easy and doesn't even bother with any effort?  It's like Homer Simpson and Frank Grimes!  Okay, so say Fiyero's changed... there is absolutely NO indication of that whatsoever.

My other problem with "Wicked" is that it really doesn't show why Elphaba turned evil.  There is one song that attempts to delve into her psyche (No Good Deed); when isn't that supposed to be the whole point of the show?  And that song has a pretty poor excuse.  She goes from being this incredibly good, well-intentioned girl to this evil chick who sets her supposed-lover on fire (watch the movie!)  It's too drastic for me, and one song isn't enough to explain that.  Also, in their attempt to round out a 2-d villain, they just created another: the Wizard.  Now I think I need to write a book/musical explaining why the Wizard's this evil tyrant!

"Wicked" is insanely popular and is kind of like the new "RENT" (another horribly overrated show.)  It seems to try really hard to appeal to teenage girls, which is probably why it's so popular.  But its portrayal of social problems like that is about as deep as a bad teen movie.  There was nothing REMOTELY likable about Glinda, even when she befriended Elphaba.  I think that the writers went out of their way to make Elphaba the only decent character in the whole thing.  It's incredibly unrealistic, and I'm not referring to the whole munchkins and talking animals.

Don't get me wrong, Schwartz has done some fine work.  I love "Godspell" and I even like his Disney soundtracks (though "Pocahontas" was a little preachy.)  But when I saw his whining about how he didn't get the Tony, I just shook my head because I'd finally gotten around to listening to "Avenue Q," and there is absolutely no question about why that did so well.  There have been arguable injustices with the Tony's in the past ("Lion King" winning over "Ragtime,"; even this year's Spamalot winning over "The Light in the Piazza") but that is not one of them.

In short, there are better shows out there.  I'd advise saving your money until you find one.
