reviewText:
This marked the emergence of a VERY negative trend in music, namely that technique and speed were far more important than creating music and actually communicating.

Al DiMeola for me epitomized a lot of things that went wrong with the jazz-rock fusion movement, which started off so incredibly innovative and exciting, Somewhaere along the way, it changed from being about exploring bold new musical ideas to rather juvenile game of "I CAN PLAY FASTER THAN YOU JACK!!" Without ANY of the sheer musical depth of his former boss Chick Corea or a master like John McLaughlin or Miles Davis, Al burst out of the starting gate just whipping off scales at 19,000 mph but saying little to NOTHING in the process except, "I CAN PLAY REALLY FAST AND LOUD".

Compositionally, most of the pieces here are not much more than textbook mathematical exercises, save for the Bach piece which actually gets a decent reading. Al's vocal spot with "Pictures Of The Sea" is pretty non-descript and pointless. Only "Short Tales From The Black Forest" stirs any interest, only because of Chick Corea's musicianship. On "Suite-Golden Dawn", Jaco Pastorious tries so danged hard to get Al to loosen up and play with some soul, but alas, 'twas not to be.

If you like super-speed shred guitar and mindless pyrotechnics for their own sake, this might be for you, otherwise, don't bother with this technique-ridden snoozefest. Al DiMeola sure proved he was far more TECHNICIAN than MUSICIAN.
label: negative

reviewText:
Since the Baroque era, the violin has been one of the most important of all Western instruments - for several reasons. The tone of the violin stands out above other instruments, making it appropriate for playing a melody line and, in the right hands, the violin is extremely agile - able to execute rapid and difficult sequences of notes. Contemporary music still embraces the violin - in sometimes new and sometimes exciting contexts - Tracy Bonham, Miri Ben Ari, Arcade Fire, Dave Matthews Band, Yellowcard...

This particular album of mostly rock tracks (or rocked-up classical compositions) with solo violin and a rock-band-augmented-backing-orchestra results in something that might be amusing as an unexpected encore at the symphony or as a novelty act in Vegas or on a television variety show. It's more gimmick than any sort of crossover genius.

I'm not knocking David Garrett's skills on the violin, but this project was poorly executed. Several of these tracks are not well suited for solo violin and those that are feel more like muzak due to heartless backing instrumentation. This is not so much the case on his earlier albums - the eponymous "David Garrett" album is a better executed set of rock/pop songs with classics mixed in to better effect.

I've listened to the entire album, not just the clips here. There was potential in spots to do something really interesting... but often I just cringed when the violin came in to awkwardly take the melody.

I'd hoped Orianthi's guitar contribution on "Walk This Way" would have been more substantial - perhaps "dueling strings"or some sort of counterpoint, echoing the groundbreaking crossover nature of the Run DMC / Aerosmith version.

A good mashup usually makes you go "Wow, how could A possibly go with B? That sounds crazy/awesome!" - In that vein, I wish "Vivaldi vs. Vertigo" had gone further contrasting the alt rock edge (U2's Vertigo) with the beautiful (Vivaldi's Winter from The 4 Seasons). I love both of the originals but this track was underwhelming.

I love Classical music. I love Rock music. I love solo violin. I think Nigel Kennedy's efforts in combining the three have been much more interesting, cool, and more likely to "get rock fans to listen to classical music" (Try "The Nigel Kennedy Experience" or "The Doors Concerto"). However, this time around, David Garrett's fusion of all 3 falls almost completely flat in a painful way. I can't imagine enjoying this album in a casual or critical listening context.

It's possible that someone out there might still find favor with the over-orchestrated, over-produced music here - the kind that was once commonly used in dentist's offices and elevators to soothe the listener's nerves. These days, while other retro music like Martin Denny can have an agreeably continental flair, Mantovani is just plain dull. This is music of the worst possible type: drained of personality and soul, where even the occasional more modern song (mid sixties) comes off as stilted. This kind of thing has long been replaced by easy-listening jazz; not even the uncoolest of the Star Search generation would be caught dead with this in their closet.

This kind of dreck gives you sympathy for the poor listener whose musical background is so impoverished as to make this music an option.

Sadly, this was not the case: unlike Nimoy & Shatner's releases, which were bad in a funny way and really good for a goof, Ms. Nichols' CD was just plain bad! Her tribute tune to the late Trek creator Gene Roddenberry is so appalling, I could just imagine him turnin' in his grave (which would be an amazing feat, since he was cremated) when this dreck hit the streets! And her little song that goes with the original Star Trek opening theme will make you wanna beam this CD right outta your player and toss it into the nearest dumpster at warp speed!
If you want Trek-celeb-crooned tunage that is bad yet still fun to listen to, take a look at Shatner's `The Transformed Man', Nimoy's `Highly Illogical' compilation, or Brent "Data" Spiner's `Ol' Yellow Eyes is Back', and avoid this musical atrocity like the plague!

reviewText: Despite selling three million copies in the US alone, Adrenalize was a huge disappointment. I know, any recording artist today would gladly give up his right arm in exchange of those numbers, but let's not forget that Pyromania sold more than ten million copies and Hysteria more than twelve million. As I mentioned in a previous review, Adrenalize followed Hysteria's overproduced pop metal formula to a tee, a move that proved fatal in the midst of the grunge explosion. So, after Adrenalize's underwhelming performance, our beleaguered pop metallers from Sheffield decided to follow the steps of countless hair farmers before them and adapted their sound in an effort to court the 90s alterna-rock audience. Unlike Mtley Cre, Poison or Warrant, who completely revamped their sound, the Leps decided to stay within a reasonable pop metal idiom despite ditching their signature multilayered production and adding some trendy industrial rock touches here and there. The main change came in the songwriting: this time around, the songs lack the melodic, in-your-face hooks and choruses that defined the band in previous albums, and the overall vibe, with the sole exception of the somewhat infectious title track, is dark, moody and reflective with much more personal and mature lyrics. Being this a Def Leppard album, really good songwriting is almost mandatory, and the band does deliver it with tracks All I Want is Everything, Work it Out and Slang. That said, I really can't find a real point in this album because a big part of the Lep's appeal was the good times summertime tone present in their music, and since it's almost completely absent here, the songs sound extremely forced and uncomfortable, as if the band members were struggling to work with a musical and lyrical identity that's not really their own. This album was ultimately a big gamble that didn't pay off, since after earning a gold certification it just died commercially and cemented the band's future status as a nostalgia act.

reviewText:
I really enjoyed the album "Begin to Hope" and felt certain "Far" would be of the same caliber. What I enjoy about Regina Spektor is that quirky,cryptic,poetic energy that she expresses with sorrow or sass. I love the kind of music that stops me in my tracks like the song "Samson". Or the song "Fidelity" which begs you to memorize the lyrics, and maybe you'd get a giggle out of "Hotel Song". There was something soulful about that album, a kind of growing pain that you could set on replay for hours.

On the other hand, I don't have much love for the album "Far". While her voice maintains something beautiful, and she can skip it around and bounce it off melodies like a stone on water... its the lyrics or content that bugs me. If "Begin to Hope" was deep, mature, and thoughtful- "Far" regresses to juvenile, boring, and weird. Yes, its all done with a beautiful voice and that same quirky enthusiasm. But as much as I wanted to be impressed or blown away by this album, I wasnt.

You can take the most beautiful singer in the world, and they can sing the dumbest song ever and you'd probably like it just because the voice was beautiful. They could sing in another language, and you'd probably love it without knowing what the song was about. But if you give a great voice a song of substance it will transcend time, culture, genere, age, etc.

Ten years from now, unless you are a die hard fan, no one will remember this album as Regina's standout piece of work. It's my opinion that when people introduce Ms. Spektor to others they will recommend "Begin to Hope" as opposed to her other albums.

reviewText:
Perhaps never in the history of rock and roll had an album been as hyped before its release. Spring's concerts were raved about by fans, but Spring had always been too insecure to release a live album. Desperate for some big bucks, his manager finally convinced his act that now was the time to strike, and strike they did, with enough pre-sales to make this 5-LP (3-CD) set debut at number one on the charts and keep them in gravy for years.

It started out promisingly enough with a 1975 song on piano. Spring performs, solo, a song that still means something to him, released on LP in 1975. Then the box takes a nosedive, jumping forward a few years. That's right, *one* song from 1975, no songs from 1976 and 1977. Knowledgeable Spring fans knew there was trouble the second they read when the songs were from. Spring and his manager-producer had decided to skip over his best concert years since they didn't have multi-track recordings of them to fiddle with and tweak.

Compounding the mistake, the general rule is that the performances selected are of songs originally released in studio versions years earlier. 1978 performances are of 1975 songs, 1981 performances are of 1978 songs, and so on. Spring has clearly lost the original inspiration he had when writing the material and plays every song as an oldie, covered as nostalgia. Spring's camp actually thought the most important thing was to have the backing group, the notoriously overrated E Street Band, not make as many mistakes (since they'd have played the songs hundreds of times by the recording dates). They didn't care that the performances themselves lacked any hint of vitality, and sounded exactly like they were, tired re-treads.

This box set also lacks any sense of flow, of sensible sequence. Compiled from numerous sources, it does not have any automatic coherence. And the multiple producers can't create any, either, from these lackluster renditions.

The sad thing is that *every* honest Spring fan knows that they've been sold a bill of goods with this set, but many drink the kool-aid all the same. All these 5-star reviews are a joke. It doesn't deserve even one star. If Spring had simply released one of the several 1978 3-hour radio broadcasts of his show, straight as-is, he'd have given fans a record of what he was all about live. What he sold fans instead was a travesty, a miserably failed attempt at tampering with his own music past, making him over as the Born-in-the-USA man.
label: negative

reviewText:
The decline of Oldfield's career in recent years has been downright painful, and I believe this is the end.  I have grown up with Mike, being born in 1978 and having had Ommadawn, Hergest Ridge, and other albums interweaved with some of the most significant and touching times in my childhood and my life.  It makes it all the more difficult, then, that he seems to be dying a slow musical death.  He has completely immersed himself in his studio, churning out uninspired landscapes of preset synth backgrounds and aimless melodies.  This musical draught has lasted for 10 years now, and it only gets worse.

What does the album sound like?  Imagine a hotel lobby.  Or a gift shop.  The first disk, Light, is definitely the better of the two, having at least a few moments of decency (the oddly beautiful "The Gate," for example).  Dark is completely terrible, being made up primarily of "techno" (I say that in quotation marks because he obviously has no idea what goes into making a genuinely good techno song).  I can say little else, because the music is so bland and uncomplicated that it is impossible to analyze.

I am geniunely sad as I write this.  How did this happen?  How did one of the most talented and innovative artists of his day become a lazy hack?  How did Picasso turn into Thomas Kincade?  I find it impossible for him to reclaim his genius after this.  His last truly good work was The Songs of Distant Earth, and that was 11 years ago.  I'm tired of waiting.  This is it.  Goodnight Mike.
label: negative

reviewText: I saw glowing customer reviews & read a professional review that compared Hoop to Joni Mitchell and Paul Simon. To quote a Paul Simon song, "One man's ceiling is another man's floor." This one's in the basement. Mama always said to start with the good things. Here are the things I liked about this CD: Damian Anthony's cover design is excellent. Jesca sitting on a stairway with a starry universe around her and a framed picture, perhaps of a mother, give an impression of a life that leads somewhere. I like Jesca's bright red skirt in the picture. I've read that Hoop is a reformed Mormon who was Tom Waits' nanny for five years. I'm glad Tom helped her. That was kind. Unfortunately, this is probably the worst CD I've gotten all year. It was excruciating to have to sit through the entire thing, which I did with headphones. The first thing that strikes me is her voice, which seems to slide between notes rather than actually sing them. Its shrill thin quality has undoubtedly proved attractive to some. The songs, IMHO, are banal. There is practically no musicality. It's as if the producer had each of the musicians in a separate room playing independently and then mixed them together. "Seed of Wonder" has a guitar that is plucked like someone who has never played picked up the instrument ten minutes before the recording began. The guitarist plucks the same six notes over repetitively throughout the entire song. The absence of melody is atoned for by the bizarre lyric which is equally awful, "Come on baby come on child - call your flo - like a seed of wonder - faith of mustard - o yeah wo yeah all is dark." Having someone sing about their monthly period may be entertaining for some. However, I wonder if the Pentagon might substitute repeated listenings of this song for waterboarding as a form of acceptable torture. The background vocals swirl nauseatingly as the track concludes with what sounds like military troops marching. The sound of an old movie machine and the scratchy sound of an old record are a good start to "Silverscreen" that quickly degenerates to an outtake from one of Yoko Ono's less successful recordings with almost no melody as "bye bye baby bye bye" is repeated endlessly. Hoop does actually sound quite a bit like Ono on this track. The track "Money" was compared to Liza Minnelli by one professional reviewer. However, Liza Minnelli can actually sing well. "Love Is All We Have" is homage to Hurricane Katrina. The six-note guitarist is back with Hoop's thin voice sounding as good as it does on this CD. "Intelligentactile 101" is inventive with different sounding instruments used. It would have been better if the instruments were tuned and playing together. "Havoc in Heaven" sounds like it was written by a malfunctioning machine. The vocals are like being nauseous on a roller coaster. I thought "Havoc" was the worst track on the CD until "Out the Back Door" came on, which sounds like it was a jam session recorded in a mental institution therapy session on a bad day. This very awful CD concludes with "Love and Love Again" that is the musical equivalent of a loose bowel. The last CD I heard as bad as this was Valley of the Doll's House by Molly Jean; so if you like Hoop, you might seek out Jean. In short, the thing I found best about this CD was the cover. Taxi!

reviewText:
Wainwright is a singularly gifted alternative pop/rock artist and singer/songwriter--let's make no mistake about that.

His affection for Judy Garland is noble and he deserves three cheers for wanting to create (or, in this case, "re-create") something of significance to underscore her influence upon his musical development, life, worldview, what-have-you.

The idea for this completely modern and outside-the-mainstream artist to recreate the legendary Judy Garland Carnegie Hall concert in 1961 was interesting and, at the outset, so unexpected as to be kind of cool. The added bonus of on-stage participation by his equally talented mother (McGarrigle), sister (Martha) and even Lorna Luft (Garland's daughter) was all in excellent decorum.

Had Wainwright himself settled for the *tasteful* success of that initial, unique, one-night tribute at Carnegie Hall, the entire concept of this project would have gone down as an uqualified coup.

But, it's become painfully obvious that good taste degenerated into waste, once the idea itself became sensationalized and blown out of proportion into a "milk-it-for-all-it's-worth" commercial "gimmick."

The problem is not so much that Wainwright sings most of these songs poorly (and he *does* sing them quite poorly), or that that he is strikingly ill-suited to the genre--he hopefuly knew this and most everyone in attendance hopefully knew it from the start. No, at its inception, this was a labor of love and homage, and, in such a case, Wainwright could have been, should have been (and indeed WAS) forgiven for his obvious deficiences as a stylist for this particular musical material, on this particular occasion.

But Wainwright made the fatal mistake of taking what should have been a  one-night-only slice of "tribute," seeing dollar signs, and then inflating the idea to proportions beyond the original premise. The uniqueness of his *own* night of "Judy-veneration" at Carnegie Hall was thus trivialized. Taking the show on the road to London, then to the Hollywood Bowl, opened the door for deserved criticism of the propriety of the main idea, and of Wainwright's inability to really sing the material at hand with anything resembling competence.

Basically, there was absolutely no reason why this "performance" ever deserved to be captured on a commercial recording. None. As a quirky, one-off concert-tribute in NYC, great. As a "brand" to be peddled commercially? Nah.

Wainwright is just plain awful on so many of these Tin Pan Alley tunes, ballads, and jazzy numbers, at least in terms of the "need" to record this evening for posterity and sell it to people who don't know any better, or who are expecting something reasonably good.

Given the brilliance of Garland's original show (and the multi-Grammy-winning, mega-selling 1961 album that captured it), this album is superfluous to the nth degree, and then some. His performances are (at best) mediocre, and the crowd excitement was ostensibly for the novelty of it all.

That being said, the only thing that should have ever seen the light of day as a commercial recording from this (initially) well-intentioned mess was Martha Wainwright's fine version of "Stormy Weather." Even then...meh.

Avoid this record like the plague and buy Rufus's fine original albums or the original Garland record. Rufus is exceptionally talented in his various "alternative" stylisms, but this is a weak effort that (as an album you might buy or continually enjoy) is rather awful...almost inappropriate. Believe me, it does not do Garland any favors (being a blatant commercial knock-off, now in album-form), nor does it do Wainwright any favors. As for the listener...cringe-city.

Again, there's no doubt about Wainwright's gifts as a singer of his own material, but one does get the sense that he really needed/wanted the easy money to have stretched this particular dime so painfully thin.

BTW: his Hollywood Bowl "version" of the "show" (which a few reviewers have mentioned here on Amazon) was indeed an absolute disaster--a shameful thing from a professional musician, especially one who was obviously using someone else's "prop" (Garland's Historic Setlist) as a come-on.

reviewText:
I never really liked The Mars Volta all that much, and this album doesn't make me feel any different about them.  People keep telling me that we're going to be looking back fondly on the Volta; that they're the Pink Floyd or Led Zeppelin of our generation.

Yeah, I laughed too.

There's nothing here but confused noodling, obtuse lyrics that seem laughably forced, and songs that stretch a good twenty minutes longer than they should.  Coming from a hardcore Sonic Youth fan who is long accustomed to ear-splitting noise, meandering improvisation, convoluted lyrics, and labyrinthian song structures, this is especially harsh.  None of the improvization on "Frances the Mute" seems organic at all.  When a Sonic Youth song crashes into an extended feedback and noise section (think "Total Trash", "Silver Rocket", the second half of "Mote", or "The Diamond Sea"), it feels and sounds like it was the only thing that could come next in the song-and it's a very satisfying feeling.  Most of what goes on in "Frances the Mute" seems like the result of a board meeting of blowhard critics, hipsters, and art majors on how one would go about making them cum the hardest.

reviewText:
Let me start off saying that I kinda liked Green Day with Dookie, but I've never been a huge fan.  This album, however, is quite possibly the worst album to come out in a long time.

It's pointless, lame, and lacks any trace of musical talent.  The whole premise and influence of the album will become obsolete before you know it.  It seems to focus on current politics the whole time and it'll be hard to relate to that in 4 or 5 years.

Apart from it's premise, the music in generall is absolutely sickening.  I must say that I have not so passionately hated a song as much as Boulevard of Broken Dreams in the history of my life.  Hearing the 12 year old girl style of vocals sing the pointless and meaningless chorous of this song makes me want to vomit.  If this song comes on the radio I immediately change the station.  I think this is the only song that makes me do this.  Wake Me Up When September Ends is another song that is simply stomach churning.  Top these off with songs such as American Idiot, St. Jimmy, and Letterbomb and you have one terrible album.  The band can be described best by the second word in the album title.

So there you have it, the album proclaimed by many as the best of 2004.  I'm not sure if i'm listening to the same album.  The music has no resemblence to that of Pink Floyd or The Beatles as some will tell you.  I can't believe someone would even be dumb enough to even compare this band with the likes of Pink Floyd or the Fab Four.  This also begs the question, is this where the rock genre, or for that matter, music in generall is going?  I mean it's just terrible, I'd actually rather listen to just about any form of hip-hop than this album.  So, is Green Day truly doing what I thought impossible?  That is, of course, make the hip-hop genre better than the rock genre.  That's actually quite a feat in a really sad, shameful sort of way.

Bands playing this sickening style of music are sprouting up everywhere such as Coheed and Cambria, The All American Rejects, and Death Cab for Cutie.  I just ask the question, what ever happened to rockin'?  Why do we have to be emotionally touched and cry whenever we listen to music now?  Thank God there are still bands such as Shadows Fall and Black Label Society that still know how to rock.

All in all, a terrible album that really suprises me in how bad a collection of songs can really be.  Technically Green Day is to be congradulted for attaining a new level of suck.

reviewText: Man, have I given this guy a chance.  Multiple chances.  Listened to the CDs, saw the big HBO special.  I mean, his career is red hot now.  He clearly has lots of fans.  Mostly college age (perhaps this should be a warning to some of you).  All I can say is "maybe they'll grow out of it."  He is NOT funny.  His act has no bite, no point of view, no opinion/viewpoint at all.  His comedy consists of spewing observations his audience can relate to (the "this is all happened to us" or "has this ever happened to you?" school of humor). "Yeah!  That's happened to me!"  "I know that reference!'  They laugh, cheer, clap, and plunk down their hard-earned dollars for his vanilla wit.  He never actually COMMENTS on the things he discusses in any intelligent, interesting way.  He has no edge.  He's not outraged by anything.  He's cute 'n' cuddly.  Richard Pryor must be rolling in his grave at the very fact that Cook is classified as a stand up comic.  "Pryor?  The guy writing this must be OLD!' reviewText: Who would guess 2'31" could seem such a long time? The band is just plain out of tune in Big Kid Table. And the jangly guitar, yuck. The vocal technique is poor and her diction is poor. The recording engineering sounds like a mic set up in a garage (although in Yes, So On and So On, there is a little reverb on the voice). Woe is me that we're living through a time period when the current "sound" is so crude and amateurish. I think poor technique is mistakenly interpreted as honesty and integrity. Bah! Don't be so easily fooled. Happily, pop trends these days tend to only last a year or so. You want unpolished integrity, go listen to your kid brother practice for his piano lesson. reviewText: At nu-metal's height, there was a seemingly endless swarm of bands that no one had ever heard of before that just all of the sudden appeared on the scene; and every one sounded exactly the same for the most part.  Factory 81 is no exception, and "Mankind" is far beyond uninspired, and is far beyond being worth time to anyone with a functioning brain.  The lead singer sounds as if he is trying to sound like a combination of Maynard James Keenan of Tool, Robb Flynn of Machine Head, Zach de la Rocha formerly of Rage Against the Machine, and naturally Jonathan Davis of Korn.  These disfigured vocals are played against a backdrop of neverending downtuned nu-metal guitars, uninspired bass work, and inconsistent drumming; a combination which is so unlistenable it makes Linkin Park look like The Who.  All in all, of all the mindless nu-metal trash still floating around, this is some of the absolute worst.

reviewText: Let me pause by stating that I rather enjoyed the Bill Laswell Panthalassa: The Music Of Miles Davis 1969-1974 project, so I'm not against remix projects, but this was stinks of cashing in, and given the drubbing that Vince Wilburn, Jr. has recently performed on the Miles Davis legacy and catalog, this is not at all a surprise. Clocking in at around 15 minutes or so, "Evolution of the Groove" features clumsy remixes that vaguely use Miles material as the source by Meatloaf guitarist Pat Thrall supported by multi-instrumentalist Charley Drayton and Vince Wilburn, Jr. Essentially, it's all aggressive beats and what amounts to a bunch of guys playing along with Miles, and it sounds like this. So much so that Miles' performance is recessed in the background. It doesn't even sound like it was mixed from the source tapes-- it literally sounds like some kid's idea of a mashup by overdubbing himself on Miles Davis recordings. Closer "Black satin" is actually pretty decent and, not surprisingly, the only track that features the original session prominently, but the bottom line is this record qualifies in the "I'll never listen to this again" pile.

reviewText:
This album is a typical example of bad things happening to a great singer. For the better part of the last decade, Whitney Houston apparently decided that she was a contemporary R&B singer and not a pop artist, turning her back on the musical stylings that attracted legions of fans to her enormous vocal talents in the mid-80s. Audiences have repeatedly refused to buy that scheme, which resulted in decreasing album sales and radio airplay. Unfortunately, neither Whitney nor her team seem to have gotten the message yet, since this last album falls into the same trap.
Not that "Just Whitney" is a total disaster - the production is professional and slick, it's short and to-the-point, and it has a couple of okay songs. The main problem is that "Just Whitney" is a very boring album loaded with third-rate material that sounds like leftovers from a Mary J Blige recording session (and given the poor quality of Ms Blige's material, that's saying a lot) as performed by a singer who has become a shadow of her former self. Whitney manages to get the right attitude on the first two songs and then falls asleep on the job for the rest of the album - just like the listener. She desperately attempts to recapture some of her magic with heavy ballads like "Try it on my own" and "You light up my life"; however this singer is not the gifted powerhouse that lit up such otherwise generic songs as "Didn't we almost have it all", "You're still my man", "You give good love" or "All at once", and the results are not as convincing.
On an even more problematic level, Whitney's vocals sound out of breath, she can no longer hit those long powerful notes, and just refuses to follow a melody, belting each note and twisting it in endless melisma to cover her unability to hit a note on the head. It's hard not to allude to Houston's private misdemeanors, but since it's not of our business either, let's just say that years of abuse have apparently ruined a genuine raw vocal talent.
By falling short of its diluted R&B pretentions, and by failing at its few attempts to pander to her former audience's tastes, "Just Whitney" is a double failure. The die-hard fans will likely pick it up or already have; as for the casual Whitney admirators, there really is no valuable reason to put your hard-earned money on this album. Live on your memories and avoid this turkey at all costs.

reviewText: I picked this record up because of its cool, Cold War inspired cover and because I am a big fan of 1980s metal (this being released in 1989).  Well, the cover art is the best thing about this album.  I find the music to be excessively noisy, disjointed, and lead by a singer who seems to enjoy wailing at the top of his lungs just for the heck of it.  I don't know how they played some of these songs, they just seem to go every which way.  Lyrically, the songs are interesting and well-written.  The sound of channel surfing separates some of the tracks to give the impression that a certain track is on a different "channel;" however, there is really one underlying theme to this album: that society is going to heck and a handbasket due to greed, bigotry, drugs, and violence.  God is brought up in many of these tracks, but their position on God is as disjointed as the music.  Sometimes, God is seen as an answer to society's sins: "We're all God's sons" ("Black and White") while other times, God is presented as false hope: "In God--our debt has been paid, still we are laid to rest" ("In God").  "There Stood the Fence" is a surprisingly decent ballad.  The rest of the music is very heavy, sometimes close to speed metal ("Spontaneous").  Their cover of Led Zeppelin's "Out on the Tiles" is almost unlistenable; in fact, most of Think This is very hard to listen to.  It is difficult to think of this that or anything while this is playing except, 'Man, I can't wait for this song to end.'  I would describe it as "Noise Metal" if there is such a genre.  I don't like "Noise Metal."

reviewText: Godsmack arrive into the rock scene a little too late to deliver anything noteworthy or original to the annals of modern hard rock or as it has been termed, "new metal." What Godsmack are experts at as a band is recycling their formulas to the point of creative exhaustion. "Awake" offers nothing but the same wah-wah solos, boring growls (there are moments when vocalist Sully Erna sounds like a bad imitation of James Heatfield) and trendy goth lyrics. Erna is a practicing Wiccan and exhausts in his lyrics the use of snakes, moons, rain etc. But Erna uses these goth cliches merely to go along with trends and commercialized forms of "darkness" so prevailant in new metal with groups like Disturbed and Staind who simply try to create a style or trend out of the issues of abuse, sadness and simply being pissed off. And it's not convincing at all. "Awake" lacks the skill of groups like Metallica or Alice In Chains (the group this band most shamelessly imitates). Consider how the material sounds so recycled, songs like "Greed" and "Awake" could be connected to make one whole song. The same goes for this album's tribal closer, "Spiral" which sounds like a bad sequel to the previous album's "Voodoo." The instrumental "Vampires" is useless distortion and sounds like a lazy attempt at heavy metal. Sully Erna is no Jim Morrison and the band is no Black Sabbath, and so they shouldn't try so hard to be them. "Awake" is nothing more than another new band trying to follow the "trends" or "what is cool," which is the total opposite of what rock n' roll is. Call me a wuss but I'd rather pop in The White Stripes anyday instead of this.

reviewText: Golden Smog is often my favorite band. I say "often" because their music is soothing in a very particular way, and whenever I reach for one of their albums I always find myself saying to myself "ahhh, this has got to be the best music I have ever heard." The Smog captures all that is good about American rock n roll in a warm, kind package. I cannot praise their music highly enough. The above is why I unfortunately have to give a Golden Smog disc one star. It comes down to this - each album they recorded during the Ryko years has a unique dynamic and pacing that flows so naturally that the songs seem like puzzle pieces fitting perfectly in place. In an effort to grab some extra dough (although I don't see how - Golden Smog is hardly popular), Rykodisc has released a compilation spanning one EP and two full-length discs. For the same price as this compilation, you could probably buy used copies of all of their albums. However, now that this compilation exists, many listeners won't do that. As a result, they will miss out on appreciating Golden Smog as the band was meant to be heard, in the original album formats. This is music out of context. Still good songs, but missing something. Has this compilation done a service to the band? Will it draw in listeners who would not otherwise approach Golden Smog albums? Will people buy the albums after shelling out for a compilation that contains most of the album tracks? These questions are, of course, rhetorical. What's here is great, although I knocked it down from my planned 2-star rating (for the overall concept) since there is a distinct lack of bonus material. By comparison, the Josh Rouse comp which Ryko released right around the same time as this Golden Smog disc contained an extra CD of bonus material and rarities that made it worthwhile for someone like myself who owns all the Ryko-era Josh Rouse albums and EPs. But here, the token bonus cuts are just a lure for suckers who own the three Smog discs and might feel tempted to shell out for the few measly tracks tacked onto this comp. Why not include a live show as disc 2? Then you'd have my attention and money, maybe even a three or four star review. So in summation, great music but stick with the albums. This is nothing but a record label's attempt to milk Golden Smog fans of some extra cash. For reference, here are links to the actual Smog albums so you can check 'em out for yourselves and hear what I'm talking about: 1. On Golden Smog 2. Down by the Old Mainstream 3. Weird Tales

reviewText:
I always though the title of this album should have been "Sad But True".  A black album cover not only showed the lack of taste in their choice of artwork, but the lack of musical creativity on the album to.  The "black album" was the biggest disappointment in musical history.

Metallica was doing fine- they had thousands of fans, plenty of money, and they made the most original, uncompromised music around.  Metallica didn't need MTV videos or rock radio airplay to win thousands of fans; they did it with the pure musical genius and the best live concerts ever for almost ten years.  I worshipped them like they were gods along with thousands of other people.  Metallica was practically the only band I listened to.
Most bands first releases are self-titled and in Metallica's case they were a new and different band.  With the "black album", Metallica contradicted everything they once stood for and said.  The hypocrisy they once sung about had become their own.  Songs like "Enter Sandman", "Don't Tread On Me", and "Nothing Else Matters" are songs that are devoid of any intellectual meaning, but that is the type of songs they had to write to win mass appeal.  There are plenty of "hey-hey-heys", "yeah-yeah-yeahs", and "whoa-whoa-whoas" to prove my point.  The music song structure was incredibly typical of pop rock and profoundly boring.  Metallica even drafted hair metal producer Bob Rock to record the album to show the obvious direction they were going. Then, there were 4 embarrasing, terrible music videos tailor fit for MTV.

When the rock critics gave the "black album" a good review, it really showed how much they knew.  The "black album" was the dictionary definition of a sellout.  People though Metallica sold out with "Load", but it happened long before that terrible album was released.  It was disgusting, wretched, grotesque, and rancid.  I have more respect for Michael Bolton than Metallica for releasing the "black album".
Ultimately, it was a good thing Metallica faded into the pop kingdom.  I searched for new music and found hardcore like Black Flag, the Misfits, and Minor Threat and other bands that never sold out.  There were also bands like Pantera, Sepultura, and Slayer that kept thrash alive.  Metallica became nothing but a ghost.

Didn't have to wait too long because the master tapes are still here at home in the good ol' USA, and has FINALLY made an official apperance thanks to some people just like us who truly made an effort.  Iconoclassic Records in association with Legacy has reissued Go All The Way, as well as Showdown, as stand-alone CDs which have been remastered from the studio's original 1st generation master tapes.  Included are Chris Jasper's new liner notes (God bless you, Brother Chris!)  I just checked out this new label's website and it is outstanding, and hope for more to come.  Someone is continuing to reissue these 70's and 80's classic jams (many on CD for the first time) and doing them right!  Good luck to Iconoclassic on future projects and hope you will be rewarded for the Isley joints and other current jewels you have worked with.

The cover stock that was used is quite possibly the thinnest I have ever seen on an American (no pun intended) release EVER!

Maybe the thin cover stock and bad cover art reproduction was used on this release to hurry up a long delayed reissue to have it out by Christmas, but knowing what I know about how fanatical Black Crowes fans can be regarding sound; this reissue may upset A LOT of them.

Great album (4 stars), just very weak attempt on execution and thus making it simply REEK of a holiday cash grab.  Hopefully if there are going to be repressings of this in the future, a little more attention to detail will be used to have this look and sound as great as it deserves.

reviewText:
Review by Cory Rennison:

When lead singer Thomas Giles Rogers Jr. of Between The Buried and Me fame makes a side project, it has to be something amazing, right? Wrong. Right after popping this CD in, I questioned, "What the hell is this?" Part way through the first track, I started thinking, "This will probably get a lot better and this is probably just an intro song." Well, the thing is, it never got any better.

Thomas's aptly titled project Giles has been advertised as something for fans of Nine Inch Nails or an underground version of Radiohead. One might question what's wrong with something like that. There wouldn't be any problem with having influences of those two awesome bands, if there was actually any influence of those bands at all in Giles. The entire album consists of cheap sounding techno beats that could have been made in a half hour on FruityLoops and the vocals sound like a bunch of nu-metal ramblings and are comparable to Jonathon Davis of Korn, which we all know he has some great vocal skills. With lyrics like "Little kitty it's time to be naughty, hop skotch to the closet of raunchy...shake your ass!" it appears that even Thomas himself thinks his project is a joke. I also have to question whether Victory Records actually saw something in this project or if they put out the album simply because Thomas is already in a band that is signed to Victory.

Nobody should expect to hear another Between The Buried and Me within the depths of this CD, but at the same time nobody should expect to hear a good album. This album gets a 2 for a rating only because the artwork is badass. However, the bottom line is, this album is the epitome of weird and you'll either "get it" or you won't; for me it was the latter. A final word of advice to Thomas Rogers Jr.: stick with your good band.

reviewText: Out Of Curiosity, I went down to the library, and checked out this CD. It was 24-bit Remastered in 2006. Not just a song here or there. The entire CD. And when you download a FROM THIS CD as an MP3, you get the actual remastered version that came in THIS CD. When you download an mp3 on Amazon, they will pull the one copy of each song they own, and use on 5 different MP# albums. What they show you, and what you download are 2 different versions. The album may say remastered 2006, and the mp3 you download is a generic one they use on every mp3 "album." If you actually wind up with the MP3 made from the file on this CD, consider yourself lucky. Most of the time the just piece-meal together a bunch of tracks to make it APPEAR like you're getting the great sounding copy, but you probably won't, and you don't know until you've downloaded the song. Straight from a kind Amazon rep who took the time to research it and let me know. Just passing it along...be careful when purchasing an Amazon mp3. Cheers.

It's not really fair since it's extremely rare for me to find a song that even hints of reggae that I'll listen to, but a pretty girl gave me a stack of CD's of people I'd never heard of before, so I had to give it a listen.  Or at least try to.  I got through the first 2 1/2 songs before, with the exception of No One Knows and Fire On the Mountain, I could only listen to about half of every song that came after.

Asa certainly can sing and while it did deviate from the typical reggae sound and instrumentation, neither were enough to make this stand out as anything more than just another reggae-esque record to me.  No One Knows almost did it with its slight hints at funk, but it really never rose above the mediocrity of the rest of the record.  I also was able to listen to Fire On the Mountain, but only so I could listen to the ridiculous lyrics.  None of it felt personal and none of it felt real.  It seemed like maybe she listened to Marley and thought, "hey, I should write something about social ills."

Some of the lack of feeling may just be the result of over-production.  The girl's got talent, but there's just so much going on, and it's all so clean and polished that whoever Asa is never really shines through.  I don't really care how pretty you can make a song sound if I can't feel what made you need to write the song in the first place.  The only time I can imagine listening to this album again is if I inadvertently wander into one of those New Age shops that sells incense and recordings of whales while this is playing in-house.

Deleting from my iTunes now...

reviewText:
Apparently this is metal, apparently this is original, apparently this about a metal band with singing, apparently this is metal.
forgive my ignorance but I truly do not understand how the lay public consider this metal.  let us take a look at the reasons why: -
1) Solos.  if I play Iron Maiden, Pantera, hell even Chimaira in my cd player.  I am rewarded with a nice solo with layered harmonies, a great starting riff and a good ending melody.  On this there are either no solo's at all or even worse solo's so slapdash that a blind five year old could do better.  Let us take 'Going Under' as an example. This song is meant to be hardcore as it is a defiant diatribe against being pampered by media and has this horrnedous four second long solo where the guitarist merely randomly slashes the strings.  it is so bad it makes a solo by Kerry King  (For the lay public who have no idea who this is he is in the thrash band 'Slayer') sound like something by Joe Satriani (God of guitar playing)
2) Lyrics; - I don't know what it is about nu-metal that means that they have to do this "We hate" or "We're not broken" and so on.  There is more to life than complaining about such superficial things as self popularity.
3) Soul: - i have read tons of reviews on this site and they are full of things like 'Such raw passion', 'Snarling aggression of an angel's voice' and stuff like that.  To me it sounds boring, Amy Lee for a start doesn't suit the music, she is awful live (I suffered a two-second snippet of their donington performance before seeing metallica on the hidden stage!) and contrary to belief is not a good singer.  Bruce Dickinson, Rob Halford and Angela Gossow (most people won't have a clue who they are) are far better.
This album to me is the perfect example of a band wanting the sales and success of a pop album, while pampering to an audience of 12 year olds.  This is an album that is exactly the reason why since 2000 the music scene has been awful.  In that time we have seen Limp Bizkit, Good Charlotte, HIM, Linkin park, Sum 41 and Papa Roach become huge.  All of them have no versatility, no originality, no soul and no point.
Do yourselves a favour and research exactly what it means to play guitar, to sing dark gothic music and to write lyrics.  Go and listen to some proper music, but pleas stay away from this.

reviewText:
I won't go into the story behind the recording of Captain Beefheart's "Bat Chain Puller" in 1975/76 and its subsequent non-appearance as anything other than a bootleg. Instead I'll just consider this current release and ask the question, what exactly is "Dust Sucker" for? As the sleeve proudly trumpets, these tracks are from "the Captain's own tapes" of the album - well that's as maybe, but what they most certainly are NOT however are the long lost master tapes. The sound quality is not measurably better on this release than on any of the bootlegs I have heard - indeed the sound quality is boomy and bass-heavy and there's annoyingly high level of tape hiss present throughout. This all serves to leave the title track, "Harry Irene", "Floppy Boot Stomp" and "Owed T'Alex" sounding like little more than demo versions of the versions eventually released on "Shiny Beast". The version of "The One Thousand and Tenth Day of the Human Totem Pole" is markedly better than that on "Ice Cream For Crow", but we knew that anyway; and while "Brickbats", "Flavor Bud Living" and "A Carrot Is As Close As a Rabbit Gets to a Diamond" are fascinating early versions, "81 Poop Hatch" and "Apes-Ma" are exactly the same as the later versions - though with worse sound quality. Which leaves "Seam Crooked Sam" and the beautiful "Odd Jobs", and what would we Beefheart fans give to hear them in their pristine glory and not hamstrung by the muddy, hamfisted mixes on this album?
This is by no means the only annoying aspect of this album. The artwork cuts and pastes the Captain and various Magic Band members, from totally different eras, into various sci-fi  landscapes - which is all good fun but what does it have to do with Don Van Vliet? Especially the Don Van Vliet who recorded "Bat Chain Puller"? The sleevenotes are a muddled mess of (uncredited) quotes, conjecture and plain nonsense. Not suprising perhaps, as they appear to be the work of Ken Brooks, a man who made some sort of living out of poorly researched and badly written books on various Rock cult figures.
The additional cuts are live versions of various "Bat Chain Puller" tracks culled at random from various sources/ gigs/ line-ups and of variable quality and, in some places it seems, variable tape-speed. Need I add that there is absolutely no information on when and where these tracks were recorded and who played on them? To add to the depressing aura of sloppiness, an extremely poor quality recording of the "Lick My Decals" out-take "Well Well Well" is added for no better reason it seems than the people responsible for this mess ("Milksafe Productions") had a copy lying around their offices. Ditto the even more lo-fi live version of "My Human Gets Me Blues" - errrrrr, why?
In short, this CD is a disgrace and rip-off and you'd be better off waiting for the Zappa Estate to get round to eventually releasing the REAL (Denny Whalley mixed) "Bat Chain Puller", which they've been threatening to do...Avoid this album at all costs.
label: negative

reviewText:
This was cut in the '80s, and it shows. I cringe every time that synthesizer kicks off "Drifting Too Far From Shore." Most of these songs weren't good to begin with, but the production sinks them completely.

There's two exceptions: "Maybe Someday" and "Brownsville Girl." "Maybe Someday" is very '80s, but by '80s pop standards, it's pretty good. It's actually an amusing, sarcastic kiss-off.

"Brownsville Girl" is one of Dylan's best epics, but if you're a bootleg collector, seek out "New Danville Girl": "Brownsville Girl" basically took that same recording, replaced the vocal track and dumped extra echo, horns and back-up singers on top of it. Still a funny epic, but waaaaaay over-produced; "New Danville Girl" is much better.

reviewText: this, like a LOT of other amazon reviewers, is, was, and always will be my favorite solo ozzy disc. i bought it when it first came out in 1982, and unlike "blizzard of ozz", i loved EVERY track on the lp! why one star? well, it's because of the desecration of re-recording something w/ new musicians that should never have been tampered with to begin with. by the way, i've noticed that a lot of reveiwers are "shocked" that ozzy could do this to randy rhoads' memory. and, i too have heard and/or read how much ozzy loved randy like a brother/best friend, etc, etc. it struck me kind of odd whenever i remember seeing ozzy live that year (it was the very last show w/ rhoads, he died the very next day), because i still remember hearing ozzy @ some point in the concert announce that his guitarist was leaving the band after that gig. i've encountered other people over the years that were at that same show, and they also claim too have heard the same announcement. another thing that i only thought of recently, is that if ozzy was SO torn up by randy's death, then why didn't he cancel the concert.?. i remember all too well that he hired guitarist bernie torme and kept right on truckin' down the road, gaining his success not necesarily from the 1st two solo lp's, but more so over the death of randy rhoads--THAT'S what propelled ozzy to superstardom, not his "ozzy the apeman" antics! by the way, one reviewer on here had a GREAT idea: let tony iommi take the 1st 8 sabbath albums and re-release them with a new vocalist, like tony martin or r.j.dio, or better yet, clay aiken (hey, i know he's a pop idol, but the mother can sing! imagine his voice w/ sabbath's mean music!). anyways, i hope i can eventually find a copy of "diary of a madman" & "blizzard of oz" that haven't been touched by sharon. (and that's why it always bothered me when people wanted to slam yoko ono for being such a provocative artist who married a beatle. at least SHE didn't try to get john to remix any beatle albums, and replace paul's vocal tracks w/ hers. yes, the new remixed versions of the 1st two ozzy cd's are that bad!! (and i love yoko, but not as a beatle!). i've always had my "suspicions" surrounding the fateful plane crash that took randy's life (even though i was never one to hold him in such high regard as a guitarist. he was good. not GOD!) and after reading in one of the amazon reviews that he and sharon had a brief romance in the early 80's, well that kind of fits right in there w/ other motivation. i don't mean to sound all "conspiracy theory", but, like i said, if oz was really that close to rhoads, you would think that the first thing he'd do would be to cancel any future concert dates; but, that falls under management...get the picture anyone?!?! oh, and when bernie took leave, ozzy STILL kept touring! he brought in brad gillis of night ranger and then proceeded to keep on touring. and don't forget that was also the year that black sabbath finally released an official live album, "live evil". it was also the same year that petty ozzy HAD to release a double live album of nothing but old sabbath songs, called "speak of the devil". when i think of what happened to ozzy during that period, and the years that followed, i can sum it up by stating what a travesty! i was a bigger fan of sabbath's, and still am. i just wish that tony iommi would kick the apeman out of the band again (even if it means losing geezer butler) and carrying on with yet a whole new line-up. or bring back glenn hughes! or any number of singers, famous or not. i just wish that iommi would realize that HE'S got his share of fans that think sabbath without ozzy is a better sabbath! Doing this material, Gaga is just as wretched as you'd expect. Her talent, whatever little there is of it, lies in other musical realms.

Tony hasn't had a new idea for 40 years and is by now unable to bring anything fresh to the mostly good, but very tired, repertoire herein. Bennett has been embarrassing himself so much over the past decade or so with his duet albums and dubious musical matings that CHEEK TO CHEEK, lousy as it is, can scarcely be called a disappointment.

Too bad. Many of his recordings of the 1960s are among the best pop male vocals from that, or any, era. But for all the acclaim and popularity the man has garnered since then, to some Bennett fans, this reviewer included, the results have been increasingly spotty.

Out of respect for Tony Bennett's accomplishments of the past, I've given CHEEK TO CHEEK one star. It deserves none.

reviewText: I know I'll get slammed for this review, so I might as well take it. First of all, let me say that I have always been a Lori McKenna fan. Her work has always been compelling, to say the least. She has lived an interesting life, honed her craft with hard work and determination, and she has become a highly skilled writer and musician.  Then something happened.  A Nashville superstar becomes her buddy, she makes around three million dollars in royalties from placing four songs on said superstar's multi-platinum CD, she appears on "Oprah" with said superstar and ....... all of a sudden her life, as she knows it, will never be the same.  I'm not saying that I fault artists for going for the money grab, but at least be honest about it. McKenna can never again sing songs about being the struggling, small town mother of five, wife of a plumber who somehow miraculously just gets by in this world.  She is now a player on the main stage, and the slick Nashville production of this CD shows it. Even her vocal delivery shows that she's been coached to deliver that Sara Evans-come-Leann Rhimes-come Wynona Judd kind of open-throated, quasi R & B voicing that I despise so much! And the songs..... what can I say? They just don't meet the standard of anything on "Bittertown". This always seems to happen to artists that are doing perfectly fine in an independent setting, who might have a publishing deal or a co-pub deal, and then all of a sudden they feel an urgent need to dive into the mega entertainment machine full force. The trouble with that is, that most artists who do this are blinded by the glitz of the big-time and stop doing what they've been doing that got them noticed in the first place. Of course, they've been convinced by hacks like Tim McGraw that they need huge polished productions and publishing house co-writers in order to meet the expectation of what it takes to sell millions of CD's.  It's very sad. Unglamorous, indeed!

reviewText:
Much as I try to avoid injecting personal anecdotes into my reviews, I feel one is necessary in this case.  Anyway, a couple days ago, during one of my interminable drives home from work, I was listening to the Afghan Whigs' album Black Love and trying to figure out exactly why I liked it so much.  After all, while it was a well-written and well-played rock album, for the most part the songs on it weren't all that original or complex.  In general, it was the type of album I usually tire of after one or two listens, but that wasn't happening this time.  Eventually, I realized just what it was that made me like the Whigs so much: emotion.  Almost every note of the album was delivered with an unmistakable fire and passion, and that energy was infectious.  The songs on Black Love were felt as much as they were played.

By now you might be wondering, what exactly does the foregoing story have to do with Nickelback, the band I'm supposed to be discussing?  Well, quite a bit, actually.  In sharp contrast to the Afghan Whigs, Nickelback represent everything that's wrong about the state of mainstream rock today: while they are technically competent, Nickelback's music is completely devoid of anything that bears even a passing resemblance to soul.  With the possible exception of Puddle of Mudd, I've never heard a band that was more blatantly going through the motions than these guys.  How You Remind Me, this album's best-known number and probably the most overplayed song ever performed by somewhat not named Celine Dion, is a perfect example of the problem.  This song doesn't song like it was written to make an emotional statement, or reflect any artistic ambitions on the part of the band; it sounds like it was written to be a hit.  Of course, How You Remind Me was in fact a huge hit, but writing a hit song isn't the same thing as writing a good song.

The rest of Silver Side Up suffers from the same problem.  Nickelback obviously refuse to jeopardize their record sales by doing anything foolish, like taking a risk or doing something original.  Too Bad is basically the same song as How You Remind Me, except frontman Chad (Jesus) Kroeger is apparently supposed to be mad at his father instead of at his ex.  Sorry guys, but that doesn't exactly count as diversity.  Never Again sounds like it was intended to be the "heavy, angry" song that established the band's hard-rock credibility, but it just comes off sounding flat, bland, and uninspired.  Pearl Jam did stuff like this better ten years ago, and even they were somewhat derivative, but at least they put some feeling into what they did.  It's rumored that there are some other tracks on Silver Side Up as well, although one could be forgiven for thinking Nickelback just recorded one more song and put it on the album seven times in order to pad it out.  If Chad Kroeger isn't the single most monotone vocalist in rock history, he's certainly pretty close.

Even worse, in 2003 these guys had the gall to make the first single from their new album Someday, which is almost a note-for-note ripoff of How You Remind Me.  Apparently stealing from Pearl Jam and Bush wasn't enough for these guys, so they had to stoop to swiping their own biggest hit.  Not that it matters to the semi-catatonic drones who listen to this drivel in the first place.  If your brain still functions, you'd be better off listening to, well, anyone other than Nickelback.

I tried soooo hard to like this new effort because of my love for Donna Summer. I played this over and over, not consistantly, but at different times to see if I would feel differently about it. Unfortunately, I could not.

Driving down Brazil gave me the same feeling the first two times I heard it but on the third listen I began to be disappointed and annoyed. The something old mixed with the something new began to remind me of an old diva wanting desperately to be remembered by the old and respected by the new. Forgetting she became who she is by calling her own creative shots and not by following others, begging to be accepted into the musically inclined fold. Especially with styles that aren't so great out there to begin with.

Example; Sand on my feet has an overly used recipe of cutesy down to earth, folksy, everybody like it, sing along song style. It became annoying pretty quickly as well.

I won't go thru every song, I am not a licensed critic. Although, some who are shouldn't be. I can say, I know what I like and I have an opinion.
Although, I may like an artist I won't look over the things I don't like about a project just because I like the artist. I think these songs suck and are beneath Donnas talent. Yeah, I said it!

Donna Summer, like many seasoned artists who have not lost their voice or flavor, lose their nerve when it comes to creativity or remembering how they got to where they are; Taking chances and not following the status quo was key to becoming what many other artist could not. Not exactly becoming greater than others but becoming their own different light on the music industry. Not afraid of setting their own standards and not what radio stations or execs say will work which most times does not.

I really, really wanted to like this because Donnas vocals are still powerful, distinctive and with plenty skills but in good conscience I could not. As a TRUE fan I could not forgive myself, if I had. She took her song slide over backward literally by taking backward steps that were all too unnecessary for a still skillful lady.

reviewText:
Well, this is one of those discs that I bought as I was browsing around and decided I would pick it up for a listen. It was in the Jazz section, so I naturally assumed that this was real jazz music and not more of that elevator "smooth jazz" crap. Granted, not all smooth jazz music is bad, but most of it isn't good. I liken smooth jazz to pop music: average at best unless there is some stunning musicianship and content.

This album is more along the lines of crap than it is good. These jazz noodlers take ten funk classics and ruin them near completely. At the end of the day you still have music that is listenable, but boy is the presentation weak (at best). I don't know of a single funk tune that deserves the "smooth jazz" treatment: water down the tempo, replace the awesome horn work with your own pseudo-jazz mangling, and remove the vocals, and you have funk as smooth jazz. All of these tracks do just that to some of the best known funk tunes out there, and they don't discriminate; they mangle a whole series of great artists from Booker T. and the MGs to George Clinton and Parliament to Curtis Mayfield and others.

Fans of the originals may be mystified as to how the artists on this album even justify the tributes they perform to these classic rock and funk artists. While there is no single track that screams "TERRIBLE! HORRIBLE!", there is no track that is even close to average. This sub-par album doesn't have much to offer musically unless you are looking for ham-handed background noise.

KoRn have emerged into the world of metal (or n-metal, depending on how you like to think about it) with great albums, they have flopped once with Issues and managed to make up for it with albums like Untouchables and Take A Look In The Mirror, which was considered by many to be the closest thing to Life Is Peachy, one of their greatest albums of all time.  Then they released their Greatest Hits CD (oh, Vol. 1... which I now doubt there will be a second one), and it included most of their greatest hits (Thoughtless excepted) and a few crappy covers... but hey, you know, it happens.

But now, my friends, I think that's it for KoRn : they're definitely stuck in the s**thole for good.  This album is the grossest attempt I have ever heard from KoRn... this is even worst than Limp Bizkit's Chocolate Starfish.  The causes : well, ok, Head did leave the band, taking an important part of the authentic KoRn sound with him, so that might explain part of it, but honestly, I think it's the critics.  For a while now, especially since they released Take A Look In The Mirror, a lot of people, even unloyal KoRn fans, have accused KoRn of not evolving, of keeping the same style and blah blah blah yadda yadda yadda.  Way to go, look what you've done now!  KoRn tried so hard to do something different that they ended up throwing away all the greatness that used to characterize their style and made it unique.

reviewText:
This has been out a while, looks like I'm going to be the only one so far to speak my mind about this. This compilation is an insult and a travesty!

I had no reason to expect better, but I wish they would have made it better. There's nothing about this collection that would distinguish it as a 50th Anniversary Celebration; it's exactly like the previous one. Even Mathis' "The Christmas Album" CD from three or four years ago had more originality than this one.  The artwork is pure Photoshop cheese and surely not worth the price of admission. There are people who didn't get to buy the Hallmark Christmas album, "Listen! It's Christmas", which was a BEAUTIFULLY done, BEAUTIFULLY produced recording, and they didn't even have the imagination to include some of those. And surely, after 50 years, there are Christmas recordings from The King of Christmas Music that we haven't heard yet because they're in a vault somewhere!

But this, they say, is the culmination of 50 years of work! Who else still alive can even say they've got 50 years of work?  This is the best they could do? Well, so be it. There are people who will buy this regardless; more power to them. Enjoy. As for me, I can't support this. I've already got the duet with Bette Midler because I've got her "Cool Yule" album, an excellent recording, and I was gifted the Mannheim Steamroller album with O Tannenbaum on it a couple years ago. I have no reason on Earth to spend $12 on this. Frankly, after following Johnny Mathis for as many years as I have, I've already got everything else.

But if I WERE to recommend a Christmas compilation, find "The Christmas Music of Johnny Mathis: A Personal Collection" from one of the used sellers if you've got to have a CD for your car, or find an mp3 download of it for cheap. They're all the same songs, more or less!  iTunes isn't allowing the single download of the Winter Wonderland duet from either this album or Bette Midler's, they want you to buy the whole album (because they know that's the one carrot they can dangle at this point), but I'd still go the download route because you're only out an X-spot.

Sigh. I guess I'll never get to hear Johnny Mathis sing "Mary, Did You Know" or "Deck The Halls". Once, I even envisioned him singing "Peace on Earth," that old David Bowie/Bing Crosby chestnut, with Sir Elton John. But these sugarplums are only in MY head, and not in those of whoever was responsible for this afterthought. Columbia blew it. They're not getting another chance to honor his longevity. The 50th Anniversary is over, and there won't be a 75th Anniversary to celebrate, and for whatever reason somebody somewhere just doesn't seem to get it.

This is the second copy of the album I have bought, and probably the last. The first copy burned up in a fire. The second, which my wife bought me to replace the original copy, broke when I attempted to remove it from the spindle it was mounted on.

 The original copy I had of The Early Years Volume 2 was a normal plastic jewel case, and there was no problem with taking it off the spindle.  As for the music on the CD (which I am familiar with thanks to the original copy which was destroyed by fire), it is truly wonderful: it reveals an acoustic and stripped down side of Tom Waits where you really see a side to his soul without the distractions of exaggerated blues influences or unusual musical arrangements. reviewText:
Having read the reviews and their comparison with the earlier NYP version, I was excited to get a good digitally recorded version of Boulez... especially one with the CSO! I'm an old CSO fan and while Orchestra Hall may not have the 'best' acoustics (hear Solti's 1972 recording of Beethoven's 9th recorded at Krannert Center in Urbana, Il. for great sonics) it's a workhorse venue and is usually fine for recordings if mic'd well.

Ugh. The dynamic range is insane. The quiet sections are barely audible and the crescendo's are so extremely loud that they are actually clipped on the disc. Yes they are. The sound is so bad I ripped it to Soundforge 10 and examined the waveform. Every loud section has the highest volume waves flattened off by the clipping of the mastering process. This is unacceptable.

The original recording with the NYP is a much less dynamically extreme version and the interpretation is at least as good. Sure you have a little tape hiss, sure it's not as bombastically outrageous, but it is not clipped either. The original is a much more listenable recording. This digital one is like the early Holst Planets or '1812' digital recordings where the producer say's "Hey, let's see what kind of bandwidth this new technology has and really push it!" Well, they pushed it too far. Strings and horns sound like mushy chatter when they are clipped and the quiet sections are so quiet that you have to turn things up so high that the loud sections are deafening.

Find the original Boulez recording with the NYP. Find the CD used or find a really good used condition LP. I have both and they are both excellent. This version is awful. Amateur mastering / production ruins an otherwise acceptable version.

reviewText:
I'm going to try to be as compassionate and kind as I can be in this review, because I love the Goo Goo Dolls dearly, and I have for almost 2 decades.  I've loved nearly everything they've done since they burst onto the scene.  But I feel like after this lackluster effort, their "Better Days" may be behind them.

This album lacks inspiration.  That's the biggest problem.  "Gutterflower", which is my favorite Goo Goo Dolls album to date, was BURSTING with emotion and inspiration.  When you have a driving force behind your music, that's when your music can best connect with people.  It was there last album with "Let Love In", and heck, it's always been there with The Goo Goo Dolls.  But it wasn't there at all this album.

Something For The Rest Of Us is a lifeless, zestless album, where the band is merely going through the motions.  Sure, you may catch a lyric or two or three that jumps out at you, and makes you feel fuzzy inside.  You might find a song that jives with your current situation in life, and you take a liking to it.  But as far as the emotional output of these things, it's just not there, sadly.  This album took a very long time to come out, and it's surprising to me that it's so empty.... with one exception, "Home". Home is actually an excellent song, which is deep and reflective.

I'm greatly disappointed with this dreadful effort by the Goo's.  I hope for a rebound in their next release, if there is one.

I've been a fan of Jane Monheit since "Never Never Land" over ten years ago.  I have all her recordings except for the Christmas CD.  She is a true bel canto vocalist.  But I cannot stand this recording.  For some reason, I did not buy this CD when it was first released.  I just received it yesterday and I cannot express the level of my disappointment.  The material is mostly weak and the presentation is even weaker.  Ms Monheit's voice never approaches the beauty or enthusiasm she displayed in previous or subsequent recordings.  The whole recording is such a muddled mess, I could not listen to most of the songs all the way through.  I wonder if this, her last Concord Jazz CD, was not thrown together to meet contractual requirements.

There's no accounting for taste.  Many people like this recording and it received some good reviews.  But I recommend comparing this CD to the ones preceding it and the follow up "Home".  To my ears, "The Lovers..." fails to compare in all categories.
label: negative

reviewText:
I thought Jeff Bridges was OK as a singer in the movie.  After all, he was supposed to be past his prime. And seeing him struggling on screen earned him some sympathy points.
However, there is no way to excuse the poor quality of the singing and songs on this CD. Didn't anyone listen to this before it was released? I've heard of vanity productions, but this is a fantasy production.  Bridges imagined that he could sing and noone had the nerve to tell him that he actually can't.
Luckily for me, I had a copy of the entire CD from the library that I could preview.  I managed to sit through the whole first song.  Then I listened to less and less of each of the next songs until I finally had to stop listening before I had even reached the final cuts.
For anyone who hasn't purchased this CD yet, my advice is to listen to the samples here.  Then realize that Bridges' prolonged singing is much more out of tune and muddled than you can tell from the samples.  And buy something else.

reviewText:
"Hello, you're speaking with Universal Imports. How can I help you?"

"Yes, yes, it is Sir John Eliot Gardiner here and I would like to submit a rather nasty complaint! I am a leading practitioner at SPECTRE (Sinister Period-Practice Enacted to Counter Traditional Readings Everlastingly)."

"I am sorry sir but I do not recognise that name. Could you be known under another guise?"

"Yes, sometimes I am called . . . . . . Jeggy." The caller whimpered.

"Jeggy . . . . . Jeggy . . . . . Jeggy . . . . now I remember you!  We transferred your file to the vault some years ago. How can I help you?"

"Well, I was walking through London the other day when I came across a Wanted Poster from your organisation which had been nailed to a telephone-pole. My name was on it."

"That should hardly be a surprise to you!"

"Hear me out! Anyway, I was rather shocked to see the price on my head has fallen to minuscule levels! Nor am I wanted `Dead or Alive' any more. And rather than being a Wanted Poster, it bore resemblance to a Community Announcement! Aren't you familiar with my late Mozart symphonies on Philips?"

"The ones that came in the orange box? I'm just checking Amazon now and . . . . . I cannot see them.  They've gone the way of the Tasmanian Tiger. Hang on - there's that single issue of Symphonies 40 & 41. Geez, they're going cheap!"

"In their day," Jeggy replied snootily, "they were highly regarded and won many plaudits from the Gramophone and the Penguin Guide. Surely the power of their iconoclasm continues to resonate down to this very day! With their advent, who can abide the romanticism of Kubelik, Bernstein or Klemperer - those lumbering leviathans! My performances are directly aligned with the composer's intentions - directly, I say!"

"Jeggy, I am reading an internal communiqu now and . . . . . . it appears that Competitor Intelligence has downgraded your threat-rating and by a wide margin.  I quote: `In this instance, Gresham's Law in reverse has kicked in with a vengeance and this disc is rarer than hen's teeth. In both performances, the phrases have more clips to them than a stationery office - the overall effect is to enervate the listener and denude the music of its innate grandeur. Turning first to the Jupiter: the surfeit of timpani and trumpets can only do so much to mask the basic lack of musicality - and it's compounded by the so-called strings of the English Baroque Soloists: they're devoid of sheen and lacking in torque. The finale of K 551 therefore is a cacophonous non-event. The opening Allegro Vivace is short-winded and inconsequential. The Andante Cantabile (Jeggy ignores the second word) sags from lack of expressive weight and bulges in the melodic line. Turning to the other symphony, Jeggy's madcap tempo in the finale of the G Minor is a gross miscalculation - it robs the music of its dignity and the scrappiness of the orchestral execution transforms tragedy into slapstick. The EBS strings in the slow movement of K 550 - twang, twang, twang - are almost unlistenable. One of the shortcomings of Gen I Period Practice was that it so uglified Mozart and here is Exhibit Number One. To sum up, these mediocre performances are no threat to our organisation whatsoever and our energies should be directed elsewhere.' There you go, Sir - does it answer your query?"

Sobs could be heard over the phone-line.

"What if I made a contribution myself to bump up the reward on the Wanted Poster?"

It must be really easy to land a major label record deal if you have a British band.  The rock critics can never get enough of British Invasion pop rock.  The good reviews a British band gets is bound to boost record sales.  That seems to be the case with Oasis.
Oasis is another band in a long line of Brit-pop corporate rock bands.  There is nothing special or original about their imitation of the Beatles and Rolling Stones.
"(What's the story) Morning Glory" sounds like a phrase that comes straight from the sixties.  It's also an incredibly cheesy sounding phrase.

In some songs they copy riffs off other artist like T. Rex and Wham.  They mask it with a little alternative style distortion so it's not so obvious.
Oasis was big on rock radio when alternative reached its peak in 1995.  Oasis was where alternative rock bottomed out.  It's really hard to believe this album was acceptable, even in the mainstream.

I've never seen this show staged, and I've never read the script, but the movie it's based upon, ALL ABOUT EVE, is one of my all-time favorite movies.  I notice that most of the other reviewers have given this CD five stars, but it looks as if a lot of those stars go to the script and to the acting, not to the music.
I had great hopes for this CD, but I have been severely disappointed.  The fault lies mostly with composer Charles Strouse:  not a single song, not even with some of Hollywood's most memorable lines for inspiration (such as "Fasten Your Seat Belts" or the title number), rises to the level of the witty movie dialogue.  (The title number starts out with promise, but doesn't reach a satisfying climax.)  Also contributing to my disappointment is Strouse's entrenchment of the score in the 1970's idiom, which today makes the show sound hopelessly dated.  Not even the acting talents of Lauren Bacall and Len Cariou can mask the failure of these tunes.
