reviewText: Upon opening the information fold-out inside the case, one reads that Bruce Fairbairn, the late album's producer, instructed the band to "make the best Yes album you can."  You'd think that would go  without saying.  Still, it raises the question: What, then, have Yes been  doing these past years? Are we to believe that they weren't trying their  best?  Judging by the results, you'd think not.  Furthermore, if this is  "the best Yes album" they can make, why is it so similar to their  dreadful output of the last decade?  The problem with not trying is that  when you're called upon to do it, you find out you've lost your chops.  Alternatively, Yes may simply have run out of ideas long ago and are  desperate to get a foot in the door.  Both these answers are likely to hold  the truth, which brings us to another puzzle.  The sticker on the case  states, "the best Yes album since Fragile and Close to the Edge,"  no less.  Indeed, a mere attempt to replicate the standards of those albums  would be most welcome.  Nothing could be further from the truth, however,  since The Ladder is a clear continuation of the bland Trevor Rabin legacy.  From Anderson's choppy and (and ofter embarrasing) multi-ethnic  signing/lyrics to the facile songwriting tailored for the even blander 90's  (a spineless pot-pourri of New Age, reggae, pomp rock, all delivered with  the right touch of political correctness), The Ladder is an excercise in  compromise over credibility. It seems more likely than not that the  reference to those classic 70's albums has become Yes' selling ploy, given  that not much they do these days sells at all.  Points such as these make  one realize just how abysmal this album really is.  Is it not  disillusionment enough that the music itself should be so uninspired  without dragging in (and cheapening) past glories in an underhanded attempt  to promote this disc?  If stooping went any lower the band members would be  inserting their heads in dark orifices.  The one star rating is solely for  the fact that they were once men of idealism and unbridled artistic  ambition.  How times change.
label: negative

reviewText:
You know, I'm not a music snob by any means, and I listen to a ton of different kinds of music and artists. From Tom Waits to Aphex Twin to Rihanna to Bad Religion to the Donkey Kong Country soundtrack, so don't think that I'm anti-pop or anything. I also don't just give out one star ratings. But from the minute Ke$ha's album started playing, and I heard the first few seconds of that...that NOISE kick in, I knew that I was in hell. Not even Stephen King could describe the horror that came over my face when I was halfway through the cd. And I'm being serious here too.

What can I say that hasn't been said yet? This album was made for the kind of women you don't want to get involved with unless you feel like making a trip to a certain kind of doctor soon after meeting them. Every single track on here...Christ, there's really not a single good thing I can say. When I first heard TiK ToK, I thought it was a joke because of how bad Ke$ha's singing is and the lyrics, but it became a huge hit somehow! She's interested in guys that look like Mick Jagger? I feel dirty just listening to this stuff. If you thought her singing was bad on TiK ToK and Your Love is My Drug, wait until you hear the abominations that are Party at a Rich Dude's House and Dinosaur. See, I don't mind party songs, no matter how lame they are (like most of the songs 80s hair bands put out), but this is really pushing it. A song about an old guy hitting on Ke$ha, after she just brought up Mick Jagger? Huh. Her singing really does bring pain to my ears, and any time I hear a song of hers on the radio, I make a mad dash to turn it off or change the station. When this cd is playing somewhere and I can't get to it immediately, I start to panic. I swear, just hearing "Wake up in the morning..." when I'm in the gym puts me in a bad mood and just makes me work out with rage.

And the music, oh ho the music, if you can even call it that. You know how everything's really electronic these days with fuzzy sounds and a lot of bass (like BEP's Boom Boom Boom) and vocal effects? Yeah, this is that. Everything here is a holocaust of audio, and these tracks HAVE to be a joke by someone who bet that they couldn't be put on an album and make it big. Oddly enough, the music counters Ke$ha's vocals, and neither is better than the other, but that just doubles the pain. As a former DJ, there's no way these tracks would get a good reaction. For starters, there's no hook, and everything just sounds so boring. 'hate to type the name of the song again, but Party at a Rich Dude's House almost sounds like something you'd hear on a Pink track, and is one of the only tracks with guitars that you can actually hear.

I know this is more of a complaint than a review of the cd, but seriously, there's not a whole lot to review when you want an album to be over 10 seconds into the first track, and it only gets worse from there. I've listened to this whole thing once, and that was twice too many. I predict that, if there is a god, Ke$ha will fade into obscurity (with no money in her pocket, as she says). Look, I like a lot of pop music like Rihanna, Lady Gaga and Madonna, but THIS? I just shook my head after typing that. If you have to, just preview the songs. But if you have any self-respect, go buy something decent with your money. Maybe some fruit snacks, or some cinnamon Pop Tarts.

(Side note- when typing up this review, I like the tags that are suggested. 'good to see that I'm not in the minority here.)
label: negative

reviewText:
I LOVE Queen. They are one of my favorite bands. That's why I'm painfully giving this new Queen collection 'Absolute Greatest' one star. Read on for further details.

In 2009, Queen released their umpteenth compilation, 'Absolute Greatest.' A career-spanning retrospective, the record spans many classic tracks of theirs, including a track from their incredibly underrated 1995 record, 'Made in Heaven.'

This record is a cash cow. That's the bottom line. If you have 'The Platinum Collection: Greatest Hits I, II & III' and 'Classic Queen,' plus the studio records, you have this already. It's a massive ripoff from Queen and the folks at Hollywood Records. How disappointing -- it seems Queen has to release a compilation rehashing all of their classic tracks every several years or so.

If you thought 'Stone Cold Classics' was bad, you'll probably flinch at the sight of this. 'One Vision' is horrendously edited, chopped down to 3:59 as opposed to the classic 5:11 studio version. That's one of my favorite Queen songs -- and what a shame that this collection offers it edited. 'Greatest Hits II' and 'Classic Queen' suffer the same problem -- 'Queen Rocks,' it seems is the only collection that offers this song in it's full-length album version.

Overall, don't buy this record. It's Hollywood Records once again trying to deprive you of your hard-earned dollar by making you pay for another useless Queen compilation. If you are new to Queen's legendary catalogue, start with 'Greatest Hits I & II' or perhaps if you want to take it a step further 'The Platinum Collection: Greatest Hits I, II & III.' And, better yet, you could buy all of the studio records, which is definitely the best way to listen to Queen.

But don't buy this record. By buying this, you're simply encouraging Hollywood Records to rehash the same material AGAIN and AGAIN and AGAIN. I can almost guarantee you this set will be out of print, by, say 2013.

reviewText:
... but he's not omnipotent or infallible. And even in 1974, when this performance was recorded, he had the resources to do better. This is easily the worst, most over-conducted, most misinterpreted recording of the Vespro della Beata Vergine ever offered to the public by any conductor with "historical performance" credibility. If it were the first Gardiner I'd ever heard, I assure you I'd never give the man a second chance.

What's so bad about it? As I said, it's bizarrely over-conducted, with arbitrary and inconsequential changes of tempo and dynamic whenever John Eliot's baton twitched. The chorus is rough and bellowy. The soloists -especially the outside voices, soprano and baritone - sound as if they're singing through a kazoo at times, or as if an 'ugly filter' had been placed over their microphones. The sopranos and tenors have gross tuning problems often enough to substantiate the critics of 'early music' who say we have insufficient training... and yet these singers, some of them at least, are fairly reputable opera stars. The orchestra is murky, loud, undependable in tuning, and not even authentic in instrumentation! If a large state university, or even a medium-sized Lutheran college in upper Minnesota, staged a performance of the Vespers, I'd expect a more musical event than this.

Besides, the recording quality is dreadful. John Eliot would do his reputation a favor by pulling this canine CD off the market. Do notice, please, that Gardiner issued another performance of the Vespers, with entirely different forces, in 1990; nothing I say in this review is pertinent to that performance.

reviewText:
Earthbound was the last album to feature all the original 5th Dimension members released in 1975 on their sole ABC label effort. Marilyn McCoo & Billy Davis Jr split from them and began their own career on ABC Records in 1976, eventually making #1 in 1977 with You Don't Have To Be A Star. ABC released one more 5th Dimension single in 1976 with Love Hangover b/w Will You Be There with 2 new members.
This album is finally released on CD and is considered to be one of the lesser commercial releases and staying true to the original sound created by them in the 1960's. Mostly written by Jim Webb (Mac Arthur Park)  and including the Beatles I've Got A Feeling (intended as the only single from the album) and The Rolling Stones Moonlight Mile. I have to admit, personally, it is not my favorite album of theirs. I do like The Beatles and The Stones, but not impressed with generic sounding remakes. The 5th Dimension developed their own style as they progressed from the 60's to the 70's and enjoyed all kinds of hits from their classic Aquarious, Laura Nyro's Stone Soul Picnic to Marilyn McCoo's Adult Contemporary chanteuse styling's of One Less Bell To Answer & Last Night I Didn't Get To Sleep At All.

Please don't take offense to this honest review. It's all about personal taste. I ordered it through CDuniverse.com because it claimed that Love Hangover and Will You Be There would be included and actually called the title of the CD Earthbound:The Complete ABC Collection. That would have made me given this a few more stars.

reviewText:
Possibly the most hated CD of all time. And for good reason. Fred Durst - and the rest - have quite possibly come up with the most hyped, yet easily most disappointing "metal" CD of the year 2001 (or any other year!).
I used to remotely like this, but once I heard all my friends noting the lack of brains in the music and lyrics, I went over the album and realised they had a point.
Breaking out in countries all over the world thanks to their version of the Mission Impossible theme, they then followed that up with one good yet monotonous song (My Generation)...and isn't it funny how that description can be applied to ANY Bizkit song? Why, yes!
Bottom line? This CD is dull, repetitive crud, destroying metal's self-respect by going mainstream, and being an embarrasement to countless fans. Haha!
Anyway, tracklisting:
1. Intro. Dull. Rock bands should NEVER apply stupid "techno" intros to their CDs without running them by anyone else. Truly boring and ...(Who's in the house?/Limp Bizkit. ZZZZ).
2. Hot Dog. As with the majority of this album's songs, Fred's inflated ego has taken command of the lyrics and made them stupid and unnecessary. In this case, 46 uses of the word f**k constitute the words. Oh how tough. That's more than most albums have (yet this one has over 200 f words and 300 swearwords in total...easily the most crude album I've heard. Maybe to make up for a lack of talent, cuss them to death!) Even having the balls to steal from Nine Inch Nails' monumental "Closer", and "borrowing" the line "Everybody knows It's On" from Korn's "It's On" (hey, they're friends so we can forgive them!), it shows how Fred has no talent. Even the riffs and song structure (the actual music) lacks a sense of cohesion..and that's what really matters in music, not brain-bashingly "heavy" music.
3. My Generation. More swearing. But no one cares after the last track. Still, this track improves on the basic musical structure of most other Bizkit songs by including both a very good (!) riff and an awful DJ solo. DJs and rock bands should stay away from each other.
Still, one of the slightly better songs.
4. Full Nelson. Even more stupid techno noises, "crushing" riffs, and stupid swearing. Yet this remains one of the tracks I still have a soft spot for. Maybe it's due to the dynamics, I don't know. It's just somewhat different. Yet if you want to get into detailed Bizkit discussion I ain't your man.
5. My Way. Clean! 3 swearwords in the song, and not 40 like others. Slightly more "upbeat" cos there seem to be major chords in the song.
6. Rollin'. Awful. The worst song ever by Bizkit, released purely for it's commercial appeal and easily imitable dance routine. Dance? I thought that's what rock was against. Still, do you find some coincidence in the fact that this was the most played Bizkit tune ever, and yet my most hated? Aaaaah!
7. Livin' It Up. Always include apostrophe in at least two songs. More of the same, very slightly above average, cos the Eagles sample doesn't sound out of place, like the album in the metal world, cos it's quite a good sample. But more bad swearing - sorry, rapping! from Fred spoils a possibly good song.
8. The One. The "mellow" track. Pretty pointless stadium filler, and Fred's attempts to sing don't work too well either.
9. Getcha Groove On. No wait, THIS is the worst Bizkit "song" ever. It's not even theirs, it has some disgusting "beats" from producer, erm, "Swiss Beatz". It's very very very bad, even Xzibit's attempts at rhyming, which work well, are drowned out by Fred's poorness and the constant nagging beat.
10. Take A Look Around. Played a lot on the radio. I'm not too sick of this song though, it seemed to be recorded at a point when Limp's talent hadn't been sucked out by the promise of money. The Mission Impossible tune seems a bit irrevelant. But hey, Fred's rap isn't self-centred tripe for once.
11. It'll Be OK. More tripe, aimed at exploiting the self-hate crowd. Dull.
12. Boiler. Boring! More MTV material, this time getting one up (or so they think) on the haters. We don't want to hurt you Fred. We just want to hurt your music!!
13. Hold On. Another OK tune, the most sensitive Bizkit song to date. Also the only one where the attempts at singing are worthwhile
14. Rollin (Urban Assault Vehicle). 2 hip-hop tunes in one album?!??! NO THANKS! We also didn't need another version of Rollin', pretty dull stuff. Except for the moment where the rappers upstage Fred by being better than him...oh, that's the whole song!!
15. Outro. More boring techno naffness. Ben Stiller sullying his name by association, then breaking up into ... giggles. Not worth it OK?
So, overall, a boring CD. Only the 2 CD set redeems the entire idea of this package even existing, as it has the videos for the best material from the last album, Significant Other, which is miles better than this, as the idea of rap-metal hadn't been ...dry by then, like it is now.
All in all, any other nu-metal group - Tool, SOAD, Linkin Park and Slipknot - are much much much more worthy of your time. Avoid.
label: negative

reviewText:
Wow, wow, and I mean WOW!  Was that enough emphasis for you?  Now this is ROCK right here!  I've never heard ROCK this ROCKIN' before!  As a soccer mom with 4 kids between the ages of 1 and 9, I've been around, and I KNOW what ROCK is, and this most certainly IS ROCK!  Everyone knows that the best ROCK artists appear on televised talent shows and shill for beverage and automobile companies before they even sign a record deal, and that's what Daughtry represents!  I don't think I've driven the point home - this is THE MOST ROCKINEST ROCK that ever ROCKED the ROCK!

What we have are heavy hitting guitar ROCKIN' jams like "Feels Like Tonight" and "What About Now" that ROCK my socks off, hardcore songs like "It's Not Over" that make me want to start a mosh pit in my SUV (I got a ticket the other day while driving to this - the cops in this state just don't know how to ROCK), and fiery death metal blasts like "Home" that cause me to bang my head against the wall!  Yes, folks, it's that fierce and ROCKIN' - believe me, because I KNOW.  If you've already picked up THE ONLY ROCK ALBUMS that have come out in the past few years, which were all done by Nickelback, 3 Doors Down, Bon Jovi, Hinder and Buckcherry, then YOU MUST have this album.  Picking up Daughtry's CD is your license to RRRRROOOOOCCCCCKKKKK!!!!!

(end soccer mom transmission)

Back to reality.  Daughtry's debut CD is glossy, overproduced, meaningless gobbledygook.  A nonsensical word, yes, but one that fittingly describes this artless piece of plastic.

Simplistic everyman lyrics are the order of the day for Daughtry.  Witness these couplets from "It's Not Over": "I was blown away / What could I say? / It all seemed to make sense ... We'll blow it away, blow it away / Can we make this something good?" - tremendous mastery of the language by Mr. Daughtry.

Musically, if you've heard Nickelback and 3 Doors Down, you've heard Daughtry.  The band offers nothing but the same tired pop/rock that's already been played to death, without bringing anything even remotely new to the table.  One gets the feeling that Daughtry simply cobbled together songs from the demos of the other bands - that's how generic this is.

What's more, all the songs on the album sound pretty much the same.  There's a few attempts by Daughtry to sound somewhat edgier (think Seether/Three Days Grace "edgy", which isn't saying much), but the vast majority of the album is midtempo pop fluff.  Another reason NOT to buy the album?  You can hear half of it on the radio, CONSTANTLY!

In summary: More generic, pure commercial product from an American Idol contestant, Daughtry's s/t album merely emulates the popular sounds of today and adds nothing to the mix.  It's like some executives went up to Chris Daughtry after he got his deal, handed him some Nickelback and 3 Doors Down CDs, and said "Listen to it, think about it, dream about it, BE about it ... because THIS is what you're going to sound like".  If you appreciate music as an art form at all, you want NO part of this album.  But if you enjoy whatever the local "Mix" station is playing to death, then one click will pave the road for your personal euphoria.

reviewText:
Cuando se anuncio que Tarja no continuaria con Nightwish mi primer
pensamiento fue que la banda se separaria y supuse que cada uno continuaria con sus pryectos por aparte, pero no sucedio asi, la banda siguio luego de,segun ellos, una extensa busqueda de una reemplazante de Tarja y es asi como una vez seleccionada la nueva vocalista que la banda lanzo para este 2007 este disco.

Pero jamas estaria preparado para lo que llegaria a convertirse Nightwish con su nueva etapa, ya sin Tarja, aunque tenia la esperanza de que la reemplazante fuera de caracteristicas parecidas a las de Tarja.

Mientras Nightwish buscaba vocalista nueva, la escena mundial de metal sinfonico evolucionaba, en mi humilde opinion para mal, pero saldria una banda nueva llamada Operatika con una vocalista que parecia cumplir con todos los requisitos para reemplazar a Tarja y mis esperanzas de que Nightwish tomara la decision correcta aumentaban.

Pero una vez lanzado su nueva produccion todas mis esperanzas fueron aniquiladas y destrozadas.
El album resulto ser una completa decepcion, su musica es simplona, con una labor de Toumas (teclados) bastante aceptable pero nada extraordinario con una visible influencia de Hanz Zimmer, las guitarras con poca elaboracion, asi como el bajo y para hacerlo peor una vocalista horrorosa, sin nada de sentimiento en su voz, fria, poco expresiva, mediocre para la calidad que habia desarrollado en sus principios la banda y todo, absolutamente todo con una clara intencion de vender discos nada mas, sumamente comercial, pero no todo es culpa de Nightwish, sino de la misma escena sinfonica metal que han visto en las voces femeninas gran potencial para vender muchos discos con tan solo modificar las guitarras hacia cosas mas digeribles, menos elaboradas, aburridas y sin sentimiento, sin sentido ni corazon, asi resumo lo que ha venido a convertirse la tan maltrecha escena metal sinfonico o doom metal en general, con bandas como Tristania, Sirenia, Epica y ahora Nightwish que ahora practican una musica comercial y mediocre.

Este disco de Nightwish debio llamarse Cold Passionless Play, pues asi describiria su musica de mejor manera, es una desgracia y muy lamentable que una de las bandas pioneras del metal sinfonico y doom metal en general se "despida" de esta manera y que por el contrario Tarja ahora como solista este sonando mejor aunque no con la genialidades de Toummas ni de una banda de renombre que la respalde pero siempre con su maravillosa voz encantando a mas fanaticos alrededor del mundo con su nuevo disco que sin ser una genialidad es mil veces mejor que este disco de Nightwish.

QUE DECEPCION!!!!!!!  BYE BYE NIGHTWISH

reviewText:
Nu-metal played fast is not death metal.
Many people, including a lot of critics who should know better, have been saying this album shows Slipknot's death and black metal influences and contains elements of both styles. This has been sacrilegiously compared to Slayer's landmark album "Reign In Blood". This has been called the direction of metal for the future.
Wrong. Wrong. Wrong.
It's just Korn on amphetamines. If this is death metal, then I'm Ronan Keating!
It's nu-metal played a bit faster than the average bunch of clown-trousered, dog-chained, whining, spike-haired wannabes. That means it has no substance, no feel, little musical skill, and is just downright dreadful. The "aggression" comes across as contrived and calculated.
The lyrics are inane, vapid, and braindead. "If you're 555/Then I'm 666". Truly insightful, I can, like, so relate to that, man, Slipknot feel my pain. And how clever is calling a song "People = S**t"! I'm gonna white it all over my school books, 'cos that's just what I feel! Enough sarcasm...
Musically, it's mush. The drumming is nothing spectacular, despite two extra percussionists. The riffs are recycled and bland, the bass is boring, and vocals are poorly executed. So the vocalist can scream and sing... Try it yourself- it's not difficult at all, and many do it much better. The addition of four extra musicians than the band needs adds nothing noticeable to the sound whatsoever.
This is nu-metal pabulum stuck in a blender. Sure, it's faster than normal nu-metal, but at the end of the day, it still tastes the same.

reviewText: Give her credit; at least she manages one decent track on an album on occasion. Here, it is the title track. "Cuts Both Ways" wasn't one of her biggest hits, only reaching #44, but it was at least sincere sounding. The utterly nothing song "Don't Wanna Lose You" was heard on the radio a lot, and it didn't deserve it. It is trite and empty, like the vast majority of her music. Absolutely nothing there! This album was also where the marketing of Estefan as a solo performer was at a transitional stage. On the cover, only her name appeared, but on the spine, it had "& Miami Sound Machine" still attached to it. Her early recordings as vocalist with that group are still her best, even though they are hardly brain stimulators themselves, at least they had some energy and were rather fun, in particular "Falling In Love" and "Bad Boy". Both of these have been ignored on subsequent collections, for no apparent reason other than Sony's not caring about completeness, something they have long been known for. Estefan is not totally worthless as a recording artist (I always contend that even the WORST acts have one or two good songs in their catalogs), but she's pretty damn close to being the female equivalent of Billy Joel. (Well, not THAT bad, actually.)

reviewText: I'm a child of the 50's who grew up in the '60's with the 'Sound Of Young America" so generally I don't take too kindly to masterpieces being remixed! However there are a few exceptions like "Stoned Love" on "Motown Remixed Vol 1" and the brilliant remix of Marvin & Tammi's "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" on the new "Ashford and Simpson Songbook" but these are rare occurrences. IMHO there is no excuse for the total lack of respect for the classic tracks which have been completely destroyed in this latest volume which I sincerely hope will be the last. To me it's a bit like someone putting a wig & false nose on the Mona Lisa! It's a gimmick & one that gets my hackles rising as I'm convinced that it's all done for monetary gain and has no artistic merit whatsoever. "Motown Remixed Vol 2" has a Latin theme and to be honest there's only a couple of tracks that sound as though they weren't remixed by Humboldt Bear & PJ! What's next I wonder; heavy metal Motown, the punk side of Motown or Motown goes country? The mind boggles. OK now that I've got that off my chest I'll go back & lie down in a darkened room whilst listening to some plain, ordinary, natural, unmixed Motown. I suggest that you all do the same.

reviewText: I've never been a fan of Baz Luhrmann. It's clear from this soundtrack that his audio sensibilities is just as garish as his visual ones. Want to have the few good songs you remember from the movie? I liked the CoCo song and the Florence and the Machine track. Well some idiot has marketed this as ALBUM ONLY. At $16.00 to boot! Often it makes sense for people to buy instrumental soundtrack albums when you have an individual composer and the sonic stamp and consistency of the music makes it an exciting listen. It doesn't usually work that way with various artist soundtracks unless they really freeze dry an aesthetic of the time - let's say Flashdance or Footloose. We've had a few various artists soundtracks that have been really good - the laser focus of Tarantino soundtracks, Coppola's Marie Antionette soundtrack. But I find it unlikely that someone would like more than 5 or 6 songs off this mess of a listen. This is going to mean low sales. Solution: $1.29 per track with 80% of downloads being ALBUM ONLY. What a bunch of crap. And finally, for anyone who was extremely disappointed by the XX's Coexist album and were hoping for them to have another shot here, don't waste your time. They provide another dire, slow, unpassionate song with no drive, melody or soul. It's so early in their career and they already sound stagnant! reviewText: I own all but one Dwight Yoakam album; I have seen him in concert a half-dozen times; I am as huge a Dwight Yoakam fan as there is; and as odd as it sounds, I believe the two greatest musical artists of the past 100 years are Dwight Yoakam and Frank Sinatra. In other words, I am a big, big fan. But the sad truth is, "3 Pears" is awful. The quality of Yoakam's recordings has fallen off in the 10 years since he split with his longtime producer Pete Anderson, and here the downward slide continues. For 10 years, each album has contained fewer and fewer good songs. And now, "3 Pears" takes us almost as low as we can go. I say "almost" because, of the 12 tracks on the disc, one of them rises to the level of "decent." That track is "Dim Lights, Thick Smoke," a pretty good toe-tapper with an OK melody line. Still, even this song would have landed in the dustbin had it been looking for inclusion on any of Yoakam's first 6 or 7 albums. Of note is the fact that "Dim Lights, Thick Smoke" is the only track on "3 Pears" not written by Yoakam himself, which indicates that a good amount of the problem in the past 10 years has been the quality of Yoakam's writing. After penning so many brilliant tunes from the late 80s through the late 90s, I fear that Yoakam's songwriting well has run dry. There's no shame in that, really, as it happens to everyone  -- from Cole Porter to Paul McCartney to Bruce Springsteen. One only wishes that a guy like Yoakam, whose voice still sounds great, would recognize the situation and reach out to other songwriters for better material. (Not so surprisingly, in my mind, his last great recorded song was "The Back of Your Hand," also written by someone else.) So what's wrong with his songs on "3 Pears"? Well, everything. Lyrically they range from thematically uninspired (broken hearts, lost love) to downright bizarre. On the song "Waterfall," here's an actual lyric: "If I had a big giraffe / He'd have to take a real long bath / And that's why waterfalls are really neat." And don't think I'm leaving out context here. The whole song features this type of stream of consciousness gibberish, filled with jellyfish and peanut butter and rocket ships and waterfalls and ice cream and war and babies. Equally inane is the title track, "3 Pears," which is really not about "pears" (the fruit) but "pairs" of things, of which there are "three pairs" of items such as "glasses" and "shades" and "shoeless feet" and "mindless thoughts" and "wishes." And in the end the lyrics wish someone happiness. What does it all mean? I have no idea. And you won't either, so don't waste your time. It would be one thing if these obtuse words were woven through pleasing melodies, whereupon a person could at least enjoy the music while attempting to find meaning in the lyrics. Unfortunately, like the rest of "3 Pears," there's not an interesting melody to be found, rendering the whole experience unpleasant. I hope Dwight Yoakam can some day get his groove back, but "3 Pears" shows no reason for optimism.

reviewText: I own about 60 Bjrk/related CDs including all of her single-released nonalbum tracks.  I have raw bootleg cuts of Bjrk singing in grade school, icelandic carols, and old Sugarcubes demo covers -- you get my point.  (With the exception of her tiny bits on Tricky's "Nearly God" album), "Domestika" and "Batabid" on this single are the most NONessential Bjrkisms in my collection yet.  DOMESTIKA is a too easily-constructed, repetitive jingle featuring Bjrk capriciously singing "Oh, where I'd put my keys?!" over and over again.  The old "My Spine" spontaneously created with Evelyn Glennie a few years ago was of infinitely better composition, if that is any indication.  BATABID is an  instrumental quickie (again, pure repetition of a few simple notes).  It's the first of all her instrumental pieces I've dismissed as a complete throw away.  Is this single a joke?  I was surprised because quite frankly I'm used to hearing very high quality in all her b-sides.  Bjrk spent a little too much time worrying about how to flaunt her nudity and choose the angle for belly-piercing in her latest video than working on extra music to make a 'pagan poetry-part two' single release justifiable.  I give it 0.6 stars above 'poor' because her voice would sound good reading the dictionary!  Not everything she releases is golden.  A sad waste of plastic.

In any event, this is really an embarrassing disc (perhaps Arrau did better later) and if you think this is great, then you should simply ignore the readings of selected etudes by the likes of Richter and Horowitz and the best complete sets, those by Ohlsson and Ashkenazy.  If you like distorted accents, lumpen phrasing, clumsy technique -- you will certainly find many of those grotesqueries here. reviewText:
Entre la fin des annes 60 et le dbut des annes 2000 Deutsche Grammophon et Plcido Domingo ont fait une vritable OPA sur Verdi. Rsultat : Domingo a chant les rles de tnor des 27 opras de Verdi et dans la premire moiti des annes 80, est venu le tour de Don Carlos. Il est difficile de porter un jugement sur Domingo qui a commenc  la fin des annes 50 et qui continue encore  chanter actuellement ; pour fter ses 50 ans de carrire, il compte mme interprter le rle-titre de Simon Boccanegra, un rle de baryton,  Berlin en 2009 ! C'est beaucoup pour un seul homme, trop en fait. En effet, malgr son immense succs, Domingo compte bien peu de vraies russites. Et Don Carlos n'en fait pas partie. Comme d'habitude le chanteur, qui n'est plus au meilleur de sa voix, donne une interprtation trs froide de son personnage, sans relle intensit dramatique. Il est de plus peu aid par les autres chanteurs :  cet gard Dieu tu semas dans nos mes avec Leo Nucci (Rodrigue) devient un duo des maons qui fait froid dans le dos. Katia Ricciarelli (lisabeth) et Ruggero Raimondi (Philippe II) font leur aimable massacre habituel, accumulant toutes les erreurs qu'il ne faut pas faire. Une manire de chanter  la fois glace et mlodramatique semble tre ici la marque de fabrique gnrale, mme chez Nicolai Ghiaurov (L'Inquisiteur). Seule Lucia Valentini Terrani (Eboli) chappe  cette malheureuse rgle ; nanmoins elle en confirme une autre, qui est celle du volapk collectif : comme dans le cas de ses petits camarades, on ne comprend absolument rien  ce qu'elle chante. Pire encore, on se demande en quoi elle chante quand on l'coute. La Chanson du voile est  cet gard rvlatrice. Claudio Abbado dirige son orchestre de manire nergique, ce qui cre des effets puissants mais limite le dramatisme de certaines scnes qui demandent un orchestre moins prsent. Il en est mme souvent trop bruyant.
La seule raison d'acqurir cet enregistrement est qu'il propose l'air entre Philippe II et Posa de la fin de l'acte II dans une version diffrente de l'habituelle (Regardez mes Espagnes... La paix du cimetire...).
Cette version a aussi la particularit d'avoir 3/4 d'heure de bonus (aprs les 3h 10 que dure l'opra). Il s'agit de six scnes qui n'ont pas t donnes lors de la reprsentation de 1867 comme le prlude L'hiver est long de prs de dix minutes, mais aussi bizarrement le ballet (pourtant donn en 1867). Avoir mis ces scnes  la fin pour des raisons musicologiques se dfend mais cela rompt compltement la trame de l'histoire. On les retrouve d'ailleurs toutes sur la version de la BBC de 1972  leur place dans l'opra.
Le livret est trs bien fait. Les analyses sont signes des deux grands spcialistes de cet opra, Ursula Gnther et Andrew Porter. Comme souvent chez DG, il faudra tre polyglotte et savoir soit l'italien soit l'anglais pour lire Porter (Gnther a droit elle  l'allemand et au franais).
Deutsche Grammophon a peut-tre ralis la premire intgrale sur cd (disponible aussi dans un coffret de cinq vinyls), mais il s'avre que cela a t une fausse bonne ide et elle ne remplace pas l'excellente version de la BBC du dbut des annes 70 avec Andr Turp.

reviewText:
Of all the work that probably went into this extensive set the first thing that comes to mind is that most of us have two working ears. There is way too much MONO! It is very clear that deception was intended by WEA/Rhino and the producers of this set. Aside from a sticker on the outside of the package, indicating that the album "Buffalo Springfield" is presented in MONO, there is no other indication that any of the other tracks were anything but Stereo. The MONO version of the "Buffalo Springfield" album is pretty rare with very few sales and  most never even made it to the cut-out bins. Included in this CD version of the album is the song "Baby Don't Scold Me" which was replaced by the also included "For What It's Worth" on the 2nd pressings of the album.

It isn't until you get into the booklet that is included  that you see that most of the songs are in MONO. There is a very tiny "M" by the selections which are MONO, which means most of the songs in this collection are MONO. Very deceptive.

As far as using the original master tape and the best available tape is a total lie. What appears to have been used are the MONO mix-down compressed tapes and a few stereo masters. Joel Bernstein obviously did a poor job of archival tape research. Redwood Digital in Woodside,  CA, did a very poor job of mastering. 24-bit/88.2 kHz HDCD digital transfer? Huh? Maybe they only did this on the few stereo recordings. That would be believable.

In conclusion, unless you are a compleatest and must have everything, I wouldn't waste your money on this collection. Take a lesson from one who did waste his money on this collection, it ain't worth it.

reviewText:
A newly imprisoned convict arrives at the prison mess hall for the first time where he hears peals of laughter ringing forth. As he takes his seat at his table, he's astonished as his fellow convicts rise one after another, throwing out numbers to uproarious laughter. "Number 3" says one to loud guffaws. "Hey, Number 21!" says another to knee-slapping chortles.

"Excuse me," he says to another con, "but what is so funny?"

"Oh," says the con, "they're telling jokes."

"Telling jokes? I don't get it."

"You must be new here. Most of us have been in here forever. We don't get any new jokes around here, and the old ones have been around for so long that we've sorta found it easier to just assign them all numbers and tell them that way. We get the same effect without all the bother."

The newbie thinks a second and says, "Hey. Do you think if I told a joke it would help break the ice with the guys?"

"Sure," says his fellow con.

"Well, do you have a good one for me?"

"Sure. Try Number 13. It's killer. It never fails."

The new convict rises and says, "Hey everybody - Number 13!!!"

Dead silence.

Chagrined, the newbie sits down. "I thought you told me that joke was a killer."

"It is," says his fellow con. "It's the way you told it."

And so it is with Sir Simon Rattle's Beethoven - it isn't the surefire music that we can sing in our sleep that's the problem. It's the way Sir Simon "tells" the music.

If I had to put it into a single word, that word would be "unmusical." One has to think that EMI could have saved themselves a chunk of change by renting out a C- or D-level provincial orchestra for this recording and gotten the same effect. Why spend top dollar on the Vienna Philharmonic if your star conductor is going to ask them to play with a tone so harsh and so aggressive that it peels paint from the walls? Why hire an orchestra known for its Beethoven tradition if you're going to have them play in a pseudo-HIP slam-bam-thank you-Ma'am style that makes the most-acerbic of HIP interpretations sound like they're channeling Mantovani by comparison? Why record them in a way that exacerbates the wrong-headed "ideas" of your star conductor, rather than mitigating the same?

And the less said about the "ideas" of Rattle in this rep the better, no more so than in the Finale of the 9th, where he has the chorus shout the words "Brder" and "Welt" in two spots, creating an effect that runs the gamut from stupid to embarrassing.

To say this set is one dimensional would be to overstate its dimensions by half.

I can't claim to have heard every Beethoven Symphony recording out there, but I can say that this traversal of The Nine is THE WORST I have ever heard, bar none. It's an Australian's nightmare of a set (let your imagination run wild). No need to go into chapter and verse as others pretty much picked the why-it-sucks bones clean on this set when it was first issued 10 years ago (check out the amazon reviews found elsewhere).

In today's market, there's a Beethoven Symphony cycle available for any taste. EMI has now produced a set for those with no taste.

BTW - EMI has knocked the price on this set down to MSRP $17.99, or about what a single top-line CD cost back in 2002 when this set was first released as a full-priced box. You can find that version elsewhere on amazon. No sense paying $68 for this set when you can get it for $50 cheaper.

That said, I can always earn another $18 to replace the money I spent on this set. What I can't do is get back the 5-plus hours of my life I wasted listening to this turkey.

But perhaps I've been too negative here. I can think of a few positive uses for this set, which might include:

* a great set to put on if you're going to be vacuuming

* a good set to load up in the CD carousel if you're planning on leaving home for a 6-hour stretch

* makes a great gift to someone who you suspect will never bother listening to ANY Beethoven set they receive as a gift, no matter how good or how much you paid

This set confirms what many of us have long suspected: that EMI stands for "Every Mistake Imaginable."

This set counts as one of their biggest mistakes, ever.

I absolutely hate this performance.  There is nothing majestic or beautiful to it.  The soloists are not pleasing, the tempi are all over the place, the orchestra is thin and hollow, like brittle cattails. Instead of rich consecrated wine, it is vinegar on the lees. I find it too awful to listen to for very long. The only thing interesting is the small detail from the Ghent Altar Piece on the cover.

Do yourself a favor. If you want an elegant HIP version, go for Herreweghe's third attempt on PHI (black cover, purple flower).  That is one of the most perfect performances and recordings I have ever heard.  Listen to this one for free on Prime (if you must) and compare.

And, by the way, skip Gardiner's Missa Solemnis. It, too, feels like the guy was just doing a quick run-through as a contractual obligation. I have one version of that by Herreweghe that is better, one by Klemperer that is majestic, and one by Karajan. The last two aren't HIP, but are wonderful.

reviewText:
It's high time the Navin brothers made their fist-pumping Heavy Metal album. Those who've had the rare opportunity to see them live (I got to see 'em on their ill-fated Pedals tour) know what %#$&-talking, shot-downing, espresso-guzzling, caustic eccentrics these guys are, and I think it's time they applied that edge to the music, if for no other reason than I'm sick of hearing them crank out the same stale, O'Rourkian techno-blip-space-lounge with every album.

Maybe that's harsh, but "Happyness" demonstrates the Navin brothers' failure to recognize that music has moved on from those wild 'n crazy lounge sounds of 1998. "Happyness" keeps the synth blips and anti-septic ambient beats coming as if the 21st century hadn't arrived yet. The same blips and beats that filled the High Llamas' wonderful "Cold and Bouncy," and the Sea and Cake's era-defining "Fawn." But now, the loungey, squeaky-clean, Thrill Jockey sounds that dominated the late 90s leave "Happyness" looking like ELO in the post-punk early 80s.

But let's make one thing clear: I *love* "Plano" and was ecstatic when it came out. A perfect fusion of Bill Nelson new wave and Bacharach flavored, late 60s AM pop, "Plano" pushed all the right buttons, offering hook after lovely hook, all bathed in gorgeous atmosphere and baroque arrangements. "Pedals" had its moments, but lumbered under an awkward weight, as producer O'Rourke sent the Navins straight to Prekop territory, where art for art's sake is the norm and sharp pop hooks are generally frowned upon. "Pelo" verged on self-parody: they seemed to forget how to write a decent tune, content with letting their flimsy songs flutter away with flaky blips and beeps. The abundance of "Pelo" copies in bargain bins proves I wasn't the only one who felt that way.

"Happyness" is every bit as forgettable as "Pelo." If you're looking for "Sugar and Promises" or "Sunday Morning" hooks, you won't find 'em. The Navins seem bent on shunning Plano's timeless pop in favor of something that will sound dated and limited in coming years. Rather than find subtle ways to keep their music relevant, they dilute what few good ideas they have left and stubbornly embrace trends from several years ago. Sterile, unambitious, and dull, there's hardly a memorable song here. I'll have to be content with Plano and its predecessor, Wonder Boy, remembering the true genius the Navins were once capable of.

reviewText:
Pink Floyd are easily one of my top ten favorite bands but even great bands can make horrible albums. In the case of Floyd, it's this embarrassingly awful funeral home that was used to promote their late 1980s tour. Hardly delicate, listening to this album is like being stuck on an elevator hearing dinosaurs fart.

The main problem I have with this album is that it is just simply BORING: dull, lifeless, uninspired and pedestrian to the bone. This is quite a shocker when you consider that Pink Floyd were one of the best live rock bands in the 1970s. There is nothing transcendent about this record; not even attempts by the band to innovate their classics on stage. Then again, that's probably a good thing because when they DO try, the results are embarrassing. Take note the hideous saxophone solo on "Shine on You Crazy Diamond" (Dick Parry, we miss you) and the agonizingly slow rendition of "Comfortably Numb", where Roger Waters' vocal parts were replaced by a bunch of average vocal harmonies that would make George Martin vomit. The worst offenders, by far, are "Money" and "Run Like Hell": the former is extended into an insufferable jam featuring horrible bass playing by newbie Guy Pratt and the latter substitutes the original's eerie menace for macho chest-beating that is exhausting rather than exhaustive. Roger, where are you when we need you?

Not surprisingly, the most listenable songs on this album are the ones from A Momentary Lapse of Reason (1987) but that's not saying much because most of the songs from the record were horrible in the first place. The only songs from this album that actually improved from their studio counterparts are "Learning to Fly", which removes that awful synthesizer riff from the original; and "Sorrow", which boasts even more impressive guitar playing than before. But whatever positives this album has (which is very few) are shattered by the negatives (which are plenty).

Anyone who considers Delicate Sound of Thunder as the comprehensive overview of Pink Floyd concerts are clearly misguided; as stated before, in the 1970s, Pink Floyd were a force on stage and their best concerts rivaled that of Led Zeppelin. It's not just because they had Waters; when they were together, Floyd produced dazzling and unforgettable music. In fact, there are many bootleg albums out there to confirm this (most notably Animal Instincts). But Delicate is not one of those albums. Far from comprehensive, Delicate confirms the inaccurate belief that Pink Floyd were a boring dinosaur act whose reasons for touring were for financial rather than artistic reasons.

Delicate Sound of Thunder is not the best place to start if you want to get into Floyd concerts, that's for damn sure. Check out Animal Instincts or even their Live 8 reunion and the difference in quality between those shows and Delicate are absolutely staggering. Avoid this Sound of Blunder at all costs.

Strong recommendation to avoid.

reviewText:
Now, don't dismiss this review as just another rant from a Dipset hater (even though every member of the Dipset is wack). Cam'ron is hardly one of the best rappers in the game; in fact, he's barely even tolerable, so it should come as no surprise that his latest album Killa Season is straight garbage.

In fact, Cam lays it all out himself at the beginning of "Get `Em Daddy", where he says: "See, the problem is, I ain't goin' nowhere." Can't argue with that. But first I'll talk about the song "You Gotta Love It", which not only sloppily disses Jay-Z but also Roc-a-Fella. Cam even says something about voluntarily leaving the Roc because of conflicts with label executives. Suuuure, Cam; leaving Roc-a-Fella was YOUR decision. Anyway, Hova's probably never going to hear this song anyway.

After leaving the Roc, Cam'ron found a new home on an indie label, Asylum Records, which probably accounts for all the unknown producers. The only producer most people have probably heard of is Alchemist, but his good beat is wasted on "Wet Wipes". And I don't know if too many people heard "Hey Lady" from Purple Haze, but it sampled Roger Troutman's "I Want to Be Your Man", and the method of lazily sampling old R&B hits on new rap songs is also evident here. "Do Ya Thing" ruins Earth, Wind & Fire's "That's the Way of the World", and "Leave You Alone", which uses Etta James' "You're Gonna Cry", has some of the worst production I have ever heard.

There are also a lot of unknown rappers on here; get this: if people named Juelz Santana and Freekey Zekey weren't strange enough, here we're introduced to Mo Money and Hell Rell. But worse than all that is Cam'ron himself: he just can't rap. In fact, his bars are so wack that you almost wish he WAS still talking about blingin' and name brand clothes (although "Girls, Cash, Cars" is confusing in that it's neither about girls, cash nor cars). Speaking of confusing songs, I can't tell if "White Girls" is really about Caucasian females or about pushing white, but at any rate, it's very uninspiring (and this is coming from a black man married to a white woman).

Another failure is when Cam tries to SING on "He Tried to Play Me"; and "Get Ya Gun" features news story "interludes" discussing the hazards of children with guns -- in the middle of a song talking about shootin' people up. Is that supposed to be funny? Finally, the voicemail interludes are incomprehensible -- not because I can't understand what Cam and friends are talking about, but because the speaking is so muffled that I literally can't tell what they're saying.

It's not that I was expecting a lot from Cam'ron, but this album is so awful that I don't even want to think about it any more. I'd even listen to Pras Michel's album before I listened to THIS again. Killa Season is definitely a time of year you won't be looking forward to.

Anthony Rupert

I'd disparage any band that released something like this -its kind of shocking, really, that this is The Gathering.
It goes beyond the mood, which I find morose and uninspired.  There is about 20 seconds of acutal valid musical content here, crammed into about 25 minutes.  Its beyond self-indulgence - in the first place, that problem implies you have some content to over indulge in.  Experimental and artistic? Over 2 hours of music was recorded and Yared gave a year to this score which he claims to be his best. Yesterday when I watched the film I paid much attention to the music and it was as predicted, the mix of previous Horner motives and themes and nothing, absolutely nothing, new.

reviewText: I tried to give them a chance after Adam left.  I tried to not be one of those who automatically dismisses someone for a line up change like this.  I really tried.  But the band just isn't the same.  They shouldn't even use the Three Days Grace name anymore with this new guy and sound.  People try to say bands need to experiment and explore new sounds.  That's true.  But at least when most bands experiment and explore, they keep their core sound intact.  This new guy is the ultimate downfall of TDG.  It's true.  Hardcore fans will stick around by the handful only.  But after this album, say goodbye to anyone caring about the bands new material.  If bands like System of a Down or Disturbed or Korn or any of these bands changed their lead vocalist, their would be an outcry.  Adams voice was a trademark to TDG.  This is full of 'ok' at best songs that sound like they would be hits in 2002.  Like I said, I tried to give this new guy a chance.  He just isn't good.  When you heard Adam you knew it was TDG.  Half the time when I hear these new songs I forget I'm even listening to this band anymore.  I've listened to the album 5 times and it doesnt work.  I'm glad I didn't buy it.  If you simply are one of the people who can't let go of the band no matter what because you're a mega hardcore fan who can't move on, then you should buy this.  If you like Three Days Grace, stay away from this.  This is one of those examples where its okay to use the phrase "their old stuff was better" and not sound like an overbearing hipster.  This is a band trying too hard to move on just to make money even if it's with horrible music.  This is a prime example of when a lead singer becomes so important to a band that they matter more than the rest in brutal honesty.  Take a look at the new Breaking Benjamin song, another band of similar genres.  The only remaining member of that band is the lead singer and their new stuff sounds amazing and refreshing.  This is very bad.  Goodbye Three Days Grace.  Live off of your royalties from previous albums and songs that you should really thank Adam for.  If you like good music, for the goodness of your sanity, stay far far away from this failing record.

reviewText: Made In America was supposed to be Carpenters' comeback album. It had been three years since their last pop album and many people were expecting Carpenters to comeback with a phenomenal album. What happened is they came back with Made In America, an album which was out of touch with the times and ended up becoming their lowest selling studio album. None of the songs had any real hit potential and many of the tunes found Karen singing in tones way to high for her own comfort zone. Much of the orchestration on the songs was overly lush and too overdone. The album lacks the magic of earlier Carpenters albums. After three years Carpenters should have returned with an album that was innovative, surprising and fresh. Instead we got an album filled with songs that at the best were just okay, it's as if they really did not put their 100% or their hearts into this album. What Carpenters needed was a comeback album that fit the times. Instead of releasing Made In America they should have released Karen's solo album which was very much in tune with the times and contained at least four or five possible hit singles.

I guess it was a bit silly of me to expect something special out of a disc that was labeled so overwhelmingly as the best representation of psychedelic-trance there is. Psy-trance is very uptempo dance music, pure and simple, although it's usually a little more complex than stuff like La Bouche or whatever is hot right now.

Unfortunately, that doesn't make it any less formulaic. All of the acts I've listened to, from X-Dream to Astral Projection to Xenomorph to Growling Mad Scientists to Koxbox to, now, Hallucinogen, seem to operate with a very basic pool of sounds, and they tend to use the same generic 4/4 beats for their music. I've always thought trance must be easy to make, and these psytrance artists certainly don't prove me wrong.

You can set your watch by the time signatures of these tracks. This is music at its cheapest, most formulaic "best." I fail to see why people hype this up as the second coming, considering that Twisted is only one or two degrees removed from EBM ("industrial dance" music), and is a close cousin of mainstream dance, as well.

My review is a warning to those who are looking to try psy-trance, thinking it's the next best thing. It's not. It's overhyped dance music. If that's what you're looking for, then this is right up your alley. If you're looking for something intelligent to listen to, try Posford's better effort: Shpongle.

reviewText:
I think this is a good opportunity to write a better review for this extremely overrated and awful album, so here's a better review for all of you.

Much like Pantera's "Vulgar Display of Power," I never understood why this joke of an album gets so much praise.  I think this album is a highlight as to many of the bad things the 1990's are associated with in relation to the heavy metal genre.  With that said, I would like to state that I'm NOT one of these people that thinks the 90's was a totally bad decade for the metal genre.  In fact, many of my absolute favorite metal albums came from the early 90's, but unfortunately, more bands in the 90's were looking to "Vulgar Display of Power" and the grunge scene and morphing the metal genre into...this.

STYLE

Groove metal, which is precisely what Machine Head's "Burn My Eyes" is, is a worthless genre of music.  This album is characterized with downtuned guitars, mid-paced guitar chugging, occasionally cool guitar solos, and bad vocals that range from pseudo-aggressive to flat-out whiny.  It's neutered music that puts up the facade of being extreme without actually being extreme.  Sure, this sounds extreme to someone who lives on a steady diet of grunge music, but play this album alongside an album like Morbid Saint's "Spectrum of Death" or Sarcofago's "INRI," and you'll see just how much of a limp-wristed album this is.

MUSICIANSHIP

Rob Flynn handled guitars and vocals on this album.  Flynn's vocals are...atrocious.  When he's not trying to do bad imitations of Max Cavalera's vocals from the Sepultura album "Chaos AD," he does even worse impressions of your average grunge/alternative rock whiner.  His lyrics are bad as well, since if they're not hammy interpretations of violent events from the early 90's, they're lame tough guy pandering or teenage whining.  Flynn was 26 years-old when this album came out, someone should have told him he's way too old to whine in his music.  The bad lyrics wouldn't be a problem if they were buried behind the other instruments, but because they're put right in the front of everything else in the mix, clearly showing their juvenile nature.  Much like Dimebag Darrell, Flynn's guitar work is really inconsistent.  His solos sound pretty neat, but his riffs are mostly bad.  There's a competent thrash riff here and there, but most of it is pseudo-metal groovy chugging that sounds totally lame.

Logan Mader also handled the guitars on this album, and like Flynn, some solos are neat, but the riffs are mostly a joke.  Same groovy plodding most of the time, with the occasional thrash burst to give off the impression of it being extreme music.

Adam Duce handled bass and did backing vocals.  Other than the opening to "I'm Your God Now," I didn't notice much bass in this album, but since all of the vocals I heard on this album were awful, I can only assume his backing vocals were awful, too.

Chris Kontos handled the drums on this album, and I honestly didn't notice any beats or fills that were slightly remarkable.  Like the guitars, when he's playing a thrash beat in the few aggressive parts on this album, they're competent, but most of the time, they were mediocre.

SONGS

Technically, none of the songs on here are good, but if there's one that I had to say would be close to good, that would be "Blood for Blood."  That song comes closest to being a proper thrasher and has possibly the best guitar solos in the album, and if it weren't for the lame vocals and lyrics, could even be a classic metal tune.

However, the rest on here are very painful to listen to with only fleeting moments of mercy to keep you from going totally insane.  "Davidian" comes close to being tolerable in that it doesn't drag, but hearing Flynn scream "Let freedom ring with a shotgun blast" made me laugh unintentionally.  "I'm Your God Now" sounds mostly like a grunge song, with its saving grace being a neat guitar solo near the end.  "Real Eyes, Realize, Real Lies" sounds like a goof-off track since it's full of distorted media samples of the 1992 LA riots with mediocre riffing in the background, with Flynn screaming the song title around the middle of it.  Songs like "A Thousand Lies," "None But My Own," and "The Rage to Overcome" repeat the lame groove metal formula, and don't stick well with me.  "None But My Own" gets pretty annoying with its guitar screeches, and it makes me wonder if Disturbed picked up on that idea and aped it on their pitiful excuses for music.

PRODUCTION

Like many other groove metal albums, "Burn My Eyes" has a too clean and sterile production for a metal album, especially with the guitars and drums.  Bass isn't really audible, and worst of all, Flynn's atrocious vocals and lyrics were placed in front of everything.  This lacks the grittiness and harshness in sound that a metal album that's truly extreme would have.

FINAL WORD

This album is just the beginning of the many musical atrocities Rob Flynn would create under the Machine Head monicker.  Flynn would ultimately show his lack of conviction in future albums by shifting styles when there was a new fad to hop on (such as "The Burning Red" and "Supercharger" being nu-metal albums during the nu-metal fad), and you're better off checking Flynn's previous band, Vio-Lence.

Here's a list of metal albums to get instead of this.

Vio-Lence:  Eternal Nightmare
Pestilence:  Malleus Malleficarum
Hypnosia:  Extreme Hatred
Toxic Holocaust:  Evil Never Dies
Sepultra:  Schizophrenia
Morbid Saint:  Spectrum of Death
Kreator:  Endless Pain
Slayer:  Hell Awaits
Sodom:  Persecution Mania

Avoid this album and Machine Head at all costs, you'll be much happier in the end.

reviewText:
It's ironic that Mann was let go by her label (after being forced to buy back the album that they rejected for release in the first place)and then was prevented from participating in a best of with her own name plastered on it. This smacks of the cash in's that were so typical of record companies in the 60's and 70's (Lennon's Roots album advertised on television in the 70's is a great example of this as well). Although this practice has never gone away, it's evidently been in hibernation at Mann's old label.
Mann is a great songwriter and she certainly deserves a compilation of rare tracks and/or a best of focusing on her earlier material. This isn't it. The worst part is that she had nothing to do with this CD at all. I won't reiniterate the story (You can read Aimee's own review for that) but I will say this is so typical of an industry that treats artist's like interchangable pawns on their chess board of success. It's also indicative of the lack of respect an artist must endure.
This was given to me as a gift by a friend. I was a little startled as I didn't know that Aimee had a "new" CD planned for release. Having these "rare" tracks on CD already I thought I'd check and see what Hip-oo was up to with this collection. First the sound quality leaves quite a bit to be desired (particularly on some of the single tracks). This could be due to the source tapes that were chosen for use or the remastering itself.  The songs are haphazardly put together at best with no thought about context (and the way they are mixed here I'd say this collection is "tone deaf").
The booklet notes are probably the worst. While somewhat accurate they make it appear that Aimee actually made comments on this compilation (they were taken from old press releases and interviews for her previous material). Perhaps the most offensive part is how the author of the notes glosses over Aimee's parting with Geffen Records (Geffen essentially refused to release Bachelor #2 but refused to give the master back to Aimee unless she purchased it--essentially holding her own work hostage).
A rather sad example of corporate America at work, this is the kind of junky release that we've come to expect from the industry. That said I'd love to see the CD single tracks (like Aimee's terrific take on Pete Ham's Baby Blue) show up on a compilation put together by Aimee with good sound quality and her own comments.

I heard the song several times and hated it right away, but at first I had no idea it was Springsteen.  It doesn't sound at all like him.  It sounds like Green Day or maybe Coldplay trying to be as sappy as they can to make the biggest possible score in the pop market.

Even worse is the video.  (That was how I found out this was a Springsteen song.)  Good God.  Is this really Bruce Springsteen?  I already knew that too often, pharmaceutical commercials look like music videos, and music videos look like pharmaceutical commercials, but this video seems to be the textbook case.  You can't possibly get any more emasculated.  "Do you suffer from feminine itch?" the screen seems to ask.  "Try Magicil.  Ask your doctor for details!"

Is this really the guy who did "Darkness on the Edge of Town" and "Nebraska"?  Is he reduced to doing macho poses with an acoustic guitar on a hilltop while a camera circles around him?  Intercut with pretentious images of "girls" of all ages staring serenely and majestically into the camera?  Did he not make enough money from this previously multi-platinum albums that he has to resort to lite FM musical stylings?

This song is so bad, so syrupy, so dull, so tedious, so awful that I wouldn't listen to the rest of the album if it were given to me.

Maybe Bruce can go on tour with Celine Dion.  As for me, I wear earplugs at the gym.

"The Fight Of Moses Early And Sir Arthur McCloud" has an acoustic guitar and a synthesized violin with one of the Bee Gees singing over it. Yuck! Quick, skip to the next track! Um, OK, so now it's Simon And Garfunkel singing a B-side for "Scarborough Fair" on the most pretentiously named song ever, "Our Darling Daughter You Are, Little Cecilia Marie". Argh! Next track, quick! Damn, that keyboard is back again, this time accompanying the Jackson Five, complete with "Doo doo dah dah" lyrics. The title? "A Death In The Family"...

OK, so the obvious conclusion is that `My Brother's Blood Machine' by The Prize Fighter Inferno is awful, and I'm not going to torture you or myself by describing the rest of the album. reviewText: I enjoyed cornell's first solo album, Euphoria Morning, and even more so over time. This effort, however, is decidedly lackluster and shockingly vanilla for someone of cornell's unique songwriting ability. Everything about this album, from the packaging to the backing band to the producer, screams "mainstream" with a capital M. No quirkiness. No power. No energy. No pulse. Producer Steve Lilywhite polishes away any semblance of rough-edged texture with a sappy mix and straight-down-the-middle performances from the backup players (I knew we were in for a surprise when I recognized one of the guitarists as Paul McCartney's sideman!). The drumming is cliche, the bass is unnoticeable, the guitars are predictable, and the rest of it is simply disposable. Cornell should have gone back to his partnership with those creative cats from Eleven--their influence on Euphoria Morning was palpable and complex. He also should have asked Josh Freese, skins-beater-for-hire extraordinaire, to come in and add some punch to these flat tunes. Frankly, Cornell's career choices since he left Soundgarden have left many a former fan scratching their heads. Audioslave was fun live, but their albums are not timeless like SG's last two efforts. I thought cornell was brave to go out on a limb with the restrained tones of Euphoria Morning, but at least that work was sufficiently dark and brooding to reveal some intriguing atmosphere and subtleties on repeated listenings. This solo record seems to have been a calculated effort to move to the middle, where sales can be spiked by that elusive crossover single. My first impression after hearing this album was--"This is an album only chicks will dig." And like a quickly forgotten chick-flick, this collection of blatant superficialities will fill up the used bins all over America as disheartened rockers cash it in for pennies on the dollar. My copy's going straight to the wife. Phffft.

Of course, saying an album isn't as bad as Knocked Out Loaded is a pretty small compliment, especially for an artist of Dylan's stature.

reviewText:
Marco Uccellini is one of several obscure Italian composers who were primarily away from their native country composing for foreign courts and patrons during the early to mid-17th Century: Pandolfi and Matteis are some of the others. Andrew Manze is also one of the leading musicians in exploring previously unknown composers from the Early Baroque period. Although Uccellini is a very innovative composer with beautiful solo violin works, as I expected, Manze's shortcomings as an actual performer made the compositions themselves on this album mediocre in terms of their final execution compared to those of Nicholas McGegan and the Arcadian Group.

Manze is at it again as with every piece he performs for the Italian style that has absolutely no passion of any sort in his intepretations. They are lifeless robotic excercises and nothing more! Manze is principally an academic performer instead of a professional one and his performances sound like scale and technique lessons instead of the passionate interpretations they are supposed to be. I can't stand them as it really only appeals to violinists who need to practice the techniques that are painfully overemphasized ad nauseam in recordings such as this one! This sluggish screeching resulting from his over-methodical applications of technique sounds like a set of nails scratching the chalkboard every time. It's self-defeating really as such over-methodical performances make him sound like nothing more than an amateur compared to McGegan who essentially uses the same techniques and type of instrument but who evokes a jovialty and warmth from them that Menze struggles to reach at best.  Manze's performaces are uniformly tedious beyond belief making me want to eject instantly every time I hear one! In terms of professional performance cirlces Manze is really but an amateur as these problems have surfaced before and not just with McGegan. Compare Manze/Romanesca and Goebels/Musica Antiqua Koln for Biber's 'Mystery Sonatas' where Manze's deficiencies are again shamefully exposed. Although both he and Goebels use traditional intruments and techniques as here with McGegan, Goebels' fluid and emotive interpretation again leaves Manze sounding stuck in the mud of his own confused renditions. There's so much emphasis on historical technique with Manze it's no longer a Baroque interpretation but a literally prehistoric one instead! To listeners who care about their ears, I tell you, avoid Manze like the plague whenever possible! Run! He knows great techniques but simply doesn't know how to properly apply them for public performance and that's a fact. In short, he simply stinks as a public performer and, despite all his technical knowledge, he is ironically one of the worst solo violinists you can get for virtually anything you might want to buy!

Uccellini is one of the more creative Italian composers from the Early Baroque and McGegan's performance is a much better example of his charm and Italian warmth than this musical mausoleum of an album.  I have great respect for Manze as an innovative musicologist-violinist exploring these obscure Baroque works and the difficult techniques they demand but he is simply pathetic as a performer and that's the simple truth! He focuses so much on techniques that he limits his ability to express the lyricism they are intended to evoke in the first place. Avoid this album and get McGegan's performance as it's immesurably better than Manze's.  Avoid Manze whenever possible as he's more an academic than a public performer and, unless you want excellent violin lessons for practice, he's not really worth a dime as a performer.  I wish to add that that is only my opinion of Manze and not the other fine performers of Romanesca who are very talented and unfortunately somewhat reduced by their lead.

In short, the only people who tend to like Sloan are Canadian nationalists, who refuse to put as much effort into appreciating bands from other nations, especially the US.  If they did, they'd realize this band has long overstayed its welcome.  I really liked the song "Coax Me" back in 1994, when I was 14 years old.  That was until I bought the album "Twice Removed" (1994) from which it came.  All the songs on that album turned out to have terrible lyrics, including "Coax Me", and the music just wasn't very compelling or original.  Sloan just sounds like a modern band trying to imitate The Beatles.
Not only are the lyrics awful and nonsensical and not only is the music dull, but each band member takes turns at singing really badly, with little range or subtlety.  I was willing to forgive them in 1994, only a few years after they started and were idiotically heralded as Canada's Nirvana -- yet again proving nationalists' strong yearning to live up to the US, while disliking it so.  However, based on their singles output, they have proven themselves unable to grow at all, and remain -- to this day -- in the stagnant status of a second-rate band, unable to attract attention abroad (not because of any nationalism in other countries) or even win major success among Canadians (despite the massive bias here).
Now "The Arcade Fire" is a Canadian band that has won acclaim internationally, but not the deserved attention from a domestic music industry hellbent on finding Canadian versions of superficial, money-making pop in the US -- Avril Lavigne, Nickelback, Sum 41, Simple Plan, Fefe Dobson, etc, which have all met with undeserved praise and awards.  Unlike Sloan and these other performers, The Arcade Fire is truly something original and special.  Check it out.

This album is the stiffest, stalest, and more importantly, most boring album ZZ Top has ever made.

The drum machines, the bass, the overcompressed guitars, the songwriting, the production... everything is done wrong. It feels like ZZ Top has turned into three Frankenstein's monsters, or that they're made out of rock. Not rock 'n' roll, but stone.

"Poke Chop Sandwich" would be good if the stiff production hadn't been there, and if the band could muster up some energy. Instead, the whole song is ruined and the band sounds and feels much older than they actually are.

Also, these "live takes" at the end... are they really live performances? They sound very similar to the other songs, features the same overprocessed guitars, the same stiff production... is it even ZZ Top performing?

Some say "Eliminator" is stiff because of its drum machines. This is way, way, WAY worse. If you want a good ZZ Top album from the 90's, don't buy this. Get "Antenna" or "Rhythmeen" instead.

reviewText:
A total disappointment and an absolutely horrendous waste of money!!! And I take full responsibility because I listened to all the posters out there, that gave the 5.1 piece of garbage, included in this box, such stellar reviews!!!
I have owned the original "Rhino" 5.1 DVD-Audio of this album, since it first came out, in 2000 and I never had any complaints about it. Then this "mess" got released, so of course, I HAD to have it!!! Yes, I am a completist. Besides the "Rhino", I have the 2007 "SHOUT FACTORY" edition, simply for the packaging (closest thing to the original album, without having to mortgage my house, in order to buy a Japanese SHM-cd copy!) And finally, I have the triple disc, 2014 "Razor & Tie" edition........I - should - have - stopped - there.
This is a six disc set. So let's go through them, shall we...
Disc 1 CD - Original album (Remastered) - already included in the triple disc 2014 "Razor & Tie" edition.
Disc 2 CD - The Alternate "BSS" - already included in the triple disc 2014 "Razor & Tie" edition.
Disc 3 CD - New 2014 Stereo Version of "BSS" on CD - not included anywhere else, so BINGO!!! - something useful!!!
Disc 4 DVD-A - Super Sonic "BSS"
  a) Original Mix in Stereo - already included in the triple disc 2014 "Razor & Tie" edition.
  b) New 2014 Stereo Mix - already included in the triple disc 2014 "Razor & Tie" edition.
  c) MLP Lossless 5.1 Mix/Dolby Digital 5.1 Mix/DTS 5.1 Mix - not included anywhere else, THANK GOD!!! I LOVE both the original
  mix and the new 2014 stereo mix of "BSS" but these 5.1's leave MUCH to be desired!!! What REALLY kills it for me is the
  opening bars of "Karn Evil 9 3rd Impression"!!! WHERE is the great, triumphant sounding keyboard melody? Why did Jakszyk bury
  it so far beneath the thunderous sounds of the Moog? It totally ruins the whole "feel" of the song!!!!!!!!! He left the stereo version
  intact!!! Why did he have to screw up the 5.1?!!!!! THIS, in particular, ruins this whole boxset, for me!!!!!!!!!
Disc 5 DVD-V - Extra "BSS"
  a) The Manticore Special Documentary - Ridiculously worthless and boring. Might have been slightly better if there was even a hint
  of an attempt to remaster and generally clean up the footage they had to work with!!!
  b) Gallery of Stills - Same pictures that are in the booklet, included in the set. Again, worthless.
Disc 6 Original Album (180gm Vinyl LP) - WHAT IS IT WITH VINYL?!!!!!!!!! What are we, in the Dark Ages? THIS travesty could have ONLY been
  excusable IF they had at least replicated the original quad-fold sleeve, down to the last detail!!! They
  most miserably, did NOT!!!
To sum up, in reality, I paid about $100.00 for one (1) CD. That being Disc 3 (New 2014 Stereo Mix on CD)!!! And it is the ONLY reason I do not send the whole boxset back!!! ALL FIVE of the other discs, in the set, are to me, WORTHLESS!!!
***I've been thinking lately that I should edit my review because, for all I know, I might have gotten a defective DVD-A, in my set. Can ANYBODY who owns this particular edition, please tell me EXACTLY what you hear, when you play the first 30 to 45 seconds of the last track (Karn Evil 9 3rd Impression) in 5.1? Does it sound, ANYTHING like the original album or even the 2014 stereo remix? My copy certainly does NOT!!! The whole mix is backwards!!! The triumphant-sounding keyboard melody is inaudible and the explosive background moog parts are WAY out, in front and obnoxiously loud!!!
If this is the way it's SUPPOSED to sound, I think someone needs to call Steve Wilson, like yesterday and have him redo this entire car wreck over again!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
