reviewText:
Upon the release of her new album "A Public Affair," singer Jessica Simpson severely injured a vocal chord, an appropriate event considering the quality of her album.

Since she infiltrated the music scene during the bubblegum renaissance of the early 2000s, she has been an average singer masquerading as a serious vocalist, and "A Public Affair" spotlights this so blatantly that a free pair of sunglasses should come with purchase.

The title track and lead single is either a rip-off or tribute (depending on your level of cynicism) to the post-disco pop that aided the careers of divas such as Madonna or Janet Jackson, complete with shameless theft from the former musical maven. Indeed, mixing the best parts of the icon's two early '80s smashes, "Holiday" and "Lucky Star," would yield the layout for "A Public Affair," complete with the same oh-so-addictive guitar licks and spaced-out synths.

Simpson's vocals are atrocious and the lyrics are bargain bin mumbo jumbo, setting the standard for the rest of the disc.

Things hardly improve with her cover of Dead or Alive's "You Spin Me Round (Like a Record)." Few classic dance songs of the past 20 or so years have been so over-exposed, making this choice for a cover ill-advised. Still, one would think a credible singer would be able to make it her own, but Simpson's limp, mechanized vocals are drowned out by walls of insipid production.

One aspect of the album that stands out is its clear aversion to the half-baked adult-contemporary goop of 2003's "In This Skin." Where an eloquent piano solo might have accentuated Simpson then, frothy dance beats now reside. Whether or not this is a positive change is up to personal taste, but without a good voice, Simpson's material remains invariably inferior.

To make matters worse, the subject matter on the record often crosses the line from ridiculous to flat out embarrassing. "Push Your Tush" promotes stereotypes of what those in rustic areas do for fun, complete with hoedowns, country hicks, joysticks and cock-a-doodle-dos, while the likes of "Between You and I" and "B.O.Y." (a musical diss obviously directed at ex-hubby Nick Lachey) seem straight out of the diary of an 11-year-old.

Her cover of Patty Griffin's "Let Him Fly" is more a blatant attempt to cash in on the media blitz surrounding the dissolution of her marriage than it is even a decent vocal performance. Meanwhile, "I Belong To Me," the controversial last-minute addition to the album, is quite reminiscent of sister Ashlee's 2005 song, "I Am Me."

Mighty self-absorbed, aren't we girls?

Overall, the reasons to buy "A Public Affair" are few and far between, especially when Mariah Carey, Celine Dion and Whitney Houston are still living and breathing. Even on her best day, Simpson would be no match for the dynamic vocal prowess these women possess. Buy one of their albums instead.
label: negative

reviewText:
This is the finest album of the past 45 years and just as X & Y celebrated the unconscious coupling of Chris and Gwyneth, this album mourns their conscious uncoupling. The way Coldplay have evolved (particularly Chris Martin) over the past decade or so is nothing short of a miracle of biblical proportions and it makes Bowie's perpetual evolution during the 1970's look amateurish in comparison. With this album Chris Martin proves that his song writing skills match those of Lennon/McCartney, Bacharach/David, Brian Wilson, Bob Dylan, etc. And let's not forget about his pitch perfect vocals. The finest falsetto in popular music since the Bee Gees' Barry Gibb, he hits the high notes every time.

Forget about Dylan's Blood on the Tracks, Gaye's Here, My Dear and Springsteen's Tunnel of Love because this is the ultimate conscious uncoupling album. It's an emotional roller coaster. It will top every end of year poll and it will forever be mentioned in the same breath as the likes of Revolver, Pet Sounds, What's Going On and Astral Weeks. Haunting, heart-breaking, boring, wonderful, dull, melancholic - call it what you want but this is an era defining and ground breaking album that reinvents the wheel as far as popular music is concerned.  In a word: Avoid!

reviewText: Am I dead? Seriously? What is with all this "its misunderstood" and "its good in its own right"? No true Pink Floyd fan could justify this album. Believe me when I say I am normally a respectful and tactful person open to other opinions, but not in this case. I have immense respect for Roger and his ATTEMPT to be lyrically vulnerable and creative. But that's just it. It was only an ATTEMPT and a failed one!!! Just because this album is emotional and tells a story DOES NOT MEAN IT IS GOOD!!!!  It is a joke as far as Pink Floyd is concerned. Go ahead and try to convince yourself that this isn't the worst so called Pink Floyd album. I'd rather blast my brain with the studio disc from UMMAGUMMA or THE ENDLESS RIVER all day long!! Many will say that the Gilnlmour led stuff like AMLOR isn't real Pink Floyd either. Yes it us and here's why. Meaningful lyrics but MUSIC COMES FIRST. Powerful sonic ambiance. And most importantly, even if only featured on some tracks, the band still regained their secret weapon: Richard Wright. Now I won't kid myself and say the songs on FINAL CUT themselves would have been any better had Rick played on them, but at least they would have sounded sonically interesting and listenable like UMMAGUMMA. The only real acclaim this album deserves is that despite how many of us wish to God it didn't happen, it had to so four years later, AMLOR could happen. If not for how terrible this album was, Dave and Roger would have tolerated each other for a few more mediocre albums before they ended up making something just as bad as this one anyway. Good thing they got this awful album out of the way quickly so Dave and Roger could just butt heads for the last time and be done with it before Floyd redeemed themselves with AMLOR, which despite the lack of Roger is an absolutely phenomenal 11 out of 10 album and the best Floyd release since Animals.  If you like this album, good for you. If you can even tolerate it, good for you. But don't say it doesn't deserve the harsh criticism it gets because it does, at least when it's coming from true Floyd fans.

reviewText: Beautiful playing, gorgeous sound.  That will only take us so far.  Abbado's rhythms have no spring to them, the orchestral colors are homoganized, the whole thing sounds slack.  This isn't just a matter of tempi, although Abbado's are on the slow side.  It's a matter of vision.  Abbado here gives us an overly-romatic, non-ideomatic interpretation.  There's little here of the Brahms who took long walks, smoked cigars and had to make his own coffee because no-one else made it strong enough for him.  There's even less of the Brahms who sought the fusion of romantic sentiment into classical form. I've played this symphony and listened to many interpretations, and this is one doesn't suit my taste or what I read in the notes I played.  For a bracing alternative, check out Klemperer's account on EMI, or Walter's, or Horenstein's.  Even Bernstein gives us more authentic Brahms than this.  Two stars for the orchestra and engineers.

reviewText: Where in the world did Meghan Trainor come from?!? Don't get me wrong, it's not like I expect there to be coherent logic to what happens in this world, or to understand how and why this barely-out-of-her-teens artist landed all over mainstream radio. It's hard to even IMAGINE pop music getting any more irritating than what Meghan Trainor presents on this 4-song atrocity. The lyrics to "All About That Bass" are a mindless variant on the idea that you should be proud of your body even if you're overweight. Folks, this subject matter is nothing new--Sir-Mix-a-Lot's smash hit "Baby Got Back", the same general thematic, came out BACK IN 1992. HELLO. The wordless "doo-wop" style backing vocals are about as out of place as ketchup on an Oreo cookie. YES, I REALIZE that we live in a Photoshop-crazy world, and that girls can socialize unrealistic expectations of what they're supposed to look like, a problem which trickles into various aspects of our world, potentially to hugely damaging effect. Having self-respect is of paramount importance, but the juvenile lyrics to "All About That Bass" miss that point entirely. That said, the lyrics to the song "Title" are perhaps even more inane--what's ironic is that, while "All About That Bass" is supposedly about having self-respect, the lyrics on "Title" present the narrator as an aspiring boy-toy with no self-respect whatsoever. That just adds to the hypothesis that this is incoherent, bottom-of-the-barrel, thrown-together drivel. Oh, and for any guys out there--if your girlfriend plays you the song "Dear Future Husband", with its self-righteous one-sided lyrics, that should be an instant red flag for you to call any potential wedding off ON THE SPOT. Meghan Trainor must have a very well-off family that was able to work out some backroom shenanigans to give her a ludicrous amount of promotion to help launch her to superstardom. I mean, I don't hear people going all crazy about the song Sexy Lady [Explicit], which SHOULD have been the female anthem of 2014, a true honoring of not just a woman's beauty, but a woman's BRAIN, not to mention the infectious uptempo beat and awesome guitar riffs. So much music comes out these days, and this time, I am truly BAFFLED at the prominence that Meghan Trainor has attained. This music is horrendous. The only explanation I can come up with is that, perhaps more than ever, people continue to be slaves to the power of million-dollar marketing, and with enough marketing power, ANY song can become a hit. TURN OFF Meghan Trainor, and TURN ON Sexy Lady [Explicit] for a REAL taste of how to pay tribute to women's bodies AND brains.

Generic metal riffs, clunky, rhythmically stunted drumming combined with vocals that sound as though Lou recorded them without listening to the backing tracks don't add up to a worthwhile or enjoyable listening experience. The lyrics are often embarrassing too. "Breezes" rhymed with "treezes", "I am the table"?!? come on dammit.

I don't fault Lou Reed and Metallic for trying something new and confound fan expectations by breaking out of the box. However neither party brought their A game to this failure. James, Kirk and Robert serve up a platter of 3rd rate repetitive metal riffs while Lars pummels his drums with all the creativity of a chimp. Unfortunately I don't think they're capable of breaking out of their particular box. It doesn't sound as though they tried very hard either. Lou Reed is a different case. But on Lulu he sounds disengaged and his lyrics are not among his best. This is a supposed concept album about a young girl who becomes a prostitute but after reading the lyrics I found it hard to grasp the concept or actually care. Perhaps if I saw the play the music would make more sense contextually. But even so there are bigger problems with Lulu. The music and vocals don't add up to a synergistic whole. They fight each other the entire time. Which makes Lulu a failure emotionally, intellectually, and musically. I'm afraid that Metallica and Lou Reed simply don't work well together. Not every collaboration works.

Btw I can't wait for the new Cher/Cannibal Corpse project. I hear that one is really going to rock!

reviewText: However lamentable it may be, it is no secret that few opera aficionados give a damn about the conductor, especially outside the realm of Wagner's stage works (and to a lesser extent Mozart's). Yet this recording of Carmen has little to recommend it aside from the name of the conductor, Leonard Bernstein, and sad to say, even his work is disappointing. The underlinings, exaggerations, and overemphases in which he indulges (often at the expense of the shape of a page or a whole scene), his neglect of the work's authentic performing tradition, and his use of an edition (Fritz Oeser's) that places the burden of large tracts of spoken dialogue upon a cast that was clearly uncomfortable speaking French--these factors and several others contribute to an interpretation that quickly passes from stunning to irritating. This is a Carmen surrounded and driven by celebrity. It was based on a September 1972 staging of the opera that was to be directed by the Metropolitan Opera's then new general manager, Gran Gentele, whose regime this new production was meant to christen (Gentele, alas, was killed, along with two of his three daughters, in a traffic accident in Sardinia in July 1972). One aspect of the production's guiding ethos--a turning of the back upon Rudolf Bing and upon Bing's decades at the company's helm--was the fact that its two leading singers (Horne and McCracken) had never sung their roles before. With the death of Gentele and the decision to place the staging in the hands of one of the Met's staff directors (a collection of nonentities that Eileen Farrell, using unrepeatable, un-PC language that would get her into very hot water today, derisively described as "skinny [boys] with clipboards"), it was hardly surprising that the bulk of critical attention devolved upon the superstar conductor, Leonard Bernstein, who had been engaged to direct the musical aspects of the production. Was it likely that the competition-averse Lennie--not yet the demigod he has since become and still a focus of contention in New York's musical life, in which he wanted to retain an important place despite his departure from the Philharmonic a few years earlier--would fail to note these circumstances, especially in light of the fact that it was almost universally taken for granted by the opera fans of the day that the casting was a disaster in the making? Indeed, Bernstein's assent to conducting Carmen was contingent upon the agreement of a reluctant Deutsche Grammophon to record the production. (Those familiar with the Met of that period will recall that its chorus was habitually dreadful--the chorus that sings on the recording under review is largely made up of freelancers--and this factor was but one of several that lay behind DG's reluctance to invest a small fortune on what it correctly thought would be a white elephant.) As for the principals, the whole is less than the sum of the parts. Horne was then at or near the very peak of her career, as was McCracken (whatever his vocal deficiencies, he was a serious and frequently insightful artist, as admirers of Barbirolli's Otello know). Their performances, however, suggest that they failed to understand the characters or else were badly directed. With his rugged voice and bold temperament, Tom Krause should have been an ideal Escamillo, yet this role turned out to be one of his few failures (his earlier Escamillo, for Schippers, was better but still not so good as it might have been). Since he shortly afterwards sang Guglielmo splendidly in Solti's first recording of Cos Fan Tutte, blaming the musical and dramatic direction he received here is as reasonable a recourse as any. Adriana Maliponte is quite an adequate Micaela, but as the part has been brilliantly sung by Freni, Cotrubas, Donath, and (perhaps best of all) Martha Angelici, adequacy simply won't do. Still, her performance is the best thing on this set. Carmen's popularity, as enormous as it is justified, tends to make any recording of the opera the object of widespread acclaim, yet fans need to be aware that far better versions may easily be found. In particular, the many admirers of Horne, Krause, McCracken, and, yes, Bernstein should know that this recording is best forgotten. For notable performances by these esteemed artists, one had best look elsewhere. Bernstein's gifts suited him perfectly for the lyric theater, and we are the poorer for his relative absence from it. Unfortunately, his character and temperament were largely at odds with his gifts, and the range of operatic repertory he chose to perform ended up being limited by both his musical prejudices and his patent requirement (once he was past his apprentice and journeyman days) that he be the uncontested center of attention in every project in which he took part.

reviewText:
Once upon a time, there was a new young singer named Faith Hill who took the world by storm with her country pop stylings.  At that time the mainstream was largely vanilla-sh pop, but the nation had not yet tired of it.  If you wanted Please Remember Me you had to buy Tim McGraw's cd.  Flash forward to 2005--now Rodney Crowell is sold at Wal-mart.  This brave new world of music is an unfortunate place for Faith Hill to make her return to stripped down, accoustic music.

Faith Hill has always had an amazing voice, and that is still present here.  However, she has always been a remarkably bad cover artist--witness her rendition of "Piece Of My Heart."  The big mistake she makes here is trying to cover three songs by Lori McKenna.  She storms through them with her usual gusto, oblivious to the idea that many of us have already heard the originals.  In 1993, when she was selling "Piece Of My Heart" to 17 year olds, that stratedgy worked.  However, in 2005, when she is selling to an older fan base and Americana is mainstream, it does not.  On "Stealing Kisses" she fails to capture the weary ache the song requires.  She doesn't have the ache required for "If You Ask."

It is ironic that she choses to end the album with a torch ballad, because she is very much like what Whitney Otto called "those fey white girls" who sang jazz classics in the 40's.  A hollowed out rendition of her genre who just doesn't seem to get it.

reviewText:
I had hoped that a few things would happen regarding the score for this production. One was that more musicians would be hired for the recording. That didn't happen. Then I really hoped (and rather expected) that more musicians would be hired for the Roundabout Broadway revival. That, sadly, did not happen either.

Perhaps I'm unfairly comparing this production to the original, which I grew up on, but to my ear this recording sounds thin and the orchestra sounds lifeless. A shame, considering the extreme passion of the performers. But, even there, I feel that the tinny quality of the orchestra negatively affects the performances, as well. The supporting cast is good in Act One and intolerable in Act Two. The very deliberate American accents (most of them an odd combination of Southern and Western, despite the fact that this portion takes place in Chicago) are simply embarrassing, and get in the way of the performances.

Jenna Russell is a stunning Dot and possibly (probably) the only person who could make me actually forget Bernadette Peters' performance for the time being. Daniel Evans, while very impressive, is a little too effusive for the "cold" George of Act One. While this may have been a tactic to prove that he is not, in fact, a cold artist, one can't quite seem to understand, based on Evans' performance, why others would consider him to be cold. However, his performance in the second act finally meets Jenna Russell's.

It's a shame that these two performances should be captured in such a shoddy recording.

reviewText: Man, this is awful stuff. I have no idea what the unusually talented Gabriel was thinking. But, this is one tough listen. If it was his intention to put his personal stamp on the works of artists he has admired, then, at that level, I suppose he has succeeded. There can be no confusing his version with the original. However, his take is invariably dour and enervating, while adding nothing and subtracting much from the power of the original recordings. One, for example, is Paul Simon's astonishing "Graceland" opener "The Boy in the Bubble". The song, while tinged with irony, and even, perhaps, anger, at the distressing paradoxes of late 20th century life, nonetheless pulsates with energy and an undeniable beauty. The music contrasts the inherent sadness of the message, but never wallows in it. Gabriel's funereal approach not only destroys this contrast, but pretty much loses the melodic content as well. One could go on song by song, but why bother? Gabriel's covers are consistently monolithic and monolithically consistent. Let's hope that he never again feels impelled to approach the material of others. Unless he's hit a dry spell in his own creativity, he has no need to do so.

reviewText:
Let me start by stating that I am a Dickey Betts fan.  I first discovered Dickey via the Allman Brothers Band, of course, and I remain an ABB fan, too.  But I've purchased every Dickie Betts solo effort, with my favorites being the first Great Southern release and Pattern Disruptive.  I also like Seven Turns by the ABB, which strikes me as essentially the Dickey Betts album that would have followed Pattern Disruptive, with Gregg Allman added soemwhere during the recording process to covert it to an ABB album.  Without knowing, I always assumed that neither Pattern Disruptive nor Gregg Allman's Just Before the Bullets Fly sold very well and that management or record company executives "encouraged" Gregg and Dickey to reform the band.  I'm only speculating on that, though.

I purchased this DVD precisely because I am a Dickey Betts fan, and I was hoping for a great performance.  I kind of presumed that Dickey would want to show the ABB how great he still is, kind of an "up yours" in response to their decision to fire him.

Instead (and I'm surprised that not one of the earlier reviewers mentioned this), Dickie shows up drunk and gives a terrible performance.  Isn't that precisely why the ABB fired this founding member?

The result?  Dickie growls/yells rather than sings his vocals.  Dickie's timing is off on what should be unison/harmony guitar lines with Dan Toler.  Dickie plays unimaginitive and repetitive solos (...yes, he's always been repetitive, but that was countermanded by his creativity...).  And Dickie slowed some of the tunes down to a lethargic pace, I presume because when he's wasted he can't play them at their more appropriate and energetic pace.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, I guess, but I am surprised that this disc has gotten any ratings higher than 3 stars.  For me, it's zero stars, and disposed of.

reviewText: Was really looking forward to a fresh take on the new Robocop score, something with power, emotion and character that paid homage to the original brilliant film music.  This is nothing more than repetitive ticking electronic whirring and shallow percussion that tries ever so hard to evoke an industrial spin on The Dark Knight or Tron: Legacy.  Other than the clubbed out version of the original Poledouris theme on the title card, this entire score is forgettable.  Had Bromfman used the effort put into this piece elsewhere in the score, he could have created something magical.  There is no theme carried throughout the music - at all.  The only highlight is Vallon's Warehouse which has a nice rhythm to it, but ends up shallow and simplistic with chomps, riffs and crunches to round it out.  It could have been a truly outstanding piece had he added the raw depth of a suite of organic orchestration to it.  I hate to compare this to the original film, but the natural orchestra of Poledouris' music and brilliant industrial creativity (banging on fire extinguishers) grounded Robocop to his human side with a tie to the machine.  This score is full on electronica, cold, repetitive, predictable and most of all rushed with zero creativity.  If you are not going to put any emotion or signature theme into a movie score, then why bother - other than to add a title to your resume?

reviewText:
This is Ultravox watered down. With the sacking of their multi-intrumentalist/drummer Warren Cann the band took a departure from strong synth rock and delved into a miasma of schlock. This is the most overdone, overproduced, and underwhelming music the Ure era Ultravox ever produced. And the records that followed were equally abyssmal.

This album has a lot of good song ideas, but the execution is that of Ure's 70's band Slik. It is so syrupy sweet and shallow, despite the heavy topicality of such songs as "All Fall Down", that is warrants nothings but going into a CD shredder upon acquiring. The music has such a depth to it that one could compare it accurately to a kiddie wading pool. With the absence of Cann in the mix the band detours into Midge Ure solodome that true listeners of the 80's era Ultravox vomit a little in their mouths with each playing.

Do you think I am being too harsh about this product? Compare this to anything else released during the Ure era of Ultravox in the 80's and even the NEW live CD of Return to Eden, then you may see/hear exactly where I am coming from. This does not hold up. THis does not age well. This looks rediculous amoung one's CD collection.

The extra tracks do NOT make up for the overall inital release. B-side are equally as tarnished and lacking any real attractive quality. This is nothing like their earlier B-sides like Paths and Angles, I Never Wanted To Begin, or even the highly experimental Break Your Back or Overlook.

If you know someone with a copy, listen to it. If you just cannot live without this addition to your collection, then by all means break down and buy it. Otherwise steer clear of this pink attrocity. It will scar the ears and memories of a true fan. It did me.

reviewText:
Since apparently Ryan Bingham's "new thing" is speaking plainly, monochromatically, and directly with no sugar-coat, I'll do the same here. After all, I'm the one who's been duped. I guess now that I'm not "getting it", I'm one of those entitled fools he's raging about, right?

I wouldn't one-star something unless I feel pretty confident repeated listens won't redeem my gut instinct, and here's a case where that instinct is all you need to follow. Replacing his usual understated elegance with an edge would have been one thing, but punishing his listeners with the cartoonish bash of bar chords, ambiguous and politically-doctrinaire lyrics, f-bombs out of the ICP Book of Subtlety, and impressionistic takes on capital-C Classic Rock are an entirely different story.  This album is the most unnerving, left-field crash-and-burn I've ever been fooled into waiting for. It would be mighty unfair to compare "Tomorrowland" to his previous three masterpieces, but it's pretty apparent he didn't intend to follow that path either, he'd rather make a "Statement". Fair enough.

This album is such an arrogant mess it's hard to lay blame on a single specific problem. The music itself is like a whiny drill that never ends, without a single place to come up for air. Apparently he feels the only way he can be heard above the din is to make his own screech, to compete head-on with the "wasteland" he used to not be interested in. And it's all a charade: "Never Far Behind" and "Western Shore" build a distant theme until you realize it's bait, you're just waiting around for the band to come crashing in, reeeeal heavy and thick, with no ability to let something unfold without narrating it with MORE slowly-building torrential chordage for emphasis. (Opener "Beg for Broken Legs" also uses this prop, and results in being the most hilarious thing I've listened to in years.) "Flower Bomb" is a yelp away from being an outtake off "The Rising", which is okay I suppose, but when Tom Petty's "Runnin' Down a Dream" is aped two tracks later (with more linear bar chords), you begin to get the point. Halfway through, I saw this as a full-on nosedive so complete, so comical that I had to laugh at "Guess Who's Knockin" and its Eric Church/arena-ready yelps designed to produce the inevitable "WOOOOO!!" from section 403. "HOW YOU DOIN OUT THERE, TAMPAAAAAAA!" And speaking of talking to his audience, the lyrics here are INCESSANT - everything is full of noise and chatter and on and on and on. By the time "Rising From the Ghetto" faded out on the chaotic mess of delay/space-echo guitar squall and bashing-over-your-head drums, I was exhausted and didn't care.

I get it, I guess. He's angry, he's mad, and he's got a bunch of new pedals he wants to try out to go along with the Marshall 8x10 cabinets. Good for him, but we're the ones that have to make the most effort here. We either get with his new program, or we get the single-digit salute he gives all over the place. But the only reason I stuck it out until "Too Deep To Fill" brought back a guilt-laden nostalgia is because this was a Ryan Bingham album. Or so I thought.

reviewText: First off, I am an EJ fan.  I own everything he's recorded.  Nevertheless, I also try and be objective and this review is more for the casual/beginning fan who may not be familiar with Elton's entire catalog.  That said, Empty Sky is very much an album for Elton enthusiasts.  It's a  sort of curio piece (or artifact) that only rabid EJ fans will find  listenable.  In truth, Empty Sky's only value is the glimpse it shows  listeners of Elton's origins.  Skyline Pigeon, is the one worthy track on  this thing.  From failed psycadelia (Empty Sky) to dull, cheerless, false  antiquity (Valhalla, the Scaffold), this is an effort that reflects the  times (late 60's) and Elton's attempt to compete with all of the other once  popular (and now utterly forgotten) "time capsule",  mock-atmospheric oddities such as Procol Harum or the Moody Blues.  Elton  was very much trying to find himself, musically, and he hadn't yet realized  his true gift: the ability to pen unbelievably catchy pop songs.

reviewText:
Fischer-Dieskau is absolutely dead wrong for Hans Sachs.  Physically, personally, it is difficult to think of a way in which he is not objectionable.  His Hans Sachs is just what Hans Sachs stands against: overrefined, overcontrolled, utterly un-vulgar.  Pretty.  Not that I have anything against a melodic high-midrange baritone singing Sachs if he has the necessary volume--Otto Weiner did a beautiful job under Keilberth's baton at Bayreuth.  But why didn't DFD play Beckmesser???  He played Fritz Kothner at Bayreuth (and shamelessly attempted to steal the first act by making every syllable sound oh so meaningful) but Beckmesser is the natural role for him: all flourishes, affectation, and head voice.  Flutey and snooty.

Placido Domingo puts so much of his time and energy into an heroic but failed attempt to get the German accent and intonation right that he has nothing left for acting.  The result sounds foreign AND unfeeling.  The German problem has something to do with the way Wagner singers back off unstressed syllables (the schwa vowell) but still make them heard, without disrupting the vocal line.  Some non-Germans get this right and some don't.  Matti Salminen, for instance, does. Jess Thomas does. James Morris does sometimes.  Domingo doesn't.

Some listeners argue that Walther is SUPPOSED to sound like an outsider.  Sure but not like a Spaniard.

Eva sounds shrill and sings without body.

Even Pogner (Peter Lagger) sounds unsure of himself.

I honestly don't understand why anyone likes this recording.
label: negative

reviewText:
James Carter seems to be apart of a new class of jazz musicians who don't understand the importance of making good music. Now granted many people probably dig this, but I don't. Here's why: anytime you have somebody like Carter, who is way overrated, you're going to have a lot of expectations, because the press and record companies create hype. I have never listened to what the critics say, because 1. most of them don't understand the music to begin with and 2. they think their opinion is some kind of grand thing when it's just an opinion just like mine. This album didn't do anything but solidify the fact that jazz today seems to have lost direction. That's why I'm so thankful for Thelonious Monk, Bill Evans, Ben Webster, Coleman Hawkins, Stan Getz, Zoot Sims, Paul Desmond, etc. They had the taste and refinement to make great music.

James Carter is just another modern jazz musician who doesn't have the know how, brains, or ability to make meaningful music. "In Carterian Fashion" is only further proof of that notion.

reviewText: John Lennon's greatest legacy might have been captured on record and in the film The US vs. John Lennon, but it certainly wasn't in this collection. Lackluster and soulless covers mar this work, making me need to reach for the original versions. From the wispy, weak vocals of Avril Lavigne sadly given the task of covering Imagine, to the non-descript cover of Working Class Hero from Green Day, this album is a big miss. Even the normally touching vocals of Youssou N'Dour miss their mark with a reading of Jealous Guy that only makes me jealous of people who haven't suffered through this collection. Who told Youssou to whistle? Oh please! Perhaps saddest of all is that two CDs are taken up for one decent song. Lenny Kravitz is the only artist to bring any soul to the project with a spirited, funky version of Cold Turkey. Flaming Lips do a respectable (Just LIke) Starting Over, but their originals are far better. The intention is good, but if you want to help the Sudanese people pull out your old John Lennon records and play them while you write a check for the retail price of this disc to Amnesty Interntational or another aid organization. And if you really want to get a taste of the sound of Sudan, check out the far more provocative Ceasefire album from Emanuel Jal (one time child soldier) and Abdel Gadir Salim, released in 2005 on Riverboat.

reviewText:
Villa-Lobos (wrote a famous piece or series of pieces called Brasil something or other, had a copy years ago, would put anybody to sleep, sort of indifferently bad, but not unlistenable) judging by this CD couldn't have written worse piano music if that had been his intention.

Hamelin is good, but I'm fed up with buying him playing things I never heard of, and hating them!  His Shostakovich PCs are breath-takingly beautiful and wonderful.  But that and his ancient Wigmore concert are about everything I can stand by him!  And I have a whole damn shelf full of his CDs!  Cziffra, Wild, Howard all play(ed) Chopin and Liszt, and they're wonderful.  But isn't there any middle ground between oft-heard warhorses and this horrible stuff?

I don't recommend this CD to anyone except people who simply like modern music which I don't.  I suppose Villa-Lobos is modern, don't know his dates.  Sounds it.  Hamelin as everyone knows is great.  So if you like this kind of thing, I can at least say that it is perfectly played.

After writing this, I went through my collection of Hamelin.  I was wrong.  There are lots of beautiful things there (this turkey not being one of them, the already garnered "unhelpful" notwithstanding).  There is Alkan (lots of him), Liszt, Hamelin's own compositions, a collection of pieces by pianist/composers, and others.  And there was (though no longer) a desecration of Chopin's Etudes by Godowsky with more arpeggios in it than I've ever heard in one place before.  (There's a remark for the "unhelpfuls" who don't write comments of their own to get their fangs into.  Lay on, MacDuff!)

reviewText:
As strange as it may sound as minister for health in rural Australia, I was asked to reduce the number of h.i.v infections in the region I represent. I asked my Canadian counterparts for advise and they were only to happy to send me over 1000 "educational kits" related to being sexually and globally educated. Inside each kit was a condom and compact disc of the band Propagandhi with the title being "Less Talk More Rock."
  Now perhaps I should back up here a bit. This part of Australia only recently got television (black and white).  Most people here don't know what a compact disc is, and the  brief instructions in the educational kit said "enjoy some music while having safe sex."
  The problem with good ideas from elitists is that the simple folk in nowhereville, Australia stretched the condom between two fence posts to make a twanging sound they could hum too, and awkwardly the males placed the compact disc on their genitals to prevent conception. Mr Cooper of Wagga said " My god this makes a good contraceptive, feels like i'm having sex with a carrot grater." Other men were badly cut up, with doctors seeming to have the giggles when certain patients said they had actually forced themselves through the round window. It was however these doctors who informed the population that the condom was not the musical instrument and that in fact there were machines that could produce music when the compact disc was inserted into such a device. At first this all seemed like more Canadian bull, but in time the population were introduced to music produced by a compact disc and the rather more comfortable condom. However yet another problem was to occur. This was summed up by Mrs Winterbottom a sprightly 72 year old from Burke (Central New South Wales) she says, " I was all ready for bit of romance and so was me husband. We had just set up our compact disc player to fill the room with joy full glory to the lord when on come the most unholy racket. Lyrics about men having you know what with other men, and all this talk about how to make money out of investing in oil............ Well this sort of nonsense may be for all those fruitcakes in Sydney, constantly dressing up in wigs and underwear and wondering which toilet they should use, but here in the country we have standards!"
  Regretfully my constituents  have spoken, and we are sending the kits off to New Zealand who we are also selling our black and white televisions too, as we update to colour.
  Regards minister for health Mr. Snicko

reviewText:
Beep Bloop! Eeep Doopie Squoop!

Hey, and I think there's a message inside here. It's like a Cracker Jack box, but then my hands are all sticky afterward and I get caramel all over the decoder goggles. It's a sick sort of sweetness, like I'm a tummy full of bees and lemonade, swirling and buzzing back up against the floor, glassy-eyed, sweat-drenched. A soggy couch surfer heaved out of the roaring jaws of Earth onto the chalky asphalt, a clown for the rush-hour crowd.

Coming from the currently en vogue school of dragging everything out of the toy box at recess and overwhelming the playmates, "Embryonic" isn't so much mid-development as mid-prog. By which I mean King Crimson covered this in 1966 -- and without the need for all the Capt. Beefheart send-ups. And, sorry to disappoint you, but Pink Floyd's got our rink's laser light night covered just fine, fellas. Yeah, it was a one-time fee. I can't afford to take on you boys, too, not in this down economy, you understand.

So go back to the drawing board, go shopping for a new suit if it helps you feel any better about your most recent failure, get a new gimmick because rolling over the crowd in a globe used to be funny, but now that it's been reported that Kim Jong Il does this at his performances, it's sort of passe. Let Kim have this one and you ... how about you find a way to squeeze your body into a peanut butter jar and let somebody else take over vocals and free up the rest of the band from your totalitarian rule.

reviewText:
Let's be honest-- most singers do their best work in the first decade of their career. If they're really talented they might have a second decade of great work. To me, that is the case with Dolly. Her 1970s and 1980s recordings were great. The quality of her work started declining in the 1990s. But she had a major rebirth with the brilliant The Grass is Blue in 1999, followed by Little Sparrow in 2001 and Halos and Horns in 2002. But nothing spectacular since then. To me, her last "good" album was 2008's Backwoods Barbie. Better Day (2011) and Blue Smoke (2014) were mediocre at best. Pure & Simple is not only laughable in spots, but sad overall considering what this great artist is capable of. Tracks like Kiss it and Make it Better and I'm Sixteen make me cringe with embarrassment to hear them. And it is a disappointment to see her constantly recycling her old songs. This is a woman who supposedly has written thousands of songs over her lifetime. Rehashing old songs makes it look like a rush job, or that she had nothing to offer.

Of course, a review is only one person's opinion, but in the future I will listen to tracks before I buy another Dolly album.

I've been a fan since the mid 1970s. I hope she has at least one more great album in her.

This CD, in all honesty, is a total waste of time.  I feel sympathy for the generation in which I'm growing with, considering a majority of them are forced to listen to this horribly-produced blasphemic compact disc.

 First and foremost, the crust to the apple pie, the beats.  Does anyone reading this recognize a dire similarity to the MIDI music used in older PC games such as "Wolfenstine 3D" and "Doom" on track 3, "Greed, Hate, Envy"?  I rarely get a laugh at such feeble attempts to create "new" music.  Each and every beat sticks to the same collection of samples, and is then applied a thick coat of "Too Much Bass" brand lacquer.  I've given a fair listen to every track on this CD, and spent the 2 hours which followed cleaning out my ears with Q-Tips (not the former A Tribe Called Quest rapper).  It hurts me as a respectable person, much like you all are, to hear and see how we kids have brutally disfigured the rap genre.  I'm a huge fan of hip-hop myself, so don't think I'm saying this from a "I hate rap music" point of view.

 Nelly's lyrical style and performance is utter garbage.  I'm taking nothing for granted by saying this; I haven't heard such false, meaningless mumbling since the days "Ma$e" was a popular rapper.  His vocals are reprinted, uninspired, and unimaginative.  As if his lyrical meaning (or lack thereof) wasn't disgraceful enough, his monotone, carry-over vocal style becomes repetitive and down right annoying after a few tracks.  I am being completely truthful when I say that hearing Nelly rap gives me a minor headache - just intense enough to spout from obviously unimpressive music.

 I do, however, feel the need to credit Nelly himself, in becoming yet another aural manipulator of children my age.  If it weren't for the boring monotony of rap in the year 2000 and beyond, mature teenagers such as myself would have no one to frown upon.  A departing tip to all Nelly fans who like him strictly for a reason besides the fact that you think this CD is good - Nelly approaches the art of being a musician from the business side of the court.  I appreciate his mission; which is solely to make money from record sales and promotion.  Making money is an every day part of life.  It is when you overturn a rusted wheel that your profession becomes a thing of the past.

 We are approaching a new millennium, and I was truely hoping to see some sort of brilliant change in rap music.  Nice try, Nelly.
label: negative

reviewText:
I had the privilege of hearing four tracks off this album courtesy of a certain sunday newspaper. "You're smoking all my stash while burning all my cash" wails Noel. Is the NME still going then? Tsk, those journalists. Lack of cash means the brothers can no longer afford boxer shorts, causing them to complain of being 'Hung In A Bad Place'. The pain in the vocals sounds all too real. The guitar twang opening this track prepares us for a news report that 'there's fighting in the streets' which doesn't materialize. No one's in the mood for a revolution or a Roger Daltrey perm, there are too many units to shift. Pink Floyd always works. Why not try that? They do, and 'Stop Crying Your Heart Out' sounds appropriately 'comfortably numb'. Difficult when you're out of stash, but there's always the pub. They're in desperate need of some 'Instant Kalma' which appears pretty sharpish on 'Force Of Nature'. The force in question being Liam, no doubt, but he has his soft side, as displayed on the self penned 'Songbird' in which a young lady comes to our bard of beatification to 'spread her wings'. Goodness, what can this mean? A little bird tells me he's not referring to personal growth. In any event, the lady in question pushes off pretty quickly thus depriving Liam of the opportunity to be a 'Jealous Guy' despite all the efforts of the music to convince us of the fact. The wistfulness of this ditty confuses all those who recall Liam proclaiming in an interview that he only ever had a quick one to give. It's time to get religion big time which the boys dutifully deliver in a trip east with 'The Hindu Times', the headlines no doubt saying 'Oasis gig cancelled due to impending nuclear conflict'. I would venture a guess that this eastern influence comes from Mr George Harrison. Surprisingly perhaps, as the Beatle never had a good word to say about the brother's band. But we mustn't speak ill of the dead. I'm talking about Oasis, here. Goodness, not only are all these artists sounding alike, they're even giving their albums the same titles (see David Bowie.)
The cover of 'Heathen Chemistry' seems to be a tube drunk's view of the lads as they stand around by the escalators hoping to be recognised. Or maybe they're busking after burning all their cash. Not that that was their fault according to the lyrics, and I use the term loosely.
There was a useful interview with the freebie in which the boys wax lyrical about the making of this album. Between the brothers Gallagher sat a chap called gem who I swear must have had plastic surgery to look just like John Lennon. If not, then he's definately in the right band. Noel tells us that the influences on this album are from all five members record collections. The cheeky inference being we are all therefore partners in crime and have no right to complain. He tells us that Liam sat in a corner strumming the same simple riff over and over again on his acoustic guitar for two hours. That'll be 'Songbird', then. It's shorter but not so you'd notice. The album is also self produced, a revelation made by Noel that causes Liam to give a barely disguised sickly grin. One imagines that the eventual bootleg of these sessions will make the notorious 'Troggs' effort seem like 'All You Need Is Love'. But one mustn't mock. The music industry is a democratic institution and all the dullards out there will no doubt be casting their votes once more to get the boys back in stash. I've got two of their singles so I know of whence I speak.
label: negative

reviewText: There are MANY recordings of "Il Trovatore" I do not regard to be very good, even the glorious Callas-recording features a problematic Manrico in lyric Giuseppe di Stefano but compared to Bocelli di Stefano is a Corelli or a Caruso. Let me quote a Bocelli-Fan here: "And I think that the size of voice would not be important in modern opera." What's this supposed to mean? That from now on Crooners and baby-voices can sing the demanding music of opera? Verdi isn't "modern" and DEMANDS suitable voices. For a more pleasing recent Trovatore go for the one with Roberto Alagna, Angela Gheorghiu and Thomas Hampson who by no means are PERFECT for their roles but they can SING it at least.  It's laughable to say that Bocelli, who sounds nice in "Con te partiro" etc. does Manrico justice. His dream of singing at the Wiener Staatsoper ended after an audition there:, The verdict: He cannot see us and we cannot hear him! Hard as this may be, it's TRUE! Villaroel is an ok Leonora but nothing compared to Callas, Price, Gheorghiu, or Milanov. Guelfi is so-so, for a real di Luna listen to Warren and Merrill. Zaremba's muddy sound I NEVER liked, go for Cossotto instead. This is a failure and an insult to Verdi. Bocelli's fans take pleasure for all I care but it's not the real thing. As this drivel flourishes the real opera is pushed aside for looks, tuned up and faked singing and publicity. And of course $$$$$ What a shame!

reviewText: I lost interest in Clapton long ago, not because he had stopped doing the "Cream thing," but, on the contrary, because he did not evolve as a guitarist. Instead, he became some sort of bland performer for all seasons, who just happened to be able to fall back on some fine guitar playing when people began to fall asleep due to his expressionless voice and bluesy noodlings. He actually became a singer who could play guitar on the side, and no one told him that as a singer he just wasn't all that great... really not. Between cringeworthy sentimental pop and tired, repetitive blues, he had erased himself off of my radar. But recently, I saw this CD at a friend's and thought I'd give it a try, for old time's sake. I was flabbergasted. To descend into mediocrity is bad enough, but to descend to the depths from which even a cohort of brilliant helpers cannot extricate you - wow, that takes some doing. This must be the most boring album of the month. I cannot believe all these five-star reviews. Man, it's great to have such faithful fans. Is it possible that none of them crave something new? This must be the crowd that is able to listen to "Darling, You Look Wonderful Tonight" for the millionth time without snoring. Well, not me. Goodbye, Eric.

reviewText:
That Laffy Taffy. Shake that Laffy Taffy." In the world of misogynistic rap lyrics that dehumanize women, we've now scraped the bottom of the lyrical barrel. It wasn't good enough to simply call the mothers sisters and daughters of the world B***** and h*** - now we've progressed to a whole new level of insulting. To the rappers of D4L, who proclaim themselves "Down for Life" on their album cover while flashing gold chains and big handfuls of hundred dollar bills, women aren't worth more than a nickel's worth of candy. And what is the setting for this degradation, where women shake their "Laffy Taffy" for their amusement? The most famous of all bations of male machismo and female degradation - a strip club.

Hip-Hop doesn't deserve the blame for misogyny that it often gets. Print media were putting women "in their place" before suffrage, and radio was convincing women there was nothing more rewarding than staying at home to raise babies a generation before TV even existed. Rock'n'Roll had just as much to do with objectifying women as any other genre of music, making the term "groupie" a household word. Music video producers locked in the eyeballs of watchers with Aerosmith style videos that were borderline softcore porn. When rap's popularity exploded in the mainstream in the late 80's and early 90's, hip-hop used sex to sell the product like everybody else. Ironically the only objection rap fans had back then was when a video featured too many white girls and not enough nubian sisters (Eric B. & Rakim's "Don't Sweat the Technique") getting equal opportunity to wear skimpy clothing and shake their Laffy Taffy for oogling eyes. Call it the equal opportunity ho employment program. These days there are no shortage of opportunities though with hundreds of cable and satellite channels, "Girls Gone Wild" videos, and the entrepreneurial ho can even launch her own website to shake Laffy Taffy - it'll cost you more than a nickel though.

So hip-hop itself is not to blame. Neither is the woman working at the strip club who takes advantage of the fact men have a natural instinct to debase themselves and objectify women. Some of these women might even be shaking their Laffy Taffy to pay their way through college and become a doctor or lawyer - more power to them. At some point though somebody has to be responsible for making a stupid song with TURRIBLE lyrics and making an equally insulting video. Thank Allah that D4L doesn't represent hip-hop as a whole. With a three note K-Rab beat and lyrics that sound like they were written by a 4th grader on a Playboy bender, D4L's "Laffy Taffy" qualify's as one of the stupidest songs of the year. It's not the first misogynistic song in rap, and definitely won't be the last, but it's certainly among the worst. It takes some doing to make Webbie's "Bad B****" sound intelligent by comparison, but D4L has succeeded brilliantly. The really awful part is that "Down for Life" doesn't show any improvement over their lead single, which I must conclude only succeeded because it was so irritating nobody could get it out of their head. That formula is applied liberally throughout the album: simplistic hooks, simplistic beats, and exceedingly simplistic lyrics.

Actually these D4L rappers have such bad diction and breath control that I can't say for sure whether he's saying "ay Rab" or "ar-rab" or "hey rap" in the quote above. Not that I care anyway. I don't even care who they are individually. There must be at least four of them in the group judging by the cover, but none of them say or do anything intelligent that merits them being singled out individually. These guys seem obsessed with the things they can or can't do ("Betcha Can't Do it Like Me"), proclaiming themselves hot s*** with no justification ("I'm Da Man" and "Game Owe Me") and issuing commands to their Bankhead groupies to "Get Real Low" when they're not busy hanging out on "Front Street." It's hard to find anything redeeming to say about this album whatsoever, but I did like the crunk beats of the opening track "Bankhead" and the dark piano backdrop of "Stuntman." The lyrics were still stupid and aggravating, especially the latter's annoying tendency to rip off Cash Money Records trademarks, but instrumentals of them would be enjoyable. "Make it Rain" is also just barely redeemable, and "S******* Me" probably would have been if they didn't end every line of the lyrics with that phrase - it's just too much. I wish somebody would explain to D4L that just because you want to make music for the South it doesn't have to appeal to a denominator so much lower than common it makes the gutter look like the skyline. File this one in the same category as Dem Franchize Boyz - rap that gives other rappers a bad name.

The once promising and inventive jazz pianist who amazed us all with his Art of the Trio series, cool versions of Radiohead and Nick Drake tunes, and the stunning solo effort Elegiac Cycle, was responsible for not one... not two... but THREE bland, ponderous, and entirely forgettable albums released on the Nonesuch label in 2006.

House On Hill has his stellar original trio coasting along aimlessly through Mehldau originals that all sound the same, the ambitious Love Sublime, a collaboration with opera superstar Renee Fleming, is a dreary, pretentious, and unlistenable mess, and Metheny/Mehldau pairs the pianist with the jazz guitar legend for a yawn-fest of uninspired noodling.

Here's to hoping Brad Mehldau gets his mojo back in 2007...

reviewText:
Look out, folks - the floodgates have been opened.  Whenever there's a sound that catches on with the mass populace, you know what that means ... send in the clones!

Fall Out Boy are not even remotely close to being original, but there's no doubt that due to their combination of sugary pop/punk and verbose self-absorbed lyrics catching on like wildfire, we're going to see many bands also attempt to take that same formula to the bank.  Enter one Panic! At The Disco, a group of teenagers that probably were playing ska or post-grunge just a short time ago.

Pete Wentz of FOB claimed that no major label would take a chance on these guys (Yeah, because they're so hardcore and indie!  Right.), so he signed them to his own label imprint, Decaydance, affiliated with the kiddie pseudo-punk factory known as Fueled By Ramen.  Decaydance, huh?  That proves it - Pete Wentz is obsessed with dancing!  Hey Pete - I heard that the producers of Dancing With The Stars are looking for celebrities to compete on the show's third season - are you in?  Go for it, and do us all a favor - take a break from the music industry for a while, our ears can only take so much of your band's sugary pop junk as well as all the sound-alikes that I'm sure you would sign to your label.

Well, let's give P!ATD some credit - they aren't just Fall Out Boy clones ... why, they also throw in some synths as well.  That's right, showing some Killers influence - the other big commercial sound of the moment!  I'll tell you, these guys prove just how calculated they are by hopping on two popular bandwagons at once!  And the synths never really dominate any of the tracks on this album, never distracting you enough from how much these guys sound like Fall Out Boy - from the singing, the overwrought and cheesy lyrics, and the glossy, overproduced corporate pop/rock sound.

In summary: Perhaps there is reason to panic, because of the influx of generic pop acts like Panic! At The Disco.  Basically, this is the band that former Fall Out Boy fans are listening to for the simple reason that "dude, Fall Out Boy used to be, like, so edgy and hardcore before my mom started liking them, but now there's another rad new punk rawk act out there called Panic! At The Disco.  These guys are so indie!  Nobody listens to them but me, because they're on an indie instead of a stupid major label like Island.  Fall Out Boy sold out, man!".  Note to this type of fan: Panic! At The Disco's label is receiving some major label funds that you don't know about (probably for distribution), and Fall Out Boy were never "indie" - they were actually signed to Island before they released an album, and put their first album out on Fueled By Ramen to give them "indie cred".  I don't see why they were so concerned with that - both of these bands sold out at their very inception by recording such safe, sugary sweet pop/rock.  This is not punk rock, it's just corporate tripe.  Heck, I'll bet the members of both of these bands were huge 'N Sync fans back in the day - that seems to be much more of an influence than any punk rock band I can think of.

reviewText:
I love Ronnie James Dio and all the music he has created ever since ELF (which was an awesome band that made catchy Lynrd Skynrd-esque tunes).

DIO the band were mammoth in the 80s.  They had huge stage productions that rivaled that of KISS, Iron Maiden, and even Pink Floyd! DIO had a huge concert following therefore leading them to play in sold out arenas world wide.  Just watch The Sacred Heart and Last In Line Concert on DVD or the rare Dream Evil Tour footage (featuring a huge robot spider, a laser shooting guitar,an elevated drum riser and towering pyrotechnics!)

Sadly DIO's quality of music began to fade in quality after the strange highways tour (1994).

Not only did the music fade in quality but so did Dio's powerful operatic voice.  Ronnie's style stayed stagnant in 1988 and he refused to update his look or the quality or sound of his band.  Therefore his fame decreased and people forgot all about DIO.

This DVD presents DIO performing in a sold out club.  Ronnie's voice is shot.  He looks as if he never changed his clothes since 1988.  He appears very old and frail but still he manages to move around the stage rather well.  He is over 60 so it does make sense that he looks old but these days rock stars usually get face lifts and hair transplants.  I guess not Dio.  Jimmy is no longer the good bass player he used to be.  Thankfully Rudy Sarzo is the newest bassist but is not featured on this DVD.  Rudy can actually play more than just three notes per song and he has much more live enthusiasm. Doug is a great guitar player but for some reason he did not want to stay in the DIO band.  Craig Goldy of the Dream Evil and Magica era has stayed loyal to DIO but hasn't yet produced as excellent quality of sounds as Doug has done.  The drummer Simon Wright can sometimes be a great drummer. His drum solos are usually amazing!  All Dio needs to do is fix the quality of his voice and stop mumbeling every time a song stops.  Also long gone are the lasers, stage props, pyro, and huge lighting designs.  Instead you only get two screens showing digital images. The film quality of this DVD release is grainy and looks worse than even the sacred heart release which was released in the 80s.  If you are a huge Dio fan from way back then you may like this DVD because the drum solo is cool and so are the songs performed.

I suggest watching Sacred Heart on DVD. It is awesome.

Well, there's the over-the-top hippy anthem Tell All the People. There are a pair of annoying good-timey blues tunes (Do It; Easy Ride) and one painfully bad one (Wild Child). There's Wishful Sinful, which is painful. Runnin' Blue, a country/soul Otis Redding tribute, is a disgrace to the man's memory thanks in part to Krieger's vocals in the chorus. The overblown, eight-minute title track is an example of how over-the-top Jim could be if he tried. Touch Me, the one everybody knows, is the second-best song on this album, but would've been the second-worst on the debut or Morrison Hotel.

I have been forced to hear this very unremarkable album a considerable number of times in my workplace and I have wondered what is wrong with me? I am a serious music lover and I love Classical music and yet Paul Potts' album strikes me as being just another tedious and unnecessary "popera" disc of basically the same dozen or so songs presented on all similar albums. Does Mr. Potts sing any Handel or Mozart or Rameau tenor arias? No, of course not! Anything from Rossini or Donizetti? Don't be daft! Of course he doesn't!

Paul Potts' singing isn't terribly imaginative or colourful. He belts the stuff out in the same way as Andrea Bocelli, Il Divo, Russell Watson, Vittorio Grigolo, Mario Fragoulis and all the other tedious 'popera' wannabes - no real music lover takes seriously. Mario Lanza did everything these guys wish they could do, and did it much better, fifty years ago.

If Paul Potts wants to be taken seriously as a "Classical" singer, let's hear him sing some of the solos from the Symphoni Sacr of Heinrich Schtz or some tenor arias from Handel oratorios or Mozart opera arias or give us a Winterreise or Die Schne Mllerin or some songs of Hugo Wolf or an album of arias from the great and obscure Verdi operas. How many times can we hear Secret Garden's "You Raise Me Up", sung by pop-singers-on-steroids, before we want to throw up?

Prediction: By 2010, people will be saying "Paul who?".

Too much production to be exact and that's the real problem with this album--it's been grossly overworked. Gaga should know that the secret to good art is to know when to pull back and when to let the viewer/listener make assumptions and interpretations on their own. reviewText:
With "Next", Sevendust rehashes the same formula they've used the formula that's been in place since their last great album, "Animosity".  Stuttering one or two chord riffs, bland melodic choruses that all seem to be in the same key, supposedly 'deep' lyrics in very very cliche terms, more of Morgan's "war chants", which consist of screaming "F**K YOU" and various phrases overusing the words "alone" and "again".

Clint Lowery's departure has really hurt this band.  All of the diversity and emphasis on great songwriting and soul has been sucked out of their sound.  The lyrics are a pale shadow of their former selves, the emotions being familiar with all of the interest and poetic value gone.  They're still using the same chords they used on "Home".

"Animosity" was a memorable, emotional and perfectly consistent album and a personal all-time favorite of mine.  "Home" and the self titled were also brilliant albums.  There is literally nothing on this album that would make me want to listen to it.  Not one great song.  "Ugly" has some old school Sevendust type melody, but songs like "Waffle" and "Denial" did it oh-so-much better, and it was fully realized and flowed.  For the first time here there are Sevendust songs that are actually badly written- they NEED a producer.  The disjointed and lyrically pathetic "Last Song" is the example.  Just another "f**k you".

Also, why is this band trying to make a 'heavy' album?  I love this band's louder side on their older albums, but this isn't some of the heavier stuff out there.  What made Sevendust so great was the passion in their songs, and the balance.  The melody.  The heaviness was a tool to get across those things.  This really isn't heavy, it's just a bunch of stop start riffing that never changes.

To anyone who thinks anything on this album is remotely creative, go get the s/t and compare the funky verse of "Prayer" or the kick ass opening riff of "Speak".  Hey, some high end guitar that's INTEGRATED into the riff!  The whole band sings!  Oh, and from "Animosity", the gorgeous and heartfelt "X-Mas Day", which has a dark tone that eclipses the sappy 'soft songs' from "Next" and contains lyrics that aren't so vague and connect to the real world.

I'm still going to see this band live tonight, but I hope they don't play much from this.  I am baffled by all the 5 star positive reviews.

I was going to give this 2 stars but I enjoy nothing about it.

Edit- After the show I now realize that "Silence" is a good song with pretty good lyrics.  If you like the "Seasons" album, go download it.  I maintain my opinions about the others.

reviewText: I hate to be a killjoy and rain on your parade, but "Come Away With Me" fell tremendously short of my expectations.  It's worse than a bad record; it's a bad record that squanders its potential to be good.  The media hype, Grammy nominations, and chart success finally made me run and grab Norah's CD.  I listened with as open a mind as possible, and after just 10 minutes my faith headed south.  Jones is an able piano player, but she and veteran producer Arif Mardin follow the rules of making a jazz vocal record so slavishly that "Come Away With Me" offers almost no surprises.  The disc takes off on a promising note with "Don't Know Why," a warm and seductive number that fits Norah's voice like a hand in leather glove.  But after that, the album lapses into a comatose state from which it never fully recovers.  The production lacks dimension; the arrangements are predictable, and Norah's voice ultimately lacks the urgency to give life to the lyrics.  "Turn Me On," "I've Got To See You Again," and the "Nearness of You" all start off well, but they ultimately lack substance, nuance, and depth.  Those who listen exclusively to Top 40 radio will swear to high heaven that "Come Away With Me" is the best thing since sliced bread.  But more seasoned, mature, and well-rounded listeners will sigh, "heard it all before."  If you truly crave for jazz, get the newly remastered deluxe edition of John Coltrane's "A Love Supreme" or the superb compilation "Verve Unmixed," which features a smattering of vocal artists from the Verve label.  Otherwise, save your money.

reviewText: This is not a review of the songs. I like them, and purchased this hoping to upgrade my copy of A TRAMP SHINING, which is a much earlier released CD. It also includes his 2nd collaboration with Jimmy Webb, THE YARD WENT ON FOREVER. There is also a version from Australia's Raven Records featuring both albums as well, entitled WEBB SESSIONS: 1968-69, but it was more expensive. Knowing Raven's penchant for sound quality (I own a few of their CD's), I should have spent the difference. The sound on this CD is horrible, "brickwalled" to the max. For the uninitiated, "brickwalling" or compression, occurs when the record companies boost the bass and lower the highs to equal the mid-range. That way, if someone is listening with an iPod or similar device, the music will be loud enough to hear every detail. The problem is, that in music every detail is not supposed to be at the same volume, but with differing frequencies, not just one. When listening to these compressed CD's/mp3's your ears get tired from the all-at-once onslaught. This is also know as "ear fatique." That is why there is a growing market for earlier generation CD's, with the music transferred properly. If you are interested in both of the above albums, purchase the Raven version, if you only want A TRAMP SHINING, click my link above, and avoid this travesty...... If you are interested in the early music of Jimmy Webb, try GLEN CAMPBELL Sings the Best of Jimmy Webb 1967-1992,Someone Left the Cake Out In The Rain: The Classic Songs Of Jimmy Webb,The Moon's A Harsh Mistress: Jimmy Webb In The 70's

reviewText:
Generally, in order to convey my disgust for modern whiny-baby music --which sadly saturates the upper percentile of the market-- I simply compose a review here on good ole amazon.com.  Well, I am confident that if you listen to this monotone-voiced, melody-starved, banal, 80s rock-rap with that typical, laughable, disastrous piano ballad ("My Immortal"), then my point will be made.  I'll only expand briefly using words, for I am optomistic that this garbage of some mutant strain can be quickly discarded after one listening, rather than by mighty keystrokes.
1) THE VOICE:  The voice, the voice, the voice.  I don't know who told this girl she possessed talent to carry a tune; perhaps it was some cruel joke.  Or perhaps her level of talent matched that of her bandmates.  If the latter is true, then I completely understand.
  The Skinny: A slender range consisting of about three notes...  possibly the most boring set of notes on the keyboard.  Additionally, those notes are held for the longest times, the singer attempting in vain to persuade the ignorant listeners that because she can hold a boring note for several seconds, blending seamlessly into the next boring note a half-step away, that she is a diva.  Don't be fooled by what the media and the music conglomerates tell you, folks: 'That kind of voice that induces insomnia,' or '...A haunting voice'.  The fact is her voice is of extremely low caliber, synonomous with the chubby high school choir girl who has no concept of melody, but rather the cringing ability to bellow meaningless tunes for unforseeable, excrutiating loads of time (which for some reason qualifies many these days to be considered talented).
2) THE "MUSIC": Bombastic.  Egotistical.  The singer's motives are clearly different than those of her bandmates.  4/4 beat, 80s rock-rap (as heard on "Bring Me Back to Life", "Everybody's Fool") and 4/4 beat, late 90s/00s cookie cutter-cliche-rock (as heard on "Going Under", "Haunted"), first of all, is not "haunting".  Those types of beats, coupled with adolescent low-chord guitar rifs --done millions of times, mind you-- were originally intended to sound aggressive, and to be complemented by an aggressive voice; this vocalist does not land in this category, or any category at all for that matter.  Perhaps the type of music suited for this fakir would have been along the lines of Sarah McLachlan, who possesses the vocal range to effectively convey "haunting" emotions, as well as a brain that tells her that her voice would not sound good over Godsmack.
Overall, this concoction is a horrible mess, reeking of the foulest of smells due to a chemical reaction gone awry.

reviewText:
A little precursor.  I am a long time guitar player and huge music lover and one of the last things I ever do is critique music. I decided after many years of listening to various different types of guitar centered music to give Steve Vai a listen. I have heard a few songs here and there admittedly popping up on my Pandora and liked them. As a long time Joe Satriani listener from the 80's up to present day- I was surprised i had never delved into Vai.  I purchased a few of the early releases on the super cheap- and for the most part was interested by the music on the early Passion and Warfare.

Next up- Sex and Religion.  It's bad people. Bad.

I have given it 2 listens- and despite my urge to turn it off- I have pushed through.  The lyrics are terrible. The guitar play gives anyone pause as it's, well- really good- but, really good in the way you see a piece of art and even though you can't understand it- and it doesn't speak to you- you can appreciate that it took a hell of alot of effort. This effort- unfortunately- is strangled by the lyrics and the singer's delivery. I have been part of and witnessed births that weren't as labored.

Did I mention the lyrics are bad? 'Victory The endless passion  For a cause  We will take an action'  'You're so cold and critical And baby that's too bad'  'Fate does call  And the sickness falls'  'What do you think you got  When you thought you had a lot  But all your feelings are dead?  And who do you think you are  When you're reaching for the stars  But all your feelings are dead?'
When I thought I might make it through the album with only minor psychological trauma- I stumbled on The Road to Mt. Calvary followed by what I think is one of the most painful 8 minutes of my life- Down deep into the pain.  I was. Down deep- 8 minutes of torture. The combination of the 2 songs- the first one was like a psychotic experience- screams- weird sounds, voices- then topped by the pain gem. It was sad. I almost lost my mind.

I am worried about the next few albums- I am hoping there are no more lyrics- did I mention the lyrics are BAD? Steve Vai- please- for the love of God- stick to virtuoso guitar playing.

reviewText:
Am I doomed to hate electronic music forever? At the present time, I can count on one hand the number of artists within it that I generally enjoy; far too small a number to sustain an interest in the genre. The problem, as I see it, is that, as a sympton of the genre's machine and synthesizer foundation, that most electronic artists are profoundly lazy. They simply let the sample and preset banks do the work for them, resulting in music that is repetitive, dull, and soulless.

Darude's "Before the Storm" is a prime example of exactly what I mean by the above paragraph. Finnish artist Ville Virtanen achieved some degree of fame with the single "Sandstorm" which actually achieved some mainstream radio airplay; you've probably heard it at least once even if you don't listen to (or actively avoid) electronic music. As a piece of music, it's purely disposable; poppy hooks, an anthemic chorus, and a simplistic and repetitive structure. Well, one single isn't enough for a full-length album, so Darude filled up an entire album (yes, a full-length LP) of "remixes" and thinly-veiled knockoffs of his smash hit.

I have scarcely encountered music more bereft of imagination and creativity. EVERY song follows the same formula: a stale, 4/4 beat with some irritating, buzzing synth samples and, if you're lucky, some irritating vocals (most noticeable on track 9 "The Flow"). EVERY song is dripping with cheesy, repetitive pop hooks and banal melodies. Like all bad electronic music, the songs go nowhere and show no progression throughout their length, despite the fact that some run on for seven minutes or more. Darude is even so lazy as to reuse the same synth samples as featured on "Sandstorm", giving the listener the impression that Darude simply cut, pasted, and rearranged "Sandstorm" to fill out a full-length album. "Feel the Beat", for example, could have easily been a simple remix of "Sandstorm".

Furthermore, I take umbrage at people labelling this music as "trance". Perhaps I'm flaunting my ignorance of electronic music here, but isn't trance music supposed to be, I don't know, entrancing? Because there is absolutely nothing "entrancing" about this album. It's shallow, cloying, repetitive, and predictable, riding the success of the overplayed single "Sandstorm". This isn't trance. This is the kind of banal, disposable pap that's done nothing but turn a promising genre into a cesspool of cheese. Look elsewhere.

reviewText:
Maybe it's my own fault that this record seems so lame, so out of touch, so down right boring--I bought it and METAMORPHOSIS, the Stone's great 1975 LP, on the same day.
When the Stones released METAMORPHOSIS they were reworking and re-releasing some classic, cutting edge, roots Rock & Roll. Jagger was still a great singer, Keith Richard an innovative guitar player, and Mick Taylor a GREAT lead guitarist. Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts were the best rhythm section around.
I guess it's the Stones playing on NO SECURITY, but you'd never know it from the sound on this second-rate live CD. It sounds more like some Stones 'tribute' band. Jagger is a mere shadow of his 60's and 70's self, the rhythm section--minus Bill Wyman--is pedestrian at best, the 'new' songs are vanilla and dull, and the renditions of classics are performed no better than your typical suburban bar band.
There are times I wish the Beatles and Led Zep had gotten back together. Then I hear a post-SOME GIRLS Stones LP and realize every band has a finite life span. I wish the Stones would just fold camp and go home; releasing this kind of record is embarrassing to listen to, and demeans what they once were.
If you think this is what the Stones were about, or has anything to do with the classic era of the band--1965-1975--you're missing the boat. They were one of the best, now they're records don't chart and their sound don't rock.

reviewText:
I like Travis Tritt. I think he's a strong and enthusiastic singer who lets it all hang out on most songs he sings. And in that positive respect, COUNTRY CLUB is no different than numerous other Tritt CDs. Unfortunately, that is the CDs only positive. COUNTRY CLUB is an uninspired collection of very "safe" songs, many written by Tritt himself. We have the "I'm proud to be a redneck and I love country music." genre. We have "Even when I was a little boy, I knew I wanted to be a country star someday." We have "Ain't it a shame that things ain't like they was in Grandpas's day when a man's word was his bond." We get, "I wanted to leave our little country town for the bright lights, but Lord this big city is so cold and impersonal and I wish I could go back home." In short, there is NOTHING innovative in the lyrics to any of these songs; nothing you haven't heard a thousand times before; nothing remotely interesting, thought provoking, or funny. Still, even cliches can be presented with the occasional bright well-crafted line; one that makes you smile when you hear it. Well, let me disabuse you of that notion in regards to COUNTRY CLUB. And, parenthetically, why CAN'T those ol' boys stuck up there in Toledo or wherever who are yearnin' for the old home place just get up and go back home, already?

The playing on this CD is Nashville-sterile - perfect yet emotionless, again with nothing new or interesting to say. These players are outstanding, but all they do here is contribute to the safe and slightly cynical vibe. Cynical in terms of, "Boys, we don't really have to do s**t here, and it'll be good enough."
As I said, I really like Travis Tritt and have other of his CDs, all of which have good things on them. COUNTRY CLUB does not. There is NO passion in either the playing or the singing and ultimately it is just plain boring. Tritt's singing can't save this one by itself.

I bought this CD on Amazon and while the price - 1 cent - was right, the $2.98 shipping costs done pretty much broke my heart and, Lord, I wish I could sell it to someone else.
