If that isn't bad enough, these aren't even the original versions of the songs you remember. The set starts off with Warrant's 'Cherry Pie' and you immediately realize that this is a poorly done remake or a demo. The third song is Quiet Riot's 'Come on feel the noise' as if you needed to buy your hundredth copy of this song, even this was remade. Every song is different than the 80's studio version. Even Lita Ford's close your eyes forever is sans Ozzy, she sings it herself.
The second CD is live performances, so if you really need to hear Great White covering Led Zepplin songs (Living Loving Maid and Ramble On), then please stop what you're doing and go out and buy this.
There are a few gems here and there. The highlight of the whole set is Paul Dianno's (original Iron Maiden singer) live version of Wrathchild. Although how he ended up on a hair metal album is beyond me, Iron Maiden was always above that.
If you are a true 80's child, you really can go without this, unless you want to waste money on poorly produced remakes and live performances that lack energy.

reviewText:
What a shock this album is. My favourite air supply is definitely 'the book of love'. Listen to the melodic genius of 'mother said' or so many other brilliant songs. This album, by contrast, is all about appearing 'modern' and 'cool', and it's just not air supply. Lots of upbeat tracks with no melodies and really annoying repetitive choruses. Russel's voice is extremely weak now, he struggles to reach high notes. Graham really takes almost all lead vocals now. He totally dominates most of the songs, singing three alone. Russel only has one lead vocal without Graham, the last track 'Until'.

Track by track analysis:

Setting the seen - 9/10 A promising start. Elements of progressive rock all over this one, multi parts, the first sounding like ABBA- the visitors, very futuristic synths and a nice verse/chorus with acoustic guitars.

Dance with me - 7.5/10 A good melody, like the bass vocals from Graham. I am amazed if he can sing that low without effect been added. This is the first example of Air Supply trying to rock in places - it works for the song.

A little bit of everything - Now this is where the album takes a nose dive. A really annoying verse, with no melody and an annoying octave apart double tracked vocal. Horrible chorus, frightful. Russel is pushed too forward in the mix and I can't stand the way he says the 't' in a little biT of everything. Yuck. 1.5/10

Hold on - I thought this was more like old air supply, with a memorable start and nice piano counter point parts. A good idea in the composition, but as with many tracks on here, Russel is straining (listen 0:52), he should not be in this range, it is frightful, his voice is just dying as you listen. When the other lead vocalist joins in, the song seems to lose all emotion and becomes another modern, emotionless ballad, with boring instrumentation. The voices do not work together. Another miss. 4/10

A little bit more - OK, this is sickening. I love soft acoustic guitar and Graham usually pulls off such a lovely melody. This has no melody, and often the track seems to distort - look at 0:32, many other places also. Graham sings out of tune at 0:42 'WANTED to' and many other places on the track. It would just be a rubbish, unmemorable track up to this point. But the chorus is just hideous. The backing vocalist puts this breathy effect on her voice and repeats the words 'just little bit more' continuously, sounding like she is trying to have an orgasm. It is truly horrific. 0/10

Alternate Ending - Russel has been absent hasn't he? More Graham lead vocals. This seems to start ok, but then Russel (mixed too loud again) comes in. The track starts to build and....oh no at 0:59 'one love...true love...' backing vocal makes this pukeworthy and trying to keep up with modern music. Heavy guitars to hip it up a bit more, then repeat the boring structure again. Verse ok, rest absolute garbage. 4/10

I won't let it get in the way - as soon as the guitar started in this, I preferred it to anything I heard since track 1. Good vocal and, for once, the instrumentation is more sparse, it works with electric guitar, piano, drums and voice. Graham sings off key at 1:05, and the track seems to distort again, but credit where credit is due, Russel's bridge vocal is a good use of melody and chords. I also like the solo. Am I wrong in thinking there is no bass on this track? Maybe it is mixed very low, but there is room for a pattern here. A better song. 8/10

Why - I just don't like it. Seems sickly to me, but at least it's different from the hip stuff here. Not sure why they included this track, as it was definitely written before the album and I heard it. 4.5/10

Me like you - OK, let's put a proper rock song on now, to show we are really cool. Best thing is the backing vocals, at least I can remember them. It is a dislikeable song, but works better than some of the sickly stuff. I would have been ok if this had been the only attempt at rocking things, but as it is, too much tuneless stuff on here for me. I also don't like Russel's double tracked lead vocals. 3/10

Mumbo Jumbo - More nonsense. This is the first track I hear a portion of, before I bought the album, and I was extremely unimpressed, but thought, surely the album must be better than this. Unfortunately it is a good example of the rest of shite on here. Another tuneless song, with meandering vocals and no decoration. Gone are the days of tune and emotion Graham was so well known for. Rubbish track. 1/10

Faith in love - As with other tracks, there is something of a good melody, buried somewhere, but the arrangement is boring. Needs a more acoustic, sparse sounds. Where is 'sunset', 'I know you better than you think', not this mindless pap. For the tune - 5/10

Can I be your lover - No melody again. Just boring and meaningless. Graham dominates again, Russel does nothing. I was just dying for the 'next' button...but the track coming next is just off puting from the title itself.
2.5/10

Lovesex - If any track is proof that air supply are no longer the band they were, listen to the intro of this. It just makes me want to puke. Listen to the album 'Yours truly'. mostly a nice album, but it has tracks on it, that are an indicator of crapshite to come. 'Body glove', 'Peaches and cream' and 'learning to make love to you'. This album is like a whole load of those tracks. This is a meaningless, emotionless pile of nonsense. Try sitting through the ;love', 'sex' bit and not have it grate on you. And of course, this is the main part of the song. Total bollox 0.5/10

Until - The last track, thank goodness, and some nice melodic parts on the piano. It is a very nice song, unfortunately Russel is beginning to sound like a lesbian singing, rather than a sorprano, and as much as he has tried, it's just bringing what could have been an amazing song down to mediocre. 8/10

Without a doubt, air supply's worst album and an embarrassment.

My regular driver will sometimes ask me if I want to open items before he leaves because he knows I am just going to have to re-box and go through the hassle of starting a return and then dropping off.

I remember reading somewhere that the Beatles only recorded something like 520 minutes of music. So one by one I opened and listed carefully. I have to say that the records that didn't have no fill issues sounded really really good to me.

On some of my favorite songs though there where definite pressing issues, on one song only one channel of sound played (weird) and on a few others the dreaded zipper like sounding of no fill noise was present. I also noted that some of the vinyl records themselves it looked like they weren't completely pressed or cut all the way through from the factory and there a bunch of long vinyl shavings that needed to be removed from the edges.

Also it should be noted that most of the records in this set also had minor warping but not enough to affect their playability on my system.

My replacement box set arrived very promptly but again was pretty banged up in shipping. The outer sleeve that slides over the set itself was somehow ripped. Still not sure how that one happened, maybe it was ripped by the amazon reboxers when they did their bubble pack job???

At that point my thoughts where unless I could get a different retailer and carrier (like Fed Ex, or even USPS) I wouldn't be getting a box set in decent enough shape through amazon and ups. But all of that may not matter due to the quality issues of the box set itself.

My thoughts are that amazon did a sub par job packing these box sets. The first one had the box set on one side and bubble bags filling the box. That may explain the crushed edge as it looked like ups had crunched the box in shipment. reviewText: Oasis's "Brit-pop" sound that was a major part of Australian radio during the 1990s was then considered to be a different form of alternative rock from the American grunge that took over the music world very suddenly with the arrival of Nevermind in 1991. Whilst there is a lot to be said against the pompous hair-metal of the 1980s, this does not excuse the total lack of melody and resultant bluntness of grunge. As for Oasis, they gave themselves a different image to grunge, yes, but there is no means by which one can say they failed to dissociate themselves from grunge. For the most part, the songs on "(What's The Story) Morning Glory?" use grunge distortion patterns that are copied with only the faintest of disguises, as on the last part of the otherwise pleasant pop tune "Champagne Supernova", which sounds nothing like 60s music as many say it does. Rather, it sound like a soppy version of grunge that retains all the horrible noise. The string-laden ballad "Wonderwall" copied this noisy character from early 1990s grunge in exactly the same way: the embellishments give no disguise. On the rockers, the band is even less tuneful: "Don't Look Back In Anger" really sounded like a half-hearted attempt to imitate My Bloody Valentine - there were traces of that dense melody - but was muffled and awful as a song. The rest of the album moved along a similar, totally slushy, mid-tempo vein that showed Oasis simply were a soggy version of (awful) 1990s grunge. If you think you will get something different from American alternative rock of the 1990s, you will be utterly disappointed by "(What's The Story) Morning Glory?". For fans, at most.

reviewText: Considering how well served this symphony is by the gramophone, and how many superb artists have given us the benefit of their reading, the praise heaped on this hysterical product is well-nigh incomprehensible to me. I don't wish to single out any competitors; but just by way of example (and because Kleiber is plainly imitating a famous precedent), listen to the first movement, alternating section by section in quick succession, between Karajan's 1962 recording Ludwig van Beethoven: 9 Symphonien and this Kleiber offering. Quick switching helps you focus on the details; and especially on how the conductor controls the dynamics. Result: you'll hear a man doing his best work and a boy trying his best to match his footprints step by step. Even the 80-year-old Bruno Walter managed to show what dynamism really means. Not running wild, like a dog chasing a rabbit. Same applies to the last movement. There is no grandeur here, just climax piled on climax in a senseless paroxysm of noise. The seventh, in contrast, is almost too demure. Maybe Kleiber felt that enough was enough; but (comparison again) you can go to Solti/Chicago SO Beethoven: Symphonies Nos. 7 & 8 to discover how truly powerful dynamics can be made to arise from a basically quite slow pace. I don't want to harp. Yet I kept going back to this album, saying to myself, "surely this excitement is not just hype -- there must be something to it?" Well, I've come to the point where I don't ever want to hear this again. Music need not be just pleasure; but it should be (especially this symphony) sublime in its turbulence, and uplifting in the grandeur of its final pages. But this performance leaves me breathless and dismayed. When it's over, you shake your head and ask, where amid this furious gesticulating is all the greatness gone?

reviewText:
I sit here writing this review absolutly amazed all by the 5 star uncritical reviews of our beloved Kate Bush's latest effort. 'The Director's Cut' is a beleagured, misguided and lazy attempt to rehash and capture aspects of 'The Sensual World' and 'The Red Shoes' which our Kate believes were missed at the time.

None of the tracks included here bar 'Rubber Band Girl','Deeper Understanding' and 'This Woman's Work' sound not to different to the original versions except for poorer vocals, instrumentation and very poor sound quality. Over the entire CD not one track stands out as being improved upon or worthy of inclusion here.
So I ask myself time and time again what was the point of this album and the answer to me is none at all. This album could easily be imagined as a left over box of demo's from the original recordings in 1989 and 1993 respectively except these recordings were from the days when Kate's vocals were out of tune.

From the start of the 'yes' on 'Flower Of The Mountain' I find myself cringing all the way through this track. There was nothing wrong with the original 'The Sensual World' and if there's nothing wrong you don't fix it. The next two tracks 'Lily' and 'Songs Of Solomon' are not too bad compared to the other duff tracks here but again they are not so different from the originals I find myself asking what on earth was the point.

I loved the original 'The Red Shoes' album. The inclusion's from here 'Rubberband Girl', And So Is Love 'Lily','Songs Of Solomon', 'Moments Of Pleasure' and the title track 'The Red Shoes'. If any of the above were perhaps done in a different style maybe but the one attempt at doing this 'Rubberband Girl is in a sort of grunge/american country style where if you didn't like it before .. you sure will love the original now.

'The Sensual World' album revists here from 22 years ago here are the worst of the lot. 'Deeper Understanding' has been transformed from a beautiful,touching song into a 6 min 31 sec NIGHTMARE. The human computer voice chorus is an embarrassment when compared to the wonderful original. On the magnificent 'This Woman's Work' an attempt to do someting different has been made but loses the urgency, emotion and potency of the original song and replaced with a 6 min 32 second ambient piece of shopping mall background muzak which would go great if you are having a cholonic bowel irrigation treatment

Never Be Mine' is one of the better recordings here but again it is so simillar to the original I ask myself ...why even bother.

So to sum it up in lyrics of 'Hammer Horror' ...was this the right thing to do' as our Kate asks herself on 'Lionheart'. The answer is NO DEAR! Your original recordings gave me many 'Moments of Pleasure' and still do. This album is a mistake which i cannot be be kind to.

reviewText:
I was excited to get the new Judas Priest album NOSTRADAMUS, as it coincided with a road trip a group of friends was planning. The open road, friends and some great new music from a band we all enjoyed. A can't miss formula for good times right?

This CD was perilously close to being chucked out the window twenty miles down the road. How could the band that wrote the triumphant "Heading Out to the Highway" screw up a soundtrack to a summer roadtrip? To put it succinctly:

1. The Concept. Nostradamus was an interesting historical figure, no question. Does that justify a concept album clocking in at a turgid 100 minutes? Debatable. Does the average Judas Priest fan care at all about the man? Doubtful.

2. The Music. Slow, dirge-like passages that go on for entirely too long and never seem to *get* anywhere. The first disc is not salvageable. There are two or three songs out of twenty three that are somewhat interesting, but only because everything around them is just so tepid. Judas Priest should NEVER make anyone sleepy, and they do a good job of that here.

3. The Production and Performances. The CD is washed out in orchestration and synths. The guitars are mixed weakly, while Halford turns in an earnest but dull vocal performance, hampered by bad lyrics. His voice is "showing" wear and it's evident in the studio now. Ian Hill is M.I.A. here and Scott Travis is just cashing a check. His drumming talents are put to waste, as he works on material most session players could handle with a yawn.

This whole endeavor feels like something a European power metal band would take on, and probably do better as this vein of concept music fits their style better. Judas Priest built their legacy on lean and mean guitar riffs, stripped down production and fun lyrics that were at turns filled with sci-fi imagery, sexual innuendo, and just plain fun times living the rock lifestyle. NOSTRADAMUS brings us a band that is too self-aware of their own place in the metal pantheon, and trying entirely too hard to deliver the EPIC they think they need to put out to blow everyone away.

reviewText:
Ever since his death in 1959 - the day the music died - Buddy Holly's songbook has been a natural source of tribute material. In the 10 years after his death, the usual culprits were Mike Berry, The Crickets, Bobby Vee and Jimmy Gilmer. There were also two other multi artist tribute albums, one in the early 90s on the French Label, New Rose was a punk tribute and totally missable, the second was a country slanted CD with the Hollies singing along with Buddy (ugh), The Crickets, Los Lobos etc, nice but nothing memorable. And now we have this album under the auspices of Paul McCartney, MPL Communications and the ever creative Concord label group which gets progressively more dire as the minutes tick by - eclectic is the best that can be said. Disparaging might be an alternative view.
In general these are pretty mediocre covers - Lou Reed (ugh), McCartney (embarrassing) and they underline just how good Buddy's original were. Check out the celeste by Benmont Tench on "Everyday" and compare it to Vi Petty's superior playing on the original. While much has been written of the tensions between Buddy and Norman Petty, the latter added much to the timelessness of the original recordings. In the vein of tribute albums, Bobby Vee had a 2000 release, "Down The Line" (re-released on Rollercoaster RCCD 4046 in 2008) which is very nice. As to the question of why the present release - could it it have anything to do with Macca owning the Buddy Holly catalog and wanting to make an extra buck? Maybe. In the meantime - back to the originals.
label: negative

reviewText:
From the cover of this CD to the music on the disc, "And Out Come the Wolves" is a polished, unoriginal album.
Two of Rancid's members came from a great punk/ska band called Operation Ivy, who never recorded a bad song.  Rancid's first two albums were descent, but they were nothing special.
"And Out Come the Wolves" was a dictionary definition of a sellout.  A year earlier (1994), punk had been officially murdered by Green Day's and the Offspring's commercial success.  Even Bad Religion had signed to a major label.  Punk was destroyed completely.
First, the "Roots Radicals" single came out which was a descent punk song.  When "And Out Come the Wolves" was released, it contained a different version of "Roots Radicals" and it didn't even sound like the same song.  The sound of the guitars were so polished that it sounded like Motley Crue.  In the background, there were melodic vocals mixed in and at one point you can hear Lars Fredrickson go "Oh-e-oh-e-oh".  What was that?
Other parts of the album were just horrible Clash rip-offs.  The Clash were not really even a punk band, but they were a critically acclaimed rock band.  Maybe Rancid was trying to get critical acclaim.
For people that think the cover is original, take a look at the cover of the Minor Threat E.P. (also used for the Complete Discography CD) that was released over ten years earlier.  It looks like they took the original picture, drew a Mohawk on the head with a marker, and then released it as their own.
It's rumored that the only reason Rancid stayed with their original independent record label, Epitaph, is because they offered the band more money than the competing major label record companies.  The official story is that Rancid stayed with Epitaph because they offered more artistic creativity in their contract.  Judging by the sound of this album and Rancid's MTV success, it seems the rumors were true.

A little over two years later we get Dedicated to Chaos and all hopes and dreams that Queensryche had truly returned to form have vanished in utter disappointment.

Why they created such an album, much like Take Cover as far as cheesiness goes, is beyond my comprehension.  This album is full of poppy and jazzy love songs--nothing even close to past themes and concepts that Queensryche fans listen to their music for.

reviewText:
Train's third album My Private Nation is a continuation of the bland MOR rock and saccharine sentimentality that has been this band's stock in trade since their 1998 debut.  Only with this album, they really pile on the latter elements and the production is polished to excess.  In addition with the lifeless musical arrangements found on these songs, it feels more like a Pat Monahan album than a group effort - the frontman is pretty much front and center the whole time and the other instruments seem to be buried in the mix.
If you haven't heard Train, it's a combination of ordinary Southern rock (this influence is pronounced particularly in the lyrics and vocals) and whatever else this derivative band gets their hands on.  Monahan is a dead ringer vocally for Chris Robinson (Black Crowes), and many of his lyrics are either trite ("When it rains it pours and opens doors and floods the floors", an example of rhyming for the sake of rhyming from "When I Look To The Sky") or just plain silly ("All American Girl").
The songs themselves are just pure vanilla: "Calling All Angels" was clearly written in an attempt to duplicate the success of "Drops Of Jupiter", "I'm About To Come Alive" is an ironic title for such a sleep-inducing song that goes nowhere, "When I Look To The Sky" has a bridge that makes you wonder if Monahan is going to shout out the chorus to "Tiny Dancer", and then there's a couple of songs with references to shaving legs - real thought-provoking subject matter to be found here.
In summary: This album is cookie-cutter generic pop/rock that only sells because the radio plays it incessantly.  Only pick it up if you're looking for something that could have easily been made by hundreds of other bands.

reviewText: I remember hearing all the hype about a new, mature Green Day; a punk rock opera, they were calling it.  A concept album that will blow you away; great, polished music. Let's face it, Boulevard of Broken Dreams sounds like the old Green Day stuff.  But the genius of Green Day (and I use that term loosely) is that they overhype everything before it comes out.  And this time they focused on the Bush Administration with rants that don't make much sense and stupid little teenage kids, with no political background, actually eat this garbage up while watching South Park.  Green Day is older now and have grabbed back their 15 minutes of fame (maybe the Beastie Boys should have taken notes) but at what cost?  Will this album be relevant 5 years from now?  No, it's not even relevant now.  People who loved to talk about how much this album changed their life have moved on now to the new Fallout Boy record saying the same thing.  Green Day will continue with their cursing and their liberal, uneducated politics, but it will always be with the same 3 or 4 chord song structures. reviewText: Like Time of No Reply, a fine collection of unreleased material from fellow troubled, British folkie, Nick Drake compiled by Island Records in 1986, Capital's 1988 Syd Barrett offering, Opel, represents a record company' realization that a largely ignored artist, signed years earlier, had slowly become a mysterious, cult legend who had gathered a devout following feverishly demanding new material. Opel is a collection of wooly outtakes from the onetime Pink Floyd frontman's two much-admired solo works, 1970's the Madcap Laughs and Barrett. Unfortunately those albums provided little unused material ready for release. Opel is simply a collection of abandoned songs and pitifully underdeveloped versions of a few released tracks. The tracks, all of which feature only Barrett on acoustic guitar, are all mere sketches. Underproduction may have worked well for the eccentric songwriter in many instances but utter incompleteness in another matter. It makes Opel a tedious, frustrating listen that adds nothing noteworthy to the Barrett mythos. Capital, unlike Island, had nothing new to offer the acolytes of their roster's cult legend.

reviewText:
The sound of Luke Bryan's new album destroys any notions of it being a country record, regardless of the genre listing on its sales tag. Crash My Party is chalk full of pop tunes not-so-cleverly disguised as country songs (a repeating two second steel ride in each verse or chorus does not make something country). Nevertheless, there are some beautiful songs on Crash My Party (the title track, We Run This Town, Out Like That), but they don't make up for the album-opening atrocity entitled "That's My Kind of Night." How Bryan can even justify putting this song on one of his albums is beyond me, but as country radio waves continue to suffer from an untreatable pop infection headlined by hardcore sell outs Blake Shelton and Tim McGraw, more and more artists are abandoning the pop-crossover title for full on, bubbly, migraine inducing pop. "That's My Kind of Night" is currently climbing the charts as more gullible, trend following, fiercely dependent on anything but themselves Americans continue to post music voting patterns that make me believe that the society depicted in Mike Judge's "Idiocracy" may be in our not-too-distant future.

 "...she was like, oh my god, this is my song."

You probably think I'm kidding, but I promise that if you pop in this record, you'll hear that line in one of the songs. When I listened to this record, the lyrics often had me scratching my head, asking why, why, why would you put that in a song? Bryan leans heavily on songwriters for the first time on Crash My Party, and it shows. While his prior albums contained songs that he had no hand in writing, the majority of the songs still had his name on them, and you could hear a little extra authenticity because of that, but on this record the lyrics are so bad that I'm surprised that the writers even bothered to put their pens to the paper. As far as singing is concerned, Bryan is a decent vocalist, but he's not nearly as good as some people would like you to believe. There are better vocalists littered all over current radio waves (Chris Young, Eric Church, and Brett Eldredge, to name a few). Either way, Luke's vocal performance is good enough to carry the lyrics to the finish line, but with sub-par material on his hands, his voice was only able to do so much.

If someone were to steal this album, I'd wonder who they'd stolen it from, because I certainly will not be purchasing this piece of trash. Yes, there are a handful of decent songs, but most of it is pop nonsense about drinking beer and girls from the past. It's a regression for a once promising artist--I, for one, was a huge Luke Bryan supporter until he released the genuinely awful "Country Girl (Shake it for Me)." People want to say that country music is evolving, but the truth of the matter is that a handful of once respected artists are reaching for pop success while being abrasive enough to act as if they're still recording country songs. Unfortunately for those of us who first heard Luke Bryan releasing wonderful songs like "We Rode in Trucks," he has jumped head first into the current pop trend, leaving his original fans to wonder what the hell has happened to his obvious talent.

Everything he shouts out sounds completely forced and obnoxious, but what's worse is that HE ACTUALLY SINGS. Cryptopsy were never a band meant for clean singing passages. It worked for Augury, it worked for Akercocke, but it sure does not work for Cryptopsy.

The music doesn't do much to impress either. It still has some elements of the trademark Cryptopsy sound, but it's all rather b-sides material that's completely sloppy and ridden with more breakdowns than a extremely aged truck with a rusted out engine. When the singing starts, it even changes pace to what you'd expect from some 3rd rate radio rock knockoff.

How the mighty have fallen. Listen at your own risk.

reviewText: What's the point? Ok, let's see, Columbia released a three disc compilation of the "Best of" Dylan, aptly named DYLAN. Kinda pointless, given they did ESSENTIAL BOB DYLAN back in 2000, but of course he's done two albums since and I guess they have to take a track or two from them. But wait, there's more. We also have, confusingly enough, this album, appropriately named DYLAN as well (so that's the third album in Dylan's discography that has DYLAN as a name, if you included the [...] child DYLAN from 1973. Dylan apparently doesn't since you can't buy it on CD in America. Oh well, that's what bootlegging and overseas and ebay is for). So what is this incarnation? Simply a single disc approximation of Dylan for dummies. Those who know anything about Dylan won't be surprised at the track list. It's about as predictable as a Beatles single disc compilation. I've had fun making my own single disc compilations of Dylan for friends, and it is quite challenging (actually, impossible) to try to capture his talent on one CD. He's just too prolific. One curiosity of this disc is the songs are arranged chronologically, all except the last song, which, strangely enough, is from the 1974 album Planet Waves. It's one of the closest things he has to "inspirational" music and end the album on an inspiration. Maybe Dylan does want to stay "Forever young". Still, kind of odd given the rest of the songs are chronological. While I suppose this is a decent single-disc version, what, exactly, is the point, given we have the new 3-CD set. That's a good question. And it's not even really that exclusive to what has went on before. Like most major artists, Dylan has had his share of greatest hits compilations, some quite recent. First, we have the first GREATEST HITS album (Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits), released in 1967 as a stopgap release. Then we have the second installment from 1971, Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits, Vol. 2. Then we have the third installment from 1994, Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits, Vol. 3. Then Columbia gave us a double-disc compilation in 2000 entitled Essential Bob Dylan . Lest we forget, we also have the deluxe, three disc version of this set, Dylan. Then we have various other Best Ofs, all released within the last ten years, including two "best of Bob Dylans". Here's a list from Amazon that pull up when you enter Dylan in the search engine: The Best of Bob Dylan ,The Best of Bob Dylan*, and The Best of Bob Dylan, Vol. 2. And a lot of imports as well. Now, if you compare the track listing to the above mentioned with DYLAN, you won't find any real difference, other than a couple new tracks from MT. Oh, and the remix to "Most Likely You Go Your Way and I Go Mine", which strangely enough does NOT show up on the three disc version. Just one more worm to bait the hook I suppose. Cheap business tactics. All this being said, the question remains: what's the point? Money, of course. There's no reason to buy this. Grab the remix off the Internet (legitimately or otherwise), and if you really want to get the DYLAN compilation, do the three disc version. Those looking to get into Dylan will be better serviced by the 2000 ESSENTIAL album. He's prolific enough he merits multi-disc compilations. Don't even bother with this. *Oddly enough, this has a warning saying "Explicit Lyrics". When has Dylan ever written anything to merit "explicit lyrics" warning?

Lars abandoned the snare but still sounds like an average drummer, Kirk rips off Iron Maiden's Trooper solo and relies on the wah proving they made a mistake by kicking Mustaine out. As soon as Lars and James no longer had Mustaine's leftover material to boost or Burton to compose the songs the band suspiciously has continued on a downhill spiral. Rick Rubin, a wannabe Phil Spector, is a horribly overrated producer. At least Bob Rock, despite all his commercialism, knew how to make recordings sound good.

Bob Rock didn't kill Metallica it was always Lars and James greed. They used their more talented bandmates to make their career and took all the credit for their hard work. Lars and James were always about the money and Metallica was a fraud. Cliff and Mustaine were great musicians not these hacks. I am not saying this as a Megadeth fanboy. Mustaine's new music, although miles ahead of Death Magnetic, is weak. So is Slayer and the rest of all these bands from the 80's who are now 50 year-old dinosaur rockers trying to recapture their youth and failing miserably at it. There is a whole new generation of awesome bands out there and I hope the people reading this will know how to find them and stop supporting them when they start to suck. Only then will we not have to deal with albums like this and the upcoming new Metallica album.

I was quite disappoited with this package.  Upon opening, I noted the disks were held in place with some sort of solid, semi-soft plastic.  Once removed, there were nearly impossible to re-seat in a firm manner.  One of the four disks had cracks around the center hole, seemingly from being forced on this poorly designed material.
Much more importantly was my disappointment with the sound quality.  I was hopeful that this remastering would produce something beyond what has previously been available.  Unfortunately, that isn't the case.  As an audiophile, with a system approaching $40,000 in value, I search long and hard for well recorded material - and I know it when I hear it.  Regrettably, this doesn't make the grade.  I compared it to my DCC gold disc (mastered by Steve Hoffman) called "Nat King Cole - The Greatest Hits".  It wasn't even close.  Steve's mastering created a spacious stereo soundstage, with well placed images, and an inviting warmth and tone in Nat's voice.  These disks were flat, compressed, and edgy in comparison - all that is despised about poorly engineered CD's by audiophiles.
While my single DCC disk could not begin to cover the fuller catalog that these four do, I find this release to be unlistenable.  In almost 40 years of buying music, I have never returned a record or disc.  This will be the first.
If you are concerned with quality over quantity, this is not the package for you.  (Unfortunately, the DCC release is out of print, but they can sometimes be found used on eBay or AudiogoN.  They are very prized by audiophiles, sometimes going for $200+)

reviewText: When are people ever going to get a clue? All these lines like, "This is Taylor Swift's big jump into pop", or "Taylor is following her own path". WHAT OWN PATH?!? This is GENERIC POP MUSIC that sounds damn near interchangeable from Lady Gaga, Katy Perry, Demi Lovato, or GOD KNOWS WHO ELSE. And yet, people equate that with Taylor Swift following her own path?!? A better term would be "sell out", although, from the beginning, she's been a sophomoric, unaccomplished "songwriter" (assuming she really writes any considerable portion of any of her songs), who had the monumental good fortune to wind up on the path to stardom, not least because she had a well-off father who could front the money and work up back-room shenanigans which helped kickstart her career, and if you think that isn't true, then you really know little-to-nothing about the music industry. And with success so monumental, what motivation does she have to actually GET BETTER? A delusional love song like the beyond-simplistic "Fifteen" (from one of her earlier albums) is the kind of thing that would make one say, "Hey kid, that's at least a start--keep honing your craft", NOT THE REAL DEAL WORTHY OF SELLING IN THE MILLIONS. "1989" is a typical, super-slick 'modern' pop album, with incessant, grating 'hooks' tailor-made for the ADD crowd with no self-respect, the insufferable "Shake It Off" being a prime example. The blink-and-you'll-miss-it high falsetto of "All You Had To Do Was Stay" is laughably contrived. "Welcome To New York" is boring, blandly-produced feel-good tripe. "I Wish You Would" finds Taylor mining that same damn "woe is me" schtick that's been one of her hallmarks, with an 'overhip' backing track and cloying attempts at emotionalism in the vocals. "Blank Space" is juvenile trash of the sort you would THINK would be beyond her by now, given all her supposed attempts to evolve, but no. It's not saying a whole lot, but to be fair, a couple moments do rise above the mire, although I think the credit for that goes to co-writer Max Martin, who seemingly managed to come up for air with a couple flashes of inspiration. "Style" has a moody mid-tempo groove that does at least get your attention, and not in a gag-inducing way. And "Wildest Dreams", despite horrendous lyrics, does have an undeniably tuneful, atmospheric chorus. But, for someone worth somewhere in the ballpark of 200 MILLION DOLLARS (?!?!?) at this point, YOU SHOULD EXPECT BETTER. A LOT BETTER. The very idea that people seem to consistently believe that she's on some kind of genuine artist mission just prove the point that PEOPLE ARE SLAVES TO THE POWER OF MARKETING. By contrast, HERE is a modern-day example of following your own path: Do Not Rebuy Your Old Favorites yet Again [Explicit]. Tons of stylistic variety, songs of protest, songs that aspire to have people BRING SELF-RESPECT BACK TO THEIR SIDE INSTEAD OF MINDLESSLY LINING THE POCKETS OF ALREADY RICH POP STARS. You can't entirely blame Taylor Swift for having a massive ego, given her ludicrous amount of commercial success. And I do mean LUDICROUS. I mean, it's mind-blowing and nearly unfathomable how anyone could be as well known as her, not counting presidents and people of that nature. But YOU, as a CONSUMER, should be able to figure out after a while how to see the proverbial wood from the trees, and to have RESPECT FOR YOURSELF. If you really can't resist getting a taste, go stream "Style" and "Wildest Dreams". But if you seriously feel compelled to buy this album, how about stopping for a moment, taking a deep breath, and then, ahem, SHAKE IT OFF.

reviewText:
Pack up the tents: the show's over: Meat Loaf''s voice is gone. When I saw him in concert a couple years ago, I thought, it's just the touring, and with some rest the voice will come back. Nope. When I heard Meat and Jim Steinman were doing an album of all Steinman songs, I thought Bat Out Of Hell III (I know there already was one, but it wasn't all Steinman songs). I wish I had a chance to listen to all the songs in their entirety before buying this mess. If someone had told me I was buying a Meat Loaf album where he isn't the loudest voice on the album, I never would have believed it.

First a disclaimer: I have every single Meat Loaf album that he's put out (yes, even Meat Loaf and Stoney), so the haters can't say I don't know all his stuff. That's why this album is such a huge disappointment. Like a pitcher who's lost his fastball, or Sinatra when the booze and butts caught up to him at the end, why bother? If this is the best you can do, really, why bother? You're just taking your fans hard earned money.  So disappointing.

Let's get to the breakdown:

Who Needs The Young: Sounds like (and probably was) a bad off Broadway intro

Going All The Way Is Just The Start (aka Braver Than We Are) This one actually had potential as it's been released before and if Meat still had a voice, he would have made it another classic. Instead he lets female vocalists (Karla DeVito and Ellen Foley) do all the heavy lifting vocally. (Something he does quite often on the whole album)

Speaking In Tongues: This one I'll let him slide on; great lyrics, great production, and Meat doesn't need to be in full voice for it.

Loving You's A Dirty Job (But Somebody's Gotta Do It). See Going All The Way...Lousy vocals and again a female vocalist (Stacy Michelle) does the heavy lifting singing around Meat. Listen to the Bonnie Tyler/Rory Dodd version to see what this song could have and should have been.

Souvenirs: Basically a watered down re-write of Left In The Dark. Meat tries on this, he really tries, but the voice just can't get there.

Only When I Feel: An intro to:

More: Nope, really Less. This song seems unsure of what it wants be. Is it Electronika? Is it a Ballad? Both? Nope neither, more female vocals and chorus to carry the vocal load. This is tepid and painful.

Godz: An attempt at Heavy Metal? (which I believe is another bad off Broadway throwaway)

Skull Of Your Country: Which came first: this or Total Eclipse of the Heart? Even re-using the "Turn Around Bright Eyes" lyrics and melody. Seriously Jim? Nothing new to offer?

This hurts deeply, being a huge Meat Loaf and Steinman fan. If THE Voice is truly gone, why bother? This seems like nothing more than a money grab and an attempt to cash in on The Bat Out Of Hell legacy. If The Voice is not gone, then why not wait until it can once again soar with Wagnerian majesty and do these songs the credit they deserve.

I realize Meat is 68 now, but that's my point: don't tarnish the legacy. Why go out with a whisper, when we want to remember the bang!

reviewText:
In Australia, where harsh environmental conditions preclude the development of the hyperfeminine singer/songwriter (even of less expressive confessional folkies), there has for a great many years been an unfortunate market for pseudo-macho women rockers. For this, this set of songs is undoubtedly to blame.
Marketed as a glam rocker, Suzi Quatro was in reality a prefabricated hit machine that was no doubt designed to shock - but did not because her music was so appealing to a country raised for two decades on exactly the simple rock and roll Quatro was playing. Chinn and Chapman, who wrote all of her many Australian hit singles, had been hired with explicitly that purpose and intent, and the songs they wrote had clear appeal to Australia's youth and female populations.

Worst of all is the horrible "48 Crash", whose backing vocals really come across as badly as would a radio announcement trying to masquerade as music, but there is equally little to be said for almost all of the other material here. Without variation, Quatro copied what male rockers had been doing back in the fifties, but imaged herself as "the wild one" in a way women had not beforehand. Her voice is not as unpleasant as Joan Jett or Alanis Morrisette but does strike one as distant: the whole thing is essentially a show-off.

This "wild" and hyper-glossy image had so much impact on such women as Joan Jett, Pat Benatar and Alanis Morrisette - all of whom have reproduced the same pseudo-macho sneering for a teenage audience - that Quatro must be seen as an unfortunate influence. Whilst this might be inevitable in Australia, elsewhere there is little excuse.

reviewText:
As an avid follower of Robert Fripp since the original KC, through all the incarnations of that band, including the ProjeKcts and Soundscapes, I have always kept in mind Fripp's motto of "no expectations". But I will admit there is one expectation that I cannot get away from - the expectation of something challenging. Now challenging does not always mean avant-garde, angular, experimental, etc, i.e. most of the terms usually associated with both KC and the ProjeKcts. Fripp's Soundscapes are certainly what would be usually considered ambient music, but the challenging part is the way that so many different textures can be created by a solo guitar (albeit augmented by racks of effects). Still, it is an expectation, so perhaps I should take my own review with a grain of salt.

Nonetheless, the bottom line is this is probably the most disappointing thing I have ever heard from Mr. Fripp. The opening track tells you this is going to be mellow - fine. No problem with that. But the next three tracks are exactly, and I mean exactly, the same. There is no evidence of anything approaching inspiration - not even inspired noodling. Not until "The Other Man" do we get the idea that they may be trying to say something, and is the most interesting piece on the album; but by then it's too late. "The Light Of Day" is essentially a soundscape with sax and vocals, but in this case they distract from what otherwise would be a worthwhile example of that genre. To compare this to the lighter side of Crimson found on albums such as "Islands" is to totally denigrate that side of Fripp's musical personality. The same can be said about his work with Sylvian. Mel Collins is totally nondescript here, and could be any studio musician playing for scale; the same for Levin, and Harrison - and that is sad.

Fripp often says that what someone says about something reflects more about them than that which they are talking about. Well, fine, but what this says about me is that I would not recommend this album to anyone. I will leave the final words to Fripp's friend Steven Wilson (Porcupine Tree) in his song, "The Sound Of Muzak":

"Hear the sound of music drifting in the aisles,
Elevator prozac stretching on for miles.
The music of the future will not entertain;
It's only meant to repress and neutralise your brain."

A depressing coda to a great man's career.

"Aerial" was genuinely moody, quiet, etherial, calm energy, a different direction for Kate. And I loved it. The natural evolution of "Cloudbusting". This is just laziness. reviewText: Sometime within the last quarter century, pundits who consider themselves hip began to shower disco with praise, herald it as being some sort of cultural touchstone of the times that spawned it, celebrate the 4/4 beat (or whatever it is - I'm no drummer!) as the pulse of life for a generation of young adults looking to escape the daily hell of their going-nowhere, doing-nothing, trailer park lives.  Feh...  I hated disco in 1977 and I loathe it tenfold in 2004 and this 800-lb. gorilla of the Billboard charts is as good a place to focus my ire as any.  Alvin, Simon, and Theodore (collectively that would be the Bee Gees) completely turned their back on some of the outright great pop songs they forged in the 60's to audition for the Vienna Boys' Choir with "Stayin' Alive," (ranking right down there with "Hotel California" as this scribe's most hated song ever recorded) "How Deep Is Your Love," "Night Fever," "More Than A Woman," "Jive Talkin'," and "You Should Be Dancing," and people just couldn't get enough.  They streamed to the dance floor like lemmings to the cliffs, like lambs to the slaughter, and the music on this album provided the backdrop.  Walter Murphy and David Shire set Beethoven and Mussorgsky  twitching awake from their dirt naps with "Fifth Of Beethoven" and "Night On Disco Mountain" respectively and that's really saying something considering how low classical music flies on my radar.  Throw in dreck like KC's "Boogie Shoes," Kool & The Gang's "Open Sesame," and The Trammps "Disco Inferno," all as irritating as simultaneously banging your funny bone on a door frame while getting a chunk of Popsicle lodged in a filling, and it's obvious why punk HAD to happen.  "Classic piece of pop history"?  Gimme a break.  It pains me to say this, but we're right back where we started, with the world's clubs packed with people standing around cheering on people cueing up records.  Nearly 30 million people can't be wrong, can they?  The apocalypse is nigh...

reviewText: Those who spot the names of Yamatsuka Eye & John Zorn & expect a revisiting of the territory of Naked City will be in for a surprise.  Once one has removed the wrapper there is no indication that Eye & Zorn are involved (two Jewish pseudonyms are used in the liner notes); what you get is a bit over 20 minutes of phony old-world Jewish music: faint vocals, harmonium & the odd bell buried under a dense swathe of sampled crackle from old 78s.  I bought this disc when I was going through a phase of purchasing everything Zorn did; it was sufficient to check my enthusiasm for completism.  Eye & Zorn did a further one of these discs on Tzadik, which I am told has slightly more musical substance, & for years were rumoured to be releasing a 200-CD set which contained only two hours of music on it (I'm not sure if this was ever released).  As the latter would indicate, their collaborations are probably going to tickle the fancy of those interested in musical pranks & conceptual art.  All but hardcore fans are advised to leave well enough alone.  The disc is inexpensive enough & I still felt gypped.

reviewText:
Mannheim Steamroller started out as an audiophile label in many ways - their music, particularly on the Fresh Aire series of albums, was dynamic, featured real instruments and was used throughout the stereo industry as demo tracks. For decades after its release, "Toccata" from Fresh Aire III was a standard demo track heard at stereo shows and stereo dealers throughout the United States until it was replaced with newer audiophile war horses like the CDs from Telarc and "Jazz at the Pawnshop."

While this appears to be a nice collection of Mannheim Steamroller songs in one place, in remastering the songs have all been made louder AND compressed beyond belief, destroying all dynamic range and delicacy in the music. If you're someone who listens on earbuds, or likes everything loud without quiet passages, perhaps this CD will appeal to you.

On the other hand, if you're a long time Mannheim Steamroller fan, you'll simply be depressed at what they've done to the music.

See the attached photo comparing the waveforms of "Toccata" from the original Fresh Aire III CD from 1985 and the 30/40 Ultimate Collection for yourself. (They also applied what looks to be a brick wall filter at 20 KHz on the remaster, but compared to the compression, that's of little consequence.)

You can just hear the limiter pushing those drum fills and slams down into a big, wimpy wall of sound.

Guess I'll keep listening to this epic work from 1969 on vinyl. I'd take the original CD version over this any day, but neither even come close to the magic sound this had on the Coliseum vinyl cut. If you have to have this on CD, I highly recommend seeking out the original release from about 1993. This version is a downgrade. reviewText:
I give this 1 star, and I have no doubt that such a rating will PO some Simon and Garfunkel fans. But just listen to my reasoning, give me a fair chance. You won't be sorry.
"I Am a Rock" is a good song, about loneliness and isolation. I listen to this myself a good bit. "Bridge Over Troubled Water" is a good love song, and the conclusive proof that Art Garfunkel was by far the better singer of the two. BY FAR. But Paul Simon writes the songs and plays guitar (which he does fairly well). Aside from these songs, there is nothing at all here that I like. "Sounds of Silence" is the most popular thing here, but there is much in the way of BIG HIT all over this disc.
These guys were not really folk, or folk rock, as they are often categorized. They are a poet and a one man band (Paul Simon)(as they sing in homeward bound), and Art G. on the side, contributing as much with his singing as Paul S. does with everything else. The problem I have is that they have no feeling. Peter,Paul& Mary had the same problem-they had good songs, smooth harmonies, and this got them hits, but the real feeling, the real SOUL, is in the grittier stuff, like Bob Dylan. A good guitarist and songwriter, a bad singer and harmonica player, but he had so much heart, and it more than compensates for what he lacks. Simon and Garfunkel, Like Peter Paul & Mary, have what Dylan does/did not-fine vocal harmonies and a smooth production. But the emotional content, the RAW part, is missing. You probably love S & G, and you'll buy this. I appreciate that. All I ask is that you give Bob Dylan a chance. Buy the early folk stuff, and/or "Bringing it all Back Home" or "Highway 61". If you can't stand the thought of something as grating as Dylan, buy the first Byrds album, the one with "Mr. Tambourine Man". Just give it a chance. If you don't care about the lyrical aspect and just dig the harmonies, listen to "The Way You Look Tonight" by the Jaguars. If you still think the poet/one-man-band with his underappreciated buddy Art are better, that's cool. maybe you think I'm way off, that there's plenty of feeling here-and maybe that's because compared to what you normally listen to, this IS more emotional. But feeling in music goes much deeper than these guys ever did. I wouldn't lie to you, give Dylan and the Byrds a chance. Give the Jaguars and classic Doo-wop a chance. I can convert you, if you give me the chance.
Whether or not you take my advice, at least "Bridge Over Troubled Water" is done one hell of a lot better here than the way that bozo did it on American Idol.

If by some insane chance anyone near to you guys is reading this, please do not take this as me hating on you guys. I love you guys. Rather, this is plea. MUSIC IS DYNAMICS--both in terms of prosody and fidelity. I can't hear either on this album because of what the master did to your music. I want to support you guys but this album sounds worse than most stuff I have heard recorded in home studios on $150 mboxes set-ups. I am very discouraged with the music world these days. reviewText:
Metallica had risen like a Phoenix from the ashes in 2009 with Death Magnetic (see my review); however, they chose about the strangest way to follow up their return to glory in Lulu - their collaboration with Lou Reed.  Let me cut to the chase and say that I absolutely hate it.  If you are like me, you heard "The View" online somewhere and thought that this might be interesting.  However I think this song was strategically chosen to appear on the web site for this unfortunate joint venture.  It is the only one that gives James Hetfield a decent share of the lyrics.  He has fewer vocals on the rest of the songs combined.  It is really difficult to find much about this that is representative of Metallica.  It certainly doesn't shred like Death Magnetic did.

As if that wasn't bad enough, we have the lyrics penned by Reed.  What he wrote is often nothing short of vulgar.  If you couple that with a voice that sounds a lot like Johnny Cash near the end of his life, and Lulu winds up being downright creepy.  It is nothing short of a disappointment for me as a Metallica fan for over 20 years.  If you are into Lou Reed, you might like this.  Otherwise run, don't walk, to the new Megadeth instead.

Download this:  The View

reviewText:
I remember a day, not long ago when Incubus was my favorite band. They had the most insightful thought-provoking lyrics I had ever heard from "New Skin" to "Vitamin" and "Favorite Things", Incubus was the most sincere group of the time.
Those days are now few and far between, due to this 'new' Incubus that has suddenly played the pretty boys of MTV doing the little Diary of Incubus TV show thing and toning down their anti-religious, free thought scream into a wimper. I saw it coming when DJ Lyfe was fired or left the band (whichever the case), and Brandon cut his dreds (wouldn't be suprised if he did it soley to become more acc accessible to the mainstream).
The music on Make Yourself was less original, and the lyrics from S.C.I.E.N.C.E were toned down. The music was also focused on being more 'mainstream rock' as opposed to the work done on earlier releases. Then I found out that Kilmore took over on the DJ position and the music was less influential BUT Make Yourself was still a pretty good cd.
Then this thing came out. What happened? Brandon Boyd has a great voice, you wouldn't think that after listening to "Wish You Were Here" in which it sounds like a whine. And the lyrics? "I dig my toes into the sand, the ocean looks like a 1,000 diamonds strewn across the plain" YaK! They are SO corny, what happened to "The things that make us human are my favorite things"? Insightful lyrics about the question of reality and the state of our minds, now this cheesy-refined-steamlined-for-the-TRL-crowd-ick. It saddens me that even their attempts to regain that very emotion feels watered down.
Don't rate this cd based on WHO they are (wheather they're intelligent or not, because I KNOW they are), but what they're doing, musically. It's bad, don't be fooled by their previous work, this is horrible. If you're gonna buy an Incubus cd get S.C.I.E.N.C.E., it is worth EVERY PENNY! It was full of heart and packed with emotion, but now those days are long gone.

reviewText:
This is one of the most fascinating pages of Amazon reviews on the entire site.  Reading down from the top, you've got Aimee's own repudiation of this collection, followed by a rant by someone named Steve Ludlum, who apparently loves Mann's music (as I do), but disapproves of her manners.

I discovered Aimee Mann relatively late in her career.  Not much of a rock fan in the horrible 80s, I totally missed 'til Tuesday.  I hopped on board about a year after "I'm With Stupid," which I discovered by accident, and listened to obsessively for about six months. I've gotten everything else she's put out since, buying the Magnolia soundtrack about a year before I even saw the film, ordering Bachelor #2 from Aimee's website before it started showing up in stores.

But one of the things I've noticed about Aimee Mann's career is the existence of a lot, probably too much, background noise. She's partly responsible, because she puts her rage at the machine in so many of her songs.  Which lover has betrayed her this week?  Which record company mishandled her career?  To some degree, you have to care about these issues to get into her music--and I'm not sure I do. But she shares the blame with the gossip-mongers and spurned lovers and business associates who seem to be overly fascinated with the doings of this evidently difficult personality.

Mr. Ludlum's fascinating, yet mean-spirited, review kind of takes the cake.  Am I supposed to enjoy the brilliant close harmonies of "Driving Sideways," or the lyrical acuity of "High on Sunday 51," or the perfect marriage of words and melody of "Amateur" any the less because Aimee broke Jon Brion's heart, disobeyed Jimmy Iovine and p---d off Elvis Costello? (A very ironic twist, there.  Has Elvis forgotten that he was marketed to his first wave of fans as the angriest new-waver on his tight little island?) Am I supposed to look at this cheesy compilation as Aimee's just desserts, and buy it to spite her?

Hey, I'm just a little old music consumer here. I don't worry about the dirty deals going down at my local pizzeria, and I don't care about Aimee's love life, except insofar as it inspires another great song. Not to put her quite the same category, but James Joyce and William Faulkner were nasty alcoholics, Sylvia Plath was an arrogant snob, and Pablo Picasso was... you get the point. If Aimee's messing up her life, that's a matter for her mom and her husband to worry about, not us.

Looking forward to "The Forgotten Arm,"... and hoping I don't recognize anyone in it,

Juan LaPrinci, fan.

reviewText:
I should have known better!
You have to be very careful when buying Marshall Tucker live albums.  Most of them have poor sound quality.
This might be the worst one yet!

I really wished I would have checked the Amazon reviews before I bought this!  Typically, the reviewers on Amazon will put up with mediocre sound quality and typically don't mention it.  But, when you see this many complaints, you know its going to be bad!

I bought this CD because it has a good song selection.  I have been trying to find an extended version of Never Trust a Stranger, ever since I heard them play it in 1977.  I really loved the drumming, bass guitar interplay.  The version on this CD is over 12 minutes long.  Does it have that wonderful drum/bass solo....you really can't tell because the sound quality is so bad.

What about the rest of the performance?  It seem like it might be good.  Who can tell?

So, what Tucker live album should you get?  It is hard to recommend any but Where We All Belong which was half live.  Most have poor sound.  The ones with acceptable sound have a lackluster performance.  Stompin' Room Only contains probably the weakest performance I have heard from the band.  It has acceptable sound quality, but does have some problems.  Rumor has it was supposed to be released back around 1976 but got shelved for some reason.  I think it is because the sound quality was not up to par.

I saw Marshall Tucker 3 times.  First time, they were the headliner and they only played for 20 minutes and then did a 20 minute encore.  I couldn't believe it.  The next time was part of festival with Fleetwood Mac.  They played for 2 hours.  The third time was in a bar.  It was a great performance.

reviewText:
... or to put it in Italian, since this was a production in the Theater of san Carlos in naples, "seriet senza squillo" -- 'squillo being the word for the ringing heroic timbre of the best Italian tenors. Squillo is what's missing in the musicianship of this performance, both in the singers and in the orchestra.

The overture to Tannhuser should foreshadow and set up all the emotions of the production, the longing, the heroism, the adoration of Nature, the redemptive exaltation -- all shades of squillo ringing out from the transformations of the central motif. This San Carlos Orchestra lumbered when it should have soared, coughed when it should have groaned. I'd swear there were holes in the violin section, or rather in the master sound track where the violins were too obviously snarly. The trombones had trouble with the beat and the cymbal player must have been doing a crossword puzzle. I have a wealth of nostalgia for this overture; I played the bassoon part in it in the Harvard-Radcliffe Orchestra decades ago. But I almost shut the DVD off at the end of it....

...and soon enough I wished I had. First there was the offstage chorus, badly out of tune. Then came Tannhuser, sung by Alan Woodrow, also less than impressive in tuning and harsher of voice than even his weariness of Venusberg would justify. Next, up waddled Venus, sung by Marianna Pencheva, alluring neither vocally nor visually, and also out of tune far too often. This first scene of Tannhuser has to be both lush and fraught with tension. Honestly, it's hard to get it right, and many productions fail, but what the audience saw and heard in Naples was closer to the mid-life spat of an overstuffed couple in an over-draped McMansion in Milwaukee.

And that's as far as I got. I'm not masochist enough for three hours of third-rate Wagner.

You can grasp what the Doors sounded like live during their prime era which influenced punk, proto-punk and goth. But the sound quality is abyssymal. They need to reissue the original master tapes to the public or at least as penance allow the next winner of "American Idol" to be the lead singer for the "Doors of the 21st Century". Take your pick. reviewText:
Like many late gen-xers I grew up listening to NKOTB in the 1980's. Then, the ascention of Nirvana and other 'grunge' bands heralded a permanent changing of the music world--the less polish, the better.
If the band was going to surive such new conditions, it needed to reinvent itself for the changing times.
Sensing G-rated bubblegum would no longer suffice in this new 'edgier' world., band member Donnie Wahlberg attempted to remix some of the greatest hits to continue the cash flow, but the direction ruined the band's reputation as the clean cut boys next door.
As evidenced by the cover photo and art, the group tried on a 'rough' image which may have been more closer to the actual outside environments of their Boston childhoods, but would drive away the pre-teen and child fans who had made their millions possible.
Especially compared to the blockbuster hits of the earlier records, sales were abysmal and the 'adult' NKOTB was shortly disbanded for (admittedly successful) solo careers. Whether this downturn was covertly planned is a matter of debate to this day, but it was the proverbial last hurrah from the "Fab Five".
Although many other greatest hit albums have surfaced since then, this work is unique because it was the death knell of the act itself.

Most of the content is numbskull commentary from a group of musical experts you have never heard of. Fans should also be aware that this product is not approved by the group, and it is my understanding that none of the musicians involved recieve royalties from the sale of the product. The short length of the clips and the presentation of the series as a "critical review" allow the producers to avoid charges of copyright infringement. reviewText: I understand that a lot of readers gonna click 'no' for this review which I happen to write in response to a friend who mentioned this album recently. It was already distasteful at first hearing when it came into release, and it made me realise that it's not worth messing around with the timeless and immeasurable quality of original classical compositions. But if an artiste has to do it, then according to this friend of mine, 1) Keep too-obvious electronica elements to a minimum. Do not overload a track with heavily synthsized sounds as it is emulated classically. Keep it simple, because such sounds are too puny to match the breadth, resonance and harmonics of actual orchestral arrangements anyway. For this point, I rate (only) Adagio For Strings satisfactorily, because it's close to the original. But really, if it sounds so similar, what's the point? 2) Do not make the tracks sound hyper. If it is necessary to quicken the pace of an emulated classical track, there is only one type of sound that can do just that all right: one that comes out of a music box. If that's the case, I remarked that even the music box version of Cavalleria Rusticana that I imagined in my head would sound much better. My friend readily agreed, and at the same time questioned if it is all right and natural for listeners to make comparisons between variants and originals. Again, this classic debate applies to film adaptation of novels as well. 3) Don't emulate classical stuff! If you want to do it, then take it to another genre or a personal style shamelessly. Ferry Corsten (for the Adagio For String remix), Vanessa Mae and even Nigel Kennedy did a good job at incorporating their professional specialties/trademarks and pop antics into the things they play. Ultimately, I believe that no matter how bad an album is, the forgiving critic would care to go through the album once and form an impression of the artiste's personal agenda behind the recording of the album. If the critic can't make sense of what he's listening to, then he can't really identify the artiste's aspirations and agenda. If this is the case, then I'm sorry to say that William Orbit has only one ultimate purpose: self-indulgence. I'm not a forgiving critic. Willam O deserves a big O (1 star is only because I need to get this review through). My friend is now proceeding to create a music box version of Cavalleria Rusticana using some music shareware program since it's the holidays, and I pray he can get it right.

But the big difference is the focus on this album is on image and self-promotion; Lady Gaga is nothing more than a manufactured moneymaker for the industry, and that is apparent by all the professionals who worked on this album. They even trotted out oldfolks Mutt Lange and the guitar player from Queen to enhance the songs.

The lyrics are just plain dumb, both banal and self-absorbed. Gaga herself seems to think that sheer will power will put her atop the charts, when in fact her singles from the album so far have not met sales expectations. Some of the songs are constructed well, while others sound like lame 1980's soundtrack material that could have been sung by Vixen, Lita Ford, or Pat Benatar. And that's not a knock on Pat Benatar by any means. But it does giv one pause when an artist like Gaga, who has not released a good single since "Bad Romance," professes to be so inventive and original. If the definition of inventive is to channel your inner 1980's Madonna and Pat Benatar, then that's a problem, because the songs just aren't that good anyways.

reviewText:
Another helping of bland jazz-country banjo fluff from Alison.  Nicely recorded and deftly played, with an excellent cast of studio musicians, but musically pretty barren.  Stylistically, it's a wishy-washy new-age product with faint country roots although it is perhaps intentionally more jazzy than country, so there is lots of pretty doodling but not much earthy gritty substance.

The compositions are mostly Alison's, with the help of the band's pianist John R. Burr, while The Road West is Mairtin O'Connor's and Forky On The Water is traditional.  The instruments accompanying Alison's banjo include piano, mandolin, fiddle, bass, guitar and percussion.

There are certainly high quality production values here.  The recorded sound is full, glossy and easy on the ears, but musically the album joins other wallpaper Americana coming out of Nashville at the moment that is unfortunately meaningless and forgettable (like Jerry Douglas's largely disappointing Glide).

I'm a fan of the banjo and of rural bluegrass generally, and perhaps my ears rebel if there's too much infused jazz, but deep musical ideas were just not forthcoming here so it didn't grab me at all (neither did a live performance a couple of years back).  One for the fans, perhaps.

reviewText:
The Doors and Warner Music Group issued a press release to promote this CD, stating: "Restored and carefully mastered from first generation tapes acquired by Elektra Records and The Doors 40 years ago, these historic shows never sounded better."

However, at least 4 tracks here were sourced from 3rd generation or higher bootlegs. The remaining songs were mastered from an edited 2nd generation 1/4" reel to reel copy of a cassette dub made from the master reels.

Neither the Doors, nor their corporate record label Warner Music Group (aka the Rhino and Elektra imprints) own the original master recordings.

The master tapes are owned by Peter Abram, who had the foresight to record the band at The Matrix (with the band's permission)--more than two years before Elektra and Paul Rothchild got around to recording The Doors in a live setting at The Aquarius theater in 1969.

These legendary 1967 live tapes were well engineered by the young Abram and find the rock band at the peak of their prowess as an improvisatory unit.

However, the tapes Warner Music Group has published on this 2 CD rip off are vastly inferior to the master tapes, brief samples of which are circulating on the Internet with Peter's permission for comparison purposes.

Some fans may choose to believe that Abram is being greedy by asking for cash for his tapes. However, The Doors manager Jeff Jampool has publicly stated the Doors' policy about acquiring live tapes is that they will only provide a small royalty based on sales.

According to Abram, he wasn't even approached to sell his tapes to the Doors for this release. And what about all those bootlegs on the market? According to Abram, all bootlegs derive from the missing first generation cassette copies in the Doors archive, which vanished in the 1970s.

The fans get a sonically subpar, incomplete product. The legality of this release is suspect since Peter owns the master tapes. Peter Abram receives zero money from this product, even though he owns the master sound recording. Meanwhile, your purchase of this material will make Warner Music Group and The Doors a little bit wealthier.

And this is the same rock band that recently sued itself for $5 million dollars over issues of "integrity?"

By the way, how much money was cover designer Stanley Mouse paid for his Matrix album cover art, while they guy that actually recorded the show--on his own nickel and made this cash cow possible for The Doors--doesn't even receive a credit as recording engineer in the liner notes?

reviewText:
As many people may know by now, Sony was recently caught with egg on their face when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit

2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.

3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.

4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

As of my writing this review, Sony has "apologized" for this incident, and claims they will "re-evaluate" this copyright protection software on their CDs in the future.

In the meantime, a virus is currently running wild, which names itself begining with $sys$ in an attempt to hide from the user and virus scanners.

Several class action lawsuits are also pending against Sony right now.

In summary, as you can tell from above, Sony's actions here are absolutely horrible. This is your music. You purchased it, and they should not have any right to dictate how you can use it, let alone install software which compromises your system security.

This is one of the CDs with Sony's XCP copyright protection software on it, and as a result, you should not buy it to send a message to Sony that this will NOT be tolerated in the future.
