reviewText:
Collective Soul is one of those bands which never ceases to sound as if they're struggling for something - musical legitimacy, critical praise, commercial success... whatever it is they seek, they seem to endure failure  after failure with continual enthusiasm. 'Collective Soul,' the group's  self-titled sophmore album, succeeds on a single front, offering a pair of  tracks with solid enough hooks to achieve chart success as singles. The  uninspired pair, "december" and "the world i know" are  dull but recognizable. Fair enough.
The album in its entirety, however,  is very very poor - largely due to frontman Ed Roland's self-important  pseudo-poetry. Roland likes to concoct silly combinations of unrelated  words to simulate some sort of goofy sophistication (witness the title of  follow-up album 'Disciplined Breakdown'). The results are pompus and  embarassing... like his "scathing" but grammatically-lacking  accusation of an ex's lust for "ambience and vanity" in  "december." Ugh.
Musically, 'Collective Soul' teeters between  overdone and just plain bad. More often the not, the tracks are plagued by  unbelievably awful guitar riffs, which repeat mercilessly through  "smashing young man" and "she gathers rain," among  others. Where the band strikes occasional gold (the simple riff of  "december" is a good example; the mushy strains of  "collection of goods" is another), all the subtlety gets bogged  down by Roland's lousy lyrcis and the bands' general tendancy to  over-indulge. It all points back to a band trying harder to win praise than  to really bare its soul... the constant showiness gets tiresome.
Phew...  this album isn't for everybody, that's for sure. Perhaps there is an  audience out there for 'Collective Soul' - the other reviews seem to  suggest there is. Hear me: there is better stuff out there, people. It's  that simple. Don't stop now - keep searching for music that realllllllly  moves your soul, collective or otherwise.
label: negative

reviewText:
I must first congratulate IE for being one of the few bands that refuse to totally give up after having had some fame come their way. Due to the quality albums Iced previously demonstrated, they rest upon a bed of good validity and they've stuck it out as much as can be expected..

  The impression first, throughout much of the album, is that this is a medium to slow (only sometimes fast) trudge through some "cut from the cloth" HM music. Though "Declaration Day" gives you the feeling you're in for something very heavy and dense. "The Reckoning(Don't Tread on Me)" does then raise the pace a bit as well... Most Rob Halford imitations work out sounding somewhat humorous, but here we realize that Tim "Ripper" Owens is sounding, for the most part, in a way that does not alert you too much of his pseudo RH-like presence....until the music picks up pace and he then tries hard to match it. But those pick-up moments are  fairly rare anyway. An "open up and say eehhhhhh" quality comes out also in the vocals, accompanied by a feeling as if TRO was concentrating on remembering the the lyrics instead of how much emotion his voice conveyed.

  Iced Earth has previously had emotional or ballad-type songs; however, they were driven by Matt Barlow's simultaneously smooth and strong voice, sounding  as though he and the band were fully conscious of the emotion behind the songs, making it all sound thorough. On this album, there seems to be patched-sounding choruses sung almost as if by the same group of voices you might hear on any standard rock album. Subsequently, each rotation stabs this quality out even further, and then you notice other things....

 Except for maybe "Don't Tread on Me," most of the entire album has an almost Rocky soundtrack or school anthem sound to it.

Some lyrics go:

 "Upon this declaration
Will come a grand new nation
Where men are seen as equal
Governed by and for the people"

 The meaning of the words are fine, of course, and these type of anthem-like lyrics merge into what you'd expect as you play the rest. The affirmation of a moderately paced: "chiga..chiga..chig..chig..chah..."..(solo)..repeat, seems to basically sum up 90% of this work. Other albums with this kind of sound have been noted as generic feeling and even as "paint by the numbers."

  On some of the material after this cd, I can hear a fair bit of rushed moments as well, though there seems to be a few rather dynamic songs on "The Crucible Of Man" to balance it all out a little bit more.

  Let's see what the future holds..

reviewText:
Midway through the opening cut, "N.W.O.," with Bush Sr. rapping at the mic, there's a moment where all the steroid-chugging axe grinding and scream-at-the-top-of-your-lungs-like-you're-a-frantic-ghoul vocals fade and the listener is left with a myopic dance beat. And that's when well-versed listeners will remember that Ministry started out (shudder at "Twitch") and was condemned to remain a sissy boogie band. Alain Jourgensen and pals merely added a Skinny Puppy motor to their makeshift parade float by the time they recorded "Land of Rape and Honey."

"Psalm" continues to lose IQ points as you delve further. The clunky wrestler's-catwalk theme "TV II" and meathead-friendly powerpuff "Jesus Built My Hot Rod" reveal Jourgenson to be in the same dopey league as the Bush clan he so constantly rails against. "Tell me something I don't know" is apropros of George Jr., as well as "Diggy diggy-don a dong dong ding-dong." But the line, "Who'm I trying to impress, who could care less?" has for me come to merely mean that Jourgensen is a man who has no faith in his convictions ... or pumps so much noise, lights, screaming and other testosterone-sized diversions into the mix that you ultimately realize he just can't take himself seriously, which should be insulting if you are a fan.

However, if the most challenging music you can handle is jerry-built by bands like Kid Rock, Monster Magnet and White Zombie, then by all means add this to your collection. However, first put down that bong and check to make sure you don't already have it somewhere in your milk-crate library.

reviewText: Elvis Costello is a strange case. Like any talented artist he has chosen never to live off his strengths. This explains why over the last decades he has continuously produced alternations of excellent and disastrous records. Also anytime he choses to go more acoustic or country, it has not been his forte. Indeed the more simplistic musical approach makes his voice seem really whiny instead of angry. He has chosen to associate once more with T-Bone Burnett after what was already a disaster (King of America) and has chosen to go down the country route again. His first venture into country almost twenty years ago was a disaster and came after a splendid run of albums (my aim is true, this year's model etc). Do not get me wrong I loved both Costello and country but as I wrote, his voice was/is not suited to the ballady type of country. It does not matter if the music is splendidly played (it is here) but it does not suit his style or voice. Then anytime the record title has been associated with moods (almost blue, get happy etc) he does not seem to handle it that well for some reason. I am sorry to say so but despite all the efforts (and coffee) put into this record, Elvis Costello has not pulled it off...again...

reviewText:
I just want to echo the sentiments of an earlier reviewer, and thank all the whistleblowers here who sounded the alarm about Sony's insidious hidden spyware. I get enough of that crap to clean off my hard drive as it is through everyday spam attacks; I don't need it coming from my music CD's as well.

Having said that, I have longed for the Diamond Days when his music (at least to me) could do no wrong. I was about eight the very first time I heard "Holly Holy." I cried. The soaring, melodic, majestically joyful combination of Neil's songwriting prowess and Lee Holdridge's arrangement made it sound like the most beautiful hymn I had never heard sung in church before. And from that moment on I was hooked.

Every review I have read here and on other music sites expresses the same sentiment: The Man Is Back! I, too, would like to have the freedom to export my music to any device I desire, since I carry a stereo CD player, and have music on my hard drives at work and at home. Which is why before I even hear the first note, I have to give it one star. Not to punish Neil, but to express my extreme displeasure with Sony. So I will still purchase it and enjoy it, but it will have to be on my portable player. As long as it has spyware on it, it's not coming near any PC I use.

And if the suits at Sony are monitoring these reviews, I think they should know that I will have to consider a complete boycott of ALL Sony hardware and software products from here on in, until somebody comes to their senses.
label: negative

reviewText:
I pre ordered this CD with great anticipation only to be so disappointed upon the arrival and eventual four listenings. I though,well I haven't really given it a chance to sink in yet or I'm not in the right frame of mind to actually hear the songs, music and receive it as intended. BUT now after four times of actually listening, I can only say, Why release this CD? Thick As A Brick by Jethro Tull is one of the all time greats while TAAB-2 is one of the all time great disappointments.
 While all who play on it are talented musicians, it doesn't get close to the sound or power of Jethro Tull nor the interesting weave of story and song dynamics.
 It starts with fantastic interest fading in from where Thick As a Brick left off making you think wow, how cleaver, the story continues and yes the first song draws you in because of that great intro and then it's all down hill from there on and boring.
 The guitarist while a good player and talented in his style but not anything close to the style, technique, power or drive of Barre or the Tull sound we all love. There is no power to this album, no drive and zero excitement......yes Tull did soft tunes as well but this is like a bad play tune one after another.
 Although I'm 65 now I still listen to rock every day and still play bass and guitar and love the Power and Dynamics Of Jethro Tull(The Band That Is). I guess some stories should end where they did originally, Great.
 Thick As A Brick was so great and TAAB-2 is really So Bad. Save your money and buy a ticket to San Francisco on Translove Airways they'll get you there on time or re-buy all of Tulls original recordings....just avoid TAAB-2 at all cost. Bland blah and boring.....I only gave it One Star because of effort and Andersons voice is still excellent for his age. Sadly you can't leave a negative star rating or I might have rated it -5 Stars.......so so sad......I'll save the jewel case and pitch the rest....It might have actually been palatable if it wasn't wrongfully titled Thick As A Brick 2...possibly Titled "Ian Anderson Sings While Boring Band Plays" would have been more appropriate...! Waste of good money and of studio time...

What right does Gibbons, Hill, or Beard have to authorize or promote the alteration and embellishment of their original session material without clearly stating on the CD This is a Remix of the Original Material to Suite Newer Listeners.  These jokers even included the ancient blurb found on early CD reissues that says, We have attempted to preserve, as closely as possible, the sound of the original recording.  This is NOT the original recording, but is instead the material altered with gated reverb and fluff to sound like ZZ Tops Eliminator and Afterburner era (when theyd basically sold out by becoming a commercial pop disco band). reviewText:
To be honest, I don't know a great deal about the artist or their history.  But upon some quick research you can tell that the beach and California is certainly loved.  Looking at the product information here, what I expected was to hear consistent atmospheric music, highlighted by Spanish guitar work.  But what was it that I got?

An act that has it's work cut out for them.  The guitar play was very disjointed.  It's as if the musicians had entirely different songs in their heads as they played.  Never mind that on several occasions you could hear that they were woefully out of tune.  But maybe more annoying on this album was that the background 'beat-machine' sounded awefully mid-80's Casio-ish.  After every song, I was left wondering if this was inspired by sailboats and the ocean, or Death Valley & tumbleweed.  If I had to say one thing positive, it would be that if there was just one guitar, and ther ewasn't any other sounds or effects in the music (this means no casio beats, no casio guitar, no casio bass), while this would still fall short, it might be better.  Assuming the songs and directions changed.  There is some talent here.  But unfortunately it's largely washed away.

I can't recommend this.  The beat's the same on every song (not that it matters, because the play .  The tone's the same & the production work is non-existent.  It's a real train-wreck.  And when the core's poor to begin with, so goes the rest of the album.  If you want to hear better Spanish guitar, stick to the masters like Segovia.  If you want to be taken to the beach, listen to bossa nova.  But this is a release that you'll be hard-pressed to ever play again.  Just listen to "Determined Drift"... a song loaded with rifts determined to make the already proven impossible work somehow; yet fail.  But the biggest surprise of all, is that this is the THIRD album they've released.
label: negative

reviewText:
I regard Jimi Hendrix as one of the greatest artists of the golden age of rock; his debut album 'Are you experienced' is one of the great debut albums of the age, 'Live at Monterey' is one of the definitive rock performances of all time, and 'Axis: bold as love', 'Smash Hits', 'Band of Gypsys' & 'Electric Ladyland' rank among the finest rock albums of all time.

However, 'South Saturn Delta', a posthumous release of senseless studio jamming, should have been left in the archives or have been issued with a warning. I bought this album to complete my Hendrix collection. Sadly, that's about where it ends - the album completes my collection but never gets listened to.

The music consists rambling permutations and combinations of Hendrix motifs that seem to come from nowhere and go nowhere. The end result is boring, completely unsatisfying, and detracts from the meteoric CV of the master. This is a sleeping dog that should have been left lying.
label: negative

reviewText:
From the first howled notes of "Old Dan Tucker," a song that nobody over the age of four cares (or should care) about, to the end, this is Springsteen's crassest yet. He simultaneously taps into the "O Brother Where Art Thou" soundtrack crowd and continues the fake-populist stance he's taken since "The Rising," an album that did nothing but crassly capitalize on the 9/11 disaster in order to bring back what was frankly a failing career.

Seeger's name stuck on this album is especially insulting. The songs have little to do with Seeger, and Seeger always had the courage of his convictions. Springsteen, on the other hand, has shown that he's perfectly willing to fake a populist stance in order to reap the financial rewards and renew his career.

I used to like and respect Springsteen. No more. This is the bottom of the barrel, and shows that in the long run he's no more principled or worthy of notice than any wanna-be abusing a cover song on American Idol.
label: negative

reviewText:
First, this review is NOT a comparison to Clay Aiken's debut CD, as the two singers represent different music styles and target audiences. Please do NOT read this review as a rejection of Ruben for any negative bias reason. As a professional music producer this review is aimed solely at this CD's content.

The song choices and production on "Soulful" is dismal. Ruben's attempts in hip hop genre are an unfortunate reversal of the musical taste of a man whose love for Opera is well known. Too often his singing is breathless, off pitch and flat on the ballads. Pitch correction is easily done during the Mastering phase with a vocal processor called a "Harmonizer". Why didn't Ruben get this benefit when needed?
"Sorry 2004" and "No Ruben" are two meaningless throw-away songs. One hopes their titles don't fortell the future of this artist who has AT LAST, brought real singing back to his culture that has, for a full decade, been represented by the vulgar, vicious and unspeakably abusive, filthy lyrics of rap, hip/hop like the appalling Eminem or 50 cent, etc. After reading many reviewers'comments at Amazon, Entertainment Weekly, etc. there is an overall feeling of disappointment even with the inclusion of "Superstar" and "Flying without Wings".
Personally, I would like to kick the collective butts of Ruben's producers who ignored the fact that many of us want to hear Ruben sing beautiful music. Other reviewers suggest that his label sabotaged Ruben's first CD with this unfortunate mix of songs.  The music industry cries and whines about flat record sales while ignoring a world of people willing to spend money on good music. Ruben can sing it, but it is not apparent on this CD.

This is a major shock and disappointment. '5 Questions' may have made a halfway decent southern soul record, but somehow I don't that was its intended market. This sounds like a demo that got released accidently-on-purpose to the uninformed, unprepared fans of the MPLS sound. Bad, bad mistake. That said, I have 5 Questions of my own for you and your record producers, Mr. O'Neal.

1. What the ---- were u thinking???!!!!!

2. Were you hanging in your hometown of Natchez, MS listening to Sir Charles Jones, Latimore, and J. Blackfoot and decided THAT was the way to go? Bad mistake dude.

3. Who told you that posing as a shady pool room character for your album cover would be cool?

4. Why couldn't you 'just say no' and leave this demo in the darkest part of your musical vault?

5. I'll always respect and appreciate you for your work in the 80s. But why won't you just swallow your pride and ask Jam, Lewis, Jellybean, and Monte for some help musically? Its obvious the people you're working with right now are steering you further and further away from the charts...and a decent recording.

Don't get me wrong. Being a native of the deep South, I like Southern soul. I really do. I feel its helping to keep the tradition and the roots of the genre alive among all these soft-voiced Urban/crossover prettyboys. In fact, if you're hip to the Soul/Blues sound you might be able to find something to like about this record. But let this be a warning to all established singers: If you're intending to radically alter your sound and style, give your listeners fair warning. It may prevent a nasty backlash.

reviewText: A work astonishing in its grandeur, all-sweeping in its innocent portrayal of the angst of twentieth century man, a defining moment in the musical progress of our solar system, and until proven otherwise, a work of musical, compositional, technical and intellectual achievement unlikely to be exceeded this side of the milky way within the remaining years of this millenium...so say some reviewers it seems. Well, I'm sorry to run against the grain but we have to be honest here. This is absolute garbage which could have been produced by sticking any bunch of talentless teenage girls together in a studio and recording them. I'm amazed that people who should know better have been caught out by the it's-so-horrible-there-must-be-something-in-it syndrome, quite common in free form jazz and progressive rock circles. Listen to their musical attempts enough times, with enough people repeating that there's something of value there, all apparently misunderstanding Zappa's irony, and a kind of collective self-hypnosis takes care of the rest. Anyone who's blown away by this can only be blown away by millions of possible combinations of teenagers around the planet. As an embarrassing musical experiment better kept in family circles, or as an amusing sociological artifact, this album succeeds. As a musical work, this is a truly dismal attempt at musical creation only exceeded by the sound of my lawnmower.

reviewText: I have read every review posted here on amazon, regarding Neil Diamond's new cd "Home Before Dark". I hestitated writing this review, because the last thing I wanted to do was write an unfavorable synopsis of this new cd.  I have never been a big fan of producer Rick Rubins stripped down guitar and voice only approach for an entire album of songs.  After several listens, I have found this cd to be uneventful and slow.  Songs like "No words", "Another day", "Don't go there", "If I don't See You Again", and most others, are basically a group of songs that sound the same, with a depressing overtone and scoring a zero on the excitement scale.  After an entire cd of the same format on "12 Songs", his prior release, I can't believe he decided to make another cd full of boring fireside strums.  Just what is Rick Rubin producing here?  There is no production.  It would have been nice if Neil jammed it up a notch, on at least half the cd.  Let's face it, Neil Diamond is a showman,  No one is going to go to his latest concerts this summer and beg to hear this stuff.  Whether one wants to admit it or not, the fans are going to his shows to hear those classics, that shake you out of your seats, like "Cracklin Rose", "Sweet Caroline", "Brothers Traveling Salvation Show", "Beautiful Noise", etc.  Some hardcore Neil Diamond fans seem to be personally offended with every negative review of this cd, you shouldn't be, just as I am not bothered by the positive reviews, it is all a matter of opinion.  My opinion is, this is a far cry from his best efforts.  One can judge for themselves.
label: negative

Andy likes his sound effects, beat box & Bacharach style melodies. Bottom line, I found this CD to be downright boring. There is nothing uptempo (can anything top "You On My Mind", "We Could Make It Happen", "Breakout" etc.?).

I have just outraged fellow SOS fans, but I am honest with my opinion. Nothing grabbed me. This is a fairly low key, mellow CD. Sure, the performance is top notch (what isn't done by programming), but it is background music at best, or something to fall asleep to. It isn't the fun, or catchy SOS power pop with catchy melodies that I am still hearing in malls today. Perhaps they haven't had many chart hits, but their music will remain a shopping center staple for years to come. I doubt if any of this material will make it that far. With each track I waited for the next one to make me say "wow", but it never happened. I found some of the mastering on a few tracks to be poor also.

This is a long overdue & welcome release, but it fell vastly short of my expectations & I don't think I'll be spinning it much. Their creativity & talent is astounding, but I'll stick with their past releases for enjoyment. Indeed, beautiful...but also a mess.

reviewText: What a disappointing album.  I was a huge Deep Purple fan starting with the album In Rock, though I now like the earlier stuff quite a bit. But I started with and loved Deep Purple Mk 2 with singer Ian Gillan and bassist Roger Glover. I weathered the change in vocalists to the duel vocals of Glen Hughes and David Coverdale and thought Purple's previous album to Stormbringer, Burn was very good although not quite as good as most of the Mk 2 albums. So I bought Stormbringer thinking I was going to get more music of the same quality as Burn, listened to it and hung my head in despair.  A once great hard rock band had devolved into a radio friendly amalgam of blues, gutless r&b and unoriginal and uninspired rock. Deep Purple seems to have succumbed to the prevailing tastes of the day circa 1974, ie. bland middle of the road mush or maybe Glen Hughes is to blame? In any case this bowl of musical outmeal was the result. It killed the band for me and apparently Ritchie Blackmore as well as he left soon after Stormbringers release. Deep Purple had a very original prog influenced hard rock sound that I loved and they completely abandoned on Stormbringer. Many of these psuedo R&B songs sound like variations on Play That Funky Music White Boy by Wild Cherry! WTF? The best songs sound like second rate Whitesnake which seeing as how Whitesnake are a second rate band means that Stormbringer sounds like crap. After this debacle Blackmore left to form Rainbow and the drug addled Tommy Bolin replaced him for the better follow up album Come Taste The Band. Untortunately for me DP without Blackmore isn't DP so I didn't buy it. They lost me. Unless you like the top forty circa 1974 or really bland cliche hard rock or cheesy R&B, avoid Stormbringer as you would a rabid cat. This is the album where DP lost their muse, their soul and their audience. Buy it and prepare to be bored.

reviewText: I love No Doubt. I guess I might have seen this one coming, but I never could let the notion sink in. Tragic Kingdom was the first CD I've ever bought for myself. Collecting little bits of money wherever I could, I bought the disc after hearing Spider Webs and Just A Girl at summer camp, my first summer away from home. Well, now, finally, it's here. Rock Steady is out and I'm speechless. What kind of redundant, pop, non-instrumental, regression is this? The release of Hey Baby as the first single caught me offguard with its nonexistent lyrics,... charged implications, and dreadful tune. reviewText:
THE ONE STAR RATING REFLECTS THE VALUE OF THIS ALBUM NOT THE SONGS INCLUDED WHICH ARE VERY GOOD SONGS.

BEATLES VI is the result of Capitol Records' strategy for releasing three Beatles albums for every two released in Great Britain using singles to fill out the remainder of the content to yield eleven song albums compaired to the fourteen song UK albums. BEATLES 65 had already used up eight of the fourteen songs from the UK album, BEATLES FOR SALE.  The Beatles' movie, HELP!, was in production and would be released as a movie soundtrack complete with incidental instrumental music as A HARD DAY'S NIGHT had been handled in the US, as such, BEATLES SIX would complete BEATLES FOR SALE, much of the material already hitting the US airwaves since "Eight Days a Week" and "I Don't Want to Spoil the Party" were released as a single. "Words of Love" was played frequently before BEATLES VI late spring release. Three songs would be from the soon to be released complete fourteen song British release of HELP!

From BEATLES FOR SALE:

Kansas City/Hey, Hey, Hey
Eight Days a Week
Words of Love
Every Little Thing
I Don't Want to Spoil the Party
What You're Doing

From HELP!:
You Like Me Too Much
Tell Me What You See
Dizzy Miss Lizzy

Also included:

Yes It Is ("B" side to "Ticket to Ride" released on HELP!)
Bad Boy (a US exclusive not released in the UK until A COLLECTION OF BEATLES OLDIES (never released in US) late 1966.

Clearly the best value and listening experience is from the British releases, BEATLES FOR SALE and HELP!  "Bad Boy" and "Yes It Is" are included on PAST MASTERS VOL. 1.

OF the US "butcher" albums, some strongly resemble their British alternatives, but some are more disjointed. Where THE EARLY BEATLES is a reworked PLEASE PLEASE ME minus three songs, and the US REVOLVER is the same as its British counterpart minus three songs, the real feel of BEATLES FOR SALE is much more evident on BEATLES 65 than what is evident here, making BEATLES VI perhaps the weakest of the true hodge-podge albums, the others being BEATLES SECOND ALBUM, SOMETHING NEW, and YESTERDAY AND TODAY. As such, BEATLES VI is a curio for only the most devote US fans. Yes, the cover shot and back cover photos are pretty darned nice photos not found on the UK albums.

TECHNICAL NOTE: The audio source for the stereo songs is from the 2009 complete catalog remaster. The mono selections reflect the complete mono selections remastered and released in 2009 from THE BEATLES MONO BOX.

reviewText:
Since most of the reviews here seem to be positive, I went back and listened to this set a second time to see if I missed something.  Sad to say, I didn't.
Yes, Ashkenazy gets all the notes in the right places, but  that is about it.  One can easily question his ability to put this music  across because he doesn't seem to identify with any of it.
One of the  reviewers below calls the Jarrett version of this music superficial and in  one sense, he or she is right.  Jarrett doesn't plumb the depths.  However,  his set shows his delight and fascination with the music at every turn.  He  plays with great enthusiasm and I suspect were he to rerecord it now, he  would provide an even more winning and profound account.
By contrast,  Ashkenazy seems bored by the music.  The "upbeat" pieces are  drained of color and light; the deeper pieces are merely lugubrious.
I  noticed a reviewer in another format who suggested that perhaps Ashkenazy  was trying to suggest the world-weary Shostakovitch of his later years.  If  so, it's a terrible decision.  This music was written for the young  Nikolaeva, who had delighted the composer with her Bach playing. He  lavished his imagination on this music.  Ashkenazy kills it.
So, I  repeat my one-star review from below.  Please try Jarrett, Nikolaeva,  Petrushansky or Shostakovich's own recordings before touching this one.  They all appreciate the wonders of the music they are playing, even if they  have occasional technical or interpretational failings.

The reason I bought it in the first place was because it was heralded as a "full band effort", rather than just Yngwie shredding fast, and, well, it is that, but the songs are still cheesy, weak, and really forgettable.  Also, Yngwie's guitar playing is just as boring as ever.  Yeah, he can shred fast, big deal.  That's about all he can do.  All of his solos sound exactly the same (Yeah, let's do a sappy ballad dedicated to my wife, and then shred over it, that'll sound good!), and his rhythm playing is pretty uninsprired.  Also, the singer on this album sounds like a 4th rate Dio ripoff, and Yngwie's vocals sound like Jeff Keith from Tesla with a cold.  And if that's not enough, the lyrics are some of the worst I've ever heard ("I'll tear my heart out and serve it to you on a plate"...uh yeah).

I really don't recommend this at all.  If you want some good band-oriented shred-type metal, get some Dream Theater or Symphony X.  If you want some full-on guitar-oriented stuff, get some Vai or Satriani.  This doesn't have you covered either way.  The only really good thing about this album is Mats Olausson's keyboard outro in "Braveheart".  But that's not really enough to listen to this.  Also, Cozy Powell plays drums on it, but it's not his best work by any means (get a Rainbow album instead).

But hey, if you really want this, you're more than welcome to my copy.  You can save it from a horrible fate of being burned, smashed, or hurled like a frisbee into a field.

reviewText:
Seeing this production in Toronto a few years ago proved to be one of my worst experiences in the theatre.
The movie should have made a fantastic musical.  And the opening theme gives the proper film noir feeling... But Andrew Lloyd Webber cheated and instead of writing a new score for this show, he chose to recycle cut-out songs from previous failed musicals.  The result is an uneven patchwork that never effectively settles on tone.  The title song, for example, sounds too contempoary for a story set in 1950.  The lyrics are bland and filled with all too obvious rhymes and slang expressions that are often out of synch with the characters. Why does Mr lloyd-Webber refuse to collaborate with a good lyricist who could make his music come across more with more effect.  (He did once, with Tim Rice... but that partnership ended.)
SUNSET angers me.  A good source was turned into an inferior musical.  Yet, simply because it was the only new book musical to open on Broadway in the 94/95 season it was awarded the Tonys for Best Musical, Best Book and Best Score.  It did not deserve any of those awards.  However, audiences were not fooled.  It closed on Broadway after a short run and lost millions.  The London production had a longer run and still lost millions.  The Toronto production lasted less than a year and lost millions.  And the national tour folded almost before it started...and again lost millions.  Maybe people are finally catching onto Webber's endless recycling!

reviewText:
I'm listening now to some old 80's bands, and it's apparently obvious that most of these old groups had about the same talent level more or less, each putting out a few hits per album..

  Many of the "heavy" bands of this time are signified by what would now be considered "power metal" with high, "untrained" or "adolescent" vocals. Things have changed up a bit now, and I'm not so sure for the better. Now it's basically not considered "heavy" unless someone sounds like they are screaming at Satan...

  In any event, after a lot of listening to music, and a held-to-light comparison, I long ago realized my brother's garage band as sounding fairly patched-up. For example, the vocals and attitude sounded like filler: "hey! yeaaa! master of..naughty things!..yeea!," errr, lol. Of course this didn't keep them from popularity. But like the bands that have improved on the tradition of Black Sabbath, the Sab remains most popular, and for all, due to simply being the first - no matter how old we realize it sounds now.

  As for this album, though even its considered cool by mums and lil sisters, I still can't confess that I fully join them on the "like wagon." There is some elements here and there I try hard to cling to, but not something I can't hear from any other band from the same time. I find myself skipping through most tracks and looking for my other music with more stirring grooves, more bass-ish aggression, more decadence, and more cohesiveness.

Sorry guys, I will have pass on this one.

reviewText: When I was a youngster just getting my indie wings with albums like Lonesome Crowded West and Doolittle, I saw this album and thought it looked interesting. With two supposed classics under my belt, I listened to this album late at night while I was by myself in my room one time (that's when I always listen to music I've been anticipating, just for the amazing atmosphere it provides, or used to) and I couldn't finish the album. I felt disappointed, like I was missing something, or there was something I wasn't getting. So, I tried again, and finally managed to finish all of it. I came out feeling pretty much the same as I did going in. Tired, a little agitated, and somewhat bored. In a few days, I bought the Mountain Goats album "Tallahassee", which is now my favorite album. Also, I later tried to get into the nitty-gritty indie albums shortly after giving up on Spiderland, and enjoyed a lot of what I heard very much and came back to it, but this is one classic I just couldn't appreciate, I guess. The lyrics are good I suppose, and I like chaotic and minimalistic music as much as the next indie fan, but this seemed to over do it a bit. I don't care for slacker music, but just flat-out lazy and droning riffs that seem almost purposely made to sound boring and flat is a little different. Also, the whole spoken word thing seems to be the same thing. Maybe they just did everything in a way that was so weird and non-technical or traditional that it would instantly appeal to fans of weird music, reguardless of whether they actually liked it or not? Or maybe it's just me. To each his own, but this just isn't for me.

reviewText:
As an avid music fan, I tuned in to Aussie Idol to see what the standard of singers in Australia is compared to the rest of the world.  Unsurprisingly, I was not impressed until Guy Sebastian came along and sang "Somewhere Over The Rainbow".  From that moment onwards, I knew Guy had to be the Aussie Idol or else I could never have even a sliver of hope in the pop music industry again.  And luckily, he did win it and my heart was lifted, my hopes renewed.  His performances in the show are nothing short of amazing, and just because he entered a 'talent competition' doesn't diminish this fact.
  However when I bought the album and listened to it, I probably should not have expected the standards to be as high as his live performances.  Rushed release or not, the record company and the musicians are responsible for the production of an album that is of the highest quality possible given the material available. What I heard were half-hearted (probably even less) efforts that uncaringly strewn together generic pop elements with a touch of uninspired R&B themes in the hope to release it before the Idol hype has died down.
  I should have realised that hoping the pop music industry would care for music rather than money is a hope in vain. They haven't before, so why should they now?  While I still love Guy and his talent, it's a sad fact that this money-driven, insultingly inane tripe may have sabotaged the take-off of his music career.

reviewText:
According to the identifying information supplied by Amazon for the recording identified as ASIN: B001N82BZ0 under the label "HHO Licensing", the conductor is Herbert von Karajan and the orchestra is not identified.  However, if you examine the sample songs you will only see three movements listed.  What seems to be missing is movement #1, Allegro moderato.  I checked the fairly complete discography available at WWW-dot-abruckner-dot-com.  The only issued von Karajan version of the Bruckner 8 lacking the first movement was recorded with the Preussische Staatskapelle Berlin in June and September 1944.  That recording is also the only Karajan performance of the Bruckner 8 in which the two last movements take longer than 27:00 minutes each.  The 1944 recording may indeed be a sterling performance (I have no idea if it is), but if this is the performance contained in the MP3 files Amazon is selling, I doubt whether most of the other reviews actually refer to the performance being sold.  Some of the reviews seem to be referring to Karajan performances with the Berlin Philharmonic; others to performances with the Vienna Philharmonic.  None, so far as I can see, refer to a 1944 Karajan performance with the Preussische Staatskapelle Berlin that contains one fewer movement than the symphony Bruckner wrote.

Buyer beware.

reviewText:
I just bought Kate Bush's latest CD, "Aerial". I wanted to like this album. I was thoroughly prepared to love it, rave about it and recommend it. However, if I were to say that I am thoroughly disappointed in what I heard of this release, it would be a gross understatement.  I will be selling my copy IMMEDIATLEY.  I am not even going to bother copying it to my HD in the hopes that the thing might grow on me. It quite simply won't.  This is the only one of Kate Bush's CD's that has made me realize buyer's remorse.  I wish I had my money back. I have no doubt the copy I have will sell, because it is, after all, Kate Bush.

Don't get me wrong. I have always adored Kate Bush. I fell in love with her the moment I laid eyes on her when she made her American debut on Saturday Night Live back in 1978.  She was curled up on top of a piano like a cat, singing her song, "The Man With the Child In His Eyes".  My reaction to her was simply,"WHO is that?!"  The next day, I went to the record store in the mall, next to the bookstore where I worked and ordered an import cassette tape of the album. It took nearly a month to get it. It was worth it. I wore it out playing it over and over again over that year.  Every time Kate came out with a new release, I was there on the release date to buy my copy. My fandom of this British songstress was rabid, and anyone I turned on to her (with the exception of one person), loved her music.  She went through some incredible changes when she discovered the Fairlight synthesizer for her album, "The Dreaming." It took some getting used to to assimilate the changes but in the end, it was all good.  Then we saw some more profound changes yet again, for "The Red Shoes".  Kate's penchant for experimentation and pushing the envelope of what her voice and instruments could do went in another direction and we loved her for it. You could pick up the influence in a couple of the tracks of her collaboration with Prince, but she was true to herself. She was always Kate.  She was the Enchantress, the Lady of the Lake, and she took you on fantastic journeys through worlds that we have gone to in our imaginations,and she made it come alive for her listeners.

"Aerial"is so far below her abilities.  Gone is the spirit of experimentation.  The entire 2-CD collection could have been compiled into an EP and you would have the flavour for the entire release.  Gone are the crisp, haunting vocals that we, Kate's fans have always loved, and in their place are vocal improvisations that are neither precise or haunting. They are sheer mush.  Her vocals sound as if she is lost in a sea of medication and just sound very sloppy.  Kate Bush has always had very good, well engineered tracks, but what is lacking is any of that bygone tenacity toward quality in her music.  She sings about her son, born a few years ago, as well as laundry and washing maschines and scrubbing floors.  What was once magical, is now meandering down a lane of boring mundacity.  Even if this were a new age album, rather than the popular / rock  music it was billed as, it would be more boring than David Winston or Yanni. There are no fairlight synthesizers. There is not one tune on this CD set that moves you at all.  It is just not the Kate we all know and love.  Other than the initial release, "King of the Mountain", there is not a single song on this CD that is at all memorable. This is without a doubt, the worst album Kate Bush has ever done. Lionheart was never that great, in my view, but at least it had  some redeeming qualities."Arial", however has few, if any at all.

It pains me to have to say things that cruel about an artist whom I have loved for so many, many years. I can maybe credit this change in direction and intensity to the fact that she is a new mother, or maybe when Kate's own mother passed away a few years ago, she lost her fire.  It is almost as if she has locked herself safely away in her studio in her home and decided she is not going to take any musical risks any longer. If that is the case, then I can only say, that would be a real shame.
label: negative

reviewText:
Very, very good album from Bryan, and in a lot of ways, more solid from start to finish than Olympia.  My one star rating concerns the vinyl and how it was "delayed" and released well after the initial CD and MP3 versions.  Does anyone even realize that the vinyl comes with a download card AND a full CD of the album?  Neither did I.  The free download is noted on the 180 gram sticker on the shrink wrap, but there is absolutely no mention of the bonus CD.  If you saw this in a store, you'd also have no idea it came with the CD.  Amazon does not mention the MP3 download card or the CD.  So, why would I be criticizing this fine album that for a decent vinyl price, that also comes with a download card and CD?  Well, because the MP3 release of this album and the CD both came out several weeks prior to the vinyl.

If you're a fan like me and wanted to buy either the CD or digital album, you'd have no way of knowing that if you were also interested in getting this on vinyl, you could just wait and get the record AND have the digital files AND the CD.  I bought the CD upon its release and would have not purchased it to wait for the vinyl release had I known it came with one.  I believe this to be unfair marketing on the part of the record label, and a way they can get the vinyl collector who also wants a CD or digital album, to pay twice for the same thing, not knowing they could have waited and got everything for one price if they just waited.  Even if the vinyl was released on the same day as the cd and digital albums, I would have been upset because it's not noted anywhere here on Amazon that you could obtain them all by purchasing the vinyl.

My other issue is that the black album cover arrived seam split on top, which is very noticeable on black.  To top it off, even before I opened up the record, I could see the cover bowing from the tight shrink wrap.  Sure enough, as with most LPs that are bowed from shrink wrap when sealed, this 180 gram record was warped!  I would normally exchange it for a other, but due to the fact I was duped into buying a CD because it was never revealed that one was going to come with the vinyl version, it's left a bad taste in my mouth and I think I'm just going to return it and wait several months to find someone with a used copy that's not warped.  Thus, my money will not go to BMG twice.  I will say that even warped, the sound quality of the vinyl is excellent.
label: negative

reviewText:
It isn't an obvious fact that Funeral For A Friend are riding in the wake of a genre that has been blown from underground into mainstream by the dozens in what seems like overnight. In this wake of emocore bands, their 2003 debut casually dressed and deep in conversation had character; Funeral For A Friend's placement in the world and innovative vocal attempts set them somewhat apart from other bands. I was anticipating positive musical growth in Hours, but unfortunately was disappointed and was thrown into the thought that Funeral For a Friend had lost their place in the fight of bands trying the same style of music. Hours plays on almost exactly the same structures, guitar riffs and song themes as every other band out there at the moment and not even a few songs scrape through. Although at times some good riffing shines through, Davies's vocal melodies are boring and repetitive and everything becomes predictable. I don't believe that Funeral For A Friend have sold out, they just haven't changed and haven't made anything worth more than one listen; this album sounds like a bunch of B-sides from 'casually dressed and deep in conversation'.

Perhaps the best song on this album would be "The end of nothing"; this song sees an actual hardcore breakdown applied and contains actual heartfelt vocals, besides the useless screaming of backing vocalist/guitarist and vocals being way too low in volume. Funeral For a Friend have failed but unfortunately so has Terry Date, this is an album that someone like him should not have on their rsum.  Unfortunately nothing else can be recognized on this album, but one this is for sure, if they follow their current trend, the next Funeral for a Friend album is nothing to be waiting on the edge of your seat for.

I also think its halarious that "Funeral for a friend" is a song by Elton John and "Hours" is an album by David Bowie in which the band do not show respect or sound anything like either.

reviewText: Pop Kulcher Review:  Even the most tie-dyed-in-the-wool Deadhead will  concede that the Dead's studio output fails to live up to their live glory.  Still, several Dead studio albums have some real merit, like the acoustic  roots-rock of American Beauty and Workingman's Dead, the dopey psychedelia  of Aoxomoxoa, and the jazzy melodicism of Wake of the Flood and Blues for  Allah.  Not so for Shakedown Street, an embarrassing product even by Dead  standards.  While few studio technicians have managed to capture the loose,  jamming style of the Dead on album, the sound and performance here is  particularly flat and lifeless.  You can almost picture some producer  standing in the sound booth yelling, "Ok, one more time, only even  more devoid of passion and energy!"  Not that the material itself has  much to offer:  no amount of energy and excitement was going to save  "If I Had the World to Give" or "From the Heart of Me."  But even the better songs are completely lifeless.  Take the title track,  one of the highlights of their live show -- here, it's like warmed-over  disco, too chipper and sweet for its own good.  Ditto "Fire on the  Mountain": live, it's an excuse for endless jamming; here, it's  suitable for the dentist's office.  And the fact that they took two cover  songs they'd been playing live since the mid-60's, "Good Lovin'"  and "New Minglewood Blues," and reduced them to short, pointless  studio versions demonstrates just how strapped for new material they were.  Avoid this dud.

reviewText:
David: Hey dear, I have some ideas for an album.

Polly: Oh, can I help?

David: Sure, write lyrics and we'll even bury your vocals in a couple of spots.

OK, maybe that is a little bit sarcastic, but unfortunately that is what this album reminds me of; a domestic happiness project. Of course the sound is Gilmour's, not Macca's, but the feel of mediocre, fluffy contentment is the same. Now there is no reason why someone as successful as Gilmour shouldn't be content and happy, and make an album reflecting the same. But looking in from the outside it's just dull and boring. The opening track has some promise, but for the most part it is all downhill from there. "The Division Bell" showed that Gilmour could follow his own vision and still come up with something with an edge to it, even if it was a different type of "edge" than Roger Waters'. But this album is not only edgeless (only "Take a Breath" has some life to it, and that track seems out of place consdiering how the rest of the album sounds), it also seems endless, as in "will this ever end?".

When one is "on an island" on a calm day one can stand on the beach and look out over a featureless expanse of sea that fades to the horizon. That is this album.

reviewText:
So Long, Bannatyne (1971) has the best overall sound of all the albums. However, there are problems here too. The sound quality is slightly sterile, and once again the vocals should be louder on some tracks. Equalization varies from song to song. The guitar solo in the middle of "Grey Day" seems to disappear instead of panning back and forth between the channels. "One Man Army" sounds good, but the mix isn't right. The strings in "Sour Suite" suffer due to the high end being rolled off.
#10 (1973) suffers from entirely too much bass on most of the album. Compression rears its ugly head once again on "Musicione." "Miss Frizzy" sounds fairly decent, although the vocals (once again) should be louder. "Self Pity" is the only track on the album that sounds like it should. The rest of the album's second side has way too much bass and "Just Let Me Sing" is a compressed mess.

Petrov, once one of death metals' most  ferocious singers, sounds whiny and warbly here; his classic death metal  roar reduced to thin, wannabe rockstar wailings. As a matter of fact, the  whole group sounds like they want to be The Next Big Thing in rock. Thin  riffs, inane lyrical content, and radio-friendly structures that are  insulting to the legions of Entombed followers. I'm all for bands trying to  find innovative ways to express their talents, but this is beyond  redemption. With release of this cd, Entombed have practically destroyed  all of their credibility in the metal underground. Entombed buries their  talent in an attempt to cash in on the already dead alternative sound.  Don't be surprised to find this in your local record stores put it in bins. A horrible misstep that might spell the end of the once  almighty Entombed.

reviewText: 12/10/2009: Do Not Buy This Record! I mean it! This A&M Group is another  rip-off in the world of the music industry, and indeed, they give record companies a bad name. I bought this, thinking that I would get the extended version of "Goodbye, Stranger," only to find these idiots lopped off 1:19 (ie:one minute, nineteen seconds)of the fabulous guitar solo at the end of the song! This is ridiculous. These guys should be beaten with sticks. Anyone who is a musician or a big Supertramp fan like I am knows this song and in particular, the guitar solo, is one of the best solo efforts by anyone in modern rock history. I love to play along with it, but cannot due to the shortening of it, for usual shortened radio FM pop-rock airplay. I don't listen to commercial radio. Can't stand it. So, I had to order "Breakfast in America" to complete the entire "Good bye Stranger" song. The entire song is there. The rest of the songs are there in this compilation, but the sound quality is not all that wonderful. I have nice stereo equipment and it seems that the separation of high end treble is tinny, and the low-end is booming too loud and too much. Maybe it's just my ears. Anyway, the other thing is, when artists of the caliber of Supertramp allows this pap to be out there leads me to believe that Supertramp probably doesn't get much, if any, royalties served up to them on a platter. That is also disheartening. All the more reason, in my view, to have independent record labels so one can eliminate the middle money-grubbers, like A&M Records. reviewText: This is without question the worst recording I have ever heard of this beloved musical. I have been a fan of Les Mis since it first came out with the London Cast Album with Colm Wilkinson as Jean Valjean. The only redeeming thing about this disc is they at least let Colm sing the meager few lines of the bishop who forgives Valjean and sets him on the path of righteousness. Okay now for the review: The lyrics have been changed in some songs which is a sacrilege in my eyes, this musical was perfect "as is" why do they always mess with it when making a filmed version? The singing is awful. Anne Hathaway cannot sing without sounding like a lamb. She is flat a lot and drags out the songs to make them even more dramatic which is unnecessary. A few people have jumped all over me saying that this is a live recording to go with the film and that once I see the finished product I will understand it better but the problem with that is that this is a musical and as such should be, well, musical! Russel Crowe is just not listenable and Hugh Jackman is only a tiny bit better. His version of Bring Him Home is the worst one I have ever heard. How can they take one of the most beautiful songs and the centerpiece of Valjean's character and massacre it? I will see this though on video next year. I cannot express how disappointed I was when listening to this soundtrack, what a tragic waste. If you want to hear Les Mis in all of its pristine glory I suggest the Dream Cast recording. These roles belong to Colm Wilkinson, Michael Ball, and Philip Quast. DO NOT WASTE YOUR MONEY ON THIS TRASH!

reviewText:
Looking at the cover and the list of songs on the back, you could be forgiven if you assumed these were all the original charted renditions, as there is absolutely nothing to indicate that some of the biggest hits included were re-recorded years later, most of them in "live" performances. Only when you open the package and check out the booklet do you realize you have been bamboozled. And now it's too late to take it back!

For the record, the following list of contents will show which are later recordings:

Disc 1: 1. Solitary Man; 2. Cherry, Cherry; 3. I Got The Feelin' (Oh No, No); 4. Thank The Lord For The Night Time; 5. Girl, You'll Be A Woman Soon; 6. Kentucky Woman; 7. Shilo (1967 hit version); 8. You Got To Me; 9. Brooklyn Roads (1986 live version); 10. Red, Red Wine (1989 live version); 11. I'm A Believer (1989 live version); 12. Sweet Caroline (1989 live version); 13. Soolaimon (1989 live version); 14. Cracklin' Rosie (1992 live version); 15. Song Sung Blue (1991 studio re-recording); 16. Play Me (1992 live version); 17. Holly Holy (1992 live version); 18. Morningside (1983 live version); 19. Crunchy Granola Suite (1992 live version).

Disc 2: 1. Brother Love's Traveling Salvation Show (1992 live version); 2. I Am...I Said (1992 live version); 3. Be; 4. Longfellow Serenade; 5. Beautiful Noise; 6. If You Know What I Mean; 7. Desire; 8. September Morn; 9. You Don't Bring Me Flowers (duet with Barbra Streisand); 10.
Forever In Blue Jeans; 11. Hello Again; 12. America; 13. Love On The Rocks; 14. Yesterday's Songs; 15. Heartlight; 16. Headed For The Future; 17. Heartbreak Hotel (duet with Kim Carnes); 18. All I Really Need Is You (1992 live version).

Combined with Heartbreak Hotel (a previously unreleased duet with Kim Carnes) and All I Really Need Is You - which was NOT a hit for Neil by any stretch of the definition - that's 40% of the contents, folks. Beautiful Noise was a # 8 on the Adult Contemporary charts in late 1976/early 1977, but failed to dent the Pop Hot 100.

The best thing about this is the 47-page booklet which contains two pages of background notes written by Neil, the lyrics to all selections, and five pages of recording credits. But that does not make up for the misinformation on the outside of the package. Compilation Coordinator Sam Cole, and Columbia, should be taken to task by the industry. Caveat emptor, indeed.

Rutherford, tras su primer, y bastante bueno, primer disco en solitario, prefiri seguir la estela de su compinche, Collins y decidi embarcarse en una empresa con ms dividendos que calidad musical. It's too bad that a disk that received public funding is not of archival grade production.  To intentionally introduce clipping and distortion in the sound renders this disk disposable in my eyes.

I'm WAY older than the average LP fan, but I've always been impressed by the alchemy of LP:  the short punchy songwriting, the dual vocal attack (the rapping contrasted well with the impassioned screaming :), the heavy walls of catchy Nu Metal guitar (a refreshing absense of noodly solos - I like guitar solos but their absense from LP made room for other things), the interesting and innovative scratching and effects from Mr. Hahn.  There is literally not a weak moment on their first two albums.  The whole was greater than the sum of the parts, and really made for great repeated listening.

Unfortunately, they've tried to "grow up" on this album.  Bad, bad, bad idea.  They've abandoned everything that made them GOOD, and made an album of BLAND and GENERIC ballads (ballads for god's sake!)... this could have been any of a thousand other forgettable bands that you hear on the radio and instantly ignore.  I literally do not understand how this album could be receiving any positive reviews at all... the people who think this is good either a) have never heard rock music before, so it all sounds new and wonderful  or b) are such passionate fans that this could have been an album of LP christmas carols and they would have liked it.

For the rest of us, don't bother.  The world is full of good music (the first two LP albums among them).  Don't waste your time with this.

reviewText:
(PLEASE NOTE: This review was actually written back in July 2002, and does not necessarily reflect my current views on her music. But I still consider it valid, as it was my initial response to the album.)

Butterfly marks the beginning of the "new Mariah"; an oversexed diva who is overly demanding and then has the nerve to whine pathetically about the unfairness of life. Her vocals through the album are much weaker than her previous efforts, and lack the emotion of her "good ol' days". The tracks all have a similar sound and seem to meld together; none of them truly stand out, and none of her performances are memorable.

The LP is laden with ballads and midtempo hiphop, and a single midtempo dance number ("Fly Away (Butterfly Reprise)"). It isn't difficult to see that this is the beginning of the end of Mariah's respectability and her career as a hitmaker. With this album, she received two undeserving number one hits, "Honey" and "My All", neither of which are likely to make a lasting impression on anyone.

The only song with potential is the title track, which cries out for the old Mariah to come out of hiding and sing.

Bottom line: Should have been long forgotten by now.

Everybody but drummer Paul Wilson (he was known as "The Thimble," if you get what I mean) had been in on what Collins himself referred to as "ram sessions." In the process, apparently Dickie B. fell in love with the Genesis frontman. I hope you realize this means that the Butler brothers were gaining carnal knowledge about one another in these hour-long daily sessions.

It's as if The Psychedelic Furs had undergone a mutation involving the shedding of an outer layer, and it is this shell that's left behind, meandering through imitations of tunes. It's an overprocessed mess, as well, a painted lady on fire in an El Da de los Muertos procession. It's like the fat Tom Hanks as Dorf on Golf. Oops, I crapped a baby. Paranoid delusions of self-importance are the mad whisperings within the cells of dis-ease. You shouldn't listen. You shouldn't turn their volume up with every gulp of wine and pills. My neck grows legs; a matter-of-fact funhouse wherein your belly grows fatter with the brutality of time and temperance. Eyes grown blind, but still seeing.

The music is barely audible at some points, so is his voice, and then there are sporadic swells of instrumental sound which roll back into the sound of soft mundane strings.

I knew from hearing the first song that I had made a mistake with this one. Peter is barely alive on this recording. He adds absolutely NOTHING to these songs that he is covering. It's to bad, these are great songs in their original versions, Peter has not done them any justice with his treatment of them. It is a lifeless, unlistenable work of drudgery, and without a trace of soul. For me, there is nothing redeeming about this mundane, self indulgent album. I say self indulgent because this album holds no real enjoyment for the listener. These songs are arranged and sung the way peter wanted to hear them, all the same tone and pace. Fit for putting oneself into a coma.

reviewText:
Okay, first off I'd like to say I have a lot of respect for this record. This is a mix of rock, funk, jazz and Indian music - I can't think of a single album that sounds even remotely like this one. It's a daring move. It's totally unique. It was very avant-garde, and well-performed. Some people see this is as a masterpiece, and judging by those terms, it's hard to argue with them.

It just isn't very good. In fact, it's my least favorite Miles Davis album.

Miles was a genius, of course. The Coltrane years and the Shorter/Hancock/Carter/Williams years are very rewarding. And while I'm not a huge fusion fan, I do LOVE In a Silent Way, and I like about half of B*tches Brew, half of Jack Johnson, bits of Live-Evil (What I Say rules!) and all of Pangaea. I do not, however, even remotely enjoy On the Corner. I don't hear any melodies in this at ALL. In fact, I don't hear much music in this at all. It's like Miles told his band, "Okay, we're gonna forget songwriting... more guitar! More keyboards! More drums! More percussion! More overdubs! More bizarre noises! No, no, MORE of it! Let's try to make this the loudest, nastiest, least listenable record of all time!" And when it came to "least listenable ever", they didn't QUITE pull it off (that title would go to the Byrds' Dr. Byrds and Mr. Hyde). Black Satin is just awful. It's not a song. It's just a mess of noise panning from one speaker to the other. And it's the BEST SONG ON THE ALBUM! Now, that's only because it's the shortest: I'd much rather hear it than On the Corner or Mr. Freedom X, which both do the same thing for twenty minutes. And I like longer songs, if they're done well (B*tches Brew itself, Shh/Peaceful, In A Silent Way/It's About That Time, Right Off, What I Say, Zimbabwe, All Blues, Sid's Ahead and Walkin' being examples from the Miles catalogue). What I don't like is twenty minutes of what my ears consider equal to the audio recording of a monkey mud wrestling match. That doesn't fly.
Let nobody say I don't like Miles Davis, because I'll tell you right now, Kind of Blue, 'Round About Midnight and In a Silent Way are three total essential beautiful masterpieces. I just don't like On the Corner. I hate it with a passion, in fact. I've heard it described as a love-it-or-loathe -it deal - in fact, by 1972 Miles' audience was already cut down to fusionheads and devotees who would praise anything he put out, and this managed to hack some of them off. I hear this as everything that could've gone wrong with fusion going wrong.
Just so you know, I'm not a jazz purist - I like rock and funk, among other genres, quite a lot. And I think that In A Silent Way (along with the good halves of Jack Johnson and B*tches Brew) were the only times that Miles succeeded in doing good things with those two genres.

I know that 80-90% of people who review stuff on Amazon love the work in question, so I am sure this will get flamed - but for anyone who is undecided about Iron & Wine, do yourself a favor, unless  you are looking for pretentious elevator music for the new millinium, look elsewhere.

Sony's copy protection scheme installs harmful rootkit software on Windows machines. This software can crash your machine, and make it easier for viruses to infect you. It also causes a small but constant drain on your processing power - even when you're not listening to music.  By design, it is impossible to uninstall without advanced technical skills.

Sony recently released a patch to mitigate these concerns. However, the patch only addresses the issue of potential virus infection. Uninstalling the software is still nearly impossible, and if attempted incorrectly can render your CD drive unusable.

For more information, search for "sony rootkit" on the sysinternals web site.

But now in her mid teens, Miss Church has yet to reach that point and one wonders now if she ever will.  Her voice has not gotten better nor worse.
Like a previous reviewer said, the strain in her voice is evident and sometimes a little painful to listen to.  There are some songs where she's straining towards a range her vocal chords can not handle and there are other times like in "Papa can you here me?" where here voice is just above whisper (cranking the volume is needed).  In fact, her pitch is not the same, at least to my ears it isn't.  It sounds as if it's been lowered a key or two.  Another thing with her singing is that I hear a lot of air before the words come out.  Her voice does not come out as clear or pure as it could be.  There is just too much whooshing sounds for me to continue listening to this CD.
I love show tunes from time to time and I'm familiar with most of the songs on this album. Although I believe Miss Church did put in a great effort, she missed her mark.  If you want to listen to an Opera/Pop/Broadway style of music, I recommend Sarah Brightman (albums: Dive, Eden, or La Luna).

reviewText:
Yes yes yes. It's cacophonous, it's gritty, it's unpleasant. Put it on at a party and watch people make a mad dash for the door. Just try and dance to some of the arhythmic beats that fill the album like a car being thrown down a large flight of stairs. It's not popular music was never meant to be and will never apologize for not being so. It is as about an acquired taste as you can get.

Nonetheless, I truly think this will be one of the albums that survives the twentieth-first century. I think people will still be listening to this in a few hundred years when the concept of music changes and dissonance and staggering rhythms are as harmonious as the choir in the fifth plane of heaven. Rock has produced nothing like this up to this point. Nothing with this sense of exploration and personal vision. Nothing as playful, nothing as fun. Nothing that stretches the boundaries of what people think of as 'rock music.'

I don't think 21st century music listeners in America are ready for this. To truly appreciate this album for what it is you need to have a different definition of music and rhythm from the norm. No words will prepare you for how jarring it is. Your friends will hate you, people will think you're insane or on drugs. My 98 year old mother still won't allow me to play it when she's home.

Well, the musings here are quite "out-there." Yes, cliche term, but, that about describes the album in the most emphatic sense of the term. It's a crazed mix of blues, R&B, garage-rock, abstract (free/avant-garde?) jazz, and modern composition, and it's all topped off by a vocalist who sounds as goofy and obnoxious as a demented cartoon character.

So, in the end, it's probably fair to say that both sides of the camp have a certain amount of validity in their responses: on the one hand, there is quite the amount of brilliant and ingenious techniques to be found here, and musicians who know their fair share about music theory and composition will find quite a bit to chew on. Barring technical details, listeners who get their kicks from things that are on the bizarre, experimental side, will have quite the opportunity to discover a goldmine. However, on the flipside, the album lacks any kind of typical or pleasant melody; melody is there, but it takes quite an effort on the listener's part to access it, especially if the listener is not used to intensely avant-garde musings.

Upon which it is clear that this album was made by a bunch of fake hippies, tootling on instruments they don't know how to play (or don't have the limbs to play, as with the two saxophones at once business), pretending to be ultra-crazy and avant-garde, and laughing all the way to the bank. An album for chumps who want to pretend that they're crazier than everyone else. Guess what, mates? You can keep it. Listen to this a million times if you want, it won't make you anything more than a buffoon with bad music playing on your stereo.

The core problem is that in my opinion, when you begin to grasp that Britany wasn't arriving at this incarnation of "music" via creativity, she was SPECIFICALLY AVOIDING traditional musical tonality. This means that it's entirely contrived, and not even close to an inspired piece of art.

.There IS melody, it can be found but it takes a determined set of ears and a love of abstract musical ideas and theory. In the Zone's drums are playing mostly conventional rhythms, though not always in 4/4. The whole album is quite spirited and uptempo, firmly in the Charlie Parker bop tradition (who was one of Ornette's most prominent influences) but abandoning the restrictions of that genre. There are some great moments on this recording--my favorite is the dual bass "conversation" between Madonna and Biritany. There are other pretty cool moments of interplay, and some great Coleman skronk too, but listening to all of this jam takes an open mind and plenty of patience. So, what we have here is a bold, unconventional, and influential recording...that does not compel me to listen with any sort of frequency. It's just not worth the effort, and believe me I have tried.

. Another reviewer termed this "for pseudo-intellectuals who need a life". I'd like to second that. Smarten up! You're no better than schmucks who like Christina Agueiliera. They like it because everyone else does; you hate it because everyone likes it. You like this album because no one else does. That doesn't make you any more original or intelligent than Christina Agueiliera fans! What a crew of sheep you are. Get a life.

reviewText: What a long, weird journey pop music has had over the last five years.  In January of 1999, a freshly turned-17-year-old Louisiana mouseketeer named Britney Spears released her debut album "...Baby One More Time," and with that release, she became responsible for launching a teen pop craze we haven't seen since New Kids on the Block and Debbie Gibson.  But more so than Gibson and NKOTB, Britney's brand of kiddie pop was criminally dull and vapid, and though her look "matured," the quality of her songs (most of which were written by Max Martin) never did.  I won't go on about her publicity-motivated marriages, her countless tabloid appearances, or her "lesbian" kiss with Madonna.  I'll go straight to her hits collection, which compiles all her singles from her last 4 (four!) CDs.  The kickoff track is a cruel desecration of Bobby Brown's new jack classic "My Prerogative," and it's rancid enough and sterile enough to make Mr. Brown refuse the royalty check.  Through the dreck of other hits such as "....Baby One More Time," "Stronger," the annoying "Toxic," and the whiny "Everytime," we find two noteworthy tracks: the Neptunes-produced "Boys" and "I'm a Slave 4 U," which still hold up as Britney's best singles.  The other hits range from so-so to thunderously bad, and Britney's thin voice does nothing to help matters.  We also get a bonus disc of remixes which could have made this set worth buying, but the CD turns out to be a major botch job.  Though we do get Armand Van Helden's funky re-working of "Toxic," the CD misses the opportunity to include better remixes such as the Thunderpuss versions of "I'm a Slave 4 U" or "Don't Let Me Be the Last to Know."  There's nothing wrong with guilty pleasure pop, but guilty pleasure pop that's banal as this hits album is unacceptable.

My only hope is that some day the people at Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs gets a hold of the original master and is able to release something decent like they did for Faith No More's "Angel Dust".  I'm a bit afraid that even the original master is b0rked though in that this is very heavily a pro tools album.  The way things are on this and other "works" is starting to give me the impression that we were all better off when recording music via analogue.  I'm with Neil Young when he says listening to 21st century recordings makes him angry.  It's not the songs that are bad, it's the compression levels and absence of any dynamics whatsoever.

reviewText:
I have listened to all of the ASOT mixes and believe my past experiences with Armin and trance music in general give me the ability to give a fair opinion as to whether mixes represent a great effort or are lackluster.  Armin's 2013 effort falls under lackluster, unfortunately.  Luckily, my expectations were low going into the mix.  You see, Armin has become a ridiculous icon of trance, a true blockbuster one might say, and has had his mind on touring, productions and his label Armada. Unfortunately for those of us who love our trance compilations, I believe this leads to less focus on Armin's part towards the compilation mixes, especially ASOT. Not to mention he also does a myriad of ASOT podcasts.

What led me to give this album 3 stars is two things.  One, this does not even come close to the effort put forth in ASOT 2011 (one I reviewed on Amazon as well) which is the best one in my opinion. If you are looking for a great ASOT, 2011 is the way to go.  Using 2011 as a benchmark, this album just does not compare, the vocals are pretty dull even given Armin's usually exceptional taste in trance vocal songs, and the drops in the club disc all feel like recycled prog trance drops from a year ago.  However, my biggest disappointment is with the beach disc, disc 1.  In ASOT 2011 you could literally listen to that mellowing, beautiful disc on a beach but this year's disc is rather heavy and does not fit the beach theme at all.  The tracks are all good but not great, there were some standouts I will be going back to, but 2011 had only standouts.

Given Armin's accolades and success over the years, and how big a fan I am, it's hard for me to be so critical over this release.  But I think it's best if we keep our expectations grounded for ASOT 2013.  Listen to ASOT 2005, 2006, 2007 & 2011. Thanks for your time.

EDIT: I had the chance to listen to this album again after coming back on here and seeing the massive amount of 5 star ratings it received.  I thought maybe I missed something.  Let me tell you, I am actually even more disappointed when I listened again and have bumped my review score down to 1 star.  If you think this is good trance, you are truly missing out on the cutting edge, exciting stuff that Above & Beyond (Anjunabeats 9, 10) and Markus Schulz (Los Angeles 12, Prague 11) are g putting out.  I listened to disc 1 again and counted the number of actual, high quality tracks and I counted 5 out of 16.  There is a stretch of about 6 songs in the middle with just downright awful vocals.  I must admit that he caps off the beach disc pretty well with some nice tracks at the end, but this does not really come close to the caliber of his previous ASOT releases.  I see what you all are saying about it being a good mix, on its own, but we must consider his past releases as well as the releases of his peers in trance to really be able to judge where this album stands.  Please, please, if you like this album, you will enjoy the releases of Above & Beyond and Markus Schulz even more.  I highly recommend you try out those artists as well.  I don't want new trance fans to get the impression that this is high quality trance music, because it's just not.  Thanks for your time, again.
