reviewText: Bocelli has a better than average voice for a pop singer, but with the best will in the world, it is not good enough for opera. It is a scary thought to see that this recording of La Boheme may very well become the best selling recording of an opera ever, especially when there are so many great recordings of Puccini's best opera. It would be useless to compare Bocelli with a Pavarotti or a Di Stefano since they simply belong to a different league of singers, but please, if this is your first try at opera, you could do a lot worse than buying Herbert von Karajan's 1972 recording with Mirella Freni and Pavarotti in London. Pavarotti had back then a truly God-given voice, and sings his heart out as Rodolfo. Mirella Freni is pure magic as Mimi, and Herbert von Karajan draws the most gorgeous sounds from the Berlin Philharmonic. Twenty years ago an opera recording with a pop singer would have been unthinkable, I wonder what the A & R people from Universal have in store for us: maybe a Turandot with Boy George, or a Tosca with Brittney Spears?

reviewText:
Ill get to Jeggy in a minute. First I want to deal with some organic pellets from the John Kwok Random Five Star Review Generator.

He writes, John Eliot Gardiner clears some of the cobwebs lingering in this venerable warhouse (sic  and it could be a mixed metaphor too), leading the Vienna Philharmonic in one of the most exciting performances I have heard of Schubert's last symphony (John, put down those poems of Jorie Graham and Louise Gluck and listen to Kna 57 et al). He omits some of the repeats usually performed in the third (this is BS - I hear repeats of the exposition and development of the Scherzo itself) and fourth movements (errr, which ones John?), but more importantly, opts for brisk tempi (drum-roll - we all know what this means: its an Ode to the God of Brisk Efficiency - Jeggys trademark). What you have is an exhilirating (sic) performance of epic proportions, in which Gardiner manages to coax the Vienna Philharmonic into sounding like a large chamber orchestra (so this performance has epic proportions even though Jeggy has shrunk the orchestra in his usual fashion?). Without question, (not so fast, John  questions I have aplenty) this is one of Gardiner's most successful Deutsche Grammophon recordings (this could mean anything), and proves that he has come a long way from being known as an (sic) period instrument interpreter of Baroque music. (if so, why was he unceremoniously dropped by DG, John? And hands up who wants to hear Jeggy in Bruckner or Richard Strauss?).

Not that it matters, but Ive been criticised of late for being so hard on Jeggy. While I have given him Five Stars on two occasions at least, I admit that normally hes the recipient of less. Alas, heres another instance where, born of his emotional repression and dogmatic commitment to miniaturisation, he has jeggy-ified a masterpiece.  SFL brilliantly asks the question A brittle, unsmiling performance - what period is this supposed to be? I think the answer is clear enough:  herein, Jeggy downsizes the Schubert Ninth so it can serve as the soundtrack to Biggles delivers the Goods or Biggles defies the Swastika or Biggles takes it Rough (whatever that means).

As per usual, Jeggy is afraid of the music that requires an emotional response. Nor is he prepared to address kerygma. Both phenomena underwrite his Cult of Brisk Efficiency  his Get out of Jail card, so to speak. While this performance of the Schubert Ninth is less calamitous than Norrington, its no better stocked than Mother Hubbards Cupboard in its impoverishment. Its an unsmiling, superficial semi-sprint from beginning to end. For instance, the famous lyrical episode at 308ff of the slow movement and 502ff with the horns are both stilted to say the least. Come the great moment of exhilaration in the Trio - 610ff - Jeggys top button and tie are resolutely done up as if hes in prep-school.  Yes indeed: its all aboard the Jeggy Light-Rail! Tickets please! Ever so predictably, the Vienna Philharmonic is skeletonised, not that it has anything to say in this domain in way of tradition . . . . . . To my ears, they're not enjoying themselves in the least  its no wonder Jeggy has been invited back so rarely since then.

Gesang der Geister ber den Wassern  a masterpiece - is another instance of emotional repression.  Leave such music to German choirs.

Short on charm, warmth and grandeur, this performance might impress a New York-based Culture Vulture but if you ask me, its another vindication of Uncle Clints observation: A mans gotta know his limitiations. Jeggys strengths  such as they are  lie elsewhere . . . somewhere . . . dunno where . . . can someone cue Monteverdi!

reviewText:
"Lulu", or "How To Kill Two Musical Legends' Respective Careers In Eighty-Seven Minutes", is the worst album I have ever heard, hands down. It should be said that I am not a Lou Reed fan, I am a Metallica fan. But I've admired Reed's work enough to think that this would've been interesting.  It is not interesting, it is horrible. I do not know what Metallica was thinking signing on for this.  After restoring decades of fan alienation with "Death Magnetic", a record that easily stands up against their seminal 80's work, Metallica consigns themselves to being the backup band to a former musical trailblazer who's clearly lost his way.

This album sounds like Metallica turned over a bunch of their unfinished demos from the "Load/Re-Load" sessions (i.e., simple, boring, chugging riffs) to Reed so he could just croak over them in a very acoustic-unfriendly room. The words he sing-speaks rarely match the music, and in fact the music often seems incidental. Or perhaps the vocals seem incidental, it's hard to say what's the most out of place here, it's just all a hot mess.  I don't think Reed even cared what music was playing behind his words, I think he just told the guy in the booth, "Cue the next one up and I'll start talking."  I don't know enough about Lou Reed to know what his fans expect from him, but I honestly wouldn't think this would scratch their itch, either.

Reed has never been a technically great singer, but we still know from songs like "Sweet Jane", "Walk On The Wild Side", "My Love Is Chemical" (remember that one? cool little lost 80's nugget), "I Love You, Suzanne", etc. that he is capable of SINGING. He is capable of forming notes on the musical scale with his voice. He doesn't do that on this record. He talks/rambles/grunts for nearly an hour and a half, often sounding like he's been on an ultra-low-fiber diet for the past few days and is now dealing with that in the studio.

And the lyrics...holy geez, the lyrics...I don't even know where to begin...all I can say is hunt around online and try to find a snippet of the first minute or so of the album.  Listen to the first words Reed speaks.  It doesn't get any better from there, let me tell you.

Avoid this album like the plague.

reviewText:
I can't believe I spent $18 on this remaster. This is supposed to be A SPECIAL EDITION CD REMASTER, but the fidelity is so horrible. It sounds like they attempted to make a "modern," "extra-loud" version but they obliterated all the magic and soul of the original recordings. I am frankly disgusted.

"A Walk Across the Rooftops" is one of my favorite albums of all time. As to Wikipedia appropriately puts it, this album "was noted for its use of empty space and detailed separation of each musical instrument, designed to showcase the Linn hi-fi equipment to best effect." Whoever was pulling the strings on this remaster had no concept of this. They crushed it (compressed it) likely in order to make it come through Spotify, iTunes, laptop speakers and earbuds immediately "louder." They also totally hyped Paul's vocals to the point at which they are so abrasive and distracting that I could not even finish listening to the album.

Congratulations mastering engineer (or record label), you followed convention and trend and gave no consideration to the fact that the target audience of this remaster MIGHT ACTUALLY WANT DYNAMICS. If anyone from the label is reading this, my gosh, PLEASE PLEASE remaster this. I am die-hard Blue Nile fan, but I am not even going to pay 18 dollars for a bunch of hyped/crushed bonus tracks. I will stick to the beautiful jazz/classical-esque dynamics of the original masters. I remember the first time I heard this album. It was an dream-like, ethereal listening experience unlike any I'd ever had before. I remember falling asleep to this album on numerous train rides throughout Europe. Everything I fell in love with is gone on this new remaster, and no I am not a purist. It is truly that bad. Anyone with a copy of the old masters and a decent set of headphones or stereo will agree with me.

I've never been a huge fan of U2, but there is not doubt about their appeal to millions and the fact that have written some memorable songs, irrespective of whether one likes them or not. However, I was curious about this new album and it has been playing no stop in my workplace for the last week.

I understand that Mr. Bono Vox has a "social conscience"? Well, if I was him, I would endeavour to discourage people from buying this third rate CD recording in these tough economic times and save their money for more important and entertaining things. Really, this is not an album one should be selling - it should either be given away for nothing or withdrawn and an apology made. Lots of people here seem to feel the same.

I know that neither of these things is likely.

PS: I have just been listening to Rokia Traor's 2009 album, "Tchamantch", and boy-oh-boy! What a relief it is to listen to something powerful, touching, inventive, passionate, intelligent, emotional, stylish and delightfully rich and colourful after hearing U2's turgid, hapless, stale and melodically barren mess, "No Line On The Horizon"! Place your copy of "No Line" in the nearest available dumpster and get Rokia Traor's album. Bono and the boys will ultimately thank you!

reviewText:
I suppose we have to that Squire and his gang of Buggle Thugs for putting out this dross.  They have served at least two valuable purposes.  First, they have saved generations of music students to come from having to wonder who was the real genius behind the great work of Yes.  Sure, there was the dreadful Drama on the one hand and the scintillating work of Anderson, Bruford, Wakeman, Howe on the other.  This indicated that Yes without Anderson is awful and Yes without Squire does just fine, thank you.  But an exception does not make a rule.  Now the proof is in.  No need ever wonder who made Yes great.  And it sure wasn't Squire, not even with the help of Howe.
Listening to this album is like eating a meal made with fine ingredients and having no chef.  There is no direction.  Solos of great virtuosity wander around in circles and dwindle into nothing.  Interesting lyrical ideas spin into clich'.  Nothing goes anywhere valid.
The second value this work has is that it finally freed Anderson from the flatulent corpse of Yes.  Now able to delve into the wonders of what Anderson rightly called the species changing event of the internet, he has already created two great works:  The Living Tree and Survival and Other Stories.
Good job Chris.  You freed Anderson and condemned yourself to immortal infamy in one blow.

reviewText:
I just listened to this box set once again in my car over the weekend and it sounds just as bad as it did when it first came out.  The high regard in which Phil Spector is held by music buffs is utterly baffling.  The arrangements, for the most part, are appalling and the mono mixes (if that's what you want to call them) sound terrible.  Most of these records are drenched in echo and the singers are overwhelmed with maracas, strings, horns and choirs.  Most of the songs sound like they were recorded on a Wollensack tape recorder with a single cheap microphone, then transferred without a mix to a crummy Memorex cassette.  From that "master", they were digitized and released as this appalling "wall" of noise.

Occasionally, the material rises above the abysmal production by this so-called "genuis".  Notably "To Know Him is to Love Him", "Corrina, Corrina", "Be My Baby" and "You've Lost That Loving Feeling".  No one, not even Spector, can ruin these great songs.  However, the same can't be said for Ike and Tina Turner's "River Deep, Mountain High", probably the worst produced song of all time.  The Animals, with a vastly improved arrangement, proved that this song was a world-beater.  It's too bad Tina couldn't have recorded it with someone other than Spector.

reviewText:
As a long time King Crimson fan, I have to admit I'm puzzled and troubled by the re-release of Earthbound (outside of the fact it was by huge fan demand). It just goes to show that even the best digital remastering implements can only go so far in cleaning up an inherently bad recording. But what do you expect, it was originally taped on a casssette recorder in pouring rain.

But the sound quality issue nearly pales compared to the performance itself, which in this Owl's opinion was HIDEOUS! What I hear is 3/4 of a functioning band bogged down by one very weak component in the system, namely bassist/singer Boz Burrell, whose vocal ability is rather dodgy at best and his bass skills rather rudimentary (he had NEVER played an instrument prior to coming onboard, Robert Fripp had to teach him by rote how to play). Instead of having a situation where the musicians challenge each other to greater heights, what winds up happening is that the musicians have to play down to that person's weaknesses. The end result, a muddled at times inept version of Crimson that had to resort to 2 or 3 chord jams to fill out things in addition to the composed pieces that Boz had just barely enough competence to play. Try as hard as they did, Fripp, Mel Collins and Ian Wallace just couldn't get the beast to wake up and roar to life. Collins and Fripp sound especially frustrated in their playing (Mel Collins skronking far more than usual). Boz's scat vocals are laughable at best, I actually would've welcomed a guest appearance by William Shatner on some of this just to make it halfway interesting.

Thankfully, this version of KC was short-lived and not long after, Fripp found the players for what would become the most loved version of KC (Wetton, Bruford, Muir, Cross).

Chalk it up to experience, never settle for less.

reviewText: Well, I'm obviously in the minority here with my opinion, but, while I do believe that Karin Allyson and her band set out to develop an album of music that inspired them, the results fall short of their reach.  Allyson's voice seems much better suited to jazz-pop standards than to the grittiness and nuances of the blues.  Her album "Ballads", which faithfully recreated the John Coltrane album, worked because it was full of those very standards.  Allyson's work here cannot hold a candle to that of an innovator like Cassandra Wilson.  Her voice and approach to these tunes is simply too pretty.  Her version of Joni Mitchell's "Blue Motel Room" misses all of the longing and the humor and, well, the nuances (there's that word again) of the original.  Even Joni's guitar work on the original is more daring and inventive than Allyson's guitarist.  And if their version of "Love Me Like A Man" is, as it says in Allyson's liner notes, what they feel to be real raw and gritty, well, it exemplifies the problem with this whole album -- an almost dainty, too studied approach, that becomes "faux gritty".  My favorite song is "Bye Bye Country Boy", where she manages to capture the flirty, lighthearted kiss-off of the song.  But it's also maybe the least bluesy song in the set, to begin with.  Sorry, this cd is going into my "to be re-sold" pile.

reviewText:
The immediately preceding reviewer writes of "the curdled, almost baritonal voice that Pears possessed" but then goes on to justify a five-star rating by saying that Pears' "noticeable wobble, not to mention his innately peculiar timbre, is the price one pays to hear a great musician."  Such is the honestly held opinion of that reviewer and I respect both it and him.  I, however, am absolutely not prepared to pay that price for the abominable Pears--not here, not anywhere, not anytime.

Another reviewer points out that "The Penguin Guide gave this recording a rosette (its highest rating)".  This is quite true and it goes a long way to explain why the Penguin Guide--and the good, grey Gramophone Magazine, too, for that matter--are never, never to be relied upon when they review British performances.

With all the wealth of fine performances of Schubert's lieder available from people who actually can sing, why does anyone waste valuable time, money and shelf space on the unhappy groaning of Pears?  And if, for some utterly incomprehensible reason, someone might actually want "a very British 'Winterreise'", as the same reviewer put it, there is always Ian Bostridge.

reviewText:
The Good
A steady guitar strum sets the pace on the verses of "Last Kiss," but the distortion and emotion picks up on the choruses. "Was a Ghost" has a few memorable guitar runs that chime in from time to time. "Dreaming Against Me" has a country feel with it's slide guitar and acoustic groove. "She Wants Results" is a pure drum track that is highlighted by soulful vocals.

The Bad
I know that a band's current material shouldn't be judged on their past efforts, but does anyone remember anything by Seven Mary Three besides "Cumbersome?" 10 years or so later the band has decided not to change with the times and rely on a sound that has been long forgotten. All the songs sound the same with the exception of a different drumming pattern.

The Verdict
Day and Night Driving is incredibly boring. This twelve song collection is void of any energy. "Cumbersome" was a killer song when it debuted and it still plays on the radio today, but nothing on this album sounds even remotely close to that song. Seven Mary Three sound like a band going through the motions very slowly. Day and Night Driving should come with a warning: do not listen to while driving, day or night; will cause drowsiness.

I'll always have a level of respect for AIR because of the sound they pioneered on Moon Safari. Much of the stuff out today wouldn't even exist if it weren't for the influence Moon Safari had on the electronic scene. But these guys have not made anything since that has come close. Talkie Walkie is just way too esoteric, aimless and ultimately pointless. There's little to grasp on to, little about the album that is memorable. I'm a big fan of melody, and you won't find much of it in Talkie Walkie, just a lot of sonic experimentation and "pushing the envelope" for the sake of pushing the envelope meandering. Let's be honest, if you blindfolded their fans and played the album for them, they would probably say it sucks if they didnt' know it was AIR. Like Beck or Bjork, AIR has carved out such a niche following that their core fans are going to eat up whatever they do, unquestionably, be it crap or not.
The one exception to me is Cherry Blossom Girl. An absolutely gorgeous song I cannot stop listening to. That is AIR at its best, and that's the AIR that I think has been lost since Moon Safari.

reviewText:
Well, that's it: after the debacle of "Sam's Town", any fans of "Hot Fuss" who still held a flickering torch for The Killers will see it extinguished by this new album. It's awful.

The main mistake made in the previous album has been reproduced here: specifically, the pseudo-meaningful lyrics. 'Lyrics from a blender' is how you would describe this jumbled heap of phoney metaphors. If Brandon Flowers had merely entitled a song "Neon Tiger", for example, that would have been daft enough; if he had merely penned the line that "Run, Neon Tiger, there's a lot on your mind" that would have been pretty awful; but instead he chose to commit this block of verse:

"I'm begging you run, Neon Tiger, run
Under the heat
Under the heat
Under the heat of the Southwest Sun
Neon Tiger, there's a lot on your mind"
[Track 8]

The Killers are not going to fool anyone with this chance-your-arm, maybe-it'll-sound-profound stuff. As in "Sam's Town", the awkward vocals from Flowers on many of these songs is evidence that he really has no idea what the song is about, and so finds that he has no particular place to put emphasis or feeling. The songs suffer terribly from being committee-written: everyone has chipped in something, with lamentably predictable results - tunes that are the musical equivalent of exquisite corpse drawings.

It's worth noting that on some of these songs the silliest lines form the chorus: that is to say, the band clearly thought they were good enough to keep repeating. But why should we condemn the album when we can merely quote verbatim from it? Here's what happens when the handle is turned on the Killer's rhyming machine:

"Out where the wind won't blow
Out here the good girls die
And the sky won't snow"
[Track 5]

How often have you ever heard anyone say "The sky is snowing"? I'd say about as often as you've heard anyone say "I heard it with my ears". Please spare me the last-ditch defense of "poetic license": a pleonasm is a pleonasm, and anyone who thinks that the above is poetry is in real trouble.

Here's the song flitting from one incoherent thought to the next:

"He looked just like you'd want him to
Some kind of slick chrome American prince
A blue jean serenade
Moon River what'd you do to me?"

Or try this for a mixture of garbled grammar and bad punnery:

"Are we human?
Or are we dancer?
My signs are vital
My hands are cold"
[Track 2]

Anyone who was hoping that the mediocrity of "Sam's town" was just a glitch will find themselves thoroughly disabused by this album. It's clear now that The Killers have settled into a comfortable mediocrity. None of the flaws in "Sam's Town" have been corrected: indeed there's no evidence the band even recognised what was wrong. More of the same is now their shtick. 'Killers fans (myself included) who really admired the great debut album  "Hot Fuss" deserved better. But after "Sam's Town" and now this, that's two strikes. They're out.
label: negative

reviewText:
The other day, a friend of mine(a bassist) said to me, "I can't believe that I used to think those Randy Rhodes era Ozzy albums were any good". I laughed and told him the story of a Band called Black Sabbath that release their first album "Heaven and Hell", and another band called "The Blizzard of Ozz" which consisted of Lee Kerslake, Bob Daisley (A Veteran like Dio of the early Rainbow Era), and hot shot named Randy Rhodes. Man that Rythm section cooks, and the guitarist isn't too shabby either.

We heard about this Blizzard of Ozz band, and when this "Solo" album was released, it was clear that someone with a big ego and mediocre voice had derailed what could have been something great. Causality? Fire the Rythm section, and the guitar player dies. Karma is...well you know.

Seriously, if it was supposed to be a solo album, wouldn't it have been self-titled? Of the two guys who wrote and played the signicant roles in this album, one is dead, and the other never got paid. But this version isn't recognizable, and some of Randy's recording mistakes are suddenly clear, as if the wrong takes were used for this mix. I'm in the majority on the original bass lines being better, so you can trash this review all you want in your fantasy land.

I told my friend how lousy Ozzy was in concert in 1982, especially without Bob Daisly. How Rudy Sarzo was god-awful, and Ozzy's voice was blown out when I saw him a couple of weeks before Randy's death. Listening to this new version is a joke. Listening to the original classic, it was clear that Ozzy was only sober long enough to contribute 10% of the lyric content, and sing the songs. 40 minutes. Yeah, thats about right. Ozzy tells people that he wrote Suicide Solution about Bon Scott, which I never believed. Actually, Bob Daisley wrote it about Ozzy and his excesses. Truth hurts I guess. Ozzy didn't write any Sabbath songs either, except Psycho Man maybe(biographical?).

*If Randy had lived, he would have been screwed as Kerslake and Daisley were, and this album would have Zakk Wylde's guitar playing on it. Yes, it would! But that is just fine for those Ozzy fans, who don't know the history of the band that gave his career as second chance. I guess some are willing to have no principles like the Osbournes/Ardens.
label: negative

reviewText:
Slow, grinding, bloodless, painful...just a few words that popped into my head as I attempted over and over to finish this monstrosity of an album. It's not to say I wasn't excited for this album: I was a huge fan of Rage and a more casual listener of Soundgarden. I figured the album should be interesting at least, if nothing brilliant; turns out I was very wrong.
When Zack de la Rocha left Rage, he took everything with him, and that includes the fiery music and message. Below his impassioned lyrics, the music was a churning, dangerous sea of volatile emotions that made Rage such a wonderful and meaningful band. Now they're just trudging through sludgy nu-metal riffs that go nowhere. This would appeal to any bonehead who thinks Nickelback is the greatest band of the decade. Is this how they sounded with Zack, if you took his vocals out of the mix? It wasn't this bad then. Tom Morello's solos, once so innovative, seem merely tacked on here: what's the point of them? Chris Cornell screams in a pale, croaky imitation of his past power about who-cares what, and the guitar solos come in unheralded, with no purpose to them, to make you wince further. The mighty rhythm of Brad and Tim, perfected on "Battle of LA", plods aimlessly along, lost in its own sea of muddle.
It's hard to see how two of the best bands of the 90s would come together and make an album that could have come from the worst of the 70s power dinosaurs. Horribly disappointing, it only throws their past triumphs into sharper relief.

reviewText: If David Gilmour wanted to continue making Pink Floyd albums, to take the  band in a new creative direction, fine, great.  He doesn't.  The 2  post-Waters albums and world-wide concert dates that followed were  approached like a bad Hollywood sequel.  They attempted to capture a  formula and harness a  band legend for profit.  Nothing unique or original  was ever attempted.  Just imitative drivel.  Perhaps nothing is more  indicative of their failure to produce anything worthwhile than the  immediate glut of live albums, two double-live offerings on the heels of  just 2 single studio releases.  The intent should be obvious:  to showcase  the original Pink Floyd material in the context of the now Waterless  lineup.  This second live release featuring Dark Side of the Moon in it's  entirety was, no doubt, a response to Roger Waters hugely successful  (televised live in every country except the U.S.) staged performance of The  Wall in 1990.  In both instances every lyric (and in most cases, basic song  structure and sound/visual effects) that passed into digitally-encoded  glory are credited to Roger Waters.  The crime here is not so much their  treatment of the Floyd legacy as it is their insistence on basing their  entire identity on creative juices not their own.  If you wasted your money  on this concert (like I did)  don't waste any more on this lavishly  produced and packaged instance of court-approved copyright infringement.

Here's some solid evidence that we've nearly reached the end of the wagon trail. Before long, music will be pumped straight into our veins calibrated to our particular mood, taste or ambition -- and still, we will gravitate toward the dizzying spectacle, the flab of the gab.

Question: Are we living in such excessive and/or inattentive times that our rock musicians have to clutter all their tunes with mixers, pedals, effects, filters, trinkets, various other whoop-de-doos, and then truck in the whole fricken high school band room? "Golden Age" is particularly unsettling, mixing Thomas Magnum's theme bassline with a sickly attempt at a "Thriller" medley. Dear lord, I thought-gasped as my earhairs recoiled at the audible tragedy that is "Family Tree," a tune that I figure would get regular airplay on an FM radio version of the Hallmark Channel.

There's this point at the end of "The Last Waltz" (a film I obviously intend to trash at a later date) where all the guest musicians gather for the last hurrah. Everyone is playing along and singing, some four-wide at the mikes. And it sounds absolutely horrible. All these beautiful, distinctive voices just battering, blistering the air -- and formless clatter lathered by too many instruments vying for attention.

reviewText:
A lot of critical things have been said about this album (see sampling below), but I think the most accurate and important one is this: "On much of the album, Maroon 5 barely sound like a band at all."

That's because Maroon 5 no longer really exists. They are no longer creating their own music. They recognized that all of the current hit music falls under categories like "disco-flavored dance-floor filler" or "dance-pop glitz," and they knew to sell songs they'd need to hire outside help. Who'd they hire? Look up names like Max Martin, Ryan Tedder, Shellback, and Benny Blanco--these people are the new "Maroon 5," and they are also Pink and Katy Perry and Kelly Clarkson and Usher and Britney Spears and Taio Cruz and Adele and OneRepublic and Gym Class Heroes and Sean Paul and Avril Lavigne and Justin Bieber and Ke$ha and Flo Rida and Pitbull. I'm not making this up--it is a fact that almost all of the music we hear on the radio is created by the same few guys whose names you probably haven't heard.

I think it would be fair to say that the Billboard 100 has never been in such a sad, homogenous state, and I think it would also be fair to say that the release of this album confirms that modern hit music is vapid and soulless--it is little more than brand names selling catchy hooks created by anonymous dance-pop gurus.

Adam Levine himself admits that Overexposed "is definitely our poppiest album yet," and he admits that he has a "love/hate relationship with it." Maybe he'll get back to doing what he loves if we stop buying dance-pop glitz.

---

Other things that have been said about this album:

* "Every song sounds as if it was custom made to play behind the montage of someone's 'journey' in a TV talent show." (The Independent)
* "It seems more like a collaboration between Swedish hitmakers and AutoTune than between Levine and members of his band." (The Washington Post)
* "Even with various superstar producers on board, including Max Martin and Ryan Tedder, the album is stridently homogenous." (Boston Globe)
* "Overexposed is a hit-seeking missile that doesn't just slaughter Maroon 5's reputation for sincerity, it festoons its corpse with glitter." (The Washington Post)

reviewText:
LTJ Bukem is certainly one of the most important DnB-DJ's. He opened the genre to ambient, Funk, Jazz etc and there are few DJ's which have influenced DnB more than him. Without Bukem, and without  Good Looking Records, DnB would not be what it is today.

Let me remind you, this is the man who created Logical Progression (certainly one of the most influential DnB albums), Progression Sessions with the wonderful MC Conrad, and Earth (which anyone in electronical music knows and loves).

Unfortunetaly, I must say that Journey Inwards just shows what I was afraid of: with the beginning of the new century, the time of the LTJ is over.

Some claim "Journey Inwards" is a logical continuation of 70's Funk, Jazz and Fusion, and that it really is "intelligent". My opinion is that it is neither funky nor jazzy nor is it DnB. Do you know these Yoga or meditation CD's you sometimes here when you are shopping? That's how this album sounds. It is totally uninspired, it is really really boring, and it never comes to a point. Its just like this man is out of ideas.

Most songs are over 7 minutes long, and you only hear some mystical sounds (again - meditation) for 2 or 3 minutes. Nothing else, no drums, no bass. And almost every song starts like that. So close your eyes, and imagine you are a tree...

I would say, Bukem has made his contributions, but his style is exhausted - there is nowhere to go with it anymore. What can you do as a music fan? Here are some tips:

Either buy all the old stuff by Bukem, or go back to 60's and 70's real Jazz, Funk or Fusion. And if you want to listen to some new very good (say 2003 and later) - and indeed quite intelligent DnB-albums, which are more "up-to-date" - then go to DJ Marky, Zinc, London Electricity or High Contrast. Thats the "intelligent" DnB of the new century.

This live album is utter garbage.  How David Gilmour could have unleashed this on his fans is a mystery.  With the exception of "On the Turning Away" (better than the studio version) the songs here all sound horrible.  It pains me to say that, because Pink Floyd are a legendary live band.  I don't know what went wrong on this tour.  It doesn't help either that the first disc is loaded with 7 songs from 'A Momentary Lapse of Reason', the worst "Pink Floyd" album ever (and I put Pink Floyd in quotes for a reason).  And literally every non-AMLR track on here can be found on 'Pulse', which is infinitely superior.

To sum up, don't buy this.  Unless you are the type of fan that absolutely MUST own every album.  Even then, get David and Roger's solo albums first.  And if you need live Pink Floyd check out either 'In the Flesh - Live' or 'Pulse'.

reviewText:
Perhaps I'm missing something here. Perhaps I'm missing the same album that others are loving....For in TX I have this record and am very disappointed.
The tracks presented here are a somewhat pleasant mixture albeit a bit fragmented in places due to the over use of samples . Although some sounded rather dated this record reminds me of a UFOrb / Orblivion hybrid - that being the 'worst' ( if there is such a thing ) parts of UFOrb mixed with the better sections of the latter. Not bad at all.
Anyway what really upsets me is the quality of the recording. In a word it's horrid. It has very little dynamic range. 80 percent of the tracks have inexcusable distortion. The deep bass suffers the most. Every hit of beat is distorted. It sounds as if the volume level meters were in the red during the whole mastering session ...This is unacceptable.
Just to clarify, the distortion is not the type that works say in an Aphex Twin release or like what occurs on an old recording. This is just plain bad.
I mean, isn't that what we want from an Orb release. To go places, to bathe in the mastery of layering textures and otherworldly instrumentation? To trance?
Not so when the quality is bad enough to cause distraction. Very disappointing. Listen to this carefully in a record shop before purchase if I were you.

reviewText:
Like most Michael Giacchino scores, the music works fine in the film but is a chore to appreciate isolated. There just isn't anything all that memorable here. I think what worked so well for composers like John Williams and Jerry Goldsmith, back in their prime, was how they could craft beautiful, complex and memorable thematic material. I've yet to hear anything like that with Giacchino. For an action film, to learn how to do it right, he should sit down and listen to Goldsmith's score to "Total Recall." Learn what makes this score so remarkable and try to do similar.

Another thing I grow tired of is the sappy general moment in the film, such as Tom's CPR sequence, where the film consists of.... a sad piano chord. Then another one. Another one, etc. What fails with this is how CLICHE this is: you can picture the composer, a somber, over-serious look on his face, playing the chord and looking meaningfully at the recording room. It's a lazy way to score a dramatic moment to just pop in a couple chords, but play 'em dramatic and leave it. It's been done too many times (didn't Giacchino do the same gimmick with Rogue One when the star destroyer crashes into the big space donut thingie?)  Complex themes, Michael. Give us something to remember, something to hum, somethings that sticks with us. No one leaves a theater humming the slow, moving chords from the CPS sequence.

Look, I could probably type up a "smart" review here, full of big words describing my disdain for this record, complex sentances and deep down thoughts and all that other stuff, but it's not my style and I don't think this record warrents that much thought.

Radiohead's "Amnesiac" is crap crappity crap crap crap. It is one unpleasant, forty five minute keyboard hum accented by a couple of "Smiths-esque"(I know the Smiths, and this ain't what they sound like)guitar lines and Thom "I Never Found A Song Lyric I Didn't Like To Mumble" Yorke, well, mubmling over the top of it all about, uhm, sad stuff. It's garbage. It's a record whose sole intention is to make the people who like it feel cool and hip, and the people who don't like it feel stupid.

Well I'm not stupid, or at least not THAT stupid. Some people will have you believe that just because a record is quote-unquote dense and should be listened to on headphones that makes it good. Sure, sometimes, like Radiohead's "OK COmputer" or even, to a lesser extent, the pretty good "Kid A". That is, when there's something there. Here? Nothing. Just a bunch of people fiddling with keyboards.

I used to dig Radiohead("The Bends" up until "Kid A", so the arguement that I just don't get it doesn't cut it friends) but after this record I approach everything they release with more caution then I do then pretty much any other band. If you had even a slight ability to hear and think then I believe that you too will despise this piece of garbage.

On the goodside, I like the line "I'm a reasonable man get off my case." Cool line that one.

The reviewer who called Mick Jagger a "Cartoonish sex symbol" was right on the money. I agree - the Stones used to be the greatest band around (before I was born, sadly). But now, they're a joke.

When Mick Taylor left, the Boys lost all the credibility they once had and became one big, unfunny joke. This can be blamed almost entirely on Mick Jagger who, like Brian Jones before him, was obsessed with style. Case in point: Some Girls was a decent record, but hurt by the group's attempt to play disco. Emotional Rescue (probably their worst album to date) also saw them taking on the disco and punk trends. And Bridges To Babylon continues this tradition, this time featuring the band trying two popular genres on for size: techno and rap. Yes, that's right: Rolling Stones rap. What happened? They sold out.

Saint of Me, the only song worth hearing, is actually close to good. But the rest (Anybody Seen My Baby, Too Tight, Flip the Switch, Out of Control, Might As Well Get Juiced, etc). is worthless. Check out Beggars Banquet, Let It Bleed, Get Yer Ya-Ya's Out, Sticky Fingers, Exile on Main Street, Some Girls, the underrated Voodoo Lounge and A Bigger Bang instead.

reviewText:
Surely the most over-praised and hyped disc of recent years. Eight grammy's?? what the hell was the competition? I bought this on the basis of good reviews and have already given it away after just one play.
And as for the Amazon's in-house reviewer, Mr Ross, - to mention Nina Simone and Billie H as comparisons is blasphemy indeed. If only! In fact Ms Jones sings 14 almost identical songs with only minor changes in tempo or tone. Her voice lacks variety but even more importantly, experience (of life as well as singing). Nina Simone? More like Bing Crosby.
The songs are trite, predictable and even embarrassing (try Lonestar, - or better still, don't), without an ounce of soul, poetry or innovation. As a whole this album is best described as MOR (that's short for moronic as well as standing for Middle of the Road) meets watered down cocktail jazz meets feeble county. The whole is an unending stream of anodyne, trite, monotonous, pasteurised and homogenised pap. Even Bob Dylan's "I'll be your baby" can't survive this treatment.
The sound is adequate and the acoustic neutral, - and better in stereo than in surround, - but who cares when the accompanying instruments are basically picking at airport lounge music in a desultory, predictable, uninspired way.
To think that this emanated from Blue Note!!  What has the world come to??!!

reviewText:
Many years ago, Jefferson Airplane put out a compilation album which they entitled THE WORST OF JEFFERSON AIRPLANE.  They were being ironic--that album contained all the BEST songs.  However, the title of this CD could be changed to THE WORST OF DEEP PURPLE, or DEEP PURPLE: AT THEIR WORST--without a shred of irony.
I'll be brief here, but if you are interested in hearing a horribly truncated (and unfinished) of the classic "Woman From Tokyo," Ian Gillian singing off-key as he does on several songs here (especially on "Highway Star" and the beloved "Smoke On The Water"), the band tripping into a Buddy Holly song (!) in the middle of another song, and in general, long rambling, ruined versions of some of their most classic tunes--then, buy all means buy this CD.  But if you're like me, and like to hear a great rock 'n' roll band performing at their best, then you should avoid this CD like the plague.
Who ever thought that this was a good idea, anyway?  I mean, anyone who has their mega-classic live album "Made In Japan" knows that Deep Purple can be incredible in concert.  Why did they do this to their fans?  I guess I'll never know.
The only good thing about this CD is their rollicking version of their all-time classic "Hush" (recorded live in a studio on Long Island, NY).  I made sure to transfer this to tape before selling my copy of this CD.

reviewText:
I have to admit, when I first heard Roberto Alagna in this performance of "Traviata," back in 1992, I thought he had no future.  The voice is thin, pallid, and constantly spreads under pressure.  And soprano Tiziana Fabbricini is even worse, having little or no voice at all.  Muti conducts pretty well, but not in a league with the best Verdi interpreters.  This recording is almost as painful to listen to (for somewhat different reasons) as the old Toscanini version.  If you want a great "Traviata," you should get the classic Cotrubas-Domingo-Milnes-Kleiber recording on DG....or, try the 1968 film version (slightly abridged) with Moffo, Bonisolli and Bechi, one of the most underrated performances ever.
Oh, and if you want to hear a Violetta who will bring you to tears...listen to Magda Olivero sing the "Dite alla giovine" duet with Aldo Protti in Amsterdam, 1968.  At the moment when Violetta realizes that she is giving Alfredo up for good, Olivero sings with the most heart-wrenching tone I have ever heard....I cannot listen to this recording without crying, it is so incredibly beautiful.

reviewText: What is wrong with this woman? Is this the same woman that established a sense of identity and self-respect on "Control"? Is this the same woman that incorporated love and equality into the musical foreground in order to elicit social awareness on "Rhythm Nation 1814"? Is this the woman who was taking command of her sexuality on "janet."? Is this the woman sublimating her rage and overcoming depression in order to reinforce a stronger sense of self-worth on "The Velvet Rope"? or is this the woman setting her spirit free after a difficult divorce on "All For You"? The problem with "Damita Jo" is that it lacks purpose, effort, and conviction. Though the blame for this travesty of an album rests primarily with Janet herself, her long-time producers, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis are also largely at blame. For 18 years the seemingly unstoppable trinity of Jackson, Jam, and Lewis released 27 singles (25 of them making it to the top 20), however, all three singles from this album failed to crack the top 40. The album falls flat, and perhaps it was a mistake to involve Dallas Austin, Babyface, and Kanye West in some of the production, but Jam and Lewis appear thoroughly uninspired and indifferent this time around. Jackson obviously felt pressure to release a new album, writing songs merely for the purpose of fulfilling a contract obligation rather than building on her career momentum and taking her music in a new direction. So what we, the listeners, are left with is a boring, gratuitously over-sexual album by a woman losing her sex symbol status at an alarming rate. Another notable difference in this album in comparison to the others is that it involves no legitimate singing. Instead, Jackson coos and whispers through each song to the point that the lyrics are almost indecipherable and no force or emotion can be detected whatsoever. Janet's apathy couldn't have been made more explicit. This album is a failure by all accounts and it did not deserve to sell a fraction of the amount it did (which is not much) and merits no respect among her fans. Regardless of the infamous Super Bowl incident (which many people misattribute for this album's lack of success), Janet seemed to be asking for a backlash. Janet's loyal followers deserve much more than this half-baked attempt at music.

KA-SSPPPLLLOOOOOOSH.

To the uninitiated, that's the sound of a large toilet being flushed. The first single was a jerky, jumpy noise that doesn't really go anywhere but wasn't terrible, but the next single ("Soldier") is quite possibly one of the worst songs of all time. Fooling absolutely NO-ONE, the three millionairesses sing about wanting to be with people from Da Hood. Soldiers, apparently. Of what, we're never told, but they bring one of them to give the most pointless rap ever. Honestly, it's like the little turd can't even SPEAK. When did that happen in rap music? Why do rappers try and sound as monosyllabic as possible? What's that all about?

Anyway, next single and it's quite obviously they're just scraping the barrel (which, at three singles in, is a sure-fire sign of a bad album). After all the honk about being Independent Women and strong and don't need men to make them happy, they release "Cater 2 U", a song about bringing their man his slippers and basically being the dominated doormats they all said they weren't in the first place.  Chicks, eh?  They love it really.

And that's that, then. One greatest hits followed, then the end of Destiny's Child. Some terrible songs, a number of interchangeable band members and some pointless "girl power". A totally unfulfilling legacy.

reviewText: There comes a time in every artists' career when they run out of ideas. This album provides evidence that they can't come up with incredible and inventive songs anymore within the traditional song structure, and they've been moving in this direction in the last couple of albums (I write to those that respond that it's just one album.)  Kurt Cobain said, "Pro Tools and studio effects can enhance a song, and there's nothing wrong with using them for that, as long as you can play those same songs without the enhancement."  Radiohead will get four stars from critics and fans alike, no matter what they do, but can anyone say that the songs on this album could be played without enhancement?  They're done.  They've overstayed.  It's time to move on.

The complete opposite is true of reckless artists like Horowitz who infuses his personality and misguided vision of how the music should be played to a point that exasperates any knowledgeable and discriminating listener.  I'm still perplexed by the popularity of artists whose main goal was to wow the public and little more.

Recently, I listened to some of Stefan Askenase's Chopin...easily some of the best readings of the music I've ever heard...a broad dynamic palette used with great subtlety, a sense of line that rivals that of great conductors and a wealth of technique put to the service of the music not just to impress the ignorant.

reviewText:
Blizzard of Ozz is one of the classic metal albums of all time.  Randy Rhoads' guitar work was brilliant.  The drums and bass were the perfect sounding board for Ozzy and Randy.  Why re-record the bass and drums???
Here is why.  They were re-recorded because of a lawsuit against Ozzy by Bob Daisley and Lee Kerslake, the original bass player and drummer from the "Blizzard of Ozz" and "Diary of a Madman" albums.  The plaintiffs claim that they were deprived of performance royalties from these albums....While I'm not sure whether they are due anything from Ozzy, I do know that his reaction (this re-released album) is a misjustice to his fans and the original recording place in the history of music.  So, to keep a long story short, don't buy this version of this album.
While I am personally a fan of Rob Trujillo, the modern-sounding drums and bass that have been mixed into this classic album of the early `80s sounds out of place...  distracting.  The bass and drums are the foundation for this classic music and should not be the centerpiece.  Imagine putting a small red rose in the corner of an Ansel Adams photograph.  Your focus would be the little red rose, not the majestic black and while landscape.  The same effect is achieved by tracking in the modern drums and bass.  I find myself ignoring Randy's masterful guitar-work and Ozzy's angst-ridden howls.  Do yourself a favor and buy the version released in 1995 (ASIN: B000002B7M).
label: negative

reviewText:
I've been listening to All Time Low since their EP back in 2006. They were a pop-punk full of energy who could make incredibly catchy songs with decent enough lyrics to get by. They were supposed to be a new wave of pop-punk to help reinvigorate the genre. They started out incredibly well with the EP and then will their first full length album "So Wrong, It's Right" Their first full length is one of my personal favorites of all time. I put it in every summer because every song is catchy and it has repeat value galore.

Now, let's move onto Dirty Work. The first time I heard "Time Bomb" I thought it was complete and utter trash. The second time, it sounded the same. The song is not inventive at all, it's using other bands who have converted already to the "Sugary pop-punk" sound and it shows. When I say bands who are "Sugary", I am referring to We The King's toned down over produced latest album and Mayday Parade's tamed down latest effort (which I still enjoy).

The worst song on the album (I know, it's hard to chose a worst when they are all awful) would be a tie between their new single "I Feel Like Dancing" and "A Daydream Away." The first song is so ironic it's not even funny. And don't worry, I understand it was written a certain way to "mock" today's standards of music and it's supposed to be awful and have dumb lyrics etc. The only problem is, this band wants to be on the radio so bad that they had to revert to making a trash song in order to do so. If anyone believes they don't want to be on the radio, you are blind. The only way for this band to make their money back is to get on the radio and get played nationwide. The lyrics in this song are forced and they are playing a song which they use to fight against so long ago. This band has sold whatever soul they have to the studios for a tamed down, electronic filled play-list which is nothing short of disappointing and awful. Now, the latter song, "A Daydream Away," this song probably has some of the worst lyrics any band has ever written. It sounds more like a Justin Beiber song than a band that use to have it all and be the most looked upon band in the pop-punk genre. All Time Low is trying too hard to appeal to the younger listener. There's a problem though, this band started out appealing to the 14-16 year old age group, but they haven't matured as their fans have. I was 16 when their first EP came out, now I'm 21 and this is absolutely terrible to my ears. There are ways of still appealing to both sides of the age group but they are so desperate to get on the radio they've lost track of what it's like to be a band full of energy writing catchy hooks etc.

I could go on and on about All Time Low. They use to be one of my favorite bands back in the day. I am done with them. I thought I was going to be done after "Nothing Personal" which, apart from 3-4 songs, is a terrible All Time Low album too, but, I gave them one more chance. They are NOTHING like they use to be. It won't be long before their songs are in Disney movies and every god damn market aimed at 14 year old girls who don't know what this band used to be capable of.

I expect some tragedy and pathos in the 6th, not torpor and turgidity. To me, this wallowing performance is terrible.  It dishonors Tchaikovsky and Tchaikovsky's abilities.

reviewText:
After 2005's mediocre at best Out of Exile, Audioslave wasted no time in directing their follow up and third in a short but already growing discography. Unfortunately, Revelations fares no better and even worse than Out of Exile managed only a year ago.

 Frontman Chris Cornell sounds brilliant. He's scraped all the grit and sediment from his throat after quitting a long time habit of smoking and drinking. While his vocals might reach the nose blood sections of Soldier Field, his lyrics would give high school students nightmares.

 Songs "Sound of a Gun" or "Shape of Things to Come" are repetitive and dull after two minutes past, while new single "Original Fire" follows suit, only to a somewhat attractive beat.

 Tom Morello, who used to pull out intimidating riffs and unique sounds, seems to borrow too much from Mike McCready's back catalogue and ironically his own. Opening track "Revelations" starts out melodic and builds into a steroid driven gun ship that fires too fast and too inconsistently.

 Drummer Brad Wilk manages to hold beat and actually keep things interesting, especially in the album's better track "Wide Awake", all the while bassist Tim Commerford ends up following rather dutifully and sounds sheepish and somewhat timid.

 One of the appealing prospects of Out of Exile had been an original sound in comparison with Audioslave's self titled debut. The lines between the members' former bands, Rage Against the Machine and Soundgarden, weren't so distinct and with songs "Doesn't Remind Me" or "Dandelion" they found their own style.

 Unfortunately with Out of Exile, too many songs fell flat and the same goes with Revelations, only this time there's more bandages to be passed around. Even if their self titled debut brought about too many comparisons with it's former past, at least the disc had replay value and a slew of memorable tracks.

 With Revelations, each song sounds too much like filler. Upon releasing the album, guitarist Morello explained their new sound as "Earth, Wind, and Fire meets Led Zeppelin." If Led Zeppelin wrote songs "Heartbreaker", "D'yer Maker" or "Good Times, Bad Times" in the same key as any of these songs, Zeppelin's greatest hits album would be a single disc.

 Apparently Revelations' twelve tracks are a result of twenty or so written. It would seem the band chiseled away too much and maybe too little with an undercooked affair. Revelations tastes mediocre at best and with some much needed spice. Hopefully, Audioslave will go back to the kitchen and rethink it out.

 Because, really, how many people enjoy undercooked prime rib?

Lily Pon's Rosina sounds dated and pedestrian when compared to later Rosinas such as Maria Callas, Teresa Berganza and Marilyn Horne.  Moreover, she was well past her best vocal days when she sang on this broadcast.  The only reason why, in my humble opinion, this set is interesting is for the singing of a very young Giuseppe di Stefano, a great tenor (with an unfortunately short-lived vocal career due to his insistence of pushing his voice into heavy dramatic tenor roles).  His voice, while youthful and fluid, as well as beautiful, is simply unsuited to this role.  The sonics on this broadcast have been cleaned up, and the remastering is certainly impressive, but the efforts should have been expended on the thousands of broadcasts still laying in the vaults.

reviewText: I hate writing this review, because Barton Hollow was a five star CD, their live performances were great, and I'd had hope that this duo could grow to become a living legend. In their previous CDs and also in their live performances, Williams and White showed that they could blend both harmony and dissonance in a hauntingly beautiful way. There is little if any of this in the present CD. Track ten, "Disarm" is the only song which comes close to meeting their previous performance level. Track 12, "D'Arline" is the only other one which in my opinion comes close to good on the vocals but it loses due to a thumping bass line and what sounds like the first run-through practice session for the finger picked guitar. White is a much better guitar player than that. Most of the rest of the album is, in my opinion, clumsily orchestrated and mixed to say the least. Most of the time White's vocals are stepped over by both instrumental tracks and William's vocals. Most of the album trends to Williams sounding strident with White, when he can be heard, sounding pretty good. If only he could be heard. White's guitar tracks appear to be presented in a manner most likely to make him look bad. Picked passages have mistakes and rhythm guitar sounds like it is being strummed with a playing card, close to what you'd get to the old Appalachian washboard sound. Electric guitar on the tracks it is used is well played but over amped - such over amping is 'right' for punk and 'wrong; for the sound The Civil Wars was trying to achieve. It comes close to sounding OK on Track 2 "I Had me a Girl" but then it gets away again. Steel guitar is very good, a marked positive, but even so is sometimes poorly mixed. And the drummer and the keyboardist from early Iron Butterfly stylism - I could go on but it is more of the same. Summary is that in the future I think we'll see White go on to do a lot better, Williams may well have peaked. No I didn't buy this CD, a family member did. But I've listened to it over five times on three different systems. I don't recommend the reader buy it either unless they find me in error by listening to the samples that Amazon presents. Edited 0n 9/2/13 to add: Today was a lazy Labor Day holiday so I listened again to Barton Hollow,A Place at the Table and Long Goodbye, all of which are four or five star CDs. Comparing it to these three I'm changing my opinion of the presently reviewed CD to 1 star. It is worse by prolonged comparison.

reviewText:
Neil Young has long ceased being the Neil that we would like him to be, the Neil of his 60s' albums and even of his enthusiastic genre explorations that were criticized then but sound great today. Somewhere about two thirds into his long and extraordinarily prolific career, it all began to unravel and has been a long slide down ever since, and yet until now, he has never produced a truly, thoroughly bad album. Well, with "Fork in the Road" he has finally achieved that.
Even at his sloppiest or most misguided, Neil Young has always shown signs of brilliance, or at the very least of true talent. Granted, he had begun borrowing more and more heavily from himself, his guitar solos that blew me away when I was a kid sounded suspiciously trivial once I actually learned to play the guitar, and after all the voyages in different directions he eventually ran out of new things to amaze us with. We know to expect a country Neil, a rockabilly Neil, a grunge Neil, and so on. But even the least inspired albums always had three or four gems on them, a sign that here was an artist whose muse had not left him. He was always an absolute master of the melody and the melodic riff or chorus, and he managed to use that even in places where you'd least expect it, such as "Mirror Ball." And there was always that electric energy, the feeling that old Neil was having a whale of a time, even if we weren't necessarily amused.
Not so with "Fork in the Road." No memorable melody, no energy, no nothing. Assuming that this one falls somewhere in his industrial/grunge catalog, it is fitting only in the sense that everything sounds like tar-logged machinery going nowhere. We plod through the songs that evoke no imagery and leave no trace in the mind. In spite of titles such as "Just Singing a Song" and "Johnny Magic," everything sounds about the same, even the two ballads. And while once he could get away with doing the same song over and over because the song was excellent, he's got nothing here that would support that. "Cough Up the Bucks" is a prime example of ugly monotony. There is no hook to sing to, it's mostly a flat, two-chord exercise, the choruses try but are too poorly conceived, the playing is amateurish, Neil's voice is going the way of all things (and, faithful to his allegiance to spontaneity, he lets all the cracks and squawks be--that concept, too, has pretty much worn out its welcome), and the lyrics are embarrassing.
The irony is that Neil is trying to fire us up, but seems to have no fire left in him. He has very often espoused topical themes, sometimes through bizarre lyrics that confused us as to where exactly he stood on an issue, but it was always good, effective involvement on his part. I, for one, liked "Living with War" very much, and still listen to it with pleasure. He had churned that one out in a day, raw as you please, yet everything worked, and the typically simple, not to say simplistic, Neil lyrics were spot on. All of that, the rawness and the lyrical simplicity, bog him down on "Fork," into some ideological morass he can't get out of. I applaud the efforts to get rid of gas guzzlers, but if we had to lobby with Neil's words, we'd die from cringing before we ever reached DC. Perhaps if he delivered wisdoms such as "It's all about my car, it's all about my girl," with the bounce of a teen singing a surfer tune, we could smile and remember cruising on a summer's day. But in the context, sung with cranky gravity, this epiphany makes you pause and think, "wha?..."
For the past decade, Neil has been including one song per album that speaks about his spiritual thoughts and feelings. It's generally a soft ballad sung in the touching way of a wide-eyed child, and while the sentiment doesn't move me, the song usually does--how could it not? Neil has perfected the intimate, soulful ballad over forty years! But "Light a Candle" is pedestrian, and will appeal only to the true believers. The album is a misery, and whether Neil comes back with something better or not, he is as of now officially irrelevant. Any pearls that come from him will be exceptions, not the rule.

At least Helfgott has his mental condition as an alibi. reviewText: I don't believe Morrissey will ever live up to the standard Smiths fanatics demand, but on this CD he barely manages a coherent standard at all. 'The Teachers Are Afraid of the Pupils' takes what I can only call an 'orchestral riff' and repeats it for 11 minutes. 'The Operation' is catchy and genuinely swings, but is undercut by offensively dull 2-minute long drum solos. Half of these tunes make no impact whatsoever, except to suggest Morrissey wants to be a singer in a garage punk band. Moz, we don't want you to be Johnny Rotten, we want frilly multi-instrument emotionally direct concise tunes. (Like what you did before this mess, and then did after with 'Maladjusted.') I'm always a fan, but this CD is a career-killer. Only 'Reader Meet Author' works well, and you can get that on the far better 'My Early Burglary Years' compilation.

reviewText:
As many people may know by now, Sony was recently caught with egg on their face when a security specialist found out that a recently purchased CD (Van Zant: Get Right With The Man) from Sony music not only installed DRM software (digital rights management, to limit and outright prevent copying music to certain devices), but it did so in such a sneaky way that it hid itself entirely from Windows, and opened the system up to security issues such as viruses.

This CD has the same copyright protection, called XCP. When installed, Sony hijacks your computer and installs custom software which:

1) Hides itself entirely from Windows by installing as a rootkit

2) Hides itself in such a manner that any files begining with $sys$ are also hidden. For example, if you install the XCP copy protection software on your machine, and rename "document.doc" to "$sys$document.doc" it then becomes invivisble to you forever.

3) Installs its own custom CD-Rom drivers to hijack your system. It also sneakily names these drivers "Plug and Play Device Manager" to seem as if it's a part of Windows. Trying to delete these drivers manually will disable your CD-Rom drive entirely.

4) Offers no uninstall option until you manually contact Sony

As of my writing this review, Sony has "apologized" for this incident, and claims they will "re-evaluate" this copyright protection software on their CDs in the future.

In the meantime, a virus is currently running wild, which names itself begining with $sys$ in an attempt to hide from the user and virus scanners.

Several class action lawsuits are also pending against Sony right now.

In summary, as you can tell from above, Sony's actions here are absolutely horrible. This is your music. You purchased it, and they should not have any right to dictate how you can use it, let alone install software which compromises your system security.

This is one of the CDs with Sony's XCP copyright protection software on it, and as a result, you should not buy it to send a message to Sony that this will NOT be tolerated in the future.

reviewText:
I have had this album for quite a few years, and it has never done a thing for me.  Tonight I took it off the shelf, dusted it off, and tried for the umpteenth time to listen to it and see what I've been missing.  After all, this is one of the most hyped bands in the death metal scene today.  Well I'll tell you what I've been missing all these years...absolutely nothing.  Utterly monotonous drumming that never varies from the same lame blast beat, monotone growled vocals, and speeding guitar riffs that are really nothing more than slightly more technical slayer rip offs.  Only one difference...slayer writes catchy, classic tunes.  Krisiun writes an endless series of "songs" that are only distinguishable from eachother by a two second pause in the blasting when the track changes.

I tried my very best to listen to this album, with the intention of hearing the whole thing.  Once again, I had to turn it off halfway through the second song because my brain literally hurt from hearing such a pathetic excuse for "music".  This is honestly one of the most boring albums i've ever heard in the death metal genre.  For the life of me I can't understand what would cause anyone to like this.

Don't get me wrong, I enjoy some pretty relentless stuff.  Nile, Angelcorpse, Disgorge, Deeds of Flesh, Napalm Death, all these bands employ blastbeats as the backbone of their music, but all are infinitely more enjoyable than Krisiun.  Even Hate Eternal, who belong to a similar school of monotonous blastology, can keep me entertained for far longer than krisiun could ever hope to.  With so much fantastic brutal death metal to choose from, why spend your hard earned money on this travesty?

Buy this only if you hate death metal and you want to show people how horrible the genre can be.

reviewText:
The problem with most of these reviews is that they are written by hard core fans of that artist.  Thus, they are not reliable.  For example, I am a huge Peter Gabriel fan.  I would give him 5 stars regardless of the content.  The most valuable reviews are those written by listeners who do not have a dying allegiance to that artist. I am not a die hard Kate Bush fan.  I am a big music fan and buy 1-5 CD's a week.  My tastes cover the entire musical spectrum from pop to underground indie.

I bought this 2 disc set because of the long absence of Kate Bush from the music scene and the "rave" reviews.  Apparently, she was working on this 2 disc set for a long time.  It does not show.  These discs are terrible. There is no cohesion to this music, it serves no purpose and it reminds me of the applicant for the high school talent show who is ignorant of the fact their song sucks.

I realize there is some music that requires multiple plays in order to fully appreciate it (e.g. Radiohead, Brian Eno, Sigur Ross).  This is not one of those CD's.  I forced myself to listen to this several times.  What a waste of time. If you are not a Kate Bush fan, save your money and move on.  You will be very dissapointed with this aggrandized elevator music.  There is not one track that is worth the time to play.  You will never hear one of these songs in your head and rush home because you need to hear it. I would give this CD zero stars but there is no option for that.

The only reason to purchase this CD is for the song Bangla Desh. While not one of his best songs, it is found nowhere else on CD.

This album is a rehash of "Comes Alive" with some new stuff that is really just an attempt to sell his later albums.  All of his better stuff is pre-"Comes Alive" (from his first four studio albums).  That's my opinion hsving only heard snippets of his later stuff plus this live album, but I think I've heard enough.
This could have been a great album if he had included old songs like "The Lodger", "Lady Lieright", "Don't Fade Away", "Just The Time of Year", and "Apple of Your Eye".  Most (all?) great rock musicians peak on their second album and then fade away.  Frampton has two really good studio albums, "Camel" (#2)and "Frampton" (#4).  Then he, like everyone else, ran out of ideas or, perhaps, just the necessary artistic edge.
I am also not crazy about his new style.  He may be a more accomplished guitarist now, but, again, he lacks the intellectual edge he once had.
So I am not busting on Frampton, I'm just saying your money would be better spent on one or more of his first four albums.  In fact, Amazon has his first two albums in a set for about $12.  Your money would be better spent on that.  Then get "Frampton" and, if you must, "Something's Happening".  Even the songs you already have on your personal copy of "Comes Alive" are very delightful on the studio albums.

I don't even know where to begin with this album.  Having been a fan of his 3 previous albums; there's no excuse for this one.  The album feels really rushed and very underwhelming.  I understand the theme is supposed to be "night life" type of songs but the problem is that the songs are weak and wack.  Can we at least get a Blame It or an Unpredictable if you choose to go that route???  He's better off on ballads/midtempos/acoustic anyway so why he would go that route in the first place is beyond me.

The production is uninspired, the songwriting is bland and uninspired, and the singing doesn't even sound like Jamie Foxx. It's horrible. I guess he just (I)phoned it in.  The guest artists do their absolute best trying to save this rubbish but there is no hope.  T.I., Justin Timberlake, Rick Ross, Wiz Khalifa, Ludacris and Soulja Boy attempt to salvage this effort but to no avail.  Quite frankly this feels like an "obligation" record to get out of his recording deal because he just threw this one together without any real push or promotion and without any care or artistry.

*Attempting to explain this travesty, a few weeks ago Tank was on Atlanta radio promoting his own album Now or Never, and come to find out that he played no role in this Jamie Foxx album.  That might explain the lack of good songwriting, arrangements and overall direction. *

On one song he sounds like Sean Garrett (who for the record is NOT the person you want to sound like).  Fall For Your Type with Drake is a good song but it sounds like a Thank Me Later leftover.

I downloaded this album and was sorely disappointed and unfortunately someone got it for me for Christmas but I have not opened it.  I want to find out where it was purchased so I can take it back to the store for a refund or store credit.  That's really how I feel.  This album will get no burn whatsoever, ESPECIALLY, with better efforts from the likes of R. Kelly, Charlie Wilson, Ron Isley, El DeBarge, Eric Benet, Tank, Ne-Yo, Trey Songz, Aloe Blacc, etc.  And that's not even to mention his female counterparts.

What happened to the Jamie Foxx that did songs like Do What It do, Heaven, She Got It, or even Blame It????  That Jamie is (almost) nonexistant on this album.  We'll consider this one a blip on the radar because it's not worth getting all excited over and hopefully Jamie Foxx produces a better effort next time around.  1 star.

For those who want analog sound in a box set of Beatles LPs, I highly recommend the half speed mastered, fully analog MFSL box set. First things first.  I'm an atheist and someone sent me Harper's The Black Clouds of Islam as a supportive gesture.  I consider that they thought it would tally with my stance against organised religion and my paid membership of the British Humanist Association. How wrong they were.

It didn't.  The song is pigswill.  It's one of the most ill-informed, casually bigoted pieces of tabloid-soaked rubbish I've ever heard.  Even ignoring its total ignorance in lumping together the numerous subtleties that propel various Islamic groups (quite brilliantly detailed by Jason Burke--who is an actual intellect--please see his book) it's little more than dull propaganda for the terminally thick.  By way of balance, where is the man's rebuke of the Christian right?  After hearing it I'm really glad that Harper has faded into obscurity and plays to very tiny audiences.  Good bye, Roy.  Good luck!

The rest of the album is equally banal.  It more or less utterly stinks.  It's made by an old cricketer that should quickly naff-off back to the pavilion and I hope someone flushes his plectrum down the bog.

Read The God Delusion if you want to know why ALL religion is terminal--not just the target picked by this buffoon.  I despise bigotry and this a purely rare example of it.  It's nasty, narrow-minded garbage recorded by an idiot with nothing at all to say.

It gets a minus ten rating and that's being generous.  As far as I'm concerned it could be minus one million.

reviewText:
Let me start by putting out a couple of my biases before getting into this review-- first, I relaly don't care for remixes as a rule, unless they're dramatic and severely restructure a song, I generally find they add little.  Second, I really don't care for "The Hand That Feeds".

Having said that, the piece is presented in three mixes, the album version, the Straight mix, and the Dub mix.  The album version has a catchy, circular guitar line and a straightahead drum beat that's actually decent until the bridge with this bizarrely irritating spoken wordish section.  Just doesn't work.

The remixes fare no better-- the Straight mix adds different rock beats and an extended introduction that eventually becomes tedious, the dub mix layers a grating sustained guitar note over a beat and a mumbled repeated take on the chorus.

If you're a fan, get it.  If not, skip this one, there's good reasons it wasn't released in the U.S.

reviewText: First of, this is just my opinion. I am very sad that many people's first experience with Evita was this unintelligable movie version. Now people are praising Madonna's soundtrack and berating this one. How sad that is. How can people say such cruel things about Patti LuPone? It was her greatest and most physically/vocally/emotionally demanding accomplishment, and she overcame those obstacles to much praise by winning a Tony award. Any actress who has performed this role on stage within a 2 hour time limit (as opposed to stopping and starting as is the case with movies) will tell you how difficult a role it is. The music is demanding but it pays off. The impressive score has always been negelcted until the movie came out, and all Lloyd Webber did was masacre his own score (maybe he knew that there were at least 7 other actresses who were more qualified to play the part and he just said f**k it when Madonna came into the picture). The original musical won 7 Tony awards, so obviously it couldn't be that bad and blasted Patti LuPone off into stardom. Evita is the quintissential powerful female role in the theater, paying mind yet to Gypsy, Hello Dolly et al, and Patti LuPone did alright for herself. The merging of her powerful voice to this driving, pulsating score is Broadway heaven. Then we have the Madonna treatment, which brings to mind when Lucy shat all over the silver screen in the film adaptation of "Mame". As was the case with Lucy, every song is s l o w e d down for Madonna so she can catch her breath, fake some more vibratto and ar-ti-cu-late every single consanant and vowel (listen to her prounciation of "Machiavelle me" and then listen to the way Patti drills her way through Rainbow High). Listening to Patti LuPone, Elaine Paige or Julie Covington sing the score of Evita sends chills down my spine whereas listening to Madonna giving her "best effort" send chills up my spine, out my mouth and into the commode. Insetad of adding the song "You Must Love Me", the should have added a song for her called "I'm Getting My Act Together and Flushing it Down the Toilet". Really people, it's a shame if you think this is a wonderful rendition of the ALW score. I would love to read the 4 page letter that Madonna wrote to Alan Parker about wanting this role. I should write a 40 page letter to Alan Parker full of death threats for making this movie. It doesn't even work in a film version. Anyone who has seen the stage production knows how Brechtian the staging is and that it was written exclusively for the stage. It doesn't work as a movie version. Especially when you put a washed up falling pop quasi-icon in the title role and then go around campaigning that she oughta win an Oscar. Ha ha. She only won a Golden Globe. There's a testimant of her acting abilities right there. I encourage everyone to give the REAL Evita a chance and don't judge it by the basterdized movie version...if you do prefer the soundtrack vehemently to the OBC, I pity you.
