reviewText:
(I know many people will say they do not find this review helpful, because most people say that when they disagree with the opinion expressed in the review, but...)
I will admit that I am not particularly a Sarah Brightman fan.  I do like her album "Dive," and "Eden" can be appreciated as background music.  With these things in mind, I thought I'd check out her new CD.  While I did not have any great expectations for this disc, even my lowest expectations were not met.  As a previous reviewer said, Ms. Brightman spends too much time at the top of her range (actually, I think she is over the top of her range) and consequently sounds like an uncomfortable (and possibly tone-deaf) imitator of the fabulous Kate Bush and produces a stream of unpleasant sounds.
There is also one thing about this disc that I find utterly infuriating.  What possibly could be the point of translating FOR AN ENGLISH-SPEAKING SINGER (and primarily an English-speaking audience) an aria from a CZECH OPERA into ITALIAN!  I'm referring to the title track, which could sensibly be translated into English or sung in its original language and remain in keeping with the theme of the disc.  Translating it to English and giving the CD the aria's familiar name "Song to the Moon" or "O Silver Moon" would not have affected the theme of the disc.  I know this quibble might strike some as petty but, to my mind, the choice of an irrelevant language seems to indicate that it was chosen merely to enable to disc to have a "foreign" title or merely to sound tonier, and that makes the whole venture seem extremely affected and pretentious.
I do hope though that this disc introduces a whole new population to the gorgeous melody of the title track and that people a proper performance of the aria.  For a gorgeous and moving performance -- and one that demonstrates that opera certainly does not have to be screechy -- check out Renee Fleming's "Signatures" disc.  (An excerpt of the aria can be heard on amazon.com -- click on track 4.)  It is a stunner (as are Miss Fleming and virtually all of her recordings) and may turn people on to a whole new world of musical pleasure.  Check it out.

reviewText:
I was excited to receive this CD as a gift because the original Vince Guaraldi soundtrack has been one of my favorite Christmas CD's for years.  Given the lineup of artists on this one, I figured it was a can't-miss.  Well, with a few exceptions they miss about as badly as is possible, particularly the vocalists. I totally agree with the reviewer above who thought Chaka Khan sounded drunk--on top of a dirge-like tempo she's nowhere near the key, and her vocalese sounds like she's going to crash down off the barstool at any moment.  Toni Braxton, there are some songs for which breathy/sexy is inappropriate, and you sure found one of them in "It's the most Wonderful Time of Year" (which, though a perfectly fine Christmas song, has no connection with Charlie Brown Christmas or Vince Guaraldi).  Even Brian McKnight, usually the king of smooth, delivers an absolutely funereal version of "Christmas Time is Here".

Even the instrumentals don't get off unscathed:  "Red Baron", by the Rippingtons, is a masterpiece of bland everything-sounds-the-same smooth jazz and also has nothing to do with Charlie Brown Christmas (or Christmas at all, for that matter), and the opening track, "Christmas is Coming" by David Benoit sounds like the opening to a Christmas musical comedy.
There are a couple of bright spots:  Norman Brown, always tasteful and creative, does a good job with "Skating", and the work of Gerald Albright, Dave Koz and Rick Braun is at least competent.
The main problem here is that nothing contained in this set improves on, or even approaches the original (assuming it has someting to do with the original in the first place, which isn't always the case), leading to the unanswerable question of "What's the point?"

reviewText:
There are few artists in the music industry that have been the subject of such intense hype - in this respect, Beyonce is in a class all by herself.  Her record label, along with mass media outlets, made Destiny's Child seem like the second coming from the moment their debut album was released - apparently the listening public bought into this but I personally didn't hear anything from them that hadn't already been done by 702, SWV, and more importantly, Diana Ross & The Supremes.
This is the debut solo release from Beyonce Knowles, diva extraordinaire, and it hasn't even come close to justifying all the hype that has surrounded its release.  The first single "Crazy In Love" drives a tired horn sample into the ground (whatever happened to using live instrumentation?) juxtaposed with an irritating, repetitive chorus that Beyonce only talks her way through - Jay-Z might state that it's "history in the making" but I don't buy it for a second.  Then we have "Naughty Girl", which has some dopey cringe-inducing lyrics and a shameless cop of Donna Summer's "Love To Love You Baby".  Then, in the track that follows, "Baby Boy", we get more uninspired lyrics - Beyonce yearns for the child that she sees in her dreams and thinks about all the time over a lifeless pseudo-sitar hook (popularized by Missy Elliott - does Beyonce have any original ideas in her head?).  After this, the album falls into slow jams with comatose arrangements and all the passion and energy of a snail, not to mention overwrought vocals from Beyonce (doesn't anyone know the meaning of restraint these days?).  Maybe I was expecting too much, but all the publicity that this album received set me up for something greater than what I heard.
In summary: A disappointing debut from the ubiquitous Beyonce.  She does have talent, but isn't applying it correctly - she needs to utilize better control over her voice and while her attempts at songwriting are admirable, they're also weak ... perhaps she should turn to outside songwriters for stronger material.  There's better stuff out there - the hype for this album turned out to be hollow.

reviewText:
Mullova used to be one of my favorite young violinists, worthy follower of her teacher, the great Leonid Kogan. Until this mediocre, sickly pale recording, almost completely lacking in energy, originality and drive.

When I first listened to the Stravinsky, it wasn't in full - I only listened to a fragment of the second movement, and was impressed by its playfulness. Since then I have tried and tried to like the rest of it, to make that first impression a self-fulfilling prophecy, but no, no matter how hard I tried the slow tempos - like an average of that of the Scre - that barely challenge the soloist (the allusion is to the conveyor-belt people movers in airports), and add to the sluggishness and lack of imagination of the piece's theme development, bore me to a degree comparable only to that achieved by purely atonal music. Whatever child-like magic the piece achieves in few and far in between fragments is lost amid the indolent drive and morose development.

And here comes Mullova and Salonen to add to the overall drabness and artitistico-ideological grayness with an interpretation so weak, so utterly lacking in passion and desire to experiment, that the performance has the singular merit of neither putting me to sleep (the sheer ugliness of its banality prevents that) or keeping my ears pricked up with curiosity and a desire for more. The talent and energy I had noticed in Mullova's interpretation of the Tchaikovsky (also with Salonen) is nowhere present here - instead the violin turns into a mosquito in the upper registers, where lies, in my not too humble opinion, one of the basic tests of violin virtuosity.  That Mullova can't perform up to par even with steamroller tempos is one hell of a disappointment, the size of a weather ballon being pricked with heavy AA fire.

When the time came for the Bartk, my hopes were high - Bartk is not as a chilly a modernist as the overrated Stravinsky, presiding minence gris of American music for God knows how many decades (that is, even after death), hanging like a gray winter day over music schools, newspapers and concert halls. But it was as chilly as the Stravinsky, with as little drive and passion, tempo modulation resembling the droning push of a water mill, and challenges to the virtuoso that barely surpass those expected of a concertmaster in Strauss' Ein Heldeleben. And the un-dynamic duo that flattened the already crumpled Stravinsky do the same with this work, with the same passion for turning music into flavorless porridge.

So Hahn, Shaham, Salerno-Sonenberg, Chang - say hello to your new comrade, youngish in the business, but already performing as if 5 years past retirement! Should Mullova put her bow down like a replica samurai sword on a horizontal stand, to perform a merely visual aesthetical purpose; lend her million dollar violin to the next generation, and dedicate the rest of her life to the raising of her family and silent contemplation of her past achievements? I really hope not - instead, that circumstance (health, worries) overwhelmed her and hurt her playing in this recording. Salonen's pallid conducting can't be blamed for her poor sound production, as I have listened to Mullova's own mentor Kogan play the Tchaikovsky as well as usual with an unsurprisingly inept, bureaucratic French orchestra under a maestro that gave the whole work something like a tempo buffo or worse - ubriaco.

reviewText:
All you fan boys, listen up!  You have got to be kidding me...you call this metal???  This ain't even music, let alone metal.
As a long time fan of heavy metal since the mid-to-late 1980s, I have followed heavy metal through-out its development (or as we like to call it now...progression) and this [The Darkness] ain't it.  In fact, this sounds like acid punk rock without the acid.  I started out with the classical metal groups like Anthrax, Metallica, Megadeth, Testament, and Slayer back in the day.  I then progressed towards groups like Fear Factory, Type O Negative, White Zombie, etc.  Then recently, I found Godsmack and the like.  But there's some underground metal that still exists and still rocks your head off.  It's called power metal or perhaps progressive metal.  A good majority of it comes from Europe, namely the Scandinavian countries, but a few are still American like Iced Earth.
I've recently heard about Darkness from my cousin who talked about their new video.  Stumbled across their video listing on Yahoo, but technical difficulties prevented me from viewing it.  So I came to Amazon here to check them out.  All I can say is thank God for Amazon preview clips.  This music is absolutely horrible.
So to praise this band, The Darkness, would be like praising the French for their participation in Operation Iraqi Freedom.  Better to have a Iraqi Fedayeen in front of me, than a Darkness CD behind me.

reviewText:
I am very disappointed with this effort and now don't understand what the band is trying to accomplish. This album is not radio friendly and there is not one dance-able track. The New Pornographers experienced broad success on previous works with tracks like "Laws Have Changed", "Your Daddy Don't Know" and "All for Swinging You Around". Each of the tunes were smart, strong, danceable pop tunes. Instead of mining that vein of success, they have in this outing, rejected the successful danceable pop style that was previously established. Each of their previous hits also featured an identifiable, powerful female front - Neko Case. Fans of the previous popular singles will be disappointed with Twin Cinema especially as Neko hardly gets a turn at the microphone.

This assemblage of talent is capable of better. I suspect that there is a battle for the microphone/fronting role. I cannot understand why the group would choose to mute the strong female vocalist who has brought them all of their broader success by limiting her role to singing backup and fronting only handful of tracks.

There is one bright spot, track 4 - The Bleeding Heart Show, is a standout for its eventual innovative wall of sound and overlaying harmonies.  The first minute or so seems tacked on with an out of style, weak male vocal introduction to some great fresh music. As with several of the other tracks it seems they wrote some good hooks and simply filled in the rest of the song. The last three minutes of this tune is smart, foot tapping, lets get out of our chair and dance song, that you want to listen to over and over again -that doesn't fit with the dramatic intro.  Coincidently, its the only time that the female front actually opens up her voice to sing with some power. Flashes of brilliance such as this are very frustrating in the Indie genre - I really think that NP could benefit in collaborating with a  successful veteran producer and defining their style/front person. Frankly, isn't pop that you can't dance to and.. "have to listen to a few times to understand "...an oxymoron?

Update 3/2007 - It really seems that this bands strenghth is writing some really great hooks - it's filling in between them that is the problem. Call Rungren.

reviewText:
If you thought I was wrong comparing these goth madonnas to Depeche Mode the last time around, the comparisons are even more obvious and the territory more redundant on "Forever." It's about as dark as Mickey Mouse in a wizard skirt. Halfway through "Written in Blood," I could swear somebody chimes in with the Inspector Gadget theme. But hey, an apologist might say, their music might be a tad simplistic but I just adore them for their deep, introspective lyrics.

OK, let's take a listen: guy meets girl; guy realizes girl is eating him alive from the inside; guy realizes this is inevitable because we are all just selfish, vacuous beasts; guy ultimately realizes he is stuck with said succubus until the end of time. So it's definitely goth. I mean, no wonder so many chicks are into the goth scene: fag hags who latch onto overly emotional wallflowers when seeking out life partners so they can wrap the twerps around their mealy fingers. But really, there's no Billy Bragg -- or even dimbulb Jackson Browne for that matter -- at work in these words. I think "Melrose Place" and other shows have sufficiently covered these boy-meets-girl themes.

By the time "She Will Always Be a Broken Girl" comes withering out of the speakers, it sounds like I'm listening to a band at the end of its tether, completely immersed in some self-destructive form of electronic masturbation. Sadly, after "This is the End," there are still five more songs to go. And boy, do they ever trounce on this dead horse. It's a mockery of a mockery. A ball of energy imploding. Innards spilling out at a car wreck. Turn away. Walk away.

reviewText:
I am familiar with the original cast, the film cast (not sung by Natalie Wood but by Marnie Nixon), the Deutsche Grammophon recording of Kiri Te Kanawa and Carreras and some other productions but I must say that even by listening to the samples presented in Amazon's "listen to samples" option, THIS IS A BAD recording of the Bernstein classic.  One has to understand that this is a groundbreaking piece of musical -- reasons: it employed the unpredictable musical tones, dynamics and tempo of Bernstein, heard in his compositions of "American" music but incorporated in musical theater -- itself an American created art form; second, being a musical, it still calls for drama and therefore, third, the audience should demand to hear something emotionally driven but fresh.  We want the singers NOT just to sing but ACT!!!  So far, this is the driest, most unsatisfying and sorriest interpretation of Bernstein's great innovative work.

Tony.  Being an a second generation American (I presume that it was his parents who were born in Poland...) still should sound American.  If not, Polish perhaps?  But not Italian.  But that is minor...Carreras was Spanish...  But if one listens to Carreras in the 1984 recording, he may not sound right with his accent, but one can appreciate the acting still though dry it may be.  Maestro Bernstein DRILLED him in singing his lines during the recording of the DG West Side Story.  I think we still have to see the tenor of this recording be drilled by Bernstein (unfortunate that he has passed away) or by someone similar just to know the complexities of the role of Tony.  It has to have passion and drama manifested in the syncopation of the notes.  Carreras has difficulty in noting the timing of "Something's Coming", this one has probably sung it with timing but definitely without the enthusiasm of the piece.  In other words, make be believe that SOMETHING is COMING.

Maria.  Dry as a desert.  One is not singing a lullaby which this one sounds like what she is doing.  Rather -- sing us your sweetness with a yearning to break free from family traditions and to be ready to just dedicate yourself to LOVE your man.  She sounds like she's singing a light ballad to make one go to sleep.  Her voice is pretty but not what I expect or even want for the work.

Orchestra -- no excitement.  Sounds like a metronome -- one two three four, one two three four...despite the calls for syncopation.

Listen to the DG version for the Orchestration because it was DEMANDED by Bernstein.  Listen to the Original Cast for Tony (sung by the late Larry Kert -- a fine voice crystal clear....).  Listen to Rita Moreno for her vicious portrayal of Anita and Marnie Nixon as Maria (it was not sung by Natalie Wood although she was tried but did not have the right vocal range and strength) in the film version.

There is no single great recording of West Side Story and each past recording as its own flaws.  One thing is certain: this is not great at all.

...NOW FOR AN EPILOGUE... for the comment that states that I was basing my review on the "listen to samples" section of Amazon, I was able to buy the CD finally after being offered on a 75% reduction of the original price.  I still have not made any changes on my opinion not as a matter of pride, rather, it only confirmed what I have always thought.  The Orchestra was heavy and treats the musical with so much drama, it drags...a Mahler interpretation of the Jazz American work.  The Riff character does not do jazz syncopation very well (lacking in lilt) just as the Tony character; although both have good voices.  They both have potential.  I do agree with the accent of Tony -- reminds me of the Te Kanawa-Carreras-Bernstein recording -- although I think it is a minor setback compared to its lack of anticipation inherent in portrayal of Tony (Somethings Coming...).  It needs lightness where the lightness is due and drama when it is called for.

But the biggest disappointment is STILL Maria.  She (conversely) lacks the accent, cannot act and has no power.  Although I do not expect bleating voices and certainly no Celine Dion do I want, it should have the capacity to just stem from a high note with power and drama (e.g.: "Oh no Anita no!!... from 'A Boy Like That').  She basically sang it like the lullaby that I described in my review...

So...probably at most a 1-1/2 star but I still stick to my 1 star rating.  I guess my CD will just be another my collection of thousands...
label: negative

Here is a review of the songs:
1. Push Play - Truth starts off on a mediocre note; voice is a little out of tune, cliche right off the bat, etc. Push next track here. 6/10
2. Addictive feat. Rakim - A very unusual and somewhat annoying song. And to think that Truth was offered an opera scholarship? 3/10

8. Not Really Lookin' - Hot beat, gonna give it to her, this is probably the best song on the CD. 7.5/10

I moderately enjoyed Chesney's 2004 release When the Sun Goes Down. I found his post-adolescent desires to return to an adolescent past charming. I liked the father-daughter song. I liked the song where Chesney's so drunk he can't keep his metaphors straight. I even liked the Jimmy Buffett imitation on the title track.

But now Chesney, who owns a home in the U.S. Virgin Islands, believes he IS Jimmy Buffett, or Buffett's heir to the pirate throne. Be As You Are marks the first CD where Chesney writes or co-writes all the songs, but rather than giving listeners years' worth of stored country goodies, Chesney instead delivers an island escape concept record, and all the stale images come rolling out: pia coladas, mangos, hammocks, straw hats, white sails, red sunsets, pirates, escaping the rat race back stateside, and so on. The most adventurous Chesney gets are two dope smoking references and an awkward sexual pun involving eating his woman's key lime pie.

My favorite dumb lyrics:

  He walked in with a salty sway
  Lookin' like Blackbeard in his day  ("Soul of a Sailor")

  Maybe I could've been a pirate
  Maybe in my next life that's what I'll be  ("French Kissing  Life")

And the songs? They're all painfully sluggish, as if Chesney could only muster the energy to grab his guitar after a long nude nap on the sand.

reviewText: Peter Murphy, solo, is a progenitor of a particularly heady brand of Goth cheese.  Sickly thin, with a piercing stare and birdlike movements, he's a mesmerizing live performer even though he comes across as a cut-rate Bowie.  Compelling as he is, he has a three note range (when he wants a bit of drama he hits his high end and, well, screams) and a ponderously opaque song catalogue.  There's no meaning; just ambient surface and atmosphere.  When his band is rocking the New Age, though, this rarely matters, which is why aLive Just for Love is such a disappointment.  These stripped-down, Unplugged versions of his songs need all the accoutrements they can get.  Many of these tunes are mid-tempo beauties in their studio versions - "Indigo Eyes", "Marlene Dietrich's Favourite Poem" - where they are densely layered with guitars and viola, percussion and keyboards - but they need their surface density to breathe.  Here, they're skimpy, and expose Murphy's vocal shortcomings more than they should.

reviewText:
Let me preface this by saying that I *ABSOLUTELY LOVE* the authentic Pink Floyd.  They were the first band I ever connected to, my first concert, and my first *musical* obsession.  In middle school I saw "The Wall" over one-hundred times, and except for my tendencies towards primal screaming, ripping my fingernails out, shaving my eyebrows and chest, leading a maniacal facist skinhead goon squad and then ending up reading weird poetry in a toilet stall in the bathroom of a hockey stadium, I'm no worse for the wear!

Anyway, I remember hearing the first strains of "Keep Talking" the day it was released as I stood out in the cold winter air, waiting in line to purchase tickets for their '94 concert tour (I was successful).  My feet were numb (and not comfortably!).  I didn't think the song was that great; more like a cheap knock off, not even of classic PF, but perhaps AMLoR-era PF.  A loyal fan and consumer, I bought "The Division Bell."  Try as I might, I simply couldn't bring myself to accept this music.  Last night I decided to give it another shot, start to finish.  This experience only confirmed one thing: this is their very worst album.  Gilmour and his friends are really sub-par lyricists, and the lyrics are obviously meant to ape the themes found in Waters-era recordings.  Do you think David Gilmour was really all that concerned about talking and intimacy, or he and the boys needed an excuse to tour and make bajillions of dollars again (I paid thirty-five bucks in 1994!)?  The very lowest point is the horrible, horrible, 'ORRIBLE piece by Richard Wright.  The guy is among the most boring singers I've ever heard, and I haven't heard lyrics that awful and trite since the last time I heard Lenny Kravitz's "Dragonfly," which thankfully has not been for a long time.  There are some nice moments (and I do mean moments, like two or three-second snippets) here and there, but all in all, Gilmour's playing is nowhere near as ferocious as it was on WYWH, Animals, or even Momentary Lapse of Reason stand-out tracks like "Yet Another Movie" and "Sorrow" (one his best moments), and his voice isn't as honey-sweet and pure as it used to be.  Then there are all the obligatory Floydisms: sax, female singers, distant voices from conversations or movies and the like.  Couldn't they have done something original?  I've read that upon hearing "A Momentary Lapse of Reason" Roger Waters called it something like "a clever, quite facile forgery," and I agree.  Even that recording used some Floydians cliches just to maintain an "authentic"  atmosphere, but at least that album wasn't awful through and through.  "The Division Bell," like "Star Wars, Episode One," is a disappointing example of totally formulaic drivel.  If you're a Floyd fan and this CD gives you some sort of deep satisfaction, then you must be a total lunkhead, because in even the most objective sense this album absolutely reeks.

reviewText:
Amazon has reviews of the various editions of "West Coast Seattle Boy" lumped together.  This review pertains to the one CD/DVD version.  You can get a one CD version without the DVD.

The audio CD consists of tracks culled from the box set.  Having heard these, I'm glad I didn't have to sit through all of it.  If you thought "Valleys Of Neptune" was crap, wait until you hear this.  The alternate takes of already issued material are pointless.  The remaining tracks are demos worth one spin.  Hendrix would never have agreed to its release during his lifetime.

Experience Hendrix could release this garbage for the next 10 years, and will as long as it sells.  Value is subjective, of course--if Hendrix was recorded belching after downing a shot, some fans would consider it a lost treasure.

The DVD was OK, but didn't reveal much about Hendrix the person (he did have parents and siblings) as opposed to Hendrix the stage act (he wanted to upstage Elvis and got dropped from the Monkees tour--so what?).  And at the end there's the announcement that Hendrix was dead, and some shots of his casket and people arriving at the cemetary.  No more groupies or royalty checks for Jimi.

Why did someone so massively talented live life in a stupor?  So loaded that he choked to death on his own vomit while unconscious.  Didn't anyone tell him he wasn't Superman?  Maybe it would have been better for Jimi if he was Jimmy--maybe he got too deep into his own BS.  We make heroes of people like Jimi, but he was just a human being.

It would be absurd to place Jimi Hendrix on the same level with Charlie Parker, but they shared the same self-destructive tendency.  On some level they both must have known they were pushing their bodies to the limit--and when you hit the limit, you're not around to see it happen.

Unless it's a live set, this is the last Experience Hendrix release I'll buy.  I'd give "West Coast Seattle Boy" ZERO stars if I could.

reviewText:
First, this is N*O*T a review about the music or performances.  Mike was a classic who could mesmerize, and I assume you are already a fan.

Over the last 10 to 15 years there has been an arms race in the world of pop/rock to create the loudest cds possible.  The businessmen want to have music that sounds louder then the competition when it first starts playing to get the listeners attention.  They do this by increasing the average (rms) volume to be as close to possible to the maximum (peak) volume.  In the old days (like 1992), music was mastered so that it retained much of it's dynamic range, which is the difference between the loudest and the quietest parts.  A drum hit would be twice (or more) as loud as the surrounding music, when a singer (like Cobain) would scream his voice would rise above the music and shake the listener, crescendos would be louder then the soft parts, and overall the music communicated emotions fantastically.  It's like with speech, if you listen to someone who talks in a single volume, you get bored and no emotion is transmitted.  So what this arms race for loudness does is it reduces the amount of dynamic range and makes all the sounds the same volume; the part of the song that is whispered becomes as loud as the crescendo with screaming.  This has three major effects.  First, it drains the potency and emotion out of music.  Second, it causes ear fatigue.  When you turn the music up a bit to listen to it, your ears will become tired and you'll want to change the music or turn it down or stop listening.  Thats why when you put on some MJ disks made in the 80's or early 90's, you can listen longer, you get more involved, and you can listen louder.  If Invincible leaves you cold, this might be the reason.  And thridly, it causes distortion and clipping, which prior to the loudness war were absolute no-no's in mastering/mixing/recording.  So, the cd portion of this set is mastered very loud, with little in the way of dynamics.  It is done cynically and without regard to sound quality.  If you want to hear the best sounding MJ, get the disks made pre-1998.  Today the word 'remaster' almost always means inferior super loud disks with no dynamic range.  I would avoid buying anything that says 'remastered'.

If you want more info on this depressing trend, look up 'loudness war' on wikipedia, or google 'pleasurizemusic' and/or 'turnmeup'.

Oh, and the video bit doesn't suffer from this problem as DVD's have standards that prevent this abuse from occurring.  That's why when you watch the concert, your ears don't become tired and the music is more involving.

reviewText: I am a major fan of the Terry Kath era of Chicago. I saw Chicago live on two separate nights at Chicago Stadium in the summer of 1975, which was sold out for most of the week with the Beach Boys. To get swiftly to the point, of all of the Chicago 'live' albums, this is one of the most competently performed, but also by far the worst recordings. You don't have to be an audiophile to notice that the bass drones on buried in mud, Kath's guitar is all but inaudible, his vocals are all but inaudible, and that even 'sound board' recordings of other bands sound far superior. The shame of it is that what little you can hear is competently and enthusiastically performed. If the original tape was horrible, then release this inexpensively with apologies in advance for the atrocious sound. But to release this with a deluxe packaging effort for nearly $40........ Do yourself a favor. If you absolutely LOVE early Chicago and would like a copy of what they sounded like live, DO NOT buy this. I've never been as disappointed with a Chicago album. I bought this thinking people had exaggerated the poor sound quality. If anything, the critics were generous!!!

reviewText:
This new "remastering" of the classic Busch Quartet's late Beethoven is more like a savage butchering.  In their effort to completely remove the inherent noise of the original 78's, EMI has also removed the entire upper frequency range.  A significant portion of the original sound is missing.

Who exactly is EMI targeting with this type of reissue?  Anyone seriously interested in old recordings knows about the noise inherent in old recording techniques.  And absolutely everyone else can tell that these CDs just sound awful.

Luckily, private collectors still hoard their old 78s and companies like Pearl (and others) treat original recordings with respect.

This is not the only recent EMI reissue to sound like this.  Tureck's "Goldberg" Variations from 1957 has been given the same treatment.  Is this how EMI plans to present and preserve their essential recorded legacy?
label: negative

reviewText: What amuses me about this chick is that she is extremely similar to the supposed manufactured musical products she is constantly dissing (both in her music and in the liner notes of her CD). At moments like that, Miss Ford just sounds like a ranting toddler who is upset that the other kids are getting more attention than her. She's desperately trying to prove her realness but just ends up sounding incredibly jealous of those she's complaining about. And her sugarcoated pop isn't any more deserving of the charts than any other teen queen out there, despite what she seems to think-she breaks absolutely no new ground, and honestly these tracks aren't nearly as infectious as those produced by Aguilera or Spears. Like Britney and Hilary, her vocals are subpar and incapable of hitting higher notes. And complaining about fame she hasn't even received yet? If this girl's mediocre sound doesn't turn you off, her unnecessary cockiness and foolish hypocrisy will.

reviewText:
This review is for the Son House double CD set entitled "Clarksdale Moan."  The performances are great throughout, that is a given... therefore I will focus only on sound quality.

Disc one is just OK in terms of sound quality.  Does nothing to improve on past efforts to present this 1940-41 material.  And I did note that "Jinx Blues" sounded better on the Biograph release of this material (BCD 118).  The Biograph CD in general was slightly clearer sounding with slightly less distortion throughout... even so, this "Clarksdale Moan" disc 1 is tolerable and listenable if you are not particular. Obviously if you already have this material there is no reason to get it here again and you would certainly be better off with the Biograph release instead of this one.

Disc two is the 1930s material.  Unlike the first disc, here they have used HEAVY noise reduction.  They just don't get it.  Taking out ALL the noise means you end up with a muffled boxed-in sound without any air whatsoever.  No highs - zero.  This is 2014 and they still have not learned that this is not the way to handle this material.  No excuses.  This disc was mastered the same heavy-handed way Columbia and other huge commercial labels released this sort of stuff 30 years ago... in recent years even Columbia has retreated from that type of heavy-handed approach.  Even so, Columbia still does do not do a good job with archival material - Bob Dylan's recent Witmark Demos release is a case in point.  The constant re-mastering of the Robert Johnson material (3 or 4 times now!) is yet another red flag.  See my reviews on both of those releases.

The packaging and booklet and information is fine.  Actually a nice package.  And yes, the 2005 discoveries of "Clarksdale Moan" and the B side of that disc are here.  Nice to have that, but probably the only legitimate reason to own this set.

In case you are wondering, an excellent presentation of the Son House 1930 material is on an instructional guitar DVD taught by Tom Feldmann.  He covers 15 Son House songs and the DVD has a bonus section with the original 1930s material (including "Clarksdale Moan") - those songs sound great on that DVD!  The hiss is left in, but it is tastefully and skillfully done - not annoying at all.  Those versions easily surpass the crappy "Clarksdale" CD being reviewed here.  Not just better - A LOT BETTER.  On "My Black Mama", for example, you can clearly hear the sharp tone and sweetness of Son's slide on the e-string - nice!  This nuance is totally lost on the crappy remastering on the "Clarksdale Moan" disc - it just is muffled out.  I plan to convert the DVD format for those songs to CD for listening in the car.... and then I'll probably drop disc two of the "Clarksdale Moan" CD in the garbage bin... where it belongs.

The Yazoo CD "Masters of the Delta Blues: Friends of Charlie Patton" is another good place to go to for much of the Son House 1930 material... and you get other artists as well on that disc.  With that release you get all the music with the highs and the hiss is left in in a tastefully way without destroying the music.  Way superior to the "Clarksville Moan" CD being reviewed here.  Much better.

I see only two negative comments for my review... probably left here by the dunderheads who produced this disc...
label: negative

reviewText:
Making records is business, like making washing powder. I have noticed one vendor claiming that "science proved" their washing powder to make whiter sheets than any other. Now I'm being told that hybrid SACD makes the Boston Symphony sound better than it did 75 years ago. Well, well!
But even if it is the case, why should anyone care when the bill of fare is a recording of MUSIC? Many music lovers these days buy mono recordings in search of that elusive "great" performance given by a Furtwangler or Toscanini. So something doesn't add up here, or am I barking up the wrong tree?
I too discovered this recording of the C major symphony in an old attic late in the Fifties; and I still own it. I've kept it all these years as an example of how awfully wrong a conductor can play music with which he's not in tune. I sometimes use it in my classes, and students rarely miss the point. You may have read in one of the other reviews about the disproportion of exposure given to strings and brass. Strangely, the reviewer in question seems not to care much about the strings being pushed so hard that they scarcely sound like stringed instruments. Or that the brass blares out with all the power needed for Tchaikovsky, so that you wonder if the composer was really Schubert. Someone else draws attention to the brisk speeds. Well, yes: an understatement. In my language it translates as total insensivity to the Schubertian melos. What's the meaning of this? Ah, now I remember: Schubert was the man who wrote all those lovely melodies! Well, there are two or twenty in this work too, but you'll have a hard time finding them.
Which also reminds me that Munch doesn't seem to have been aware that the Unfinished Symphony has a very different feel and mood, as well as orchestration. The way he conducts it, it might as well be two more movements of the C major.
I suspect you will read this as a personal reaction to music making which I find utterly unsympathetic. So right. And I have not changed my mind in seven decades. This is because in music history, Schubert is a romantic, indeed one of the arch-romantics; and I expect musicians to treat his music accordingly. Schubert's music has the power to make us happy amid grief, but the musician must allow his heart some leeway. Munch does nothing of the kind. So the effect of this recording on me is the opposite: it makes me unhappy.
Well, you might not care for the sentiments I've just expressed. Then go for it. But bear in mind that even in America, recordings were made at roughly the same time that are more "musical". Bruno Walter's recording with the Columbia Symphony sounds, to my ears, much better, because it is warmer and has a more hall-like ambience. As a reading of the music, it towers head and shoulders above this RCA offering. So you do have choices!

reviewText:
There are a few things wrong with this release besides the music.

 First of all, to advertise it as a 'super band' is a joke because most of the players never even met. Schenker mailed his solos in over the internet after listening to the backing tracks, just like he did on the first one. This to me, signals the coming of the apocalypse. When it reaches the point that musicians now longer even bother to meet each other to record in the same room, for ONE lousy album, all I can say to them is 'screw you'. I wouldn't give a dime to anyone who participates in bogus 'recordings' like this. All I hear when I listen to this is the reality: Schenker sitting alone in his hotel room, playing along to backing tracks. It's ridiculous. I do that all the time, and I certainly don't -and should never- get paid for it.

We all know Schenker is notorious for not keeping anyone in his band for more than one album, but now it's reached the point where he can't be bothered to even meet the musicians once. If you want to be a hermit, that's fine, but don't try to sell your  attitude to the public. I usually buy everything Schenker does, but I will not support mailed in solos, especially when the cd cover shows a picture of all of them supposedly playing together. It's even called 'The endless jam'. Hello? Jamming means to play  together, you know, like on the same stage, being experimental and taking risks, like Gov't mule does every night of the year. That's what a 'jam' band does. To insinuate/advertise this as a 'jam' is despicable beyond comprehension. I will seriously consider vetoing any future projects that are excreted from the Mike Varney factory of 'quick buck' making.

Now, about the music. Why bother re-doing any of these tracks? Not one of them is better than the original, or offers anything substantially different, like a new arrangement that would at least make it interesting to hear it in a new way. I've always loved Davey Pattison as far back as Gamma, but he's wasted here. Listen to him on the new Trower Cd and then you'll know how much this sucks in comparison. And Schenker is just not a blues player. He's covering the wrong kind of songs. 'Layla'? You've got to be kidding. I winced when I heard this. Schenker is great when he follows his own muse, his own style, but he just does not fit these songs. Remember his cover of 'shapes of things' from the first CD? Again, why bother? Gary Moore did the definitive 'metal' version of that song way back in 1983, and Schenker's solo isn't anywhere near as inspiring as Moore's version.

This is for completists only, and for those who support musicians who prefer to 'mail' in their work. It's a fact Schenker is in desperate need of cash these days due to his complete lack of business acumen, lawsuits from psycho ex-wives, groupies, etc. (go to [...] to read the VERY scary truth under 'to my true fans' section)

So, since Schenker is practically bankrupt, can you blame him for jumping at Mike Varney's offer of a couple grand to mail in some solos for this abysmal 'non band' and 'completely unnessary' effort? Shame on Schenker and shame on Varney.

reviewText:
The songwriting (and by that I mean the musical composition, not the lyric-writing) on Kiss Each Other Clean is so incredibly unengaging, bland, and boring!  And this from a man who gave us a master class in songcraft with his first two releases! Not to mention the three EPs!

There is not an interesting or compelling chord change to be found in this entire record, it is pure pop blandness.  And I can't believe I'm writing this about Sam Beam... which makes me afraid that there were Warner Brothers people over his shoulder saying "Keep it light, we've got to reach the masses via Top 40 or Adult Contemporary radio." Or perhaps picking only the dullest songs and leaving the others on the editing-room floor?

If it wasn't them, then Sam is simply out of gas.  Don't know what else to say, but after three full unenjoyable listens I plan on dispatching this CD.  Major major major disappointment.  I understand that we will never again get the amazing, wistful, lo-fi magic he created in his bedroom -- I can handle the layers of production -- it's just that the songs aren't any good now.  It's like he abandoned every interesting guitar chord or chord change in his arsenal.  I don't think there's even a minor chord on this entire CD!  Ah well, guess I'll await the next great folk artist and leave Sam to the masses.  Thanks for the memories, Mr. Beam!

reviewText:
This CD starts out with a British female DJ saying that she will not put up with any of that rock superstar bullshit.  But, that is what this whole CD is.  Old rockstar overdulgence.
Pyschoderelict is another concept project from Pete Townsend.  There are 2 versions of the CD.  There is a "Music Only" CD which contains just the songs.  This CD is only about half music.  The rest is a radio play, with the actors talking over the songs.
I only have this version of Psychoderelict.  There appears to be some great songs here.  But, you can't tell because there are only pieces of the songs, and people are talking over most of what music there is. There is a reason why you can find it used for under a dollar. But, from what I can tell, the songs seem to be some of Townsend's best work.
Psychoderelict is about an aging rock superstar who brings a young female singer under his wing.  She starts cheating on him and stabs him in the back. There is some humor here.  Townsend does make fun of aging rockstars.  And, he shows the downfall of his young female singer by having her sing a Britteny Spears type song.
This is part biography, but also appears to be part of Townsend's fantasy (taking a young singer under his wing, molding her into a star and becoming her lover).  Townsend was recently arrested for having kiddie porn.  He said he was researching a project.  I hate to think what his next fantasy is.

reviewText:
Some music critic, I think Stephen Thompson is his name, came on NPR Radio and plugged this CD.  So I bought this and their other CD.  So now I need to confess to what is probably a very cynical understanding  and I need to realize something and take it to heart, and that is probably that in exchange for good interviews Music Critics probably get recognition and access friends in the Business.  Or music critics can be really tone-deft and beat-less no talent idiots, or they would have been musicians themselves.  Or Stephen Thompson was some lonely desperate nerd and those two young girls aren't so prudish as they sound on their CDs.  Or Stephen Thompson wanted to be gallant, and help discover these poor needy girls.  Or he had the delusional ambition  to find the next Joni Mitchell or something as though it is a matter of luck or percentages, and not a matter of whether or not these stiff and stodgy girls had any real talent as singers, musicians and entertainers.  Or maybe it has come to the point  where Music Critics now have to be investigated like the Radio Stations in the 50s were investigated for payola  accepting gifts and money for promoting records.  Yes, so many possibilities, but something needs to account for why the worst CDs I have heard in a long time have been plugged on a radio franchise, NPR, that is heard around the World.  It is so out of place that one cant help but to suspect unethical interests were somehow at play.  After all, there are Record Companies out there with huge resources, with the best Agents, Producers and Engineers and Editors, in cities where Talented Musicians flock because of their rich music culture, and these Record Companies have thousands of Acts to choose from, and they only sign the Best.  But, somehow, that NPR Reviewer, Stephen Thompson I think his name is, he picks an Act that was recorded by some unrecognizable Record Company (honestly, the print on the CD was so small I could not distinguish the name of the Record Company) in Bloomington, Indiana  which is too North for Country Music, and not on either the Left or the Right Coasts where cool Rock and Pop resides and not even near Chicago.  My guess is that these CDs were Vanity CDs  that the girls weren't signed by the Record Company, but that they walked through the door themselves with small bag of money, and out came these budget basement CDs, that is, produced very cheaply.  It doesnt seem quite fair, does it, that the Consumer has to pay full price for a CD that was produced for a fraction of a penny on the Dollar that a Quality Record would be produced for?  And all while NPR Music Critic Establishment was clamoring for us to buy buy buy it.  It all feels like a big rip-off, and I am sure that NPR will never ever get another pledge from me.

So, what is wrong with these CDs anyway.  Well, every song sounds the same.  Same instrumentation on every song.  Heck, it even sounds like all the Control Board and Effects setting never budged.  The CD covers give credit for Drums and Percussion, but I don't hear anything.  After all, the songs are so flat and without any lilt or rhythm , that I would believe that a drummer would have a difficult time trying to figure out exactly what to drum to.  It is obvious that there was not enough Budget available for the Producer to bring in Arrangers and Song Writing Consultants, to help punch up the dreary  and shapeless material that the girls walked through the door with.  So whatever the drummer did try, simply didn't work, and the Engineer earned his money by editing it out.  Oh, and I suppose the girls insisted on playing themselves  one on piano and the other on guitar.  Really, was the Budget so constrained that they could not get Real Musicians to play.  It really doesnt sound like these girls have been musicians for very long.  No smoothness or elegance, but just careful plodding along, making sure they were hitting the right basic chords  not very inspiring no flights of talent to sweep us away, but the impression we are standing outside the door of a Music Lesson in progress.  Oh, wait, the Production Team did reach out and hire a real good Cello Player, Shannon Heyden the only listenable music on both CD is Shannon Heydons Cello rising and falling with a sublimity that she must have brought to the game herself, because none of the other musical parts show  any such inspiration in their arrangement.  Everyone else plodded just behind the just learning how to play playing of the two beginner girls.
The Critic raves about the girls exquisite singing.  Well, how would anybody know?  In both CDs the singing is slid back behind a veritable fog bank of reverb and echo effects maybe some chorus to fatten up their thin and shrill voices if they are thin and shrill, but buried in so much and many Effects, who knows what they actually sound like.  But if so much work went into augmenting and disguising their voices, then isn't it highly probable that if they sang into a Clean Channel that it would sound very much as though their voices needed a lot of work.  Well, that should be nothing a discerning Music Critic should be raving about.  Oh, even a lot of the instrumentation was fogged over with effects as though the band is playing a quarter mile away between glass office buildings with sound bouncing in and about from everywhere.  It reminds me of those old Enya Records from the 90s  it was supposed to be some sort of a New Age sound, but really it was just twisting up the effects knobs  a lot of echo, reverb, chorus, tone stretch and overlap all to take off any natural edge and make everything sound , well, not warm and fuzzy, but round and fuzzy.  Maybe the girls were big Enya fans and thought that sounded neat.  Or the Production Team figured that the Enya Formula was their only chance to find a willing audience for this unique material.  You see, the girls aren't County, they aren't Rock, they're too dull  and un-catchy to be Pop, and too plain and basic to be Jazz, and so the Production Team turned up the  water-color and pastel Blur and let the Effects Fog roll in and the girls could be the next New Age Nebula.
But, back to the singing.  We also hear from the critic about the wonderful close harmonies.  Well, yes, there are close harmonies, but why are there never any far harmonies.  It always seems the same interval.  It is as though the two sisters started practicing singing together, and learned just one harmonic interval, and froze in place, never ever learning anything more, and decided that that would be their style and they would stick to it for the rest of their lives.  There is no back ground singing, no counterpoint, no framing, no weaving, no syncopation, no duets.  Nothing but their One Trick Pony  the Close Harmony.  One girl simply shadows the other girl exactly.  They both rise together.  They both fall together, keeping the same tonal interval.  It gets tedious very quickly.  It is especially bad that in both CDs there is not a single catchy musical phrase.. nothing to remember nothing to tap ones foot to.  You definitely will not have to worry about whistling while you work after sitting through either one of these girls CDs.

And there is a huge stylistic problem one concerning a very reasonable and practical musical convention.  You see, the lyrics and the singing squeeze out any opportunity for the Instrumentation to provide any Contrast, Framing or Texture.  The girls never seem to pause they never shut up!  They could have had the best studio musicians in the World, but the girls droning was endless and uninterrupted  the musicians would never have stood a chance.  It is as though these girls have never heard a song before, where  the Singer sings, then the instruments play.  It isn't rocket science!  Somebody needs to buy those girls a radio or something.

reviewText:
With this sophomore effort that falls monstrously short, Velvet Revolver has "fallen to pieces"...they've gone "Down" in quality relative to Contraband...they sound like they're "Dead and Bloated"...listening to Libertad is like a "Big Empty" feeling...what I'm scheming to express is that Libertad is the epitome of the sophomore slump. I used STP song references to comedically pun on the failure of Libertad. Clever, huh????

All sardonicism aside, Libertad absolutely is a godless, merciless and brutal failure of an attempt at a CD, a collaboration by a so-called "supergroup," and just as music!!!! Before the VR-sheeple get incensed to the point of intolerantly detesting me, let me just clarify that I loved Contraband and also STP as well as Guns N' Roses. That's why my unassailably virtuous critique of Libertad is so painful to me, personally: I had to become intellectually honest with myself and liberate myself from the stubborn blinders I had on for wanting to like this CD just because it was VR. Pitifully, I see that many VR-sheeple are still suffering from having blinders on, which leads to their shortcoming of evaluating Libertad on an intellectually honest basis.

What I want--nay, DEMAND, in fact!!!!--is that the misguided reviewers who are unduly praising Libertad to the high heavens stop lying to people and misbehaving like VR's publicists. These censurable rogue reviewers have feloniously embellished Libertad as the record of the decade, as something avoiding the sophomore slump, and even (egregiously) as an improvement over Contraband!!!! These claims are merely hardcore lies by these reviewers who must be VR ideologues who just refuse to criticize Libertad for what it is: a nightmarish failure of cataclysmic proportions. I implore these brownnosing reviewers to stop lying to people to get them to part with their money to support VR's sub-par CD. An unemotional, independent and objective examination of Libertad will prove that it's inferior to Contraband and anything that STP and Guns N' Roses, respectively, have ever emitted.

I admit: upon first going through the tracks on Libertad, I, too, endured the same, sheeple-minded mentality of these reviewers with their blinders on. I was actually deluding myself to imagine that Libertad was a stellar CD, that Weiland's voice sounded awesome, that Slash's guitar-playing was sweet, that the songs were memorable. But, after confronting myself with intellectual honesty--which I insist these VR-sheeple do at once!!!!--I was easily able to recognize Libertad for what it is.

Libertad, indisputably, is a CD which Weiland and company hyped as "exactly" the record they wanted to make on account of its writing and song structures allegedly being "tight.". However, listening to Libertad, we discover the songs are rushed, uninspired, and redundant. Many songs are disorganized/chaotic (Spay), sentimentally sappy (For a Brother), rehashes of ballads of both groups' previous albums (Gravedancer), immature (Mary, Mary), or inane (...Quick Machines?).

Two of the faultiest parties on Libertad are Weiland and Slash whom VR fans should primarily come to hear due to their respective singing, guitar-playing abilities. However, on Liberad, both Weiland and Slash come abjectly short as Weiland's voice sounds impermissibly high-pitched and lacking a "punch." Slash's guitar "work" disappointingly sounds like it was sloppily rushed and thusly sounds uninspired, careless and just chaotic. This sub-par failure from Weiland and Slash is not what VR listeners should tolerate because we all know both are obligated to do so much better.

Weiland, after all, comes from the STP school of singing (roaring, crooning in a somewhat baritone pitch), especially with Core and Purple. In fact, he's maintained this superior form of singing even on later STP songs like Down, and on Contraband, many songs also feature this better singing style. For almost all songs on Libertad, Weiland sings like his privates are in a vice as he struggles with projecting a truly booming, deeper sound. Slash is a gross disappointment because he's one of the best guitar players around, yet on Libertad his solos are wretchedly sloppy. NOT ONE SONG has any inspirational guitar work where the listener can marvel at his usual guitar-wizardry.

My accusatory thesis that Libertad is the epitome of VR's ignominious sophomore slump is vindicated by the real-life under-performance of this coaster-posing-as-a-CD. Whereas Contraband debuted at #1 on Billboard in 04, Libertad bombed with a #5 debut and quickly fell off the Top 100 in album sales in only a few weeks. This supergroup officially has to be tarnished with the brand of "sucking!!!!" Unless VR atones and returns with a CD that's truly worthy of the expectations that former STP and Guns N' Roses members instill, VR should disband and quit because they're just a mortification.

I bet many VR-sheeple are imperceptive to the fact that Duff McKagan has a financial degree and manages a small portfolio on the side. If VR's trajectory continues down this slide, McKagan should consider quitting music and focusing solely on managing his portfolio as a fund manager!!!!

reviewText:
It's no secret that LL Cool J has been around for a very long time, but the problem is that he hasn't made a truly great album in quite some time, or even a fairly decent album. Well, I can honestly say that he has reached his nadir with his latest album, Todd Smith.

Aside from the fact that people may be growing tired of L naming his albums after himself (Mr. Smith, The G.O.A.T. Featuring James T. Smith), the fact of the matter is, this album is his absolute worst album to date -- yes, worse than 10; yes, worse than The DEFinition; yes, even worse than 14 Shots to the Dome. Speaking of 10, though, I was wondering if L was going back to kickin' it for the ladies because the liner notes feature nothing but pictures of his chest. I was also wondering that when I heard the lead single, the J. Lo-assisted "Control Myself" (which is straight-up wack, by the way). But what if I told you that that was actually one of the BETTER songs?

This is another one of the many rap albums that is littered with guest stars; LL is only alone on one song ("#1 Fan"). And there are mistakes aplenty, like when L recruits Juelz Santana, of all people, for the tired "It's LL and Santana" (great title, guys). The Jamie Foxx-assisted "Best Dress" is forgettable, and L's latest single, "Freeze" (with Lyfe Jennings), makes absolutely no sense.

LL is also rapping too softly for us to understand what he's saying on "Ooh Wee" (featuring Ginuwine). And speaking of has-beens, City High's Ryan Toby sings the hook on "I've Changed", but he comes off like a Michael Jackson impersonator. But the song was pretty pathetic anyway, especially when L kicks lyrics like: "Please find it in your heart to forgive me/Realize only God can convict me/We all make mistakes; so have you/If God showed mercy on me, then you should too."

Songs continue to fail, as the Mary Mary-assisted "We're Gonna Make It" proves that LL Cool J and gospel are like oil and water. And as far as the subject matter in "Preserve the Sexy", well, I sure hope Teairra Mar wasn't still 17 when they recorded the song. The only song on here that's really worth hearing isn't even LL's; it's a remix of Ne-Yo's "So Sick". Although I'm tired of people using Michael Jackson's "Human Nature" music, it actually works well with the song (not that "So Sick" wasn't a great song to begin with). But LL's rap during it doesn't help or hurt matters.

Todd Smith proves that although LL started out in the rap game, he really needs to hang up the mic and stick with acting now (doesn't that remind you of what another rapper-turned-actor who was also born in 1968 and ALSO has the last name "Smith" should do?). As far as keeping from using this CD as a Frisbee, well, it's hard to control myself.

Anthony Rupert

I hate having to write a review like this,especially when I'm a fan of Zorn's other work and groups like Boredoms/Ruins/Melt Banana. Inevitably you will find useless reviews here where close minded people go on and on about how THIS IS THE WORST ALBUM EVER!!THIS IS NOT MUSIC!IT"S JUST NOISE!!!

Funny how these people can tolerate actual"noise"artists like Merzbow,Masonna,etc.and think Melt Banana is"NOT MUSIC!!!!"

Anyway,the point is,this album should have been much better than what these guys gave us. Zorn is a legendary avant sax player/composer and Eye Yamataka cut one hell of a path through the world of audio art with Boredoms.

This is nothing but two guys,probably on limited time schedules,messing around with instruments and toys and recording EVERYTHING without a second thought. There are some interesting ideas on here,but they are rushed. The whole thing sounds like a big joke. Bad Hawkwind,as other reviews have noted,is garbage. 18 minutes of virtually unchanging looped screams by Eye. Letting Eye scream in different ways and THEN splicing the results together with some dynamic shifts would have been a better idea.

Initially I thought this album would be just Zorn on sax and Eye on vocals,the two improvising as they did on a few tracks from Zorn's legendary Naked City album Heretic.

A whole album of Zorn and Eye improvising,screeching sax and screeching vocals would have been much better and a more acceptable artistic product than this wast of tape.

Preview the tracks yourself and decide,otherwise,I say,don't waste your money. Buy any of the early Naked City albums instead.

reviewText:
That's right. I have been a fan of Dredg for a very long time. I would go as far as saying Leitmotif helped shape my music taste into what it is today. It was probably one of the first 20 or so albums that I bought, and one of my most-listened-to albums ever. Every listen was a new discovery, I felt like a kid in a candy store on an unlimited shopping spree. Every album from then on, I bought on day one without even thinking, and have always been pleasantly surprised. But not this time.

You know, I really don't care if a band changes their style. In fact, I welcome most bands doing so, and recognize most bands will gradually change their style probably without even realizing it. I didn't even read anything about this album being different, or who was producing it or anything like that. I didn't think much of it - I figured I'd buy it anyway. Trust me - my problem isn't that the album has an electronic or "pop" style overtone at all. In fact I have many albums that I would consider to be in those genres that I enjoy immensely, even a few that could be considered "Dark Pop" which are done very well. I also don't think that they've "sold out" necessarily because this style is probably LESS radio-friendly than most albums, especially "Catch Without Arms" which I was totally obsessed with when it came out.

It seems like this album was certainly rushed, since it came out not even two years after the last, (by far the shortest amount of time between full-length releases) but even that is no excuse for how bad it is.

The first thing I noticed, other than the electronic overtone is that the vocals sound extremely weak. They sound like you're listening on a fuzzy AM radio station or something. Not only that, but they seem too quiet in the mix and have no dynamic range whatsoever. They're extremely bland, whiny, and completely unflattering. Honestly the production on the entire album sounds like utter garbage and I don't understand how a band can all of a sudden sound like that on their fifth album, especially one that is promoted as "pop". Heck, some of the percussion sounds like they may as well be banging on garbage cans with spoons. The somewhat experimental and electronic melodies just sound like a complete mess and a sad attempt to make things interesting.

The first song is somewhat half decent, but it only goes downhill from there. By the time I get to the third track, "The Tent" I'm ready to shut it off already. The vocals are EXTREMELY repetitive, and they sound like half-asleep mumbling over an 80's porn soundtrack in slow motion. I have to spend so much extra energy trying to find something interesting about this song that it's exhausting. The only other song that hints at a glimmer of how Dredg's songwriting should be is "Somebody is Laughing".

As if this isn't bad enough, they had to re-record a grand song like "The Ornament" and turn it into a sopping, tedious bore-fest with monotonous vocals and one-tone rhythm. "Kalathat" almost had a spark of potential, with a nice acoustic melody but the potential quickly vanishes since the same 3 notes are played for the whole duration and absolutely nothing interesting happens.

Also, what happened to the thought-provoking, creative lyrics of the concept albums? The lyrics here are elementary at best ("The Thought of Losing You" - really?), further indicating that this album was rushed. Also, this is the shortest album, clocking in at only 41 minutes (which is probably a good thing).

All I can ask is, what were you thinking, Dredg? And all I can do is hope that this is just a crazy failed experiment. If that's the case, I forgive you, Dredg but please take your time on the next album and don't turn into one of those bands that I can only listen to their "old stuff". I will have to hear at least something before buying from now on because if albums continue to sound like this, it's time to move on. All good things must come to an end, I guess. Please understand that it hurts to put one star on a Dredg album, it really does, but I really have no choice.

reviewText: Sadly, this famous much-reviewed, much-cherished performance has been revealed to be patched together from REHEARSALS for the live event. The actual concert was quietly released in 2008 on the ORFEO label and available from Amazon. Beethoven: Symphony No. 9 The ORFEO release was cleared and approved by Bayreuth. The notes for the new release specifically state the EMI release of a performance we THOUGHT we'd grown up with was assembled with "obvious edits and corrections using material that differs from the performance that took place 29 July 1951." Wow. This deliberate fraud - and that seems to be what it was - has been talked about since the authentic performance appeared in a Japanese release. Dade Thieriot, president of the Wilhelm Furtwangler Society of America and someone likely to know about these things, wrote: "The hack job that Mr. Legge did is an embarassment and an insult to the Furtwangler legacy, and while it is in and of itself a memorable version, it is nonetheless not what it has always claimed to be. Dress rehearsals spliced together with chunks of the live performance is not in any case the real thing." He added that the applause at the end of the EMI release was added to create the "live" recording. By the way, the ORFEO performance is astonishing and remastered very well. It's a better version than the EMI since it's the real thing: a live Furtwangler performance. Beethoven: Symphony No. 9

reviewText:
If you are one of those people who simply saw the track listing that included a song called Thunderstruck, Lord have mercy on your soul, because even if you crave that song, the rest of this album very likely doesn't equate to the money you spent on this album. AC/DC was in an absolute freefall after the death of Bon Scott, and this disc is just more proof of that. Here's my breakdown of each song:
1. Thunderstruck: a very strange song, very different from the classic formula they had going in the 70s and early 80s, and for some odd reason, has struck a chord with the general public. It has no real cohesive purpose or story, it's just an excuse to belt out "THUNDER! na na na naa na na naaaaa..." a chant that has become the call of a generation. Personally, this song grates on my nerves, but I suppose it would be considered a "classic" because it has been so engrained in the public's subconscious.
2. Fire Your Guns: This song may seem just fantastic the first time you listen to it, but for me, it's deteriorated over time. It reverts somewhat to the fact that Brian Johnson's voice can destroy ANY fantastic guitar work.
3. Moneytalks: a timeless classic...guitar-wise. It's one of Brian Johnson's better vocal forays, but going back to that ruining some ingenious guitar work...he still manages to overpower some great playing by Angus with his voice that strains the definitions of gravelness. Nonetheless, still one of the top three songs on this CD.
4. Razor's Edge: a fantastic opening, has the potential to be a very eerie song, in the league of their earlier work such as Night Prowler, but then, it fails to pan out. Still, a half decent effort.
5. Mistress for Christmas: brutal. Nothing more than that. Look at the other reviews of this album, many of them say that Mistress for Christmas is one of their weakest efforts in awhile.
6. Rock Your Heart Out: awesome. The highlight of the CD, bar none, although it really never gets the recognition it deserves. Brian tones it down a bit on this song, is actually understandable, and is actually bearable to listen to, and the guitar riff is classic AC/DC. One of the top 5 AC/DC songs ever, in my opinion.
7. Are You Ready: Certainly not as awful as some of the other stuff on this album, but proof that AC/DC's best was far behind them. If this gets classified as "not filler" then it really proves the mediocrity of something like this CD.
8. Got You By the Balls: this time, instead of bad vocals from Brian Johnson, it's really the terrible, stupid lyrics writing that ruins another catchy guitar line from the Brothers Young.
9. Shot of Love: like Fire Your Guns, sounds great the first time you hear it, but then, eventually one realizes that this really isn't that fantastic song. Although this is one of the more energetic offerings from this album.
10. Let's Make It: wow. This and If You Dare are just terrible, in my opinion even worse than Mistress for Christmas. In these two songs, the band falls short of coming up with a great riff, or an immortal chant, or anything really, these are two of the most non-descript songs imaginable.
11. Goodbye and Good Riddance to Bad Luck: contrary to the two train wrecks on either side of it, this song ranks right up there with Rock Your Heart Out as one of the two highlights of this disc. A great, memorable guitar riff, and just a great salute to the blue collar society.
12. If You Dare: sadly, I must refer you to the the comment about Let's Make It.
Overall, this really makes a die hard AC/DC fan like me hearken for the days of Bon Scott and Phil Rudd, when the band had energy, attitude in its playing and one amazing fireball of charisma and wit in Bon Scott. Make no mistake, Rock Your Heart Out and Goodbye and Good Riddance are two of my favourite AC/DC songs, but even they only amount to a star combined when put up with the rest of this album. If you are just an AC/DC fan from what you've heard on the radio, for sure you should get this album, it's got two of AC/DC's most instantly recognizable songs in Thunderstruck and Moneytalks, but if you are a true AC/DC fan, or more specifically, a Bon Scott fan, I'd advise to get this just to round out your AC/DC collection. Just so that when your friend is over and sees you have AC/DC, and since they've only heard AC/DC from the FM radio, asks if you have Thunderstruck, you can pop it in and show it to them. While in your head, you've got some truly great songs playing from the Bon Scott time, the glory days of a great band...

reviewText:
Let's be honest: Radiohead were never an "albums band".  Even their most homogenous release to date, 1997's OK Computer, devolves into a series of anticlimactic murmurs and at least one recycled song from the A-side of the album -- no surprises means some seriously let down listeners.  Clever artistic choice?  That still doesn't mean I'm listening past track six.  So.  Now we get around to possibly the least surprising Radiohead album of all: Amnesiac.  Even the most unwavering radio-'heads were readying their counter-arguments to the protesting cries of "Kid B??", and the metallic atmosphere being rehashed through these vapid lullabies doesn't make it hard to decipher why.  Unfortunately, the legions of yes-men armed with blue Radiohead blankets are missing the real chink in the armor -- the fact that this is a collection of uninspired, uninteresting, and underdeveloped sleeping pills.

The record opens with a trademark weird sound (thank you, Brian Eno), before the monotonous hum of "Packt Like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box" buzzes by your head and is gone.  Wait, did someone just hear a Radiohead song?  Oh well.  But actually, just a moment -- the next sound to grace the record is one of the three tracks Radiohead has cut that could almost be called beautiful.  "Pyramid Song" is startlingly pretty, features some arresting lyrical imagery, and to put it in short terms, positively shimmers.  After that.... lights out, kids.  The show's over.

"Pulk/pull Revolving Doors" is that long-awaited song to us artistic purists: the Radiohead song that even die-hard fans can't say they like.  Approximately one sentence of this review will be devoted to the boring soulless ballads, "Paranoid Android" (Act 1) revivals, and hookless failed experiments that make up tracks 4 through 10 of this record.  We've been listening to this album for well over a half and hour and we're desperate for something to stick... and, thank God, it does.  "Life is a Glasshouse", along with "Pyramid Song", is one of the two good or otherwise memorable tracks on this whole piece, and is destined to have legions of fans crying "Look!  It's jazz!"  Aside from the fact that horns do not equal jazz, and Radiohead has never shown any penchant for a jazz influence, this is a pretty solid track.  The New Orleans funeral march is an interesting sound for these guys -- too bad they had to take a few more scattered stabs at it on the similarly hollow Hail to the Thief and ruin all the fun.  Meanwhile, those of us who like our avant-rock with a jazz twist are off listening to Talk Talk's Laughing Stock.  And no, that doesn't involve a wall of horns.

Goodnight, Thom.

reviewText:
Here's an amusing anecdote for you. You know how old people always say they remember where they were the day they heard Kennedy had been shot? I think our generations alternative is going to be "do you remember where you were when you heard Diana was dead?" And that's a real shame, because, according to eye-witnesses, I told them about it after hearing it on TV at four in the morning. Trouble was, I was blind drunk and completely forgot about it the next morning. I woke up and was like, "oh, really? Wow." So does that count as the first time I REALLY heard it? Answers on a postcard.

I suppose my alternative "do you remember" question could go something like this.. "do you remember where you were when you were bowled over by the unbelievable hypocrisy and fake sentiment surrounding this parasite's demise?

The answer would be no - because it came so thick and so fast (and so frequent) that I could barely breathe because of it.

Let me cast your mind back, before Diana's driver tried to do a Kittie Pryde. Guys, Diana was a JOKE. A laughing stock, seen as a yo-yo knickered airhead who tried to con and manipulate the media for her own gain. A day didn't go by that the tabloids were mocking her or the media were exposing her. It was accepted, it was who she was - a Royal - a complete waste of time.

Then, BAM! All of a sudden she does the biggest, most succesful career revival ever and snuffs it. Then you cannot MOVE for newspapers telling us how great she was, the media telling us how much she was loved and how she'll be missed and how the "world was in mourning". And, for some reason, she was now the People's Princess, "England's Rose" and about a million other utter LIES. It really was an eye-opening experience for The Curmudgeon.

And this God-awful CD is just an example of the mawkish drivel we had to suffer for (what felt like) about two years straight. Ah yes, you really can sum up the way the "nation is feeling" by playing "Mama" by the Spice Girls. The deeply meaningful lyrics of Angel - "I walk into an empty room, and suddenly my heart goes boom" is a great representation of "our suffering", but then the song IS called "Angel" so it's got to be included. I can't believe they didn't include Meredith Brooks' biggest hit. What a wasted opportunity.

Look at that track listing, and think about what its supposed to be for, what "devine cause" its supposed to support. I mean, God almighty, who BOUGHT this junk?? That this CD was ever made is the REAL tragedy here.

Roast in Hell, Diana.

reviewText:
I have been a hardcore 30STM fan and Echelon member for something like 4 years now, and I was counting the days to this album release. Sad to say I was VERY let down. I wear my wristband inside out now in shame.

30STM's first album was amazing. The guitar was heavy, there were ambient electronics and sounds coming from all directions, the lyrical content was ambiguous yet off the wall and interesting, and the drumming was stellar, with the electronic sound thudding through.

Beautiful Lie basically has NONE of the aforementioned elements that made them unique and made me a fan. The guitars are dull, the vocals sound more mainstream, especially his half screams, the drumming is mixed way back so you can barely hear it, and almost all of the ambient electronic sound that made the last album sound so spacious and epic is sadly missing.

This album feels like a really bad attempt at getting radio airplay and a spot on the Warped Tour or something. Too much touring with Chevelle and the Used seems to have infected the band with a terrible case of SUCKASS.

I hope to god they can redeem themselves with a third album that returns to their once great and unique sound. Until then I will continue to listen to the debut release and despise this one.
