reviewText:
Ostensibly, From the Hot Afternoon is a showcase for a couple of post-Jobim/Gilberto Brazilian song writers and for some new Brazilian instrumental and vocal talent.  This sounds like an interesting idea for an album.  To be sure, Desmond had a remarkable flair for the bossa nova style.  He even recorded an album with Jim Hall in 1962 called Bossa Antigua which contains several of Desmond`s own lovely bossa-style compositions.  (This, despite the ruefully punning title, was only two years after Getz and Byrd recorded the ground-breaking Jazz Samba, which introduced American jazz fans to the "new thing" and started a craze in jazz and popular music of the time.)
Anyway, it must have seemed like a good idea to everyone, even as late as 1969, to return for another take on the Brazilian jazz-samba style.  Unfortunately, the two featured composers--Milton Nascimento and Edu Lobo--are not remotely in the same league with someone like Antonio Carlos Jobim; nor is the rhythm section (with the exception of Ron Carter on bass) up to the caliber of Jim Hall's guitar and Connie Kay's drums on Bossa Antigua.
But these problems would not alone be enough to completely sink an album featuring the incomparable Paul Desmond.
What does succeed in ruining it, though, is Don Sebesky.  For some reason, Sebesky was hired to add light orchestral arrangements ("sweetening" it was called) to many jazz albums that were produced by Creed Taylor in the late 70's-including several other Desmond/CTI releases as well as sessions by other jazz greats.  Whether the incorporation of these dreadful over-dubbed orchestrations was a symptom of blatant commercialization, or whether Taylor genuinely thought it constituted some kind of revolutionary pop/jazz/classical fusion, I don't pretend to know.
But I do know the results are, to say the least, un-jazzy.  Sebesky's arrangements are so insipid that they make elevator music seem exciting--so pop and goofy that they make new-age music seem hot.  Moreover, they are so poorly realized that they even submerge the principal musicians!  You have to constantly switch channels just to hear Desmond over all the strings, flutes, French horns, clarinet, oboe, harp, and electric piano.  Can it be that some engineer really thought Desmond's alto merited no more prominence that the first violin or the oboe?
The final result, then, is a miasma of muzak, with the ghost of a jazz giant floating around in it.
Still, there is a reason for a diehard Desmond fan (like myself) to own this re-release; and that is for the extra takes that are laid down without the overdubbed orchestra parts, thus giving us a chance to hear Desmond in his natural, small-group setting.
Sad to say, however, these takes seem uninspired at best-especially when compared with the same sort of music and the same sort of instrumentation that resulted in the effort captured on Bossa Antigua.  On the Hot Afternoon tracks Desmond sounds like he's spinning his wheels, rather than giving out with the remarkable lyrical invention that graces all of his work prior to and after this lamentable Sebesky period.  On most of these cuts, he takes a modal and undirected approach to his improvisations.  He seems to be playing almost as if he knew that his voice would be lost in the mixing anyway--playing like an accompanist, rather than like the featured soloist.  Moreover, the cuts are all traditional pop-song length (two and a half to four minutes), which is not a format Desmond ever used, or sounds good on, either with the Brubeck quartet or with his own groups.
Desmond once remarked that he was not the type of musician to dominate a session-that his work very much depended on a rapport with his fellow band members.  This album seems to prove the point: without a seasoned rhythm section, good material, and room to stretch, even the greatest of alto players found himself far too constrained to produce his best work.

reviewText:
One of the worst side/solo projects from anyone from the Yes camp.  I'm a big Yes fan; I love all aspects of Yes from its entire history.  But I could not listen to this.  It gave me a headache quickly.
Most of these songs are turgid mid-tempo pop-rock numbers, with the less-than-stellar vocal harmonizing of Squire and Sherwood being the acid frosting on the tasteless cake.  "The More We Live-Let Go" was heard to better effect on "Union", largely because Jon Anderson is simply a better singer than Billy Sherwood.  If these were the songs Chris and Billy were working on before the Union project became a reality, it's no wonder the entire band felt adrift.  "Red Light Ahead" is the other good song on here, and even as such, Chris has written far better songs than this.
For all Yes fans, try to imagine "Open Your Eyes" without Jon Anderson's vocals or Steve Howe's guitar flourishes and you'll have this album.  It's THAT bad.
There is hope; on an Inside Out music sampler, I've heard a Conspiracy song from their next album, and it sounds MUCH better than this.

reviewText:
One of America's most treasured Rock `N' Roll bands Aerosmith is perhaps Rock's ultimate ballads band, they came with some many great songs and ballads like "Dream On", "Angel", "Don't Wanna Miss a Thing" and so on. Some of these ballads are really special and have stood the test of time; many of Aerosmith's ballads are still played live today. Releasing an album of Ballad content only is not a new idea and certainly not a very original one. For Aerosmith you'd figure that with the amount of great ballads they made over their lengthy career that one could make a great collection of ballads. That's what Tough Love: The Best of Ballads attempts to do and fails miserably at. First of all I'm not even sure who this is supposed to aimed at. Maybe the casual fan who only or mostly likes Aerosmith's ballads? Tough Love isn't all ballads, it features Hard-Rock songs as well but this ruins the concept of ballads. If you're going to have a ballad best-of album and include some rockers why not buy a better and lengthier compilation at a similar price with the ballads and the bigger hits that does a better job at summarizing Aerosmith.

Tough Love is not a great Aerosmith compilation and while it does have the band's greatest ballads in one place, it falls short of whatever it's supposed to do. Some of the songs like "Livin' On the Edge" and "Rag Doll" probably have no business here at all. "Love In An Elevator" fits the concept of love but is not really a ballad. With only 12 songs, this is a pretty poor compilation that doesn't offer much.

It's been a while (and too many compilations) since the last Aerosmith album and it seems that fans are always promised a new album that never quite happens. It's been said before but the amount of Greatest Hits albums and collections with the Aerosmith name stamped on top of it is definitely too many. I can't even tell how many there are, I lost count a long time ago. Get the classic Aerosmith Greatest Hits, Oh Yeah! Ultimate Aerosmith Hits or even Big Ones if you're looking for an introduction to the band that is often considered the greatest American Rock'N' Roll band. At the price you're better off with almost any other Aerosmith compilation from which you have many to choose from (my favorites being the older Greatest Hits and the two discs and the more complete Oh Yeah! Ultimate Aerosmith Hits which are both far better introductions to the band. 1/5.

reviewText:
I've already written my long form review on Prog Archives, but I still have two cents worth to spend here.

This album is pleasant. But, when I say pleasant I spit the word out. Pleasant is dull and lifeless just like this album.

I really liked (most of) Fly From Here (see my review), I really liked Magnification, I really liked The Ladder, I love Relayer, I like almost every Yes album for what it is. Ready for real blashpemy? I like Union. Yep, I'm easy. I'm a dyed in the wool Yes fan since I first heard the Yessongs album (while contemplating the universe and Timothy Leary).

I don't believe that a good Yes song needs Jon Anderson's writing. There are a number of songs I really like that were principally written by Trevor Rabin and the Drama era members.

I don't believe a Yes album needs Jon Anderson's voice to sound good. I like Trevor Horn's voice on Drama, and I really love Benoit David's voice on Fly From Here. Benoit's vocals on Mystery's last album are simply awesome.

My point here is that I'm really open minded to whatever Yes put's out. Now don't get me wrong. I'm not trashing Jon Anderson here. The best Yes songs sprang from Jon's mind and throat. That alto, northern England velvet rasp is icing on any Yes cake.

Now there's Heaven & Earth. It pleasantly (hock-ptooey) plods along with nice vocals and stupid lyrics and then it ends. I had no inclination to start it over and listen again. I didn't hear any passion. Chris Squire. You're in charge so you're responsible for this pablum. For heaven's sake start working with Billy Sherwood again. That would be an improvement.

It is with a heavy heart that I say this is the worst Yes album ever. I won't be pitching my shekels into their pot this time.

One last thing. If this album was released by a lesser band I would have easily given it two stars, but this is Yes. I expect a bit more from Yes.
label: negative

I was introduced to this group through Austin City Limits on PBS.  I thought and still think that this is a very talented group of musicians.

 This DVD however, is for me a big disappointment. I truly try to understand what the group or the person(s) who filmed and edited this was thinking?

In all honesty, it appear to be a collection  of home video, cell phone camera pics and security cam recordings made by a high school student whose ego was greater than his/her ability and whose artistic passion conflicted with an intention to depict the musicians and their music.

The video quality ranges from mediocre to downright bad.  The sound ranges from acceptable to music over a bad telephone connection.  What was lacking in video quality is "compensated" by "creative" video editing with "artistic distortion"  to the point that I found myself very frustrated.  My expectation in this purchase was to observe the artists and their music with sound and image.  I am badly disappointed.

I am sorry but at fist view, I regret having purchased this DVD, and would recommend against anyone else doing so.  To the group Arcade Fire, you are very talented, and your music deserves better than this.  In fact, such a DVD may turn potential fans who do not know you, off.

reviewText:
I understand that bands evolve, and that they often emerge with different styles on different albums. I agree it is always good to keep things fresh. As far as the direction the chili peppers are going, on paper it sounds great. The softer, more introspective songs on Blood Sugar Sex Magik and other albums were brilliant. For them to drop the funk and expand on those kinds of songs would be cool with me as long as they maintained the same standards of quality and musicianship.
  Unfortunately By the Way does not utilize the awesome musicianship of Flea, John Frusciante or the rest of the chili peppers. The drumming is especially lackluster considering we know how good Chad can be. Why waste all of this talent? There are some decent songs here and there, but overall this album is quite bland. Anthony Keides' lyrics have lost their bite and often come off as cliche.

  I consider Blood Sugar Sex Magik to be one of the top three albums of the nineties. At the time it was released it was different from anything they had done before. The musical genius of every member was used to its fullest and they tore through funk, hard rock, more mellow tracks, etc. While I am not one to constantly compare albums, it is hard to overlook the ridiculously simple drum beats, lifeless bass hooks, and trite lyrics of By the Way when you know how fresh and inspiring this band can be in all genres- including mellow songs.
  It was not my favorite, but I enjoyed most of Californication because the songs were well structured and their musicianship was at least somewhat utilized. Like I said, if they want to mellow out thats cool but "mellowing out" doesn't equate to writing poor songs and forgetting to play their instruments to their fullest ability. There are very few moments on this CD when they really "get down" and play like they're putting their soul into it. Even One Hot Minute, despite being somewhat misguided, had some great moments.
  I haven't given up on the chili peppers- I know they can write some damn good "mellow" songs. Still, I never thought the day would come when I would listen to a chili peppers album this poor.

reviewText:
Dylan was in the midst of a creative debauchle when he embarked on the tour with the Dead in 1987.  My own personal belief, however, is this is a vitally important record in Dylan's career.  This is the album, and tour, that proved to Dylan he needed to rethink his music, and needed new ways to reconnect to both his lyrics and his audience.  DYLAN & THE DEAD is like a phoenix dying and bursting into flames.  But take hope, because the phoenix will be reborn.  Dylan would recover, even though it sure didn't look like it from crap like this.  Like Steve Miller said, you got to go thru hell before you get to Heaven, or, in Dylan's case, OH MERCY, Travelling Wilburys, TIME, L&T, and MT.

1987 was a bad year for Dylan.  Actually, the late 1980s, the period between 1985 and 1988, Dylan was in a bad way.  Read Chronicles.  He was confused.  He lost touched with his songs.  Dylan couldn't relate to his songs, and his concerts and performances were unmitigated, unfocused messes.  Bob was getting a lot of acknowledgements from the rock establishment, recoginizing him for his past glories, but his art had the time had got in a bad way.  A very bad way.

Enter The Grateful Dead.

Bad mix.  Personally, I love the whole idea of The Grateful Dead and Bob Dylan touring together.  I think had they done the tour in a different time in Dylan's life, you could have got some great stuff.  But no, DYLAN & THE DEAD is outright horrible.  Dismal.

As far as the Dead are concerned, I like them, but I understand why people don't like them.  They are a jam band first and foremost, and they can stretch out any song to an ungodly length.  The first concert I ever took my wife too was Dylan and the Dead (this is when we were dating), and amazingly enough she still married me.  Personally I thought the concert was great, but if you're not into the Dead or that whole scene you really won't get it.  And trust me, that was more of a Dead concert than a Dylan concert.

A big problem with Dylan touring with the Dead is his method of work.  Dylan just starts playing and wants the band to fall in line, and doesn't really give any clear cut direction on how he wants the music played.  Some bands that work.  But with The Grateful Dead it's a marriage made in hell.  The Dead are notorious for their jamming and oft times rather directionless, stoner improvisation.  Get an unfocused by trade jam band like the Dead, pair them up with a at that time completely directionless singer like Dylan, and the results are before you.

Bob Weir said for this tour they rehearsed over one hundred songs, but each song they only did two or three times and that's it.  Garcia was so exicted to get to perform with Dylan, he really wanted to perform a wide variety of songs from the Dylan canon.  And then on some of the opening shows, it was Dylan who really wanted to expand the set list out to include several new songs the band didn't really know that well.  By the time he shook up the set lists they had about six shows to really get it nailed.  And they didn't.

The music here is bad.  It's recorded bad, sung bad, played bad, mixed bad, and just overall has a bad sound.  Dylan, always one for marbles in the mouth, completely massecres his songs here, forgetting words and whole verses, mangling the whole affair.  You really can tell he's lost touch with his work here.  The time's off.  The Dead took a while to figure out Dylan's cues, or what passes for cues.  And who the hell mixed this album?  God, the mix is horrible.

Sadly enough, Dylan is largely responsible for the final product.  Dylan has a rather perverse history of mangling his studio albums, and he extends that practice to this live album, if you can call it an album.  Garcia and the band had several different performances lined up that they wanted to release on the album, but Dylan rejected them.  There were three songs, "Wicked Messenger", "Ballad of Frankee Lee and Judas Priest", and Dylan rejected them, instead placing the two old warhorses "Knocking on Heaven's Door" and "All Along the Watchtower", both of which had appeared more than once on a Dylan live album.

As far as touring goes, this 1987 tour is the bottom of the pit for Dylan.  While he has been wildly uneven in concert, he was at his consistent worst here on this tour.  This is Dylan at his most adrift.

While Dylan and the Dead were rather bad on stage, I've got several hours worth of boots of their studio rehearsals, and I will say they are quite entertaining to listen too, and not (thankfully) because they're trainwrecks but because they're actually good renditions of Dylan's songs.  And, contrary opinion, there are actually a few scattered peformances throughout the tour that could have been assembled into quite the passable, though not necessarily great, live album.

As bad as this live album is (easily Dylan's worst official album; there's a lot of live boots that are better than this), the 1987 tour proved to be immensely important to Dylan psychologically.  He talks a lot in CHRONICLES about the tour, and how he knew he had to get back in touch with his music.  It was only a year later in 1988 that he began the Never Ending Tour.  This is the period Dylan had to go thru to rediscover his music.

Anyway, this is a bad album.  Don't bother with it.  Great cover though.

Have to be dead to be reborn

reviewText:
as i type this, the 50th anniversary of their arrival in America looms. it's a more than worthy sentiment to make such a gesture, but this monument to not-so-artistic license isn't the most flattering of testimonials, to say the least.
i am so much second-to-none in Beates fanaticism that (as the astute reader will of already noticed) my Amazon alias amalgamates two of their triumphs. so yes, having to give them a paltry one star feels not unlike badmouthing my mother, but it should be noted that the "Fab Four" themselves are not to blame. the true villains of this little melodrama are record company muckety-mucks with dollar signs (as opposed to pound signs) in their eyes.
the content stems mostly from the early days of Beatlemania. for some bizarre reason the American distributors couldn't at the time be content to simply release the albums that arrived from the U.K. their tampering was pretty much for the sake of tampering, and was emphatically NOT to the liking of the ones coming off as the auteurs. it took Paul's personal request that Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band be left intact for us Americans to finally get the same albums as the Brits.
their incessent reshuffling of playlists had little or no logic behind it. why, for instance, relocate "I've Just Seen A Face" from Help! to Rubber Soul? why harvest Rubber Soul and Revolver to create a whole new record that would serve only to stir up controvesy with it's grotesque "butcher" cover? what were these American record execs thinking? pretty much "we can, so why not?"
if that's not a sufficient sacrilege, how about their tendency to reduce the albums from 14 songs to 10 or 12?
and here's the capper: contrary to the gossip, Meet The Beatles! was NOT the premiere American release. a record called Introducing...The Beatles predated it by several months...but is now conveniently missing in action. so really, the set isn't even completely true to it's own misguided purpose!!
in one of my favorite Peanuts strips, Charlie Brown is reading an "adaptation for children" of Sherlock Holmes, which he ultimately compares to "a diluted root beer." what we have here is a simliarly diluted root beer, in a much larger glass. it literally boggles my mind to think that there could be any demand for this truncated selection in a world where the legit U.K. albums - the albums The Beatles themselves made - are readily available. there's even a similar compliation set of them from Apple.
so my rather obvious recommendation is to get that Apple set instead. all this scanty set can ultimately offer that that comprehensive one can't is a few album covers...and those you can see for free at Wikipedia!

reviewText:
For starters, I'm not Gen-X or Gen-Y, I'm a few years from fifty and a huge Linkin Park fan.  I do not have enough praise for Hybrid Theory and Meteora [and Reanimation].  But I have to [reluctantly] say that my reaction on first listen was torn between:

1)  Stunned:  I listed to the first 4-5 cuts and just couldn't stand it anymore and started cueing each song for 10-30 seconds before cueing the next cut

2)  Profound Disappointment:  What happened?  This is not growing, this is forgetting who you are and from where you came, not to mention how you got there.

I read the booklet while I listened to the few cuts I did and the short samples I could tolerate afterwards.  I enjoy reading their notes on their songs and moods and thoughts while recording, writing and mixing.  A pattern was developing - many notes contained:  "Rick felt we should do this..." or "Rick said we should try that..." or "Rick told us that...".  Three words guys - BLAH BLAH BLAH.  I finally thought to myself, if Rick Ruben told each of you [or collectively] to jump off a bridge, would you do it?

Being a musician/composer and producer myself, I realize Rick Ruben is a well known, well respected, talented and award-winning producer.  With that said, perhaps Mr. Ruben should stick with the Chili Peppers, Johnny Cash and the Beasties and stay away from Linkin Park.  Not everything he touches turns to gold and this is both a reminder and visceral proof.

If this new direction is his idea, he has done the band a real disservice.  You will not have to read many reviews here to find out that they decided to take a detour in their usual sound and style.  Now whether this is due to the perception that rap/nu-metal has seen its heyday, or Mr. Ruben's suggestions, or Warner Brothers legendary A&R paranoia or other demographics I couldn't say.  What I do know is that Linkin Park had a unique sound between their hypnotic mix of power metal, Shinoda's rapping & turntable scratching, Bennington's seemingly limitless vocal power and truly amazing and flawless production.  They were ALREADY unique and beloved and really had no need to change their sound or follow a different direction, at least not for a while.  It IS possible to stay within a niche while still growing and expanding.

One of the few songs that Shinoda does rap on is backed with pipe organ and marching snare drums [PIPE ORGAN AND MARCHING DRUMS?  GROAN!]  I heard maybe 2 songs plus the intro that were tolerable and reminiscent of the LP sound but the rest were horrible, intolerable or at the very best, not what I was hoping for from their new release.

Again, let me reiterate that I'm not slamming Mr. Ruben - I certainly recognize his long string of successes.  Perhaps, Mr. Ruben can dig up Johnny Cash and get into the posthumous album release craze.  I'm not slamming the guys either - perhaps you all can give Don Gilmore a call, apologize like you never have before, beg his forgiveness and hire him back as co-producer.

Guys:  More scratching, more rap, more of Chester's euphoric wailing, more chunky beats, more slamming bass and more crunchy metal.

DO WHAT YOU DO BEST - IT HAS BROUGHT YOU TO WHERE YOU ARE!

It's always nice to aspire to be more, to reach out, to grow.  But it's also a crime to lose track of who you are and from where you came, which strikes me as the case with this album.

I sincerely doubt this CD will ever take another spin on any player of mine.  I did relent and took it in the car with me a few days after my first disappointing listen, but I could not tolerate much there either and switched it off about 4-5 songs into it.

But I'll give you one more shot guys - I'll buy your next album, without hearing a thing, probably on pre-order once again.  But if it's like this one, Ciao-Baby - we officially part paths at that time and I'll just treasure Hybrid Theory, Meteora and Reanimation for the works of art that they are and wish you all the best.

Nuff said-

Respectfully submitted-
label: negative

reviewText:
I've heard it said before. If there was a rock and roll equivalent of Mount Rushmore then surely four lads from the United Kingdom known collectively as Led Zeppelin would  have their faces (for better or worse) gracing the mighty rock. I can even sort of picture it now. Jimmy Page, perhaps chiseled into the rock with a slightly sallow, greenish complexion compliments of some condition picked up from another misspent night with another misplaced hypodermic. Bonzo Bonham, bloated, face like a bowling ball to reflect the many pounds his poor frame endured from chronic alcohol abuse. Robert Plant, head full of dirty blonde, unruly hair, and perhaps the goatee he's taken to sporting in recent days which makes him look like an even lamer version of Sammy Hagar. John Paul Jones, can anyone even remember what John Paul Jones looks like? Neither can I.

It is with not a little awe and certainly a handful of piety that one should gaze upon this collection of washed up ex-junkies, ex-boozers, ex-hippies. Unfortunately the only thing that hasn't been "ex-ed" out yet is the fact that they still insist on trying to make new music. They are for some inexplicable reason, venerated as the Gods of Rock by sundry music lovers. Sadly, unlike most people's more traditional personal gods, whether it be Yahweh, Allah, Christ, or whatever, they refuse to stay out of sight and more importantly, out of sound.

40 years ago, this ragged, unkempt parade of wanna-be's unleashed their second effort in which they successfully exported someone else's ideas to a mass audience. In the case of their particular passion, the blues, they offered absolutely nothing of consequence to a style that had been performed decades before by Black American musicians. I wish to compare and contrast a terrible, shameless band of no depth or orgnality like Led Zeppelin and their treatment of the blues (perhaps better said, their thievery of the blues) with someone who also took as his foundation, blues music, but unlike Zep, he made it his own. I apologize in advance because I'm going to be referring to a very literary and intelligent songwriter and this is anathema to Zeppelin fans. Not to mention it will likely strain their comprehension skills to breaking point.

If we compare Led Zeppelin's embarrassing plundering of the blues style on their first two albums, it should strike any informed fan as the pathetic meanderings of a talentless gang of rip-offs inundating the senses with something that is derived 100% from a sound and style that was decades old at the time. One cannot over-emphasize the word "derivative" enough. It conjures up images of exactly what they are and excel in, hack job replicas, completely second rate, but much more commercial than the original articles they have plundered. The very first track on here was partially nicked from a blues player born in the 1910's called Willie Dixon. As a person who is not fond of the blues played either by the orginal generators of it or their sad rip-off's, I find it uninspiring lyrically and usually dull muscially. The lengthy wailing guitar solo's are simply tedious. However, compare Zep's copycat act with Australian singer/songwriter Nick Cave's first two albums and you will see that they weren't only separated physically by miles and miles, but that Cave is light years beyond them in terms of orginality, intellect, and just simple talent.

Now I'm sure that Zep fans are arduously scratching their heads at the name Nick Cave and aside from the reverberation of the usual empty clinging sound, are at a loss. Cave's first two albums came out in 1984 and 1985. Several years after Zeppelin and he is several years younger as well. It may seem unfair to compare artists that far apart in time, but if it was possible to use the blues as your starting point and still manage to create your own style, it would have been easier to do it in Zep's time. By 1984, the blues was even older, even more plundered by Zep and their sad acolytes. Cave managed to do it then simply because he had something Page and company never will. Brains, talent, skill, ingenuity, creativity, artistry, etc.

Musically Cave and the Bad Seeds entailed four musicians like Led Zeppelin. Unlike Zep however, this quartet who did use blues as their starting point, created something unique and original in spite of the fact. While Jimmy Page abuses his instrument with more frustration and indulgence than a pimply geek on prom night on virtually every song, you'll find not a single guitar solo on either of Cave's first two albums. Not one. Why? Because it's dull, because it's derivative, because it means **** all to anyone who isn't themselves a pretentious white flop trying to ape the blues. "Whole Lotta Love" is ripped off from blues man Wille Dixon, and it's clear. It has about as much uniqueness as any other Zep song on the first two albums, which is to say, none. Lengthy, mind numbingly dull guitar solos and a drummer likely in an alcoholic haze struggling to keep the beat. Cave's "Tupelo" employs minimal instrumentation, it is virtually the bass alone that propels the song along eerily as Cave prophesies the doom that lay ahead for the inhabitants of the birthplace of the King. I'd love to see the hacks in Zeppelin create a song that is driven by little else but the bass guitar, but at this point I'd settle for a Zep song that didn't have a pathetic pseudo-bluesy guitar solo. "Saint Huck" is another that is propelled largely by an eerie bass line and again a demented Cave detailing the doomed Huck's venture from the river to the city. "From her To Eternity" most prominently contains crashing keyboards as well as a rivetting bass. Throughout, the guitar is hardly noticeable, much less aped to the point of fawning adulation as Jimmy Page excels in.

Music aside, perhaps the biggest contradiction is in the lyrics. Whereas Robert Plant appears to have the mind of a petulant child perpetually p*ssing and moaning over matters of the libido (matters one suspects he lacks the maturity to even understand) Cave expands in a unique and original way on elements of blues that were always there. Plant takes elements that were always there in blues lyrics and pretty much regurgitates them verbatim to a white audience (with cutomary orgasmic yelp of course). Cave takes the themes common in blues music, melancholia, despair, hopelessness, bad luck, and then precedes to elevate them to a higher, more literary, adult level. Cave's lyrics explore religion and God and those that they have condemned. They explore dirty death row floors, the psychosis of a broken and jilted lover, the mythology of evil symbols and figures and what it is claimed they foretell. Loneliness, isolation, despair, abandonment by God and/or man, all elevated to a level that is then crammed down the listener's throat with violent assaults of voice and sparse instrumentation. There's not a lot of electric guitar on those first two Cave albums and there's many tracks when the drums are either absent or tame, but this combination contains within it approximately 1000 times more force and power than the "pedal to the medal" pseudo-energy of Led Zeppelin. Perhaps Zep had to be harder and faster in an effort to conceal how truly unoriginal and derivative these guys are. Perhaps it had to be harder and faster to conceal that the Emperor indeed has no clothes on.

reviewText: This album brings with itself a sad history... Here we go: I don't mind the fact that SCORPIONS tried hard to change their music to gain notoriety in America and other markets. No. Due to sheer determination, they deserved success, whatever way it came. They began to fight hard for the desired success when guitarrist Matthias Jabs replaced guitar-hero Ulrich Roth. THe first result of this new "phase" was the album "LOVEDRIVE". Then followed "ANIMAL MAGNETISM", "BLACKOUT" and "LOVE AT FIRST STING". Altough totally different from the Roth's days and commercially driven all the way, these albuns still had the quality to produce some great hard rock tunes. So, the next step was, logically, to release a live album to consolidate the success of the new "phase". This album was WORLD WIDE LIVE. It contains not a single song from the albuns before Matthias Jabs, as if the band wanted to make it clear that all was left behind forever. Ok. But, why, for God's sake, the production destroyed this album?? WHy the sound generated one of the most heartless albuns that I've ever heard in my entire life? THis was a disservice for a band that worked so hard to acheieve mega-stars status. Hermann Rarebell's drums are lame, awful, terrible, I can't understand how he played like that, comparing with his own performance in the superb TOKYO TAPES !!! The guitars are totally dead, flat, sleeping. Even the cover art suggests a product made without the slightest intention of delivering good music. A shame, German boys. I don't need to tell that after this they embarked in another "phase", this one to be worst still...
label: negative

reviewText:
I have to admit, I'm not the target audience for an album like this. However, my GF left it in my car's stereo so I decided to give it a listen. And yes, I did listen to the album...I'm not just "bashing" for no reason. I actually listened to it from front to back 3 times.

I don't really get Kesha (and I refuse to put a stupid dollar sign every time I type her name). What's her message, exactly? This album is utterly confusing. In between songs about sleeping around with random men, she decides to toss in a love song. Kinda hard to take a love song as genuine when she repeatedly reminds the listener that she just wants to "get in your dirty sheets" with random Joes.

It's not just that stuff that confuses. It's also the fact that she constantly talks about "fighting" like she's some part of movement for misunderstood youth. What exactly are you fighting for, Kesha? Why do you insist on starting some sort of revolution? A revolution for what? Promiscuous women getting drunk?

She also talks about the "simpler times" and how she misses them...like when she had no goals and lived in her car and (surprise) had sex with random dudes. She misses being a screw-up slut? Well at least now she at least has money, I suppose.

The lyrics leave absolutely nothing to the imagination. It's actually cringe-worthy just how bad of a lyricist she is. Don't get me wrong, I didn't think that somebody with a dollar sign in their name would be some sort of epic wordsmith, but still. Just like her messages, many of her lyrics really have no purpose or meaning or make sense. "Shoot the lights out like a machine gun" comes to mind. What the hell is she even talking about? Or how about "Cut you like a knife, kill you like a dagger"? I don't know about you, but I haven't seen a dagger since Lord of the Rings. Knifes are actually much more common weapons...and they kill you just as well as daggers from sword & sorcery novels.

Speaking of lyrics, I don't even think she knows what to put in half her songs. One track is basically the same lyrics/song and then simply repeated. It's like she wrote half a song and just hit "repeat" during the recording session. Seriously. And why does she insist on repeating words in so many of her tracks? Annoying.

Her voice teeters between god-awful and decent enough for a mass-produced manufactured pop star. That's, of course, when she actually sings...which she only does for about half the album if that. A large part of her vocal "prowess" includes talking over a beat and rapping. Her rapping vocals make her sound like some spoiled suburban brat that hates their parents because they got her an iPhone 4S for Christmas and not an iPhone 5 and now the world is ending. At least that's the image I got in my head.

There's really absolutely nothing of value here, IMO. But hey, I gave it a few tries.

reviewText: I will start off saying that I used to be a Nickelback fan.  Nickelback has come out with some great songs and great albums in the past.  However, I'm afraid the downward spiral continues even further with this band.  Remember when rock bands were able to create rock songs that appeased both rock and top 40 fans with hits?  Songs like "1979" by The Smashing Pumpkins and "Better Man" by Pearl Jam enjoyed massive appeal for both rock and pop fans.  There are even good songs that have been recently released that can find both success on both genres such as "Lost In You" by Three Days Grace or "Hesitate" by Stone Sour.  When Nickelback released their massively successful hit "How You Remind Me" it became big on both rock and top 40 charts.  They were once able to have crossover potential with past hits like "How You Remind Me", "Rockstar", and "Saving Me".  However, that has now stopped for this band.  I feel that this trend of lets make half our album hard rock songs and the other half poppy songs to please both audiences is annoying and nothing more to retain popularity.  It kind of started with All The Right Reasons but really became even more so with their previous effort Dark Horse and now even more so with this album.  In my opinion, "When We Stand Together" has got to be the worst song Nickelback has ever created.  It is nothing but a generic twangy-pop song.  Not only that but the melody in the verses sound awfully similar to "All or Nothing" by Theory Of A Deadman.  I can't help but cringe every time when "When We Stand Together" comes on the radio knowing that this is the same band that got me into them in the first place with their first hit "Leader of Men".  Can you honestly say that "When We Stand Together" is on par with past hits such as "Too Bad", "Never Again", "Because of You", or "How You Remind Me"?  I don't see how, but anyways, I'm glad when I see bands find success with their music but to start making an album thinking, hey "Bottoms Up" is a pretty cool rock song for people to rock out to at the bars or strip clubs...but oh wait it won't be good for little kids as well and that we will write "When We Stand Together" and release them both as singles at the same time is uneven and, dare I say, selling out.  The same happened with their previous effort by writing light adult contemporary songs like "Never Gonna Be Alone" but writing sexually explicit rockers like "Something In Your Mouth" that some people may find inappropriate.  Now I am afraid Theory Of A Deadman, a group founded by Kroeger - go figure, is suffering from the same fate with their latest effort as well.  I know a lot of Nickelback fans will be displeased or angered by what I wrote in this review but it's just my opinion.  But going furthermore into the album itself, can you honestly say songs like the sexual rehash of "Midnight Queen" and the "I'd Come For You/Someday" sound-alike of "Trying Not To Love You" are that good?  I hope it's not just me, but it seems as if they want to constantly write about sex and drinking and also reuse older song melodies because they know those songs will make it big.  Nickelback know they could write songs about different topics once in awhile still can't they?  I thought "Something In Your Mouth" was catchy and good at first because it had a different sound but come on now, do we have to keep rehashing the same subjects in your "rock" songs.  I'm not offended at all by sexual lyrics but if that's ALL you feel you need to write about in the majority of your songs for the fact to continue to sell records then it does get annoying.  Does anyone remember great rock songs that contained different lyrics with different subject matter they put out in the past like "Just For" or "Where Do I Hide"?  Anyways... the only song that I really enjoy from this album is "This Means War".  "Don't Ever Let It End" is also a decent slower song.  Other than that, you will get songs like "Bottoms Up" which sounds like a sped up version of "Shakin Hands" or a slowed down version of "Animal".  Or also, how about "Midnight Queen" which is somewhat a lyrical rehash of "Something In Your Mouth".  On the plus side, one thing I do give them props though is for the fact that they can actually tune their guitars differently with songs like "This Means War" and "Gotta Get Me Some" to actually make them sound different from songs they have done in the past.  However, on an ending note, if you want to hear new material from Nickelback, listen to the samples first before buying the whole album.  I would much rather you save a little money and download the songs you find you'll enjoy listening to.  If you want to purchase a Nickelback album as a whole, I recommend their classics "Silver Side Up", "The State", and "The Long Road" which are great rock albums.  This album is far away from those and is not that good.  It seems these guys like to play it safe rather than take any risks.  Maybe if they experimented with their sound a little more instead of recycling song riffs/melodies it could be a breath of fresh air for these guys.

reviewText:
Unfortunately for the current future of mankind, we humans (and particularly, we Americans) find ourselves in a particularly regressive state.  We would rather watch a plethora of reality shows than CNN, we want superficial movies with talentless-to-only-somewhat-talented actors and actresses, we seem to find it perfectly acceptable that athletes and glossy Hollywood types get paid millions per year while teachers and scientists are often struggling to get by, and we mindlessly accept pretty-packaged musical atrocities as art.  Whomever first described the musical fare in the vein of Britney Spears as "sugary" was absolutely correct.  To the passive listener, Britney's music tastes good going down, but is ultimately not only of no value to the body, it is actually harmful.

From her first album until now, Britney has been the poster child for all the popular music cash cows that the greedy record executives anxiously sign to their labels.  The philosophy is simple:  make as much money possible by any means necessary.  To do this, songwriters and producers are brought in to provide serious support to the usually barely-talented (if at all) "artist".  The most financially-rewarding demographic has demonstrated in their buying habits that they don't want lyrics that make them have to think, they like sexual content (whether explicit or implicit), and they like catchy melodies and harmonies.  Thus, the artist doesn't need to have even decent vocal ability.  What is commonly referred to as "auto-tune" will make sure no off-puttingly wrong notes are hit, songwriters will write tepid lyrics (usually representative of immature modes of thinking), and producers will create the vocal melodies and accompaniment (or what is simply referred to as "beats" in the popular culture) that are easy to remember (and, oftentimes, easy to dance to).  All of this serves to hook the *passive* listener on the music, which can result in any combination of album, ticket, perfume/cologne, toy, and clothing line sales.

Most music reviewers are proving that they really have no authority to be ranking albums, as they seem to be unable to tell just how terrible Britney's music is.  I have already seen some far too optimistic reviews given to this album by critics, while the few truly artistically-impressive albums coming out are getting reviews that are just blatantly insulting when compared to those of "artists" like Britney.  What seems to be impressing the critics is the production on the album.  Sadly, the production is often credited to the performer when it should really be credited to the producers.  Britney has certainly acquired an astonishing amount of money by now, and she brought in "it" producers who be able to carry her album for her.  However, despite the constant criticism of her terrible vocal abilities (and probably terrible aural skills, although we can't be sure of that, since she continues to lip synch in her performances), Britney has demonstrated her infamous ignorance yet again and has STILL hasn't pursued serious vocal training to improve the quality of her singing.  On top of that, her lyrics are still terribly lacking in creativity, uninspiring, and simply immature (and sadly, she had to pay people to write them for her because hers would be even worse).

Based on the other new releases for this week that I have seen, as well as the ridiculous amount of news coverage this album is getting (due to Britney's other parts of her life that she is also insanely ineffective at managing), I expect this album to debut at #1 on the Billboard album sales chart next week.  However, that doesn't mean that my message will have been for nothing if I can convince even one person who is thinking about buying this album from doing so.  We human beings are supposed to be progressive thinkers, as we are the most cognitively-advanced creatures on this planet.  Music is art, and we deserve better than this as our art.  We deserve for high-quality music to once again be the "popular music" of our culture.  We have the power to decide what the record labels feed us, and one way to do that is to refuse to give them our money when they try to feed us this "sugary" music.  We have to regain control.
label: negative

reviewText: Jordin Sparks basically had two ways to go after her self titled debut. That to either continue in the direction she was going in,or forge ahead musically. By the time of this album Jordin was just past adolescence and was choosing to make some more independent creative decisions such as co-writing some of her songs. Trouble is she's playing it very safe because musically this is one of the most irritatingly cliched albums musically I've ever had to hear. The production and songwriting embody almost every negative stereotype most people would have about EDM (electro dance music),and the rockier songs have very dull garagy guitar riffs that just aren't full of inspiration. Her vocals have grown a bit,but singing one or two phrases in almost every song here again and again isn't the best way to express that. Only one song stands out,and stands out strong. That's "Faith",one of the songs she co-wrote and it's a beautiful,melodically complex gospel/soul song with lyrics full of depth and delivered with total vocal conviction by Jordin. Now if your one of those people who enjoys dancing to music that's little more than of a simple beat with nothing but surface glitter bubblegum variety,than the majority of this album might just be for you. But as you get into it,there are signs of her talent making room for badly needed expansion. Harvey Mason Jr.s rhythmic complexity that begins "Watch You Go" is another sign,however the shallow musical cliche's that muddle much of this album take that over before it develops much further. It's clear on this and her debut that Jordin Sparks is at this point looking for more or less commercial success,putting musical development and vision a second or far third in her list of creative priorities. Recently my exposure to her music came from her most recent (and so far most creatively satisfying) music in the soundtrack for the remake of the film Sparkle: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack. And honestly? If your looking for a good creatively oriented introduction to Jordin's musical talents,I'd go more for that soundtrack or download the song "Faith" from the Amazon.com MP3 department because this album especially just doesn't cut the mustard musically as a whole.

reviewText:
I was living in Minnesota at the time and got free tix to see Lynch Mob playing live. I didn't know there was a new album until they took the stage (very late). Now, George took a huge leap of faith with this band and this recording, and he's since admitted he regrets the damage done. There are a few good tracks here, certainly, but I couldn't recommend you spend your cash just to find them.
But where this album picks up that solitary star is when I saw it LIVE. They were tight, they were rocking harder than Pantera, and the crowd was really into it. Well, except for those of us who saw Dokken play back in the day. For us, this album sucks muddy water. For fans of Korn, Limp Bizkit, etc., it's probably enjoyable. And while they toured on this CD, LM played completely different versions of Dokken classics, versions that were amazingly cool. For that, I stayed halfway thru the show. But then George actually stepped back and let the new guys take over the show and the spotlight, and that's when I walked out.
It doesn't matter to me whether George releases another CD: I've had enough of his self-indulgent, semi-musical meanderings. This CD ends my interest w/ Mr. Lynch's career. He has talent, or at least he had talent, but clearly he doesn't know what to do with it. This recording, even with a few decent tracks and a live performance that went from scorching to burnt, is a sad testament to the faded glory that once was a great 80's talent.
RIP, Mr. Scary.

reviewText: Gross, Homer Simpson-level incompetence. Soulless dreck. Music that struggles and fails to be cutting-edge. You'd never think that U2 would make something like this, would you? Well, you were wrong, then - this represents their lowest low. Distorted, processed electrofunk is not U2's strong point, and you probably could tell that by listening to "Babyface" and "Numb" (with a vocodor! On a U2 song! Seriously! The Edge raps on it, too... urgh...). I mean, at least Achtung Baby had some really high highs, rather than awful imitation Prince fused with techno such as "Lemon" (which was somehow a charting single - when you're massively popular, you can get away with anything). The only song with organic elements, "Stay (Faraway, So Close)"!), is a pathetic flop with some of U2's worst lyrics. Said awful lyrics show up to plague "Some Days Are Better Than Others", which does have a fine bass groove going for it. It's the only song on this monstrosity I can tolerate for more than a half minute, and even then I have a hard time with the instrumental break. At least "The First Time" and "Dirty Day" have nothing to do with techno, even if I can't remember a thing about any of them. Oh, and did I mention the title track, less a song than an excuse to whip out as many headphone tricks as possible? Or the execrable Johnny Cash duet "Wanderer"? No? Wondering why? I hope not. This is the ultimate low for U2. Painful. Just painful.

reviewText:
Why are we still reviewing this? For that matter, why are you even selling this, Amazon? "Angel Dust" was years ago exposed as a mere corporate stunt and, even if you've been stuck under a rock, comes off as an awkward exercise nearly 20 years later. An exercise that, frankly, Suzanne Somers wouldn't even try with a Thighmaster.

So, if somehow you didn't already know, I'll give you the Cliff Notes of the "Angel Dust" debacle: The year was 1992 and Geffen Records pimp David Geffen had just broken up with Warner Bros. Records chief Mo Ostin, after catching him fooling around with Lorne Michaels and the Artist Who I Think Is Currently Known As Prince in the "crystal baths" at the Burbank YMCA. After Ostin learned that Geffen was "on the rebound" with then-Disney boss Michael Ovitz, he set out to deflect the "grunge" movement by signing Body Count and (you guessed it) Faith No More, pumped methamphetamine vapor into the studio and dressed them in Run-D.M.C. outfits for photo shoots. However, Geffen countered with Guns N' Roses' "The Spaghetti Incident?" and won the round through the sheer WTF factor alone.

And I gotta hand it to Mike Patton, boy does he try on this Jason Voorhees version of suburban soul -- what with his ever-earnest aural gymnastics (see the militant, Tone Loc-flecked "A Small Victory") -- but it's like Bill Bixby channeling Constantin Stanislavski in "The Incredible Hulk," the rest of the cast molesting the proceedings like a nun wearing a confederate smock to an Al Sharpton barbecue.

If I may, I'd like to sum up some of the "stoner critiques" that have come before mine so you don't have to go through the torture of reading them yourself. You're welcome.

A closet opera freak by the name of S. Janowski ambled out of hibernation a mere 15 days ago to chisel out an ode to this inspiration for screamo, in which he basically states "Angel Dust" is one of the best albums since music began because the songs are great. A genuine genius analysis, sir! Ranger92175 admits he is such a pothead that he can never make it past the first three songs before losing consciousness, although he still gives it the requisite 5 stars. N. Hall shares a term paper he wrote in community college with us which made my head hurt. Christopher Roche "real gone" shares how listening to the album made him so psychotic that he thought Mike Patton should have been the one with an amusement park in his backyard and a detachable nose, always hanging out with homeless kids in Bangladesh. Et cetera.

reviewText:
When Ja first came out in 1998 on Jay-Z's smash platinum hit single "Can I Get A..." people thought they had discovered the next great rap superstar. Having fought off gruling critics & naysayers with DMX comparisons, he released his debut album Venni Vetti Vecci in 1999 to the delight of street fans everywhere. Unfortunatley for Ja and his dreams of becoming a millionare, his lead single never picked up on radio and the album quickly tanked and vanished into dust covered shelves in record stores. Realizing his approach hadn't worked, Ja completely abandoned his all about the streets thug persona to go commercial with the release of his 2000 album Rule 3:36. With the help of upcoming female singers like Christina Millian & Lil' Mo and Murder Inc's gorgeous new female rapper Vita the album took off and spawned 3 top 10 singles and sold over 3 million units.
On his third album, 2001's Pain is Love, Ja again used his leading ladies to fuel the success of his album. His songs were more radio friendly then ever, and relied heavily on the strength of the females performance. At the time Murder Inc. had just signed RnB sensation Ashanti, and one of the game's best female rappers Charli Baltimore so both of them were thrown on the singles and there sexy appearence helped fuel the success of the singles at radio & on national television.
Now, Ja uses the same formula that has worked in the past on his fourth album, The Last Temptation. Ja's pitiful rap approach sickens me as he reliqushes the position of main attraction on his own albums. Using the controversial singer Bobby Brown on the album's lead single "Thug Lovin" was a fantastic move by producer & Murder Inc CEO Irv Gotti, because with Brown's constant problems with the law, both the album and single would receive tons of free promotion. However, its once again Murder Inc's leading ladies who steal the spotlight. Ashanti Douglas, appears on the album twice, on the album's second single "Mesmerize", and on the "Pledge" (Remix), a track that was a previous hit though remained unreleased for a period of time.
The only decent moment on the entire album though, is Charli Baltimore's performance on the album's title track. Baltimore, who has already cemented her reputation as some serious compition to the rap throne currently shared by Foxy Brown & Lil Kim, continues to out perform every other artist on Murder Inc Records. Her all to quick verse makes fans yurn for the release of her debut full length LP, The Diary set for release early next year. The album also includes guest appearences by new Murder Inc artist & Ashanti clone Alexi ('Murder Me'), Cadillac Tah ('Murder Me'), Nas ('The Pledge Remix'), Tupac Shakur ('The Pledge Remix') & Chink Santana ('Emerica') which leaves room for only 3 solo songs.
The album is 13 tracks long, 2 of which are interludes & 3 of which are solos. Do the math, that takes you down to 8 tracks, three of which ('The Pledge Remix', 'Thug Lovin' & 'Mesmerize') have already been released to radio. Do yourself a favor and skip this.
label: negative

reviewText: Jessye Norman has a gorgeous voice and superb breath control.  The problem  is that her and Masur's tempi are so slow that the songs are brought to a  grinding hault.  Particularly in "Im Abendrot," the pace is so  slow that this incredible song is turned into a shapeless ruin, with no  sense of line left in the orchestral music.  Again, Norman's breath control  is miraculous, and if you can make it to the end of the song you will be  amazed at her talent.  Strauss, however, gets left behind.  The early  digital sound is not great, and the playing time, at around 46 minutes, is  outrageous for a full-price reissue (this is about 36 cents a minute, as  opposed to Karajan/Janowitz's 16 cents a minute).  There are no  translations except for "Im Abendrot", and that isn't even next  to the German text!  To be avoided at all costs, unless you are looking for  a lesson in how NOT to perform these songs.  Turn to Janowitz and Karajan  on DG for a recording worth listening to.

reviewText:
In case your wondering, it's not just amazon that has shipped bad sets.
I bought mine from Music Direct as a Christmas present to me and my 10 year old son who loves the Beatles.

The condition of the vinyl is totally unacceptable!!

Was packed nicely. I have not played any of discs as I am in process of purchasing a turntable but I had to open this set early, with all the bad reviews I could not risk missing my 30 day satisfaction guarantee.
So all I say from a purely visual perective.
First the box is glossy, would have much preferred a matte or harder rough cardboard with maybe some metal protection on corners and maybe a clasp, but no Biggie so far.
The jackets? Well, I was expecting a thicker stock card board, these are almost as flimsy as English jackets of the 60's but without the laminate. Very disappointing. So thin that ring wear is appearing already on Rubber Soul, Revolver, Abbey Road, and Let it Be.
The Original inner sleeves are not reproduced from originals, although SGT Pepper inner sleeve is here.
From there it gets worse, but won't bore you with all the details, although ask and I will respond.
Let's just say, almost all of these vinyls have slightly rough to extremely rough edges, with a couple of the albums having large chunks hanging off the edge.
Many of the spindle holes and labels are inaccurately cut, either fraying vinyl or paper label problems, sometimes crinkled label or bubbled label, and some appear to be off center.
A couple of the albums have feel able blemishes, uneven run in edges.
MMT and SGT Pep jackets are dinged, and the 5 x 7 band photos in White Album were all pinch in the binding, thus bending all the photos.

Do I really need to listen to these before returning this Box set?
Of course not, although I would like to, but like I said,  I am currently without a turntable.

I'm just glad I opened it, so I can now start my probably endless routine of shipping returns back to Music Direct.
It looks like I am going to have to pay for all the shipping and re shipping costs.
When all of this is done, I will be sending my shipping receipts to EMI.
Thanks a lot ya EMI wankers!

reviewText:
It would be impossible to think that in the 1940s Bruno Walter was the placid, serene old gentleman who never said a bad word to his players.  I'm told, but haven't verified, that a heart attack changed almost completely his approach to music.  Regardless the cause, the change is surely evident to even the most casual listener who compares  his stereo recordings made just before he died in the early 1960s.  By then he was considered the saint with a baton by those that heard only his slow Mozart and Haydn; his Beethoven lacked thrust and his Mahler had little of the drive in his prime.  Some will argue that late Walter's conducting is a "second prime".  I can't disagree completely.  Mozart's Prague Symphony is played with a zen like quality in the slow movement.  The same is true of the slow movement of Mozart's 40th.  Sadly, though, CBS withdrew the mono recordings so the ability to compare these two very different approaches to leading an orchestra were lost to most listeners for decades. His live broadcasts from the 1930's to the early 1950's have in many cases become widely available.  How wonderful to discover, to borrow that cliched phrase, "Everything old is new again!"

So, I wanted to hear more of this master's early conducting.  I wanted to learn about Bruno Walter - the firebrand.  Listen to a few of his broadcasts with the New York Philharmonic from the 1940s; the volcanic eruptions of sound lay the bedrock for the great works of the 19th century.  Once I heard what a demon he could be with that tough crew of players who were the New York Philharmonic of the post WW II era, those "nice" stereo recordings, while always pleasant, seemed quite pallid in comparison.  I've always preferred live "historic" recordings in any event.  So I couldn't wait to hear this EMI collection that promised some great performances.  They're there, but are so badly transferred I can't listen to them.  In short, these performances that range over several continents and at least two decades have been homogenized to sound as though they were recorded in one sitting!  The idea is absurd at best.  Muddy acoustics are married to a flabby bass register making the entire enterprise a disaster.

Finding a good comparison to use against this set was simple:  I chose the 1931 Brahms Second Symphony, Fritz Busch conducting, and the Staatskapelle Dresden being broadcast live from Berlin's old Philharmonie Hall.  The recording can be found on a four CD set produced by Germany's small Profil label.  This much older recording was definitively clearer than EMI's transfers of Walters 1953 CBS recording of the same work with the New York Philharmonic.  Though Walters Brahms should be a model of clarity, instead, whole lines disappear in the maddening quagmire of reverberation and pumped up bass.  Walters efforts are lost in the muddle, making the EMI/Profil 1931/53 comparison take on ludicrous proportions.

Now that I've done my best to explain what's wrong, let me recommend the Brahms Second led by Busch that I've just mentioned.  He has a studio version from the 1940s, but it does not have the biting syncopations and agogic accents found in this '31 performance.  This may be the only Brahms Second Symphony on record that so clearly exposes Brahms' affinity for the musical vocabulary of Robert Schumann - not to mention his affection for Clara, Robert's wife.  I know of no other recording of the Brahms Second whose tempi emerge with this kind of mania. What conductor today would dare to try and get away with such a bold, but very satisfying statement.  In fact, I'm not sure many collectors even know of this recording's existence - I only discovered it thanks to a friend; that was only two years ago.  The set includes a Tannhuser overture from the same era that is unrivaled even by todays high definition sound.

I don't recall giving a CD one star before.  I hope it helps to make my opinion of EMI's serious error in it's "Great Conductors...." series crystal clear.

reviewText:
For those who might think that `80's glam metal may have had a rebellious, fiery beginning before it became mainstream, they won't ever be able to find it.  Def Leppard and Van Halen founded the glam metal scene and they were both pop bands from the beginning.
The cover of "Pyromania" is extremely misleading.  The destruction depicted on the cover is a great picture and may be interpreted as a hatred of the mega-rich record companies.  But, the sound of the album is a record company executives dream.
It's incredible how annoying the songs on this album really are.  Unlike some pop songs that may have some pleasing effect the first few times around, these songs are annoying the first time and only get worse.
Lyrically, "Photograph" caters to a junior high mentality of the hurt of not receiving a picture from a girlfriend.  The other hits off the album, "Foolin" and "Rock of Ages" are devoid of intellectual content and should be downright embarrassing to the band.
Joe Elliott's voice is the worst part of the music.  He seems to be stuck in high-pitched mode and almost screams at parts.  It could be mistaken for a woman's voice very easily.  When he does the chorus "F-F-F Foolin'", it sounds like a soprano singer with a speech impediment.
If the vocals weren't high-pitched enough, they add high-pitched guitars to further damage the listeners hearing.  They almost always use pop melodies, instead of riffs that define real metal.
"Pyromania" was made to please MTV and rock radio.  The album is extremely polished with a calculated attempt to seem energetic and uplifting.  There's nothing natural about this recording.

reviewText: The press release proclaims this to be Springsteens 19th album. Well if you count the live and greatest hits releases then yes, this is number 19. However, in reality it's only his 13th album of new material in 32 years. Then, if you minus the real clunkers like Human Touch, Joad and now this debacle you are down to 10 exceptional albums in 32 years. It's not the stuff that legends are made of but here we are reviewing Devils and Dust from what many believe to be a true music legend. How strange when you do the math. First please stop the Dylan comparisons. While both are on the back 9 of their careers, Bobby tours incessantly with a band and an opening act and only charges 40 bucks for a show. Not to mention treating his fans to 40 plus releases and a complete overhaul of his back catalog. Meanwhile, Bruce still pedals CDs released with 1980's technology (his back catalog is an industry joke), charging 80 bucks for a solo tour and now doesn't have the smarts to know how limited the dual disc technology really is. Who advises this guy anyway? On to Devils and Dust. I find it a bit odd that a grown man with children would write a song about anal sex with a prostitute as Bruce has with the song Reno. That nugget and flipping the "F" word is the reason for the warning sticker. How sad for parents who have been bringing their kids to his recent tours to explain this downward spiral into a morass of debauchery. I'm sorry; I don't expect the teen angst mentality from an artist of his stature. As for the tour well let's just say this is his big political statement, one he started while stumping for John Kerry. Bruce is more than entitled to his opinion, however, by loading his statements from a stage to a captive audience and not offering a single solution is nothing more than a drive by shooting. I'd like to see him being interviewed and answer some tough questions. I think he would not come across as a great intellect but rather an elitist with no ideas whatsoever. He said as a child he asked his mother what party they belonged to and his mother replied we are democrats because they are for working people. Well, she was right about that statement back in the 60's. However, 40 years later, democrats are for wealth redistribution and have become more socialist then democrats. They keep poor people poor and rarely profess self sufficiency. While Bruce offers no ideas to improve the public school system, his children go to the most prestigious private school NJ has to offer along with Bon Jovi's kid. What this illustrates his pure hypocrisy because what he's saying is that capitalism and the free market system is okay for his wealth accumulation, but the rest of us slobs need to be cared for by the government from cradle to grave. I don't buy that and neither should you. I've been a fan since the Palladium in NYC in 1978. reviewText:
If you're looking into this band, you're probably already a fan of Pink Floyd.  So I'll describe them in terms of Pink Floyd:

You know how Pink Floyd had this habbit of putting in these extended bits of not-quite-music between their songs.  The weird noises between tracks on "Dark Side of the Moon", the boring bits of "Shine On You Crazy Diamond", and the quiet bits in "Dogs" and "Sheep"?

These guys have made entire songs out of this stuff.  Twelve minute tracks - or a single "song" that extends over seven tracks.  Burried in all this highly produced but fairly un-musical waffle is the odd bit song.

These actual songy bits are alright, but they're few and far between.  They have a wild, spastic quality, and sound more like Zepellin than Floyd.  They might actually be really good - its hard to tell after only a few listens.

Even so, a few bright moments of brilliance can't really sustain an entire album.  It actually almost seems like these guys came up with this material, and said to themselves "well, we could put out five short songs on a little EP and become a Dillinger Escape Plan type band, or we could couch this stuff in a whole lot of overwrought soundscapey stuff and break into the prog-rock scene".  It actually feels that pretentious.

The benefit of couching their bombastic stuff inside all the waffle is that the loud, fast stuff sounds that much louder and faster after seven minutes of sustain effects and sampled bird noises.  It's effective, but it doesn't make it good.

People obviously enjoy this, but really, I'm the sort of person who tolerated the filler on Floyd albums because it didn't take up too much space, and their actual songs were good.  Obviously, if you're the sort of person who enjoyed the filler, this might be your album.

Personally, I find it to be tedious, pretentious, and, well, not that good.

reviewText:
This album was one of the low points in Manowar's career. They had always been a very over-the-top kind of band, but with this album they got downright silly. The album is full of uninspired music, ridiculous (and sexist) lyrics, church choirs, some more church choirs... what a stinker!

The 1 star is for the opening track Wheels of Fire, which is a killer song, equally good as Manowar's finest anthems (Fast Taker, Battle Hymn, Blood of My Enemies, Kill with Power, Thor, Black Wind Fire and Steel). And I guess the final track Blood of the Kings is quite okay if you can stomach the intense silliness of the lyrics. But what's in-between is a collection of painful mistakes that you wouldn't want to touch with a stick.

Maybe I'm being too harsh, but that's because this album for me marks the point where Manowar's music came to follow this formula of very simple chord schemes and hollow attempts at being 'epic'. And even worse, it made people identify the whole power metal genre with this kind of simplistic stuff, while at one point Manowar's music (not talking about their image or lyrics) had been really quite intelligent, energetic, and even 'avant-garde'. So my advice is to get acquainted with that side of Manowar, and to buy the Battle Hymns and Hail to England albums instead, which are both 5-star records.

reviewText:
As a music snob I didn't buy this album expecting a masterpiece, but I did expect rather semi-pleasant background noise I can listen to that will put me in a good mood and make my head bob. I enjoy mindless music just as much as anyone else when I'm in the mood for it. I wouldn't call myself a fan of Miley Cyrus, but I do enjoy her music (come on who doesn't know all of the words to Party in the USA and secretly love it, or at the very least doesn't mind it being stuck in their head?). I don't mind the raunchiness, I understand that when you're a female in the big boy pop industry you will at some point have to act like a ho in order to advance (or keep) your career once you're of legal age (and in some cases maybe even before) so it's not even the content that irks me, but rather the sheer laziness of the people who are putting together an album to sell. These record execs are so greedy and want to pop out another crap cake album to sell so quickly that they don't even try and focus on an artist's strengths and weaknesses (which isn't exactly a news flash). In Miley Cyrus' case her voice is her selling point because it's unique and distinguishable. I will at least give her that. If you're listening to the radio and a Miley Cyrus song comes on you KNOW it's Miley Cyrus because she doesn't blend in with the millions of other artists (and I use that term loosely) that have (or had) a career paved in gold that sound exactly the same as the artist that probably won a grammy only a year before and were quickly forgotten. So why oh why would you get her to make an album where she either talks through or "raps" through the whole song? It's going to suck people because Miley Cyrus is no Busta Rhymes. Also Mike Will...... that name has forever been burned into my mind because his name is mentioned in EVERY single song. Thanks. At least now I know who not to get to mix my pop album if I ever decide to make one. I personally would not want my name advertised in every song. I wouldn't want people to know I was in any way responsible for any of the crap on that album. None of his tracks are unique or even go anywhere interesting. (Rule number one when mixing a dance/hip-hop/pop album. While an artists may have a good voice the music is the strong point, or rather whatever buttons you push in random order on a control panel is the pulse. It has to at least go somewhere interesting and change every now and then.) I wish I could get a job mixing crappy pop albums it doesn't seem to take any talent at all....

Also I've heard some pretty crappy songs that I still like and consider listenable (enough) because the beat is good and it's at least catchy, but god some of these songs just made me cringe inwardly because they were SOOOOOO bad. For example (from the song Love, Money, Party) "A party ain't nothing but a party, when you party everyday, it ain't nothing but a party". Just out of curiosity I read through all of the liner notes. I honestly cannot believe how many people it takes to write a crappy song. Apparently for this album they hired a lot of songwriters who were fresh out of Ke$ha's school of basic rhyme with Miley throwing in a couple of words here and there. Not to brag but I could write better lyrics than that. I'm sure the majority of people with a brain could.

I'm also sick of people saying that Miley Cyrus is going in a "new direction" with this album. *ahem* New? How so? If it were a different artist I wouldn't even remember who it was or be able to distinguish it from whatever song was being played before it. I can't really blame Miley because I'm sure that when you're a pop star you have zero input as to what music you're going to sing or whatever sound you're being told to endorse so all you can do is just roll with the punches and hope to god eventually someone will let you do something halfway decent, or just become completely numb to it go on auto-pilot and enjoy watching the cash roll in.

Anyway, rant over. My review in a couple of sentences; The only good catchy song on the album is "We Can't Stop", other than that the rest is forgettable. I just saved you the embarrassment of wasting ten bucks on crap, you're welcome.

reviewText: Almost amusingly bad, which actually reflects the group's status since 1977 or so. But when that happens, here's what you do: go on the world tour, make a crapload of money, and disband, rather than torturing us with this. There's literaly NOTHING on this album I'd want to hear again, though I'll admit it is amusing to hear them imitate U2's Joshua Tree-era sound on Take It Back, it's the kind of amusing that hearing Iggy Pop doing a Jim Morrison impression on the Stooges' Ann is: amusing with more than a tinge of annoying. Dave Gilmour's taken over the songwriting, and the group in general, and he takes Roger Water's concieted, pretentious streak to new highs (or lows, if you will). Not even Gilmour's guitar heroics on Poles Apart (the closest thing to entertainment) save this mess, since he practically repeats the solo on A Great Day for Freedom. Hell, I could sit here and take potshots based on the song titles all day: they were indeed Lost for Words (a hybrid of Money and Wish You Were Here), and not exactly Coming Back to Life. A decent album was what we wanted from you; after hearing A Momentary Lapse of Reason, it's not exactly like anyone had High Hopes. Stop talking - it'll be A Great Day for Floyddom when you realize you're over the hill and break up, leaving us with fond memories of the early-'70's albums.
