reviewText:
Even an ardent Boston fan should not consider buying this album unless one enjoys having their soul crushed. Yes, some of the material is recycled (not just the recycled songs, but a lot of the instrumental hooks steal from earlier Boston material). I suppose we should have recognized that Tom Scholz has been recycling his own material for years (i.e. see the weird recycling of Amanda on "My Destination" from Third Stage). However, this album is truly shameful. Beyond the recycled material, the mix is awful. Few tone-deaf teenagers with Garageband could create a worse mix. The drum machine is tinny,out of sync & highly out-of-date (i.e. late 80's Casio), many of the keys are cheesy and poorly played, bass seems to largely be absent from most tracks, and the vocals are inconsistent in volume, frequently hidden in the mix. At best, this album constitutes a very raw demo. No serious musician would ever release such an unfinished product. Instead, maybe its time to recognize that Scholz has become an eccentric who's lost his ear and lost his perspective on what makes for good rock music. There are nice moments on the guitar, but there's no approximation of a band in this album. At best it's "Guitar Hero" video game quality.

Scholz had to understand that this album was to be his swan song. Right? Those of us who are good at math understand that a 66 year old musician who makes albums once every decade has little chance of ever recording another rock album. That's fine...sometimes there's something to be said of quality over quantity (i.e. Bob Dylan has recorded some quality tracks, but also released a boatload of utter crap). Sadly, Scholz does neither. "Corporate America" was poorly mixed, but there was more of a sound of an actual band. There's no such sense on this release.

It's just a painful listen that's embarrassing to any long-time Boston fans. If you're such a fan, do yourself a favor---pretend this album doesn't exist. It's better to remember Scholz as a musician who was supremely talented in the 70's through 90's than to see this hack besmirch his own reputation.

reviewText:
Fear Factory, oh Fear Factory, sometimes I just can't figure you out. I thought things returned to normal with Archetype, so what happened? Archetype was so much better than I could have ever expected from a band and Fear Factory has, once again, officially taken 10 steps backward with "Transgression." If I didn't know any better, I'd think they like the idea of writing a bad album every other release so they can really feel the pressure the next time around.

The album itself is such a disappointment. Remember that feeling you had when you listened to Digimortal and you said "what the hell is this?" Get ready for that feeling all over again. I will admit I found "540,000 Degrees Fahrenheight" to be quite an enthralling listen and then I listened to the rest of the album and wanted to cry. On Archetype, it didn't even seem like the band missed Dino at all. On Transgression, it's clearly apparent that they do. The riffing is so dry, plain, and redundant I can't even begin to explain it. All you really need to do is listen to the title track and "Contagion(which could be the WORST song Fear Factory has EVER WRITTEN)." In fact, I think Burton has amazing vocals but he's loosing his touch, stretching himself into areas he shouldn't be going, and between that and uninspired riffing, Fear Factory has once again plummeted themselves to the bottom of the barrell... and dare I say that the snare on this album sounds almost like Lars Ulrich's on St. Anger?

As if it wasn't bad enough in the first half of the album, it completely falls apart in the latter half. "I Will Follow" is literally a pop rock song and it's done oh so horribly. Unfortunetly, this album could be worse than Digimortal. That's not to say that it sounds like "Digimortal", although, "Transgression" does contain quite a few "nu metal" overtones(is it 1999 all over again?), the simple fact of the matter is that this album will sit right next to "Digimortal" as being the weakest material the band has ever written. When I need a Fear Factory fix, I'll take out my copy of "Demanufacture" or "Obsolete." Maybe next time.

It's sad, I used to think that the earlier more lyrical, emotional Brad Mehldau, et al, were the best thing out there. Look to his various Art of the Trio albums, or Anything Goes for much more involving music.

I keep waiting for the obviously talented Mr Mehldau to put his heart back in his playing, instead of flashy technique...

Caveat Emptor. Let the buyer beware. Definately audition before purchase.

Don't blame me, I'm just trying to save your money. I've always felt anyone can write an unreflective good review, including the artist himself, the record label and his friends. That's why there are so many of them. But if someone takes the time to write a negative one, to tell you why an album is not worth buying, they probably care for your money. The TV travesty known as THE JERRY SPRINGER SHOW is already a paraody of itself..so how can one successfully parody a parody? You can't.  Richard Thomas and Stewart Lee created the score. Their wit is limited to schoolboys making rude comments. Examples? Just look at the song titles: "Chick with a Dick", "Diaper Man", "Montel Cums Dirty." The lyrics are not especially funny, and the music is absurdly unmelodic.
The recording (made live in the theatre, so you can hear the tepid audience response) is muddy as all live recordings are. The package includes a synopsis and a few color pics but no real info on the show.
Plans are underway to bring this show to Broadway next season.  It will need considerable revision and some genuine wit to make a go of it on the great white way. The greatest sin is the cutting in two sides of a blistering That's it for the Other One, one of the best versions played that year, in a year of high level Other Ones. The song easily would have fit on one side. A 30+ minute Lovelight does require a split, but did anyone think other edits through?
Two count 'em two drum solos further clutter what could have been a definitive Grateful Dead vinyl masterpiece. Even at $70 this is still overpriced. It easily could have fit on 4 lps. Shame on you Brookvale for screwing up what could have been amazing. Sound and manufacturing are exemplary, but it's just not worth the financial layout. Get the CD.

reviewText:
NOTE:  This review is ONLY for the version sold as BMG 09026-68642-2. That number is also on the disk, in very small type. Both jacket and disk have the black horned helmet on a red background. Amazon seems to be putting these Nevsky reviews here and there.

anyway.....

I give it three or four stars as a movie soundtrack.

But, since it is packaged and marketed as a piece of music to play in my living room, it gets one star.

This recording (and performance) absolutely pales in comparison to my Ormandy LP. This performance is gimmicky and poorly-edited, sounding almost like patchwork. The sound is thin, harsh, and poorly-recorded and mastered. However, it is movie music, so the producers might have been aiming at a different market than those who buy Ormandy conducting Prokfiev's cantata as written.

The percussion, in particular, is almost clownish. If nothing else, the guy on the panel gave them way too much mic.

However, the Russian choruses are excellent. Well-sung and well-recorded, without post-production interference or jiggery-pokery.

In fairness, the sound quality is indeed far better than my (early) VHS commercial recording of the movie, but it still sounds like an early '80s CD. I would almost go so far as to say that the sound of the same performance on my VHS commercial version is better than the CD. This is not terribly hard to understand, as analog tape really smooths out rough poorly-done digital. But, I am surprised to see this in a mid-90s recording. I have to wonder what on earth happened to the VHS movie sound when they put it on CD. Other reviewers have commented on the poor transfer from the restored VHS to DVD, so the same inept team might have been responsible

The movie is so powerful that the original VHS version leaves one hungry for decent sound. Such as something that matches what Ormandy and the Philadelphia have already given us.

However, when I watch the restored movie (VHS) with this soundtrack, I am OK with it, because it is secondary to the movie, but it serves the movie well, perhaps as any music can serve a movie. Playing this disc on my stereo system, I am entirely focused on the music, and it falls short.

Perhaps I made a mistake in buying the soundtrack version, and should have just stuck with the way Prokofiev wrote the concert music instead of somebody else's patchwork quick-cut version of how it should be.

 I believe Prokofiev's vision of this music as a concert piece (cantata) to be far superior to that of the crew that put this disk together.

My advice to anyone who thinks they might like this CD is to go ahead and find the '95 restored Temirkanov VHS of the movie and watch the movie and enjoy the sound together. It's music and visuals are masterfully combined. A stunning experience for both movie and music lovers.

I have not seen the DVD version of the mid '90s restoration, but am expressing my satisfaction with the restored '95 VHS version.

If you want Nevsky as music on your stereo, skip this and find the Ormandy performance. The only way to enjoy this performance is when watching the movie.

reviewText: I always liked this LP, because it included some un-released studio and soundtrack recordings that had never been released before this LP first appeared in 1970. However, there have been a few slight changes in the CD version, which were kind of dissapointing. The song "Mama", which is an out-take from Elvis' movie "Girls! Girls! Girls!, is not the 2:12 mono version from the original LP...it is the 58 second, stereo version that was first included on the "Double Features" series. This shorter version was probably included because of the better sound quality and the fact that it is in stereo, although the actual reason is not quite clear. The shorter version is actually the original, the way Elvis actually recorded it. The longer version is spliced from Elvis' version and the Amigios version, which was probably done at the same session. This is the version that was used in the film, and Elvis probably liked it enough to record a version of his own...probably as a tribute to his mother. It is also possible that it was originally intended for the film, but never used. The other change here is with the song "Let's Forget About The Stars". The version included on the CD is the same take as the one on the original LP...however, the LP version included a piano track that is missing from the CD. Again, the CD includes the stereo version that was included on the "Double Features" series, probably because the original LP included the song in mono. It's possible that the master, which included the over-dubbed piano track, has been lost. Still, this CD is not a complete dissapointment, because the versions of these two songs included here are still very good. My only complaint would be that this version of "Mama" is much too short, and this LP only included 9 songs and had a short running time to begin with. These original Camden albums on CD are selling for only about 5.99, so at least they are not over priced, which makes them well worth purchasing. Still, anyone who has waited for this CD to get the versions of these two songs as they were released on the LP will be a bit dissapointed.

reviewText:
This recording of Don Carlo taken live from the Vienna State opera in May of 1979 is a huge disappointment.  I was looking forward to hearing this 'famous' performance conducted by Herbert von Karajan and found myself pacing around as I listened, grumbling in disgust.  The horn blooper in the opening was a poor start.  The Vienna State Opera orchestra aka the Vienna Philharmonic, sounds a little sloppy to me and is certainly no match for Karajan's Berliners on the EMI studio recording.

What really irks about this recording at hand is that Karajan was not content to leave the 4 act version alone.  He snips large bits off in the most vile manner and for no apparent reason beyond three of his leading singers needing all the help they could get to make it through the evening.

The revised aria for Carlo in the monastery in Act 1 (Act 2 in the original version) is preceded by a banal Wagnerian prelude, reminding me of some of the tunes and chordal progressions in the Venusberg scene in Tannhäuser.  The Tannhäuser and Lohengrin echoes continue to be heard until Rodrigo arrives.  This is the first time in any Verdi opera that I have noticed the Wagnerian influence on Verdi's compositional style.  I don't think Verdi's genius was firing on all 8 cylinders when he made the revision.  It shows elsewhere as well, especially in the extensive foreshortening of the last scene of the opera.

The monk's beautiful music is grievously shortened in this version, which is a shame as Luigi Roni is one of the better sounding basses in this role on recording.  Carlo's revised aria isn't a patch on the original and sits strangely in the monastery setting.  It sounds tacked-on. Of course there is a huge ovation at the end of this scene following the famous and ever-more tiresome duet between Carlo and Rodrigo.  The Viennese making a big deal out of the Meister's presence really do over-egg the applause, reminding me of the feather-brained audiences often heard on the matinee broadcasts from the Metropolitan Opera.

The church bell prior to the famous duet is out of tune and is a bonging annoyance.  And for the first time in my listening experience of the homo-erotic duet my eyes rolled.  It's too much.  I think this was largely to do with Karajan's oozing and self-indulgent slow tempo.  In general his conducting in Vienna is much more leisurely, sluggish even, than the EMI recording the year before in Berlin, with largely the same cast.  A cast that was in much better vocal shape than they are here.

The next scene is in the garden with Eboli and her ladies.  The outrage here comes when Karajan surgically amputates the second verse of the Veil Song.  And Agnes Baltsa's breathing is so stentorian as to ruin any sensuousness that she may be emitting from her vocal chords.  The Tebaldo of Marjon Lambriks is fraught with some questionable intonation, but as the guts have been ripped from that role it hardly matters.

What ensued next sent me to the couch to hang my forehead in my hands in despair.  José Carreras has been shouting since his first entrance and now Mirella Freni begins her screaming match with him.  The love duet is hardly enticing in the least.  They both sound like they are in  'survival' mode.  And, here's the worst of it, Karajan cuts the lines beginning 'O, Prodigio!...'  !!  This is one of the most magical moments in all of opera and he cuts it!!!!  I was incredulous at this vandalism.  It was at this point that this recording became merely three stars.

Ruggerio Raimondi's King is a known quantity from other recordings, notably Abbado's French version (DG) and Giulini's classic set on EMI.  Here under Karajan's leadership (he also produced and directed the stage action) Raimondi's King comes off like one of those modern Metro Men.  No offense intended but this king has no balls.  He whines.

The vehement trio with Eboli, Carlo and Rodrigo is over-acted in Grande Guignol manner, all three singers pushing their voices to unpleasant extremes.  Baltsa grows especially tiresome with her consistently high octane singing, making me think she was over-parted in these heavy Verdi roles but recorded them well under studio conditions, like so many of Der Meister's principal singers on record.  And Karajan rather zips through this important ensemble.  His conducting of this performance, in general, is one of the most eccentric and illogical things I've heard from him on record.

Act 3 scene 2, the famous Auto da fé.  The women of the Vienna State opera wobble, sounding like the elderly ladies in Der fliegende Holländer.  There is one particular soprano who catches the mic with her shrill singing that is most unattractive.  The Wiener choir does not shine in this recording, to put it mildly.  Then the little choir of inquisitors stumps on to the scene.  Karajan's conducting makes them sound like a crocodile of elephants in the circus, holding on to the tail of the beast in front of them with their trunks.  It is risible.  Karajan usually shines in these big spectacle numbers but his direction makes this music sound like a local band in the town square bumping through La forza del Destino overture, not like Verdi at his greatest, which is what this opera is!

Thomas Moser (the royal herald) sings the a-capella ditty like he was singing Celeste Aida or something.  Very overdone and unsubtle and not ceremonially grand or impressive at all as EVERY OTHER herald on record manages to do, and with much less voice than Mr Moser possessed.  Again, I suspect Karajan's bad taste was the culprit here.  The Auto da fé scene slogs on with the droopiest bunch of Flemish ministers imaginable.  Sadly this DeMille spectacular ends with Edita Gruberova's hard and clunky singing of the Heavenly Voice, who sounds more like she came from the Other Place.

Act IV is my favorite act of all of Verdi's output.  The King's study is the scene of a gripping meditation for Philip brooding about how the queen never loved him.  Verdi reveals this very complex personality vividly and most movingly.  This is immediately followed by the over-powering confrontation with the Grand Inquisitor, always, for me, the great highlight of this opera.

Raimondi does a good job, very good in fact, though he sounds over-directed by Herr Meister and his voice sometimes disappears into sudden sloughs of diminuendo that are hard to hear.  And Karajan lapses into Liebestod mode at the end of the King's monologue, all tremolo strings and shivering mysticism that isn't suitable to this character or this opera.

The main reason I purchased this set was for Matti Salminen's otherwise unrecorded portrayal of the baleful Grand Inquisitor.  He satisfied my expectations.  His magnificent bass voice is the equal, if not the superior, to his compatriot Martti Talvela (Solti). He alone uplifts this performance to the levels of greatness, even though Karajan's conducting is too smooth and lacking all volcanism.  Salminen, however, sounds far too young, virile to the point of athleticism, not the voice of a 90 year old decrepit, albeit dangerous, priest from the Pleistocene Age.

And Karajan fails to generate any sense of growing danger or hellfire spirit in this great scene.  The tension does not build in the least.  His conducting is flaccid and smooth.  The awesome surging of the lower strings near the end of the Inquisitor's threats goes for little.  It's all very neat and clean and pretty, but not powerful.

Agnes Baltsa's 'O, Don Fatale' is marred by her gasping for air, same as in the Veil Song in Act 1.  And she runs out of breath on the last high note and goes flat as the voice slides away.  She is heard to much better effect in the EMI set from the previous year.  If you want to know what a great mezzo can do in a live performance of this role listen to Elena Obraztsova for Abbado in Milan.  And SHE sings both verses of the Veil Song, plus the often-omitted scene with Elisabetta when she dons the queen's mask, which is the cause of all the trouble to come, and proceeds to blast the putti off the plaster pilasters with O, Don Fatale after a very long evening.

Cappuccilli cracks slightly on the last note of his big aria before he is shot.  No applause.  His death is melodramatically performed, smacking of Karajanitis again.  Cappuccilli and Raimondi suffer the most from the Meister's amateurish stage direction.

José Carreras is good but tries too hard.  He is much better on the studio set where he had time to rest and recoup over what must have been several days of recording sessions.  Mirella Freni forces too often to be touching in her two big arias.  The deeply moving aria  'Non pianger, mia compagna' is crudely sung by Freni.  There isn't a shred of heart, just vocal showing off, and it isn't much to show off, frankly.

Her 'Tu che le Vanità is almost 'bad'.  She screams her way through it and her low notes are non-existent.  No subtlety at all.  Listen to Margaret Price on Abbado's live set from Milan and the difference is like night and day.  Like Freni, Margaret Price was a lyric soprano, and not naturally suited to the heavier Verdi roles, but Price, with her bigger and more beautiful voice, invests every note she sings with her heart and soul and a great deal more nuance than Freni can muster.

Austrian Radio's sound is good enough but the mic'ing is lopsided and brings too many wobbly sopranos in the chorus to the fore.  Overall the singers do not disappear into the depths of the upstage area and are always audible.  Their diction is also generally very good as well which is something in a live performance.

Karajan is the fiend here.  Self-indulgent in the extreme in what appears to have been a big ego fest for him and his followers in Vienna that night in May of 1979.  And to add insult to injury he introduces an enormous Ima Sumac GONG crash as the mysterious monk reappears at the end of Act V.  This is simply vulgar.  He used a gong in his party recording of Lohengrin (EMI) too.  Gongs are not used in Wagner and the only gong I have heard elsewhere in Verdi is in Gardelli's recording of I Due Foscari, an early opera from Verdi's melodramatic years.  But he never used it again as far as I know.

Really, sometimes Karajan was so kitschy it is almost impossible to take him seriously.  Then you hear his last and magnificent recording of Bruckner's 8th or Sibelius 4th and the conundrum is complete.

The last pill associated with this release that I refused to swallow is all the gushing adulation of the booklet blurbs, written in the the most nauseating sycophantic language.

This is the worst recording of Don Carlo that I've ever heard, worse even than Pappano's live version from the Chtelet Theater in Paris. Pappano had the advantage of a very good lead couple in Roberto Alagna and Karita Mattila which makes up for the deficiencies elsewhere, notably the worst Eboli EVER in Waltraud Meier.  And there are also some interesting differences in the French version he adopts, a hybrid of some kind, and Van Dam's King is good as well.

I admit to not caring much for the revised and 'improved' Reader's Digest four act version of this glorious opera but knew Karajan never conducted any of the five act versions, either the original French or the various transmutations in Italian.  I love the five act 'Modena' version.  It is basically the original French version translated into Italian.  Abbado recorded it live in Milan in 1978 (available on BellaVoce in a fine sounding transfer) and Levine for Sony in 1992.  Both of those sets begin Act 1 (the 'Fontainebleau' act, eliminated in the revised 4 act version) with the chorus of peasants and not the hunting horn calls which always begin the more familiar 5-Act Italian version.  Whatever version you hear you will still hear some of the greatest music ever penned by Verdi, or anyone else for that matter.

If you love Don Carlo don't waste your money on this Karajan circus abortion, unless, like me, you want Salminen's gargantuan voice as the Inquisitor, then it is almost worth the high cost of this release, but he doesn't get his awesomely threatenings lines in Act 5.  And this IS an expensive proposition from Orfeo, seeing as the performance has been sliced and diced to such an extent that it would almost, by about 6 minutes, fit onto two compact discs.  Act IV begins  on the 2nd disc here so Baltsa's not-so-great 'O, Don Fatale' would end the disc.  As a result the 3rd disc contains only 34 minutes of music.  And don't think that for $44.00 Orfeo will supply you with a libretto, let alone a translation.  The booklet is all balls-aching hyperbole about Karajan and photos of the production.

Unless you are a glassy-eyed Karajan completist this release from Orfeo is a rip-off .  I felt like a sucker for falling for it, but I wanted Salminen's Inquisitor.  His EMI set is the better 'performance' though it is a product of the Karajan recording cannery.

For those who are not all that familiar with this towering masterpiece and haven't fallen under its spell I strongly recommend Solti's set from the 1960s at Covent Garden (Decca).  His Act IV will knock your socks off with Nicolai Ghiaurov's King and the unequaled Martti Talvela's Inquisitor going at it vocal hammer and tongs to electrifying effect.  You will never be the same.
Giulini's great set on EMI is also a wonderful recording.  And, surprisingly, Bernard Haitink's set on Philips is quite wonderful as well.  You should have all three of those, plus Abbado's French original on DGG.  Levine's Sony set is hobbled by a matronly and wobbly Elisabetta in Aprile Millo and an Eboli, Dolora Zajick, who seems more interested in imitating an air-raid siren than she is being a human character, but she sings magnificently nonetheless.

For a great live event you can do no better than the Abbado/Milan 1978 Modena version on BellaVoce with the glorious Margaret Price, Plácido Domingo, Elena Obraztsova, Renato Bruson and a splendid King in Yvgeny Nesterenko.  That evening makes ditch water out of Der Meister's wallow in Vienna.

Not their worst, but certainly a failing effort. The only Marilyn Manson I can reccomend is "Mechanical Animals", which, although a turnabout departure from their familiar black/goth stylings, had a host of sonic equity to spare through the entire record. Not one track on "Golden" comes close to matching that record's glam-rock swagger. Perhaps they need Michael Beinhorn back at the producing console. Also, Manson, I reccomend you look deep inside, instead of at the universal exterior, to come up with personal meaning for your next musical objective. Third, and finally, "Independent Woman PART 1." "PART 1?!?" Where's "PART 2" or "PART 3?"

reviewText:
Back when they first started putting environmental ambience on vinyl disks, the people who put the albums together used to actually do things like go into the woods during a rainstorm and record the natural sounds.  I guess those days are gone for good.

Now they seem to feel a burning need to either "enhance" the nature sounds with bland music (thankfully that's not been done here), or to "simulate" natural ambient sounds with various studio techniques.  As far as I can tell, if this has ever been done successfully, it's not been available on CD.  And it's not available here:  this recording is one of those failed attempts at synthesizing the natural.

Most of the rain here sounds like it was looped from the sound of water running out of a leaky gutter into a narrow cement-surfaced alley.  And I am being charitable with that description: my first impression was that this was recorded in somebody's bathroom, with the shower running.  Real rainstorms are rarely so heavy for so long, nor so densely "wet" sounding.  The real sound is more like white noise with the occasional gurgle of water, and not like a firehose turned on a swimming pool.  This alleged "rain" is anything but "relaxing" -- listening to this makes me feel like I'm about to drown.

reviewText:
Yet again, the Zappa Family Trust have botched up an archival release - feigning to have paid some attention to the needs of the more knowledgeable fans, before delivering a...perversion of the fans' suggestion!

Memo to the Zappa Family Trust: If you're confining yourself to a single CD in which to represent the Petite Wazoo, you most definitely do not include this kind of material at the EXPENSE OF the many superior, less guitar-heavy improvisations this band played (what of "Little Dots/Approximate"?), and their superb arrangements of tunes like "America Drinks And Goes Home", "Don't You Ever..." and most of all "Duke of Prunes" - all of which have been bootlegged in the past.

Yes, there was a need for a Petite Wazoo CD - so long as it documented what made this band special: the arrangements and the variety of soloists on hand.  This does not.

Only two tracks are satisfactory: "Farther O'Blivion" (aka the "Greggery Peccary"/"Bebop Tango"/"Cucamonga" medley) and the excellent "Been To Kansas City In A Minor".

The rest - oh dear!  The title track is an underwhelming bit of funk - this and the subsequent "Montreal" may feature someone's idea of "hot guitar solos" but they'll bore the hell out of other listeners who recognise that Frank The Improviser was far from his best at this point: easily the worst soloist in his own band.

"DC Boogie" and the "Oddients" intro may be fun pieces of stage folklore, but they don't belong here.

The four tracks mentioned above would however have been acceptable or at least forgivable in the context of a double-CD.

reviewText:
I don't know what all of the 5-star reviewers are listening to; maybe I got a different version of Sam's Town.  All I know is this album is a complete mess.  I don't understand how a band can put out a nearly flawless debut album, a couple of good extra tracks in the interim ("Glamorous Indie Rock and Roll" and "The Ballad of Michael Valentine"), and then crank out something as bad as this.

I wasn't expecting them to give us Hot Fuss 2, but I certainly wasn't expecting this.  It is hard for me to put my finger on exactly what is wrong with this album, but I think alot of it has to do with the absolute disconnect between the vocals and the background tracks.  I'm not exaggerating when I say that I could only listen to about 5 or 6 tracks before I got a headache.  It sounds like they laid down the background tracks first and then had Flowers stand at the mike and make up the vocals impromtu--it's that bad.  What makes things even worse is that the lyrics are as insipid as lyrics get.  You get gems like "feel my bones on your bones"  and "I see London I see France"--no wait it's "I see London I see Sam's Town."

All in all, Sam's Town was a tremendous disappointment to me.  This was an album I had been looking forward to for months because their first album was so great.  But, it looks like some people really liked it, so I maybe I just don't get it.  But I would definitely borrow it and give it a listen before you go and drop $15 for it.

reviewText:
Talk about a fall from grace. Wait, wait, back up. Talk about dropping all you have off a cliff. I consider Jethro Tull's work from 1969-1972 classic, with the best being 1969's Stand Up. But this... what is this? For one, it's one of the records that killed progressive rock's reputation. (I enjoy the genre a lot, too, and feel it gets unfairly underrated) - the other two are Yes' Tales of Topographic Oceans (I love Yes, but I never saw where they were going with that one - amazing instrumental work, though), and Genesis' Lamb Lies Down on Broadway (which I, in spite of being a moderate Genesis fan, have never heard). Really, this has got to be the worst of them. And Thick as a Brick was stellar! My second-favorite Tull release, in fact. That was a dead-on satire of "over-intellectualism" and "prfound thought" that, in its own way, managed to be a deep look at how easily society is manipulated by poets and wise men spouting nonsense. That's exactly what Anderson becomes here: a wise man spouting nonsense, only Bibically inspired nonsense. It has none of the quick-witted sarcasm that made Brick such a riot. And the stylistic variety that kept Brick from wearing thin. And the little instrumental blurbs that gave Brick its variety. They're there, but there's no balance in them. TAAB gave Anderson, Barre, Evan, Hammond-Hammond and Barlow equal time to shine. This is almost entirely devoted to Anderson and his variety of woodwinds, which has at this point expanded into soprano and sopranino saxophones; and Evan, who plays a LOT of organ and pseudoclassical piano. Martin Barre, who was always my favorite musician in the group, gets pusehd aside.
I commented earlier on the lyrics, but I thought I'd go in depth with that. What inspired Anderson to go from mocking pompous pseudomysticalism to actually singing pompous pseudomysticalism? Ian's obviously quite sarcastic - that's his whole schtick - which means it's also quite hard to believe whether or not he's ever sincere - the Aqualung album being my exception to that rule. So that makes me wonder: was Thick as a Brick representitive of Ian's honest thoughts on overintellectualism? Or was he, in essence, mocking those who mocked it? Or, alternatively, did he just let Thick as a Brick's success go to his head, which in turn led to him saying, "It's okay if I write these overblown, dead-serious lyrics, just because it's me doing it. Everybody else who does so is a wanker, though"? Really is something for me to ponder. I'll get back to you when I've made up my mind on it.
Right, and here's the biggest problem: Anderson got so carried away with his cliche-loaded, keyboard, flute, and sax happy Grandiose Statement that he forgot one tiny little detail: writing any real melodies that really stick with you. That's another thing that Thick as a Brick had going for it. All kinds of melodies. I'm not saying everything has to be shallow, vapid, face-value entertainment (I am a jazz fan, after all), but there's just nothing to latch onto here. For me, music needs some form of hooks to keep it from going astray - the lack thereof was precisely what went wrong with King Crimson's Moonchild, but that's another story. It's also one of the many things that goes wrong with this album. The only melody that really grabs me is the "Overseer Overture" part, which is my favorite bit on the whole record. On the other end, my least favorite is probably the opening three parts: "Life Beats" (just random noisemaking, again like Moonchild), "Prelude" (mericfully brief indulgent jamming), and "The Silver Cord" (gives us a taste of what the lyrics will be like, though the piano's pretty). I don't approve of either "Forest Dance", while I'm complaining. Though the entire album is just dry, unimaginative, overblown, and lacking. Basically, I can't recommend this. I know it has its ardent supporters, and I'm not here to give them a hard time about it (though I know SOMEone will give ME a hard time about my intense dislike of this disaster). I'm just saying, I don't think it's very good. And I would love to read a review of this by someone who thought this was the masterpiece and Brick was the indulgent bomb. But yeah, this doesn't make the grade. I guess sometimes the band catches fire, but it's a very occasional thing, and when they do, they don't keep it going for long.

Nick Cave and his Bad Seeds have produced some monumental albums - Your Funeral My Trial, Tender Prey, The Good Son, Let Love In.  But somewhere around Nocturama the wheels started getting all wobbly.  It happens in a career of this length.

Blixa Bargeld left.  Jim Sclavunos started taking over the drum seat from Thomas Wydler.  Then the final nail... longtime songwriter/arranger Mick Harvey left.  Cave was now writing mostly with Warren Ellis, and while they've produced some great soundtracks, I just don't like the direction they've gone.  Not only has the personnel completely turned over, the sound has very little to do with the golden years of the Bad Seeds, when even the ballads had a sense of malice and brooding danger bubbling beneath the surface.

The last 10 years just seem to be riding on the fumes of past glory, and what's amazing is they're more successful than ever!  Just goes to show...

I hope that Maiden doesn't rest on this.  This would be a sad end to an illustrous career.  Think Sabbath's Forbidden in 1995.

Kevin Shirley can't get anything out of the band.  He is clearly a "yes man" because he brings nothing to the table.  What a joke.  Get Birch, get Tsangarides, get Roy Z, get anybody else!

Poseurs will deride me, true fans will listen to this album and realise how bad it is.  There is nothing remarkable about this album.  BNW had several good songs.  DOD had Paschendale and Rainmaker, AMOLAD was excellent!  I am not just against new Maiden, I am against bad Maiden.  Speaking of "new Maiden", there are no fast paced Gers songs.  No Gers at all except for one rather bland track.  There is nothing on this album worth hearing, even Adrian Smith sounds lazy.  Buyer beware!

reviewText:
I guess that makes sense, since Journey's music is incredibly slick and processed - it represents the triumph of commerce over art, which plagued rock music until the early '90s.  Some people might have enjoyed this back in the day (you had to - radio stations played them incessantly) but for anyone that enjoys it, it's a total guilty pleasure - how many people do you know that blast Journey out of their car windows, or wear their shirts?  I thought so.
Credit where it's due: Neal Schon was a heck of a guitar player, and Steve Perry actually can sing.  However, the band couldn't write songs to save their lives, and Perry's voice was better suited for Broadway instead of a rock and roll band.  Sure, the songs might have had memorable choruses, but at their core they were completely empty - dependent on repetition of the chorus to the point where it will make you scream.
Subject matter is a weak point with this band - there's such a dearth of inspiration with these songs.  Apparently the only thing that they were capable of writing about were relationships - that means there's plenty of drippy "I'll love you forever" stuff and breakup songs as well.  For a band that is as popular as these guys have been, listening to these songs will make you wonder what everyone sees in them.
In summary: Pick up this album if you enjoy hearing overwrought, hackneyed, slick corporate rock.  There's more cheese on this album than you'll find in the state of Wisconsin!

I remember reading in a newspaper, a few years ago and a teacher saying to his pupil: "you have the worst singing voice I have ever heard in my life".  The pupil in question was Sting.  Indeed, I find it very hard not to agree with his former teacher, for this is the kind of voice that no amount of singing practice would improve - colourless, emotionless and powerless, akin to the sound of a saxophone being played with a damaged reed.  Nonetheless, his music seems to have found favour with some music consumers, reflected in inexplicable record sales figures.
Despite having not been blessed with a heart-warming, microphone-breaking voice, there is a hint of quality in his work both musically and lyrically, where some political and environmental issues are addressed.  However, not even the best session musicians that grace some of his albums, is enough to lift them above mediocrity.
One shouldn't be fooled into thinking that because environmental concerns are expressed in Sting's songs, one is hearing the voice of someone with immaculate green credentials.  In fact, quite the opposite is true.  This is the classic example of "do as I say not as I do".  Here we have a man who has a few abodes scattered around the world(some of which he rarely visits), where he travels in first class along with his entourage and reportedly once requested that one of his personal cooks, travel an outrageous distance just to prepare a meal to a particularly demanding member of his family, because in true British, fingernail-sparing fashion, his wife can't or won't cook, the latter being the most likely.
Walking past a shopping centre in Geneva(Switzerland)in the late eighties, I noticed an unusually big queue stretching out onto the pavement, with people clutching records and books.  Consumed with curiosity, I approached to have a closer look.  A long-haired man was sitting at a desk and scribbling his signature on books, while barely lifting his head to ackowledge the enthusiastically grinning buyers.  It was Sting.  Sitting beside him, was a half-naked indian, from an Amazonian tribe, sporting a disc on his lower lip that stretched it to a painful and unimaginable size.  I was informed that he(Sting) was on a book-signing world tour, promoting a book about the Amazon rainforest and the plight of its tribes as a result of deforestation.  There was people trying to have records signed, only to be ignored or told that it was against the publisher's wishes or more importantly, in this case, Sting's.  No item other than Sting's book would be signed.
While I have nothing but praise, when celebrities come together to raise money for humanitarian causes, I am sceptical when they try to lecture the world on issues beyong the scope of their professional activities and cannot credibly look at them without thinking that there might be a more sinister, underlying reason.
This was the most nauseating display of hypocrisy and greed I had the misfortune to witness.  It almost spoiled the rest of my day.  A conspicuous publicity stunt, in which a poor indian was being paraded around the world and used as a marketing tool in order to sell books and in the process, inflate the bank balance of unscrupulous publishers and the so-called environmentally conscious.
Sadly, the poor native Amazonian indian got very little in return for all his trouble, as the trees in his beloved rainforest continue to be relentlessly felled at an alarming rate.
Undoubtedly, Sting has seen a gap in the book market, where there was money to be made and promptly exploited it, with rudeless efficiency.  This, in itself, should be enough to persuade him to give up his lousy music career and become a businessman.
As for his environmental concerns, it seems that unorgasmic, energy-saving tantric sex, are Sting's only green credentials.

reviewText:
The Curmudgeon never has been, nor ever will be, what you would call a major Michael Jackson fan but there really is no denying that, before the baby dangling and kiddie fiddling antics and the frightening plastic surgery and, well, everything else that turned him into an off-putting laughing stock, before all that - Michael Jackson was quite simply one of the greatest pop stars on the planet. Innovative, exciting, mysterious - basically everything that absolutely NO pop star is nowadays. Jackson really did seem like he came from some fantastic alternative universe, creating some jaw dropping, magnificent pop records - Thriller being one of them.

So it comes as absolutely no shock that one of the all-time essential albums gets a 25th anniversary edition. Quite as to WHY we really need another edition, when you consider that it was re-released as a Special Edition a few years back, not to mention the fact that every single was re-released only last year - really Mike, how much longer do you expect your glassy-eyed, weirdo obsessive fans to buy the same music time and time again?

Anyway, you're probably wondering WHY Thriller, one of the greatest albums of all time, from one of the greatest pop stars of all time, is sitting alongside the very worst Amazon has to offer in the Curmudgeon's reviews?

Because, not only is it a cheap cash in, not only is it unwarranted, not only is it MISSING actual album tracks from the previous Special Edition, but because the main selling point here isn't Thriller itself - more the "previously un-released" (read - knocked up about a week ago) bonus tracks, featuring remixes and covers from such luminaries as Will. I.Am and Fergie.

Are you scared yet?

Gentle reader, you SHOULD be. For tacked on at the end of the album are 5 horrific, worthless, pointless remixes that clearly anyone could and should do without. Did you ever want to hear Dead Eyed Peas "singer" Fergie strain through "Beat It?" Not in a million years, obviously - but you can now! Did you ache to hear a new version of Wanna Be Starting Somethin', but this time with Akon and Will. I.Am? Only if suicide swiftly followed, surely - but it's on here too.

People like Akon and Fergie don't even deserve to be mentioned in the same sentence as someone like Michael Jackson, yet here they are stinking up a classic album, an album that some poor kid is going to think is the REAL Thriller record. It's like Bob Dylan re-releasing Blonde On Blonde but with Fred Durst on vocals.

An abomination, then. By all means add Thriller to your record collection. In no way, shape or form make it this version.

reviewText:
Time machine to 1995 trance anyone?  Where do I start... well CD1 was alright, but nothing too special; pretty forgetable really.  Around track 12-end we begin the time warp that REALLY continues on CD2.  Seriously this is the most formulaic trance one could possibly create.  One could write a computer program to spit out tracks like this.  Here's how it goes (see if this sounds familiar to you):

1) track starts off bumpin' following a played out, static 8 count rhythem of A-C-B-D pitch (ie high sounds 2 count, low 2 count, almost as high as before 2 count, lil lower than the low 2 count) ...or quickly builds to this point
2) suddenly the bass/beat/everything completely stops ~1:30 to 2:00 into the song
3) 2-3 seconds of silence
4) enter either: a) operatic/cheesy female vocal; b) high synth you've heard 1000 times before
5) surprise surprise! track starts to slowly layer back in the mid beat and build up volume/"wall of sound"
6) a COMPLETELY played out very fast dut-dut-dut-dut-dut beat or static note signaling the big climax!
7) the bass beat finally re-enters and the song is bumpin' as before (by now we're about 3:00-4:00 into the track)
8) static 8 count of A-C-B-D follows for 1 minute
9) bass drops out again, but not the mid beat so as to create a slight dip in the song once again, yet still dancable and rocking, just not as much as before
10) full bass quickly returns within 30 seconds
11) static 8 count once again follows for another minute or 2
12) next track mixes in abruptly, but is OK because it's the same bass tempo and same sound
13) rinse and repeat

Seriously!  Play CD2 tracks 9, 10, 11 right now and tell me you haven't heard this 1,000,000 times before!  YOU CAN'T DENY THIS IT IS FACT!!!  I've been listening to trance/techno/EDM/house/progressive/D&B/dubstep/etc. since the early 1990's and as I listened to this I seriously was asking myself, "Is this supposed to be the best of trance?  Maybe I just don't like trance anymore?  All these songs sound the exact same and on top of that, sound the exact same as tracks that came out 15 years ago.  I've been listening to a lot more progressive/house/dubstep lately..... so MAYBE IT'S ME???"

NO!  It's not me!  I love good trance and this is garbage!  Even the latest Anjunabeats was weak and forgettable.  DJs/producers keep recycling the same sounds vs innovating.

ASOT = the new Ministry of Sound

Really though, you should look for these songs as performed by great Jazz artists like Diana Krall, Frank Sinatra, Chet Baker, Eileen Farrell, Bill Charlap, Stan Getz, Tony Bennett, Ben Webster or Billie Holiday.  You would be amazed at how great these songs are when performed by someone with the musical ability to provide a valid interpretation.  Rod must be laughing all the way to the bank!  His rock and roll material is awesome-no question. But he has neither the talent nor the skill to successfully interpret this material.  His croaking efforts make me cringe!!!!  Perhaps Kermit should consider recording some romantic songbook material?

I just hope other aging rockers don't decide to cash in and emulate Rod. Can you imagine Robert Plant warbling "Stairway to the Stars"? Or Mick Jagger growling "You'd Be So Nice To Come Home To"?  If Jim Morrison were still around, I guess I wouldn't mind hearing his version of "Sleep Warm".  After all, he was a serious fan of Frank Sinatra and had the chops to successfully mimic some elements of Frank's style in some of his better love songs!

One rock artist who can turn in credible interpretations of this type of music is Brian Ferry. Check out his "As Time Goes By" CD. As Time Goes By

reviewText:
I thought I had written a review for this product when it released, but I was apparently so angry I simply imagined doing so.

All you really need to know is that much of the music used in 300 was plagiarized, most notably from Elliot Goldenthal's work for Titus.  I am not speaking of a fleeting reference or inspiration here, folks, but of verbatim copying.  Orchestration, rhythm, dynamics, tempo...all identical.  I am, of course, specifically referring to Bates copying the piece from Titus entitled "Victorious Titus" to compile "Returns a King."

How Tyler Bates managed to get away with such blatant theft and continue to score subsequent films is truly baffling.  Many criticize other composers of copying constantly (Hans Zimmer's Gladiator from Gustav Holst's Mars, John Williams' Jaws from Antonin Dvorak's From the New World, etc.), but Tyler Bates has set a new standard for thievery in the modern age of film scores.
label: negative

reviewText:
The other day, while surfing through music sites on the net i saw Marilyn Manson's name twice (on different sites) being mentioned as "Marilyn Mainstream". Now, there's some food for thought.
This album did -of course- ride the charts as had previous horror "Holywood". Mission then accomplished.
  Manson has been constantly undermining whatever it was that he stood for (and there could be a whole catalogue of opinions about this). The momentum, but above all, the excitement generated by albums like "Antichrist Superstar" or "Mechanical animals" or even, before these, the more indepedent releases (Portrait of an american family) has withered to a long forgotten but sweet memory.

  I hear (and read) that Manson wishes to relive an era of pre-WWII-Berlin with this album. Ok. There's nothing wrong of course with installing some healthy retro touches into your music. Not if there's any substance to it. But is there any here?
  With song titles (and lyrics) that resemble something like "Kabooma-booma" or "Bazza-buzzo-bozzo-mojomuffin" any discussions about substance are far stretched. And the music? All done before but better (even by Manson himself) with the added element that not one of the here offered songs approaching the "memorable level". I apologise for being mild by the way.

  Another thing that impressed me is that Manson has reduced himself to a kinda Eminem-metal guy thumping his chest and screaming how's he's gonna write a rock n roll hit and what he's gonna do with all the dough he's gonna pull in from it. Hmm. That's all very nice and interesting but why should we all care?
  Fact is, increasingly more people are refusing to care about Manson's wishes. That might not hindern Manson from riding the charts, but then again, C.Aguilera is riding the charts too and so are dozens of boy groups and other oddities as well. Manson is beginning to be in good company. Because if horror is his mission i couldn't imagine a bigger horror than glancing at the charts at any given day.
  Having uttered what i just did, i think that the Alice Cooper sequel for this era has reached its sad end. For those a little older in age, it must be mentioned that Cooper's artistic end wasn't pretty. You noticing any similarities?
  Overall, this is an album-monument to nothingness. Musically, lyrically and image-wise. Being that it has -naturally- quite some success financially as it fits perfectly with its times. But this is exactly the juxtaposition, the contradiction here. Manson built his name by trying to oppose his times.
  May the next Alice-Cooper-Manson take the stage please. Oh, but wait till the elephants and the clowns have left first.

reviewText:
This album is from 1994 and is Emerson, Lake and Palmer's second studio album since reuniting in 1991.  It has 10 new tracks for a total of 50 minutes.  It includes a new 15 minute version of Pictures at Exhibition, for a total of 65 minutes.  Sound quality is excellent.
Most of the songs on this album are pretty bland but bombastic.  It follows the same style as the previous Black Moon.
The best track on this album is a Greg Lake patented ballad called Daddy.  However, it is one of the most depressing, disturbing songs you will ever hear.  It is about a single father who has his young daughter kidnapped and murdered.  Although the murderer is caught, they are never able to recover the body for a proper burial.  All throughout the song, the father imagines his daughter calling out to take her home.
The only other good song is a cover of Dylan's Man in the Long Black Coat.  Street War is OK.
This version of Pictures At An Exhibition is supposed to be special because it is recorded with an orchetra and was recorded in Dolby Digital.  It is just another unnecessary version of the piece.  It is already on 4 other live albums.  And this is one of those truncated versions, so it comes off as sounding just like an excerpt.
Emerson, Lake and Palmer's reunion was not very succesful.  The two studio albums contained mostly bad songs (I don't how anyone can say one was great while the other one was bad.  They both sound basically the same).  Their live albums from this period were fairly unimpressive.  There was a very nice version of Tarkus on Live at Albert Hall, but the rest was just old rehashing.  It was interesting to see to them on Jay Leno though.  It just seems wierd to see these rock bands on the late night talk shows.  It used to be that rock was outside of the mainstream.

For some reason fans of Ulver continue to hang on to this band and pretend everything they release is pure gold. It's not. It's pointless noise. All their music sounds like random bits of guitars, vocals, keyboards and synthesizers slapped together with no real purpose. And don't give me the "that's how it is meant to sound" line. Hogwash.

Ulver is a band who likes to experiment with sounds. That's it. You're not hearing something everyone else is not. This album does nothing to change my mind. To quote Type O Negative: don't mistake lack of talent for genius.

If you like droning, pointless noise then this is your album. If you like substance, if you like creative song structure rather than random piecing together of sounds, if you like your music to sound purposeful rather than accidental then go look somewhere else on Amazon and stay away from Ulver.

And why do so many people continue to label this band as metal? Black metal even! Metal fans -- especially black metal fans -- don't be fooled by the labels. Ulver is about as metal as a plastic spork. At one time they may have had some black metal elements, but that was a long time ago. If you like all the elements of black metal besides the guitars, bass, drums and vocals then go ahead and give it a try. Imagine Dimmu Borgir with no guitars, no drums and no vocals. Maybe that's black metal. Maybe it's just noise.

tastefully done.  I'm usually one of those who hates doctored up old recordings, but this is so well done. It's okay.
The German collection also has more songs which includes great recordings from the other labels Decca and Commodore. For some reason the set is missing four great tracks (Strange Fruit, Yesterdays, Fine And Mellow and

Fine and Mellow either. The American set only deals with the Columbia sides, but does give you lots of
alternate takes, which the set from Germany avoids. But that's alright, I just want the official recording, not
the alternates or outtakes as I call them.
As far as packaging, the American set wins hands down, but the imported German set does have a nice
40 page booklet and is better about protecting your CD's and most importantly...far better sound quality.

reviewText:
Hey I understand that most rock musicians see hearing loss as a badge of honour, and want their gigs 2 dB away from ear drum perforation, so I suppose they might not know just how bad this cd sounds.  But if you have normal hearing and are under 90 you'll probably think your stereo is broken when you put this disc on.  The only other rock disc that sounds worse that I've heard is the '97 remaster of Iggy & the Stooges' Raw Power.

For those that don't know, this cd is the product of the so called "Loudness War", you can Google that term for more info.  In a nutshell, what that is is the attempt by the mastering guy (although sometimes the mixer and the recording engineer as well) to jam as much signal as possible onto the recording medium.  How they do this is they make the loud parts quieter so that everything is one volume.  Then they can amplify that volume to the maximum.  That is why a cd from the 80's is approx 1/2 the volume of one from the 00's.

They make the louder parts quieter by digital manipulation, and when it its taken too far you get digital distortion, clipping, and zero dynamics.  The end result is loss of audio information, degradation of the sound, and the removal of any dynamics.  And dynamics are important, it is a vital part of how we express emotion through sound.  Mozart believed a singers ability to modulate volume within a single note and between groups of notes was so important it was the first thing he looked for when evaluating talent.  He saw it as a vital means of communication and a vital part of the power and emotionality of music. (you can read more about Mozart's thoughts in a book called "Mozart Speaks", which collects some of his letters).

Anyway, this cd has clipped waves galore, approx 4 dB of dynamic range, and will induce listener fatigue in a matter of minutes.

reviewText:
Stay away from this CD if you're a fan of the Jeff Beck who brought us "Blow by Blow," "Wired," "There and Back," "Guitar Shop," "Jeff," "You Had It Coming" and "Live at Ronnie Scott's." This new CD is a snoozefest compared to any of them. This CD should have been called something like "The Mellow Moods of Jeff Beck," but even the word "mellow" suggests there's more energy in this music than there is.

Seriously: Beck playing around with "Over the Rainbow" doesn't belong on a CD. It's best left to his six-string musings in his living room. The problem with this song is the problem that plagues most of this disc: He doesn't sound emotionally engaged. I'm a fan of the Jeff Beck whose guitar squawks like a squeezed cat with fireworks shooting out of its a**; the Jeff Beck who sounds as if he has eight fingers on each hand because no one could possibly play what he does with just five fingers on each hand. There's almost none of it on this disc. And when he does try to amp it up with "Hammerhead," he apparently forgets that some of us are old enough to remember Hendrix's "Voodoo Chile (Slight Return)."

reviewText:
Bush remains to this day one of the bands least deserving of its success. And yet they still manage to sell millions and prompt positive critical response. Since its release this album has gone five times platinum, on practically no merit.

This album is so derivative it hurts. Listen to Smells Like Teen Spirit from Nevermind, then listen to Little Things. The ... from Nirvana are grossly apparent. Kurt is rolling in his grave.
And when they're not ripping off Nirvana, they're swiping riffs and even entire song structures from the Pixies, Pearl Jam, and a million other alternative bands that are far more worthy than Bush will ever be.
The lyrics are just thrown together, stream of consciousness ramblings penned by Gavin (OOO, he's so HOT!) at the last minute. It's clear that the band members have no technical ability, and just repeat the same stale grunge riffs over and over. Even the production is a waste, and makes this music sound even less energetic.
I've talked to Bush fans. Even they admit that they can't stand three-quarters of Sixteen Stone, and only listen to the singles (Everything Zen, Comedown, Machinehead, Glycerine). I'll admit, the singles are a little catchy. But original? Interesting? I'll take the Pixies, Nirvana, or Soundgarden over this turgid mass-market slop anyday.

reviewText:
From the lean, mean, thrash machine they once were, Metallica have become fat, bloated rock dinosaurs of the type they once despised. The transformation from velociraptor - speedy, sharp and dangerous - to diplodocus - slow, docile and blundering - has been distressing for long time fans to watch.
The biggest problem here is that most of the songs are simply not suited for orchestral accompaniment. Like attempting to mix oil and water, it just doesn't work. The band really would have been better to admit the experiment did not work, cut their losses and release a four song EP of the tracks that actually DID work.
Let's be positive here. The tracks that they do pull off are excellent. The obvious one is "The Call Of The Ktulu". The instrumental from 'Ride The Lightning' is the oldest track here, and definitely the best, which is a shame because it's straight after the intro track, and the next two hours are basically a waste of time. Strangely, the only other song from the first four albums which even approaches "The Call..." is "For Whom The Bell Tolls", which is given a huge, militaristic movie soundtrack feel, like something out of `Ben Hur' or `Gladiator'.
"No Leaf Clover" was obviously written with this performance in mind. The band lay off a little, allowing the orchestra to flood through. The strings, woodwind and brass sections weave in and out of the simple melody. Unfortunately, the other new track "Human" is, for want of a better word,.... The gentle "Nothing Else Matters" is given added facets by the orchestra, although they are obvious, as the original also has orchestral backing.
"Bleeding Me" almost works, as do a number of other tracks, but they are very patchy. The odd introduction or bridge is good, but it is never consistent enough for a whole song.
Thrashers like "Fuel", "Master Of Puppets", "One" and "Battery" are absolutely ridiculous. Violins, horns, and triangles just do not belong in a song where someone is shouting "Gimme fuel, gimme fire, gimme that which I desire!" over them. Nor do Jason Newsted's barked backing vocals fit.
In other places, violins play the counter-guitar lines, which are either multi-tracked or where Kirk Hammett's leads would normally be. A third guitar player would have been better than making some unfortunate violinists who have spent decades mastering their art fill in the gaps around a simple plodding guitar riff. That is when there actually are gaps. Much of the time, the orchestral instruments seem to be straining to be heard, and come off as superficial decoration. Much of Metallica's career has been built around a gargantuan rhythm guitar sound. It simply stomps over the subtleties of the orchestration, like Godzilla let loose in the Louvre. At other times, the orchestra is a nuisance, where just hearing the band on it's own would be a classic metal moment.
If Metallica were really considerate to their fans, as they used to claim to be before we all started sending them to the poorhouse by stealing their music off the internet, they would have released a reasonable sized unaccompanied live album (not like the overpriced 'Binge/Purge' box set) with the aforementioned orchestral EP as a bonus. Instead, we get the fat Elvis version of Metallica, a self-parody, the once shiny faade dulled by decadence and overblown egos. If you really want Metallica live, get hold of one of the hundreds of bootlegs made of the band. They do not deserve your money for this album.
label: negative

The production is okay but Ja's lackluster rhymes and Bobby Brown's dated over the top singing make the track worser than it had to be. Mesmerize feat Ashanti is hands down the worst song on the album and is the worst song Ja ever made period. The track is too mushy for comfort and corny beyond belief plus the fact that the video was modeled afer the movie Grease is a good enough reason to call for Ja Rule's ousting out of the rap game. Who knew that years later his baby iguana faced archrival 50 Cent, would make a track that is equally as bad that is called Candy Slop. Go figure. Ja butchers Toto's Africa in Murder Reigns also feat Alexi and turns it into boring nonthreatening joint. More butchering would follow as Ja mutilates the Tony Toni Tone's classic Anniversary with a cheesy chick record called Murder Me also feat Cadllac Tah and Alexi. Dishonorable Mentions: Emerica and Rockstar.
Bottom Line: The Last Temptation is the worst album of Ja Rule's career. The production was rank, Ja's rhymes were weak and his singing was horrendous plus the guest appearances(with one exception) hurt the album more than help it. Even if you like Ja Rule don't buy it. Its not worth it.

reviewText:
"What If?"  Indeed...  I never have been a fan of Mr. Big, despite the obvious talent of the blokes who comprise this band.  No doubt Eric Martin has a good voice and Billy Sheehan is one talented bassist (just check out his playing on the first 2 David Lee Roth solo albums for example), and Paul Gilbert's Racer X stuff isn't bad at all either, but Mr. Big just never did it for me and this album does nothing to change that.  Fans of the band will disagree with my review and that's fair enough, everyone is entitled to their opinion and here's mine - like it or not.

The best song on the album is undoubtedly the opening track "Undertow" but even this is nothing special.  Yes the guitars (especially the bass) are very Van Halen-esque but it's nowhere near as good a song as just about any Van Halen tune.  It's just the best of what I can only describe on this album as a collection of very bland, quite often lame to insipid songs.  After the opening tune things fall away pretty quickly with the second track "American Beauty".  The slower paced track three "Stranger In My Life" isn't bad, but again really nothing that good either.  Yet it's way better than the god-awful two tracks that follow in "Nobody Left To Blame" and "Still Ain't Enough For Me".  Then things only get marginally better with the following two tracks "Once Upon A Time" and "As Far As I Can See" because at least they do have a bit of a harder edge.  Next in the track list is a pathetically boring, lame, soppy, semi-pop crap song "All The Way Up", but at least the title is appropriate as the song does indeed cause the contents of my stomach to come all the way up.  "I Won't Get In My Way" follows and this rocks about as hard as the opening the track and would be the second best song on the album.  This one sounds a bit Bon Jovi-esque, as does track 11 "I Get The Feeling" but again these just aren't as good as just about any Bon Jovi tune you care to name.  The album should have ended there but unfortunately I have the version with a bonus track so I had to suffer through one more song which I really could have done without because it's not really worth having.  In fact it wouldn't matter how many bonus tracks they threw on this album, it wouldn't make it good.

I tried to give this album fair playing time before writing this review, to see if it would grow on me but I really would have better spent the time scratching my a#s, removing navel lint or picking my toe nails.  And yes I could still do those things while listening to this album, by why should I make those experiences unpleasant?

What If this was a good album? Well for me the cover says it all.  This is one of the worst albums I've listened to in a long time, and should only be recommended to fans of the band because I expect that they are just about the only people who will enjoy it.  I just can't see them winning many new fans with this stuff.
label: negative

reviewText:
This is the worst R. Kelly CD I've ever heard in my life. He has been the King of R&B (not Bobby Brown, sorry Whitney) for so many years, making hit after hit, I guess it was time for him to make an "oops." Everybody is entitled to an "oops" and this one is his.

He's right up there with Marvin Gaye, Luther Vandross, Donny Hathaway, Brian McKnight and Gerald Levert as far as male vocalists go, but this CD is just garbage. There are only 4 songs that are worth listening to, "Get Freaky in the Club", the song he made for the Virginia Tech victims, the "I'm A Flirt" remix and the song he does with Ludacris. That's about it.

"I'm A Flirt" has an infectious beat but the lyrics are weak. "Don't bring your chick, 'cause I might leave with your chick." Huh? "She be calling me Daddy, I be calling her Mommy, she be calling you Kelly, when your name is Tommy." Huh? Did you write that all by yourself? "Don't bring a b---- to the club when you first meet her." Oh, okay. Maybe after you've known the "b----" after 90 days it'll be okay to take her to the club. You may like "I'm A Flirt" if you listen to the music, but I'm a lyric person and the lyrics are whack. Therefore, I can do without it. Matter of fact, I could do without the whole CD. The only reason I am going to keep it is because it was a gift. I'm glad I didn't pay for it.

Most of these songs are meaningless and he refers to women as b------ quite a bit. "Real Talk" is just embarrassing to listen to. It should have been titled, "Cursing You Out On The Phone." And who wants to hear about two guys being with the same girl? Usher and R. Kelly in the studio together (a magical moment) and they couldn't do any better than that? And how many of us can relate to the guy in prison who loses his girl to his best friend? Yeah, I've been waiting a long time for someone to record a song about that.

It's hard to believe that this is the same man who composed, "You Saved Me." I don't know if he's going through a mid-age crisis, if he's having problems at home, if he's been spending a lot of time in the club or if he is trying to appeal to a younger crowd. If he's trying to reach a younger crowd, I hope they'll continue to support him because if he keeps putting out mess like this, he is going to lose a lot of fans in my age group (mid-30's).

I hope that whatever he is going through that he'll snap out of it and get back to writing songs that have meaning like, "Homie, Lover, Friend," "The Greatest Show on Earth," "Happy People", "For You", "I Believe I Can Fly", "If I Could Turn Back The Hands of Time", "I Can't Sleep" and "Heaven I Need A Hug." And let's not forget the songs he's written for others, "You Are Not Alone" (Michael Jackson), "Magic" and "Charlie, Last Name Wilson, (Charlie Wilson), "More and More" (Joe) and "Quality Time" for Hi-Five.

I still love R. Kelly and I believe that he will redeem himself.
label: negative

reviewText:
Most, if not all, of the seven albums the Moody Blues recorded from 1967 to 1972 are, without argument, among the most innovative and resplendent jewels in the entire history of the rock epoch (although I have yet to espy a five star rating for any of their releases in the numerous rock record guides and encyclopedias currently available).
The Moody Blues, as we all know, initiated classical-rock. Each album was a ruminative landscape of sound, where queries about the cosmos and the essence of being were framed (some fans even approached them for "the answer to the universe" and "to be blessed"!). What seemed like a galaxy of instruments, played gossamer ballads that segued into fulminating rhapsodies. Fluency of melody and pleasantly fluctuating rhythms, combined with the lugubrious poetry of minstrels, became their trademark. For awhile we were, no question, swept into another dimension. Sure, their Weltanschauung may have sometimes been a bit pompous, but this was just their intrepid nature purveying them with limitless imagination--without which no great work of art was ever created. This is what made Berlioz and Wagner orchestral heroes in their day. A plethora of imitators endeavoured to follow the Moody Blues' exemplary vision, many floundering with their soon forgotten trifles.
What the Moody Blues accomplished in their first decade of existence should have awarded them their throne in the temple of titans, where the Byrds, Doors, Jefferson Airplane and others sit in eternal veneration. Yet, as of this writing, induction into the Rock'n'Roll Hall of Fame has eluded them. Why? Perhaps comparing the material they put out from 1978 (after their four year breakup) to the present, with what they did in their glory years in the '60s and early '70s, would provide some elucidation. Excluding the "Journey Into Amazing Caves" soundtrack, in which only a couple of new Moody Blues songs are featured, "Strange Times," from 1999, is their first new offering in about eight years. It approximates just what they have been doing in the studio the last couple of decades: making albums wherein most of the pieces consisted of weak melodies, humdrum rhythms and lyrics about cloying love affairs. But "Strange Times" is the nadir of their output because, unlike their other elevator music recordings, it contains no memorable tunes. This, like all the other stuff they have tried to pull off in their latter days, in no way even approaches what they did in their first decade, described earlier. The intricacy is gone and the mystique is dead. Therefore, there are no works on this CD I would adumbrate as my personal favourites. It is no wonder the Moody Blues--once a legendary rock band that I exalted--are not in the Rock'n'Roll Hall of Fame. The Hall's voting members probably considered what the Moodies had done in the past long while and were not impressed. It hurts to hear them go down like this.
label: negative

reviewText: I'm a fan.  I liked Incesticide.  I liked Sliver.  I liked the deluxe re-issue of Nevermind.  I really dig "Old Age" and "Clean Up Before She Comes".  There are a few really good tracks out there that did not get released on a proper album while Kurt was still alive. Or, if they did get released, they ended up as hard-to-find B-sides.  I'm sorry, but 90% of THIS CD is pure dreck.  As the soundtrack to a documentary, it works.  As a stand-alone product it sucks.  This isn't good music.  This is a series of home experiments that was never meant to see the light of day.  Most of them are unfinished.  Many of the ideas were orphaned, and they deserved to be.  I think that Kurt was great, but that doesn't mean I want to listen to over an hour of him noodling on the guitar into a cheap tape recorder and trying to sort out his ideas.  Not everything he did was commercial, and not everything was even artistically viable.  That's O.K.  My admiration for him remains undiminished, but this CD appears to be a waste of money.  After hearing this, I am now absolutely convinced that there is nothing left to hear from Kurt Cobain.  May he now (finally) rest in peace.
label: negative

reviewText:
This music, with only a few exceptional moments, is just another example of the same meandering theatre pablum we've been hearing for too many years.  Unexceptional melodic phrases leading to long held notes -- this same rank formula over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over, ad nauseum.  The writers try to be as brilliant and "important" as Sondheim on his worst day, resulting in lyrics so jam-packed with MEANING that one simply grows tired instead of inspired.  [I kept thinking that this work was like Craig Carnelia on his best day, which isn't an admirable position.]

Musicals nowadays are either dry as dust [like this one] or relentlessly wacky fun, like "Avenue Q" -- where are the shows that had drama and comedy combined?  "Most Happy Fella," "She Loves Me," even, dare I say it, "Fiddler on the Roof" -- works with tremendous heart, admirable skill, and a nice dose of humor.  I'm all for the art form growing and improving and changing, but not into dour, humorless works like this.  I'm not a fuddy-duddy, but why has the term 'musical comedy' become anathema?

Miss Carmello is again in top form; she makes the most of this limited material.  Mr. Ludwig, however, manages to be utterly bland and utterly annoying; one dreads hearing him after a very short while.  Though his basic vocal technique is solid, he has a notably limited range of vocal colors/expressions.

I got this recording in hopes of finding new material; the pursuit proved fruitless.  Ho hum.

reviewText:
Boccherini - GUITAR QUINTETS - Newton Records

These quintets for guitar by Luigi Boccherini have long been an established part of classical guitar repertoire; guitarist Massimo Scattolin, violinist Franco Mezzena (whose previously re-released CD of violin and guitar sonatas by Gragnani is lovely) and the rest of the quintet play them with skill and sensitivity.
Sadly neither they nor the music here is well served by this very odd sounding recording. Somewhere along the line from microphone placement, to "live" mixing, to later remixes, mastering and manufacturing, someone seriously dropped the ball.
The result, with its wildly uneven dynamics, is nearly unlistenable (like having the worst seat in the house) whether heard on a car stereo, home audio system, or ghetto blaster.
Anyone really interested in getting to know these quintets would be better off with the Phillips recording of Pepe Romero and the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields Chamber Ensemble.
Newton Records has done a generally good job of making out of print recordings available to a new audience; their re-issue of works by the Amsterdam Guitar Trio has been particularly well received. Unfortunately, "Guitar Quintets" with its wobbly sound quality, cannot counted as one of their notable successes.

  Not recommended  Oscar O. Veterano
label: negative

The title of this album should have been "Dennis Edwards and his background singers a.k.a. The Temptations." He's about as bad as Diana Ross when it comes to hogging the mike. David Ruffin led one song and Eddie Kendricks led none. What were the producers thinking about when they went into the studio? The only good song on this album is Rick James' contribution, "Standing On The Top." If you can find this song on one of Rick's greatest hits, do so. Don't waste your money on this.

Like one of the other reviewers asked, where was Stevie Wonder? And where was Lionel Richie when you needed him the most? I believe even Teena Marie could have pitched in on something! You know all they need is a pen and a pad: automatic hit. Oh well...

I didn't even listen to the last track, "Money's Hard To Get" all the way through, it was just awful. Obviously, some good material was hard to get too. The only reason I bought this album was to honor my dad. He's no longer with us and I bought this because I remembered that he had it. I love you and I miss you Daddy but the next time I want to honor you, I'll just stick with The Delfonics, The Manhattans, Blue Magic and The Main Ingredient.

And like Peter said, don't buy this for over $15.00. Matter of fact, don't buy this for over $5, shipping included. $125 is too much to pay Dennis Edwards personally to sing these songs to you in your living room. It's a shame that some of the original Temptations were together in the studio one last time and didn't get a chance to really do their thing before God called them home. Uhm-uhm-uhmph. I guess some good ideas should just stay ideas, like the Otis Williams character said in the "Temptations" movie. I couldn't agree with him more.

reviewText: I normally don't write reviews on CD's that I disliked, but I felt that I just had to express my opinion on Puddle of Mudd's 'Come Clean.'
