However, I was gravely dissapointed with the painfully slow riffs and the almost absent bass. Wes' voice is irritating at times and can get very tiresome, the drums aren't that great, and some of the songs here sound really terrible.  I figured for a long time that maybe the music would grow on me, that although I hate it now does not really mean that I won't like it in the future.  Well, I've had it for about four months now, and Come Clean is doing nothing for me now except collecting dust on my CD rack.  What's worse about this CD is that it sounds kind of poppy at times, reflecting more of a boy band trying to play guitars rather than real rock.  I am not trying to sound offensive or anything, it's just that this was a huge disapointment to me, and I will never listen to this band again willingly.  I really thought this was horrible, whiny, and too mellow.

reviewText:
Here they are, ladies and gentlemen, the Limp Bizkit, no!- the INSANE CLOWN POSSE of the classical world!  Assembled by Simon Cowell - that perpetually irritated Brit with hair designed by Frank Lloyd Wright (is he sure AI stands for American Idol and not Artificial Intelligence?) - these four plastic-faced young lads can make you weep like a baby, though not from the soaring emotion in their voices (there is none), but merely from the immense pain they will inflict upon your eardrums.  You see, Simon Cowell is an expert at crushing the dreams of youngsters hopeful of a career in music, and with Il Divo, he's successfully crushed my dream, as well - the one where I envisioned a world where music like this doesn't exist.

I can't quite decide which is the worst aspect of this music: the unsubtle, glossed-over arrangements; its shameless marketing angle which tries to pass it off as classical music when it is actually mainstream pop sung with operatic vocals, or Il Divo themselves, who, with each successive album, sound more and more enthusiastic about the fact that they are howling together like a quartet of banshees.  Honestly, do they have to use a wind-tunnel's worth of vibrato with every single note they sing????  No, they don't - because when they do, and harmonize together with it, the composite timbre they produce wavers so much that they may as well be singing in different keys.  Really folks, these guys are incisive as a Jimmy Buffett lyric - as soulful as a Heart guitar solo.  Wait, did I call this "music," earlier?  Note that I'm using that term loosely.

Also note that since Il Divo have rehashed the same basic album's worth of material three times now and simply slapped a new cover picture and title on it each time - failing at every turn to muster up any inkling of progress or creativity - that I myself shall replicate their incomparable lack of effort and repost this same review on all of their material!  What's the difference anyway, ay boys??!!

And so now we must ask ourselves, where will Rocketship Il Divo finally land?  What fate beholds this blindingly chiseled foursome who dare to call themselves "singers."  Well, hopefully a few years from now, after the last scratched-up Il Divo CD lands in your local used record store's 99 cent bin, and after the last half-deaf grandma empties her change purse to buy it, maybe one or two of these guys will succeed in a semi-respectable opera career, still blasting a melody from their vocal cords, composed by someone else, still (for ever and always) a dangling puppet of the mainstream music machine.

One of the worst groups ever recorded.  Period.

reviewText:
Another in a long line of 'greatest hits", Then & Now doesn't even come close to being comprehensive. There are too many missing gems (like Relay, Let's See Action, Join Together, Anyway Anyhow Anywhere, etc.) and the inclusion of weak new songs dilute the potency of the songs recorded forty years earlier. And the new songs are the only reason a Who fan would get this collection anyway.
Real Good Looking Boy has the misfortune of directly quoting the famous Elvis Presley song "Can't Help Falling In Love With You". Has Pete Townshend totally run out of ideas? Old Red Wine is a little better but still rather dour and never really gets going despite Roger Daltrey excellent singing.

With only two remaining original Who members one has to ask: At what point do you stop calling these projects The Who? I guess Pete Townshend can get more mileage out of The Who's name brand than his own.

I would have much rather heard an entire recording under the Townshend/Daltrey banner than this waste of plastic.

I have asked this question before, and I will trouble myself to ask it once more. Who pays money for these completely crappy, outdated mixes? Most of these songs can't actually be classified as music, and the ones that can were overplayed in march. The first eleven tracks (all in the R&B/rap genre of course) range from bad to terrible. Songs like Hollaback girl should make you want to gouge your ears out. Another question. What on earth happened to gwen stefani. No doubt was a good band, but most of her solo material is painful. Next time I listen to her is when she goes back to her band. In the meantime, skip ahead to track twelve, "ordinary people" by John legend, a good, if slightly boring slow song.

The only other decent songs on the CD come from 3 Doors Down and the killers. Everything else is mediocre, boring, repetetive, or cringe inducing. Coldplay's song is alright a few times, but can't escape the fact that its basically clocks remixed with different lyrics, and seeing as that song got old several years ago, I don't feel inclined to listen to this one.

I can only imagine what goes on in the heads of whoever makes these mixes. The 3 Doors Down song, which came out all the way back in february, would have fit nicely on now 18, but now that it is so sickly overplayed, and still being killed by radio stations everywhere, I do not feel like I need to listen to it in CD or mp3 form. The only thing done correctly on the mix is that they managed to get the killers. Anyone who says any other song on this CD is better simply has awful music taste. She writes a song about Bush, deriding him for alcohol abuse and drug use in his youth, and then she also writes a song about how much fun it is to get drunk all the time!

She writes a song about materialism and about the poor people who cannot have such luxury, then she also writes a song about her excessive materialism on the same album!

Other commenters call her "brave" or whatever for "taking a stand" against the President. Instead, I find her hypocritical grandstanding quite pathetic and insincere, and I think that only the simplest of minds would be swept up in adoration for this confused pop-tart.

Judging by the 5-star reviews, I have to assume that Pink's childish anti-Bush tirade and her glaring inconsistencies are small change when compared to her allegedly awesome abilities as a songwriter and musician.

The music on this CD is not bad, much of it is catchy and is great to dance to. But I have trouble taking someone seriously when they cannot even recognize their own hypocrisy. Pink is an entertaining pop star who provides young teenage girls with some sort of role-model/counter-culture figure to look up to, which is also disappointing.

I am no die-hard fan of the President, but it is ridiculous to have a semi-educated pop star deriding the President while at the same time promoting the same types of drug use and greed! She is calling the kettle black. It's a shame that her fans cannot tell the difference between a hero and a hypocrit.

3 stars for a CD that features plenty of listenable music. It's nothing ground-breaking or genre-bending, but the songs are not bad enough to cause me to stand up and hit the "next" button. But those 3 stars are chopped down to 1 lonely star when her hypocrisy casts a shadow on the whole experience.

reviewText: This review is concerned with the quality of the product at hand, not the music itself, which in my opinion would rate three stars. "String Driven Thing," their first release on the Famous Charisma Label imprint was in actuality their second release, following their 1970 also self-titled Concord album, now available as Early Years Mark Two. The artwork, liner notes and photos are top notch, which seems to be the norm for all Esoteric Recordings releases, it's the sound quality/remastering that sinks it. When listening to the previous 1998 Ozit Records release titled In The Studio '72 plus Live In Switzerland '73 & London '95, which contains the same tracks plus five live 1973 tracks and a track from a 1995 reformation, the music sounds well-balanced with the just the slightest hint of what is probably tape noise/hiss, inherent due to the age of the recordings. It doesn't distract from the music, but when I saw that Esoteric had put out a remastered version, I was curious if the slight distortion was still present. Well, I'm sorry to say it is, but this go-round in spades! It sounds as if the tapes used are the same as the Ozit release, but were pushed beyond "red levels" during the remastering process. The Ozit version seems warm and spacious compared to this brittle fuzzy mess. Not to say thst ALL Ozit releases are so well done, their recent offerings of the two original member Graham Smith-only long players, Please Mind Your Head and Keep Yer & On It pale in comparison to the grey market versions on Red Fox, Please Mind Your Head/String Driven Thing and Keep Yer 'And On It/The Machine That Cried. The recent pricey Japanese mini-lp sleeve releases (Please Mind Your Head and Keep Yer 'And On It) are to be avoided as well, since they utilize the same terrible "Graham Smith's Personal Tapes" as the Ozit releases! Esoteric also has available a newly remastered and upgraded version of the band's critically acclaimed third and most popular album "The Machine That Cried" which has been released numerous times over the years by Ozit (The Machine That Cried: The Band's Official Version), Repertoire and SPM/World Wide! I review the new Esoteric CD here: The Machine That Cried......

reviewText:
No question about it. Ozzy was a force to reckon with in his day. He lived the rock and roll lifestyle to its fullest, and came close to cashing in his chips many times. Songs like "Crazy Train," "Flying High Again," "You Can't Kill Rock and Roll," and "I Don't Know" are definitive Ozzy Osbourne. (Man, I love those songs) He definitely earned the title of "Madman of Rock and Roll" in the 80's and into the early 90's.

So what's an aging Heavy Metal star to do in his later years? You've got to keep those paychecks rolling in. And while you still enjoy making music, singing about Crazy Trains, Barking at the Moon, and how you Can't Kill Rock and Roll begins to look a little goofy after you're well past the age of fifty.

Do you quietly fade away, enjoying your golden years, or do you release an album of odd cover tunes? Why Ozzy chose to put his legacy and reputation on the line with a tired sounding covers album, I don't know. "The Osbournes" made him out to be somewhat of lovable, crotchety, bumbling old man. This CD doesn't help.

As much as I love what Ozzy's done over his amazing three decade career, I think the time has come to call it a day. But for one reason or another his camp has decided to release an embarrasing collection of cover tunes that fall outside the music genre he's known for! Ugh! Why?

Now there are certain artists that have successfully gone outside of their normal musical styles -- Elvis, The Beatles, the Rolling Stones -- but they are the exceptions rather than the rule. There are so many more that crash and burn. This, my friends, is yet another sad flame out.

What might have worked better? Sticking to music that suits his voice. And let's face it, Ozzy has a distinctive voice with a narrow range. Songs like "In My Life," "Go Now," and "For What it's Worth" are great for vocalists with the range to do them. From Ozzy, they are fingernails on a chalkboard.

What did work on the album? To some degree, Mountain's "Mississippi Queen," and King Crimson's "21st Century Schizoid Man."

I'm all for taking a risk -- but make it a calculated risk. My guess is that no one in the Osbourne camp is willing to admit that the emperor has no clothes.

reviewText:
This is not the Nickelback we once knew, and it's not for the better. I've been defending these guys for years. Trying to show other fellow metal heads and hard rock fans that there are indeed a plethora of great songs to be had in Nickelback's repertoire. "Don't let the popular singles fool you," I'd tell them. I'd pull out stuff like "Never Again", "Little Friend", "Side of a Bullet", "Just For", and "Flat On The Floor". However, those songs are not in this album. Not one. Edge of a Revolution is about the best it gets here, and even that song leaves you thinking this is just another generic fist-pump song that got thrown onto the album without much thought. Everything here belongs on a major pop artist album (and yes that is a bad thing). Whatever happened to the song writing that came out during the initial era of Nickelback (Curb, The State), followed by the era in which they broke out into the mainstream (Silver Side Up, and The Long Road) is LONG gone. This band's ability to be heavy and gritty has been losing ground over the past 10 years or so, but the breaking point is finally here. With every album starting with All The Right Reasons their ratio of heavy songs to pop songs has been swinging in more and more in favor of pop songs with every album, and now they don't even hide who they want to be anymore. This album is a disgrace to who they once were. Don't give me the whole, "But they're changing with the times" routine. Most new music is bad today anyway, and this album just proves me even more right.

If you're a hard rock fan looking for new music, might I recommend Filter's "The Sun Comes Out Tonight". That album is how Hard Rock is supposed to sound like with today's technology and "times".

Lou Reed's career has as many low points as high ones.  This is one of the lowest.  Bland, anonymous studio musician rock with lyrics that are so over-the-top that they become unintentionally funny. Eventually, though, even the humor factor wears off and it quickly becomes unlistenable.
The scam, at the time this came out, was that this was REALLY Lou Reed - no, REALLY, the REAL Lou Reed, talking about his REAL life.  Really! Honest!  Of course anyone who believed that would also want to invest in Lou's shares in the Brooklyn Bridge or his offering of great real estate in South Florida.
The best thing about this album is the cover.  Nothing else on here is worth bothering with.  Most of Lou's output on Arista records showed him at his least interesting, and this one unfortunately is one of the worst (only surpassed by the truly abysmal "The Bells," which no one should be forced to listen to).
God bless Lou Reed, but give this one a pass.

reviewText:
I haven't listened to a Prince album since 1987's "Sign O' the Times," and after listening to "Musicology," his latest proper full-length, I guess I know why.

 In the late 70's and early to mid-80's, his body of work was so original and uncomprimising, that although it was heavily rooted in funk (and I hate funk), I still loved it. "Dirty Mind" and "Controversy," up to "1999" and "Sign," they're all classics that no one who proclaims to "love music" should be without.

 To this day, I don't have a problem with him (aside from the $99 price tag on tickets for his current, non-arena tour), but I was never interested in what he was doing with the New Power Generation, and changing his name to a symbol was just a preposterous, pretentious thing to do.

 That phase is over, and "Musicology" is more akin to his earlier, one-man works, with the trademark blend of funk, rock, and modern R&B, but there is absolutely nothing on here that stands out. Each track blends into the other, nothing is exciting or fresh; it's all stale. It's sad to admit, but I had a feeling that would be the result before I even heard this album. If you still like post-"Sign" Prince, you'll probably dig this, but it does absolutely nothing for me, especially coming from an artist who was once one of the most original out there.

reviewText:
A great soundtrack should perfectly capture the mood and/or themes of the movie that it represents and be a collection of good songs that can be enjoyed out of context. A decent soundtrack might accomplish one of those goals. A bad soundtrack accomplishes neither. The soundtracks to the first two Hunger Games films are examples of great soundtracks (especially Catching Fire, which might have been the best soundtrack I've ever heard). Naturally, I had high hopes for the Mockingjay soundtrack as well.

Unfortunately, this soundtrack is far from great. Mockingjay's soundtrack was curated by Lorde, and you can tell because she is all over it (appearing in four songs). I admit that I am a fan of Lorde, but I don't go crazy over her like a lot of people do, but I did love "Yellow Flicker Beat" when I first started hearing it on Alt Nation. After hearing this soundtrack, though, I am wondering if she has ever even seen a Hunger Games movie or read a book. If she had, she would know that none of the songs picked for this soundtrack (with the possible exception of "Yellow Flicker Beat") fit the mood of the film. The dark folk/indie style of the first two soundtracks fit the films so well. Furthermore, it was easy to see how the songs on those two soundtracks, lyrically, connected with the films. It's hard to make that connection with the songs on this soundtrack, and musically, the songs do not fit at all. All of the songs are upbeat electronic pop songs... not at all what should be found on a Hunger Games soundtrack.

I can get past the fact that it doesn't feel like a Hunger Games soundtrack if the songs were at least good. They're not. Outside of the Chvrches and Tove Lo songs, and the two versions of "Yellow Flicker Beat", not a single song stands out as a good song. Some are unlistenably bad even.

Look... I get that Lorde is popular and well respected... but maybe she should stick to what she's good at. For the next soundtrack... maybe hire a legitimate music supervisor... you know, someone who does that for a living and knows what they're doing, rather than a kid who just wants to put all her favorite songs on a playlist.

-KC

reviewText:
"To convince an audience that an illusion is real, the magician creates a plausible diversion."
That's the main idea behind VICTOR/VICTORIA a gender bending musical comedy adapted from Blake Edwards's acclaimed 1982 movie. VICTOR/VICTORIA was notable chiefly for bringing Julie Andrews back to Broadway in 1995. The reviews were mixed, but the only Tony nomination was for Julie. The show was bypassed for a nomination as Best Musical. Julie got her nose out of joint, called a press conference to say she was declining her nomination to stand in solidarity with her "egregiously overlooked" co-stars.  The grandstanding gave the box-office a boost but cost Julie her award.  (She has never won a Tony: Not for MY FAIR LADY or THE BOY FRIEND or CAMELOT. Hard as it is to believe.)
Truth be told... VICTOR/VICTORIA did not deserve any awards. Or any nominations. It was a patchwork show, slapped together with little care.  When composer Henry Mancini died, Frank Wildhorn was called in to write new songs.  NONE of the new songs by either composer are a patch on the songs from the 1982 movie.
Along the way from screen to stage much of the humour, much of the warmth, and even a good deal of the story has been lost.  Instead we get cheap jokes, lacklustre production numbers and no real true character development. Good musical theatre writing should do this through songs, but many songs in VICTOR/VICTORIA are time-wasters.
Nowhere is this more apparent than in "Paris Makes Me Horny" - not only the show's worst number but also one of the worst songs in the history of musical theatre.
The ONLY reason this show ran was Juliue Andrews.  When she left the show quickly folded.  Those in search of the true VICTOR/VICTORIA should stick with the film and the movie soundtrack CD.  Both are much more enjoyable than this awful recording.

A soundtrack for the summer...yes.  If you are ten years old.  There is a very juvenile feel to this album, which is really quite fine if you are 12 or under.  If not, this is the sort of album you would never play when driving around with your friends.  In fact, its the sort of album you would stash under your bed when they come over just so they don't know you own it.  The songs are poppy, and often quite catchy, but other than that there isn't a single reason to own this album.  The extremely high levels of enthusiasm and earnestness in the music and lyrics gets really annoying, really fast.  Much closer to pop than rock, nothing experimental.  The melodies are very simplistic and childish, singsongy almost.  Also, I find something extremely disturbing with how the singer seems to be almost happy when singing "Jumper", a song apparently written about a friend who was contemplating suicide.  Personally, I would never write a pop song like that about any of my friends unless maybe I wanted to embaress them.  But then again, Jenkins doesn't appear to have much integrity so I wouldn't be surprised if that song really wasn't about anyone real at all and just something he dreamed up because he though it would make a good hit song.  A lot of the lyrics also seem annoyingly self-righteous, and they give you the feeling that Jenkins is the kind of person who just looks in the mirror every morning and thanks god for being such a good-looking guy.
PS:  If "Graduate" isn't a purely commercial song with a sole lyrical intention of empathizing with schoolchildren, I don't know what is.

reviewText:
No, but close.

This mid 1980's release is a monumental example of everything that was lame about 80's music in particular and the rock/pop genre, generally. It is exactly what you would expect from Mr. Phillip Collins and co., a sad snapshot of a sad period that a space alien could identify as coming straight from the 80's. There's a reason why so much of the eighties' biggest stars are instantly recognizable as eighties music and why they have all dated so very badly. It's simply because they had no depth, range, or frankly, any talent to begin with. Now, I'm not saying the members of Genesis aren't accomplished musicians, but that doesn't translate into being good or interesting song writers. I believe Rutherford or Banks could have (and should have) made fine session musicians for some other, more credible singer/songwriters. Mr. Phillip Collins, well that's a little more difficult, but I've long suspected a career as a circus midget might be his true calling.

As for the songs themselves, we have a healthy smattering of everything that makes this band so atrociously bad in the first place. Yes, Phil and the boys have left no stone unturned as they drag every crappy and cliched trick of the 1980's up from the mire where it belongs. The vapid, shallow pop of the title track is enough to make any serious music fan shove pencils through his ears. It, as you might expect, has a tired keyboard heavy performance throughout, with of course, the by now obligatory disposable fluff that pass for lyrics as only Phil can write them. "Land Of Confusion", a watered down, sanitized commentary on the political climate of 1985, 1986. Clearly, Phil didn't understand very much about what was going on politically at the time or was much too afraid to convey a meaningful message in a more powerful way lest he dampen his mass appeal to other little, middle aged balding men commonly known among those in the know as Philites, the fans. It was probably a little bit of both, but to be fair, when you have your head stuck chronically up your own anus it could be a little difficult to have proper perspective on what's going on in the outside world.

Next, we get the usual display of poorly written, emotionally manufactured love songs. "In Too Deep" and "Throwing It All Away", lyrics which I'm sure fans will insist must have come during a difficult time in Phil's love life, but in fact sound like they were most likely inspired by the vapid up's and down's of characters from daytime soap operas, which I've long regarded as the visual equivalent of Phil's "music". Finally, we toss in a nod to Genesis early days by way of the 11 and a half minute "Domino". Here the boys flex their musical muscle in a vain effort to provide a little credibility in the face of the album's otherwise non stop onslaught of "made for the charts" fluff-pop. Unfortunately, the lads failed to realize that the song is boring and prog-rock in general is boring, but it was also the decade before. "Domino" proves definitively that they can escape the worst musical (and for that matter lyrical cliches) of the 80's, but only by travelling a decade backwards. "Domino" tries hard to lend a smidgeon of credibility to a pathetically bland and overly commercialized album, but in the end merely re-affirms that this album is a crime against the eardrums. I don't believe that anyone could publically admit to owning this album with a stragiht face. If nothing else, it would turn beet red in sheer embarrassment.

Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher, The Contras , The Falklands War, all sad products of a largely embarrassing decade. This album belongs in the same class of happily forgotten 1980's disgraces. Leave it there.

reviewText:
This was one of the truly BAD albums of the late 70s and, unfortunately, not in the so-bad-it's-good kind of way. From the material to the performances, this record tends to underscore the glaring reality about Minnelli: she has always been an enthusiastic but very one-dimensional, limited vocalist with a rather abrasive instrument.

Moreover, her selection of material over the years has been little better. 'Tropical Nights' exemplifies this problem to the hilt. While Minnelli was ideal for the brazen 'Cabaret' film and score, it's wise to recall that she hit her career peak in 1971-72...and it's been one long flatline (with a few minor blips) ever since. 'Tropical Nights' surely could not have helped.

The album seeks to fit Minnelli into the pose of a seasoned jazz/blues/disco stylist, when she is technically and inherently incapable of any of those genres. Again, the problem stems from the voice and her narrow delivery. Many have naturally compared Minnelli's voice to that of her mother, but in truth the two voices are vastly different. Overall, Garland possessed bell-like tone, great control in all registers, masterful phrasing, and interpretative powers second to no singer ever on earth. Garland could cross genres with ease and conviction in her heyday (which lasted a long while). Minnelli possesses none of these qualities. On this album, especially, she comes across as a woman trying and failing to sound like Judy Garland, but coming quite close to a poor-man's Ethel Merman.

Neither Minnelli nor Merman have ever been conventionally pleasant on the ear, with their braying, bellowing approach, but both (curiously enough) decided to accost innocent '70s disco beats with their throttled vibratos (see the ETHEL MERMAN DISCO ALBUM). On 'Tropical Nights,' Minnelli butchers and mangles every single number--and it doesn't help that most of the numbers were poorly written to begin with.

The cringe-fest opens with a travesty called "Jimi Jimi," in which Minnelli actually tries to "get her funk on" and the result will drop jaws to the floor. She has no timing or rhythm whatsoever for this disco/funk fusion, her phrasing is mind-bogglingly bad ("...or some fuh-LASH that wuh-HUZZ"), and of course there is the unwieldy vibrato that is as shrill and repellent as the vibratos of Dion, Streisand, and Garland are rich, pleasant, and warm. Minnelli sounds like a frantic chicken desperate to lay a painfully impacted egg on "Jimi Jimi" and, boy, does she ever lay a stinker.

Things don't get any better. Hope seems to flicker for a bit of "I Love Every Little Thing About You," which sports sort of a smooth, jazzy arrangement and innocuous lyrics, until Minnelli's contemptible phrasing gets in the way again--like she's got a mouthful of gravel. She's off the beat, off the vibe, and off the rails. She seems to "gulp" her way through much of this song and several others, frog-like.

The title song, 'Tropical Nights' features Minnelli at her most enthusiastic (does she know any other mode?), but again she cannot catch-up to the messy disco arrangement with any discernible clue as to what she's doing, or how to sing it. The trademark Minnelli "nails-on-chalboard" technique tries to win the day, but the result brings both singer and listener to the brink of desperation.

The remaining songs are equally offensive to humanity.

"New Best Friend" is a jaunty piece of tripe wherein Minnelli seems to quack her way through the miasma. One can almost picture her recording this in a gigantic duck-suit.

Why Minnelli (or any of her handlers at the time) thought this sort of record would seriously fly for her, one cannot hazard a guess. She's a delightfully competent actress and comedienne, but the voice was made for bawdy, brazen stage-musicals ONLY. Don't give her a microphone. Please! If a song requires itself to be screamed and hollered with no regard for subtelty, phrasing, or common sense, she's your gal. 'Tropical Nights' would likely stand-up in a court of law as undeniable proof of that.

This album almost makes a great companion-piece for Merman's late 70s disco album, save for the fact that Merman's record is funny (and hence mildly amusing) in its incongruity, its novel quality, and its badness. Ain't nothin' funny 'bout this record. I can't believe they deemed this worthy of a CD reissue, but Minnelli does have ardent fans. You'd have to be ardent.

Before I start my review let me clear one thing, My rating has nothing to do with Chris Brown's personal life. Yes, I'm aware of the fact that he's a misogynist with anger management problems. I'm a woman and totally anti violence in all its shapes and formes but celebrities personal lives and their mistakes no matter how grave does not affect mine in anyway so why should I care? I'm here for the music that's all.

Chris Brown as an artist *if you could call him that* has a good singing voice. Not the most remarkable vocals you'll ever hear *God Forbid* but given the right amount of effort, amusing or somehow meaningful lyrics and catchy beats the overall production of his works are not that bad. Some of his past achievements or contributions to the music industry if one will consider anything by Chris Brown to be regarded as an Achievement *this is a tone in cheek way of saying earlier works not something I'd take seriously* were quite entertaining, Which I think is his strongest suit he stands out as an entertainer more than anything else. A Quality that is clearly lacking in this album as well as any sings of depth or sincerity. There was a release of some singles back in January & February to promote for Fortune which were somehow catchy but the overall product falls flat. My complains are just like every 1,2 star reviews there is an abuse of auto tone which doesn't help any, the lyrics are simplistic and come across as offensive and well tiring *how many times can a person hear about sex without being overwhelmed eventually?* and the spark is just not there. There is no message to be sent in this album or at least not any I can consider. It's filled with sexual innuendos, partying, alcohol and drugs. Much like every other song played on the radio and in clubs. Which doesn't make the tracks on here stand out or commit to memory. Sooner or later the listener is going to realize that it's not just one awful song after the other it's one awful song over and over again. You can't distinguish between the tracks themselves they all sound the same and have the same feel, message and theme to them. The Music Videos and Album cover as well as the logo, mostly give this Science fiction appearance to them which gives you the impression that Chris Brown is now a robot in the year 3000 on a save the world mission or something but this chosen persona does nothing to redeem the album once you start realizing that wether he's a robot thousands of years from now or an average backstreet guy he's still gonna sing about sex and all those things.

Lust *the main subject this album evolves around* is a one dimensional emotion and it fades as quickly as it appears. Same thing goes for this albums. While F.A.M.E was entertaining and optimistic mostly, and Graffiti was sweet in nature. Fortune doesn't provide anything memorable or new to the table. Easily the most forgettable album of 2012 & by Chris Brown to date.

Is it Recommend?  Yes, if you were super drunk, in a club and just want something to jam into then this album will be somehow bearable although god knows there are way better options out there.

reviewText:
While there are definitely people who seem to like 3LW on their artistic merits alone (I'm not one of those people), it's time really time that someone identifies what the true problem with this group is.  It's not lame lyrics or unoriginal music.  It's the fact that 3LW is another example of a disturbing and increasingly frequent trend in pop music to grab attention and sell records by emphasizing the sexuality of underage girls.  While Adrienne Bailon is now 18, she was still underage when this album was being written and even more underage when this group's previous album was released.  The other two members, Keily Williams and Naturi Naughton (no longer with the group) are both 16.  To see these girls regularly dress in clothing (or lack thereof) that would be inappropriate even on South Beach and dancing bump and grinds in a such a way as to make the most permissive parent blush, is to realize that something has gone terribly and horribly wrong in music today.  While young artists have always been a staple of pop music industry, the concept of selling their bodies and their sexuality as the primary means to sell the records is a fairly new development.  Britney Spears can be thanked for this trend, which made the taboo 'Lolita' syndrome okay in mainstream society.

"Girl Can Mack" is an embarrassing and inappropriate album, both in song and video.  The debut single off this album "I do" is a classic example of what's wrong.  The lyrics show the girls 'singing' about partying and clubbing all night long.  The video shows them bumping and grinding with very little clothing on with men who are nearly twice their age.  Their vocals demonstrate how out of league they are with this material.  The verses, the chorus, and the intro all have the sound of girls in a high school freshmen talent show.  They simply sound too young to be singing about topics like this.  Other songs reveal even more inappropriate material, like "Ghetto Love and Heartbreak", "Neva Get Enuf" and "Leave wit you (I think I wanna)".  What are an 18-year old and two 16-year olds doing singing about things like that?

It should come as no surprise that one of the members of the group, 16-year old Naturi Naughton, left the group because she didn't feel comfortable with the image she was portraying and being forced to take part in.  There appears to be some relief on the horizon, though.  With Britney's popularity fading at an astronomical rate and producers doing more the keep clothes on their new young artists like a Vanessa Carlton, Michelle Branch, or even Hilary Duff, there's a chance that this brief, shameful dalliance with promoting the sexuality of underage children is on its way out.  We can only hope that is the case.

reviewText:
Since the Beatles disbanded in 1970 a misconception has developed that they were all about Love.  Forget those songs of alienation, biting wit, loneliness, satire, and detached surrealism . . . man, those cute moptops were just all about love.  Love, Love, Love.  Their edge, the sardonic humor, the attributes I've most valued have been worn away and in the popular view that has evolved we have Saints John, Paul, George, and Ringo beatifically preaching their gospel of love.  (Can one be a saint while still alive?  I'll leave that one for the religious scholars to debate.)  The hard-edged songs - "A Day in the Life," "I'm only Sleeping," "I Am the Walrus," etc. have all been de-clawed.
The Messrs. Martin have pulled off a very clever musical feat, but when I hear the results of their labors, and imagine the unlikely contortions the Circque de Soleil performers no doubt perform while that music is playing, I give the click wheel of my iPod a quick twirl.

Ladies and gentlemen, Ashlee Simpson finally has some competition to worst album of the year and her name is Lindsay Lohan who has just released her second album, A Little More Personal (Raw). For anyone who has had to wait in line at the supermarket and glance and the tabloid rags with Lohan dancing on table with the like of Tara Reid and Paris Hilton could easily tell that Lohan has daddy issues, but that didn't keep Lohan from writing songs about it including the album opener, Confessions of a Broken Heart which lyrics sheets reads like a diary entry from the annoying moody chick in Middle School who just got grounded for the first time. To add to the agony, the song even stoops to the worst clich in songwriting, ending the song with exactly the same line which started it. Okay, you're waiting for the postman to bring you a letter, I get it. Maybe you should check your e-mail every once in a while too.

Thing don't get much better from there. Where Ashlee Simpson at least sound like she has had some vocal training, not much, but at least some. But for the most of the album, Lohan hits almost every note as if she has never read sheet music before and that's when she's not screaming at notes why out of her range as if she was auditioning for Rock Star: Pantera. The only time she remotely comes close to reaching the right notes are on the already established cover song in Cheap Trick's I Want You to Want Me which is the closest to entertaining that this album gets. And it's only entertaining in the way a drunk chick singing the song at karaoke is entertaining, even Antonio Sabato Jr. was able to do a better version on But Can They Sing? Unfortunately her stab at Stevie Nick's Edge of Seventeen failed miserable because, for some reason, she tried slutting the song up.

There is also a funny exchange at the beginning, where Lohan says, "No I like when people talk in the beginning of songs I think that kinda rad," to which someone relies, "I don't think you should use it." I had to laugh because they should at least take out the dude because he was right and only made Lohan look foolish. Of all of her own songs, the only redeeming one is Who Loves You which wisely pumps up the techno beat while toning down Lohan's vocals where she coos the title over and over. At least that is until the ending where she screams it only to coyly says, "Me" afterwards, but that just means it fits in well with the rest of the album.

reviewText:
I'm really sorry to say this because I was originally an Ace of base hardcore fan : on board right from the start. I so loved Wheel of fortune and  All that she wants, bought their first album blindlessly (the 1st European version even, I was there and I'm very proud of it !) and I remember the angst of buying their first album knowing only 2 songs from them before being blown away and overjoyed just after hearing the first notes of Voulez-vous danser for the very first time !

There it was, finally : the best thing that ever happened to the music world from Sweden in years and Happy Nation and the following hits and albums right up to Wheel of fortune 2009 so proved me right ! I bought everything they have ever done : the remixes, music videos, all of their albums and singles (in all of their multiple releases in Europe, Japan and the U.S. like the albums Flowers [Europe] / Cruel Summer [U.S./Japan] or the singles Life is a flower [Europe] / Whenever you're near me [U.S.] etc...) I really mean everything !

I was so proud to say to the whole wide world back in those days that Ace of base was and always have been my favourite group in the music biz, and I did it for almost 16 years non-stop ! even getting mad everytime I heard someone saying something like : "Ace of base ? Are they still around ?" Of course they are, to me anyway, there was no doubt about it.

Even when I was disapointed than Linn's role in the band got slimer and slimer (she was my favourite singer and voice : so fragile, so unique), I was so glad the group kept on running even without her just with Jenny's voice : hers was a little bit different, it's true but still enjoyable nonetheless.

So believe me when I say I was really ready to accept almost anything for my favourite band ever to live on and I tried to like this album, my God, I really tried, but sorry I just can't.

Some songs are almost as great as in the good old days "Black Sea" and "Doreen" for example and if I didn't liked "All for you" at first, I must admit it grows on you but like another reviewer said everytime I would hear these new songs, I'll always surprise myself trying to imagine what they could have sounded like with Linn or Jenny's voice on it, I just can't help it but it makes me sad.

I'll always be greatful to "Joker" and "Buddha" for all these years of happiness and joy : I remember the first time I heard The Sign and I thought to myself right away : "My oh my : this song is so good, its success is going to be huge !", I was so right then and so proud too when it got to number one worldwide. Likewise I remember being so happy to spend all my summer of 98 listening to Adventures in Paradise or Tokyo Girl ! So thank you guys for all of this, I'll always have a special place for you in my heart but you shouldn't have called this ratio thing an Ace of base album just because it's not.

Like I said in the title of this review, to me, this is no resurrection at all, it's a betrayal and even more than that, it's a major slap in the face to all of your hardcore fans. I was so glad recently to discover on youtube an extended version of Hear me calling I've never heard before (it's one of my favourite songs !) : this is what you should release on CD guys, this I will buy :  extended versions of old tracks or rare songs from THE REAL ace of base but not this album.

Even Lady Gaga's Alejandro sounded more like Ace of base than this album, isn't that pathetic ?! Personnally, since I liked Ravine and Experience pearls in 1995 (solely written by Jenny in their 2nd album The bridge) I guess I'll just go and buy Jenny's album now : it's the only reasonable thing to do until the guys ever decide to get me out of this bad nightmare because even though their indeniable musical genius can still be found here and there at times in this album the magic and the soul of what made this band great is gone.

My advice to you Jonas and Ulf : put back those kinky girls in the gutter where they belong because my ears bleed when I hear them sing sometimes. Moreover being French myself I so laughed out loud when I heard the way one of these girls said Montparnasse (which is the name of one of our most famous Towers in Paris) where Linn and Jenny sang so perfectly in French in Voulez-vous danser or C'est la vie : I'm so ashamed for you, really.

So do anything to get whether Linn or Jenny back in the band again whatever the cost might be, or else God is my witness : I will never ever buy an Ace.of.base record again. To me, your last album will always be Da Capo and this band died with the 2009 Greatest hits album.

Come back with the real deal or don't come back at all.

And to end this review with a little humourous note in Ace of base style :

All I wanna say to you (is that what you did to us) is nah nah nah nah,  unspeakable ! :)

reviewText:
I've always loved metal more towards Type 0, Metallica, Pantera, Opeth and lots of power metal bands, but when getting into death metal like Cannibal Corpse I discovered this band and gave them a shot. I bought this album because I've heard a lot of people seem to like these guys, without really knowing anything about Nile. So I figured I'd give it a try. Boy, was I dissappointed.
Sure, the lyrics aren't all about death, they talk about ancient Egypt and the theme of the whole record (most especially the final instrumental) sounds very much like what death metal would sound like if it was around in ancient Egypt, which is a good change. Secondly, each song has it's own story behind it on the lyrics CD booklet, interesting to learn a few things. Then when it comes to the songs themselves, the talent is definitly there. Most especially the drummer. The drums play a VERY significant role in this record, it's almost like he's the lead and not the lead singer. Where most records out there use percussion as background beats, this one pushes it way up front and the drums lead, and don't follow the guitars almost. It's fast, furious, etc. In one phrase: This drummer is fantastic! The down side to this is that the guitar riffs become somewhat in audible, because I couldn't really make out the riffs (especially bass lines) when the drums were going crazy. It just sounded like mindless distorted plucking at some parts. A few of the songs were decent, ironically it was those where the drumming wasn't leading.
On to the downside and why I gave this a low score. NONE of the songs are really good songs. I mean, I know death metal isn't supposed to sound like progressive and power metal where melodies are dominant, but music really does have to have some melody to it, to keep things interesting, and death metal nowadays really is TOO rhythm driven. I mean, Cannibal Corpse may have hard riffs galore but these are kickass fast riffs that'll get you headbanging. Anyway, excluding tracks 3 and 6 which were pretty good (not GOOD though), the rest of the record lingered on monotonous bordem. It was to the point where I didn't want to listen to the rest of the record because I knew what the next song was going to sound like, but I stuck with it. The songs were slow and dragged endlessly. So sure, the first song may have had great drumming, but I prefer the sound of a good guitar riff or solo, or even a kickbutt bassline over a drum solo anyday, I think most people would too. During this first track a keyboard is used to input some eery tunes throughout, which is the only saving grace this songs had from being relentlessly boring.
So I don't know what else to say except that this record bored the hell out of me, I'll probably sell it or something. My suggestion is that if you want to get into the death metal I'd suggest starting with Fear Factory's first album "soul of the new machine" which is very beginner friendly (not that you should stick to FF b/c their new stuff is utter crap). But NOT this, it will dissappoint you very much and you'll probably close the book on death metal all together. I really don't understand how people can think this album is interesting or deserves anything more then 2 stars. Once again I say, do not mistake abstract art for good solid entertainment.

reviewText: This is Faure with star power, and the result is painful, to my ears anyway. Faure is many things: subtle, elegant, graceful, melodic, and haunting, all about in equal measure. This recording is too seldom any of  those things for very long. The major problem is the two big  "show-stopper" numbers, the "Pie Jesu" for Bartoli and  the "Libera me" for Terfel. Faure certainly didn't intend these  lovely pieces as show-stoppers, but that is what we get here. Bartoli's  solo is beautiful in a show-offy self conscious sort of way. She has a  great voice certainly, but this music would be better suited to a more  restrained performance. But one could learn to live with her  interpretation, I suppose. The real problem is Terfel, who belts out  "Libera me" as though he were leaning into a Puccini solo in full  force. It is very hard to describe just how monumentally wrong-headed his  approach is--the proverbial bull in a china shop. For those of you familiar  with Faure, you may want to hear Terfel's performance once for its shock  value, but this Requiem is most likely not going to appeal to you for very  long, unless, of course, you are a fan of the Ethel Merman approach to this  repertoire. For those of you unfamiliar with this work, there are literally  dozens of more attractive recordings of this work. My favourite is the  Montreal/Dutoit version that generously includes the lovely Pavanne as well  as the Pelleas and Melisande suite.

reviewText: The product description claims this 5-CD set from JSP Records is "Remastered by renowned engineer John R.T. Davies". As far as I can tell, this is untrue. First of all, notice that other JSP recordings that actually were remastered by the late Davies, such as Cab Calloway The Early Years: 1930-34 and Bix Beiderbecke Bix & Tram, declare so prominently on the cover. This Louis Jordan set doesn't mention Davies at all, not on the cover nor anywhere in the notes. Second, I ripped a couple tracks from this JSP set and did a A/B comparison to the same tracks from the Bear Family box Let the Good Times Roll: Decca 1938-54: they sound identical. Moreover, the waveforms look virtually identical when compared in Audacity. This leads me to conclude that JSP appropriated the material for its set from the Bear Family box. Apparently this sort of appropriation is legal wherever JSP is headquartered, but morally it's distasteful, to say the least. Personally, I think Bear Family charges far too much for its products, but does Bear deserve to have its hard work sold on the cheap by its competitors? It's up to you to decide by voting with your wallet.

reviewText:
The thing is, they were always the choice of the highbrows. While The Beatles spoke to the masses, the Stones were always favoured by the college crowd. Yet, it was the Beatles who evolved and deepened and matured, and who had the wisdom to quit before the well ran dry. The Stones are still going at it forty years later. Not going strong, just going through the motions. Their well dried up years ago.
Being of a certain age, I remember when "Satisfaction" first topped the charts. So my disappointment with this album does not stem from the foreshortened view of history that sometimes afflicts the young. It's actually a grown man's lament that a bunch of otherwise talented guys can't find the courage to grow up.
Bridges to Babylon is a paean to arrested adolescence. It is dumb, transparent and banal. It repeats everything the boys were screaming about decades ago, except that the "boys" are now senior citizens.
It is important that I make myself clear about this: I believe that growing old is one of life's gifts. I have no desire to revert to youth. Been there done that. But surely if growing old is to have any significance, it must involve an evolution for the better: the deepening of wisdom and the amassing of experience.
This album contains none of these things. It doesn't even make a passing bow to nostalgia or reflection. Just inane songs about how desirable, mysterious and dangerous women are. The stuff third-rate poets have been nauseating about for thousands of years, and the Stones for going on forty.
It took the Beatles less than seven years to progress from the frivolity of "She Loves You" to the introspection of "Let It Be". We saw them find wisdom before our eyes. It was wondrous to grow up with them. But the Stones lost that sense of wonder long ago because they refused to grow up. For more than twenty-five years now, we have been stuck on the same old ride in the same old time loop. This album is the worst sort of exploitation: a cynical vehicle to print money by recycling the ossified reputation of a band permanently parked in puberty. Sad.

"Girls don't like boys, girls like cars and money
boys will laugh at girls when they're not funny
and these girls like these boys and these boys like these girls"

As for the actual melodies... there's no substance to them... they strike not one emotion in me. Lifestyles of the Rich and Famous pretty much lacks any semblance of this, being mostly drums and Benji's irritating-as-nails-on-blackboard attempt at singing a comprehensible melody. The Anthem is just plain annoying, sounding like something they'd play at a pep-rally. Hold On attempts to speak to a crowd of angst-ridden teenagers, which, from my experience, are declining in number, with the heartfelt words of "this world is co-ho-ho-ho-hoooollldd", showing that 'GC' as all the preps say, can be both bubblegum-pop fun and "meaningful" on the same album! After all, who wants to hear some positive, uplifting lyrics like those from Killswitch Engage when you can hear an album entitled "The Young and the Hopeless?"
Thirdly, the marketing image they're making and their egotistics are really starting to pee me off. I don't care how punk they supposedly look (I don't define myself by the way I dress or the music I listen to although others obsess over it), I don't care if they SAID they're punk or not, that's irrelevant, it's the fact that they get raving reviews for lyrics shallower than a hot tub and music that has no emotional substance to it and in which the guitars are two-dimensional (if they play them at all).
What this band needs to do to be any good:
1) Lose the corny name (bands named after someone's mother's name isn't the in thing)
2) Take instrument playing 101
3) Learn that there's more than one chord or riff possible to play on the guitar

Until then, all this deserves is one star, because that's the lowest rating I can give.

reviewText:
Anyone interested in purchasing the recent Robert Palmer reissues from Culture Factory or Edsel would be wise to read these two articles from SuperDeluxeEdition:

#1: Online music forums are buzzing at the moment with fans claiming that Edsel's recent Island-era Robert Palmer reissues show signs of being mastered from an MP3 source.

Using sound editing software such as Audacity, audiophiles often like to `look' at the sound of tracks via waveforms - it's a way to check the state of the mastering. Some fans of the late English singer have been doing just this with the latest reissues and are unhappy with what they see. "There is absolutely no musical information above 16 kHz, which is a dead giveaway" stated one person - the implication being that this was an indication of an MP3 source. Many fans have emailed us in the last 24 hours asking if they should not buy the reissues and if we knew whether there was any truth in these claims.

So we put these allegations to Edsel label manager Val Jennings and he was adamant that the masters had been nowhere near an MP3 file.

"We were given flat transfers by Universal for all the albums and bonus tracks, on CDs with Universal's Belsize Road Tape Library inlays. Since they came directly from the tape library, I can't see how MP3s would come into it. The CDs certainly don't have MP3s on them", he said.

When pushed about the actual source and details around the transfers themselves he told us:

"I can but assume that they would have been new transfers from the tapes with no extra EQ. They were done in 2006 for Universal's very own catalogue team, who were all set to reissue the albums, until the whole project was shelved for reasons no-one involved can remember".

Clearly frustrated with the situation Val added, "I really don't know what else to say. It's shame that people can't just be glad that someone has reissued the records, instead of trying to find or invent faults."

#2: When Edsel Records reissued Robert Palmer`s Island era albums on CD, we were delighted. Regular SDE readers will know, we rate the Yorkshireman's diverse '70s output highly and like many fans were frustrated with the lack of activity around his catalogue.

Although the (Edsel)reissues that came out at the end of August were budget conscious combo-packs, with two albums in each set (three, in one case), the packaging itself was excellent, with slipcases, thick booklets, essays, lyrics and some great archive photography and scans of sleeves and record labels. Most of the albums also came with bonus tracks.

Unfortunately, enthusiasts who'd purchased these sets started reporting in online music forums that the sound quality was not what you might expect from an original tape transfer. Some were stating that the albums looked like they'd been mastered from MP3s.

That got us thinking. If the new Edsel releases are indeed less-than-optimum, then what is the best way to listen to Robert Palmer's Island albums? Exactly which CDs sound the best? Are the Edsel reissues, really that bad?

There are a number of different masterings, and rather than heap amateur analysis on top of amateur analysis, we asked mastering engineer Nick Watson to give us his professional opinion. In his 23 year career Nick has worked with bands like Faith No More, The Kinks and The Libertines and he co-owns (with Tim Debney) of Fluid Mastering in London.

We gave Nick three versions of Palmer's 1976 album "Some People Can Do What They Like" and asked him to analyse them. One was the new 2013 Edsel CD, the second was an original Island CD from the 1980s, and the final disc was the 2011 remaster from US label Culture Factory. To keep things simple this comparison is based on the first track of the album "One Last Look." Here's what Nick had to say.

The spectrogram image show(ed) clearly that there is no useful audio data on the CD above 16kHz, and the blocky nature of the display is consistent with the audio having been subjected to some form of data compression such as MP3 or AAC or similar. The sound of the disc is also consistent with this, with the top end of the recording appearing to switch on and off, the stereo image flinching, and some twittering artifacts in the top end, as one would expect from low resolution data-compressed signal. As a test, using a clean uncompressed version of the same track as a control, I found that a reduction of the bitrate to about 192kbps was required to reduce the perceived quality to something similar to the Edsel CD (see this image to illustrate).

Apart from the data-compression artifacts, the album sounds quite thick and bloated (too much low-mid) and very closed off in the top end, although this latter point will be partly to do with the data-compression.

This CD sounds exactly as one might expect for a reissue done at this time. The EQ is quite thin and the sound is slightly brittle - although once the listener has adjusted to this there are no unusual or distracting artifacts. The stereo image is open and consistent. This sounds like an album that could do with being properly remastered, from the original tapes, with a little extra warmth and bass in the EQ and the more natural and transparent sound of good quality modern A to D conversion.

Looking at the spectrogram, (I could) see that the frequency response continues upwards from 16kHz and there is none of the blockiness of the Edsel image. Another interesting point is at the extreme high end you can see the response tails away smoothly, but rapidly, at about 21kHz. This would probably be due to the more aggressive filters used in A to D converters in the 80s and early 90s.

The spectrogram on this version has no blockiness and no rapid rolloff of the high frequencies. This would demonstrate that as far as digital processing is concerned, this version has suffered the least degradation, i.e. it has not been data compressed and was converted from analogue to digital using more recent technology.

The sound of this version however is dreadful. The tone of it would suggest that at least 8 dB of boost has been applied at around 2kHz giving it what you might describe as a telephonic kind of brightness, and the stereo image swerves from side to side wildly and seemingly at random, with the left channel becoming so loud at times that clipping distortion is audible. Given that no engineer in his right mind would do this to a recording (and I'm allowing for the fact that plenty of engineers do some pretty awful things in the mastering world) I can only assume that on this occasion the guy left the room and WHAT WE HEAR ON THE Culture Factory CD IS THE RESULT OF THE CAT WALKING ACROSS THE CONSOLE. All of which is a real shame as it's a great album, and one that I would enjoy listening to for pleasure.

Conclusions

Given the choice between these three CD editions, the hands-down winner for me is the original '80s Island reissue - which, for all its faults (faults it shares with pretty much every other reissue of that period) it at least doesn't suffer from strange sonic artifacts or appallingly harsh EQ.

Coming back to the much discussed Edsel reissue finally, one might wonder how such a thing could have happened. Well, I'm not going to speculate about that and can only talk about what I find on the disc itself. However, in general terms, I can perhaps allude to the fact that before computers and music became so closely intertwined, mastering was something that could only be undertaken by professional engineers. Today, however, anyone with a computer, whether they work in a studio or an office, can pick up a disk or download a file, and do stuff with it. Not everyone for instance knows how to make a 1:1 copy of a CD, and might load it into some freeware in order to attempt to do so, perhaps resulting in some inadvertent degradation. I even know of record company employees who do things to audio masters using applications such as iTunes, without really knowing what they're doing or why, other than it being something that they have been shown how to do by someone else in the office. It's almost akin to say, 20 years ago, them taking a master tape out of the box, and unravelling it and then editing it using scissors and sellotape. Except that that would never have happened.

(by Nick Watson, minor edits by me)

But I plodded on, wondering what this "soup of the day" really was. Were those bits of carrot or flesh wounds? And it didn't matter because we had techmologicalized. We were pushing buttons now and DNA-approved to gain access to pay-per-view oxygen. We evolved through hope and memory loss. By the time I reached "Whatever," I really didn't care, which provided perhaps the finest moment of this failed experiment -- a time-transcendent conversation with Gnarls truly, wrapped in tusks of irony. reviewText: I listen to a lot of comedy albums. A LOT. My favorites include some staples, like Dave Chappelle's sets,early George Carlin, and Louis CK. I also like everything Paul F. Tompkins has ever done, and I still can't get over how great Norm Macdonald's latest album is. I'll listen to the clean guys (Brian Regan, Jim Gaffigan) as well as to the relentlessly crude (Patton Oswalt, Daniel Tosh). I'm no stranger to the angry comedian shtick, although it's not what I actively seek out. I see eye-to-eye with most of the angry comedians -- David Cross, Doug Stanhope, Bill Hicks -- but it's not enough for me to hear well-articulated rage. There must be, y'know, something funny about it all. In my mind, Lewis Black comes closest to mingling his punches with punchlines. I find that many of the others -- including some of Carlin's later stuff -- tries to just ride the rage without really doing anything clever with either the subject matter or the words used to describe it. It's less about being funny and witty, and more about how viciously you can tear into the topic. I'd never heard Maron's stand-up before, but his podcast has been highly touted by all in the know, and as a huge fan of comedy, I figured I'd give it a listen. After my first listen, I was not just disappointed but also irritated and bewildered. I really, honestly, seriously couldn't understand why this was supposed to be considered funny. I make it a habit of listening to all albums twice before I consider reviewing them, but it took me many months to build up the willingness to sit through this record again. Maron hates himself. He hates his audience. He hates his job. He often mocks the audience for not getting a joke long before he's even told the joke, as if he is preparing for failure. A self-fulfilling prophecy, if you ask me. Only two of his bits did I even mildly enjoy -- tracks 7 & 9. I enjoyed the former (The Creation Museum) because he does a good job of spoofing Creationism without coming across as mean-spirited, and he makes a great and amusing point when he compares militant atheists with militant Christians. The latter track (Earl's Rooter) is notable for being one of the few times when Maron ISN'T railing against himself, his life, his ex, or the state of the word today. It's just a fairly humorous tale about his first experience with clearing a septic tank. Obviously comedic sensibilities differ. Some people love a good venting, and even vitriol can be engaging when it's tightly-written and delivered well. Maron's bits, however, mostly sound like him rambling impromptu into the mike, with occasional asides when jokes don't land like he wants them to. Overall, it's just dark, dismal stuff that sounds stream of consciousness. There were times when I felt sorry for him. Other times I simply felt relieved that I wasn't him. Still other times he simply got on my nerves, and I wished he'd finish his point and move on. But I rarely, rarely laughed or even smiled. For fans of Maron, obviously this review isn't helpful. For newbies, however, consider what other comedians you like. If you regularly enjoy David Cross, Bill Hicks, George Carlin, Doug Stanhope or Lewis Black, you might get into Maron's style. Everyone else should know that, as far as this album's title goes, it has to be funny far less than it has to be mad.

reviewText: When in high school I almost destroyed my treasured "Yes" LPs, because I listened for these albums for hours and hours - as thousands of other suckers did, searching for some secret knowledge and hidden message. Bugger it - there is none. Centuries later I suspected already the existence of Internet, but I didn't know anything about Amazon - otherwise I would have bought them from Amazon and save the trouble of a trip to "Tower Records" in London. Well, I bought them on CDs and kept listening to until I came to a painful conclusion: we are dealing with musical Maoists who are in the dark room searching for a black cat, and they don't even want to admit that it's not there. Somehow the music reminds an elaborated and over-decorated facade which hides an ugly naked truth - a simple concrete pavillion of a public WC. "Yes" are exceptional musicians who go on and on into lengthy improvisations, showcasing of instrumental prowess and complicated construction of songs, while tin falsetto of Anderson wandering above - looking to which part to stick to. It became a music for self-appointed cognoscenti and illuminati - not literate enough to know classical music, but wishing to be above "art crowd". All these virtuoso ventures to my most humble opinion cover one simple thing - "Yes" plays instruments, not music. Meditating with the candles was a good try, but the inspiration obviously got lost in the darkness, while the candles should have been used for better purposes. Composing is not their forte, all these artificial complexities cover a sheer misery of melody. It was a good show, I really loved it - time to face the truth. I got rid of my "Yes", and listen mainly to "Rare Bird", "Frumpy Live" and - if you want progressive - Czeslaw Niemen. Until now I keep some LPs - because of Roger Dean. P.S. By the way, Touch - most humbly, but strongly recommended - did it all in 1969. Actually, pre-dated and blew away (if given a chance) many of British prog-rock peers.

reviewText:
This may be the second worst Priest album after Ram it Down. Rocka Rolla can be excused because the band hadn't found its sound yet, Turbo and Point of Entry are excuseable because the band (and the fans) looked at both albums as experients. There's no such redemption here, this album is every bit as bad as Ram it Down. Granted, then first two tracks (Freewheel Burning and Jawbreaker) are awesome songs, the rest are all completely forgettable. Even look at the stupid song titles (Love Bites, Heavy Duty, Turn On Your Light). Love Bites is a mind-numbingly awful track with stupid lyrics about Vampires (Vampires are awesome but not here). Heavy Duty and the title track both stink, in fact both are the two worst priest songs ever. Some Heads are Gonna Roll has a good solo but that's it. Eat Me Alive has a good intro, and then goes downhill from there.

And another thing, the lyrics are TERRIBLE. Yeah Painkiller had stupid lyrics too but it could get away with it because the music was so damned awesome. There's no such redemption for that too, the lyrucs are stupid. With dumb lyrics like "We're gonna rock you till your metal hunger's fed", "Let's all join forces- rule with an iron hand- and prove to all the world- Metal rules the land" as well as "With animal lust they'll devour your life- and slice your word to bits like a knife". This is especially shocking since Halford wrote the lyrics. Wasn't Halford supposed to be the "Metal God" or something? As for the production is terrible too- the guitars sound like keyboards, the drums sound like Holland is banging on a plastic cup, and the bass is too loud. THere are noticeable volume drops on the album too.

How this trash got the reputation of "Best Priest Album" is beyond me. Cut your teeth on "Killing Machine" or "Sad Wings of Destiny" or even "Painkiller" instead, if you must.

reviewText:
How is it that Whitney Houston can take a long break between albums and then still make an album that sounds like it was thrown together? You'd think that with a slim ten tracks, you'd find at least ONE song worth listening to. Well, you don't.
But I think we all should have seen this one coming. Whitney introduced this album with a bad first single ("Whatchulookinat"), and, well, a bad second single ("One Of Those Days"), and...hmmm, a bad third single ("Try It On My Own"). That already covers the beginning, middle, and end of the album (tracks 10, 1, and 6, respectively).
And as so often is the case, the guest stars don't make things better. I guess Tweet was just honored to be working with Whitney, because the two ladies deliver bad harmony in "Things You Say". And her husband joins her on the predictable "My Love". (By the way, doesn't Whitney's calling Bobby "the king of R&B" make you want to throw your television out the window?)
Lazy sampling doesn't help this album either. "One Of Those Days" samples The Isley Brothers' "Between The Sheets" for the millionth time. And it doesn't help that the song doesn't go anywhere. Then her rendition of the classic Debby Boone song "You Light Up My Life" isn't the best, and I really hope she doesn't release it and then it becomes a monster hit (Whitney always seems to get props for songs that aren't hers...must I bring up "I Will Always Love You"?).
We all know about Whitney's problems, and we also know that the quality of her music has been going downhill ever since that corny sing-along "My Love Is Your Love". But I didn't think she'd hit rock bottom. In reality, Bobby Brown's Forever is better than this album. Leave it alone.

reviewText:
Jessica Simpson's re-release of "In This Skin," originally issued last August, does little to improve a weak album.
The original tumbled down the chart due to its first single, the Diane Warren-penned "Sweetest Sin." Although excellent lyrically, it was too softly cooed by Simpson and lacked a hook. The success of "Newlyweds" on MTV put her back in the public eye, though. Then, the second single, "With You," entered pop radio and became a hit. With the help of constant CD signings (and in some cases, tuna can signings), people started to buy "In This Skin" again.
Apparently, having Simpson on television, in gossip columns and on radio wasn't enough. So the decision was made to re-release "Skin" featuring two new cover songs, a rearranged tracklisting, bonus DVD and new artwork. And, it worked -- going all the way to No. 2.
The two cover songs included are Robbie Williams' "Angels," on which she gives a decent performance, and a completely hideous rendition of Berlin's classic "Take My Breath Away" from 1986's "Top Gun." Any fan of the original has been appalled by this remake, and yet the song is becoming increasingly more difficult to avoid. Why? The answer is simple: Hype gets attention, not talent.
If Simon Cowell ever said one correct thing, it was when he said Simpson's voice is not impressive. Although he is not completely correct, since "I Have Loved You" and "Underneath" are moving performances on the disc.
With the right material, Simpson can sing. However, she cannot sing or write as well as her idol, Mariah Carey, or even Christina Aguilera. Indeed, she lost out to Aguilera when auditioning for the Mickey Mouse Club after getting intimidated because Christina "sounded like Mariah."
It is confusing why anyone would buy this album. The DVD does contain footage of the first season of "Newlyweds," and her wedding to Nick Lachey on the DVD -- but don't we see plenty of them on a daily basis?
Unfortunately, artists with sheer talent and integrity sell fewer records and garner less attention because they don't have the audacity to cover classic songs such as "I Got You Babe" on television specials and walk around in front of cameras for all to see.
Mark these words: Jessica Simpson, though moderately talented, is unlikely to survive much longer in this business.

In my mind, at least, it makes more sense to provide people with the oportunity to here songs that many Floyd fans don't even know exist, rather than slap togeather "hit" songs that everyone has already heard before anyway. I myself have most of the unreleased Barret material-mostly from bootleged copies- its hard to find but it IS out there(go to ebay and look around). There is easily a full albums' worth of unreleased Barret stuff. It is sad to know that the record companies and David Gilmore are more concerned with making even more MONEY rather than providing the avid Pink Floyd the opportunity just to here more of their wonderful music.
In closing, its offensive that great songs from "Dark Side"(Breathe, Brain Damage, Eclipse)were substituted for mediocre ones from mediocre albums(the fletcher memorial home???come on).

reviewText: I'm baffled by the amount of praise this album has received from fans and critics alike. I'm even more baffled at how often the band repeats itself here. The obvious thing is this: Petrucci and Portnoy had a writer's block before recording this (and they still have). So what did they do? They came up with a concept album which is (more or less) connected with a song from their earlier, better material; this enabled the band to extensively reuse themes from that song, change a few notes here and there, tack on some indulgent instrumental wankery, put a few forgettable, soggily orchestrated ballads in between and repeat the damn thing in every possible way over and over again. Sorry people, but this has nothing to do with musical genius but rather plays like a mean prank on the loyal DT-fanbase and the ignorant mainstream masses who are searching for a good prog-rock CD.

It's almost like she's saying, "I'm Beyonce, I'm amazing, and people will jump on anything I create, so why even make an attempt."
I'm one of the idiots who purchased the deluxe album, and after unwrapping it at home and actually checking out the track listing and such, all of these songs could have DEFINATELY fit onto one album. There was nothing deluxe about it.
After listening to the first disc, I almost felt I had to check my stereo to make sure I didn't have the same song on repeat over and over. The entire first disc is nothing but power ballads, that lack just that, power. There was no emotion, they all sounded exactly the same: bland, dull, and over-polished. It made me feel like she went into the studio and just recorded each track to the same intrumental, back to back, and called it a night.

The second disc I'm assuming was supposed to be the disc with club anthems, party songs and such. It had the typical "independent" ladies song, and the typical "boast like a man" song. I forced myself through the whole thing just to say I gave it a shot.  Basically the only song worth anything on this entire collection is the song "Single Ladies", which I'm still not bananas about.
Beyonce, you're incredible, but this album was a slap in the face to all of your fans and anyone who even mildly liked you. Giving it two stars is generous, and I wasn't in the mood.

It definately seems like I'm bashing Beyonce in this review, but I'm not bashing her, I'm bashing her feeble effort in this album release. I'm sure she'll notice the poor feedback from this cd and the next will be incredible. She should definately take her time and create an album with songs that have some staying power. Because if there ever was a Beyonce album to forget in the dust it's definately this one.
