reviewText:
Ladies and gentleman: meet the latest indie-rock darling!  Andrew Bird enjoys a devoted and growing fanbase who will eagerly snatch up his CDs and concert tickets.  Disliking Andrew Bird is about as easy as hating a puppy which is why writing this review is so difficult.

Armchair Apocrypha, like all of Mr. Bird's studio releases, falls well-short of his live performances.  Longtime fans already know that his "Fingerlings" releases showcase the real Andrew Bird: haunting and spare performances that are impossibly eclectic.  Armchair Apocrypha, on the other hand, is a rather overwrought and bloated offering.  Too often, Mr. Bird chooses to overproduce the songs with armies of overdubs that squeeze the life out of the songs.

And therein lies the problem.  A glance at the liner notes reveal that Mr. Bird himself is the producer, with some other guy co-producing.  In live settings, Andrew Bird is limited to what he can do with his loop machine, thus creating a "less is more" handicap that works well for his songwriting.  In studio with no one to rein him in, Mr Bird is free to orchestrate to his heart's content.  This is not a good thing.  The problem with Andrew Bird playing with a roomful of musicians is that it makes him sound, well... ordinary.  Armchair Apocrypha is a pleasant little collection of songs but there is absolutely nothing that sets it apart.

Case in point: Andrew Bird's performance on Letterman.  He could have put on a sublime performance, imagine him playing solo and wowing the crowd with something on par with, say, a version of Master Fade from the Fingerlings 2 era.  Instead, it was just a watered-down performance with superfluous accompaniment.  Mr. Bird could have challenged the subversiveness of the Radiohead's October 2000 performance on SNL but instead he went for the forgettable charm of the Gin Blossoms July 1995 Letterman appearance.

I concede that it's unfair to completely write off Armchair Apocrypha.  Stand out tracks include "The Supine" and the amusingly titled "Yawny and the Apocalypse".  Both are instrumental pieces that capture Andrew Bird at his best: brooding soundscapes built with looped background instrumentation.  "The Supine" features some cathedral-esque reverb that immediately sets the gothic tone.  You almost expect monks to start singing.  Meanwhile, "Yawny" opens with birds chirping and the piece really _does_ sound like a meditative take on the apocalypse.  The end of the world never sounded so beautiful though.

The rest of the CD aims high but falls short of the mark. "Imitosis" (which originally appeared on the CD Weather Systems) is recast with a bigger monster stomp sound though it's unclear why.  "Heretics" features an annoying singalong chorus and a guitar riff that doesn't quite riff.  "Scythian Empires" is a neutered, studio-version of the much more dynamic live arrangement that appeared on Fingerlings 3.  "Spare-Ohs" gets a little lift from Haley Bonar's guest appearace on vocals but it's not enough to overcome the fact that the song is rather non-descript and pedestrian.

Which brings me to my next point: the vocals.  Mr. Bird's singing tends to be hit and miss.  At his best, he sounds like early Michael Stipe with a bit more range: lots of syllables and key phrases that leap out of the inspired mumbling.  At the other end of the spectrum, Andrew Bird completely oversings ("Dark Matter") and risks sounding like That Guy From Matchbox Twenty or, even worse, The Guy From Live Who Also Had A Cameo in Fight Club.

Me, I'd take Andrew Bird's live (and solo) performance any day over Armchair Apocrypha.  He can accomplish much more with just his guitar, violin, glockenspiel, whistle and voice than with a roomful of dead-weight musicians.  Not that my opinion matters.  There are countless fans (hello MySpace!) who will mindlessly lap up his uninspired releases and even more who will buy his music because it's "hip".

Now if you'll excuse me, I'm listening to a vinyl copy of the latest Arcade Fire and I have to go flip the LP.  Plus I have to go iron my Modest Mouse t-shirt.

reviewText:
I have heard "Running on Empty" a zillion times on the radio in my car (cheap car, cheap factory stereo) and always really liked this song. I finally found a remaster on hdtracks and bought the CD. Boy was I surprised!

My first thought upon listening to my new purchase on home stereo system was, "This is a live version and it isn't very well recorded. I must have bought the live version by mistake. Maybe the studio version is what I'm used to hearing on the radio and maybe it sounds better". So I looked through all of Jackson Browne's CDs on Amazon and didn't find any studio version of this song. I even went to Jackson Browne's web site and looked through all his recordings and found that there is no studio version of this song - this live version is what I've heard on the radio all these years!

The song "Load Out" is 6 min 3 seconds long and was recorded live. The last five or ten seconds is a transition into the next song, "Stay". On the original master tapes this was probably one long continuous recording with no breaks but on the CD, "Load Out" gets cut off just as it transitions into "Stay". So, you're listening to "Load Out" and it is transitioning into "Stay" and then there's this abrupt silence where the mastering engineer decided to create a new track out of "Stay". "Stay" picks up, note-for-note, right where "Load Out" ended. Either the engineer or the label decided, arbitrarily, to split this continuous "double" song in half. The first time I listened to it I thought, "what the h*** has my CD player done to this song???!" After listening to the two songs again and again, I decided to merge them into one song using a free tool called "Audacity". I just basically took "Stay" and stuck it right on the end of "Load Out" and saved it as a single song and burned me own copy of the CD with this "whole" song on it. It sounds much better to me this way - there's no idiotic, arbitrary, and unsettling hack between these "two" songs.

On the song, "Cocaine", the last 30 seconds of the song is the crazed mutterings of, I guess, the band, and they sound stoned! The first thing you hear after the music ends is,"sniff, sniff" - I guess someone snorting coke (or at least is supposed to sound like it). Then a couple of voices start talking about "it takes a clear mind to make it? It takes a clear mind to take it", followed by weird laughter. Very weird.

This is a strange set of recordings. On "The Road", it sounds like a studio recording for the first three minutes, then at exactly 3:00 minutes into the song, you hear a crowd cheering for a couple of seconds, then the song resumes but the sound of Browne's voice on the recording has changed - now, all of a sudden, it's big and boomy and you hear the echo of the auditorium. I wonder if they dubbed half studio/half-live together into one song here.

One thing I do like is David Lindley's lap steel slide guitar on a lot of these songs. I've always been a fan of slide guitar and I really like David Lindley's guitar playing. For me that's a positive thing about the CD.

This CD isn't all live. Apparently some of it was recorded live, some of it was recorded in hotel rooms while Browne was on the road, etc. Overall, it's a really dull, flat, lifeless. heavily compressed recording a good system, sadly. The last song, "Stay", is probably the one I like the most from the point of sound quality.

As others have pointed out, the lyrics on some songs are pretty dated, referring to the days of yore when CB radio was popular (that was a LONG time ago - about the same time disco was popular).

SO if you plan to buy this CD or download the mp3s, be aware that this is not a very good recording. You may like it for other reasons - nostalgia, the lyrics, etc. but don't expect it to sound anything like what you're used to hearing on the radio.

I'm really disappointed. I was really hoping to enjoy this music!

reviewText: As with other reviewers, I've wondered what the record label has been thinking when it comes to these jazz boxed sets. The Miles Davis, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Charlie Christian sets...all issued in "deluxe," "creative" packaging that comes up short, shorter, or shortest in the two areas most important to me when I purchase these collections (not counting the music itself, of course): safe storage of the discs and readable, organized liner notes.  Well, this latest fiasco is the last straw. I have a long-running interest in Herbie Hancock's music and was interested in this boxed set...but I will not purchase it unless/until it gets reconfigured in a user-friendly package (hint: start with jewel boxes and leave the "innovations" to the musicians).
label: negative

reviewText:
Paul Oakenfold would love to take credit as the man who introduced trance to America, but all he does on TRANCEPORT is display a mix of commercial tracks, cheesy synth lines, and music with little artistic quality. It's a shame that this caught the public's attention while quality mixes like Sasha and John Digweed's Northern Exposure series are unknown outside the circle of progressive dance music cognoscenti.
While the track's here are bubble-gum pop entertaining, they have no value that contributes to the evolution of dance music. About the only highlight of TRANCEPORT is that it is one of the few places to hear the Sasha V The Light remix of gusGus's "Purple," honestly one of the best trance remixes ever, elevating the original (excellent) song to even higher peaks of aural bliss. However, every track on this disc is anthemic, and nowhere does Oakenfold include subtle tracks that would give the mix peaks and valleys.
Avoid TRANCEPORT, it's commercial and doesn't reflect what trance music was originally about, the underground sound pioneered by DJ's like Sasha, Dave Seaman, and Jimmy Van M.

reviewText: I have been a fan of the group since back in the earliest 70's; discharged from the Marine Corps, wondering what to do with my life and listening to Renaissance on late night WYSP out of Philly. Intensely powerful music and lyrics, the captivating, haunting voice of Annie Haslam whom I immediately developed a crush on (some wonderful photos of her from that period- all very sexy- all very fine). Okay, so enough background credentials. I loyally followed the group to the bitter end and agreed with their decision to break up. Their last few albums were atrocious- trying to appeal to a market which no longer wanted them in lieu of monstrous garbage flooding the airways. I met Ms. Haslam in '06- at Al Stewart's Winterfest concert in New Hope PA. I was nervous. She was distant. Photos were taken, one of which currently hangs over my desk. I praised her work with Renaissance. She mentioned her solo career- of which I have not been thrilled. Don't ask a question if you do not wish the (rare) honest answer. THIS point brings us long-windedly around to this current Renaissance endeavor. Annie Haslam can't write worth a damn and shouldn't. She is a dramatic lyricist, but as with her solo albums which ran the gambit of god worship and praise these lyrics are dull, drowned in orchestration and weak in the bargain. I can- and have- written better while intoxicated, back in the days when Renaissance was a force to be respected and reckoned with. The loss of Dunford is tragic without doubt, however they should hire on Ian Anderson full time and cut the flute master loose to replace Michael. Grandine il Vento is ponderous. The instrumentals harken back to Turn of the Cards, or Novella for example, but the lyrics are just weighty and weak. Likewise I had to refer to the liner notes to even catch what she is saying. she seems more concerned with hitting the high notes than clear pronunciation. Conversely, don't let the guys sing- NONE OF THEM. in comparison to her they are howling beasts and should stay behind the instruments rather than in front of the microphones. I anticipate much flak from this review, however it is the truth regardless (albeit mine). Chris Lay (disappointed fan)

reviewText:
This album is absolute trash. It's really tragic that Jerry Only has decided to keep on trying to tour under the name of The Misfits with whoever he could find at the Punk Rock Retirement Home. Only may legally own the rights to the name, but every Misfits fan knows that his band is nothing more than the worst Misfits tribute band working today. I was really excited about the idea of a new misfits lineup until I saw some clips of them performing. You would think musicians who have over 30 years of experience playing in bands would be able to make it through at least one song without completing losing their sync, yet this group seems to do it every time.
Devil's Rain is the result of what happens when a bass player decides he should sing and write songs. Not only are the lyrics to every track nothing short of cringeworthy, but the vocals are so poorly delivered I couldn't believe they didn't autotune him just so he'd sound like he had some idea what he was doing. He's flat, he's off key and he doesn't seem to understand that a singer can modulate the pitch of his voice up and down. He's a backup singer and he should have kept it that way. Forgetting entirely that this album has a Misfits logo on it, like let's say the band was called Jerry and The Onlies. It would still be awful. It's just a bad record, there's no getting around it. The songs are not catchy or clever, the lyrics and vocals are terrible, and the guitar sound is so off the mark that it doesn't even sound like rock, punk or metal - it sounds like a teenage kid who just got his first distortion pedal and hasn't figured out the settings yet.
Sadly, the rest of the veteran punk rockers in the trio don't really pick up the slack - some of the most boring, repetitive, songs I've ever heard. There is no groove like what we're used to hearing from Misfits songs, no energy, none of the elements that made the band popular to begin with. This is simply Jerry Only trying desperately to justify his taking Danzig to court years ago. He took an intellectual property that could have made him very successful for the rest of his life and he completely ruined it. This "Misfits" is a joke.
Danzig and Doyle perform misfits songs together. Doyle and Chud have a new band. The Misfits are doing just fine without Jerry. As far as I'm concerned, a Misfits reunion happens every time Danzig goes on tour. They may not legally be able to call it The Misfits, but all the fans know the reality. Jerry Only's Misfits are a huge failure of a delusional old man who tried to screw his old friends over and failed miserably. The result is Devil's Rain, a blight on the name of The MIsfits that should have never been produced. It's just bad.

reviewText: Robert le Diable is a rare opera, but nevertheless there are a few different recordings in the catalog to choose from. One criterion in selection is whether it contains a libretto, since so many current opera recordings don't include one. And the libretto for an 'unusual' opera can be extremely hard to find otherwise. So the fact that this one happily proclaims, 'LIBRETTO DOWNLOADABLE AT [website name given]' does play a HUGE factor in selecting this recording. WARNING: it is a con job to achieve exactly that result. First of all, the website name they give doesn't exist. But I don't mind that. A little googling can locate the libretto and it is obviously for this item because it is for Brilliant Opera Collection with these artists. The problem is, it's all in French. No English translation. Now, it's a very long opera, comparable to Wagner's Siegfried. And that much text in French alone ... well, it's completely unrealistic for I would estimate 99% of opera listeners in the U.S. And is it unreasonable to fail to mention it is in French only? I say yes, it is unreasonable, for an English-language label in an English-language market. But ... they are covered. They are covered. After all, they only promised "Libretto available for download". They didn't promise "English translation". So, they are covered, they have your money, and you are screwed. Well, I still do have Amazon Comments, so I can warn anyone who would like to know. Addendum: the Dynamic CD set DOES include the French libretto and English translation. I haven't yet seen if it matches the Brilliant CD. Any opera this long is bound to be cut here and there and can't expect the librettos to match exactly.

The background noises and samples take on a life of their own in such a way that the main reason you would listen to this type of music (the beats, rhymes) become difficult to hear. There is no crispness to the sound as is heard on virtually every other professional recording in any genre. The sound is so blurred together it's hard to decipher what exactly El-p is talking about. reviewText:
[PLEASE NOTE: Dengue Fever have posted a nice response/review below. Please read it and decide for yourself! I'll leave my review up there, as it still reflects my feelings, but I really appreciate Dengue Fever getting online and explaining what was unexplained in the album package.]

...I was psyched (no pun intended) about this compilation, having seen Dengue Fever live and really enjoyed them. I was looking forward to hearing the music that inspired them...and, for the most part, this is cool, cool stuff: winding guitars, keening vocals, woozy organ, etc.

But, I can't help but wonder if these tracks have been messed with. I think they have. There are some cheezy electric piano sounds and some drums that really, really sound like they were grafted over the top of the original recordings. These unwelcome, history-distorting additions aren't on every track, but when they are (like on track 2) they make the song pretty much unlistenable.

reviewText:
Aside from Universal's obvious search for another stream of revenue from a well-worn music catalog, there's one other wrongheaded reason for this collection to exist: To provide an ego trip for a bunch of mixmasters -- to let them say, "I put my stamp on a Motown song." For the most part, they shouldn't be proud of this.

What most of the producers have done here isn't as much rework the songs as suck the life out of them. In their original forms, these classic tunes were magical coexistences of melody and beat. Here, the songs, with a couple of exceptions, have become slaves to the beat, bent to conform to rigid, ill-fitting suits of rhythmic armor. I mean, did the world need a crunk version of "ABC"? What was once an exuberant, explosive tune is now caged inside a crappy beat. "My World Is Empty Without You" is empty of soul here. Rare Earth's "I Just Want to Celebrate" wants to turn in and call it a night instead. And -- the worst offender of all -- if you didn't know better, you'd swear there was a totally different vocal take on "Let's Get It On." Marvin Gaye's original, framed by that wah-wah guitar, was as raw and as mighty and as over-the-top of a plea for love (or sex) as has ever been heard on record. The new mix emasculates Marvin's vocal, turns him into some cheap, slick, subdued lounge pick-up artist -- and it's the same exact vocal track as the original!

The only two cuts that make the grade are ones that at least stay faithful to the roots of their respective songs: Jazzy Jeff & Pete Kuzma's low-key romp through the low-key-to-start-with "Papa Was a Rollin' Stone"; and the Futureshock Main Ingredient rendition of The Undisputed Truth's "Smiling Faces Sometimes." The latter is actually enhanced by guitar and electronics that wouldn't have been out of place on a 1971 recording, which this was.

As for the rest, it's just an abomination. To these "producers," the track could have been a Motown gem or a Beethoven symphony or an automotive how-to instruction manual -- as long as they could force their beats upon it. And that's just what they did.

reviewText: OK, let's just set some things straight.  Great movie.  Rotten soundtrack. Badelt has composed some truly original melodies and rythmns in other scores, and it's too bad that he doesn't seem to have had a lot of influence on this score. If you care little for texture and depth, or if all you do is listen for bass and Zimmer's same ol' recycled rythmns and hokey synthetic sound effects than you'll like this CD.  If your ear is tuned to the great swashbuckling scores of Korngold (Sea Hawk, Captain Blood), Debney (Cutthroat Island) and Williams (Hook) than you'll hate this CD.  It's to bad really.  I liked the movie.  I wanted to like the soundtrack.  Unfortunately I bought the CD trusting in Badelt before I saw the film. I got ride of it in less than 24 hours. If you do like this stuff please take my advice: sell the CD and go take a course on Music Appreciation.  This kind of cheap music production is what gives the "Film Score" a bad name in the world of music.  It's too bad I can't give this less than one star.

reviewText:
Whenever I read positive reviews for this Pantera album (and Pantera in general), it really boggles my mind as to why people think so highly of this rather derivative and inoffensive "metal" band.

Before I logically deconstruct the music, I'd like to cover some history about Pantera so that people can get a larger picture than the band and fans would like people to know.  Pantera started off in 1981 and just about everyone knows that hair metal was one of the hottest music trends in the 80's and guess what, Pantera played hair metal.  However, unlike the insipid swill like Bon Jovi and Poison, Pantera never really went anywhere in the 80's.  Then again, do you really think a band with brilliant songs like "Ride my Rocket" and "Metal Magic" would ever get anywhere beyond the drunken nightclubs in Arlington, Texas?  As the 80's were getting towards the end, Dimebag (then known as Diamond) Darrell knew they had to find a way to change the band so they would survive the upcoming 90's, so they kicked out original vocalist Terry Glaze and roped in New Orleans native Phil Anselmo, who also brought an Exhorder demo and told his new band mates to water down Exhorder's sound and market it as their own.  Guess what?  It was a smash success!!  I know that in the world of metal bands, bands put up some sort of image as part of their aesthetic and don't really believe what they say (unless if we're talking about Varg Vikernes of Burzum), but when bands change their image and sound just to fit with the current trends, that screams phoniness.

Now to the music.

For an album that's supposed to be considered a "classic" and a "masterpiece," I was extremely underwhelmed by the sheer lack of quality pervading on this record.  They took Exhorder's sound and diluted it to make it more digestible for the mainstream masses.  Exhorder was a good band, not masters in the genre, but at least they actually played thrash with a hint of NOLA sludge.  It's like Pantera took said sound, stripped away the thrash element (which was vital to Exhorder's formula), and replaced it with sluggish, groovy, and repetitive downtuned chugging to make the songs seem "heavy," completed with the occasional "burst of aggression" to make it seem "tough" and "brutal."  Now I don't have a problem with metal bands using slower, downtuned guitars so long as they actually craft good,  heavy riffs.  Examples of bands doing this right would be Black Sabbath, Cathedral, Ahab, and Asphyx (referring to each of their prime work, of course).  However, Pantera don't use their downtuned instruments to make good songs.  A fine example of this sonic flatulence would be the song "Walk."  It has the repetitive and ultra-silly start-stop chugging, and the fact that this swill is quite slow makes it all the more laughable when people actually label it as "heavy."  For all of you who champion Pantera as some great band yet pan equally detestable (if not more so) nu-metal feces like Slipknot, Korn, and the Deftones, take a look at where these imbeciles got their ideas from.  The first wave of nu-metal bands loved Pantera's sluggish, repetitive chugging that passes off as "heavy riffs" and they loved their angst-laden lyrics about how much they hate life (while some others strut around as being tough).  Granted, while Pantera wasn't nu-metal, they essentially laid out the groundwork for that detestable form of music.  While there are some songs like "Mouth for War" and "F***ing Hostile" that crank up the speed, making them more tolerable, they're still coupled with the sluggish guitars, and it doesn't help that the production is too clean and sterile for a metal record, taking away any sort of grittiness that could have helped these songs out.  As much as I hate to say it, Dimebag was capable crafting good guitar solos (not great ones, though).  However, his riffs were terrible and if you want good metal songs, you need good riffs to start and to complement them, you can bring in good solos.  Even though Dimebag's solos were pretty good, I can easily get my fix for cool solos satiated by popping in a MUCH superior metal album that has both great riffs and excellent solos, such as Megadeth's "Rust in Peace" or Deicide's "The Stench of Redemption."  Now to the vocals.  I really hate Phil Anselmo's vocals because he tries to be "diverse" by doing really bad pseudo-death growls, really bad hardcore shouting, and singing melodically (and badly).  It's bad enough that he's trying to sound like the toughest guy from New Orleans, but when he tries to sing in order to look "emotional" and whatnot, it comes off as hilariously pathetic.  The lyrics don't help "Vulgar Display of Power" one bit, either.  It's the banal swill about the band screaming "We're the toughest mofos down in these here parts and if you get in our way, we'll kick your as$!!" with the occasional "singing" about damaged relationships (yuck).  All around, save for some neat guitar solos, this album is worthless.

For those of you who think that "Vulgar Display of Power" is the best album of 1992, here's a short list of metal albums that came out in 1992 that are light-years better (and yes, I own all of them):

Nocturnus:  Thresholds
Demolition Hammer:  Epidemic of Violence
Solstice:  S/T
Asphyx:  Last One on Earth
Immortal:  Diabolical Fullmoon Mysticism
Darkthrone:  A Blaze in the Northern Sky
Hypocrisy:  Penetralia
Pan. Thy. Monium:  Dawn of Dreams
Atrocity:  Todessehnsucht
Sodom:  Tapping the Vein
Deicide:  Legion
Vital Remains:  Let Us Pray
Napalm Death:  Utopia Banished
Unleashed:  Shadows in the Deep

Do yourself a favor by referring to the above list to bolster your metal collection and let the copies of "Vulgar Display of Power" collect dust on the store shelf.

reviewText:
I wonder how this is one of the big sellers on Amazon. Is it simply because it is a box set of all the symphonies, by a great conductor?
For beginning listeners, I will say just this: if you're considering buying a set of all the Beethoven symphonies, JUST forget this one, and look elsewhere. Karajan, for example, or Kleiber, or Bhm. These CD's will give you a distorted idea of what Beethoven's symphonies are meant to sound like.
For the rest of you, who have heard several recordings, and who are familiar with Solti, I must say that these recordings were total disappointments for me, especially because I often favor Solti-CSO.
You might think that Solti's loud, thundering style which works well for so many composers, might suit the 5th and the 9th too. You might as also think that Solti, being the conductor that he is, could be 'trusted' with the Beethoven symphonies - but the fact is that these recordings fall flat on their faces.
So that I do not launch into strings of negative adjectives, let me just tell you about some of the more terrible parts of these recordings.
1. In the beginning of the 5th, before the build-up, Solti makes it go very, very slow, as though it might heighten the effect of the build-up later on. Try to imagine this: instead of a brusque da-da-da-DAH, we have a slow da-pause-da-pause-da-pause-daaaaaaaaaah; then an even larger pause; and so on.
2. In the fifth movement of the Pastoral - if you can recollect the song-like flow of Karajan - you'll find it entirely missing here. "Happy and thankful feelings after the storm" sounds more like "Statement of the storm having passed", if you'll pardon the poor analogy.
3. In the scherzo of the ninth - and this is a real joke! - if you can recall the part close to the beginning of the movement, the light, sharp taps on the tympani stating the first subject - Solti makes a mess of it: the tympani actually THUMP and CRASH out the first subject, losing it altogether!  If you can imagine that, it should be enough to put out the idea of Solti-CSO for the Beethoven symphonies altogether.

reviewText:
Jennifer Lopez's third full-length album was a disastrous valentine to her ex-boyfriend Ben Affleck -- goopy, watered-down and thoroughly dull, with a vague hint of voyeurism. So maybe she was trying to tell us something when she named the first single from "Rebirth," her new pop album, "Get Right." Sadly, this doesn't get right. It doesn't even get okay.

The idea of "Rebirth" seems to be to make hip-pop with a more acoustic sound -- hence things like the horn solo in "Get Right," which is the only memorable part of the entire song. What remains are bubbly little pop tunes and the odd mournful ballad, usually about How Much I Love Whatsisname And Will Love Him Forever, Or Next Week, Whichever Comes First.

After a bunch of club tracks, "Rebirth" gets sidetracked with bubblegum pop, and weepy, adoring ballads. One is (bad omen here!) a duet with her husband, Marc Anthony, who proves himself the superior singer as he soars above Lopez's childlike voice.

But at heart, this is no rebirth. Rather it's the same ol' same ol' from Lopez -- generic ballads and unexceptional club tunes, which are catchy but essentially forgettable. Only the odd song has a moment that is memorable, such as the aforementioned horn solo, which will set your teeth on edge after a few repetitions. The rest of the time, it's just highly repetitive beats and swoony bubblegum.

Lopez can certainly be counted as a singer, because she does sing. But as her assorted live performances proves, she isn't a very good one. Admittedly club tunes don't require the voice of an angel, but Lopez's are flat; they also have the over-polished quality of vocals smoothed over too much. And she falls flat on the emotional notes as well -- though she tries to convey deep passion in songs like "I, Love," she sounds like a teenager French-kissing her pillow.

Not that the songwriting on Lopez's album can possibly make up for her lack of vocal ability. For example, one song rhymes "the strange way you turn me on" with "as if you really didn't give a--unh!" Not impressive, rhyming a word with an inarticulate grunt. Sadly, no other songs manage writing more intelligent than comparing love to cherry pie. (Let's all say it in unison: Huh?)

A real "Rebirth" would be good writing, more imaginative music and more than one beat. But Jennifer Lopez strikes out yet again in her latest "rebirth," leaving only a handful of bland hip-pop tracks in her wake.

reviewText:
KITTENZ AND THEE GLITZ, Felix Da Housecat's long-awaited LP, is sixteen tracks of New Wave comeback funk. In 2001 Felix Da Housecat released two records which became hits in clubs, "Silver Screen Shower Scene" and "Harlot." These two tracks made for high expectation for many dance music fans such as myself.
However, KITTENZ AND THEE GLITZ is rather disappointing. I was looking forward to more tracks like "Silver Screen Shower Scene," 4/4-time tours de force that have invigorated the progressive house scene. Instead, I got an album full of sonic-noodling that can be compared most easily to the goofy interludes between songs on His Name is Alive's album FT. LAKE. Few of the tracks stand out, they are all mired in Felix's obsession with this genre and his lack of innovation.
Furthermore, the artwork here is terrible. The American version has drastically different artwork from the original British version. The import is designed to look like a British tabloid, the same theme Felix used on the dance records he released in 2001. The American version, on the other hand, has a rather tacky 70's blaxploitation look. Were one to purchase KITTENZ AND THEE GLITZ, I would suggest getting the import.
I can't recommend KITTENZ AND THEE GLITZ, there's really nothing new here. "Silver Screen Shower Screen" and "Harlot" are great tracks, "Madam Hollywood" is pretty good, but it's not worth buying the entire album just for those.

reviewText:
Ever since Otmar Liebert, every music producer doing something in the same genre seems compelled to (mis)appropriate the title "Flamenco."  Please understand one thing:  This album, nor Otmar Liebert, nor anything  like it, is "Flamenco", either "new," "old,"  or anything in between - and it is ESPECIALLY not like Flamenco as  interpreted by Spanish Gypsies, so it is doubly disrespectful of the  "real thing."

The proper word for this type of music was  coined in Spain long ago:  "aflamencada," meaning "flamenco  like" or "flamenco inspired," but NOT flamenco.  This is to  true Flamenco what a timid gelding is to a proud and fierce stallion.  Think of standing in an elevator suffering an interpretation of the Rolling  Stones' "Satisfaction" played by "The Hundred and One  Strings" and you'll get the idea.  And that's what this album is:  elevator and dentist chair music.

I feel compelled to write this addendum to my above 11/28/1999 review since the consistent criticism that I and other critics of this form of music receive (see, e.g., J. H. Minde's review) is that we are "purists" or "traditionalists" who are either unfamiliar with "new" flamenco or just refuse to acknowledge that there is such a thing as "new" flamenco.  Such criticisms only serve to reflect the writer's profound ignorance of the subject, the size of which may be glimpsed by the fact that many hundreds of volumes on flamenco exist in the Spanish language; there are major centers for flamenco studies in Spain; and the discography is in the thousands.

I am neither a "traditionalist" nor a "purist".  A "traditionalist" is like a museum curator - someone who has found something he or she loves so much that they want to preserve it intact for future generations.  A "purist" goes a step further and declares that the thing under the glass is the ONLY "authentic" one of its type and that all others, however similar, are, at best, only imitations of less quality.

There is indeed a "new flamenco" of which I and all other serious aficionados are extremely well aware.  Flamenco is a living art and as such continues to grow and change, and like any other passionate art has its fair share of "cutting edge" artists, radicals, and revolutionaries who are alternately praised and pilloried.  Some of these call themselves "flamencos", others reject the term even though their music grew out of a thorough immersion in the art and culture of flamenco.  Together with the more  traditional evolutionaries  they form the group of "nuevos flamencos" - which is EXACTLY what they are called in Spain.  The label "new flamenco" is not new.  It began to emerge in Spain in the late seventies in the immediate post-Franco period.  The envelope began to be seriously pushed by Paco de Lucia in "Almoraima" (1976) and Camaron de la Isla in "Leyenda del Tiempo" (1979).  You want radical "new"?  Try Kiko Veneno, Pata Negra, Ojos de Bari as but a few examples.  "New flamenco" which has a traditional underlayment but experiments in numerous (and some quite tasty) directions?  Listen to any album by Ketama.  THAT is "new flamenco" and NOT the endless albums of rumba rumba rumba produced in this country by guitarists with little to no training or experience in the flamenco culture in Spain.  It is indicative of the ignorance of and lack of respect for the art of flamenco that Otmar Liebert recorded "Nouveau Flamenco," the album which started this whole craze, after only a few months of flamenco lessons.  (It takes years of full immersion to even begin to scratch the surface.)

In sum, I have no criticism of any kind that many people enjoy the (mostly) American, Otmar Liebert style of soft rumba, or even of Otmar Liebert and his many imitators per se.  If it has musical value it does not need to masquerade as something it is not, but should instead stand on its own under some other more appropriate label.  (Strunz & Farah, for example, have always had the class and good taste to not label their music "flamenco."  It is no coincidence that they are also the two most accomplished guitarists in this whole group.)  So please, please, have a little respect, show a little humility in the face of a highly developed and centuries old art form and its many dedicated artists by not calling this form of music "flamenco" - old, new, nouveau, neue, nuevo, whatever.  It just simply is not "flamenco."

reviewText:
When you are one of the most loved pop musicians in history and yet your twenty-songs greatest hits album contains quite a lot of filler, something is definitely wrong.

And it's not hard to figure it out. Lennon was a polarizing character, a perennial maker of front page news, and a wannabe revolutionary (to his credit, he had the courage to admit he hadn't change anything) but most of all he was a mediocre musician. He did write some beautiful songs, quite a few forgettable ones, and a whole lot of utter trash. This is accurately reflected in his Greatest Hits. Even some who gave this album rave reviews admit they skipped over some of the songs because they don't remember them -they are fillers in a top hits compilation.

Old coots like me who lived through the Beatles and post Beatles period remember too well that, after 1975's Rock and Roll (just a covers album), he was pretty much forgotten. No records, no tours, nobody wanted to play with him, while the much reviled Sir Paul nailed hit after hit, although the critics labeled him "commercial candy". Many years after, Paul's post Beatles career includes a boatload of amazing songs, and new generations still love them. Now ask any contemporary (or old, for that matter) listener how many Lennon songs he/she knows and loves other than Imagine.

reviewText:
I am a big fan of the first "Journey to the Centre of the Earth" album. It has a kind of delightfully cheesy grandeur mixed with a genuine sense of mystery -- while some of the lyrics, flat vocals, and fantasy-art concepts migh provoke a chuckle or two today, I think the whole thing works wonderfully well because it really believes in itself. It tells an interesting story in an interesting way, and for 40 minutes of proggy bliss, you are swept right along.

Unfortunately, Wakeman's "Return" utterly fails to live up to the original. First of all, the storyline is dull and unengaging -- written by Wakeman, it merely rehashes Verne's original, substituting a few alterations here and there. There are no surprises, and even the few original touches -- such as the fireballs -- seem out of character. Then there is the music. Wakeman was once one of rock's greatest keyboard players, but here the narrative is carried by relentlessly bland orchestrations, hackneyed harp trills, and only the occasionally keyboard solo, none of which stand up to anything he's done in the past. The lyrics are wretched; and worse, the "song" portions of "Return" are only tangentially related to the narrative itself. In the original, there was more of an operatic approach -- the "characters" sung about events in the story, and while an epic song about battling dinosaurs might bring a smile to one's face, it's an indulgent smile, and that's half the fun. Here, the songs are just lame -- shallow attempts to create songs that may have "life" outside of the narrative. I'd even call them "commercial" if I thought they had any real potential!

I realize that many fans have weighed in with five stars and tons of accolades, but I just don't get it. (Though, yes, Patrick Stewart's narration is of course charming.)  If you are a fan of classic Wakeman, and feel disappointed or alienated by his output after the Seventies, I suspect that you'll feel as I do about "Return." Avoid this CD, it is uninspired from start to finish.
label: negative

James Bond w/o the JB theme; Superman without his theme; Spiderman similarly - the Green Hornet, the Flash and the Man from Uncle even, all have themes that tell you when the hero is back; that he is the hero; etc. etc. I really despise them for making such a fine movie and then not be willing to hire Elfman or else to at least pay some homage to him and/or the scores to the non-Elfman Batman movies such as Batman Forever or Batman and Robin so that the fans get music that can be added on to existing music for the hero. Star Wars has consistently hired John Williams to do exactly that; Bond had John Barry and more recently, David Arnold. Obviously Batman is not with it and the Warner Bros franchise is to blame. I bet dollars to donuts the reason was financial; to hire Elfman was more money than giving newcomers a shot at glory. Worst soundtrack of this sort since maybe Goldeneye for Bond or the music for the Hulk (another notable study in mediocre music). Too bad for the fans.....

reviewText:
First off, I was into this band WAAAAY before you. I saw them in a small shack in Oklahoma in 198-something in front of like 10 people so EVERYBODY ELSE BUT ME shouldn't talk about how amazing they were I AM THEIR ORIGINAL FAN AND EVERYONE ELSE is a BANDWAGONEER who only got into them because of their TV ads.

This is a literary, sonic creation of being and sound. It is dark, it is light. It is the space between the dark and the light, it is up and it is down. It is the space between the up and the down, that transient period between up and down. It reminds me of Rimbaud, Emerson, early Pink Floyd (NOT the MAINSTREAM STUFF of course, because no one who really knows anything about music would DARE listen to anything but the early stuff), Nietche, Whitman, and philosophy. It reminds me of Syd Barrett and Can, and experimental stuff that is really deep and no one has ever heard of. I think there are some parts that sound like TANGERINE DREAM, which is experimental and revolutionary. This is the first album which is philosophical. I think Wayne Coyne has been reading philosophers, because this album is about LIFE and life's darkness. I especially think it is like Nietche because Nietche is about good versus evil, which is what this album is all about. It also reminds me of the paintings of Jackson Pollock and cinema verite. I see many influences of the writings of Plato and the films of David Lynch, which is also dark. I also see the poems of Ezra Pound, and dadaist art.

Wikipedia describes "darkness" as a transition period between two spaces of light. This is intense, and it is EXACTLY what this album is about. It also reminds me of the many layers of being, like an onion. You have to peel an onion, and you have to "peel" this album in order to UNDERSTAND IT. This is something that alot of people miss because THEY WERE ONLY INTO THEM BECAUSE THEY GOT POPULAR. It's good that they made this album now because all the people who were into them for this reason won't like it. I have them all to myself now!

Anyway, the songs remind me of the chapters of the poem "The Waste Land" by T.S. Eliot. I think this is really important. The album is deep, and has to do with the downfall of society and the environment, and the election. Lots of people thought they would "get positive" but I didn't. I knew they would get really dark, because see I have been into them longer and I KNOW WHAT MAKES THEM TICK. They do exactly the opposite, like yin and yang. This is something called "the tao".

Anyway, buy it. And if you don't then you were only into them because of one song.

 Performances range from merely okay (Natalie Cole) to outright disastrous (Elvis Costello). A version of "Begin The Beguine" transposed into an inappropriate key by Sheryl Crow does not "transform" the song so much as "disfigure" it.

 Far from making these already immortal songs "accessible" for a "new generation," this soundtrack trashes some of the greatest popular songs ever composed. What a shameful wasted opportunity, when there is in fact a "new generation" of jazz- and cabaret-inspired singers who could have done a much, much better job.

reviewText:
I'm gonna take a wild, wild guess and say that mr. Wyndorf (that would be the Magnet's singer) didn't bother to look up "monolithic". Had he done so he'd have found out that in its metaphorical sense it means "one-dimensional" or also understood as boring.
  It's becoming saddeningly clear that Monster Magnet's good days are fading away into the past. The last worthwhile album they brought out was "Powertrip" and that was dangerously flirting with the mainstream, but after that the wheels have come off and the wagon is heading straight for the cliff.
  "Monolithic baby" is the kind of rock album that fits perfectly in a biker's bar, complete with choppers parked outside, messed up billiard tables, and women that lost their femininity long before they got baptised. I guess in such circles it could pass off as "great stuff (man)", but take it outside of that context and it reveals itself for what it is:
  cheap rock for the masses, with dumb cliche lyrics about "babes" and what the singer wants to do to them.
  Which, could, come to think of it, be positively ignored, were it containing great music like so many Magnet albums have in the past. But no. This is one bad song (the eponymous single), extended to 11 even worse versions of it so it can make up an album.
  No point going on burying this disaster, I've enjoyed M.Magnet's music too much in the past to unleash even more excoriating critique on this LP.
  Pick a good wall, paint it with wild colors and watch it dry instead.
label: negative

After the audition of Susan Boyle and the fiasco of how badly the judges treated her prior to her performance, Simon Cowell has since become a changed man, a humbled man, a better man. Gone is the arrogance that had become a hallmark of his personality.

reviewText:
When U2 released Achtung Baby in 1991, it was their first album in the decade, and the follow up to the somewhat flop of "Rattle And Hum." This is my favorite U2 album by far. The CD doesn't really sound remastered, only louder. It was a full digital recording to begin with, so perhaps there wasn't that much to do. Including a disc of demos of the album was a great idea, however, some of the tracks sound like 2011 Bono singing to 1991 U2 playing. This is a shame. If the tracks did not have vocals, simply release them as they are. Why only One Star??? The music deserves around 400 stars, but U2's Management released a statement basically calling it a cash grab. 6 CDs and 4 DVDs sound great. This set was not made for the casual U2 fan. The Casual U2 fan is not about to plunk down $126 for a Box Set. The problem, is that hard core fans like me were horrified to find out that the Zoo TV DVD Live In Sydney was part of this set. This is something Die Hard fans already paid for. More than Once. We bought it on VHS, some bought it on the old Laser Disc format, then on DVD. They could have chopped off $10 or so on the price, and not make us buy the same thing twice. I can't give the band a free pass on this one. They have so much money, they have to understand that their die hard fans who want the box set are going through tough economic times. This set is better than Sting's latest Box Set that is a total rip off. I still have to rate the set with one star, as this band goes to much trouble to market themselves as philanthropists, and now they are robbing their own fans.

The demo Cd is the reason to buy the box. It is great hearing the songs as they probably were before the final album. Like I said, some of the songs sound doctored up a bit after the fact. A lot of artists do this, so I guess I'll have to deal with it. I have not watched the entire doucmentary DVD yet, however, it is very good, and a big positive when considering if
to purchase this. Again, the failure of U2's Manager Paul McGuinness to understand their die hard fans is hard for me to
take. I've spent thousands of dollars on this band, and figure they couuld've dropped the Sydney DVD, and given us a unreleased
concert from the same period, so that we don't have to give our money to bootleggers who charge $35 or more for a poor quality
release.

One last complaint, is that there were a lot of unused songs from both the Achtung Baby, and Zooropa era which did not make the cut. I really could do without all the remixes, as I own all the CD singles as well, like most Die Hard U2 fans do. They
easily could've made it 7 CDs and taken out the Sydney DVD, with or without another concert.

Still, most die hards will have to buy this, warts and all. It's just with somebody like Bono, you would think
he would have the understanding that including the Sydney DVD was a slap in the face to the real fans. I won't be lisening to "Scarelt" from October tonight, and will not be singing "Rejoice." Shame On You, U2.
label: negative

reviewText:
They say this is supposed to be Ian Hunter's return to form.

"Guiding Light" does sound a lot like "Ballad of Mott the Hoople," "Fuss About Nothing" reminds one of "All of the Good Ones Are Taken (the fast version)," and "Read 'em And Weep" does recall "Irene Wilde."

However, don't expect any angry lyrics like "Now it's the middle of the night on the open road, and the heater don't work and it's oh so cold," or party lyrics like "Head one's a saw-bones and he wrecked my chair, Said 'how'd you like to do it in a room downstairs'. And it's just another night. Oh, just another night." There's certainly no party chants like the "oh oh oh" that you'd find in "That Girl Is Rock 'n' Roll." Instead, we get fluff like "the paper's full of January sales, I guess I won't be buying fairytales," or "If it's left to the left, There won't be nothing left." What's so finely crated about these lyrics?

I own just about every CD Ian Hunter ever made as well as an almost complete catalog of Mott the Hoople CDs, and am sad to see a continued deterioration of the music that he has been making since "Yui Orta." I am completely disillusioned by this CD. Nowhere did I find anything even remotely resembling "Once Bit Twice Shy," "Just Another Night," or "All the Way from Memphis."

Ian Hunter has departed from the style of music that made his legacy since "All The Good Ones Are Taken," which in itself was an ominous start of the departure of his musical direction up to that time. While one can give him some latitude for an occasional dud (e.g. "Overnight Angels"), but Ian Hunter always somehow managed to return to form with several great CDs.

However, with three CDs of original music ("Dirty Laundry," "The Artful Dodger," and "Rant") that are full of duds, a bunch of compilations and concerts in between which add nothing to his "body of work," it is sad that Ian Hunter may have finally lost his creative sparks for good.

There will always be an audience out there for music like "Who Do You Love," "Cleveland Rocks," or "Central Park West." If Ian Hunter cannot muster enough creativity to make this type of music that he is admired of, he might as well as pack up his guitar and let his fans remember him fondly for the great music he created.

reviewText:
I bought this cheap on Marketplace because although I love Rameau's keyboard works and want to know the operas better, I suspected that despite its enthusiastic reviews, it would suffer from the usual expectation and tolerance of dreadful, weedy, throaty, constricted non-voices murdering the music. And indeed so it proved; the singing here is dire: Ragon is an embarrassment as Plate - give me Snchal's very French but so cultivated tones any day rather than his bleating - and the other strangulated, tremolo-ridden, weak-tea tenor, Guy de Mey, is hardly any better; just sample his first aria, CD1, track 3 and giggle at the nasty sound he makes. I wonder that Jennifer Smith was ever able to make a career but having heard her awful traversal of Faur's songs I now understand why she retreated to recording Baroque opera where nobody seems to notice screeching, wobbling, rudimentary French or aspirated divisions. The bass has been plucked from the usual fruffly-fruffly crowd with no resonance but lots of "funny" inflections.

Furthermore, I have never accounted myself in the least politically correct but the basis of the plot is cruel and offensive to modern sensibilities: it revolves around mocking the idea that the King of the Gods could ever fall for the water-nymph Plate because she is so vain - OK, not nice - and ugly; ha-ha. Michel Snchal at least made us sympathise with her which in a way makes it worse as her humiliation is the climax of the tale.

The orchestral playing is of course vinegary and clipped; they scrape away energetically and at least sound energised. The cuckoos' and frogs' choruses are fun; they redeemed a few seconds of this entertainment. The new bargain issue offers no libretto but there is a synopsis.

I put this straight on the give-away pile. Goodness knows what the five-star puffers are hearing but I kindly request them please to form an orderly queue in order to bestow their outraged negative votes upon this review.

reviewText:
First of all, I want to make clear that I think this is a phenomenal, 5-star album.  This review is for the remastered edition of the cd only.  If you already have the original cd release of this, hold on to it.  That one has problems, but it at least sounds true to the original album.  This remaster is an atrocity.  The drums dominate the mix (sorry Cozy -- I don't love you THAT much), while the vocals float in the background.  Worst of all, you have to strain to hear the guitar in many parts, with the synthesizer far more prominent.  Whoever remixed this is an idiot.  Evidently, they think that Ritchie Blackmore was the LEAST important person in this band.  I assume that most Rainbow fans would disagree--with no disrespect to the rest of this legendary lineup.  Rainbow Rising is classic rock for people who enjoy guitar, not nu-metal for people who want to demo their subwoofers.  It should have been mixed that way.

Beyond the sound of it, all these Rainbow remastered re-issues are a rip-off in every other way, as well.  No liner notes.  No lyrics.  No bonus tracks (not even the inclusion of "Jealous Lover" with Difficult to Cure, which was on a cd single at the time of the album's release).  These re-issues are the worst I've seen from any band.  Compare them to the Deep Purple anniversary remasters and it becomes obvious how much more could have been done with these.  In my opinion, this is an insult to the diehard fans who are purchasing these releases for the third or fourth time (lp, first cd release, Japan import cd, and newly "remastered" version).  If you don't have this yet, you should buy any version you can find as quickly as possible, because you've been missing out.  But for anyone who already has a previous release of this cd, you should just save your money.

You know, I was never a big fan of Magoo, but he was tolerable over Timbaland's production. This time out, he dropped Timbaland (which is ALWAYS a bad idea), bought some incredibly goofy lookin' sunglasses, and turned in his best Rick Ross impression. The thing that irks me the most is that he changed his name to Shawty Lo and started rapping like Young Jeezy instead of giving us the Q-Tip imitation that he's been known for all these years. He's never been all that great on the mic, but Magoo...I mean, Lo...really embarrasses himself this time out. Joints like "Dunn, Dunn" and "100,000" are straight up corny. As a matter of fact, every song on this album is doo doo, straight up. He basically made the same song 15 times and he's obviously fooled a small number of people on Amazon -- at press time, two people -- into thinking this album is original or, at the very least, noteworthy when it's nothing more than a link in the chain of terrible "music" flooding the market. And what's up with the whispering over every track? He runs Bankhead talking like that? lol Well, if he runs Bankhead -- which I highly doubt -- then he should probably tell a good number of them to buy this album as I'm afraid that's the only way he'll keep from going wood on the charts.

The only two positives I can think of is the fact that Magoo/Shawty Lo kept it under an hour. The production, though terribly generic, is good for bouncing to as well -- thus the  star I gave it. I find it gives me the energy to do my daily chores with zeal. Outside of that, this album is a steaming lump of zebra poo.

Units In The City is simply another in the long line of forgettable "dope boy" albums. Fans (?) will play it to death and move on once it wears off in a week or two. I'm pretty sure this album will be making a pilgrimage in staggering numbers to a dollar bin near you within the next 4 or 5 months -- you can quote me on that. I can't recommend this album to anyone, but if you must own this, wait until that happens. Or, you could download the lead single for free and keep it movin'.

The thing is I really enjoy bands like KMFDM, but if you're going to go for that sound you need to do it well. This, is just not good, not in any way.

The more traditional death metal tracks here vary from good enough(Nevermore)to kinda boring but passable (Blades for Baal), yet none of them are interesting enough to rise above the truly awful, and I do mean awful, trash on here.

reviewText:
Seriously.....WTF happened with Yngwie?

His last great album was ALCHEMY..........after that we got the same album over and over again. I challenge anyone to guess to which album any song belongs after WTEAW. All songs sound exactly alike.
The mastering was tolerable in ATTACK! and a bit on UNLEASH THE FURY...........but the rest is plain down horrible.

Down to this particular album.........again, the same old story. Repetitive compositions, no proffesional singer, bad recording engineering, bad drums, bad mix....

Regarding the "songs".....looks like Yngwie tries to recreate the feeling of Facing the Animal, but fails of course, and he just repeats the same process over and over, trying to see if he can get it right in another song.

Another concern is the "instrumentation" of the album is suffocating. It's a mix mass of sound which can't be hold for much longer. Your ears literally get tired: Drums clipping, Heavy distorted rythmic guitar at full volume, with a full volume heavy distorted solo guitar, with the harmonic 2nd solo also full volume, Bass repeating the rythmic guitar part (making it totally pointless), plust the keyboards playing absolutely nothing, therefore also totally pointless......and Yngwie's voice lost in between

Basically, I could call this CD a one hour demo reel of Yngwie improvising over and over again, with no distinctive melody that calls your attention.

I could tolerate the bad mixing with good compositions, but after the 5th album with mediocre mixing and the same music over and over again is enough.

Not recommended at all. AVOID this album. We have to show Yngwie he has to stop bombarding us with this "less effort" productions.

reviewText: The albums in this box-set feature some of the worst "loudness war" mastering I've ever had the chance to analyze. I'm not going to get into much detail on what the "loudness war" is - look it up on Google and YouTube for a few thousand examples. In simple terms, a recording is said to have been victimized by the "loudness war" when it was mastered with the audio volume so high that it exceeds the limits of the CD format specifications. Among other nasty effects like unwanted distortion and loss of dynamic range, this usually causes "clipping", that is, parts of the audio simply don't "fit" into the CD's volume range and are cut off, or in other words, lost. It doesn't matter if you play a "loudness war" CD at low or high volume - it will always sound distorted, uncomfortable to listen to, and you simply won't be hearing everything that was in the original recording because much of the audio was lost or damaged in the production of the CD. Recording companies have been cannibalizing musical masterpieces like these albums for years now, and I wonder why no class action has been filed against them yet for what is, in a nutshell, a crime against the consumers.

reviewText:
This is ridiculous. The plaudits being heaped on this compilation are misleading at best and criminal at worst. And the latter probably strikes closer to the truth. For those of us who had the cosmic luck to start listening to the Project from their inception, their albums simply cannot be broken into pieces, with selected bits being reassembled into anything that is in the least way credible.
Each of the Project's albums was conceived, assembled and executed as an organic whole. They each have an internal logic that manifests itself only as an entirety. A listener not only has to listen to the whole album from beginning to end; he must do so carefully, placing subsequent songs in the context of preceding ones. Even the breaks are integral to the flow, like pauses for breath in an extended aria.
This compilation completely destroys the very essence of the Project's structure. It's like taking the First Movement from Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, the Second Movement from the Seventh Symphony, the Third Movement from the Sixth and the Fourth Movement from the Ninth, and calling it a "definitive collection". Sheesh.
This travesty is the art rock equivalent of those candlelight dinner compilations sold on T.V. complete with close-ups of fireplaces and Pacific sunsets. Think "Hi-lights of Mozart" or "Bach's Greatest Hits". The worst disappointment of all was the knowledge that Alan Parsons himself performed this act of self-mutilation.
The Project produced some of the most sublime art rock albums ever. Sometimes bordering on the pretentious, more often achieving magnificence, but always, always, a structural whole. Some albums worked better than others, but they all gifted us a journey with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
If you wish to discover the Project, please PLEEEZE buy one of their complete albums. I would suggest starting with Tales of Mystery and Imagination or I Robot. Just don't settle for this Frankenstein's monster of amputated body parts.

reviewText:
First things first.  Rush = 5 Stars.  Some great songs here also 5 Stars.  This MASTERDISK pressing itself of the vinyl is ALSO 5 Stars for overall quality, but that is where it ends....

This review is directed at the Vinyl remix release.

I was super excited to see this was a MASTERDISK release!  Like the original pressing of yesteryear that STILL sound great.

The problems begin with possibly the original mix and subsequent remix.  The "Wall of Sound" as others have pointed out, and attempts to tame it with the remix simply do not translate to a quality vinyl playback experience.

For high end vinyl geeks, I 'attempted' to enjoy this on 3 turntable setups.  Everything from a linear tracking Technics SL-7 w/Jico Shibata stylus, Highly Modified KAB-USA 1200M5G w/Ortofon BLACK, AT440mla, DL110, and a friends VPI Classic w/Sumiko Blackbird Stylus.  In all test, the amp(s) were set to "Source Direct" so as not to add eq.  Speakers were B&W 800's.

To summarize.  Muddy, muddy, muddy on the most guitar dense tracks.

-The Ortofon Black, and Jico Shibata seemed to overemphasize Alex and the mids.  However, Neil came through pretty good.  This setup did NOT make me want to listen to this Vinyl ever again.

-Denon DL100 - Mud, but with a Radio/Broadcast quality.  Geddy too far back.  Drums a bit muted.  Would NOT listen to this again with this setup.

-AT440mla (Baerwald Alignment) - (I have a love hate relationship with this, but keep it in the stable for experimentation).  Guess what!  This setup made the Vinyl sound closest to the CD.  However, in all fairness, sounded a bit more like a high quality MP3.  In doing so, surprisingly made it most listenable.  It pulled Geddy's vocals to the front, and brightened/cleaned up some of the mud by pushing Alex's chord wailing back a bit.  Neil sounded 'good' with pronounced cymbals and a slight taming of the Kick & Snare.  Geddy's Bass moved back a bit, a bit too far perhaps for my liking, but ultimately helped clean up the mix.  (This setup also made Caravan vinyl more listenable)

-VPI Classic.  Marginally better than what I achieved with my modified KAB-USA 1200M5G & 'everyday' AT440mla.  Given the price point though...

So, if you are buying the Vinyl for a 'superior, sonic listening experience', I would say don't bother.  If you have a $$$$$ setup, you might accomplish a CD sounding Vinyl.  If you are buying the Vinyl to support the band and to collect it on the shelf, BUY IT.

Final pet peeve with the Vinyl is it is a 2 LP set, stuffed into a regular sleeve.  It is NOT a Gatefold, and needs to be.  Especially with the 200g weight.

The following Rush Vinyl Releases are a bit disappointing:
1.  Moving Pictures ~ LIVE 2011 ~ - DO NOT BUY.  I have heard better sounding YouTube videos. :-(
2.  Feedback (Similar to this Review, sounds like a 44/16 CD to Vinyl transfer, CD is excellent.)
3.  Vapor Trail Remix (this review).  Buy only to collect.
4.  Caravan (Similar this Review, but with spotty Vinyl production quality.  Took me 4 sets to not get a warped/damaged set)

SUPERIOR Rush Vinyl:
* The new Mercury Catalog DMM Releases seem to knocking it out of the park.  I was blown away in every way by the Rush reDiscovered release.  I am hoping that quality carries through to the re-releases coming out starting 1/2015....

Cheers!

reviewText:
Nina's been promising a new rock album for years, but I don't believe it will ever happen. She's lost so many fans after her last two CDs of "Big Band" music, that I suppose I shouldn't be shocked at this new religious CD.

I love Nina's early music and have been an avid fan for decades. So it is with great regret that I have come to realize she's lost it. Her voice has diminished some, but that is to be expected over time. It's the type of music she's been doing for the last several years that bores me to death. I found the 2 Big Band CDs extremely disappointing and lacking imagination. Go ahead and do cover versions of classics like "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" if you want, Nina, but do something different with them! Unfortunately, she didn't. I can't listen to either of the Big Band CDs, and this new CD is not only unoriginal but so overloaded with Jesus lyrics that I can't stand it. Even the Depeche Mode title song, and I liked the original, sucks as it is redefined by the new Nina. If you like that old, tired religion music and/or accordion and banjo music, you might like this CD; all it does is make me sad as I recall how great Nina used to be.

First she was "the mother of punk" (not really), then she had her alien contact (she beefed-up what she saw and heard more each time she told the story), then she was the Goddess of Love and Peace (until her young husband left her, at which point she became the Goddess of Hate-Spewing), then she had her Hindu guru period (the music wasn't bad, sometimes very good, at this point, but this period marked the end of the good stuff), and now she's found Jesus. When is she going to find Nina again? Likely never. I'm neither religious nor anti-religious, but there's nothing original or interesting on this CD. Farewell, dear Nina, I truly loved thee well!

reviewText:
Let me start with an analogy. At the end of the comedy "Forgetting Sarah Marshall," we're treated to a short musical scene about Count Dracula, where the actors are puppets. The scene is a hysterical parody of Broadway shows, with lyrics and music so pretentiously bad that they are comical. That's how I would sum up "Theory of Everything" by Aryeon. I'm a huge prog rock fan and expected to like this concept album, as it includes some incredible players and the music is influenced by some of my favorite bands. But the music is definitely not to my taste.

The music brings to my mind a famous psychiatric disorder, called the Capgras delusion, in which the sufferer believes that everyone around him has been replaced by exact replicas. They look and sound exactly like his friends and family, but somehow they don't seem real. The music on "Theory of Everything" similarly has all accoutrements of symphonic progressive rock, like odd time signatures, walls of sound, flutes, strings, etc., without actually being good. I find the compositions to be fairly static regarding the instrumental lines and harmony. You can hum a single note for like 60 seconds and it continues to fit the music. That's not good in prog rock, where the listener expects more variety. (Unless it's space rock.)

I also found the lyrics to be uniformly irritating. Every other song seems to have the same sorts of phrases: "How did I get here? What is going on?  We will never understand. How could I have done such a thing?" And on and on and on and on. I know there's a story behind it, about searching for the ultimate answer, but I couldn't bring myself to care because the overall effect was so grating.

Someone clearly spent a long time creating this album, so I can appreciate the huge production effort and the playing skills, just not the musical results.

reviewText:
Following Sammy Hagar's post-Van Halen solo career hasn't always been the easiest thing to do. Rewarding at times, yes, but certainly not without a great deal of work. His first release sans his former band was 1997's Marching To Mars, a truly excellent recording that filled listeners with hope that there would be more of the same to follow. Unfortunately, Hagar followed things up with 1999's Red Voodoo, his first collaboration with backing band The Waboritas and the first hint that things were on a slow downhill ride. While containing some truly satisfying moments, the album was comprised with a great deal of filler that made a start-to-finish listen nearly impossible. Subsequent releases (2000's Ten 13 and 2002's Not 4 Sale, for example) followed the same trajectory as the one before it, with stellar tracks being harder and harder to weed out amongst the half-baked rockers and overtly-chintsy ballads.

Enter Cosmic Universal Fashion, Hagar's latest entry into his solo catalog. Here, weeding out the good stuff from amongst the filler proves either nearly impossible or remarkably easy, depending on how you look at it. This is largely due to the fact that album is virtually devoid of any memorable or meaningful tracks, a handful of underdone genre experiments and poorly-thought out cover selections in their place. In fact, the only truly memorable moment on the entire record comes in the form of a Van Halen cover, a live capture of a "Dreams" and "Cabo Wabo" medley as reinterpreted by Hagar's solo band on his last tour. Hagar manages to strip away the bombast of the original Van Halen versions without sacrificing the power of the song, a testament to the intense talent of his songwriting partnership with Edward Van Halen.

The most glaring problem with the album is calling it just that: an album. With ten tracks clocking it at barely forty-five minutes, this hardly constitutes an album by the current definition of the term. Toss in the fact that the songs have no cohesive bond and there are two covers in the mix and Hagar's really got himself an EP. Had the singer/songwriter submitted Cosmic Universal Fashion as a collection of unreleased tracks and oddball cover tunes, it probably wouldn't hurt that it isn't very good. But to pass it off as an album leaves the listener feeling cheated and pining for something more.

Another key problem with Cosmic Universal Fashion is that the rock feels somewhat forced here. It's hard to tell at first, as the rockers are drenched in Hagar's usual mix of carefree pseudo-spirituality and teenage-like abandon. But at age 61, the latter of the two characteristics borders on ridiculous. At this point, there's no reason for Hagar to "fight for the right to party" - he's a successful millionaire who own a tequila-based club on the beach in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. The man's got the right to party and no person of the age when the lyrics to "Fight For Your Right" mean something is looking to Hagar for guidance on the issue.

His reluctance to let go of the constant theme of partying is what does Hagar in throughout the course of Cosmic Universal Fashion. After all, the music to some of the tracks is downright wonderful. "Psycho Vertigo," "Peephole" and "Loud" all contain some of Hagar's best constructed songs musically of his entire catalog. Unfortunately, the lyrics are just plain silly at times and render the songs unlistenable. The singer fairs a little better lyrically on the album's lead-off single, "Cosmic Universal Fashion," which focuses on the issues of the day a la Van Halen's 1992 hit, "Right Now." But that's one fleeting moment of relevancy amongst a cavalcade of mediocrity and ultimately serves as a reinforcement to just how good the album might have been had Hagar delved deeper into more of those lyrical themes.

reviewText:
Except for two Randy Holden songs, "Fruit and Icebergs" and "Peace of Mind", which are probably two of the best songs BC ever recorded, this is, by far, their worst album! The LP itself is really a "tale of two bands". The original 'side two', containing Holden's contributions, is chronologically 'side one' in reverse. The fact is, Randy Holden's singing, songwriting, and guitar playing abilities could have saved this record from disaster and caused it to live up to its "New! Improved!" billing, had he not left the band midway through its recording. When he left, taking his talents with him, you can almost hear the album getting progressively more directionless and lost--and I do mean--LOST! How did a band who pushed the envelope of hard rock on their first two albums, regress to the point of sounding like Herman's Hermits on songs like "West Coast Child of Sunshine" and "When it All Gets Old"? Those rock critics who trashed their first two albums--is this what BC thought they wanted to hear from them? If Blue Cheer was a band built on the strength of its lead guitarist, Randy Holden's replacement, Bruce Stephens, brought nothing to the table on this LP. Admittedly, he entered a situation that was in shambles, and things would get much better on the next album, simply titled: "Blue Cheer". I don't even blame the original drummer, Paul Whaley, for leaving the band after this record, either. They were changing styles, and his hard-hitting services were no longer necessary.
"New! Improved! Blue Cheer" is an interesting study of how one member's departure halfway through the making of the album can change its whole dynamic. I would say for the sake of posterity and historicity, the record company should reverse the track order of the CD, making Holden's songs first, but perhaps leaving "Honey Butter Lover" last on the disc.
Fortunately, the band did not completely fall apart after this album. As I referred to earlier, the next album, "Blue Cheer", would be much better, moving more in the conventional, mainstream direction they wanted to go, having also had more time to write decent songs. However, I can't say the same for the two albums after that, "The Original Human Being" and "Oh! Pleasant Hope", which were just wimpy, drugged-out affairs.
This album was the sad story of a band who could have gone to the next level. "One star" for "Fruit and Icebergs" and "Peace of Mind". "No stars" for the rest!
