reviewText:
(Actual Rating- 1.5 Stars)

Pilgrim(1998). Eric Clapton's Thirteenth Solo Studio Album.

After the critical smash of 'From The Cradle', Eric Clapton's comeback album, he then rocketed to the bottom of charts and critics with his New Age, Trip-Hop hybrid expiriment, and the resulting album, 'Retail Therapy'. For his first studio album in years, Eric Clapton decided to do another Blues album, and in 1998, 'Pilgrim' was released. Upon its release, 'Pilgrim' was greeted with decidedly mixed reviews, but nonetheless the album debuted at number four and stayed in the Top 10 for several weeks on the success of the single "My Father's Eyes." Over the years, the album has been criticized, yet hardly ever recognized. So, is 'Pilgrim' and underrated blues masterpiece or just a plain boring album? Read on to find out!

Track Ratings-

Clapton went for a decidely more R&B/Blues/Jazz/Gospel style of music, and on 'Pilgrim', you can't help but tell. "My Father's Eyes" is an R&B ballad, but nothing other than the chorus stands out. Through and through, Clapton disappoints, with "River of Tears" using boredom as an instrument and the album's title track giving new meaning to the word repetitive. "Broken Hearted" features background additions of Bagpipes and Acoustic Guitar, yet the melody's just boring. Would you like me to waste any more of your time? Take my word, "One Chance", "Circus", "Going Down Slow", "Fall Like Rain", "Born In Time", "Sick And Tired", "Needs His Woman", "She's Done", "You Were There", and "Inside of Me" are all tired R&B/Blues ballads, with Clapton's *boring* vocals and depressing lyrics about his son's death marring down the album. Sure, there's a few parts that actually sounded like Cream and Blind Faith's former guitarist was here, but just imagine Boyz 2 Men with an electric guitar. If YOU like that, you might as well pick this album up! If not, back away from the "Cart" button!

Overall, 'Pilgrim's a disappointment, and it's sad to see an artist who was once in Cream and Derek & The Dominos reduced to this. If Clapton's supposed to be one of the greatest guitarists of our time, then how come he sounds exactly the same and tired on each track? Obviously it's time to retire! Actually, just start doing ROCK music again, and we might actually like you.

NOT RECOMMENDED UNLESS YOU'RE A FAN OF R&B BALLADS, BOYZ 2 MEN, OR A DIE-HARD ERIC CLAPTON FAN! HOPEFULLY, ERIC CLAPTON WON'T MAKE HIS FANS SUFFER THROUGH THESE SONGS IN HIS CONCERT!

Recommended Instead-

Slowhand- Eric Clapton

Disraeli Gears- Cream

reviewText:
I was surprised to learn that this is the result of five years of work.  In brief: I found AN's latest CD bland, monotonous, boring, and overall unconvincing in the Verdi repertoire. She does not have the requisite Italianate expression, the phrasing is choppy, and the musicianship lefts a lot to be desired. Her top notes are sometimes strained and her low register is seriously underpowered and unattractive. Her voice is getting darker and (to my ears) unpleasantly so. The trills in the coloratura are still questionable. The best pieces are from Lady Macbeth; the worst are Elena's Bolero, Tu che le vanita, and the excerpts from Il Trovatore.

For Verdi soprano arias you are better off if you stick with the classics: Callas (for Lady MacBeth), Tebaldi (for Giovanna d'Arco), Caballe (for Il Trovatore and Don Carlo), and Cerquetti (for I Vespri).

reviewText:
Avoid this new rendition of Bach's "St Matthew Passion". I would not recommend this version at all as I found it to be lifeless and weak in spirit. It is probably of interest soley from a trained musician's standpoint, and even then only as a curiosity or an experiment for those long familiar with this well-known work.
I am not a musician by any means, so my review must be understood as coming from one with an "untrained", yet as such, an unbiased ear. I only can comprehend the work as a whole and this work, to me, just sounded dull and lifeless. Gone is all the deep strength that you might expect from a Wagnerian opera. This version of Bach's work is presented almost minimistically and very soft. It has none of that manly, almost operatic Germanic and gothic feel that I just can't help but believe that Bach's original music must have sounded like to some degree. Or perhaps that is just wishful thinking on my part and I am guilty of transcribing more Romanticism on Bach than he could have possibly had.
I would prefer an old-school and "traditional" rendition of the St Matthew's Passion instead. This McCreesh version lacks the theatrical quality, the entertaining "feel" that most modern non-musicians have come to love and indeed, expect. Perhaps I'd even go so far as to wish that some "showmanship" go into the recording of the "St Matthew" a.k.a. John Williams. Indeed, one of the versions of the St Matthew's Passion that I feel contains the strongest and most spiritual "feel" is from the George Lucas science fiction film "THX-1138" starring Robert Duvall from 1971.
Anyone with similar taste should probably stay away from this "limp" version of the St Matthew by McCreesh and the Gabrieli Players.

I had been on an Ant kick lately, rediscovering Kings and Prince Charming. I take his music with a grain of salt. It's a bit goofy, but has a lot of style. Some of it can be intelligent and creative. So I saw this in the record store for $3.00, and figured, what the hay. I'm a huge Prince fan, so I was curious to hear his former best-friend Andre Cymone's production.

Wow. This music is so 80's sounding. But it wouldn't have sounded innovative in 1984, let alone 1989 (and obviously not 2005). The problem is not so much with the songs, which are overly pop and overly cute, but somewhat catchy. The problem is that the production is so stale and generic that Adam is completely lost in the mix. This sounds just like any bad 80's pop singer. What made Adam was his individuality, and this record has none of that. And the songs have no dynamics. The whole thing feels like a flat line. I would place the blame on Andre Cymone, but Adam was involved, too. And the songs wouldn't be that great with another producer, either.

There are a couple good songs Room at the Top (which sounds a bit like Spinal Tap's Big Bottom) and You Can't Set Rules About Love. USSA rocks just a bit. But, sorry, I felt the $3 just wasn't worth it. Not even as a guilty pleasure.

reviewText:
The latest album from Avril Lavigne, an "artist" that was put on a pedestal by the media the second that she arrived on the scene.  Without her, we wouldn't have such "profound" lyrics as "He's just a sk8er boi / She said see you later, boy" and "I'm not the milk and Cheerios in your spoon".  And you have to love her affected angst whenever she's on television, in her misguided attempts to prove to us how "hardcore" she is.  I can't wait to see her in concert with Simple Plan - I'm sure the mosh pit is going to be the most brutal one in the history of punk rock!
All kidding aside, Under My Skin is Lavigne's second album, and instead of collaborating with those corporate hacks of The Matrix, she opted to work alongside Raine Maida (frontman of Our Lady Peace) and Chantal Kreviazuk, among others.  However, upon listening to this album, one wonders about the nature of the contributions from these talented songwriters; all it takes is one listen to see how flawed the songwriting is, and Lavigne's flat voice doesn't help matters much at all.  And for some reason, she continues to pronounce all of her "s" sounds like "sh" - i.e. "Guys are sure hard to trussht", "I'll have to kick your ash".
Surprisingly, Lavigne seems to have the critics in her corner with this album, as many have commented on how she "bares her soul" with Under My Skin.  This much I'll give her credit for - there is nothing as embarrassingly juvenile as "Sk8er Boi" on this album.  But there is also nothing that lends any validity to Lavigne's claims of being a "hardcore punk" on this album either - it's filled with the same tame, docile teen pop/rock found on her last album.  If anything, the sound of this album is even more controlled and safe than the last album, if that's possible.  The album sounds like the work of an innocent girl in her early teens, which is in contradiction with the image that Lavigne portrays.
The songwriting is where this album really falls apart.  Examples: "It's there inside / All I do is hide / I wish that it would just go away" ("Take Me Away"), "You held my hand and walked me home / I know / While you gave me that kiss / It was something like this / It made me go ohh ohh ... Did you think that I was gonna give it up to you / This ti-e-i-e-ime" ("Don't Tell Me"), "This is when I start to bite my nails / And clean my room when all else fails / I think it's time for me to bail" ("He Wasn't").  Keep in mind that I'm only scratching the surface here - this style of writing is the general rule rather than the exception.
In summary: Another lackluster effort from one of the most overrated acts in the music industry.  Lavigne fails to impress with Under My Skin, a very ordinary, unspectacular collection of pop/rock lacking any kind of depth or substance.  Don't fall for all of the publicity that Lavigne and this album have received - this album is not worth your time.

reviewText:
Jennifer Lopez's latest release, "This is Me... Then" revisits themes close to her heart: She's humble and down-to-earth and adoring and she REALLY adores fiance No. 3, got it? With vapid lyrics, one-dimensional vocals and a lack of any zest whatsoever, this serves its purpose better as a coaster than as a CD.
Among them are the lifeless "Still," flat "Loving You" with its halfhearted drumbeats, the cringeworthy "I'm Glad" ("I'm glad when I'm making love to you/I'm glad for the way you make me feel" -- like Shakespeare, ain't it?), the frankly embarrassing goo-ballad "Dear Ben," the rather tuneless "All I Have" with L.L. Cool J, the abortive dance song "Jenny From The Block," fluty ballad "Again," and a cover of Carly Simon's "You Belong to Me" (which, from Lopez's lips, sounds a bit possessive).
Lopez has become almost a parody of herself in recent years, and "This" does nothing to decrease that parody. "I'm real, I thought I told you!" she reproves the listeners. We heard you, Jenny; we just don't believe you. What's worse is the Ben Affleck-centered gushing, adolescent crush songs that gave me the uncomfortable feeling of voyeurism.
With a more talented singer, these empty songs might have sprung to life. But Lopez's voice is thin, high and inflexible. And the songs are among the worst-written I have ever heard. Among them are "I love you, you're perfect/a manifestation of my dreams," "I dig the way that you get down/(you get down for 'bout)," and "Perfect blend, masculine." It's enough to bring tears (of laughter) to your eyes.
It's hard to take Lopez's latest offering seriously, especially since she definitely does. In the end, this syrupy collection of ballads will serve only as an embarrassing, poorly-written reminder of Lopez's much-publicized romance.

reviewText:
I must stress that I am not a fan of this outfit, nor do I own any of their records.  The purpose of this review is to warn any potential buyers of what they would get if they were to purchase this DVD.
I had seen a number of musical performances, both classical and rock, at the Sydney Opera House, when I was in Australia back in the late nineties and absolutely loved the venue and its acoustics.
Recently, I came across this DVD, recorded at the same venue and by curiosity, decided to look if it was available to rent, until I found it had been uploaded on youtube.  Having viewed and listened to this performance in its entirety, I struggle to find attributes strong enough to describe the dreadfulness of it all.  Not only do they sing out of tune, but when they attempt to harmonise, the result is even more abysmal, making a pair of Colobus monkeys in the breeding season, sound like the embodiment of two-part vocal harmony perfection.  This leads me to believe that their voices must have been subjected to a great amount of tweaking, using studio wizardry, when they were making records.  At one stage, during the proceedings, they try to spice things up a bit, by telling shallow, predictable jokes, perhaps with the intent of diverting the audiences attention, from their musical shortcomings.  If any of the members of the great local LRB (Little River Band) were in the audience, hed have been shocked and used earmuffs.  Had I been there, I would have left as fast as I could.
As if the quality of the performance wasn't bad enough, the work of the cameramen complements it, being very poor and amateurish.
That the Australian audience, on that day, was enthusiastically applauding such performance, I find rather baffling and musically undiscerning.
Whatever price they paid for their tickets, they didn't get value for money and were undoubtedly ripped off.
America (the country) has given the world some outstanding rock bands.  This duo is certainly not one of them.  They arent, have never been, and never will, be part of the rock music elite. They are second rate musical lightweights, who filled, with some degree of success, a musical space left temporarily vacant by CS&N (Crosby Stills & Nash), whom they grotesquely imitated, with their slight, pedestrian and pubescent songwriting.
The production company, who deemed this DVD acceptable for commercial distribution, should be ashamed of themselves.  Such performance should be withdrawn from sale with the warning unsuitable for human consumption and ultimately destroyed.

Unfortunately, the caustic bombast that profusely blasts  from this SONY "vanity disc" simply appalled me. Could music this abyssmal actually gain public forum with Ma, Zinman and the Philadelphia Orchestra taking the reins? At its very best, the Danielpour Concerto for Cello is an absolute musical monstrosity--- abrasive and an insult to one's intelligence and  sensibilities. Kirchner's tedious Music for Cello and Orchestra is a hectoring compilation of notes; and the Rouse Violoncello Concerto--- abominable and confrontational. I find the lack of insight, imagination and humanity pixilating.

reviewText:
After years of neglect the Buggles are showing up on many compilations. It's true, Video Killed the Radio Star was a sizable worldwide hit. Except the US. It managed 1 week on America's Top 40. I can still imagine Casey Kasem..."Starting off this week's countdown is a band from England called The Buggles??? Far out! We'll be hearing from these guys for years to come!" I'm not sure what's worse for a band, having your only US single chart at number 40 for one week or not at all? (If I were ambitious I'd make a list of bands that had one number 40 hit for one week.) The thing is, Video Killed the Radio Star was a hit in 1979 with a few declining chart weeks in 1980. Sure, it was on the chart during 1980, but it's star shone brightest in 1979.
What's more embarrassing is it's parent lp 'The Age of Plastic', didn't even bother the US album chart.
'Video' did make a very minor appearance on the first Stars on 45 album. Which did chart.  And what most people don't know is Bruce Woolley and the Camera Club recorded and released their version of 'Video Killed the Radio Star' before The Buggles, but sadly failed to chart anywhere. I'll take The Buggles second album "Adventures in Modern Recording" which is, by far, superior to any of the above mentioned singles or albums. This even did chart on the US Album chart (#161), but not many remember. Go for the 2010 reissue on the ZTT label (sadly recently vacuumed up by the company trying to accumulate all entertainment in the known 'universe'). Btw, that would be Universal who conveniently released this flabby excuse on pvc. I do hold a grudge with the company. They gobble up more entertainment faster than a black hole in a gas and dust field. Their proto-black holes didn't fool me at the Orlando theme park. I was aware of every minute queued up in those attraction lines.
The 80s music can be divided into two eras. Spearheaded by British bands 1981-1984 was the Golden Age of Pop. This had some overlap in 1985 (I'm calling Dead or Alive's "You Spin Me Round" the halfway point) leading to 1986 and beyond. This second part deserves no name. It ended abruptly with the Seattle myth. There was pop music during the 90s. In the US it was pretty bad. You had to go to the UK (like always) to get great pop music. You could still get proper singles in the UK. In the US you were forced to buy an album for that one mediocre track. Mostly because radio had 'independent promoters' telling them what to play. (For more info search Payola)
If you've stuck around this long. Thanks. Wish I could give out prizes, but Amazon gets all my loot.

reviewText:
I made a tremendous mistake thinking that I could trust Rhino. I've purchased many of their releases in the past and have almost always been quite happy with them. Their two Nuggets box sets are a joy. But this DVD box is just a plain mess and a total disappointment! If there are specific performances that you want, stick to the individual DVD's which are also being released separately.
What's wrong with this? Geez, where to begin?  First, the entire running length of this nine DVD series is less than nine hours, meaning the discs average less than one hour each.  Thus, the entire set could easily have fit on four DVD's.  The performances are arranged in a very clumsy way so that bands like The Beatles have their clips scattered across several DVD's.  Liner notes are non-existent and the viewer must rely on between performance commentary to pick up info, which sometimes doesn't even include original airdates. And several perforances are repeated in the series, including The Jefferson Airplanes' "Crown of Creation" showing up twice on the same disc! What the hell is that all about??  There are other problems and little annoyances spread throughout, such as box set credits rolling two to three times on per DVD, Ed's endless signoffs and many truncated versions of songs.
All in all, I can't remember being so disappointed with something that could have been so great. This set is a plain waste of money. Rhino should be ashamed for foisting this on the public.
The ONLY reason that this set deserves one star is because much of the old footage is beautiful to watch and several of the performances are really good. But don't let that fool you into plunking down big bucks for this!  It's a very poor value.

reviewText:
When Green Day announced they were making not one, not two, but three new albums to be released over the span of five months, the small portion of the world that still gives a flying rat's behind about Green Day did what we all do when bands announce such ambitious projects like this: brace themselves for a disaster. Furthermore, when Billie Joe had his little meltdown on stage back in the fall, it was only a hint that this album would end up being nothing more than a vanity project for Joe. And everyone was right on both counts.

That's right, despite Mike Dirnt's face being on the album cover, both this and it's Predecessor UNO! Are all entirely Billie Joe centric. If I had to guess, Billie Joe must have written all the lyrics and riffs and just hired Mike and Tre as session musicians, because neither would be capable of putting out such atrocities as this. If I had to make a comparison, remember when you were a kid and your neighbour's dad embarrassed both himself and you by trying to show off how cool he was? That's exactly how this album feels. Billie Joe is 40, has two kids and you'd think that he'd show a bit of maturity in the songwriting department if he's going to be a dominant force of the three albums. And even if this album is supposed to be a breakaway from the bloated boring rock opera stuff, and back to basics old school stuff, you'd think he'd show a bit of maturity there.

Well, there's two songs that show just the slightest smidge of maturity. The opening track, "See You Tonight" is a very nice Beatles/Simon and Garfunkel sounding intro that does set the (false) tone and leads you to believe that this will be a good album. Problem is, it's immediately followed by the unfortunately titled "F*** Time". Even the title alone just makes me want to cry. I nearly chucked the CD into the trash the first time I read the title, but I decided "never judge an album by a song title" after all, and listened. And it was exactly how I thought it would be- boring three chord trash with immature lyrics. The next track is decent musically, but problem is, it uses the whole "word vomit" thing I mentioned in my review of UNO!. "I'm drinking the Kool aid/I jumped on the grenade". Really? is Armstrong even trying anymore?!

The rest of the album isn't much better in terms of lyrics or music.  Alright, I guess "Stray Heart" might be decent lyrically, but is sonically an insult, with the boring three chord progression that just does nothing but solidify the trilogy's status as the new "St. Anger". Yup, that's right, Metallica. St. Anger doesn't look so bad anymore, we have a new sinker in our midst. And such proof can be found on tracks like "Lady Cobra". Or the hokey and boring "Wow! That's Loud".

But it gets even worse, believe it or not. If you haven't ingested vats of rat poison and cyanide by the time you reach "Nightlife", that song will really push you over the edge. If you thought "Kill the DJ" was bad, it's a blessing compared Nightlife. It's essentially "Kill the DJ" but with added rap. That's right, RAP. The rap wouldn't be so bad if it actually added something to the music, but it doesn't it just feels forced. And by the time album reaches "Amy", which is an acoustic ballad that's a tribute to the late Amy Winehouse, you're wondering what the point of releasing a trilogy of crap is. Amy is the only good track on the album and it's absolutely beautiful lyrically, yet even that song is musically in pretty gory shape.

Like it's predecessor UNO! and most likely like the following album, TRE!, DOS! has no reason to exist, will not attract any new fans to the and old fans will probably just dust the album off their shoulders. Hell, when KISS makes a better album than you, you really need to rethink your position as a musician.

reviewText: After the power-punch return to melodic metal rock with 1984's `Animalize', and the recruitment of yet another lead guitarist in Bruce Kulick (who would stay til they once more donned their make-up 12 years later), Kiss's 1985 album, `Asylum', proved a pretty lackluster offering. Paul Stanley produced the album. But without the powerful drum sounds captured by producer Michael James Jackson on `Creatures of the Night' and `Animalize', the original mix sounds very thin (though, the 1998 remaster gives it some much needed oomph). The band returned to co-writing with one another on much of it, but the results are generally weak and on the pop rock side of things. Even input on six out of the ten tracks from staple 80s and 90s hitmaker, Desmond Child, fails to produce results. Paul Stanley's `Tears Are Falling' is the only standout. The opening `King of the Mountain' is reasonable, but would have sounded far better with heavier production. The rest are on the puerile side (`Uh! All Night' etc), sounding very much in the vein of the crop of weak-kneed 80s US pop metal hair bands at the time. The over-riding sense you get from `Asylum' is that the contract required it and the band wasn't really committed.
label: negative

reviewText:
I'm responding here to the recent hype around Skrillex as a "dubstep artist." I'd like to take this opportunity to set the record straight for those of you just encountering the dubstep genre through Skrillex's music. Skrillex is not dubstep. He takes the worst and most cliched conventions of dubstep ("wobbly bass," for example), mashes them up with glitch techno bleeps and electrofarts, and wraps them up in emo/aggro rock posturing.

I find Skrillex's music shrill in tone and sophomoric in content, nothing like the subtly unsettling atmospherics, rolling basslines, and unconventional rhythms of quality dubstep from artists such as Shackleton, Burial, Kode9, Zomby, and Benga. I'd recommend any of those artists and the "5 Years of Hyperdub" compilation for a peek into what dubstep is really about.

If anything, I think (hope) the so-called brostep trend led by people like Skrillex will eventually open a few doors into better music for younger listeners, rather than exploding into another vacuous, faux-adolescent, emo/aggro rock lurch (cf. circa late 90s/early 00s Korn, Limp Bizkit, etc.) dressed up as dubstep. Trust me, there's more sophisticated music out there that rewards with repeated listens. I've listed a few artists above. I'd encourage Skrillex listeners to check them out.

Thanks for reading.

reviewText:
Unfortunately for the current future of mankind, we humans (and particularly, we Americans) find ourselves in a particularly regressive state.  We would rather watch a plethora of reality shows than CNN, we want superficial movies with talentless-to-only-somewhat-talented actors and actresses, we seem to find it perfectly acceptable that athletes and glossy Hollywood types get paid millions per year while teachers and scientists are often struggling to get by, and we mindlessly accept pretty-packaged musical atrocities as art.  Whomever first described the musical fare in the vein of Britney Spears as "sugary" was absolutely correct.  To the passive listener, Britney's music tastes good going down, but is ultimately not only of no value to the body, it is actually harmful.

From her first album until now, Britney has been the poster child for all the popular music cash cows that the greedy record executives anxiously sign to their labels.  The philosophy is simple:  make as much money possible by any means necessary.  To do this, songwriters and producers are brought in to provide serious support to the usually barely-talented (if at all) "artist".  The most financially-rewarding demographic has demonstrated in their buying habits that they don't want lyrics that make them have to think, they like sexual content (whether explicit or implicit), and they like catchy melodies and harmonies.  Thus, the artist doesn't need to have even decent vocal ability.  What is commonly referred to as "auto-tune" will make sure no off-puttingly wrong notes are hit, songwriters will write tepid lyrics (usually representative of immature modes of thinking), and producers will create the vocal melodies and accompaniment (or what is simply referred to as "beats" in the popular culture) that are easy to remember (and, oftentimes, easy to dance to).  All of this serves to hook the *passive* listener on the music, which can result in any combination of album, ticket, perfume/cologne, toy, and clothing line sales.

Most music reviewers are proving that they really have no authority to be ranking albums, as they seem to be unable to tell just how terrible Britney's music is.  I have already seen some far too optimistic reviews given to this album by critics, while the few truly artistically-impressive albums coming out are getting reviews that are just blatantly insulting when compared to those of "artists" like Britney.  What seems to be impressing the critics is the production on the album.  Sadly, the production is often credited to the performer when it should really be credited to the producers.  Britney has certainly acquired an astonishing amount of money by now, and she brought in "it" producers who be able to carry her album for her.  However, despite the constant criticism of her terrible vocal abilities (and probably terrible aural skills, although we can't be sure of that, since she continues to lip synch in her performances), Britney has demonstrated her infamous ignorance yet again and has STILL hasn't pursued serious vocal training to improve the quality of her singing.  On top of that, her lyrics are still terribly lacking in creativity, uninspiring, and simply immature (and sadly, she had to pay people to write them for her because hers would be even worse).

Based on the other new releases for this week that I have seen, as well as the ridiculous amount of news coverage this album is getting (due to Britney's other parts of her life that she is also insanely ineffective at managing), I expect this album to debut at #1 on the Billboard album sales chart next week.  However, that doesn't mean that my message will have been for nothing if I can convince even one person who is thinking about buying this album from doing so.  We human beings are supposed to be progressive thinkers, as we are the most cognitively-advanced creatures on this planet.  Music is art, and we deserve better than this as our art.  We deserve for high-quality music to once again be the "popular music" of our culture.  We have the power to decide what the record labels feed us, and one way to do that is to refuse to give them our money when they try to feed us this "sugary" music.  We have to regain control.
label: negative

Could the man  have devised a less subtle approach? Could his music more closely resemble  a rejected segment from the 'America Sings' ride at Disneyland?

reviewText:
To briefly state how I come to a conclusion of how I feel about an album, the primary focus is the songs.  How many are stand out tracks, instant classics, how many are decent but require more listening and how many filler/bad songs are there.  And if my star rating wasn't enough of a spoiler for those who don't want to read a long winded review, this album had 1 decent song that requires more listening and a bunch of filler.  And 1 bad cover song.  Get Death Angel's the dream calls for blood, much better album in my opinion.

I wasn't there from the beginning, but I really enjoy the Barlow years of Iced Earth, the first one anyways, and the versions of the songs from the first 2 I have are from the Days of purgatory and live albums.  I also really enjoyed Dystopia, and between that album and the 2 Into Eternity albums I became a Stu Block fan.  that guy can seriously do any style of metal and probably rock he wants.

All that being said I'm not a fanboy and have to point out when a band I like, no matter how much I like them, puts out sub-par material.  That's what they put out here.

After the last album I was really excited about the new disc.  And then I heard it.  It's not that it's necessarily bad, it's just not good either.  The style is kind of a mix of the various IE styles over the years.  Anyone expecting them to suddenly change their style will be disappointed.  And really you can't fault a band over the past 15 years for not changing their sound.  Most bands, especially rock and metal bands don't these days.  So I have no complaints with the style, however as I said it's a mix of stuff you've already heard before.  So if the material itself isn't very good then I might as well listen to the old stuff.  And the songs on here aren't very good.

And that's the problem, I'm not the only one to feel this.  The songwriting just feels lazy.  Jon really should reconsider making himself the band, because he's surrounded by talent.  The production sounds ok and the musicianship is capable, if not a bit uninspired.

And for the whole something wicked story which continues for half the album, I feel this story was beaten to death in the double album of last decade.  I only heard the Crucible and the 3 Barlow re-recordings, not a ripper Owens fan, and while there were some good songs in the bunch, geez did that 1 album tire me of that story.  It should have stayed as a theme for a couple songs on the 1 album.  Instead we get songs with this theme on here.  I guess it's ok because the songs aren't very good anyways, so if Jon wants to continue telling the same story again and again it's not a big deal.

Stu does an alright job here.  he definitely sounds like an IE vocalist.  I'd like to have heard more of his range as he can do pretty much everything.

Plagues of Babylon starts off with a pointless song lengthening intro which pretty much does the same thing for 2 minutes almost.  Really boring if you asked me.  And you did:)  I could see an intro like this for 20 seconds or so, but after that we get the idea, and it's time to move on.  When the song actually does start it sounds like it'll be an in your face thrasher.  Nope it's a mid tempo forgettable song that really never gets going and ultimately just feels like a waste of time.  It's not horrible, but geez is it boring.

Democide is a fast paced metal song that's ok, but it sounds just like songs I've heard before.  It has grown a little on me but it sounds like Pure Evil, which is a much better song.

The Culling has a decent chorus, however the rest of the song sounds flat and tired.  It's ok, but that's about it.

Among the living dead actually moves with a nice enough guitar riff and rhythm section.  Unfortunately the melodies just aren't there, and this could have been a better song.  I'm listening to it right now and I can't remember how it goes.

Resistance is another slower heavy song.  It's got a faster part in it, but the verses are slower.  Again it doesn't do anything for me and while listening to it I can't remember how it goes.

The end starts off quietly with clean guitars and vocals.  The song gets heavier and a little more upper mid tempo.  It picks up speed later, but again and you'll notice a theme, it's forgettable.

If I could see you is a cheesy ballad, which does show off some more of Stu's range, however we've ehard this before on the last album done better.  I liked this song much better when it was Melancholy.

Cthulhu starts off quietly with clean guitars.  After a minute or 2 it gets heavier and picks up speed.  The riffs are nice and the drums and bass are solid.  Stu's vocals are excellent.  this is the only song on here that actually flows really well, and gets me to stop paying attention to whatever distraction I've got myself into to not pay attention to this album.  I love this song, and it's easily my favorite song on the album.

Peacemaker and Spirit of the times could just as well be the same song.  They really sound that much alike.  geez every song on this second half seems to have a soft part.  Peacemaker gets heavier for the bulk of the song while Spirit is a ballad, but the intro sound the same.

Parasite is another slower tempo metal song.  This song might be more boring than the opening track.

The Highwayman Hahaha what a terrible song.  This has to be the worst thing recorded under the Iced Earth name.  Terrible song.  I can't speak to the original, but this version is not done well at all.  The melodies are awful and I don't care for the performances of the guest vocalists.

So if you only want an Iced Earth album to have the same style as you're use to then go ahead and buy this, however if you want good songwriting you'll want to look elsewhere.  This isn't a terrible album, but you've heard it all before done much better on previous albums.  But listen for yourself and judge it on your own.  I just find this a chore to get through in 1 listen, and can't really do it.

reviewText:
I was going to keep mine sealed until I went back and looked at the reviews. I decided I had better take a listen. I broke out Abbey Road. Side 1 played fine. Side 2 (Here Comes the Sun) was absolutely horrible. So much static that it distorted the playback. It is truly unbelievable that this product was shipped. Non-existent quality control. I also experienced, like others, the shipping debacle. Mine came in an over-sized box with some air cushion material but not enough to keep the product from bouncing around during shipment. Luckily, my box was not damaged (light dings on the corners) but I did think to myself at the time "you have to be kidding me - who packs this way?". Net, I returned mine. I'm going to wait until EMI decides to ship a quality product and then repurchase. Obviously this initial batch is what we vinyl collectors refer to as "junk vinyl".

FOLLOW-UP: Cleaning does not help. I have a professional disc cleaner and cleaned Abbey Road after I listened to the record once through - no improvement. I'm a hard core Beatles collector. I must have over 1,000 collectible Beatles LPs from all over the world (Butchers, the rare Revolver red Capitol "bulls eye" label, the first pressing of PPM on the Parlophone black and gold label, etc.) and I have never ever experienced anything like the junk in this box set. I can pick up a used Beatles LP on eBay or at the flea market which is 30 - 40 years old and it plays better - much better. I am amazed at what some people will accept for the money they put down. I'm reading about dishing, warping, off center spindle holes, misaligned labels and some reviewers saying "but the sound is great"... seriously? For $319 everyone of us should have received a pristine set - as in perfect. The box set should have records that rival the Mobile Fidelity pressings from years ago. Instead we were shipped a defective product with the burden on the collector to return, swap out, etc. to get something passable. My suggestion is everyone send this crap back and make EMI do it right.

reviewText:
...and I'm Batman. Rarely have I encountered an album seemingly as undeserving of praise as this. What you might call a classic Black Metal album, I call a godawful mass of auditory rape.

"Oh, you just don't get it!" I hear you say. "Transilvanian Hunger is tr00, necro, grim, and/or kvlt!" You might also say that Darkthrone is one of the few bands that stayed "true" to their Black Metal roots, compared to sissies like Dimmu Borgir or Cradle of Filth. Well, I'd say you're right on both counts, but that doesn't change the fact that this album STILL sucks.

I don't know who first got it into their heads that Black Metal albums should all sound absolutely terrible in the production department. Sure, the thin, distant sound to Emperor's "In the Nightside Eclipse" helped it to sound more cold and evil, but for most Black Metal albums, I find that the bad production doesn't make the album sound evil, it just makes it sound, well, bad. Of course, when it comes to bad production, "Transilvanian Hunger" is quite possibly the absolute nadir. My first impression was that it sounded like some distant drums and some guy screaming over them, along with an earful of radio static. Oh, wait, that's not static, that's supposed to be the guitars! Do they honestly expect me to sit through this nonsense for 39 minutes, especially when the music itself so maddeningly repetitive and simplistic? Most of the songs barely change over their (interminable) running length! Sometimes, you can hear a faint tinge of a melody, variation, or a faint scrap of actual music, but it's all buried by the disaster of a production. Yes, Darkthrone, I get it, you're against all that slick "commerically" produced music, but that's no excuse to sound this bad!

"Oh, but Black Metal isn't about raw musicality or virtuosity!" I hear you saying. "It's about the atmosphere!" Again, you'd be right, but when it comes to "Transilvanian Hunger" I must ask...what atmosphere? How can any album have "atmosphere" when it sounds like nothing more than two guys sloppily playing about in some shack somewhere whilst recording their "music" on a Fisher Price tape recorder? "Transilvanian Hunger" sounds about as evil as a bawling infant. Loud and grating, yes, but in no way evil.

To make matters worse, Darkthrone, in their infinite necro-ness, decided to label their music as "Norsk Arisk Black Metal" (Norse Aryan Black Metal) and proclaimed that anyone who criticized this album should be admonished for their "obviously Jewish behavior." Of course, I can't say if there is any racist content on the album, due to the fact that all but the title track is sung in Norwegian, but the whole "Norsk Arisk" bit comes off as an absolutely moronic publicity stunt, especially coming from an elitist band like Darkthrone who apparently think there are only two ways of doing things: their way, or the wrong way.

"Transilvanian Hunger" is an absolute mess of an album, with production below bottom of the barrel, and the sloppy playing of two guys who think they sound much more evil than they really do. How can anyone even PRETEND to enjoy this?

reviewText:
This doesn't shock me, offend me or scare me. It just bores me. It's so repetitive! It's basically the same damn song all over again. "Postmortem" has essentially the same riff as "Jesus Saves"; "Criminally Insane" has the same drum break intro as "Epidemic"; "Alter of Sacrifice" has the same riff as "Reborn"; "Angel of Death" is one of the most overrated songs I've ever heard, just pure noise without any redeeming facets. I don't even mind loud music - I actually like it when it's done well. But when it's noise for the sake of noise? Forget it. And Slayer is just that. And as for the riffs themselves... "DUH doot duh-duh-duh DUH doot duh-duh-duh- DUH doot duh-duh-duh DUH doot"... what's brilliant about that? It's like Slayer decided that playing as fast and as loud as possible would make up for the fact that none of them could play. The lyrics... well, they aren't shocking at all. If a guy in a Cookie Monster voice grumbling about how he plays pool with Satan's uncle on Tuesdays shocks you, you're obviously easily shocked. Then again, nothing's shocking anymore. Or I'm jaded, one or the other. I can't think of a single reason to listen to this. If I want something fast `n' hard, I'll go with The Clash, who had plenty to say, and a lot of imagination. More than Slayer at any rate.
One more thing: people can say whatever they want, but that won't change the fact I think Slayer sucks and sucks hard. Just so you know.

reviewText:
I had the faint hope that "The Delivery Man" would  be a solid and tuneful set of punchy rock and roll and sharply writ lyrics as was Costello's previous "When I Was Cruel" from four years ago, but such is hardly the case.

The songs are wander bits of amorphous mood setting, vaguely sad, melancholic, inward drawn. The worst of "Painted from Memory", is irresolutely medium tempo collection of muzaked dirges with Burt Bacharach (both of whom apparently forgetting that Bachrach's work is marked as much by quirky, uptempo tunes)  meets the pulse less shoe-gazing sniffling of "North".Costello has been trying to show everyone how much he's matured and grown as an artist and writer, but unlike someone like Paul Simon , who improved dramatically in his solo work after he finally bid adieu to the collegiate poesy of Simon and Garfunkel's too-precious word mongering, Costello tries to get it all in, to say it all in one song, and then again in the song after that. His songs tear at the seams, and there is not the overflow of talent you'd like, but rather an uncontainable spillage. Simon , through "Rhymin' Simon" and onward, knows the meaning of restraint, containment, care in image and metaphor. He remains a songwriter with an especially strong sense of pop structure, a matter that forces him to make each song the best he can do at the moment. Costello is, on occasion, a better melodist than Simon and a more interesting, verbally dexterous lyricist, but it is his lack of care that sinks him here and through out most of his output in the 90's.  Tom Waits, his closet in terms of sheer talent, does the sloppy and the unrestrained with the kind of genius we reserve for Miles Davis and Picasso. Costello is shy of genius, is a brilliant craftsman when he applies the technique, and reapplying himself is exactly what is called for.

The songs on the new one are unfocused and drift in structure--Costello seems to be trying to convince that playing being indecisive about how he wants a melody to unfold, or what mood and psychology he wants to get across is enough to evoke Hamlet like assumptions of deep thought and artful equivocation on key narrative points. He sounds like he's trying to be artfully oblique, but what Costello forgets is that his greatest talent was his ability to absorb the styles of fifty or so years of rock,pop and rhythm and blues styles and then compose a fantastically buoyant music that was at once subtly argued in the lyrics and intensely rocking with the music. Costello must not like to dance anymore, and has entered middle age with some overblown assumptions that he needs to be artier, moodier, more depressed, more diffuse, more obtuse than he was when he was a young punk trying to make a buck off his bad attitude.

There are those die hard fans who would counter that Costello's lyrics are the subtlest and most literary of his career, something I would argue against, but all the same this is a weak defense of the general torpor that saturates "The Delivery Man". Even if it were so, albums that are more interesting to read than to listen to are fit, on principle, to be used for target practice at the next skeet shoot.

Sorry, just thought I'd write a sloppy, all-over-the-place review for a sloppy, all-over-the-place, crapped out in two weeks just to beat the actual Queensrche band to the punch abomination of an album.  It would be one thing if Tate hired his "all-star" band to write an actual piece of classic heavy metal, or even heavy prog, but he just needed some credible names to attach to it to differentiate it from his solo crap.  The ironic thing is that he accuses his former bandmates of tarnishing the Queensrche brand for reviving their classic style, then he pieces together a quick collection of solo grunge/nu-metal/radio rock and recruits about a dozen hired guns to help record it, as if this somehow adds something of value to the brand he's so worried about.  Add in the horrendous quality of the four re-recorded songs, and you have a legitimate trainwreck on your hands.  June 11th will see the release of an actual Queensrche album with their new vocalist, while April 23 will be remembered as a huge "FU" to anyone who ever appreciated this band.

reviewText:
LL Cool J is a legend in the hip hop community and is one of the top ten greatest mc's of all time.  His catalogue is enormous and quite frankly I cannot remember which album this is.  He's found a way to play the middle between the streets and the mainstream with tracks such as 4,3,2,1 and I Need Love.  He has many hits under belt and has dropped platinum album after platinum album.  However, this may be the end of the road for him.

This album, Todd Smith, simply put is wack.  This may be good for pop music but as hip hop I can't put my stamp of approval on it.  Every song has a feature and the feature is an R&B artist.  It wouldn't make a difference if the songs were good because they certainly had the potential to be good.  With guests such as Teairra Mari, Ginuwine, NeYo, Mary Mary, 112, Lyfe Jennings, Jennifer Lopez among others.  The songs just don't turn out to be very good.  The first single with Jennifer Lopez - Control Myself was a song made strictly for the clubs with no replay value.  It was ok when it came out but now its just annoying.  The second single Freeze with Lyfe Jennings is flat out horrible.  As a matter of fact the only good songs are the collaborations with Mary J. Blige and Jamie Foxx.  Favorite Flavor with Mary J. Blige is really a great song and the light airy beat screams summertime (this should have definitely been the second single), and Jamie Foxx puts his touch on Best Dress (they must have put aside their differences).  Down The Aisle with 112 is alright but other than that the rest of the tracks are throwaways.

LL Cool J may have ran his course and there should be no shame in him hanging up his mic and passing the torch.  His legacy is solidified but if he wants to continue on he can as long as he does better than this album it will be fine.  Personally, I can't listen to the album but may still check for something if he decides to drop again. 1 star.

reviewText:
Human life sometimes turns out the way God wants it to be. Human life is also the sum total of all of the historical, sociological, psychological, economic, and biological forces that impinge upon us, mixed together with the large number of thoughtful choices that we make in each and every day of our lives. We also have fluctuating feelings; we often act as we do feel. Each and every day of our lives presents us with wonderful opportunities to think, feel, learn, and grow in new and different ways. So I have devoted one day of my life to listening to, feeling, thinking about, and learning from Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection. Since this five cd set has been successfully remastered, we hear Janis Joplin and her bands sing and play more clearly than ever before! And what do we learn from this listening? We learn that Janis began her musical career singing folk rock music (cd #1). We learn that Janis Joplin's recording career lasted only a few short years and that her career was only somewhat productive of high quality music. We learn that Janis' life was quite troubled, and that this trouble was gloriously and often outrageously expressed, and thus given personal meaning and purpose, in her music. We learn that Janis Joplin's voice, her music, and her influence upon popular culture were so very powerful and so very unique that her voice and some of her music defined and actually became A SEASON OF OUR LIVES for those of us music fans who are part of the baby boom generation. We learn why classical musicians of the time, who were formally educated in music, thought that much or all of Janis Joplin's music was junk. We learn that only cd #1 (folk rock) and cd #4 (Pearl) are coherent enough to be considered true works of art. We learn that the music found on cd #5 is a complete waste of listening time. We learn that Janis Joplin's musical legacy, like her shortened life, is very scattered, with much unfocused, probably alcohol and drug driven, energy. We learn that reviewers who give Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection a five star rating are either very ignorant of high quality music or extremely irresponsible in their ratings. We learn that reviewers' ratings of cds on amazon.com are not a valid or useful indicator for consistently purchasing high quality music. And finally, I learned that the season of glory, discontent, alienation, outrage, and unfounded dreams, which was the season of Janis Joplin's music, is a long-gone season in my own life. I gained further understanding of Janis' musical legacy from Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection because the sound quality of this five cd set is so very clear. However, I did not truly, consistently, and deeply enjoy listening to a vast majority of the songs on Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection. I was very disappointed in the small amount of listening pleasure that I gained from this five cd set. I will sell Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection at a used cd store. In summation, my wisely informed and strong recommendation is that you NOT BUY Box of Pearls: Janis Joplin Collection. I instead suggest that you purchase a Janis Joplin greatest hit package that skips all of Janis' songs that did not even chart during her own lifetime.

John

Geez..so this is the new Springsteen. I've been on board this bus since I worked at Discount records in St. Louis where one day we checked out this guy in the 'Folk" isle and we played the Wild & Innocent. Hey, he's not folk!

So my buddies and I'm were hooked and now I'm 56 living in Orlando. Every Springsteen new release hits some type of player 8 track, cassette, turntable, cd, computer the day its released. 23 times in the clubs, halls and arenas to see him live. My ex-wife and I even planned our honeymoon around the 'darkness' tour 7 shows in 12 days in a VW bug following their bus.

But man I gotta tell you. This stuff's getting ragged. Surprise, Surprise, Surprise! Yeah, I tell you I was Surprised all right. What the 'L' is that all about? Whew! And that cowboy thing that opens this collection...amazingly I read somewhere here on good 'ol Amazon that one of these reviewers compared it to Jungleland! Ok pass the pipe, I've got to get a hit of what you're smoking.

Overall this collection of dreck has a little better edge than that last rotten egg that was laid called Magic. I played it once and said - 'hmmm must not of been in the mood today for Bruce' played it twice and said - "could this really be as boring as I think it is" waited a month - played it again and when I heard that ' Girl in the Summer Clothes' thing I ripped it from my car cd player and frisbeed it out the window.

Devils and Dust in a word - BRUTAL. This Dream thing, the acoustic stuff has merit. Are there any rockers on this thing? Can somebody give me a hand here?

I know, I know he's almost 60. So am I. But honestly folks, you want good Springsteen? Then start with BTR and go right directly through every release including Live 75-85 till you hit Brillant Disguise and stop. That's it! You've got everything you'll ever need. No reason to expose yourself to this dreck that gets released now.

Bottom line if the first Bruce cd was Magic and Dreams was the second....you'd never hear a 3rd.

I love you Bruce but its time to go back to that mansion in Rumson and weave those tales of the road to your kids.

See you at the Super Bowl.

reviewText:
...digital-era pseudo-1950's formula duds under the name of the world's leading imposter horrorpunk band.  Except this time, the songs aren't cover songs.

So many things in life aren't meant to last, and the false Misfits of the new millennium are no exception.  Nothing near as refreshingly violent, melodic and unique as the Danzig era was; allthewhile lacking the roar and re-inspired drive of the Graves era.  Dez Cadena's guitar sound doesn't seem to hold up with the production and completely cowers in comparison to what was previously Doyle's.  And Jerry Only, the almighty "leader and founder of the Misfits," IS perfectly capable of holding a tune.  But so what?  Many people are.  That doesn't mean they should be a lead singer in a formerly-reputable band with the vocal tracks doubled and very up-front in the mix.  In fact, I have to say that Corey Graham's review here basically nailed it on the head with, "Only's singing sounds like your drunken dad stepping up to the mic late in the wedding reception."

I only have 3 positive things to say about this album:

1. There's no denying that the album cover has character.
2. The storm pauses in the title track are a brief, but cool vibe.
3. Eric Arce does well at capturing a good cross between the styling of Googy and Chud, yet moving the sound forward.  He actually may even be the closest thing to anything sounding authentically Misfits-like about this album.  Unfortunately, he also has to wear that stupid-ass makeup.

But overall, the album is dull, comes across as feeling repetitive, and is just plain cheesy and difficult to take seriously, considering all the work Jerry has put into claiming ownership of this band and it's future. The songwriting as a whole lacks originality and ranks as mediocre-at-best as the common run-of-the-mill horrorpunk band consisting of people half Jerry's age or less.  I give the guy big props for his tenacity, but the result is just embarrassing and doesn't hold up well at all against the original era OR even its "resurrected" era, for that matter.  For the most part, it's produced well... but that doesn't mean much when the songwriting sucks.

PREPARE YOURSELF FOR THE TRUTH:
If you prefer music of the 1950's, this album is a harsh travesty in comparison.  Stick with the original stuff.

reviewText:
The above title was my reaction after hearing WORKS I when it was originally released in 1977. Unfortunately, it hasn't improved over time for me at all.

This and Works II were a horrific example of egos out of control and the resultant schlock. The 3 individual members by this point weren't even speaking to each other and had their own separate managers and travelled separately as well. And it shows in the music to an alarming degree.

A lot of things that made the earlier ELP efforts so cool here are largely absent. For example, there's nary a trace of Keith's distinct Hammond organ playing, and in its place some of the cheesiest, schlockiest synth sounds ever devised. Keith's amateurish attempt at a post-Brahms/Rachmininoff piano concerto would actually be somewhat entertaining if he wasn't taking himself so seriously. Greg Lake's predictably sappy ballads are no help and Carl Palmer's material is pretty much forgettable.

The two group cuts are just pure cheese-whiz, the reworking of "Fanfare For The Common Man" makes Mannheim Steamroller sound like Stravinsky by comparison, and "Pirates" just sinks under its own weight as Greg Lake barks up a storm.

This Owl thinks they should've quit while they were ahead with Brain Salad Surgery, undoubtedly their finest moment, but alas, their egos did not permit them such an indulgence of common sense.

reviewText:
This is more a complaint about the press release than the CD itself (although I do believe that Baez, at her best, is trite).

"Before Joan Baez, the closest thing to a female folk singer was Jo Stafford".  Huh?

Leaving Ronnie Gilbert of the Weavers aside for the moment, Carolyn Hester recorded "Scarlet Ribbons' in 1957, BEFORE "The Kingston Trio", the album that precipitated the 60's folk boom.  She followed it in 1960 with the "Tradition" album and, in 1961, her Columbia debut featuring Bob Dylan on harmonica, Bill Lee on Bass and Bruce Langhorne on guitar.  Carolyn's perfect soprano bell-like tones and Spanish-language folk songs were the obvious prototype for Baez's uneven career.

So, if you're going to write a press release promoting someone, don't make it so obviously fatuous!

reviewText: This album, in my humble opinion, has absolutly nothing going for it. Apart from the first cut ("Hell Or Hallelujah"), not one song drew my attention. I bought the CD cause i'm a KISS fan and i feel obligated to do so. For my collection. And the first song will surely go in my own compilation CDs of the band. But to me, Paul Stanley and Gene Simmons are simply not good enough composers to make a full album on their own. They might not want to but i think that they need outside writers. Some of their best hits were written by outside writers, mainly DESMOND CHILD. I know, "I Was Made For Lovin' You" wasn't a typical KISS song. But what about "Heaven's On Fire"? What about "Uh! All Night"? Or "Who Wants To Be Lonely"? Yes, Desmond Child mainly worked with the band during the eighties and that period isn't the favorite of most die-hard fans but, to this date, "Heaven's On Fire" is still one of the band's best success. A true anthem that's sure to be popular in concerts. Still today. Who can say that a song like that wouldn't fit "Monster"? Or "Sonic Boom" before? Desmond Child has written some of the best songs in Rock History (Bon Jovi, Kiss, Alice Cooper, Joan Jett, Aerosmith, etc...) and he is still composing hits even today. "Live To Win", a great song by Paul Stanley on his last solo effort was a hit and guess who helped write it? You got it. Desmond Child. All of the songs on "Monster" sound like a collection of fillers from past CDs. Songs that you would find on B-sides. At least, on "Sonic Boom", you had "Danger Us" and "Say Yeah!" that were truly "KISS worthy". But on "Monster", nothing. Well, just the first song but still, it's not even one of their best. Just like Meat Loaf who refuses to go back to Jim Steinman and keeps putting out insipid records, KISS is staying away from their hitmaker (Desmond Child)and keeps coming to us with lesser efforts each time. I appreciate the effort on their part but my opinion is made. Without Desmond Child, they will not survive another album like this. They need another "Heaven's On Fire".

reviewText:
Review by MARK TEPPO at igloomag.com

(03.23.05) Shortly after 18 was released, I seem to remember an interview with Moby where he laid the blame for depressed sales of that record on the shoulders of the peer-to-peer file networks. "Kids," he claimed, "are trading my record instead of purchasing it." I didn't buy the argument because every CD store I visited (and I visit a lot of them, music whore that I am) had four to six USED copies of 18 in their bins. No, Moby, the kids weren't stealing your record; they just weren't buying it because they thought it was terrible.

I'm reminded of this as I listen to Hotel, Moby's latest bid for rawk star status. I must have missed the announcement where Moby came clean with his desire to be a pop star; it's the only rationale I can find to explain why Hotel is a continuation of everything that went wrong with 18. Gone are all the sumptuous textures and orchestral flourishes that propelled the little idiot (and, no, I'm not being an pretentious ass with the name calling, check his publishing credits) into superstardom in the first place. Maybe he never wanted to be remembered as the guy who imported the symphony and the blues singer into the laptop and fused it all together with a drum machine and a series of DSP patches. Maybe Moby just wants to rock out; maybe he just wants to bring the lights down for an intimate power ballad for a stadium full of his newest best friends.

Maybe. If that is the case, he's certainly picked a tepid way to go about it. While a few of the tracks on Hotel have a bit of a hook ("Raining Again" and "Lift Me Up" for example, though even these seem like Moby's only fishing for minnows with the shallow hooks he's using), the majority of the tunes are pale narcissistic pop songs that will be relegated to incidental music for Deepak Chopra seminars and elevator musak for tired urban hotels struggling to stay hip.

That said, Hotel: Ambient is gorgeous. Packaged with Hotel as part of a limited initial release, this companion CD is an ambient retread of the record. His explanation in the liner notes for the title of the record says, "I don't feel like making music that is airless and lifeless because I also really like people and the messy miasma of the human condition and I want to make messy, human records that are open and emotional." Maybe it says more about me than him that I find Hotel: Ambient to more evocative of the human emotional experience than the trite lyrical content and shallow pop constructs of Hotel, but Hotel: Ambient glistens with charm and innocence, a seductive lure of slow tones and fathomless textures that is far more than just aural wallpaper. This is incidental music filled with longing and heartbreak, loneliness and hopefulness. This is the womb of your hotel room: the space that enfolds you, that holds you tight when you are separated from the ones you love, that tries to alleviate your need for home with its tiny amenities and spartan intimacy. Hotel: Ambient understands how alone you can feel in a numbered room high above the world, and just wants to hold you tight.

If you like what Moby did with Voodoo Child's The End of Everything (and even the ambient bits of Play), then Hotel: Ambient will make you happy. It is just disappointing that you have to put up with Hotel to get to it.

reviewText: This is pure "Free Jazz" --it is totally devoid of a recognizable form.  If you are looking for melody, harmony, and rhythm (i.e. the traditional building blocks that make music what it is), you will not find them here. Indeed it is difficult to believe that this is the same musician that gave us "The Four Brothers" and "The Train and the River." It is obvious that these are accomplished musicians who give us well executed arpeggios, scales and other snippets, but these disjointed fragments do not fit together to produce anything that seems musically satisfying. It is more delicate and not as overbearing as Ornette Coleman, but it is just as boring if not unnerving--it is an incoherent jumble that just doesn't feel like music. I found it very hard to give this CD a fair listen--the temptation is extremely strong to switch to something else. I honestly cannot find anything redeeming to recommend this album.

reviewText:
I keep asking myself why this recording was even considered; it's that bad.  Ms Fleming may or may not be a good singer, but her attempts at Mozart show blatantly all of her short comings, both artistically and technically.

Ms Fleming got her first big break singing Konstanze.  But the very demanding aria "Ach, ich liebte..." is far too much for her.  It's like watching a car careen out of control down a narrow, winding mountain road: at any minute you are sure she will just spin off all together.  And the other selections are not much better.  I should think that Mr Mackerras would have handed her the Urtext at some point during the recording sessions to point out all of the wrong notes she hits.  Some times, it's like a an exaggerated appogiatura, where she steps an extra note too high, but it occurs at many other spots as well.  "In quali eccessi" is particularly bad; write at the close of the aria she jumps so far off what is indicated in the score, it makes a true Mozartian sick!

The selection of arias is also somewhat strange.  Most of the arias are more about lost love than being in love ("In quali eccessi", "Ach ich fuehl's) or have nothing to do with love at all ("Nehmt meinen Dank").  In the end, it would have been nice to hear a few arias from Cosi, or one of Zerlina's arias from Don Giovanni.  But there is danger in those selections as well (her recording of Fiordiligi with Solti on Decca is not one of the highlights of her career).

Ms Fleming will never been accused of being a coloratura soprano.  She has a very lyrical tone, to be sure, but lacks the strict vocal tightness to cope with the arias presented on this recording.  It is far too sloppy for my liking.

To be avoided!

reviewText:
I think reviews that are hyping this album as a great and underappreciated gem are doing potential KISS fans a disservice. This was the first KISS album I ever bought, and it's a wonder it wasn't the last.

The Elder is a concept album. Yes, a concept album from KISS. Never a band known for their deep philosophical musings, the guys sat down with Bob Ezrin and based an album around an idea for a movie from Gene about a race of immortals, and a "chosen one" who has to meet his destiny. Or something to that effect. It doesn't really matter what the concept is, as long as the music is okay, right?

That's where this album fails miserably. This albums best songs are listenable and okay (The Oath, Dark Light, a World Without Heroes) but when it's bad, it's laughably bad. Songs like "Odyssey", "Mr. Blackwell", and the cheesy self-affirming "I", almost ruined KISS single-handedly. At times, it's so bad I wonder if they actually *tried* to make it sub-par.

New fans should avoid this album until they are well acquainted with KISS' GREAT albums from the 70s, starting with stuff like "Dressed to Kill" and "Destroyer". The Elder is only for completists.

reviewText:
Welcome to the MTV Generation, where all you need is an attractive look in order to attain success.  Trivial things such as talent are not necessary, and those who have it need not apply, because it's only "hot and sexy" people that we are looking for.  Therein lies the appeal of 'N Sync: Their core audience (mostly young girls, 15 and under) find them easy on the eyes, and along with radio and MTV playing them ad nauseum, they were able to manage enormous sales (over 2 million in the first week alone!) of No Strings Attached.  Millions upon millions of 'N Sync fans can't be wrong, right?  Or could they?
For anyone that doesn't go to slumber parties, doesn't buy Hello Kitty merchandise or shop at The Limited Too!, No Strings Attached is an audio assault that's about as much pleasure as pouring hot acid on your ears - and just about as fun.  The songs veer from the typical slick, saccharine, melodramatic balladry typically associated with the teen pop genre, to songs that are allegedly "innovative" but aren't if you've ever heard any real techno/trance music before.  If you can get through treacly tracks like "This I Promise You" and "That's When I'll Stop Loving You", you must have a stronger stomach than I do.  The blatantly cheesy "Space Cowboy" and "It's Gonna Be Me" are enough to make anyone cringe, and a song like "Digital Get Down" (for anyone that doesn't know, it's about "cyber sex") should have kept parents from buying it for their kids - and let's face it, the vast majority of their fans fall into this category and probably have outgrown this music four years after it's release (and judging by the incredibly high amount of used copies offered, that's certainly a possibility).
In summary: Dated teen pop that offers nothing with substance or originality whatsoever.  The lyrics are juvenile and poorly written, and basically 'N Sync is nothing but a glorified New Kids On The Block tribute group (as if they needed a tribute!).  I don't recommend this album.

reviewText:
I have known this work in score (all 413 pages of it) for nearly 50 years now - and have been attentive to every recording that has surfaced. Some performances cut the guts out of the piece making a mockery of Gliere's carefully crafted architecture. Others come close to the mark. The only recording to follow GLIERE's markings accurately is  still available and is conducted by Harold Farberman. The only recording which, if not entirely accurate tempo-wise, is sonically quite spectacular, and that is Sir Edward Downes'.
The present recording is a colossal disaster from every perspective. When a recording announces itself as being "complete and uncut" and yet, in this case, has a performance time of 72 minutes, you know something is terribly wrong. I was antipating a solid performance from Leon Botstein, and spectacular sonics from Telarc. Neither is the case. Telarc's engineers have totally missed the boat on this recording: The LSO sounds like it was recorded in a Turkish bath house, the acoustics are so terrible. There is no definition, no balance, everything sounds muffled and totally out of kilter. This is astonishing given Telarc's past record of superlative orchestral recording.
The LSO plays at its usual high level - but is totally sabatoged by Botstein's absolute dismissal of Gliere's tempo markings, either specifically or conceptually.  The architecture of the four movements of this work are very carefully constructed - such that the first, second and fourth movements each have performing times between 27 and 28 minutes: yet Botstein manages the first in 22 minutes, the second in 20! and the last movement in 22. Botstein's tempi in the first movement are often not even in the same universe as Gliere's - i.e. the all important bits of liturgical chant at Rehearsal #8 are completely wrong, first measure to last. The materials given here are critical to the rest of the piece and are blown away as if they were a bit of meaningless trivia. The fourth movement, for example, begins in a "slower" tempo, progress through a series of accelerating tempi and then arrives at allegro - but is, rather, played at the arriving tempo - you know the conductor either does not know the score, or has totally misread it. The second movement builds entirely out of the "creepy" sul ponticello augmented triad blurr with which it opens - and the progression is supposed to be very, very slow. Gliere gives only one tempo marking for the movement: quarter=54. There are no accelerandi marked anywhere in the movement, and only one very brief retardando. Many of the complex figures are unplayable if the tempo is too fast - the result here is a hideous kind of sloppy rhythmic hyperventilation, not the orgasmic agitation which is, in fact, what is in the score. Here, it is all matter of fact without any feel for the "geist" of the music. The third movement lacks clarity and projection altogether. It is unlistenable. The long peroration at the end of the fourth movement, itself a very ingenious recapitulation, al roverso, of the materials that preceded it, is meaningless when it happens too soon. (See "accelerando" above). For all these (and many other reasons) I would have hoped that Mr Botstein, who is also known as a musicologist, would have paid more attention to the score. Certainly, he could have followed Gliere's markings "more closely." That he did not gives us this egregious bit of interperative charlatanism. The power of this music is fully revealed in that most fundamental of musical attributes: time. The piece works because things happen "at the right time" as much as a result of "what" happens. Gliere knows his business - and it is totally indefensible to tell the composer "you didn't write the correct tempi" in your score. Such arrogance! Such chutzpah!
Avoid this recording like the plague. It is absolutely, totally wrong and negates, at virtually every point, everything that's in the score.
label: negative

reviewText:
Interesting that the two French DJs known as Daft Punk would imitate robots, because their music is as mindless and repetitive as something that would come from an automaton.

I've listened to a lot of bad albums, but Discovery stands out as one the most uniquely unpleasant listening experience I've ever had the misfortune of enduring. Not being satisfied with one listen, I instead subjected myself to the entire CD's length at least three times in the vain hope that it would somehow grow on me. Quite the opposite, as I found myself despising it with a greater and greater passion with every listen.

Can one honestly tell me that any effort was put into this CD when nearly every track is repetitive and cylical to a downright ludicrous degree? With the exception of "Digital Love" (the only halfway decent song on the album), each and every song consists of a single hook looped fifty to a hundred times over a simple beat for nearly the entire length of the song. Tracks go nowhere, build to nothing, and only if you're very lucky will they ever change at all. Take "Superheroes" for example, where a single vocal sample repeats for nearly three quarters of the song's duration. This wouldn't be so bad (at least, not nearly as unbearable) if the songs were at least somewhat catchy, but they're not. There's nothing remotely memorable, and at a later time I had difficulty remembering anything about any of the songs. This isn't minimalism; this is music at its most lazy and uncreative. The only circumstance in which the songs on Discovery would be remotely listenable would be if I were high out of my mind, and even then that would be doubtful.

As if maddening repetition were not enough, Discovery is replete with irritating synth samples that sound like they were dredged out of the worst of 80's synth-pop. Vocoder vocals are used throughout, and only create further irritation and disgust. The whole album comes off as sickeningly cheesy and unaware of it. If Daft Punk had conceived this album as a mockery of Dance and House music, it would be a downright brilliant satire. More cynically, Discovery sounds like it was tailor-made for television commercials; each song containing just enough material for a half-minute jingle, and repeated over and over to stretch it out to a full album.

Your tastes might vary from mine, but I don't recall ever disliking an album as much as this one. Most bad music makes me feel either disappointment or boredom, but Daft Punk's Discovery is the first to inspire outright loathing and disgust. To my amazement, I have heard that Daft Punk's latest album "Human After All" is even more repetitive in nature than this.

How is that even possible?

Nothing changes with Godsmack. They are stale, monotonous, and their music is repetitive drivel...which is probably why their commercial appeal is so high.

However, they truly did earn at least one star from me, because at least the songs on this album are a scratch more bearable to listen to then all their preceding garbage.

My recommendation? If you're a fan of Godsmack, then you will probably see this as an interesting and intelligent change of sound for the band, so buy the album, but only if it's cheap because it's less than 30 minutes long. If on the other hand, you have a grip on reality, I recommend you save your money. There's no new sound on this album, and as bad as Godsmack's other albums are, the remakes here are nothing special. Yes, the acoustics sound good despite the bad songs, but Sully's horrific voice eliminates any remaining possibility of this album being any good. Sully has a nu-metal voice, not a acoustic accompaniment voice. Godsmack should never try anything like this again, though I'm sure they will. Twice more. In an attempt to mirror AIC.

reviewText:
Coltrane's 1961 Village Vanguard engagement is legendary - both for the quality of the music and for the controversy it generated at the time.  This reissue contains the Live at the Village Vanguard album, nothing more, nothing less, and to my mind offers a very poor value for most listeners.

There is another release - the Village Vanguard Master Takes - that offers the 3 tracks here, plus two others ("India" and "Impressions").  These are the 5 tunes from the 1961 Village Vanguard engagement released during Coltrane's lifetime.  To be fair, you can still get those 2 missing tracks by buying the album "Impressions", but leaving them off here seems like a case of runaway original-LP-fetishism.

Another option most listeners should consider is the 4-CD box set which contains all the recorded tracks from the Vanguard engagement.  This isn't something for everyone - the box is pricier, and most of the tunes (including 4 or 5 that are not available on the Master Takes disc) are given multiple interpretations that may go over the head of the Coltrane neophyte.  Nevertheless, the more you listen to the music, the more the variations between these radically different versions (each night has a different approach) come to the fore.  Unless you are the kind of person that will end up with no more than 5 or 6 Trane discs, I would consider saving up the cash and getting the box.

As far as the music, the most famous track is "Chasing the Trane" - a bare-bones blues with Coltrane on tenor, backed by only bass and drums.  While later in his career would push the music out even further, by the standards of 1961 this was a very radical performance, with Coltrane's squawks, growls and screams as well as highly dissonant note choices.  "Softly as in a Morning Sunrise" is the most traditional track from the box, showcasing how well Coltrane's quartet could function even in a more conventionally swinging format.  Listen to Elvin on brushes!  Finally, "Spiritual" anticipates some of Coltrane's later music - "After the Rain", "Alabama", "Song of Praise", A Love Supreme - though in this case, he's literally playing a tune based on an African American spiritual rather than expressing that sentiment.
