reviewText: I love Ratt and regard all other releases as at least good if not excellent.  This is a huge disappointment.  It was Ratt trying to be whatever they felt they needed to be in the "modern" era and trying to redefine themselves rather than play in the classic Ratt style.  The vocals and drums are still there... but gone is the crisp classic Ratt guitar sound and the well blended rhythm guitar work.  Warren De Martini instead wants to blues up the band.  Not a good thing.  The solos are utterly forgettable and saturated in blues style rather than rock style... some of the songs might be good, but its hard to tell given the bad, lackluster, low energy guitar sound that drags down the entire effort.  Ratt used to be very upbeat and melodic... neither of which can really be used to describe this album.  Its all roll and no rock.  They got songwriting help from Great White's Jack Russel and I believe Jack Blades as well... and, honestly, I think Ratt was better off writing themselves and needed no help (Come on, Ratt's collection of best songs beats Great White and Night Ranger combined).  Listening to this CD makes me tense and aggitated.  I think it is a blemish upon their legacy.  Shame on DeMartini for destroying Ratt.  I would give this a zero if that were an option.  I own thousands of CDs and this is definitely in the bottom 50 or so.

reviewText:
"There was a time I was one of a kind."

That's true. There was a time Britney was the most special and beloved pop singer in the United States. Manufactured, safe, but still creative enough to not solely be a musical puppet. That time was 2003 with the release of her forth studio album In the Zone, which to date stands as her only real statement as an artist. This was also just before her complete mental breakdown and alleged drug use. I always said that I had to give Ms. Spears all the credit in the world for not committing suicide given just how cruel and malicious the media was to this woman who really did not deserve all the abuse she was receiving. I swear the media was nicer to George Zimmerman than it was to Britney Spears. Her crime? Well, I still haven't figured that out. And in a way, this time in her life both made her a stronger person, but also a complete shell of the pop singer she used to be. She's clearly lost a little of her equilibrium along the way, no longer singing and dancing as well as she once did. And what's evident is her lack of effort on every subsequent release. Blackout and Circus are, to date, her greatest records-- unfortunately, she had absolutely nothing to do with that. She wrote not a single line, her voice is auto-tuned and processed to the point where it transcended a human quality, and she looks half-asleep in all the promotional material. At least to me. But at the end of the day, those two records had some of the greatest songs of her entire career (Piece of Me, Gimme More, Circus, Radar, Shattered Glass).

But the days of Britney getting all the best tracks seems to have come with a close, a trend first started with the one-single "3", which commemerated a greatest hits package. What followed was the disaster that was Femme Fatale, a lukewarm, bland pop record void of any sort of personality or presence. I dare say it, the drunken party girl Britney person she used on Blackout and Circus was at least interesting. For as hard as she tried to not try at all, Britney had transformed into the Courtney Love of pop princesses, and she was damn good at it. Femme Fatale was Britney's rebirth as a mature woman. But the songs were awful, none of them had any sort of hook, and the lyrics weren't even close to clever or sexy. I predicted it was the end of the road for Britney Spears, no matter how well or unwell the material would go on to chart. The album was a moderate success, its single overshadowing the final product as a whole-- this is perhaps the first time that had happened since her sophomore album Oops...I Did It Again. But the guilty pleasure fun that Spears provided me was missing, and I had to admit it, but I was disappointed.

I struggle with whether or not I call myself a Britney fan. She's everything I dislike in an artist: she's not particularly talented; she can't supplement her lack of talent with personality; she hasn't evolved since for about six years now; she lip-syncs on stage; her lack album was a mess and I loathe almost everything she released before 2003 (which is two albums worth of material). And now, after her role as "judge" on the American version of The X-Factor, I have to say that I am definitely no longer a fan of Britney, as a person or as a popstar. I don't really understand why she was allowed to be so rude and cruel-- perhaps just as cruel as the media was to her after she was turned into a social perriah.

Now comes along Britney Jean. I'm already soured on this woman. It's clear I don't like her, and I don't necessarily wish her any more success. But I'm still gonna listen to it. I mean, I need my dose of guilty pleasure, inane, fun pop songs. Well, much like Femme Fatale, I'm just not finding anything even remotely interesting. The sad rave that was Blackout and then the shrooms trip that was Circus was a left/right two-punch knockout. Femme Fatale was a weak slap in the face, and Britney Jean is already on the floor unable to even swing. In an interview, Britney said she only does this for fun and doesn't really care how it does. Well, that seems like a half-truth. It seems more that Britney does this for contractual obligations rather than "fun," because she sounds sedated and sleepy throughou the entire project. But let's break this down. Britney Jean was produced in large by Black Eyed Peas abomination will.i.am, a mediocre, self-important infant playing with his big brothers' toys. If you didn't like Scream & Shout, you likely won't find much here you'll like either. His signature is all over this project with its generic beats and flate, late-80s vibe. The EDM-inspiration works the same way the dubstep-inspiration worked on Femme Fatale-- its a gimmick and serves no real purpose as only one of the songs is truly marinated in this genre (Til It's Gone). But by and large, this record's instrumentation sounds more like a glitched Dance Dance Revolution cabinet during a power outage. And then you have Britney's nasally vocals thrown on top of them. I do appreciate the lack of blatant auto-tune, though. It's use is far more subtle. But really, Britney's voice isn't aging well. It has that girlie hiccup to it, but she hasn't honed her skills whereas her mentor Madonna had (Evita).

Spears receives co-writing credits on each song, but I do have to wonder just how much she had to do with the lyrics. One could hear her contribution on In the Zone, but any she may have written seems to be lost between the lines written by her studio hands. Passenger, a song written partially by Katy Perry, really has no place on this album. Spears attempts to push her vocals beyond where they are comfortable, and really, this song should have been released by Perry. Or Christina Aguilera, perhaps. And say what you want about Aguilera, but at least she's not afraid of taking risks (Bionic). Spears has been contributing the same amount of boring for about a decade now. Blackout and Circus are products of their time, when Spears had absolutely no control over her life. And those times are likely never coming back, so for now we're stuck with mediocre pop song collections until her RCA contract runs out. Like we need songs like Alien or Work B****, the latter of which serves to do nothing except giving me a headache. Perhaps the biggest mess here is Chillin' With You, which is, for all intents and purposes, a country song masquerading as an R&B slow jaw. And perhaps most embarrassing is that the guest vocals from her little sister Jamie Lynn are far stronger than her own. How sad.

Overall, Britney Jean, her second self-titled record, has nothing good or bad for Spears' career. It's a non-entity, lost in a sea of other boring 2013 releases. It's Artpop. It's Roar. It's Miley Cyrus. It's just boring.

reviewText:
What is this crap?!?!?!
I've been a fan of King's X since their first release back in 1988. I thought that debut album (Out of the Silent Planet) was amazing, unique and an instant classic. Gretchen Goes to Nebraska confirmed my opinion. What a masterpiece! Each successive album continued to excite me, move me and make me eagerly await the next one.
Dogman was a bit of a disappointment, however, but I grinned and beared it, hoping the next release would be an improvement.
Ear Candy rubbed me the wrong way from the first time I saw a different looking King's X on the back cover. I initially thought their sound had changed along with their looks. Not so. I actually like Ear Candy more than Dogman.
Tape Head was okay, sort of falling in between Ear Candy and Dogman. Not one of their first five classics (what could ever top Faith Hope Love or their self-titled follow up to that incredible album?).
Along comes this bottom-heavy, nearly melody-less album, Please Come Home...Mr. Bulbous. As much as I liked King's X, I have to admit this album isn't going to find itself in heavy rotation any time soon. In fact, it may find itself in a used bin the first chance I get... Whatever. This album is dark, heavy and devoid of trademark King's X sounds and songs. If you're looking for a ray of sunshine, forget it.
"Fish Bowl Man" starts it off, and in an off-beat way. Distortion, free-form bass riffing, and discordant playing fade in -- then become a bone-crushing riff and a spoken verse that soon gives way to more free-forming, this time with verse, almost like a '50s word-association Beat poet. Or one of Jim Morrison's prose/poems. Yuck.
"Julia" is equally as dark. But at least it's slower.
The next track, "She's Gone Away," continues with another bass-heavy intro...then the guitars crash in, nearly burying the vocals and harmonies.
I could go on and on. But I'll spare you the details. The lyrics are virtually impenetrable (even by King's X standards). The musicianship sounds like the band was depressed to the point of hopelessness. In fact, nothing on this album sounds happy, upbeat or positive.
The trademark King's X sound (tight, creative drumming, crisp but raspy bass playing, a unique guitar sound and vocal harmonies that compel and soar) is gone. In its place is something found just about anywhere these days, in any city or state.
Interestingly, the most upbeat song on the album is track 6 ("Charlie Sheen"). It's actually fairly catchy, although I can't for the life of me figure out what they're singing about.
If you're a fan of King's X, do yourself a favor and skip this disc. It'll make you cry. If you're not a fan of King's X, this album won't make you one.
If you really want to know what true creative excellence and uniqueness sounds like, I suggest buying one of their first five albums. Those will go down in history as high points in 20th century music.
This album is merely going down...the wrong path.
Please come home...Mr. King's X. We miss you.
label: negative

reviewText:
The Good
Motley Crue bassist Nikki Sixx wrote a book about his life and struggles with drugs entitled The Heroine Diaries. In a unique marking tie in, he formed a new band to create a soundtrack for it. The album mixes passages from the book read by Nikki, with music no-doubt inspired by the story. Our story begins in 1986 at Christmas time. "X-Mas in Hell" twists a holiday classic with a section read from the book. The dark track "Van Nuys" would have you believe that whole town/city is drug addicts.

"Life is Beautiful" is the lead single from the album and has a great hard rock crunch and emotional chorus to it. "Pray for Me" is most likely about Sixx's failed marriage with Donna D'Errico (or Brandi Brandt). He laments on how she tried to help him, but he only hated her for it. "Dead Man's Ballet" delves into Sixx's near-death experience as he regrets leaving loved ones behind but spits venom at his father. The track runs the gamut on emotions and tempos.

The Bad
The album is probably better understood after reading the book. Trying to profit from stupid, irresponsible, and dangerous life choices is just wrong.

The Verdict
While The Heroin Diaries Soundtrack is hands-down Nikki Sixx's best non-Motley Crue music project, I simply cannot endorse anyone that glamorizes a lifestyle of drug abuse. Sixx can hide behind the claim he wants to help people so they don't make mistakes like he did, but in reality, people will feel that they too can survive a lifetime of drug abuse and may even come out a millionaire or celebrity because of it. reviewText: Oh punk rock, where have you gone? I was subjected to this album last year by a friend, and needless to say, I wasn't pleased. It's sad that punk rock, once a vital and powerful artform, has been co-opted and watered down into sort-of a sub-power pop, "alternative" rock mashup for a new generation. Simple Plan are to the Ramones (or even Green Day for that matter) what Candlebox was to Nirvana. No Pads, No Helmets...No Talent (eerr, No Balls) is a bland collection of Deep Blue Something tunes played at 45 rpm and dressed with a hodge-podge of laughably trite lyrics written by a 20-something about how hard it is to be 16. Not that there's anything wrong with writing a song about your teenaged years, but Simple Plan completely trivializes the experience of growing up (if you want a good song about being young, try The Replacements' "Sixteen Blue"). It's downright insipid. It's not even about the music being punk (it's not punk though); any way you slice it, this is bad stuff. It's the kind of music that insists that rebellion is about telling your parents to f' off because they want you to do the dishes. It's sad really, that a genre that used to base itself on rejecting conformity (musically, politically, etc.) has become pre-packaged drivel that goes against all the values it used to stand for. Not that it's Simple Plan's fault that they're marketed as punk, but the fact that it is passed-off as such is a tad disheartening. I could go into a long rant here, and I don't want to. If you like this sort-of thing, fine, but I think it pretty much speaks for itself. If you have any interest in punk rock at all, though, pick up a record by the Ramones, The Clash, or The Fall.

reviewText:
First, let's be clear on one thing: As my moniker says, I am an electronic music fanatic. Period. But as I've stated many times, ALL genres of music have their great music, their fair-to-middling music, and their god-awful music. So, please understand that my giving this release 1 star is only because it...well, it didn't grab me like I hoped it would. Zelda-werk stated it pretty clearly: If the majority of the "singers" on some of these tracks would have kept their traps shut and just let the music do the talking (or, as some of the smarter musicians did, put their voices through a Vocoder or an Eventide Harmonizer), I might have enjoyed it more. Their "singing," for me, ruined what otherwise might have been some overall enjoyable tracks. But, it's plain upon listening to this disc that a lot of heart, soul and good intentions went into it. So, if you're the type who would enjoy a hybrid cross of Kraftwerk's music with the average electronic pinball machine, then you will find this CD very, very enjoyable.

Now, if I were to try to line up a roster of artists to do a tribute to Kraftwerk, here's the list I came up with: Brian Eno. Depeche Mode. New Order. Gang of Four. Witchcraft. Steve Roach. Jonn Serrie. Constance Demby. Kevin Braheny. Robert Rich. Jean-Michel Jarre. Tim Blake. Vangelis. Rick Wakeman. Keith Emerson. Chick Corea. Robert Carty. Stomu Yamashta. Kitaro. Even their fellow kraut-rockers like Kraan. Tangerine Dream (the classic lineup of Franke/Froese/Baumann). Klaus Schulze. I am sure there are many other illuminaries that I neglected to mention, but this was just off the top of my head. Can you IMAGINE the kind of music a lineup like that could yield? reviewText: Only one star? Yes, again Biret's Chopin does not warrant more than but the one star. As so often, her playing distracts rather than attracts the listener as to the masterful inventiveness of these Sonatas. It is often claimed that the First Sonata is no masterpiece. In relation to what the teenage Chopin was to create a few years later, that is quite true--at least Biret is in no way able to provide any counterevidence. Nonetheless, turning to Ohlsson's reference version, one realises how much pleasure there is embedded in the seemingly somewhat puerile notes. Neither the Second nor Third Sonatas fare much better. Probably, the rhapsodic first movement of the Second Sonata is least ill-suited to Biret's erratic pianism. Conversely, the trio sections of the second and third movements almost lose all their shape and structure in Biret's hands. The excellent Bsendorfer instrument is, as always in Naxos's Tonstudio van Geest, captured almost without any beauty or warmth but rather with that unpleasant metallic edginess. For a complete Chopin Sonatas disc, there is only one near-perfect version--Ohlsson (Garrick Ohlsson - The Complete Chopin Piano Works Vol. 1 ~ Sonatas), with a reference First.

reviewText:
I've already alluded to these terrible performances in my review of his even more outrageously anemic performance in his Rachmaninov disc.  I don't know what to say.  What passionate fan of the piano oeuvre doesn't know The Tchaikovsy 1st (this review will focus on this since I really do not care for the Mendelssohn)? Having heard the Tchaikovsky hundreds of times, not always by choice, I regretfully admit that I know this piece like the back of my hand, every single note and chord.  How on earth can Lang Lang justify this pseudo-intellectual, pedantic, "I'm on valium" account?  This is a show piece, meant to be played to elicit excitement.  Pay attention to the tempo in the first movement, and you'll notice that it's 4-5 minutes longer than usual! 4-5 minutes longer in the first movement!

I challenge anyone to compare this recording to any number of Horowitz performances (particularly the legendary 1943 and the angry 1941), Argerich's, or Freire's, for example.  This isn't hard.  Go home, put the Lang Lang on, then immediately put the Argerich or the Horowitz on.  If you think Lang Lang's version is "legendary" like some have claimed but you want to know the truth, then you'll try this exercise.  If you can't handle to the truth, then you'll...well, you know very well this won't occur.  Same with his Islamey.

You have to understand that these works are show pieces.  Whether you like show pieces or not, you have to admit that you must fulfill the original intent of the works.  Islamey and the Tchaikovsky aren't profound pieces like Brahms or Busoni.  It won't make you learn something about yourself like Mahler or Bruckner.  It wasn't meant to learn something about nature like Beethoven's 6th.  They were composed for the sole purpose of being the virtuoso vehicle for the pianist.  So, why does Lang Lang play like they are works of Herman Hesse or Dostoevsky?  Why does he suck all life out and try to intellectualize it?  I was flipping through the channels and caught Lang Lang on the Tonight show, about 1/3 way into Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No2.  I remember asking myself, "How on earth can someone this bad get so much props?"  That night, he managed to something that is almost impossible--make the Hungarian Rhasophy No2 sound boring!

I'm not a religious person but I say a few prayers before I go to sleep.  I pray that Hamelin eventually gets his dues in this country.  I pray that Hyperion continues their trail blazing recording efforts, surviving the lawsuit by an imbecile musicologist.  I pray that record companies follow the the examples of Hyperion and Naxos, and record NEW music, and stop recording warhorses like Tchaikovsky or Rachmaninov concertos (except his 4th concerto).  Finally, I pray that record companies stop promoting average pianists like Lang Lang (no matter now their teachers are).

Lang Lang is a sign that classical music is in a bad shape.  Like Travis Bickle said in Taxi Driver, someday a real rain will come down and wash this all away.  I pray and pray every night that this will happen.  If it doesn't, I won't have anything to offer to my children.  How sad will that be?

reviewText:
Lou Reed is an punk/rock icon. Metallica is an influential rock band. They are also both known for performing with numerous other bands/artists with much success through the years (ie. Marianne Faithful, Bob Dylan, etc.). These are the simple facts so far. Now enter Lulu, a collaborative effort of said icon and influential band. One might expect a creation of pure strength and musical magic. This would be wrong.

Whether it is too much ego on one album, or the two sounds are just not meant to merge, Lulu is what one might call an epic fail. This is rather unfortunate, because both Lou Reed and Metallica are the best of the best, and together they should be unstoppable. Something happened along the way during the creation of this album. Their quest to be grittier and more raw turned into a seemingly pretentious mess, and is at times simply unlistenable. The barrage of noise and ridiculous lyrical banter melds together to create a sound that does not seem to have any audience. It is certainly not up to the iconic, influential standard that is expected.

The only redeemable, listenable song on the album is 'Iced Honey,' which is more in the rock-with-a-punk-edge direction one expects from the combo. It does have a nice beat and groove to it, and the lyrics aren't entirely obscure. Even at that, it is evident that Lou Reed's voice is not what it once was. True, it has never been a lyrical voice, but rather the rough punk voice that was just perfect for what he created. Sadly, it sounds too rough and abrasive to accomplish what he is trying to do now. As a band, Metallica did not do a bad job on Lulu. They do seem to be a backing band to Lou Reed's unfocused, delirious attempts, though. It feels as though the band is the afterthought, which may be a large part of the downfall of this effort.

It is proven here, that sometimes artists really want to work together, but just shouldn't. Epic collaborations can be magic. Or they can be Lulu- a disaster that is heartbreaking and saddening.

I was really anxious for October 9th and the release of "Monster". "No Filler" I've been reading about...then, I listened to it and after one pass, I thought, "Okay, that wasn't anything special." This one, accompanied by quite a bit of "It's their best album in years" hype, got me thinking that maybe this would be a "Creatures of the Night II." One bright note: "Eat Your Heart Out". I love this song. Most of the others just kind of blend together and are just ho-hum songs and what is with "Wall of Sound"? It's SO out of place.

This is not a "ZERO" star review, but I do give this release "ONE" star, for the one song I like and that there is nothing BAD (except, Wall of Sound) on the album, it's just another, "Been there - Heard that" from a band trying to relive some glory.

reviewText:
First of all I have to say that I was never gaga's BIGGEST fan. I always thought she was a bit over the top and just overrated.
However, there were always several songs from ALL of her previous albums that I loved, and still love to this day.
But upon hearing "Applause", I had a bad feeling about her upcoming album - and that bad feeling was right.
The first song on the album, "Aura"...I honestly can't even put into words what a mess it is. If it's supposed to be art, it's actually the farthest thing from it. This song actually makes me laugh because it is just so weird and..well...HORRIBLE.

You know I could go on and on about how atrocious this album is, but it would just be far too lengthy and I feel like I'd be wasting my time seeing as all her diehard fans will probably love this CD anyway.
But I will say this - I am a huge fan of all different types of music (especially EDM, which she made an absolute JOKE of on this album), but this CD has to be one of the WORST CDs I've heard in a very, VERY long time.
Have a listen for yourself if you don't believe me. I played some of the songs to friends and they all had the same reaction I did.

I can't even list a few songs that are highlights of the album because there literally are none.
But if I had to choose, I would say "Dope" and "Gypsy" are among the few decent songs.

**Last thing I would like to say - we all know what a mess Miley Cyrus has become these days...but I have her recent album as well, and I have to say that her CD "Bangerz" is honestly 100 times better than Gaga's "Artpop". I know, I know, it sounds hard to believe...but trust me, I would be the last person to give Miley Cyrus credit for anything these days. But if you're comparing the two CDs, "Bangerz" could win a Grammy.

WOULD IT MATTER IF THEY SOUNDED LIKE THIS CD IN CONCERT???

Dream Theater is my 6th favorite band and this pains me dearly...to have this done to the retail cd of this release just takes all their hard work and takes a big ---- on it. Very sad. When does the madness end? When will the powers that be turn the volume control knob back over to the listener?

This retail cd is completely BRICKWALLED...stripping it of any emotion, impact, and power. A complete shame and in-excuse-able with all of the knowledge now out there on this topic. Yet it continues through willful ignorance.

RECORD LABELS, SOUND ENGINEERS, AND PRODUCERS...IT'S TIME TO WAKE UP. LOUDER and compressed isn't getting it anymore. The bands also need to speak up. Dream Theater, honestly, do you like all your hard earned work to be in the end squashed down/whimpified and mastered for the teeny-bopper "I-everything" listener? Or do you want power and punch in your sound? Many listeners out there just do not understand this concept. A quick A/B would clarify.

When we can finally arrive at the point where us consumers can get PROPER MASTERING on the RETAIL, we can then proceed to the enjoyable task of discussing the actual music.

reviewText: Don't get me wrong, the first ten years of Jimmy's career was sheer genius.  Along with James Taylor, Gordon Lightfoot and Steely Dan, I cannot imagine any artist that can place you in a situation via song better than he.  He is sort of a Stephen King of music.  I would LOVE to give his first 10-15 albums five stars, but I can't because they still have yet to be remastered.  I have the original cd releases and they are no better than the ones available today.  The input is low and the sound is flat.  I imported them into a WAVE program and remastered them myself for my own listening, so I don't know why a more proficient engineer cannot do the same.  I have been awaiting the full remasters for nearly thirty years, and it is a shame that there aren't any at this point.  If you are starting your Buffet collection, by all means buy these; they are very cheap (in both senses of the word).  If you have the originals, try to be patient!

reviewText: Ringing? More like clunking. Way back in '56, Comden and Green sat down and wrote a musical for their chum Judy Holliday. The original recording---recently reissued with bonus tracks by Sony Legacy---is also a classic, and belongs in every show music library. This recording of the recently deceased Broadway revival does not. The music and lyrics are still wonderful and moving and funny, but star Faith Prince is cloying and charmless. Sorry, wrong number.

reviewText: As a die-hard Bryan Adams fan, I was very disappointed with this outing.  Without the input of Jim Vallance and Bob Clearmountain (song writers and producers of "reckless", "Cut's like a knife", etc.),  Adams song-writing has clearly gone down hill.  Klunkers such as "I  want to be your underwear" and "Black Pearl" are scrapings  from the bottom of the barrel.  "Mutt" Lange's finger-prints are  all over this album, from the corn-ball lyrics to the hackned riffs and  choruses.  Mutt produced one of the greatest albums in rock history, Def  Lep's Pyromania, but since has done nothing but trivialize the genre.  I'm  sorry, but this album lacks quality and substance.  The production is good,  though.  The vocals and guitar work are clear and crisp, also a Lange trade  mark.  I look forward to an Adams album when he's reunited with Vallance  and Clearmountain.

reviewText: Why sugarcoat it...this album is one of the worst records ever. Boston, who we all loved in 1976 with their debut, and 1978 follow-up Don't Look Back, got weird after that. They released their next 3 albums 8 years apart...a gap of 24 years for those counting. By this time, their fan base had long gone. Five years after their 2002 debacle Corporate America, lead singer Brad Delp committed suicide. Tom Scholz, the mastermind behind Boston, released this one last album in 2013 (I wonder why they didn't release it in 2010 to keep alive the 8-year interval streak). This album is even worse than Corporate America, the tunes aren't melodic, and don't rock. I tried to listen with an open mind, but listening to this album just made me want to reach for their first two albums to remind myself why I liked Boston in the first place. I suppose Boston may put out another album in 8 more years, but I'm not sure anyone would even notice. They shot themselves in the foot by waiting way too long after Don't Look Back, and have never scaled those heights again (even though Third Stage produced their only #1 hit, "Amanda," which is a nice song but nowhere near as well remembered as "More than a Feeling.")

But what's worse than 5 boring techno tracks with little samples of the original pasted on is the fact that the original version is not on here (though it is included on the UK release I think).  I thought it was being that one of the 'versions' was by Nine Inch Nails, assuming I did that if I didn't like the rest of the tracks I'd still have the original, but no.

reviewText: REM was a fine, albeit not great, group in the mid eighties to the early nineties (from Murmur to Automatic for the People).  Great artists know when to put the brush down, to put the final period on the short story, to stop writing songs once they become only a shadow of what they were once capable of creating.  Both U2 and REM have milked it for fifteen years, tbeir work becoming more tiresome with each new release (which regrettably do not sound new but like retreads - and flat, bald retreads at that).  Those who feel Led Zeppelin should have continued without Bonham, take heed.  Stipe's lyrics have always been dangerously close to mindless gibberish, but at least the music was good.  I wish they would stop tarnishing their image and give it up while their fans have enough good will to disregard the albums after Automatic - two more albums as weak as this one will bury any fond memories and make us believe that the early albums were flukes.  What is perhaps most eggregious is their attempting to resurrect their earlier style and plagiarize themselves for big bucks.

reviewText: If Paul Stanley's album was the best of the four simultaneously released solo efforts from Kiss in 1978, Gene Simmons' was without a doubt the worst - and the oddest. Calling in stacks of guest performers and musicians, he aims high at points, but ultimately the entire exercise flops like some sort of terrible expensive joke. Simmons' problem had always been his monotonous over-reliance on repetition in his song-writing - and it would continue to be throughout the career of Kiss. On this record, it is hard not to think that, if he had employed as many co-composers as he did performing guests, things might have been decidedly better. Sharing the same producer as Peter Criss' album - Sean Delaney - most of it sounds like the dregs of a Kiss album, including a redo of `See You in Your Dreams' from 1976's `Rock & Roll Over'. However, there are a few rather charming moments - all middle of the road or slow in style. `See You Tonight' is uncharacteristically tender and `Mr. Make Believe' - the best track on the album - is positively heart-rending. But the real eye opener is his cover of `When You Wish Upon A Star'. Disney-esque in approach, it is truly lovely and almost (but not quite) worth purchasing the CD just to own it.
label: negative

I never thought I would write this kinf of review for a Juno Reactor release, but this album is truly, TRULY terrible.  Were this released with a different band name I might have given a higher review.  I felt about the same way about this CD as I did with Future Sound of London's 'The Isness' - I wondered WTF I was listening to.  I kept thinking this can't be Juno Reactor.  There are lyrics... and they're really bad and really repetitive.  There's nothing but the same loop over and over in every song.  And they're boring loops.  This was until the last 2 songs which are way too awful for me to listen to ever again, especially the country & western bit at the end.

Ever since I heard Juno Reactor for the first time I was anxious for their new releases.  I rushed off to get Bible of Dreams as soon as it was released, and then every other JR work since, as soon as I could get my hands on the CDs.  Most of the time the efforts paid off.  Not this time.  I kinda wish I could get my money back.

There is one other thing that bothers me a little bit.  Two of the tracks were taken from a Matrix video game, and it seemed like there was no real work put into making them stand alone songs, unlike Labyrinth's remix of Mona Lisa Overdrive.

Overall, this was one of the biggest musical disappointments I've had.  Prodigy's last CD was painful, but this truly was a shot to the gut.  I hope JR gets back to what it does best.  Experimentation is good sometimes, but this was uncalled for.

Nice cover, though.

I haven't heard a decent musical project by Waters since he either left Pink Floyd or they bounced him (I believe it was the latter).
His voice sucks and his musical ideas are so mediocre - to be kind - and sometimes even bizarre as to make one realize that it was David Gilmour who was the big talent in Floyd.
Though it's true - to give the Devil (a word I think Gilmour would agree with) his due - Waters, whose self-centered nastiness alienated him from the rest of the band, once had a decent voice, it's long gone. It's painful to try to listen to him anymore.
I'd say that's a shame but he's so offensive as a person that I weep for him not.
Save your money. You'll be disappointed. Check out David Gilmour's albums - and the last Pink Floyd albums, without Waters. That's music.

reviewText:
Released in 2002, The Ozzman Cometh was the first compilation available to the mass public for Ozzy Osbourne's solo career and a reissue of 1997's The Ozzman Cometh featuring newly remastered tracks(That means it sucks!).
OK Ozzy, we get it! Just because you don't want to pay up to your original band members doesn't mean "Re-Recording" all of your  original albums  with new bandmates so you don't have to dole out a few dollars in the millions you have! And of course, Ozzy re-releases his Ozzman Cometh hit set because it contained the original songs, so he had to destroy all these songs for the new re-issue of the Ozzman Cometh with his incapable band. How the mighty have fallen! A combination of Black Sabbath and Ozzy Osbourne's solo career, this compilation spans over 20 years of material in 15 songs. Is 15 songs enough to cover one of the most popular heavy metal artists of all time? Read on to find out!
PROS-
IT'S OZZY YAY!- Ozzy is one of the most memorable Heavy Metal artists of all time, and this album has Ozzy on it. Therefore, that's all I have to say good about this album!
CONS-(PRE-HEATED TV DINNERS HAVE LESS THAN THIS)
-BLACK SABBATH MATERIAL IS SERIOUSLY MISJUDGED-If you are going to put Black Sabbath material on here, I think you would need more than three songs to do so. Ozzy made a serious error when he decided to put Black Sabbath material on here, as too many songs are missing, most notably "N.I.B.", "Iron Man", "The Wizard", and many more. If we wanted Black Sabbath, Ozzy, we wouldn't be looking here would we?!
-BLACK SABBATH MATERIAL SOUNDS TERRIBLE-For some reason, Ozzy decided to put the early "Basement Tape" versions of the first two Black Sabbath songs, and the sound quality is simply terrible. The only way you would get any enjoyment out of these songs is if you were seriously drunk or mentally challenged. The other Black Sabbath song, a live take on "Paranoid" from the album Tribute stands as one of the only good songs on The Ozzman Cometh.
-ALL THE TRACKS AREN'T EVEN THE ORIGINALS EXCEPT A SELECT FEW-All the songs from before the album No Rest For The Wicked are all new "Re-Mastered" versions Ozzy has done with his new band, so all the songs you hear are not the originals at all, but just a bunch of tribute songs! Also, No More Tears is edited for some unknown reason!
-THE LAST TWO TRACKS ARE NOT IMPRESSIVE- The previously unreleased track "Back On Earth" and "I Just Want You" from Ozzmosis catch Ozzy in his creative decline where guitars are less significant than the overdone synthesizers. I'm okay with synths, but Ozzy just way overdoes it. Not his best work!
-WHERE IS "FLYING HIGH AGAIN"?WTF!-Without a doubt, along with "Crazy Train", "Flying High Again" has to be my favorite Ozzy songs, and since it's a MAJOR radio staple its abscense here is unforgiveable, but at least you don't have to hear the terrible edited version of it!
-WHERE IS "I DON'T KNOW" AND "SHOT IN THE DARK"?WTF!-Without a doubt, "I Don't Know" and "Shot In the Dark" are two of Ozzy's biggest hits, so their abscense escapes reason! Why put "Goodbye To Romance" on here, which is not very famous, instead of the radio staple "I Don't Know"? The reason "Shot In the Dark" isn't on here is because Ozzy doesn't like the album Ultimate Sin, of which its from, but still it should be on a Greatest Hits package even if Ozzy doesn't like it!
-"I DON'T WANT TO CHANGE THE WORLD" LIVE ISN'T THAT GOOD!- Why put an inferior version of a good song? This version pales in comparison to the studio version off No More Tears, and I don't see why Ozzy makes us suffer through a live track!
-TOO EXPENSIVE!-Even if Amazon says it only costs 15 Dollars, at most stores this collection costs almost 20 Dollars, and that's a complete rip-off! For 15 terrible tracks, you shouldn't have to pay a rip-off price!
-SEEMS LIKE AN AFTERTHOUGHT COMPARED TO THE ESSENTIAL OZZY OSBOURNE!-That collection has a much better track list and it has the original recordings of all the songs, so The Ozzman Cometh is looks like dog crap in comparison! That collection is also much better, and will only cost you a few more dollars than this travesty!
Overall, this is a terrible compilation that only has about 4 tracks that have been unaltered, while all the rest have been changed and tainted with. Ommisions of songs like "I Don't Know", "Flying High Again", and "Shot In the Dark" make this collection incomplete, as those songs are some of his biggest hits. This was the first taste of Ozzy for me, and I almost didn't get any of his other stuff because this collection stunk so much. Thank god I picked up an original remastering of Blizzard of Ozz! Even the 1997 issue of The Ozzman Cometh is lacking, as it has "Shot In the Dark" yet doesn't have the other songs I wanted including "Miracle Man".
NOT RECOMMENDED! EVEN IF YOU ARE A CASUAL FAN, THIS COMPILATION IS TERRIBLE! IF YOU WANT TO GET INTO OZZY, BUY BLIZZARD OF OZZ OR DIARY OF A MADMAN, AS THOSE ARE MUCH BETTER STARTS THAN THIS CRAP! IF YOU REALLY ONLY WANT A GREATEST HITS PACKAGE, CHECK OUT THE ESSENTIAL OZZY OSBOURNE! DON'T GET THIS, BECAUSE I DON'T WANT YOU TO GET THE WRONG IMPRESSION OF OZZY LIKE I DID! Thanks for Reading!
label: negative

After being a huge fan of Ministry and almost all Industrial music for years, I am saddened to say that this album is atrocious.

I usually hate when musicians go on a political tear, and I had my fill with uncle Al's last three Anti George Bush albums (House of the Mole, Rio Grande Blood, and Last Sucker). They were decent in their own right, but a little too politically charged for me on the whole. Plus why now with the semi-new President in charge are people still not annoyed by his complete lies and non "magical" change for all of those who came out to support this great hope!?

I then find out that Ministry or Al with some friends at this point, is doing a new album! What do we get more of? Politically charged music...

The lyrics are very amateur and repetitive, the beats and music are also boring, and the Git up and vote song I had to shut off mid play, along with 99 percenters.

I understand that musicians are people too, and have their opinions. But when the music goes from angry metal with a cool message into a president or United States bashing I am out. If I wanted politics I would listen to the news. At least subtly throw the message in and surround it with thought provoking music and lyrics. This also goes for you Dave Mustaine, and Trent Reznor!

Sadly this album is a mess, with poor execution, horrible repetition, and a crap message IMO. This is not the Al/Ministry everyone came to know and love, he is too wrapped up in his political rants and has lost his edge. For anyone that was a fan of old Ministry, do yourself a favor and try to stop at House of the Mole or even Animositisomina.

reviewText: Tommy Shaw's vocal range and talent has never been in question. But why he felt the need to do bluegrass is interesting. Tommy bailed out of Styx because he didn't like the way DDY was trying different styles of music (Kilroy, more operatic themes, wonderful ballads) and stomped off, saying he just wanted to rock. And now HE wants to do something really different, saying that this bluegrass was inside of him, wanting to come out? I'm sure DDY felt the same way back in the day, but because Tommy refused to perform any music other than pure rock, it cost us one if the best bands from the 80s. Disappointed that TS couldn't appreciate this concept of trying new styles sooner. So here we are, TS can clearly leave rock and roll far behind and do something completely different. Thanks for at least realizing that there are many kinds of music, often found in many different singers, and to experiment with them is not a bad thing. Too bad the epiphany came so late. The voice is still good, but unfortunately the info above is all I can think about when I try to listen to this CD, and I just can't get behind it.

reviewText:
I have started working my way through the Hawk catalog in chronological order. The first 10 albums I've listened to have been really great, and I've rated all of them 5 stars except one which I gave 4, so this one came as a huge shock to me.

The music is beyond terrible. It is essentially strait ahead late 70's British heavy metal with no melody, no hooks, no power, and bloody awful singing...totally without redeeming value. Which is especially disappointing given the fantastic preceding 3 albums with Robert Calvert.

I've read that they were without a record deal at the time, and the only reason they got one from Bronze Records was because of the success of Motorhead. Gerry Bron of Bronze records reminisced, "I don't think we would have signed Hawkwind if it weren't for Motorhead, I can't say I was that interested." So I suppose it's not too surprising that Hawkwind ended up sounding like Motorhead wannabes on this album.

The mastering on the 2009 Cherry Hill/Atomhenge remaster is suitably dreadful. The 1992 Castle release if far far superior in every respect. The 09 version suffers from all the problems of a 'loudness war' remaster (google 'loudness war' for more info), including mastering induced distortion, zero dynamic range, and clipping. In addition, the 09 version has had the bass pumped up and it swamps the mids and highs. It is really disappointing, because the 3 or 4 other Cheery Hill remasters I've heard sound very good.

Recommendations:
Do not buy this record. And if you absolutely must, get the 1992 Castle cd.
label: negative

reviewText:
Once upon a time Ian Astbury and company built a legendary status that bridged the seemingly non traversable gap between alternative post punk and heavy metal. They did it with memorable hooks, a doors-like image and sound, and heaping helpings of word of mouth hype. They deserved all the accolades and attention they received, though most of the music press derided them mercilessly.

Now, 20 years or so later, we find most of the same players, with a bit more of their sound leaning towards the heavy metal side and less on the alternaive side, but sadly, very lacking in hooks and solid song writing.

The songs here all sound very pedestrian with simple, banal lyrics and no real memorable moments throughout the entire album. This sounds like a band cashing in with nothing but flash and no substance. Perhaps it's lack of substances (of the illegal variety) that has caused this band to lose their creative way. Now, while it must be said that the playing is first rate, Astbury's vocals are strong and still very accomplished, and the production and recording are first rate. But the songs are simply just not there.

Ironically, and perhaps fittingly so, the very best song only exists only on this special edition of this album. "Stand Alone" could qualify as the best choice for a single. It immediately inspires the listener to hear it again, with a soaring chorus and catchy melody. But nothing else truly stands out. "Dirty little rockstar is just embarrassing. Cliche filled lyrics, non creative guitar playing, uninspired aimless melody. The rest of the CD meanders without substance or character. Outststanding production and performances are literally wasted on some of the worst written songs you may ever hear. It's that bad.

So, along with some much older croakers: The Who (endless wire), The Stones (Bigger Bang) and Lou Reed, who actually has now recorded 2 of the worst albums of the decade (The Raven, and Hudson River meditations). The Cult with "Born into This" have joined the infamous few who have only succeeded in embarrassing themselves terribly with their most current releases. It's a shame really, because all listed here still possess some phenomenal talent, especially when witnessed live, but their most recent studio work is quite honestly, just abysmal.

As much as I wanted to like this and wished to be able to recommend it, it would be an unfair lie to those that are contemplating purchasing this CD. Spend your money on one of their many live CD's released last year. Or better yet, look into some really great studio releases from these newer groups: Doves, VHS or Beta, Spoon, Bellavista, Secret Machines, Interpol, Kings of Leon. All of whom have a somewhat derivative sound, but are writing some truly great songs, and sound many times more inspired than the old guard listed above.

reviewText: Six years of waiting and THIS is what we get? I am afraid Rush has gone the way of other great prog bands like Yes, Queensryche, and even recently Dream Theater (with their horrendous Six Degrees of Inner Turbulence). Rush, like these bands, has so far removed themselves from what made them great that they no longer resemble the brilliance or even the band they once were. Rush is my favorite band. Well they were until they released Presto, then Dream Theater took over. Ever since Presto, they have slowly started slipping down a slope. With Vapor Trails they have hit BOTTOM. This is the messiest, noisiest, nonsensical album I've heard in a long time.. let alone from Rush. Let's face it, a non-progressive/"mainstream" Rush is NOT a pleasant listen. Don't get me wrong, I don't need another 18 minute song like Hemispheres (although I LOVE that song and album), but man this album is BORING, sloppy, and WAY too heavy for Rush - Who told them they were good as a heavier band? They are not. Who is on the drums? Because that sure as hell can't be the mighty Neil Peart. Jesus, a 17 year old in his basement could do a better job on drums. I understand Neil had 2 huge tragedies and didn't play for awhile, but come on, he could do better than this! Geddy's melody lines have been suffering for about 10 years now. He's not singing anything even remotely catchy or pleasant. I know Geddy still has a LOT of his range still and yet he hasn't used it in years. And in the few moments he DOES hit some higher notes, he buries them in the mix or under those ultra-bland and annoying vocal harmonies he's become addicted to.  Also, his bass playing on this album is nothing. Period. Bass chords?!?! Who the hell wants to hear Geddy Lee playing CHORDS on the bass? And Alex has just plain forgotten how to solo. I haven't heard a good solo from him in I don't know how long. And on this album he isn't soloing AT ALL!!! Without Rush, Dream Theater(though DT still has time to recover), Yes, Queensryche, or any other truly great Prog band, where can we turn for great prog music?? I've always expected all other bands to let me down. And I was silently hoping after the past 4 let-downs from Rush that they would finally wise up and give us something brilliant. Well, they haven't. And now I have to admit that Rush is finally dead.

This twofer pairs two albums that, honestly, I have little use for.

It could just be me, I'm definitely a fan of the artistic peak of the Beach Boys rather than the hits stuff, but the whole "Party!" concept sits wrong with me.  The idea (if you don't know) was to record stripped back versions of songs like would be played at a party (acoustic guitars, hand drums, multiple lead vocals in sing-a-long fashion) and then add background noise to it to sound like a party.  The result?  Good performances are marred by background noise.

Mind you, I don't really feel there's many good peformances on the disc-- its all pop songs from the past few years, largelyfiller except a pretty fun version of "Tell Me Why" and a great "You've Got to Hide Your Love Away" by Dennis.

"Stack-O-Tracks" is interesting, conceptually-- Beach Boys songs without vocals, but largely unnecessary-- the better of the material is the Pet Sounds stuff, all available as backing tracks in the Pet Sounds Sessions box, the balance of it is a couple songs from "Wild Honey" ("Darlin' and "Wild Honey") and a bunch of older tunes, most of which lack the complex instrumental arrangements that were present on later Beach Boys albums.

Really only for completionists or anyone who would be interested in hearing the backing tracks isolated from the vocals.

reviewText:
Please keep in mind that Iron Maiden are my favourite band ever when reading this review.

It's bad enough that Maiden can't seem to be able to go a year or two without releasing a compilation of all their best material, but i didn't see THIS coming at all. Yes, it's great that for once, we have a remaster of the classics coming straight from the original master tapes, but that's immediately corrupted by them being picture discs. It's almost as if all the artwork and fancy design is the point, and the album itself is an afterthought.

I have the original NOTB picture disc, and the original Harvest Records vinyl, and the picture disc is just unlistenable. It sounds just like the painful to listen to 1998 remaster, if maybe even worse. In fact, this pic disc sounds slightly better than the original pic disc" Thankfully they didn't make the pivotal mistake of including Total Eclipse (one of only two Maiden songs I don't like), but problem is, this is just a bare improvement upon the original pic disc, and it ain't flattering.

Maiden's pic disc releases, in terms of sound, are hit and miss- Rock in Rio, DOTR, Flight 666, the compilations,  and The Final Frontier sound great! But everything else in the post 2000 catalog sounds awful on pic disc (especially AMOLAD- on CD it's one of the most handsome and brilliant sounding albums I've ever heard, on pic disc it sounds like Vlado Meller mastered it). And be it no surprise that this sounds... well, as expected, miss!

Look Rod, I love you and all, and I appreciate your trying to rectify the awfulness of the 1998 remasters. Even the 1987 discs, which obviously sound better, still have a small and slightly noticeable level of compression (they still have lots of dynamic range), but please give us CDs taken from the master tapes if you want to rectify the problem! Sure these discs sound better than the post 2000 catalog and the 1998 remasters but just barely, and the dynamic range is almost gone because of it.

Though I will say, thankfully we will be getting Maiden England this year finally after a 16 year wait on DVD and blu-ray, as Arry recently confirmed in a German iterview, and Arry is trying to reinstate the encores too. Let's hope, at least.

reviewText:
I won't comment on the actual music here - I love many of the songs and Jennifer's voice is absolutely spectacular, especially on "Tonight."

What I will comment on is the vinyl pressing.  While the songs themselves sound good, the pressing is the worst I've heard since mass market  labels were cranking out product in the mid-80s.  Simply put, it's rather noisy, with scratchy noise embedded directly into the clean grooves.  I scrubbed the record pristinely clean with the use of a highly regarded vacuum record cleaning machine with no change in the grunge and crud pressed directly into the album.

So while I doubt you'll hear the music sound better on any other format, when the songs get soft all you hear is crud, and between tracks it's shocking how bad a pressing this really is,

I may have been spoiled by listening to many audiophile 180 gram pressings lately, but this LP represents all that was wonderful and horrible about the LP era - great sound but it's apparent the record label just didn't give a flying fig about the quality of the vinyl they were turning out. Note this isn't the fault of the mastering, which is great, or the music, but of the plant cranking out the vinyl LPs.

In short, I'll have to buy the CD now and can say I've learned my lesson about buying vinyl on non-audiophile labels blind, even today when vinyl runs are so small the label could afford to turn out a quality product... if they really wanted to.

What happened to this band? I ask myself that question a lot lately. Shallow Life has a bit of the old Lacuna Coil 1999-2000 sound mashed with a little bit of techno-like mix, Linkin Park and an Alice and Chain chorus (Sung By Andrea in one song). The only trace of Karmacode in the album is in 'I Survive'.

It's obvious why the band made this album. This week they are #16 on the Billboard charts, smacked in the middle with pop tarts like Kelly Clarkson and Beyonce. Cristina posted on her myspace how she was dying to see the charts to see how the band did. She was more then happy with her #16 spot. This is the problem. The band no longer make music for the passion but for the profit. I never seen a band fall out of grace as hard as Lacuna Coil. The fact that they mocked Evanescence in a few interviews because of their popularity makes them hypocrites now. One thing is sure, The Open Door was as far from a commercial sounding album as a rock band can be and that album sold 5 million copies. Amy Lee didn't have to sell herself out. Nor have other bands like Within Temptation and The Gathering. All 3 bands have been true to their art and sold albums extremely well. Lacuna Coil should take notes.

There are only two good tracks on the album. Wide Awake and Oblivion.

Wide Awake is classic Lacuna Coil. Andrea doesn't even sing chorus, therefore the song is not ruined. Cristina's voice is wonderful on this one. The second best track is a song that's not even on the album. It's a B side called Oblivion. That song is also a classic Lacuna Coil song,
which gives me chills down my spine at how f*****ing beautiful it
is. Even Andrea doesn't sound so bad. The interplay between Cristina and Andrea is perfect which blends gorgeously with the music and lyrics. Very 'In a Reverie' dare I say.

The rest of the album is FAIL.

The lyrics are terrible. Appear to have been written by a 5 year old. The band said they wanted to write more direct less poetic lyrics for this album. They aced that with flying colors. They also aced with hiring one of the worst producers in music, Don Gilmore. A person who produces Avril Lavign and Linkin Park, jesus christ. With 'I'm Not Afraid', I felt like that song was a left over song from Linkin Park's first album.

The worst is 'I Like it'. I cringed and shook my head in disbelief when I heard it. If you thought 'Closer' from Karmacode was bad, get a load of 'I like it'. Sounds like a song penned by Demi Lavato, Avril or Ashley Simpson.

The rest of the album is so dull it's not worth mentioning. Same verse chorus, verse, bridge, verse, chorus, end technique. This band is pretty much done and over for me unless something miraculous happens on their next album. Maybe they'll go back to making REAL MUSIC and stop giving a s**** about $ and fame.

In the meantime, Flowing Tears 'They Kingdom Gone' and The Gathering's 'West Pole' is playing full blast on my stereo.
label: negative

Oh my worms, listening to this 1978 debut was a *nightmare*. Kate Bush sucked me in with her "Hounds of Love" LP first. Then a friend recommended "The Kick Inside" and that spewed me right back out.
Obviously, many enjoy this album; but let me warn you: it is NOT for everyone. All I heard were intolerably high pitch shrills and squealing of a talented young Irish bumpkin stuck in too-high a vocal range alongside dreadful songs with inconsequential piano music. It was extremely irritating to me (like nails on a chalkboard). I couldn't help but envision Kate as the old stereotype of the teenage girl singing near a pink, ruffled canopy bed, gazing out the window at horses in the foggy field, wondering what the outside world holds ... all while the hormones of insecurity explode through the music.  (Incidentally, I AM a fan of the shrills and sopranos and piano of bjork, elizabeth fraser & enya, suzanne ciani, respectively.)
Sadly, after listening to this I haven't searched further into Kate's repertoire pre-"Hounds of Love" in fear of touching on the sound of this CD again.

reviewText:
I'll make this quick.

Look, I own 1000s of CDs in my collection, and the 2009 Rolling Stones remasters are among the worst-sounding CDs I have ever heard. Obviously, the music is great on all of them, but the sound just sucks. Remastered? Try OVER-remastered, if that's possible. It is compressed, distorted, and edgy, none of the above things you want in a Stones album. If you have the 1990 Columbia pressing or the 1994 Virgin Records pressing, stick with that.

'Sticky Fingers' is worse than any of the other 2009 remasters. This actually may take the cake for the worst remaster/reissue I have ever heard. The organ on 'I Got the Blues' is just deafening. 'Can't You Hear Me Knocking' features a great saxophone/guitar interplay, but that now also sounds just grating. Everything has been mixed waaaay too high with these reissues. Shame on you, Polydor, for releasing these pieces of crap.

As I said above, don't sell your 1990 and/or 1994 CD pressing of this. This is one of the best albums ever made, and everyone should hear it in one format or another, but you wouldn't know it by this 2009 remaster. Dreadful, just dreadful. I sold my copy of it to my local record shop and made some good money for it. If you have this, I advise you do the same and use the money you make from selling this to buy a '90 or '94 pressing of this (if you don't have one already).

NOT RECOMMENDED.

reviewText:
When Angels and Serpents Dance is a blast from the past, and not in a good way; rather, more a fetid, stagnant rank draft of the nu-metal that so unfortunately ruled rock radio in the late `90s and the beginning of the new millennium. P.O.D. was the scene's resident Christian "rock" band, combining heavy bass, distorted riffs, and syncopated rhythms with singing/rapping about God, loving God, and finding God.

A short listen to When Angels and Serpents Dance finds that little has changed. The guitars are still defiantly de-tuned, the singing is still mostly consisted of screaming and angsty yelps, and the lyrics still sound like they come from a demented hymn.

"Addicted" rips off the chorus melody from their earlier hit "Alive" and sounds exactly like it could have come from 2000. "Shine With Me" contains such cringe-inducing lyrics as "shine with me like the beautiful star you are" and Bob Marley-esque sentiments like "one love." There's even a whole verse where vocalist Sonny Sandoval just sings "la la la la la la la," etc. Seriously.

The music is meat-and-potatoes rock pioneered by bands such as Nickelback and ape P.O.D.'s "influences" shamelessly: "Condescending sounds like Rage Against The Machine's "Killing in the Name Of" if written by a Christian band. The band's one exploration, the reggae-tinged "I'll Be Ready," is derailed by Sandoval's uninspired lyrics and fake-Jamaican accent. Simply put, those kinds of things just don't work.

The survey of Symphonies 88 - 92 set Haydn's cause back ten years Haydn: Symphonies Nos. 88-92; Sinfonia Concertante. I do not want to rest on my laurels here at SPECTRE but they continue to irradiate the composer in the minds of the public. Better still, at my behest Number 7 Trevor Pinnock and Number 13 Ton Koopman recently conducted the Berlin Philharmonic. In the old days under the successive 007s, such fixtures would never have occurred." Number 2 winced at this point. "Well done, Number 3. Even Mister Bigglesworth gets narky whenever I play your Haydn in the Bentley. We will now turn our attention to the Head of the Warsaw Station, Number 58." A youngish gentleman cleared his throat. "So Number 1, you have finally heard my performances of K 491 and K 467. What do you think?" Hogwood-Blofeld pursed his lips. "Number 58, I congratulate you for your clipped phrasing. It leaches so much of the vitality from the works. It's the hallmark of SPECTRE. I also appreciate the use of a solo violin in the first movement of K 491 when our enemies, following the score, use the full deck. Indeed, I had never heard it before. It was a triumph of miniaturisation." Number 1 placed his hand on a level. "Our expectations, however, were higher. SPECTRE is a fraternity whose strength lies in the integrity of its members." Mister Bigglesworth hissed at Number 58. "You played the entire first movement of K 491 at super pianissimo." The head of SPECTRE rumbled. "Not only is that hyper-romantic, it's also affected. We too have standards at SPECTRE. Romanticism also rears its ugly head in the slow movement of K 467. If you cannot decide whether you are for us or against us, it's time for you to go." The guitars growl and the drums snap and explode.  But the vocals are something else.  At first Justin Hawkins sets out upper mid-range akin to Steve Marriott then he kicks into a falsetto that makes the BeeGees reek of testosterone by comparison.  I can't get into it which is a shame since I like the songs.  I mean that falsetto puts me off so much that it ruins this record for me.
Maybe you'll like it.  But I doubt it.  Be forewarned!  If you have even inkling that this vocal style would annoy and bother you, stay away.  God bless the English.  They always come through in a pinch for us Yanks.  But this is a pint of ale I'll have to pass on.

reviewText:
Sunset Boulevard is certainly one of the best scores Andrew Lloyd Webber has ever written. The composer admitted that it was his wish for a long time to make a musical based on the 1950 classic movie directed by Billy Wilder. After the successful 1991 revival of Joseph and the amazing Technicolor dreamcoat, Webber began working on Sunset together with Don Black, his long-time lyricist on "Tell me on a Sunday" and "Aspects of love" and Trevor Nunn as a director.

 The plot concerns Norma Desmond, once a big silent movie star, who, after 20 years of being out of the picture business, still believes to be "the greatest star of all".  She accidentally meets a 20 years younger unemployed writer Joe Gillis, who grabs the opportunity to edit the script she wrote for her big comeback to the screen, even though he knows it will never happen. That fact is also evident to Norma's butler, Max, but none of them has the heart to tell her the truth. Eventually Joe becomes Norma's lover and uses all the benefits that a life with an elderly and a rich woman has to offer. In the end, when Norma finds out that Paramount won't shoot her script and that Joe is in love with a young girl, she shoots him. When the police arrive at her house on Sunset Blvd, she is in a world of her own, completely unaware of who or where she is, thinking that she is in the studio making her comeback movie and says to all that she is "ready for her close-up".  The plot itself is very beautiful and original, showing what can become of a human being when one can't deal with the rejection or acceptance of the present.

When it became known that Andrew Lloyd Webber is going to make the musical based on this classical film, almost every woman in show business wanted the role of Norma, from Angela Lansbury to Meryl Streep or Liza Minnelli. However, the honor went to Patti LuPone, who became well-known in the musical theatre after she played the lead in the Broadway production of Evita in 1979. She delivered a stunning performance at Webber's Sydmonton festival in 1992, refusing to use the book on the stage, which, together with her amazing vocal abilities, secured her the role. The contract was signed stipulating that LuPone will play Norma in London as well as on Broadway.

The show opened in July 1993 in London. The reviews were mixed, as they usually are, but LuPone was fantastic in the role, as well as was Kevin Anderson who played Joe Gillis and Daniel Benzali in the part of Max. The LA premiere followed in December with Glenn Close playing the lead and Alan Campbell as Joe, with George Hearn in the role of Max. Rumors started that Paramount, who was co-producing the show with Webber, wanted Close to reprise her role on Broadway. Webber kept repeating that LuPone will take her Norma to New York, but in the end he yielded to pressures and canceled LuPone's contract, making Glenn Close her replacement. LuPone sued him and won a hefty out of court settlement. And this is the main problem with this recording: Glenn Close is singing the lead. Singing it BADLY. Unfortunately, Ms. Close's vocal abilities are more than limited as this recording is proving: she is struggling all the way through; unable to hit the notes and find her voice. But that's not all. She decided to overcome the lack of a good voice by screaming and sobbing the dialogue parts. The result was anything but satisfying: she is totally unconvincing. Her stage presence may be strong, as seen in the Lloyd Webber's Royal Albert Hall DVD, but the bottom line is she doesn't have a singing voice and range. She won a Tony only because Broadway had no other new musical to compete in the 1994 season. Patti LuPone's performance on the London cast recording is quite the opposite: she has a beautiful voice that can sing properly all the notes as it were intended and acts the dialogue in a very subtle and persuasive way.  In other words, Patti gives an impression she IS Norma, while Ms. Close sounds as if she is acting it BADLY. The bad choice of the leading lady certainly didn't help the American premiere. It was probably one of the main reasons why the show didn't last too long on Broadway.

The same thing can be said for Alan Campbell, who plays Joe Gillis on this recording, as he suffers from the same lack of good singing, not like the original Joe, who is superbly portrayed on the London cast recording by Kevin Anderson. Judy Kuhn as Betty and George Hearn as Max are good, but I like their London counterparts better.

As far as the score, it is simply beautiful. The rich and lush melodies perfectly bring the old Hollywood alive, and jazzy threads work perfectly. The themes tend to repeat themselves, but that is almost a Lloyd Webber standard, and here they form a nice whole so you don't notice it much. The two big numbers, "With one look" and "As if we never said goodbye", performed by Norma, are pure gold. Other melodies include "The greatest star of all", sung by Max; "The perfect year", Norma's hail to the New Year; "Sunset Boulevard" in which Joe sings about her new life with Norma; "Too much in love to care", a beautiful duet between Betty and Joe and many more. The orchestrations on this recording, however, sound a bit metal to me and aren't as good as in the London recording. The material here is revised and some new passages are added, together with a new company number, called "Every movie is a circus".  The fact that this is a digitally remastered new release is not an important fact, due to the problems mentioned above.

The score here is complete but that is not much of an asset due to the lousy cast performing it. Therefore I would advise the potential buyers to skip this recording without thinking and purchase the original /world premiere/ London cast with Patti LuPone. That 2 CD recording has all the musical numbers and music, with an edited version of dialogue; just like the original recording of The phantom of the opera. . Only original recording will give you all the benefits of this show, while this one will only make you wonder.

Unless you are a die-hard Glenn Close fan, avoid this at all cost.

Ever listen to something that was about as fun as being stuck on the John (porcelain throne) for 3 hours? Well I think that accurately describes the experience of listening to this 1982 Rush album called Signals.

Fans can be convoluted sometimes. This is not a good album. The band members themselves hate it. It was SO AWFUL that immediately after this was released they fired Terry Brown, a man who had produced and crafted a wonderful relationship of 8 years and 8 studio albums with.

Reader be forewarned; my thoughts on this sonic bowel movement differs greatly from
the majority of reviews on this website. Come to think of it, I really don't understand how the majority of fans can honesty be handing out 4 and 5 star reviews to Signals. Something is awry here. Simple put, Signals is the first blunder Rush ever hatched. It's like a pile of fresh fecal matter after a bad meal that you were disappointed in and wished you just stayed away from. Unfortunately unlike fecal matter, this record will still be around. I don't know how on god's green earth they released something as magnificent sounding as Moving Pictures only 1 year prior, then release this P.O.S. Up until this point, Rush never put out anything that would be considered "unlistenable", however in 82 Rush surprised everyone when they released this god awful bowel movement from their musical bum-bums. The album cover art even depicts a dog going to the bathroom right on the front. I suppose that was an indicator for what would be inside...

So, what went wrong? I'll tell you what.

Ther4e are 2 big reasons why this record is so bad.

1) This has to be one of the worst 'sounding' albums that's ever graced my ears. And when I say sound I am strictly talking about the production/mixing here. After the first listen I though my CD was defective, literally. Every song on Signals has this awful fuzzed, washed over harsh feedback sound going for it. Nothing is clear sounding at all. Terry Brown MUST have been drunk or on serious illegal substances here, because he really dropped the ball in the knob twisting department. All of the instruments except for the vocals and keys are terrible under mixed, poor Alex is submerged in excessive  tasteless synthesizers because Geddy hasn't learned how to play them yet. Thank Jesus he took some lessons after this because his keyboards were much better on GUP.

So the record sounds like complete $ h ! t.

2) Lack of songwriting. I know most will think I am blaming Neal for this but I'm not really. The lyrics themselves are pretty good. Not his best but there are some literary jems in there like Subdivisions, The Weapon and Countdown. But on a sonic level the songs just sound boring. The arrangements just lack any sort of excitement and you just sooner wish then record end rather then listen to this $ hit. It's as if The boys just wanted to rest on their laurels with Moving Pictures and phone it in for the rest of their career. Way to be lazy guys....the hunger, creativity and passion you heard on 2112 and Permanent Waves is long gone. I'm serious here, couldn't they have tried a little harder? It's Rush after all, their smart guys and good with their tools I would of expected something better then turds like The Analog Kid Or Digital Man.

Simple put this record should have never existed. It's that bad. I find it crazy that this actually made it past a record company and made it to  music store shelves. Whats even more crazy is that it was put out by Rush. Thank Satan that they were able to recover and put out 2 great records after this (GUP and Power Windows) that would help deodorize the $ h i t stench left over from this disaster.

It's easy to forget now, but their albums were huge sellers in the 70's. 5 of their albums went to #1, so they were more than just a hit singles machine. This comp also overlooks the strong songwriting and contributions made by the non-McCartney members of Wings. Where is Jimmy McCulloch's Medicine Jar or Wino Junko? Where are Denny Laine's great songs like Time to Hide, Deliver Your Children, No Words, or Again and Again and Again? Or for that matter, some unreleased Wings tracks like Cage or Waterspout? There still is not a definitive Wings comp....probably never will be.

reviewText:
I was skeptical of this album for a long time considering the departure of singer extraordinaire Jorn Lande, but having heard and reasonably liked the lead single "Lost and Gone" . . . and having read review after review for this album being so supportive of the change---and positive overall---I finally said "what the heck" and picked it up.  What a mistake.  I should have stuck with my gut.

I want to make it clear I'm casting no aspersions on replacement singer, Mike Dimeo.  While he's no Lande, he is in fact a very talented vocalist, and he's similar enough in style and delivery to Lande that he could have made a completely acceptable replacement.  This album's failure certainly isn't his vocals.  For one thing, the vocals are mixed too low and in a couple spots are almost inaudible . . . it's as if the band said to themselves: if you can't really hear the vocals, but what you do hear sounds close enough to Jorn, then maybe no one will notice the difference.

Beyond that, the songs on this album are just sloppy, under-developed attempts to recreate the first Masterplan album (which to me was perhaps a little heavier but inferior song-wise, and with a more dated, stuck-in-the-80's sound than the excellent Aeronautics . . . which in contrast successfully captured an 80's and classic rock vibe yet still very much sounds like a 21st century record).  The songwriting on MK II is just lackluster, throwback Euro hard rock by-the-numbers, with a few virtually pointless, meandering instrumental breaks thrown in to add some measure of a "prog" element.  In particular, Grapow seems to lose control of some of his solos (and I like him as a guitarist) with frantic, speed licks that go off-key and at times are altogether out of synch with the rhythm of the song.

Worse are the lyrics.  Again, I almost feel as though the band hoped you didn't pay much attention to the vocals other than to perceive enough of a superficial resemblance to Lande that you would just nod and smile and move on.  While Lande's lyrics certainly contain their share of shameless "Whitesnake-isms", they at least convey enough of a coherent theme or narrative to make logical sense and communicate some tangible emotion.  The lyrics here are just a completely random string of every 80's hard rock/metal cliche you've ever heard.  They don't even seem to make sense in many cases.

All in all I was sorely disappointed in this album, and frankly I felt duped by all of the supportive reviews that promised quality close to that of the previous releases.  Bottom line: the songwriting spark that Grapow, Kusch, and Lande brought to Masterplan collectively is completely lacking here.  And despite the debate over the relatively  heavier, more metallic attack of the debut album vs. the slightly more catchy, song-oriented approach of Aeronautics, the fact is Jorn Lande and the vocals overall were the driving force of this band.  If the band had embraced that notion and actually took the risk of letting Dimeo step to the forefront on MK II, perhaps they would have created something with similar appeal.  Alas, they played it safe, de-emphasized the vocals, and just shot for enough of a sound-alike approach to get by.  The result is a well produced (except for the vocal level), mostly well played, but utterly empty pastiche.  Too bad; this band was on its way to greatness before this woefully self-conscious misstep.  Perhaps they'll pull it together for their next release.  This one left a bad taste, but not so much that I won't give the next one a chance.
label: negative

Judging by the fairly positive response this CD's gotten here so far I'll assume this CD's par for the course for this band, but I found it incredibly boring. One low to mid-tempo track follows another for the entire CD...they all sound the same, they all lack any sort of hook, and all lack any excitement whatsoever. It's the type of CD where after listening for a while you'll forget you even had it on.

Soul Meets Body was easily one of the best songs I'd ever heard, and yet still I didn't buy Plans, the CD that was on. Determined not to make that mistake again, I checked out this CD, Narrow Stairs, after LIKING (but not loving) the single I Will Possess Your Heart (the long intro's really the only thing that makes the song stand out)...unfortunately, even that "good" song isn't matched by anything else on this CD.

The only tolerable songs on it were, of course, the 1st single I Will Possess Your Heart (what a surprise that it's much faster and more melodic than...anything else on the CD) Bixby Canyon Bridge (incredibly annoying outro aside,) and Your New Twin Sized Bed. That's it. After several listens those are the only songs that stood out in any way for me, those are the only ones that seem to do anything but drone on and on.

Obviously if you're a fan of this band you should know what to expect. New listeners who haven't owned one of Death Cab's CD's before should be warned, however. Personally, I'm getting tired of bands creating very misleading 1st singles that sound nothing like the rest of the CD...it's CD's like Narrow Stairs that explain why so many people today illegally download music.
