reviewText:
If you're looking for good Aftermath-produced or G-Unit affiliated music, here's which artists to go to and which to stay far, far away from:

50 Cent-- Go nowhere near The Massacre. You're 5% more likely to suffer a slow, painful death just by touching the case. It is the worst CD you could possibly ever hear. Same thing goes with the movie soundtrack.

Get Rich or Die Tryin (the original) on the other hand, is solid... especially on those bonus tracks (Heaven, Life on the Line, U Not Like Me), Patiently Waiting, 21 Questions, and anything featuring another G-Unit member. PIMP, with its lack of Snoop Dogg (which the music video seemed to promise), High All the Time, Many Men, and Wanksta can kind of get old though.

The thing about 50 Cent these days is that by himself he is no longer any good at all. He needs to be held up by a crutch of some better rapper before he can make good with his own rap. The reason he succeeds so well in his collaborations with The Game in The Documentary and Eminem in The Re-Up is because he has actually GOOD rappers holding him up. He's like the Abbott of the comedians Abbott & Costello now. He has nothing worth contributing without his Costello of some kind to be there for him.

The Game-- As soon as I heard this guy's album and compared it to 50's Massacre, I knew that if G-Unit was going anywhere, this guy would be the one to take it there. And now it turns out he left. Can't blame him when the clique-label's leader is so dumb. Was the most progressive rapper of the crew, and his reason for leaving is probably because of how anti-progressive 50's Massacre was. Has the best, deepest subject matter within his songs, if not the best flow (Although his underground 300 Bars song would automatically crown him king if he did that well all the time on his main albums). As far as the mainstream and not underground CDs go though, I'd give him a 2nd best for flow of the G-Unit crew.

His Documentary album has been called the third Chronic, and has the best of Dre's beats you'll find on any G-Unit CD. Criticisms are that he name-drops Dre & NWA a bit too much, but overall, I think it's not that big of a deal. He's a big hip-hop history fan, and he's still a little starstruck over the chance of being able to work with Dre. Given a very brief profile of the rapper, he fits into an uncomfartable stereotype, (average-looking rapper from Compton who's been shot a few times), but he immediately carves a personality of his own in the Doctor's Advocate and his even better The Documentary.

Young Buck-- I'd say probably the best G-Unit member still in G-Unit. This guy has the best flow, as far as mainstream CDs are concerned. He also seems to be the 2nd-most concerned about the world (a.k.a. 'progressive'), with references to the Illuminati amongst other secret organizations. I like this guy the best of the remaining G-Unit. 2nd best comes sort of close to him, but still doesn't match Buck's raw skills.

Lloyd Banks-- This guy is second best. His flow skills somewhat tie for 2nd place with The Game's, or at least land in that area. He, Buck, and The Game are my top three for G-Unit (even though The Game's not G-Unit anymore). Anybody else you can probably pass up. I'll go over them real quick just to make sure you know who the others are beforehand.

Tony Yayo-- The one male member who is worse than 50 Cent. In the G-Unit CD, they always shouted 'Free Yayo!' and now he is free. The G-Unit had done a terrible thing by campaigning for his release. His is of no benefit whatsoever to them. He might even be responsible for the gradual dumbening of 50's style & outlook on life.

Joe-- The kind of R&B star you'd expect to sing chorus or backup on an Outkast track, mixed with a bit of R. Kelley and a very small splash of Stevie W. He's not bad I guess. I hated him completely on 'Wanna Get to Know You' of the G-Unit CD, but would definitely still listen to his 'Ride Wit U' track off his own solo album.

Olivia-- Pssh, are you dumb? No. She's partially responsible for Candy Shop. That should be reason enough to hate her full-on and never turn back. She kind of can't sing either. Bad move to make an R&B CD without being able to sing, I think.

Lil' Scrappy-- This is the same Lil' Scrappy you heard on Lil' Jon's "What U Gon Do?" track. He's pretty good. Decent at least. Definitely not as decent as 50 Cent's original Get Rich or Die Tryin, but decent. He's got a good enough style though that places him above everyone else still in G-Unit, excluding Lloyd Banks and Young Buck, but including 50 Cent by himself.

I think that's everybody. So... now you know all about G-Unit, and who's good and who's not. If you HAVE to buy G-Unit, now you know who to avoid and who to embrace. If you plan on buying the original Get Rich or Die Tryin, I suggest you don't. Burn it, or have a friend burn it for you. 50 doesn't need the money right now or ever again. If you decide not to buy G-Unit, then more power to you. The Game is actually now sort of the anti-G-Unit since he left, because, you know, the majority of their members still suck.

I'd suggest Mos Def's Black on Both Sides instead of any of this stuff though... even if you were planning on buying G-Unit. That's probably the best hip-hop album I've ever heard, or will hear.
label: negative

reviewText:
First of all,I LOVE MARY J. BLIGE!
She is a legend in modern terms. I mean no one gets realer or grittier than Mary! The word incredible is an understatement.
Mary's two masterpieces-all of her albums are above average-BUT
1994's "My Life" and especially 1999's "Mary" really show whose Queen showcases a woman who was looking for serenity but just couldn't grasp it.
So when Mary released "No More Drama",her fifth studio albums in
nine years,everyone finally thought that the Queen of Hip Hop Soul
finally found the happiness she so deserved. Well,Mary was getting things together BUT her material was unraveling.
"No More Drama"-the original issue-was very unsatisying.
There was so much filler on that album and undercooked songs that
I couldn't believe that Mary J. Blige-the Queen herself-would dare release such a half-done sounding album. Save for the emotional
Jimmy Jam & Terry Lewis produced title track,"Where I've Been"-
featuring Eve,and a couple more tracks(the brutally honest "PMS";"Steal Away";the overplayed "Family Affair"),"N.M.D." wasn't cutting it.
Happily in early '02,Mary and her label,MCA,decided to reissue
"N.M.D." "Yes",I thought. Finally we get the Mary that all we know and love. Not really,"NMD"'s reissue has the same
borderline tracks and to cover it up,her label added four new bonus tracks not added on the original issue(two unreleased songs
and two remixes of the original "NMD" tracks "No More Drama"
and "Keep It Movin'").
The two new tracks are very intesting."Rainy Days" featuring current radio darling Ja Rule,is the type of material that does nothing for Mary. It's obvious the folks at the label felt that
having a currently popular radio-friendly artist like Ja Rule
would make the song an unabased hit a la Ja's collabrations
with Jennifer Lopez("I'm Real","Ain't It Funny":both hit #1).
BUT hello!,Mary is not "J.Lo"!She is  a true artist. Mary is a grade-A vocalist. She's almost on the save level of Aretha Franklin(if not already there),she needs songs that move. Not generic chart stabs like this. That may work for a heavily glossy
packaged "act" like Lopez but when it comes to Mary,you better do better than that!!
BUT "He Don't Think I Know"-the other unreleased new track-is more like it. A wistful,compassinate ballad that sounds like something that could've come from the "Mary" album. THIS is
the Mary we know and love. Why wasn't this on the original anyway?
I mean I know the album was supposed to be "No More Drama"
but if "Drama" sounds this good,then bring on the drama.
The two remixes are OK.Mary and her former muse,Puff/P. Diddy,
reunite on a remix of "No More Drama" and Common blesses a new mix of "Keep It Movin'".Not bad.
I'm a Mary fan. But hopefully the next album will be the Mary that
we all know and love. No more drama or not.

reviewText:
I guess this is the "best" of Bon Jovi in the sense that it includes many of his and his band's big hits and covers various points in their career. That said, I have a couple of problems with this collection. One -- and I know this is subjective -- is that it doesn't necessarily contain the songs that I personally think are his best. In fact, my favorite Bon Jovi track -- the solo hit "Midnight in Chelsea" -- is missing.

The bigger problem, though, is that Bon Jovi's music in general is incredibly pedestrian, VASTLY overrated mall rock. I'm not saying that everything has to be Chopin, Rodgers & Hammerstein or The Beatles, by the way; there is definitely a place in this world for mall rock. But if that's what you're into, there are better places to look -- Def Leppard, to name one. Jon Bon Jovi is a pretty awful writer and an even worse singer. One of the reasons I like "Midnight in Chelsea" is because his singing on that tune is uncharacteristically restrained. Usually, his vocals are heavy-handed. As for his writing.... I think back to a review I read in Rolling Stone years ago that started out by asking, "How many rock and roll cliches can you string together into a single song? Not as many as Jon Bon Jovi can." Truer word was never written. It's as if this guy has never had an original idea in his life! Even the TITLES of his songs are often stolen from other musicians. "I'll Sleep When I'm Dead" (not included here) was stolen from the late, great Warren Zevon, and "It's My Life" was stolen from Talk Talk.

If we're going to be honest, there are two big reasons that Jon Bon Jovi has a career: his looks and his lineage. He's obviously a good-looking guy who's aged well and who appeals to the ladies. And his uncle was a successful producer. If you took these two things away, Bon Jovi's career would have been much more on the level of Jackyl or maybe Warrant at best. I know he wants to be taken seriously as an artist --  to be mentioned in the same breath as Bruce Springsteen -- but outside of being from New Jersey, these two guys have almost nothing in common. Springsteen can write, play and sing (not to mention he's a great live performer).  Jon Bon Jovi can't really do any of those. He just might be the most overrated man in rock and roll.
label: negative

reviewText:
If 1993 had Snoop Doggy Dogg, 1998 had DMX and 2003 had 50 Cent, then 2009-10 had Drake: The heavily saturated newcomer with mountains of industry-manufactured hype. Except the Toronto native born Aubrey Graham already had the profile of a superstar a year before the release of his debut album (national ad campaigns; several hits on commercial radio; magazine covers; mountains of press).

That a rapper like Drake is taken seriously in 2010 says a lot about the state of (mainstream) hip hop because to put it quite bluntly, his official debut album, Thank Me Later, is god-awful. Damn near unlistenable to these ears. Why?

*sigh* Where do I start?

Maybe it's the annoying, fake Southern accent he raps with, sounding like a white prep school kid doing his best Lil' Wayne impersonation? Straight up, this guy sounds like Jamie Kennedy doing a bad Memphis accent when he raps.

Maybe it's the hilarious (auto-tune aided) attempts at crooning? What's worst is that the majority of TML is actually comprised of this haphazard attempt at singing! When I first heard the single "Find Your Love", I honestly thought I was listening to an amateur 'boy band'....the flat in-the-shower singing; cheesy mid '90s Euro synths; cornball hook...and he's not trying to be ironic!

Maybe it's the drowsy, samey downbeat production that makes most of the tracks sound indistinguishable from each other?

Maybe it's the annoying and immature self-importance that shrouds the album? Drake comes across as a sheltered, pretentious, pampered white school kid who thinks that his (rather insignificant) thoughts are somehow profound when they're actually fairly vapid, dull and common.

Maybe it's the sheer corniness that is obviously just Drake's nature? The painfully corny punch lines, the phony "emotionalism", the wimpy lyrics. Hip hop is a style that's known for it's sheer swagger. This man has absolutely NONE.

All of these above reasons makes me scratch my head not at Drake's massive current popularity (he was shoved down the public's throats and the American public, by large, practices groupthink-questioning or deviating from the established common consensus is discouraged) but by the fact that many hip hop heads actually take him seriously. It's amazing that MC Hammer was seen as a dancing sell-out 20 years ago or that even a party rapper like Coolio was dismissed in hip hop circles two decades ago yet in 2010, a (bad) singing, unapologetically corny former teen actor who makes dour pop music is called the "future of hip hop" by some. Sign of the times, indeed. It confirms that hip hop's interest is now 100% corporate.

Thank Me Later is pure product and not a very good one at that. It sounds like a even duller, lamer fusion of 808s and Heartbreak (which this album's approach, like Kid Cudi's similarly awful debut, is based on, even by Drake's admission), British R&B/pop dullard Craig David and the Backstreet Boys. Except even cornier. Will the same bandwagoners who currently sing his praises be bumping this album in 2 years? We all know the answer to that question.

Instead of drinking the (dying) music industry's Kool-Aid, check out REAL emerging young rappers like Jay Electronica, J. Cole, Fashawn, Blu, Nipsey Hussle, Curren$y and B.O.B. (whose poppy major label debut, while not bad, doesn't display his full rhyme genius).
label: negative

reviewText:
To spice it up, I'm going to make my review into a story.  Gather around children.

Long ago when the CD first came out AOL offered a free download of Ohio Is For Lovers.  I seemed drawn to the title as it reminded me of commercials for the state of Virginia.  So, I downloaded it.  The thing is that I seriously thought it was a joke.  It didn't even register in my head as an actual song, I thought Hawthorne Heights was perhaps the best joke band ever.  Now, you must remember at this point in time they didn't have groupies or fans or whatever so there was nobody around to correct me.  I have to admit, that song was hella catchy, so when I saw the Hawthorne Heights CD in a dark, dank, corner of my local Sam Goody I just giggiled.  "Oh look it's that band."

I picked up the CD.  Suddenly I felt a sense of evil and dread.  At this point I know everyone thinks I am joking, but trust me, I'm not.  As I further examined I started to have doubts about my joke band theory.  Something in the cover art told me that they seriously must have thought they were somekind of emo prophets.  I shuddered and the rest of the day sat in my room and thought to myself, "Are they really serious?  No way, it HAS to be a joke."

Time passed and for the most part I completely forgot about their existence.  Until MTV found them.  Before I knew it Hawthorne Heights t-shirts were spread around the school like the plague.  It is at this point I was sure that emo had hit critical mass.

Now in 2006, I still have to sit through the deep discussions on Hawthorne Heights "meaningful lyrics".  When they came to town on tour I recall the guy sitting next to me beam with excitement at the prospect of going to the concert. "I get to go see Hawthorne Heights!"

After throwing up a little in my mouth I drew the following conclusions:

Hawthorne Heights is quite possibly the worst band in the world, but have mastered the art of subliminal messages.  They can somehow speak to the mindless masses in ways I don't yet understand, but above all else.  They must be stopped.

reviewText:
There is indeed a mystery that surrounds this project: what was Mickey thinking?!?!?! I first want to establish that Mickey Hart is one of my heroes; I've seen him live in various incarnations and I have all of his recorded releases. Now that I've set down my credentials, I can write that this is Hart's worst album. Beyond weak songwriting, the Mystery Box sound is sickeningly conventional. I would only expect this recording to appeal to 16 year girls on Long Island circa 1994. This misadventure occurred despite good ingredients and a decent recipe. The project included Robert Hunter, Zakir Hussain and conguero Giovanni Hidalgo. The Mint Juleps sing well. Beyond these qualities, the Mystery Box was a genuinely unique project for Hart. Moreover, the idea of a pop crossover in itself wasn't a bad idea -it just didn't work in this situation. So what went wrong? That's the mystery! Now if I could only find that darn box, the answer to this enigma may be inside.

Before me, all other critiques gave this outcast of the Rykodisc family five stars. It's laughable that listeners put this on the same level with the Grateful Dead's "American Beauty," and the Beatles' "Sgt. Pepper's." These reviewers are either teenyboppers (you guessed it, from Long Island, NY) or they're being way too generous, awarding five stars just because it's Mickey. At the time of review, about a dozen copies of this potential beverage coaster could be purchased for less a buck through Amazon's marketplace sellers. Why? The answer to that is no mystery.

Yundi Li's performance was uninteresting and empty. His pianism also had very little to offer - no touch, no pianissimo, poor pedaling (dry or total blur), in cords he hears only tops and basses, no sense of musical time - he often breaks it without reason - and there was no vision of structure of the piece, otherwise the tempos in the score would have been respected (after all Liszt was not an idiot and knew what HE wanted to say). I don't even mention the dramaturgy of this masterpiece, it would be too much to ask...
I wish people stop react on names and trust more their own senses. This pianist's success is clearly all about marketing.

reviewText:
Firstly, I have to say that I have lot of respect for Reznor and Ross and I have nothing against Mariqueen. This is nothing personal, just a review of this particular album, so if you're one of those people who looks at the rating and then feels it necessary to comment with a bunch of immature nonsense, don't bother. Also, I want to note that I would like to give this album a 1.5/5 review, but Amazon won't let me.

I can't believe how many people have been referring to this album and the EP preceding it as "improvement". With the exception of a few musical elements on no more than three tracks, there is nothing on this record that stands out or conveys any point at all (at least in my opinion).

I thought the last EP was "average". Never felt it was good, never felt it was bad, and almost all of it was weighed down by one track. It is incredible how much your opinion can change with the rest of the album. For starters, musically this is hit and miss - mostly miss. Some of the percussion on "And The Sky Began To Scream" is appealing and pretty much all of Ige Age sounds nice. Pads towards the end of "How Long?" are interesting. It's not up to Reznor or Ross standards but it's not bad...on those tracks. This record will have a pattern where there's a track that's real nicely layered, with detailed sample work and a nice atmosphere, and then the next track has percussion that sounds like it was made in FL Studio out of stock samples taken from an old drum machine. Same goes for melody, you'll get some really nice leads and backing pads, and then the next track will be something that sounds utterly broken. Not broken in a good way like an old Skinny Puppy album or the like, broken like sine waves being randomly thrown in at intervals of the beat, completely dissonant, with no structure or build ahead of that dissonance to give it any context at all. Both the intro and outro are excruciatingly weak, especially the outro. It's 7 or so minutes of a repeating, uninteresting beat, with some piano notes, as a "The Frail"-esque ambient background comes in along with a few other backing sounds-and that's it. Nothing we've not heard before, in much better form from Reznor. That's what's so funny about all the people going "if you're looking for an NIN sound, you won't find it here". The album actually retains TOO MUCH of an NIN sound and because of that it comes off musically as a combination of Year Zero, Ghosts and the first HTDA EP, except being weaker than all three.

Now, let's get on to the biggest issue of this album: the lyrics (and I mean the lyrics themselves, many people will complain about the sound of Mariqueen's vocals but honestly that bothers me much less than what she's actually saying). Jesus Christ, they sound like they were written by a 12 year old. He's not by any means an amazing lyricist but there's no way Reznor wrote these. Lines like "the more we change, everything stays the same", "the beginning is the end" and "how long can we keep holding on" frequent the album. The former is expressed more than once, another example is Ice Age - "I find it looks the same but everything has changed"...except now they totally contradict each other. Here's some more:

"Worn the skin off both my knees
Waited oh so patiently
Staring straight into the sun
Never thought you would've come

No, no
No, no
No, no

Somewhere sits an empty throne
Like we've always kind of known
Variations on a theme
And the sky began to scream"

It's seriously hard to even get through the tracks without cringing. It almost seems like they were written with literally the most vague of ideas, with word choice adhering to the most basic rhyme schemes possible, without being revised even once.

Take all of these issues and wrap them up in an album complete with that pretentious "Hey Look we're choosing to puNctuate this HOW we want to_____" stylization on the titles (WHICH ARE INCLUDED IN THE ID3 TAGS!) and you have Welcome Oblivion.

I had a lot of hope for this band. A lot. I've listened to this thing many times since it was first available on Pitchfork's Advance service and now in lossless quality. It has not grown on me. I have appreciated, to some degree, all of Ross and Reznor's work in NIN, the soundtracks and HTDA's EPs to some degree, but I just can't appreciate this. If it were completely instrumental it would be better, but even still just average at that. There's a lot of things they could have done to make HTDA its own thing and not have it sound like NIN. They could have dabbled into IDM territory. They could have aimed for a more organic sound. Hell, they could have gone Throbbing Gristle style and decided to make some actual industrial music since NIN gets so much flak for being called inappropriately called industrial. What they did was none of these things, and I honestly would say that this sits fairly below "Things Falling Apart" quality in the scope of Reznor's work. I tried to enjoy it, but I just have to be honest. I hope that whatever he works on in the future will not be in this sort of style again.
label: negative

reviewText:
Ive been an Otep fan since their first release, but I have noticed that their last couple of releases are lacking imagination....and honestly....creativity.  Atavist takes this dilemma to a whole new level.  It essentially buys into the argument that "heavier" must equal "better."

Two of the tracks on this album are 5+ minute spoken word ensembles.  They are 100% filler material.  Suggestion:  Publish a book of poetry.  The first track is all instrumental.  So that leaves you with 9 tracks.  The last track is a Doors cover and if you've never cared for the Doors music, then this isn't going to do anything for you either.  So now we are down to 8 tracks.

"Remember to Forget" has almost the same exact riff as "Blood of Saints" - it almost makes you wonder if the songs were originally combined at one point.  The vocal delivery is as you would expect.  The lyrics are very tired.  It's quite obvious that Otep has a very limited vocabulary and repeats the same phrases over and over again.  Yes, we get it - Otep is proud to be gay and hates republicans, is this all you have to say?

The bright spots on this album are "We Dream Like Lions" and "Blood of Saints".  "Lions" is an acoustic song that's well-written and shows what can happen when you think more about writing songs that are good versus writing songs that are strictly moshpit material.  "Blood of Saints" has some great riffs and vocal work in it - pretty catchy.

The rest of the album reminds me of the metalcore genre.  Songs that never really fully form, feel forced, and get repetitious mid-way through the album.

This is by far Otep's worst album.  Which is unfortunate since she appears to have so much potential.

Perhaps this is another casualty of an artist who's more obsessed about making political points than actually writing good music?

Let's all be as real as we possibly can be and face the truth...after grunge populated the airwaves and then suddenly vanished, those corporations that made millions of dollars off of the angst-filled population of our world scampered left and right to try to fill the void, and their wallets again.

Enter a host of bands that sound suspiciously similar to many of the early 90's bands, only newer sounding.

Enter Godsmack, a sort of heavy metal band that borders more on a heavier version of the commerical sound that Metallica refined. Dark, brooding is the general feeling of this bands music, and while very catchy and enjoyable as "radio" music can be, its hardly satisfying and gets rather repetitive really fast.

Bands like Godsmack, are like fast food. It sure tastes good, its fast, its there in an instant. But there is no nutritional value inherent in the goods, and it really only serves to temporarily satisfy you, though it rarely does.  There are hundreds of these bands, they crop up everyday. Where they come from, is anyones guess...

In the end, like fast food, this music makes you fat and bloated and sick - metaphorically, people. It poisons your mind and warps your vision of what amazing art and entertainment COULD be.

What I am trying to say, is that while Godsmack's debut has songs that many "angry" youths and misguided adults will enjoy and TOTALLY relate to, it serves as a brief relief from an eternal hunger for something more filling, more healthy.

reviewText:
Since the Baroque era, the violin has been one of the most important of all Western instruments - for several reasons. The tone of the violin stands out above other instruments, making it appropriate for playing a melody line and, in the right hands, the violin is extremely agile - able to execute rapid and difficult sequences of notes.  Contemporary music still embraces the violin - in sometimes new and sometimes exciting contexts - Tracy Bonham, Miri Ben Ari, Arcade Fire, Dave Matthews Band, Yellowcard...

This particular album of mostly rock tracks (or rocked-up classical compositions) with solo violin and a rock-band-augmented-backing-orchestra results in something that might be amusing as an unexpected encore at the symphony or as a novelty act in Vegas or on a television variety show. It's more gimmick than any sort of crossover genius.

I'm not knocking David Garrett's skills on the violin, but this project was poorly executed.  Several of these tracks are not well suited for solo violin and those that are feel more like muzak due to heartless backing instrumentation.  This is not so much the case on his earlier albums - the eponymous "David Garrett" album is a better executed set of rock/pop songs with classics mixed in to better effect.

I've listened to the entire album, not just the clips here.  There was potential in spots to do something really interesting...  but often I just cringed when the violin came in to awkwardly take the melody.

I'd hoped Orianthi's guitar contribution on "Walk This Way" would have been more substantial - perhaps "dueling strings"or some sort of counterpoint, echoing the groundbreaking crossover nature of the Run DMC / Aerosmith version.

A good mashup usually makes you go "Wow, how could A possibly go with B?  That sounds crazy/awesome!" - In that vein, I wish "Vivaldi vs. Vertigo" had gone further contrasting the alt rock edge (U2's Vertigo) with the beautiful (Vivaldi's Winter from The 4 Seasons). I love both of the originals but this track was underwhelming.

I love Classical music. I love Rock music. I love solo violin. I think Nigel Kennedy's efforts in combining the three have been much more interesting, cool, and more likely to "get rock fans to listen to classical music" (Try "The Nigel Kennedy Experience" or "The Doors Concerto").  However, this time around, David Garrett's fusion of all 3 falls almost completely flat in a painful way.  I can't imagine enjoying this album in a casual or critical listening context.

reviewText:
REVIEW: With all honesty: John and Yoko's "WEDDING ALBUM" (the third and last of their avant-garde/experimental collaborations) is the absolute pits. Whereas the audio verite of "TWO VIRGINS" had at least a similtude of inspiration (a la The Beatles "Revolution 9"), and the all-out white noise of "LIFE WITH THE LIONS" made for an all-too-real snapshot of personal pain: the lame "John & Yoko" (where our newlyweds holler out each other's names for twenty-three freakin' minutes) is pure egocentric horse s**t. I could edit a half-hour tape of me farting, and it would sound more interesting than this bunch of nonsense. The second side is a bit better: an audio documentary of the Lennon's bed-in in "Amsterdam" prologued by Yoko's "John, Let's Hope For Peace" and ending with a halfway decent acoustic guitar/vocal improvisation that goes "stay in bed...grow your hair" followed by Lennon cooing "Goodnight" from The Beatles' "WHITE ALBUM". It may not be worth a couple of listens, but at least it is worth SOMETHING (although naive in their politics: they do make some interesting points such as "there isn't one European country that hasn't had its Hitler...we're violent people...but I prefer myself when I'm non-violent. I prefer my friends when they're non-violent. It just makes for easier living"). The original LP was accompanied by a gargantuan box set filled to the brim with booklets, a fascimile of J. and Y.'s marriage certificate, photos, and a picture of a piece of wedding cake. Obviously Beatle John desired to celebrate his marriage to Yoko, but I wonder if the elaborate packaging was used to compensate for the lack of originality (and utter triviality) of the "WEDDING ALBUM" itself. Completists will treasure it more so than the casual Beatle listener even though the three bonus tracks do help to make it a much better bargain. Yoko haters should quickly turn the other way and run: this isn't going to win you over as a fan. I am a Yoko fan, and I can honestly say that I love "Who Has Seen The Wind?" and "Listen, The Snow Is Falling". But the other selections aren't worth defending.

reviewText:
I have tried for weeks to like this album. Really.

As a long time Maiden listener, who still listens to their early catalog frequently, I just can't hear ANY of the genius that was once so prevalent back in their prime. Do I expect TBOS to compare with these early albums when the band was rising to fame, world domination in their sights, and a burning desire to prove what great metal should sound like? Of course not. I realize that the driving flames have dwindled, age has set in, and let's face it, they have nothing left to prove. They'll go down in history, and deservedly so. Ultimately as an example of a band who has been able to capture multiple generations of fans by evolving their sound.

But "WAIT", you say. "Maiden has always been Maiden. That's what makes them so great".

Not True. So not true.

When I fell in love with Iron Maiden it was about musicianship. It was about the riffs, the leads, the dual harmonies played so fluently and beautifully by Adrian and Dave all while Steve kept the bass lines underneath tight, intricate, and interesting. You could always count on Clive and (early) Nicko to not just keep time, but also to show off their chops and provide interesting fills within each song. You listened in awe and most importantly you never got bored or tired from repetition. Sure the lyrics were cool, and Bruce's singing was strong and powerful, but it was MUSICIANSHIP first and foremost. TBOS has NO dual harmonies, NO interesting musicianship, absolutely nothing to make you want to grab your guitar, bass or drumsticks and learn or jam along to. Instead it focuses on storytelling and verse after verse of redundant singing of lyrics, never really reaching a pinnacle or musical highlight.  Did Dave, Adrian and Janick even show up to recording each day? (-1 star)

Speaking of Dave, Adrian and Janick. Where are the extended guitar solos and long instrumental passages? Early Maiden had a ton of this! I remember when guitar solos were a song in themselves. Parts to look forward to when listening to the song. Hell, often times they were the best parts of the song. Dave and Adrian would feed off of each other, complimenting each other's style. Bouncing back and forth they'd sweeten an already killer tune with intricate staccato licks and blazing legato runs. I'd often rewind those parts just to comprehend what they were doing. I'm sure they inspired countless young listeners into their local Guitar Center with piggy banks in hand. (think Aces High as a prime example of the guitar solos adding punch by not just senseless notes, but licks designed to mimic machine gun-fire and bullets flying thru the sky). So I ask, what happened to this focus? Where are these crafty solos on TBOS? Absent. Painfully absent. (-1 star).

While we're on the subject of guitar, Janick has proven himself incapable of intelligent guitar playing/soloing and shouldn't even be in the band. (-1 star)

Lastly, I just want to make note of TBOS overall sound quality. Before the age of compressed files and earphone listening, it was important to engineer an album utilizing the entire available bandwidth. Listening to older Maiden albums, nothing sounded muddy or compressed. Every instrument had its room to breath and it sounded AWESOME. Even with only two guitar players, the guitar sound was full of life, layered and with audible nuances. Steve's bass sounded tight and clean, and Bruce's voice cut through like an air-raid siren. This is a far cry from what Maiden has created lately, specifically TBOS which sounds compressed and lifeless by comparison. I've tried to find a moment when I can hear all 3 guitar players at once, but often all I hear is ONE. (And too often its mimicking the vocal line, YIKES!). Also back in my day, Maiden's attitude was clearly different when it came to instrument choices. Pianos, Keyboards, synthesizers were adamantly avoided. (read POM liner notes or watch "Behind the Iron Curtain" for proof). I don't knock them for instrument evolution mind you, but it does go to prove my point. I however cannot overlook the wretched and uninspired sound/recording quality of TBOS. I hear a DRASTIC difference (-1 star). Do you? Probably not.

Probably not, because Iron Maiden has evolved into something I no longer recognize. It has legions of loyal fans that simply don't care about how well an album is mixed and recorded. Who apparently don't care about musicianship, dual guitar harmonies, great guitar solos, but instead are perfectly content and thrilled by storytelling and long drawn out lyrics. Who will love any simplistic muddy guitar riff as long as they know Dave, Adrian or Janick is playing it. To say TBOS is epic or the "best album of their career" simply baffles me. I read these 5-star reviews in utter confusion. What are they hearing? What parts are they enjoying? What are they smoking?

So I have to hand it to Iron Maiden. They've captured the hearts and minds of a whole new generation who will certainly hate this review and defend anything they create like religious-folk defend their GOD. Honestly, I probably would have done the same back in the day.

All I can do at this point in Maidens evolution is try to enjoy a new album for what it is. I realize the guys have matured and have lost some of their spark, (plus it must be a burden carrying the dead weight that is their third guitar player) but with every new release I still hope to hear a few moments that resemble what made them stellar back in my day. And until this latest album, I could find reasonable doses peppered throughout. (Final Frontier is actually quite good). Even to my teenage self it was clear that Brendel ignores 90% of Beethoven's dynamic markings (unlike) Cortot and Schnabel . . . . Artists who followed in his wake avoided the instrument in question like red-spots on the undercarriage. He or She had become It.

reviewText:
I may not be a musical scholar of any sorts, but I sense plenty wrong with this soundtrack and I'll voice my issues as best I can while not savvy in musical terminology. I may do future edits when I can word my opinions better, but for now endure my rant.

My basic thoughts on soundtracks for Nolan's Batman films.(Might write their reviews one day)
Batman Begins: Intriguing enough, establishes the mystery and heroism decently with a dash of mysticism that actually works swell. Weak 4 stars.
The Dark Knight: More obnoxious and redundant, but still some listenable highlights. Strong 2 stars.

But this, this is last straw. Most of this is mindless raves about how it brings things to a conclusion. I don't see how, if it didn't really go much anywhere to begin with. This could deserve two-stars at best, but that's too generous.

Nearly all of it is just copy and paste from the last two soundtracks. Repackage them with sound editing to supposedly make it a refreshing experience. What may sound 'new' on the album, is actually the same what you heard from the last films only being released now. TDK OST suffered from this, but this running out of presents so instead put more boxes in boxes to fill the void.

It's not a matter of whether anything you'd find whether "Bonus" or "Unreleased", it's just more Zimmer dicking around saying there's more if you search harder, while there isn't. "No Stone Unturned" for example. Can't I just go back and shuffle through the last two OSTs? I can find them still the same as usual rather than buy exact replicas all over again.

"Storm is Coming" & "Death by Exile" - Totally WORTHLESS. Just 30 of seconds effects to segue into the next track. Anyone would sooner call this a sound-bridge used in film editing than anything musical.

"On Thin Ice" - My God, a whole third addition note is actually hinted at here for Batman's ever so meaningful two-note piece. But just faintly here, the rest is just strings and we never hear of it again.

"Mind if I Cut In" - When he does resort to instruments other than low strings(still haven't heard a woodwind from him in eons) he applies to the lowest denominator on trigger a audience response. Piano for instance can only serve two functions for Zimmer, tragedy or wittiness, there's no middle ground the keyboard is divided by only two.

"Gotham's Reckoning" & "Fire Rises" & 'others I can't name right off' - A one note, one trick pony. Not only does this apply to only half of Bane's character, his brutality not his intelligence, his attempt to capture the militant masses goes full circle to capture none of it's essence. There's no variation where it could apply to each unique situation, the members growing by additional groups as the movie suggested, or the next plot point when the tone changes from foreboding to consuming. It ends the same as it began. That online crowd-sourcing was just a publicity stunt for Zimmer to gain more underserving hype. 'We'll fine tune it later,' Zimmer said. No sh*t, you muted anything unique or variant. You could have just gotten a dozen man's choir chanting on repeat and you'd get the same result you have.
Congratulations on a such a wasted opportunity.

"Underground Army" - Just "And I Thought My Jokes were Bad". Doesn't matter is sound-editing made a certain 'umph' to it. Why am I listening to the same theme again if these new enemies have no connections with the Joker? Answer: Serve it's basic function as foreboding music to create the 'mood' and move on.

"Why Do We Fall" & "Despair" - Advancing character and story moments, but all significant moments are irrelevantly the same according to Zimmer. Very basic tone of uplifting, as our heroes at their supposed lows rise again. These new, harder obstacles of broken Batman rising from the pit and returning to Gotham should be whole new experience. But, no Zimmer decides bigger and louder, because up the volume and bass is easier to convey 'triumphant' than writing additional material that could convey a sense of development and advancing of character and story.

That's why stagnant mood music or constant ostinatos STIFLES progress. The characters may grow, change, and learn but the music sure IS NOT. And subconsciously that sterilizes the joy of the film even. When all three of the film's villains were defeated each film, who they are may have represented totally different themes in the batman, but Zimmer doesn't bother to make the distinction outside of 'this cue is when bad guy gets defeated... Wallah!' It's all the same to him and his indifference.

"Rise" - The most insulting track of all. For the climax, the final decision and ultimate sacrifice for Gotham all that Zimmer did was just copy and paste parts of "I'm Not a Hero" & "The Dark Knight" from The Dark Knight OST and "Barbastella" from Batman Begins OST. Treat every plot point no matter how PIVOTAL to the story, is just going to be the SAME! Revisit the boy soprano to reflect the deaths of Wayne family is fine, but there is a difference between having parents slaughtered by a thief and a man sacrificing his life for the whole city. And that should be revisited with a varied emotion, not just apply the 'one size fits all' tragic sad boy singing solo.

And that's my complaint with the Nolan's Batman in terms of music: Nothing is developed, it's just on repeat. Nothing grows, just tweaked a bit or made louder. Story and character cannot grow in an abyss, but Zimmer sure is reluctant to never have a solitary musical identity advance outside his fixed ostinato that would remain attached for a whole trilogy. I could go into greater detail how Star Wars Episodes 3 and 6 and LOTR: Return of the King trump anything Zimmer attempted but I'll just exhaust myself in this rant.

He's not focused on a fully fledged human identity at all here. Just focusing on minimalistic motifs for a couple characters, and copies and pastes filler everywhere else to create moods to serve the scene to the lowest denominator.

Well, I don't see costume or set designers stick to one color to create a 'mood', they'd be called lazy for not giving the material the attention to detail it deserves. Actors playing one-note performances serving solely to generate knee-jerk reactions would be criticized for not deserving an acting career. Imagine if he did mountain climbing disaster flick, he'll just sound edit an avalanche or gusts to make the 'mood'.

This year we've been treated with three superhero films with varying soundtracks. "The Avengers" was average but served it's audience with bravado that heroes deserve. "Amazing Spiderman" was flawed, but accomplished duality of outrageous heroism and fragile humanity far better than Zimmer did with his hazy sound-scape you can't distinguish Batman or Bruce Wayne from it.
Even "Wrath of the Titans" that fell under the influence of Zimmer's suggested techniques is a joy to listen despite being a chaotic mess.

This album is nothing short of AWFUL. And this is coming from a HUGE Sinatra fan. I have every commercial release on CD. I have the boxsets, the albums, the original CD's, the remastered CD's, and the remixed-remastered CD's. I've taken all the singles from the '40's, and arranged them into playlists by style. I replaced Nice 'N' Easy from the Nice 'N' Easy album with the correct 'The Nearness Of You.' If you don't know why that makes sense, then you're not a big a fan as i am. I just wanted to point all this out to you fan boys who will lap up anything Sinatra spit out.

That all said, the problems with this album are many. For one, every song (save 'Send In The Clowns') suffers from the horrible soft rock beat that became largely standard of much of FS's recording output at this time. It makes him sound like someone's grandpa trying to be cool. In addition, there's the annoying choir on 'Noah' and the cheesy, over-the-top 'power ballad' choruses of several other songs. And what about those sickening lyrics on 'There Used To Be A Ballpark?' 'The air was such a wonder from the hot dogs and the beer??' Are you freakin' kidding me??? I CRINGE hearing Sinatra sing that. This album makes me beg for a whole album full of duets with Dagmar!

His version of 'Send In the Clowns' is not bad, although his all-piano version from a couple years later is much better. But that's about all i can say that's positive about this album. Actually, Jenkins' string flourishes are pretty good and well-placed, but the rhythm section is tired, cheesy, and poorly arranged.

If you're a casual Sinatra fan, take note. He had 16 albums on Capitol Records (1953-61) that ranged from pretty good to fantastic. He had another half-dozen or so from the early '60s on Reprise that are mostly good, plus a couple later albums like the Jobim album, and his near swan song, 'She Shot Me Down,' which are classics. Not to mention about 75% of his Columbia material from the 1940's that's classic. You can have a collection of 500-600 great Sinatra songs, without having to waste your time with the inane drivel on 'Ol Blue Eyes Is Back.'

reviewText:
More than one reviewer trashing this recording said that it was this pair's "anti-Romanticism" that completely destroyed whatever grace they may have been able to infuse on their interpretation. I would say that the problem, as in many recordings with the mercurial Argerich, is her refusal to let anyone else take even a little part of the show from her. The result is that she tries to get ahead of poor Gideon, one of the few really talented living violinists out there, turning andante or allegro-like movements into prestos, with barely any attention paid to dynamics. It reminds me of that famous cartoon of someone playing the PIANOforte with hammers, and makes me wonder if the instruments she plays in have to be overhauled right away because of all that too-passionate banging.

Kremer is better known for his interpretations of modernist and post-modernist composers like (specially) Schnittke, but critics are wrong in their portrayal of him as too cold for romantic music - they should all listen to his recordings of the Beethoven (the one  with Harnoncourt and the Euro. Chamb. Orch. has some new, pretty good cadenzas composed by Kremer himself) and  Tchaikovsky concertos. Both of them show that Kremer knows how to put passion on his playing... without losing his cool, which is what often happens with Argerich.

This isn't the first time I have had the Argerich experience: the same thing happened in the otherwise excellent recording of Schumman's ensemble works she did with some of her friends, live at the small hall of the Concertgebouw. It was her colleague Alexander Rabinovitch that stood out for that subtlety of interpretation she lacks almost completely. I fear that all that technical virtuosity goes to waste when it isn't tempered by concern for the intentions of the composer, not that this means that there's such thing as an absolutely faithful standard for interpreting Beethoven or anyone else. When a soloist dragoons her agent into stuffing two or more full concertos by different composers into *half* a night's programme, which is what Argerich did last year at the Carnegie (it was more shocking to read in the TONY that it was possible she wouldn't show up at all), I fear she may be following Battle's path into artistic oblivion.

reviewText:
Well, as the title states, this was the beginning of the end of a once great band. Replacements put out a few amazing records that epitomized hardcore/punk-ish emo/indie from around 1980 on. But on this one finally did a 180 and changed direction. A change that some of us didn't like. Yet so many see this as some sort of landmark monumental release. Maybe for someone whose standards have been dumbed down and don't care about listening to punk any longer this might be great. That isn't me. They still have their share of hardcore ties to their past on this record in various forms but they still went down the tubes anyway you look at it.

But anyone who truly loved what they did on Sorry Ma all the way through to Hootenanny would vomit in their mouth (as I did) after listening to this horrible sign of their catastrophic decline. This was the followup to Hootenanny and supposed to be their trek into more mature songwriting but something caused them to abandon who and what they once were.

This album takes the poppiness leanings of their first 3 records to such a (lack of) ambitious slant that it sounds like any other "alternative" pop band at the time played on the radio. Gone is the roughness, cheap production values, uniqueness, and devil may care attitude that made them the Replacements. But it was all sadly replaced by a radio friendly, mainstream, glossy, overproduced, sellout piece of garbage caricature of what they used to be. And it would only get worse on every record after this until they closed up shop with each successive album selling less and less. By their last record, which was nothing more thana glorified Paul Westerberg solo recording, their transformation into Britney Spears pop territory had been complete. On here they were almost half way there.

If you know music and the Mats like I do, buy Sorry Ma, Stink, and Hootenanny. Erase everything else they did afterwards from your memories. I know I have ;)

Then, there's "Nutshell", also very beautiful and giving you a mixed feeling. You can feel both happy for it's beauty as well as sad because it is truly a "preety-sad" song.
"I stay away" reminds me of good times spent in a place in Lisboa called "Bairro Alto", where me and my friends used to hang out and there was this joint that played this album over and over. So this song always reminds me of those great summer nights spent there having loads of fun, preety much s***faced but for those who know the place, you know that's the feeling. And for me it's the optimistic "lift up" of the album!

The whole song sounds like a reply to "Don't follow" I won't reccomend this album for the fans, because i believe they have it (and i was lucky enough to get "Jar of flies" and "Sap" in the same pack!) reviewText:
Rhydian's initial outpouring was pretty awful, but it doesn't come anywhere near this cretinous, concilliatory effort.
Oh yes, he's trying to distance himself from nasty lizard Cowell, and a lot of the songs on his debut were thrust upon him against his will, so 'Oh, For Tuna'  should be packed to the seams with red-hot, passionate NEW songs, interesting, unconventional arrangements, and topped with a fiery spirit of subtlety and progression.

Not a bit of it.
It's the same old safe, conservative clap-trap that got dished up - ooh about this time last year, funnily enough - without a tweak or forward thought to its agenda.
Being a ferocious right-winger, consumerism is something I normally haven't a problem with; but at this level, and of this magnitude, even I begin to reel at the stench.

Aiming something this squarely at the over 60's and/or the totally mind-swept and mono-dimensional is both heartless and monstrously exploitative. Far from being the voice of an angel, Rhydian is in fact, the face of the corporate Satan - rubbing his hands yet again at the slovenly, bone-idle Christmas shopper, reaching for 'Tuna Sandwich' as a present for the old folk, instead of trying to think of something decent.

I'm horrified: the retro-hymn 'How Great Thou Art,' 'Annie's Song' (honest!), the I'm-proud-to-be-Welsh-even-though-I'd-steal-the-coins-from-your-dead-relatives-eyes token 'Land of My Fathers' and the utterly terrifying 'Myfanwy' are the picks which peck at your ears first, but there's more - oh so much more.
It's exactly the same mix as before, only this time he looks like a murderer on the cover.

Hymns, light classical, movies....echoing vocals, choirs, pompous orchestra....o yawn.

After all the noise his clucking, sychophantic supporters made defending his debut - predictions of an electrifying second album free from Cowell and all the trappings, 'Tuna Bake' is a sickening kick in the teeth of the highest order.

The only good thing I can say about this cruel release, is that at least it doesn't contain 'You'll Never Walk Alone' - the worst song ever written.
He's keeping that for next time...

reviewText:
The Prima Donnas' playing of the NY Phil are faithfully reproduced in this recording! As usual, there is no dynamic balance, and the dynamic levels are the usual LOUD and LOUDER of the NY Phil!  "Pianissimo? What is that? We don't do this around here! In the NY Phil it is every man for himself!" The playing in this recording is shamefully sloppy! There are missed notes and bad entrances, pitch problems, especially in the horns, etc....For example, check out the Cor Anglais entrance at the end of the third bar after rehearsal number 129, where Mr. Michel Nazzi consistently misses at least one or two notes of the chromatic solo entrance leading into the alto flute solo!  Later, five bars before the Danse Sacrale (5 bars before rehearsal number 142), the bass trumpet in Eflat also misses part of the same chromatic scale repeatedly! Another example of sloppiness, is a bad entrance of one of the trumpets in the "Dance of the Earth" at the end of the first part! While Bernstein chooses an exciting fast tempo for the final Danse Sacrale, there is a serious problem with the last bar! The upbeat run into the last chord is not heard clearly, and it ends up blurred and sounding together with the last beat! Arthur Nikisch said: THERE ARE NO BAD ORCHESTRAS! THERE ARE BAD CONDUCTORS! I wonder which one applies here! Perhaps both?!  This is not to say that Lenny is a bad conductor. I have played with him, and I know he was good! Just that his efforts here do not cut it, for he was up against an orchestra that was hard to tame!  This CD is not even in the same league with Stravinsky's 1960 version with the Columbia Symphony Orchestra version, Boulez's 1969 version with the Cleveland Orchestra, or even the 1990 Dutoit/Montreal recording! I am sure that Stravinsky's comment after the "WOW" exclamation was not "how wonderful this recording is", but his thoughts had to have been:"WOW, This really STINKS!"

By the way, I have also played with Stravinsky, and I know that (unlike many half-baked comments) he COULD CONDUCT WITH MATHEMATICAL PRECISION, and this is what is required for this work with its intricate polyrhythms, and complex texture, but seriously lacking in this CD!

reviewText:
First of all, I'd like to say right up front that I am a tremendous admirer of Andrew Lloyd Webber. I am not one of those people who write reviews only to bash him and denounce his life's work as unsubstanciated trash, nor am I one of those manic "Phans" who are all torch-and-pitchfork for any attempt at a sequel that comes rolling their way. I'm simply a fan of both him and his previous works who was highly disappointed.

 When I first found out there was going to be a sequel to "Phantom", I hoped Sarah Brightman and Michael Crawford would come back to repise their roles. After listening to this album, I am so glad they didn't. I was sorely let down by the quality of "Love Never Dies", and taking part in it would have only brought them down in my own estimation.

 I had heard alternately positive and negative reviews for this show; being a big fan of the original, I was a little curious about this, though leery of the setting at Coney Island. After some deliberation, I decided to just go ahead and take a listen. My fears were justified.

 Love Never Dies is a tremendous monstrosity. Set in 1907, ten years after the events of the "Phantom of the Opera" (Time discrepancy anyone? I thought the original took place in 1881. Hmm...), and set in New York; or more specifically, Coney Island, of all places; the Phantom has built himself up as an innovator for the freak-shows and attractions at the park. Calling himself Mr. Y, he devises a plan to lure Christine from Paris to sing. To make a long story short, she arrives; tragedy ensues; and the whole thing ends just as abysmally as it starts.

  The plot is ridiculously kitsch and predictable. You needn't even have to see it live to know what direction it's going to take, and even then it is beyond unbearable. Even the title itself is deplorable, for SPOILER HERE: one of the principle characters is "done away with", for lack of another phrase, in a rather merciless and unnecessary manner, proving that love does indeed die (I hope I didn't give away too much). Lust never dies would be a far more fitting moniker. What should be a celebration of the strength of love and its ability to persevere through any circumstance is instead reduced to a wake, displaying in vivid color the irrevocable tragedy caused by it and the destructive effect it has upon people's lives.

 As a word of note to fans of the original, I would like to point out how far removed and very different from "Phantom" this is; much too different. Andrew Lloyd Webber freely admitted that this was going to be a completely separate work, and in case it doesn't meet your expectations (it REALLY failed to meet mine), he at least met that one.

 In case you're wondering, don't go looking for any continuation musically. There is no romantic lullaby like "Music of the Night" or a beautiful, longing ballad like "Wishing You Were Somehow Here Again". Instead, those greats have been replaced by songs like "The Beauty Underneath", a weird, pounding, rock-stomp, or "Beneath a Moonless Sky" which left me feeling sick to my stomach. We all knew ALW was secretly bursting to include more rock in POTO. In LND he's gotten his chance; and boy, did he go all out.

  Even character-wise, nothing is the same. The characters are desecrated and made largely one-dimensional, with enough problems to fill an entire season of "As the World Turns". All of the beautiful characterization that was put into the Phantom himself is done away with for LND. I never though Ramin Karimloo made a very good Phantom, and, unfortunately, it seems the revised character was written around his lackluster portrayal. The Phantom is made very uninteresting. He has no style, no grace, no nobility, and no personality. He's little more than a shadow of his former self. He's no longer a genius, but a freak-show sell-out, everything he aspired not to be in both Leroux's novel and the original play--heck, he isn't even scary!

The rest of the cast is also changed considerably. Meg (little Meg Giry!), has seriously gone to the dark side in her role as the lead "Ooh-la-la girl", a group of seriously underdressed showgirls. For supposedly being French, she comes off too brash and brassy, and not at all the sweet little member of the corps de ballet. Christine is too flat and boring, and doesn't have any of the really sweet, innocent qualities she used to that made her such a compelling character. Oh, and to top it all off, Raoul is a bitter, gambling drunkard, totally lacking in sympathy and warmth. What a group of winners. None of them are in any way appealing; there is far too much anger running through them, enough that it makes you, as the listener, uncomfortable. It really left me wondering,"What was anyone thinking?" or more probably, "Were they thinking?". And the resounding answer to that question is No.

 What really tore me up emotionally was the lack of sympathy and honest devotion between the Phantom and Christine. Their first meeting, for instance, which should have been a sweet homage to their parting at the end of POTO is nothing more than a gruff confrontation, ending in a sickening duet showcasing an overabundance of bawdiness. The only touching emotional conflict in the whole show is that the Phantom hasn't written any decent music since Christine left him, and has instead produced cheap side-show jingles. A nice tribute, but it leaves me to wonder, did he write the music for LND too?

Concerning the music, Andrew Lloyd Webber has really lost his touch here. The entire score feels like it was written by someone else. Grating, disturbing, and for all intents and purposes Tim-Burton-esque, it is slow-moving and nowhere near the caliber of any of his other work. It doesn't leave you feeling uplifted, but drained and unsettled instead. There is nothing pretty or romantic about it. It has has none of the sweeping, grandiose melodies of POTO, and if you didn't know any better, you could easily pass this off as a very poor imitation of a usually good composer.

 The songs here aren't even sappy. They're just bad. I actually had to stop and walk away from listening for a while before I got through it, they are just that terrible. They sound like cheap, third-rate songs tossed hap-hazardly into your average third-rate American musical. There is all flash and no substance, and what a weak flash it is, too. The lyrics are clunky and cumbersome, and if they weren't so utterly ridiculous, maybe you'd be able to focus on some of the better points of the score itself. There's hardly a tune out of the whole lot I can remember enough to hum or would even care to. None of them are memorable and certainly will not be ones that are still popular some 20-odd years later. The only exception is the title song "Love Never Dies", which is very beautiful and classic, a real show-stopper; but is sadly the one and only, and is nothing more than an ominous portent when taken in context with the show.

 All of the gorgeous operatic sensibilities that made the original Phantom stand out have been uprooted for the sake of appeasing those who objected to "too much Opera". Excuse me? It was set inside an Opera house, written by a man who was an opera critic, and has the very word displayed quite blatantly in the title.

As a major fan of POTO I admit to have listened to the original album more times than I can count. I certainly couldn't stand to listen to this album more than once without my head exploding or my eardrums bursting from the overwhelming shrillness of each piece, coupled with the overly-repetetive introduction of electric guitars. The cast as singers are only annoying and seem perfectly content with their terrible habit of over-acting and under-singing lines, which is only magnified by what dribble the material is that they have to work with.

 The score by itself certainly has some merit, but with different lyrics and better story I can see working, ideally, in another show, one totally unrelated to "Phantom"

 Those who are more familiar than I am with Webber's earlier works will probably deem this classic ALW; edgy, slightly irreverent, and definitely different than anything else standing in musical theatre; but for something as a follow-up to a show based in an opera house, that style just doesn't fit.

In few words, Love Never Dies is a chaotic, unexciting spectacle (and I mean spectacle in a bad way). It certainly has no makings for being a theatre classic, nor a timeless masterpiece. It doesn't have the nostalgic feel of "Phantom of the Opera", nor the sense of tension or anticipation that was so apparent throughout all of the score. The dismal choice of setting is so completely unsuited to the core subject, it's hard to even believe anyone gave it the green light. I completely understand that ALW aimed to be different, but honestly, when you're dealing with a sequel, shouldn't it at least be a little cohesive to where you started from?

I really blame Mr. Webber for his choice of Glenn Slater as lyricist and Fredrick Forsyth's novel as source material. Don't get me wrong; I think Mr. Webber is a gifted composer who has produced some of the best theater works in the last forty years, nearly all of which have  been received as world-renowned smash-hits; but I personally don't see this as one of his best. The stinker lyrics and bad choice of source material bring it all down. I honestly believe he would have done much better if he had tried to come up with a story himself, rather than depend on the atrocious sell-out "Phantom of Manhattan" is.

  In tone, the show is far too dark and depressing. There is no mystery and absolutely no magic; humor is nonexistent. The romance and wonder is gone, only to be replaced by a drawn-out nightmarish bore. It has none of the poignancy and brilliance of the original, and doesn't carry over well as a continuation of the original story. Honestly, it reminded me of the Joel Schumacher movie adaptation of "Phantom": bad acting, bad orchestration, so-so singers, and enough grit to sandpaper superglue off a wall. Those who enjoy bodice-busting tales of carnage might like this one, but for those of us who liked the Phantom the way he was, beware.

 To quote the Phantom himself (not Karimloo's Phantom, but his earlier incarnations), Love Never Dies is a "lamentable mess", to put it kindly, and if you are a fan of the original you'll avoid this one. I sure wish I had.

reviewText:
Norah Jones is part of a popular trend that's going on right now: putting a pretty girl behind a piano. I really expected more from Norah because of the ravishing reviews and Grammy nominations, I really did, but this CD turned out to be as tasty as a rice cake. Norah has "sultry" voice, but she lacks any kind of vocal range and doesn't display any kind of emotions throughout her songs.  "Come Away With Me" starts off on a smooth note with "I Don't Know Why" and makes you think that you'll be in for something more, but after that song everything that comes after it just goes downhill. If you're not paying attention to the CD it would be hard to find out if a song has just started or ended because they all sound the same; there is nothing unique about any of them. I was hoping there would be some experimentation with certain sounds and that she'd have some East Indian influence in her music, but there is none.
How is her music considered jazz and who had the nerve to compare her to Billie Holiday? After I listened to Norah's CD I listened to Billie's CD- immediately and thank goodness it was close at hand- and I realized that there is nothing similar between the two of them. While Billie was able to express emotions through an array of beats and melodies, Norah's "sultry" voice- along with the music- remains stagnant and monotonous throughout "Come Away With Me." I didn't feel relaxed or inspired at all, just bored and anxious. Sure, Norah wrote some of the songs, but that doesn't make her better than other *real* jazz greats like Billie and Etta like one reviewer tried to imply. It's not *what* you do but *how* you do it. Billie didn't write many songs, but it was her voice and feeling that she put into the songs that touched many people. Norah writes lyrics, uninspiring and dead lyrics, and puts no magic into them.
While Norah Jones may want you to "come away" with her, she ultimately leads you nowhere. Don't believe the hype about this CD. It's definitely the most overrated album of the year. "Come Away With Me" has just tied with Sade's "Lover's Rock" CD for being just one long boring song. If you want to listen to REAL jazz, skip this floozy and get Billie Holiday or any of Sade's earlier work.

reviewText:
Let me start by saying that the one-star rating is in no way a reflection of my feelings about Dokken or this album. Classic 80s Dokken is the best hard rock of the era; Breaking the Chains is a damn good record.

I was ecstatic when I heard Rock Candy, who does some of the best remaster/reissue work of any company out there, was going to be reissuing some Dokken albums. When I heard that the first record was going to be amongst those reissued, I was all the more delighted, feeling that the pros at Rock Candy were going to dig into the vault and give us the original Carrere Records versions of the tracks as bonuses.

A brief history lesson for the uninformed: Before it hit American shores in 1983, Breaking the Chains was released under the Don Dokken solo name on European label Carrere Records. This early, rare version of the album featured alternate mixes of the tracks, and two are drastically different from their International Release counterparts. On this early version, Live to Rock (Rock to Live) is entitled "We're Illegal" and has totally different lyrics, and Paris is Burning is actually a studio version (international albums have a live version.) These tracks are the holy grail of Dokken obscurities and rarities....

....so why did Rock Candy not include them here?

I absolutely love Rock Candy for what they have done for reissuing great classic hard rock and AOR albums, but there are a few dimwitted incidents where they overlook great potential bonus content, and this sadly, is one such occasion. The expanded liner notes are nice and the sound is truer to the source than any earlier release, but hold out for a true deluxe package that has the alternate Carrere Records versions as bonus tracks.

reviewText:
First off, I LOVE, LOVE, Mudvayne (they're in my top 5 fav. bands & have been since LD 50)... I also LOVE (most of) Pantera... and I've lived most of my life in Dallas. Unfortunately, HellYeah, despite being comprised of some of my favorite musicians/artists, stinks to high heaven... and there's one very simple (and obvious) reason for this: You've got an IL (Illinois) front-man, trying to write "southern-rock" songs.

I don't really even like "southern-rock" all that much... I've only heard a few bands in my entire life, that sounded decent doing it -- and it's because they were born &/or raised in the South... but I digress...

There were only 3 songs on the 1st album I liked (the 1st three... the 2nd being the best)... and most who bought that album felt similarly. I, unlike most of them, didn't expect a Mudvayne or Pantera album... I expected a Southern-Rock album (a good one)... but it just didn't fly.

I decided to give HellYeah one more shot for a few reasons: 1) Fav guys, as stated earlier __ 2) Read pre-release interviews from Chad saying the writing & so on, went much smoother & came easier, having worked with everyone for the last album (ie, they had a chance to get to know each other & compliment each other, better... at least, that was the intended message -- one I fail to hear in this album -- but again, I digress) ___ and 3) Because I'll give any band (especially one with talented members) a 2nd chance...... unfortunately, this one is even worse than it's predecessor.

(most fans either didn't buy this album, or chose not to write truthful reviews about it, out of loyalty & wishing to see Chad, Vinny & the guys do well in sales... but it's my opinion, that if they want good sales, they should put out good music... not hope their "rabid fans" will take mercy & keep quiet.)

Do yourself a favor... if you absolutely have to show your support & buy the album, then buy the regular edition... at least you'll save a couple dollars..... your ears will probably still spew out a gallon of blood as you listen to it; but at least you'll have saved a couple bucks.

(The music, ie, drums, guitar & bass, is pretty good... but the lyrics are terrible.... sung well, in Chad's style of course; but he's proven twice now, he's not the right guy to front a southern-rock band... regardless of how close/comfortable he is with the other members. It pains me to say that, because I LOVE Chad's Mudvayne work... but it's the God's honest truth. Hopefully he'll spend more time with (and concentrating fully on) Mudvayne, and less time with HellYeah, from now on.)

PS: I'm reading the "tags" others have left, LOL!! What the heck does this album (or band) have to do with KoRn &/or Jonathan Davis!??? Wow!? LOL. Whatever. (I like KoRn too; but come on guys, really... Stampede is being compared to KoRn... talk about night/day, apples/oranges!) ;-)

reviewText: This is purely based on the product quality. Why does a record company bother to master a vinyl release then decide to cut corners on quality control. The faster speed magnifies any imperfection in the platter. So 60 bucks later--I DID try two copies--I have a download. And with the remainder of their catalog due for reissue, I'll be hard pressed to take another chance. Buyer, beware.

reviewText:
THIS ALBUM HAS BEEN RE-ISSUED AS PAST LIVES.
Past Lives is a double CD, containing this CD plus another CD of live material.  The sound has been cleaned up to a great extent.  It is not perfect, or even professional quality, but it is much, much better than before.  The perfomance still sucks.

This is not a good live CD. It has many, many problems. The sound is horrible, performance is off, and the song selection is weak. This does not do the band justice. For anyone to give this thing 5 stars, they are enhancing it in their minds, building it up to something we all wish it could be. This is 58 minutes long.

One of the biggest problems is that Ozzie Osborne keeps yelling out things in the middle of songs. He screams, "Everybody Stand Up" or "We Love You All". Personally, I don't listen to a band called Black Sabbath to hear the lead singer say he loves me. And why does he have to tell the audience to stand up? It must be some poor performance if the audience isn't already on its feet. Any great hard rock band should have audience spontaneously charging the stage during the first song.

The sound quality is the worst I have ever heard for a commercial release. It is even worse than King Crimson's Groon or Epitath or Hawkwind's Early Daze. There is no high or low end and the sound is completely muffled. I have the Castle Records release and it says it was taken from the original master. But if the master tapes are bad, there isn't much you can do.

The overall performance seems weak. Maybe the poor sound quality makes the performance seem weaker than it is. You really need the full dynamic range to enjoy Black Sabbath, with the rumbling bass and the screaming guitar and vocals.

The songs are 3 to 5 minutes long, with the exception of a 7 minute Sweet Leaf and an 18 minute Wicked World. The band plays most of the songs just like they are on the studio albums, but only with not as much energy or emotion. The band never really opens up. You can understand why Osborne must yell at the audience to get them off their butts. There is a nice guitar solo in Sweet Leaf, and the band does seem to have some fun during Wicked World. But it is hard to enjoy either with the poor sound quality.

I don't know if Black Sabbath was ever a great live band. I know they have had some bad performances. Yes got its big break by being the opening band on a Black Sabbath tour. Yes just totally blew away Black Sabbath. For many fans, that tour marked the group's decline in popularity.

This album comes from a concert somewhere around 1974. It was originally released in 1976 as a single LP in England. It was missing Wicked World and one other track. In the US, it was only available as an import. In 1980, it was then released on CD with the two songs added. The CD doesn't have any liner notes or pictures. There is supposed to be a new version floating around with new expanded liner notes. I don't know if the sound has been improved any, but I doubt. I don't know if the current version being sold here has expanded liner notes.

reviewText:
Another reviewer(R.Hutchison) was totally correct.

This is shallow music. It is slick and very well orchestrated but so is much film music(think of the brilliant Elliott Goldenthal).Why Adams is seen by many musically educated critics as the greatest current American composer I don't know.

Adams has a brilliant technique-that cannot be denied. He has actually written some good music-Harmonium is a lovely piece,almost visionary in its scope. Unfortunately in my view he has succumbed to what many American composers have done-crowd pleasing showy orchestration but with music of little substance. Harmonium was a rare example by Adams music of substance and good orchestration.

The piano concerto,like the violin concerto,sees the soloist wasted on banal meanderings while the orchestra assaults us with even more banal repetetive phrases. Poor Emanuel Ax. The slow movement is really banal.

Loopalooza is very clever yes(even catchy) but again gets really irritating so by the end you couldn't give a ...k.

The Slonominsky piece is the best piece by far but again leaves you with the the conclusion 'good orchestration but so what'.It AGAIN descends into obsessively repetitive phrases that drive you mad!

Adams music on this disc is a curious mix of Steve Reich,Stravinsky,Schoenberg,Copland,and his own Shaker Loops but without the unity. We get slushy 'apple pie' Americana Copland/John Williams/Disney films harmonies(you know what I mean!!) colliding with atonal music I thought he didn't like! Maybe he wants that mix but it drives me nuts and doesn't work. It wouldn't be so bad if it didn't sound all so slick,flash and mechanical.

reviewText: On paper, the concept is pure genius: Madonna, pop tart of the 1980s, teaming up with Britney Spears, pop tart of the new millennium.  The collaboration could have been as titillating as the lesploitation kiss they shared at the 2003 VMAs.  Instead, we get a generic dance single that's silly, boring, and goes limp faster than Britney's marriage.  "Me Against the Music" stiffed on the charts upon release, and you can credit that to the forced come-ons and lack of chemistry between the two singers.  In fact, the duet sounds so impersonal, Madonna could have very well recorded her vocals on an Mp3 file before FedExing them to Spears.  "Hey Britney," goes Madonna, "you say you wanna lose control?"  Well, if both singers lost a little "control" and got a tighter groove, "Me Against the Music" would be the killer dance tune it could have--and SHOULD have--been.
