reviewText: The Shadow was a great radio program. If you've found this collection, you probably know what to expect from the programs themselves. The 20-disc CD compilation has a balanced selection of episodes starring the three most famous radio "Shadows": Orson Welles, Bill Johnstone, and Bret Morrison. The discs are handsomely housed and the enclosed booklet is a nice bonus. Why only one star? The sound is generally horrible. I have home-made multi-generational cassette copies of many of the episodes in this collection that I got in trades with other OTR (old time radio) collectors twenty or more years ago that sound *infinitely* better than the "remastered" versions on this set. "The Gibbering Things" is a prime example: my 20-year-old tape sounds crisp and clear with plenty of high frequencies and sibilance. The version on this CD sounds so muddy as to be nearly unintelligible, and portions are plagued with tape "warble." Clearly, they got it from a tape copy many further generations down the line. After years of listening to my home-made tapes, I thought that I'd do the "right thing" and buy the licensed versions of these programs and hopefully upgrade the quality as well. This set was a major disappointment. I might have given two stars to the set for the decent booklet, but the programs themselves are the real selling point here, and they sound *so* poor compared to other versions of the same episodes floating around out there that I can't recommend this at all. Ordinarily, Radio Spirits puts out a good quality product, but they really missed the boat this time. With a little bit of effort to find better source material, this could have been a really wonderful CD set. Avoid!

reviewText:
Assassins is a masterpiece of American theatre. Through a revue of skits and songs, it examines ideas we don't want to face, and shows us the flip side of the American Dream. The score rates as one of Sondheim's best, and the overall effect, when the show is performed well, is incredibly powerful. For years, people have wanted to mount a production on Broadway.

Given this result, they needn't have bothered.

I am still amazed at how much this production got wrong. The principal cast is nothing short of dreadful: the acting is almost laughably overwrought; the pacing keeps getting disrupted by pauses held too long and lines spoken too slowly; some singers are frequently behind the tempo (notably Michael Ceveris as Booth), while others are painful to listen to (like Jeffrey Kuhn as Zangara and Mario Cantone as Sam Byck); the new orchestrations allow for more musicians in the pit, but are much less effective than the earlier arrangements.

To top it all off, this production includes "Something Just Broke", a song sung by the Ensemble as various "average" Americans of different time periods recalling where they were when the president was shot. The song was introduced in the London production, presumably for people who didn't understand the show to have something to latch on to, but it was mercifully kept out of the published vocal score and libretto. It's not a bad song in and of itself, but musically it does not fit in with the rest of the score, and dramatically it doesn't fit in with the rest of the script. Worse, it is placed right between the Kennedy assassination -- the climax of the show -- and the finale, thus skewing all the dramatic momentum and depriving the show of an effective resolution.

The result of all this is that the comic moments aren't funny, the powerful moments fail to move, and the wonderful music is left ho-hum.

I realize that the extraordinary cast of the original production of Assassins presents a dauntingly high standard for everyone else to compare to, but the college productions I've seen were better than this.

reviewText:
Sourced from inferior two track masters widely used (and plagiarised) for its multi release on numerous cheap budget record labels from the 1970s onwards. The sound is poor. Look elsewhere.

Everest represented the peak of recorded sound back then and this set, as with other Belock recordings, well worth getting, but only as outlined below. Otherwise do not waste your money on cheap re-issues, though I notice this isn't exactly cheap!  Insult to injury?

To get back to the original audiophile quality of the recordings you have to invest in the collectible Vanguard reissue, where the original 3 track 35 mm master tapes have been transferred via lovingly restored 1960s valve electronics to 20 bit SBM CDs. The sonic results are light years ahead of this cheap bucket job which I consider an insult to the Belock recorded legacy as a shortlived but brilliant stereophonic record label between 1958 and 1962.

The performances are middle of the road. Without being historically informed, Krips' direction and view of the music isunerringly right - as you would expect, his Mozart cycle with the Concertgebouw for Philips is a reference recording - and he was used to working with quality orchestras. In this case the LSO was, as now, one of the top symphony orchestras in the world. In particular the LSO strings have always been admired. Here, in unbuttoned mood, with recording dates outside of the pressures of the busy concert season, we have joyful, eager and sensitive playing light years away from the hard driven bolshy Germanic readings which seem to dominate from Karajan to Solti.  Krips' intelligent performances are also superior to the current vogue for HIP from the likes of Gardiner and (arghhh!) Norrington.  The thing to look for is musicianship - not historicity whatever that is - and nice sound - not scratchy strings - and these recordings are loaded with superior muscianship, instrumentals and lovely strings. The Beethoven orchestra is quite small compared with its later Romantic counterparts, so a monumental scale if it is to be achieved must be done within these restricted means. The Everest recording values authentically give a realistic audio picture that is familiar to anybody who has listened to the symphonies live in a concert hall. This is infinitely preferable in my view to sonically bloated recordings which followed, utilising a regiment of microphones, 16 track or more mixed down to 2 track masters. Even so-called authentic recordings using period instruments are so extensively cosmetically engineered as bear no comparison to what the concert goer would hear even in the "sweet" spot of a great auditorium, in a centre seat, about 10 rows back, costing about 100$. One might as well have stuck microphones INSIDE Gardiner's musical instruments given the adrenalin steroid pumping sound of his recent "live" cycle. And so it goes.

Thankfully, with this Everest recording, you know where you stand: in the real world...a world that has drifted away in most modern recordings. So if you value a traditional concert hall sound, get this - but not in this edition, which is a betrayal of the original audiophile source and intention.

Although some 35mm Belock recordings have been transferred to DVD-Audio and even SACD (Classic Records) we have now probably come to the end of what can be done with the original aging analogue film masters. So this is it: the legacy that has been preserved by Vanguard and Classic Records. There are also the original blue/silver LPs from that era if you can get them mint (again not cheap!) But to my knowledge the Beethoven cycle came too late for release on audiophile quality vinyl as by the end of 1961 Belock Instruments had sold off Everest Records, it's equipment and studio in New York going to Mercury, to become a budget label based in Hollywood.

Therefore for a great set of enjoyable performances recorded with the non pareil clarity of Belock's state of the art 35mm recording process, in a naturally wide and deep acoustic soundstage, using traditional LR stereo and avoiding the over miked hard driven versions that abound, then Krips' cycle is for you.

It will cost you about 500 or more on Vanguard as a complete set - or 20 or more per individual disc - if you can find them!

Don't buy this cheap rip off thinking you are getting a bargain. You aren't. It's a waste of money. Really this CD box set is a disgrace.

Go for the Vanguard set and splash your cash.
label: negative

reviewText:
Now that the days of those, like me, who bought "Hard Nose the Highway" when it was released, are drawing like Mr Morrison's, to a close:  Is the best yet to come, my friends?

We, dwellers on the threshold, a little further down the Vanlose Stairway, who have followed Van Morrison this far, hoping to catch him looking ahead to see across the bridge where angels dwell, are likely to be demoralised by this offering and the news that, because there is NO PLAN B, we are going to have to lump it.

Before the dawn of the new millennium Van Morrison's matchless "High Summer", moved away from his usual worship of Celtic light.  We witnessed him courting the forces of darkness.  According to Dennis Wheatley, only a spiritual adept, the like of an Aleister Crowley, could survive such a cataclysmic confrontation.  The Lucifer in the red sports car arriving at "the mansion on the hill" leaving behind the professional jealousy that has cursed Morrison for years has no rendezvous this time with the "Queen of the Slipstream"; but a woman of a different order who, making a stand against the light, hums "Thank God the dark nights are drawing in again".

BORN TO SING provides the latest evidence that Morrison's encounter with the forces of darkness has done the man no favours. The whole of this negative album is morose, drawn out and dull.  He sulks: "There is no pot of gold at the end of the rainbow".  Almost every Van Morrison album has some exquisite example of the High Priest's art; but for a long time the best of the regalia has been ruined by being encroached upon by inferior settings.

 In the past, Morrison has shown those of us patient enough to follow the man's drift, how we may be friends with God and his angels; how we, like Ford and Fitzroy ourselves, might break laws for a muse such as Madame George.  Only a great artist can invite us, as he does, to have a friend in the Lord and yet speak with just as much affection for Lucifer: "He is a light out of the darkness."  It is God himself who Van Morrison addresses when he sings: "Have I told you lately that I love you?"  Perhaps, in advance of the new millennium, he gambled that selling his soul to the darker side might pay off.  Perhaps it has.  In this century we have the songs "Stranded" " Celtic New Year", "Keep it Simple", and "That's Entrainment".  There are a few others but most of the albums have struggled to match those.

"OPEN THE DOOR TO YOUR HEART" suggests that money is just to pay the bills. After wasting too much of my own on albums like "Philosopher's Stone" or "Too long in Exile" it is no comfort to be reminded of what I don't want to hear.

The money that covers the singer's mileage GOING DOWN TO MONTE CARLO, presumably in the interests of tax avoidance, may be certainly reclaimed as a business expense: "After everything I worked so hard for, I'm not goin' to give it all away". The town of Nice (25K from Monte Carlo) usefully rhymes with "peace". "Nice" also rhymes with "briefs"; although the revelation about being "without my brief" is saved for the lifeless MYSTIC OF THE EAST where "geese" and "teeth" make up, if not boxer shorts, at least a rhyming pair.

Van Morrison is a windbag with a divine sense of humour. His "Blah blah blah blah" is divinely inspired in "Behind the Ritual."  But BORN TO SING costs 8.99 as I write on Amazon. It's not funny.  For 3.99 including post and packing you can save 5; and experience Van Morrison's latest sound, if you are prepared to search on eBay for "Inflatable Li-Lo Air Bed".  The product is available in three colours.  If you let out the half of the air you can hear, in the exhalation, the baleful sounds of self-reproach that mark this album; particularly if, by sitting on the air bed, you can modulate the note as it passes the valve. On the closing track our Li-Lo idol even blubbers on about a "global elite"

Few of us who prefer to live in that place "where poetic champions compose" will ever be praised for having brought Promethean fire down to earth.  Van Morrison is one of them who deserve such honour from us, and in all his recorded work he has either refined his abilities, or assured himself of divine privileges by admitting weakness; and by his truly disarming blatant honesty.  BORN TO SING offers none of these things however; but by its absolute dullness it reminds us of the old crown jewels, of the "Queen of the Slipstream" for example; to remind us of the eternal sparkle and the living vibrancy that they always had.

Those of us framed to look for spiritual succour in the world have found enough beneath the refectory of Van Morrison to keep going back. Some of Van Morrison's spiritual insights are worth having. "Keep it Simple" and "That's that!" are two of them.  There are exotic morsels and crumbs too beautiful to eat still; but once upon a time there was real plenty.

The morose preoccupation of this album is with money. Perhaps the most miserable record that has ever been made, IF IN MONEY WE TRUST will try the patience of anyone looking for the joys of "Virgo Clowns" or for another glimpse of the blush of his muse; or for lines like  "You have crossed many waters to be here my love; and will you still be my special rose?"

MY RETREAT IN VIEW is without any amazing or saving graces.
PAGAN HEART is an insult to John Lee Hooker's work.  This really is PSEUDO JAZZ. Have a listen to John Lee Hooker when he duets with Van Morrison on "Gloria" or "I cover The Waterfront" to surprise us with the real thing.

reviewText:
For years now, Billy Joel has been threatening to quit rock & roll and go into a classical career. Judging by the performance on his new double-CD, and to quote the man himself, "this is the time." Recorded live at Madison Square Garden, Joel treated (or subjected, depending on your  point of view) the hometown crowd to a set of 35 songs--24 of which appear  on 2000 Years. For all intents and purposes, Billy Joel's creative peak  came in the late 70's, and with a few exceptions, he's been fizzling out  ever since.
There are a few high points on his new album, but most of  the time he's oversinging and turning the songs into a much larger  production than is necessary. There are entirely too many musicians/singers  onstage for much of the show. Does he really need seven backup singers on  "Big Shot?" Of course not. "The Ballad of Billy the Kid" (one of his  all-time best songs) suffers from too many horns.
Speaking of the horn  section, they sound horribly out of place on just about everything except  "Big Man on Mulberry Street"--one of the few high points you'll find on  these two CDs. The only other high points to be found are "Prelude/Angry  Young Man" and a cover of "Honky Tonk Women."
You're probably wondering  about the low points. Well, I won't list them all (we do have space  limitations here), but here's a rundown of some of the worst. "Movin' Out"  ( ) when it was released in the first place. Did anyone really think it  would sound any better now? Ordinarily "New York State of Mind" is a high  point in the set. Not here. Sure, he has Rich Cannata come in and reprise  his sax solo, but unfortunately Billy feels the need to oversing  again--this time to the point where it sounds like he's in pain by the end  of the song.
Joel says before "I've Loved These Days" that it's the  first time he's played it since 1976. Maybe if he hadn't blown his voice  out on the last song, he wouldn't have had to lower the key to sing it  here. Before his overblown rendition of "Only the Good Die Young," Joel  tells the crowd "after this song, you have 15 minutes to have a whiz." Very  professional, Billy--especially on the CD. "I Go to Extremes" was one of  the piano man's few decent songs of the 80's. Unfortunately, here it's  marred by a generally lame performance that Joel tries to cover up by  oversinging. Are we detecting a pattern here?
The next highpoint is  "Goodnight Saigon." This was one of the few tracks (along with "Big Man on  Mulberry Street") that actually surpassed the original. Enough high points,  let's get back to the low points. "Auld Lang Syne" is awful. Someone  should've given Joel a monitor so he'd be able to tell when he's offkey.  But wait, it gets worse. Up next--the undisputed low point on the CDs,  "River of Dreams." The backup singers hit all the high notes for him; then  all of a sudden, he starts to scream like a wild banshee. He throws in a  verse on "Land of 1000 Dances," but even that can't save this from being  just short of six minutes of pure torture.
I could go on, but I'm sure  you're getting the point. It's a shame that someone with Joel's potential  has to subject his fans to a third-rate live album like this one. It  would've been better if he had just released an EP with the few good songs  on it and called it quits on a positive note. reviewText:
The idea was a good one: a newly repackaged album in mini-lp sleeve replica albeit very highly priced but they forgot the most important thing; in keeping with the old cliche 'you can't judge a book by its cover', the sound quality is absolutely horrendous.

This version isn't remastered or even mastered well at all to begin with.  This may well be an album that's more deserving of one star but who could tell?  You can't hear a darn thing with the horrible production job.  I couldn't believe it at first as I had just got "Lionheart" in this format and the sound quality was excellent until I took a closer look at the credits on the cover: produced by Kate!

Let this be a lesson in that people who don't know what they are doing should leave the job to one who does.  Even the great George Martin of Beatles fame who although was executive producer, still allowed the likes of Glyn Johns and Geoff Emerick and even Alan Parsons at one stage to do the actual mastering, all renowned sound engineers and who have gone on to become great producers in their own right.

Kate is a great performer and usually, with this album as a possible exception, is an excellent songwriter but she's definitely not anywhere near as good a producer as is evident here.  Very low sound levels and when you raise the volume you get very muffled and grainy sound and all this added to subpar material means that this is highly not recommended.  You are better off holding on to your old versions of this album or getting cheaper remastered versions that are out there.

Oh lord... It's both unfortunate and ironic that the first band to actually get busted for paying for radio airtime happens to be both terrible and incredibly popular.
I actually think a few of the people in Limp Bizkit are quite talented and deserve respect- both guitar player Wes Borland and drummer Joh Otto could find a much better gig playing music with some kind of artistic value. I think they both have unique styles and technical proficiency which could be used to a far better end in a different band.
What makes Limp Bizkit, and in particular this album, bad is Fred Durst. He is a talentless hack who couldn't rap his way out of a paper bag. He was clearly in the right place at the right time when he went from chubby, mediocre tattoo artist in Jacksonville, FL to chubby, mediocre frontman for the Poison of our time. The only track I've ever heard in which he showed any kind of talent was Ntogether with Method Man, and this was because he was just mimicking Meth. I can see it now: Behind The Music, in about three years or less. The man to blame for the downfall of the band will be their whiny, shrill-voiced singer.
I hate to refer to other reviews in this one, but 99 out of 100 good reviews for this album are misspelled, non-punctuated, aimless rants written by preadolescents. I weep for the future when I see these reviews, as I know in 20 years these kids will be speading their poor taste thoughout the world.
Something to consider is the fact that every musical era breaks down and disappears when the artists involved become more concerned with their public image rather than creating art. Limp Bizkit is a perfect example of this. They were signed by successful friends and their popularity was paid for by their record label. Can the end be far?

This is a review of the sound quality only, not the music.

I think this could have been a beautiful and powerful record.  Unfortunately, the mastering guy was told to make it as loud as possible.  So large portions of the album suffer from mastering induced distortion and clipping from brutal dynamic range compression.  There is a whole generation of music that is being damaged for no other reason than they want it to be as loud as possible so it's not quiet on someone's ipod.  Look at 'loudness war' at wikipedia or google it.

I'm not entirely sure why artists want this type of processing applied to their music.  If I had labored and sweated over an album I would want it presented in the best possible way, especially if I was already rich like Alanis.  But instead they intentionally harm the sound because they think people don't know how to use the volume button, or volume normalization/replaygain.  I cannot help but think that if an industry puts out an intentionally inferior product, fewer people will buy it.  And so I wonder if the downturn in the music industry over the last decade is just because of p2p.

And this version will most likely be the only one we get to hear as this record is not a likely candidate for a mofi type remastering.  C'est la vie.

reviewText:
Seems that marginally-talented popster/reality-TV star Ashlee Simpson is still trying to carve out an identity for herself. First she fills her first album with angst about her sister overshadowing her, and then she titles her second "I Am Me."

But after a year of pure P.R. disaster, there's one lesson Simpson hasn't learned: how to make really good pop music. Instead, this is the MTV music du jour: pop that styles itself as rock or punk, but has neither the spirit nor the skill. It's more of the same, and somehow it seems even more childish this time.

It kicks off with "Boyfriend," a guitar pop song that strains mightily to be counted as rock, but is too simple and radio-bouncy. The song's point: Simpson.... well, she basically claims that "you got it wrong/I didn't steal your boyfriend!" The popster doth protest too much, methinks -- it wouldn't even be an issue if she hadn't brought it up.

The songs that follow aren't much more memorable, with cries of "L-O/L-O/L-O-V-E!, and radio-friendly guitar pop without much actual melody. Just electric guitars cycling around in circles, with Simpson making an effort to really, really sing in a memorable way, and failing miserably. Even balladry -- a relatively easy kind of song -- falls short, since the lack of cover-up music reveals what a strained voice she has.

In "I Am Me," Ashlee Simpson is apparently trying to prove that she is a good vocalist with true artistry. Unfortunately, she only emphasizes that the album is artistically empty, and that she cannot sing well, even with the help of studio wizardry to smooth over her vocal straining.

The biggest problem is that Simpson fills up the album with her efforts to soar vocally. A lot of good pop singers don't have great voices. But hers is a scratchy, small-ranging voice, and the more she tries to soar, the worse she sounds; it just emphasizes that she has very little range and no smoothness to her vocals.

Nor do the songs make up for these. Most of it is instant teen angst, concerned primarily with boyfriends, public embarrassment (it's, like, SO awful to be booed!), and written in a lowest-common-denominator style. "Burning Up" is crippled by a seemingly endless stream of "I...I...I...I..." Elsewhere, we have instant cliches like "Every day is a new day!" If I were Simpson, I wouldn't hurry to share credit for garbage like this.

Like her debut, Ashlee Simpson's "I Am Me" stumbles over it pretensions and its lack of content. It's empty on all levels -- musically, vocally, and lyrically. If "I Am Me" is Ashlee, then she's terribly uninteresting.

reviewText:
Now here's an artist that has been praised and given the whole song-and-dance treatment by the media, but regardless of who you are, you are bound to be disappointed by the finished product.
Norah Jones's follow-up to her inexplicably huge-selling debut Come Away With Me is filled with more of the same - smooth jazz-pop with tepid arrangements and lyrics with little effort put into them, almost as if they were an afterthought - basically it's good for background music at a formal dinner or as treatment for insomnia but that's it.
The difference between this album and the last are hints of country music, which come off as totally contrived and as an attempt to appeal to a different audience, rather than the authentic article. reviewText:
I don't understand why fans of Ryan Adams forget to mention 2003's Love Is Hell when speaking of his career "pinnacle."  That album is a staggering work of beauty and melancholy unlike anything I've ever heard before or since from a singer/songwriter.

Everyone says Ryan & Co. reached their peak with Cold Roses.  Cold Roses doesn't matter in the slightest to me.  The songs are watered down versions of Love Is Hell material, and bad Grateful Dead rip-offs.  I would never recommend Cold Roses or Jacksonville to someone unfamiliar with Ryan Adams.  I would ALWAYS recommend Love Is Hell, however.

Now, as for Cardinology...I'd only recommend this album to someone who enjoys bland average "old guys" playing pop/country tunes that occasionally touch on "rock."  This album is perfect alongside the likes of recent albums by The Eagles.  Ryan Adams even sounds like Glenn Frey much of the time.  Over 1/2 of Cardinology's songs sound like the same one song.  Then you have "Cobwebs" ripping off Easy Tiger's live standout "Off Broadway."  "Magick" is nowhere near as charming or engaging as "Halloweenhead."  Everyone knows that "Evergreen" is Jack Johnson with deeper lyrics.  And "Stop" is beleaguered and overdramatic (as are most closing songs on Ryan Adams' albums).

This comparison to songs off 2007's Easy Tiger is only to show that even that album, recent as it was and while it also is no Love Is Hell, was far better.  It had the tunefulness ("Everybody Knows"), lyrical bite ("Oh My God Whatever, etc."), and edginess ("The Sun Also Sets," "Nobody Listens To Silence") that are nowhere to be found on Cardinology.

It now appears Ryan Adams is taking a step back from music i.e. retiring for a period.  Maybe this is a good thing.  But if this were his last album, it would be a shame to see him go out on such a lackluster and feeble note.

My only guess is that they needed more money and knew that their fans would run out to buy any old garbage they would release. reviewText:
Anyone interested in purchasing the recent Robert Palmer reissues from Culture Factory or Edsel would be wise to read these two articles from SuperDeluxeEdition:

#1: Online music forums are buzzing at the moment with fans claiming that Edsel's recent Island-era Robert Palmer reissues show signs of being mastered from an MP3 source.

Using sound editing software such as Audacity, audiophiles often like to `look' at the sound of tracks via waveforms - it's a way to check the state of the mastering. Some fans of the late English singer have been doing just this with the latest reissues and are unhappy with what they see. "There is absolutely no musical information above 16 kHz, which is a dead giveaway" stated one person - the implication being that this was an indication of an MP3 source. Many fans have emailed us in the last 24 hours asking if they should not buy the reissues and if we knew whether there was any truth in these claims.

So we put these allegations to Edsel label manager Val Jennings and he was adamant that the masters had been nowhere near an MP3 file.

"We were given flat transfers by Universal for all the albums and bonus tracks, on CDs with Universal's Belsize Road Tape Library inlays. Since they came directly from the tape library, I can't see how MP3s would come into it. The CDs certainly don't have MP3s on them", he said.

When pushed about the actual source and details around the transfers themselves he told us:

"I can but assume that they would have been new transfers from the tapes with no extra EQ. They were done in 2006 for Universal's very own catalogue team, who were all set to reissue the albums, until the whole project was shelved for reasons no-one involved can remember".

Clearly frustrated with the situation Val added, "I really don't know what else to say. It's shame that people can't just be glad that someone has reissued the records, instead of trying to find or invent faults."

#2: When Edsel Records reissued Robert Palmer`s Island era albums on CD, we were delighted. Regular SDE readers will know, we rate the Yorkshireman's diverse '70s output highly and like many fans were frustrated with the lack of activity around his catalogue.

Although the (Edsel)reissues that came out at the end of August were budget conscious combo-packs, with two albums in each set (three, in one case), the packaging itself was excellent, with slipcases, thick booklets, essays, lyrics and some great archive photography and scans of sleeves and record labels. Most of the albums also came with bonus tracks.

Unfortunately, enthusiasts who'd purchased these sets started reporting in online music forums that the sound quality was not what you might expect from an original tape transfer. Some were stating that the albums looked like they'd been mastered from MP3s.

That got us thinking. If the new Edsel releases are indeed less-than-optimum, then what is the best way to listen to Robert Palmer's Island albums? Exactly which CDs sound the best? Are the Edsel reissues, really that bad?

There are a number of different masterings, and rather than heap amateur analysis on top of amateur analysis, we asked mastering engineer Nick Watson to give us his professional opinion. In his 23 year career Nick has worked with bands like Faith No More, The Kinks and The Libertines and he co-owns (with Tim Debney) of Fluid Mastering in London.

We gave Nick three versions of Palmer's 1976 album "Some People Can Do What They Like" and asked him to analyse them. One was the new 2013 Edsel CD, the second was an original Island CD from the 1980s, and the final disc was the 2011 remaster from US label Culture Factory. To keep things simple this comparison is based on the first track of the album "One Last Look." Here's what Nick had to say.

The spectrogram image show(ed) clearly that there is no useful audio data on the CD above 16kHz, and the blocky nature of the display is consistent with the audio having been subjected to some form of data compression such as MP3 or AAC or similar. The sound of the disc is also consistent with this, with the top end of the recording appearing to switch on and off, the stereo image flinching, and some twittering artifacts in the top end, as one would expect from low resolution data-compressed signal. As a test, using a clean uncompressed version of the same track as a control, I found that a reduction of the bitrate to about 192kbps was required to reduce the perceived quality to something similar to the Edsel CD (see this image to illustrate).

Apart from the data-compression artifacts, the album sounds quite thick and bloated (too much low-mid) and very closed off in the top end, although this latter point will be partly to do with the data-compression.

This CD sounds exactly as one might expect for a reissue done at this time. The EQ is quite thin and the sound is slightly brittle - although once the listener has adjusted to this there are no unusual or distracting artifacts. The stereo image is open and consistent. This sounds like an album that could do with being properly remastered, from the original tapes, with a little extra warmth and bass in the EQ and the more natural and transparent sound of good quality modern A to D conversion.

Looking at the spectrogram, (I could) see that the frequency response continues upwards from 16kHz and there is none of the blockiness of the Edsel image. Another interesting point is at the extreme high end you can see the response tails away smoothly, but rapidly, at about 21kHz. This would probably be due to the more aggressive filters used in A to D converters in the 80s and early 90s.

The spectrogram on this version has no blockiness and no rapid rolloff of the high frequencies. This would demonstrate that as far as digital processing is concerned, this version has suffered the least degradation, i.e. it has not been data compressed and was converted from analogue to digital using more recent technology.

The sound of this version however is dreadful. The tone of it would suggest that at least 8 dB of boost has been applied at around 2kHz giving it what you might describe as a telephonic kind of brightness, and the stereo image swerves from side to side wildly and seemingly at random, with the left channel becoming so loud at times that clipping distortion is audible. Given that no engineer in his right mind would do this to a recording (and I'm allowing for the fact that plenty of engineers do some pretty awful things in the mastering world) I can only assume that on this occasion the guy left the room and WHAT WE HEAR ON THE Culture Factory CD IS THE RESULT OF THE CAT WALKING ACROSS THE CONSOLE. All of which is a real shame as it's a great album, and one that I would enjoy listening to for pleasure.

Conclusions

Given the choice between these three CD editions, the hands-down winner for me is the original '80s Island reissue - which, for all its faults (faults it shares with pretty much every other reissue of that period) it at least doesn't suffer from strange sonic artifacts or appallingly harsh EQ.

Coming back to the much discussed Edsel reissue finally, one might wonder how such a thing could have happened. Well, I'm not going to speculate about that and can only talk about what I find on the disc itself. However, in general terms, I can perhaps allude to the fact that before computers and music became so closely intertwined, mastering was something that could only be undertaken by professional engineers. Today, however, anyone with a computer, whether they work in a studio or an office, can pick up a disk or download a file, and do stuff with it. Not everyone for instance knows how to make a 1:1 copy of a CD, and might load it into some freeware in order to attempt to do so, perhaps resulting in some inadvertent degradation. I even know of record company employees who do things to audio masters using applications such as iTunes, without really knowing what they're doing or why, other than it being something that they have been shown how to do by someone else in the office. It's almost akin to say, 20 years ago, them taking a master tape out of the box, and unravelling it and then editing it using scissors and sellotape. Except that that would never have happened.

(by Nick Watson, minor edits by me)

reviewText:
The fact that the Reqiuem stands at the very pinnacle of the classical repertoire is beyond dispute, but I'm afraid that I don't have too many nice things to say about Mr. Abbado's go at it.
His overall approach seems to be to treat the work as a sort of quasi-baroque compostition: the orchestra is scaled down far too much and plays with far too much staccato (especially when that is not how it appears in the score).  One, not knowing which orchestra is playing, would be surprised to hear that it is the Berliner Philharmoniker!  No power, no weight, little beauty!
The score itself is the source of endless scholarly debate as to how much is Mozart and how much is Sussmeyer.  This recording utilizes one of several re-written scores whose aim is to make it more "Mozartian."  It is chiefly the Sanctus that is affected, but so also is the Agnus Dei.  To be honest, I'm not so sure that they accomplished their objective: it sounds less like Mozart, and one might even be so bold as to say it is down right bad.
The tempi are never quite right: either too slow or too fast, but it is generally on the fast side.  This, along with Mr. Abbado's quasi-baroque approach, serves only to remove any real drama and tension from the piece.  And when we come to a movement like the Dies Irae, where we want a little fire, the tempo becomes too mellow; no drive at all.
The choir is very crisp and accurate but has no warmth or real power behind them.  The soloists are only just sufficient.  Bryn Terfel is certainly a consumate Mozartian, but does not give a very memorable performance here.  And the other soloists tend to fall flat as well.
This recording was something of a memorial for Herr Karajan, who passed away 10 years previous, but I can't think of a performance that does so little to emulate the style of conduction that Karajan championed.
If you want a real recording of the Requiem Mass, stear well away from this CD and go with one by Karajan (my favourite is the 1976 recording with the Berliner Philharmoniker, the Wiener Singverein, Anna Tomowa-Sintow, et al).

reviewText: If there was one thing that Soilwork had shown during its first few albums, was the bands ability to mix so many forms of metal into one, and make it work. When I heard the first few works by this band, I had thought they were the most unique band since "Hypocrisy". Even though I am not die hard fan of Soilwork, I still enjoyed what they had to offer, and found myself sneaking in a listen every now and then. As the albums and time went on, it was apparent that Soilwork was starting to change over their musical style. They had seemed to abando some of their Death and Thrash metal sound, and were almost crossing into a more Nu Metal sound. That is fine. Even though some Metal Heads critize Nu Metal as being generic and poppy, that is a really broad statement. There are some Nu Metal bands that are fantastic. True, some are generic and sound like every other, but some try their best to create that sound, while still creating thier own "Bells and Whistles" to stand out from the rest. So on to "Stabbing the Drama" When I first heard it, I was ashamed that Soilwork would even be dabbling around with this generic sound. Gone was everything they had built, only to be torn down my genric pop Nu Metal core, almost like the band was releasing something for the masses of pop radio, and not for the fans who so dug the sounds that made them stand out from the rest. True, there are fans and people that will love this album, but I tend to be really critical of bands that have a ton of talent, and then release an album of this calibur. Korn, Metallica, Machine Head, Pantera and Coal Chamber are all bands that I had either loved the debuts, or some of the bands early works. Then it seemed that they crossed over in sound, and in my opinion, this was done not because of a want to make something different (most of us know that as we get older, we all seem to have changes or long for something different musically)but they did it to sell more albums and appeal to the masses. Some of those bands recovered, some didnt, but the damage was still done. So the conclusion is, what will you think of "Stabbing the Drama" It depends on what you are looking for. New to Soilwork? Like a more generic Sound or simple Metal? Yes, you might like it. Even fans of Soilwork might appricate the change here. I look at this as strictly a marketing gimmic. As such, I was waiting with bated breath the release of Shogun. Unfortunately, the group seems to have been pressured by their "hardcore" following to return to the 'screaming' style of vocals. The songs suffer, and it's a shame because this is a group of musicians that are on top of their game. EVERY Song on this release is marred at one point or another by the cookie monster vocals.

Why would a band sacrifice musical and vocal quality in this way in order to "save face" with their fanbase? In summation, if you are a traditional metal head who enjoys melody along with pummelling riffs, stay away from this but hold onto your copy of Crusade.  However, if you enjoy metalcore and screaming vocals, you will find this to your liking.  I can't expect Trivium to make it to the next level of metal greatness unless they go back to the more traiditional metal style of Crusade.

Remember No Limit Records' heyday from 1997 to 1999? No matter if the artist was good or bad, if a new No Limit album came out, you would rush to the store and buy it to add to your NL collection. I know of nobody who can admit to owning this, not even the most "bout it" fan, and I'm from Milwaukee, where Dirty South music is played nonstop.
This album doesn't sound like a debut for a promising artist. It sounds more like a contest winner who earned the opportunity to work with Beats By The Pound for a day. Songs like "It's Your Thing" (a poor interpolation of Dave Hollister's "My Favorite Girl"), "Pony Ride", and "I Need a Thug" showcase elementary production (a shocker since the album is mostly produced by the Pound), and bad rhymes and vocals. It's a shame when an artist can't sing OR rap because s/he has nothing else to fall back on. There are more bad songs than this but I can't remember them, and I can't tell you about them because that would require me to listen to this album again.
Too many female rappers limit their topics to being the baddest b, taking on any dude because she's just as tough, or going downtown, and Mercedes is no different (see "Kiss Da Cat" and "Talk Dirty to the DJ's"). And in my opinion, her singing is worse than Mia X trying to sing. But most No Limit music is trendy anyway (do you know anyone today that still bumps Ghetto D or Charge it to the Game?), so this album is probably long forgotten. If you're feeling nostalagic and wanna get rowdy rowdy again, feel free to get any No Limit album you want, but in my opinion, skip this one at all costs.

reviewText:
I didn't think it could get any worse than "Jugulator," but it has with this ... disc.  Rob Halford clearly was seminal with the song-writing on the top-notch older stuff (i.e. "Defenders of the Faith," "Hell Bent for Leather," "Screaming for Vengeance"), because now that he's gone, Priest is left with Glenn Tipton's inane lyrics and Ripper Owens' ill-fated attempts at emulating Halford.  Deductive reasoning, you see.  With Halford, Priest was great.  Without him, they're God-awful.
Also, where are the classic Tipton and K.K. Downing solos?  They've gone the way of the do-do bird, replaced with monotonous riffing.  Ripper Owens can certainly hit those high notes, but is little more than Halford clone.  And what's with the cursing?  This isn't the Priest of yore.  This is something else, proving once again that different doesn't always mean better.
Avoid all JP albums after "Painkiller," which was also heavy, but still great.  Why?  Halford, of course.  Also, it had tons of searing solos and great compositions.  Really, I could care less if Rob Halford is homosexual.  It's too bad TIpton, Downing, and the others did.  Halford is a metal legend, an incomparable frontman with an exorcistic voice, and a credit to the music industry.
Nevertheless, Halford has had the last laugh.  His solo career post-Priest has produced two masterpieces, "Resurrection" and "Crucible."  Priest, on the other hand, is washed up.  In fact, they're relegated to playing at second-rate venues and desolate festivals.  That usually happens when the genuine talent leaves.

reviewText:
As lead singer Richard Patrick recently turned 40, he must look back at how different his life and his band are now. Gone is the anger of his youth, and his introverted outlook on life, along with all of his Filter bandmates. Geno (guitar), Frank (bass), and Steve (drums) from the last two releases have not returned. And long gone is his original collaberator Brian from the debut "Short Bus."

Musically:

Attempting to fill in the gaps, Patrick has brought in Wes Borland to write/perform a track, and John 5 does the same for a couple more. Aside from these songs however, there is a noticeable lack of the guitar presence that Filter fans have become accustomed too. Too often the riffs seem boring, radio friendly acoustic is common also.

Session star Josh Freese fills in on drums, and more often than not sounds lost with his task. Generic drum beats cover most of the album, and this is by far the most basic and limited work that I have ever heard from Freese.

Lyrically:

Aside from the musical changes, the songwriting is the major letdown here. Patrick seems dedicated to anger, even if he has none. An upcoming  father, recently sober after a post "Amalgamut" stay in rehab, and middle aged for the first time, there is just not much to be angry about.

Thankfully there is an unpopular war in Iraq. Although Patrick is a few years late, much of the album centers on Bush Administration criticism, deception, and "lies." A word that you will hear frequently throughout this album. The anger and rage feel forced here, as Filter was always best at straying from political commentary.

Finally "Can Stop This" picks up from "The 4th" on the last album. A way-too-long instrumental filler piece that makes this album appear longer than it actually is.

Conclusion:

Overall this is one of two things:

A sign that Richard Patrick and Filter have lost their inspiration. It may mean that "Anthems for the Damned" is better off in the hands of new listeners not expecting such powerful former singles as "Welcome to the Fold," "Hey Man Nice Shot," and "Where do we go From Here." This may be a welcome change for someone more tailored to the current modern rock field.

Or, hopefully it will be looked back on as just a lost album among future great ones. Maybe Patrick can regroup after this tour with his new bandmates, new energy, and new inspiration. Maybe they will head back to the studio and re-claim Filter's legacy, it would be a shame to end on such a weak chapter.

One of the reviewers hit it on the spot while comapring this to the smooth, diluted syrupy jazz of Spyorgyra. Case in point - Violet Love with its saccharine driven sax leads. Seriously, we expected a LOT more from Densmore....maybe next time. On the other hand check out Manzarek's Love Her Madly. A great documentation of taking the music to the next level, stretching it out, brewing the vamps it in the electronic(a) pot, all the while maintaining the vibe he created alongside the late Jim Morrison. reviewText:
Remember the style of music that came out in the late 70's called Punk?

The pioneers of this type of music were bands such a Clash, The Sex Pistols, The Ramones and the Talking Heads.  The style becamse somewhat funk-influenced to the gut-wrentching hardcore metal influenced sounds of The Dead Kennedies and Ministry.  Even Social Distortion had their own little sound to offer.  This is how it went through the 80's.

Yet, after the who Nirvana-mania that saved music from Whitesnake and Warrent, Punk, as well as many other sounds, seemed lost until...

Green Day comes around with "Dookie."  This continued the punk sound into what we know today.

So in the words of Oasis:  "Where did it all go wrong."

It's not that this sounds on it's own is bad.  When Blink 182 first came out, they had a lot of fun to offer.  But gawd, where do we draw the line?  After that, we had ( in no particular order) Sum 41, New Found Glory, My Chemical Romance, Showoff, and jeez, I could go on forever.  They all sound so much alike.  Still they were once tolerable.  But with simple plan, (sigh), enough is enough.  I can't even tell the difference sometimes between these guys and Bowling For Soup.  And I don't easily confuse bands.

Really, though, these guy call themselves Punk.  But last time I checked, Punk was about rebellion, Anarchy, disatisfaction with where humanity is going, all that stuff.  Ex Sex Pistols "Anarchy In The UK" or Ramones "I'm Against It."  Now Listen to some of the titles off this:  "I'm Just A Kid," "God Must Hate Me," "I'd Do Anything."  Difference?  You'd have to be blind not to see one.  These guys have jumped on the "poser" bandwagon that every other "punk" band on a major label has jumped on, and thus, mainstream punk is doing the same thing heavy Metal is.

They trivialize the canon by vacuuming each lyric of its contextual emotion and any irony - all for the stab at `prettiness'. Yet, their robotic vocals consistently drown any beauty with persistent tortuous detail.
It's an exuberant, classic gene pool mutated as soporific inertia. Chynna Phillips, perhaps the most unmelodic singer in pop history [sorry, Jessica Simpson] sucks the exquisiteness on every track she tackles. And if Chynna defines tuneless monotony, then Wendy personifies stupefying naivet - she attacks her leads as a nave high school chorus member with no understanding of nuance of content. And poor Carnie remains the biggest curio - always the most talented of the tacky trio - which doesn't mean to imply that she - or they - had any - it seems any trace of vocal capacity dissolved away with her gastrointestinal bypass surgery.  Strongest contender yet for worst CD of 2004.  My grade: D+

reviewText: I'm sorry to say it, but In Flames, one of the greatest Swedish exports since Volvo, finally fell into their own trap. I've never been a fan of the early In Flames-era, I never picked up on the charm in The Jester Race for instance, but I still felt that their three latest albums all had something to bring, with Soundtrack to Your Escape being the all-out best, packed with melodic hits just begging to be unleashed and explode (you literally cannot sit still to that album). There was much fuss over Come Clarity, and granted, some of it was justified. Come Clarity is a solid album, with sturdy power, a beautiful title track, and a superb collaboration with Lisa Miskovsky (who could've seen it coming? - and yet it makes perfect sense). And then, all of a sudden, came A Sense Of Purpose. In the wake of Come Clarity, the album seemed to just drop out of nowhere all too fast. Can't we let the last one sink in for a while? And what immediately struck me when I listened to it was..nothing. It was In Flames on auto-pilot, doing what's come to be expected of them, right down to the guitar hooks. All you hear on this album has been said and done before, and better at that. Reroute and Soundtrack have the "hits", the melodies you can't shake, and Come Clarity certainly has the more grounded touch, especially the calmer title track. So I'm afraid it's exactly that - there's no point or purpose to A Sense Of Purpose. There shouldn't have been such a rush. I hope they take the time to really develop the next album, because this is just a colon in their catalogue to me.

reviewText:
It's amazing how hype can carry someone so far when they have delivered so little.
After the massive hype when the album launched, you would think Leona had done the unthinkable for a talent show winner and come up with a distinctive debut that really established them and set them apart from the crowd.

Sadly, it's just another classic example of PR and label execs hyping up something not up to scratch.

I don't mean to be scathing and I'm not having a go at Leona... She deserved her victory on the X factor.. You can't argue with her voice, it's a mega find. But winning the x factor was really the easy bit and you'd think Simon Cowell would have learned this by now with how many young kid's dreams he's built up, profited from and then shattered. Her 10 months spent away really gave me hope that only the best songs would have been chosen for her to record. I had foolishly believed that the length she had spent making this was a good sign. I was sure nothing bland and derivative would pop up.

This album is nothing better than the rubbish Westlife churn out every year in time for Christmas sales. Leona sang other people's songs on the X Factor but made them sound great and her own. Here she's given the sort of pap Westlife call exciting original music in between their covers when their writers "creative spells" dry up. It's bland ballad after bland ballad. This really could have been a Westlife album. On the X factor, she sang songs and really made you feel them. Here she's been given a load of bellow par songs. Honestly, I defy Simon Cowell to argue that any other artist could release any track off this album other than the cracking Bleeding Love and have a hit. The reality is it's not Leona's fault. Her voice is excellent, Simon Cowell has failed her. He didn't find anything exciting other than Bleeding Love that was worth the wait.
Honestly, most of the tracks here don't and won't stand up over time. Bleeding Love is an instant classic and has carried Leona this far but what does the next few months hold... I fear a bit of a media backlash because she won't sell much more albums anyway, this has sold over a million to date, the media will have a field day knocking down what they helped to build up only months before, the label will cleverly blame huge album sales for poorly performing singles and Leona's dreams will be slipping fast away.

 I really can't see her having any other hits off this album. After a while they all start to sound the same, start with a piano refrain and build up to a modern beat that carries them to their conclusion. Take a Bow is an attempt to break this cycle and try modern RnB. Beyonce and co won't be having sleepless nights anyway. It's painfully bad. There's really nothing else that stands out. Whatever it takes is okay, catchy maybe but nothing to get excited about.

At the end of the day, Leona's voice is great but the material is bland and unoriginal. As for cracking America, Bleeding Love might deceive some into buying this lacklustre album, but she runs the risk of being a one hit wonder there and elsewhere in the world because she simply doesn't have the material to back her up or the same hype. In the uk/ Ireland , I'm sure we won't see more than three singles max because they simply aren't here. Maybe, they'll repackage the album with some new tracks but that would be just cynical and greedy.. so they probably will do it! It's a shame Leona's debut hasn't lived up to the hype.  I wanted her to do well and have a long career.. she deserves it but based on this , the jury's definitely out still.

reviewText: Normally, a new Dream Theater album is an experience worth waiting for. This was certainly the case with every one of DT's previous albums, including their 3 live albums. Unfortunately, this is not one of those instances. This album lacks focus, sounds too pop-pish, doesn't have enough heavy music, tries to be too many things for too many people, etc etc, you get the drift. Every song is a disappointment. After suffering through the first seven tracks, I had high hopes for the closing, 24-minute title track. I should have known better. The intro is a shameless rip-off of Pink Floyd's "Shine On You Crazy Diamond'', right from the gentle atmospheric keyboards to the distant, chiming guitar riff. The rest of the track rips off Yes and Genesis, even down to a reference to a ""machine messiah'' which is a Yes song on their Drama album. If I had to use a single word to sum up this CD, it would be ""insipid''. Petrucci's guitar sound is weak and buried in the background, even for the few solos he plays. As a guitar player myself, this is sacrilege. Rudess' keyboard sound is fine, but the melodies are nothing great. Portnoy and Myung do their part to hold it together and adding an orchestra was a nice touch but it isn't enough to save this bloated, over-indulgent waste of money. I own all DT's records and DVDs and all have been played at least 10-20 times. This won't follow suit.

reviewText:
I've never understood the fuss over No Doubt.  They started off as a decent ska-influenced band - they originally had two singers and the energetic music was enough to take the focus off of Gwen Stefani's often nasal, irritating vocals.  Then they became a sensation when they streamlined their sound and became a new wave dance/pop group on 1995's Tragic Kingdom album.  Since then, the band has continued to regress, with each release becoming poppier and more banal than the next - clearly the sign of a band trying desperately to hang on to that brass ring.
As far as this album goes - why bother?  It's all the singles that by this point you're probably sick of, as most of them are played ad nauseum on the radio.  You've got "Just A Girl", the subject matter of which would have been fine about 40 years ago, but the song has been rendered meaningless in this era of equal opportunity.  Then there's meaningless ditties like "Spiderwebs" ("I'm walking into spiderwebs / Leave a message and I'll call you back"), melodramatic ballads ("Don't Speak", "Simple Kind Of Life") where Gwen is crying out for sympathy but only leaves the listener feeling annoyed, and ridiculously vapid songs like "Hey Baby" which make "Spiderwebs" seem downright profound in comparison.  And then there's the cover of "It's My Life" which has had all the passion and resonance sucked out of it by Stefani's lackluster voice.  Only "Trapped In A Box" is worth listening to - at least that song is somewhat unique and well performed.
In summary: Slick, overproduced, overexposed pop music lacking substance.  This album is far from a necessity.  Support some bands that need the attention instead of this overrated band.

reviewText: Caveat:  have loved Red House Painters since their inception, saw them in London and LA and SF very early; have greatly enjoyed early Sun Kil Moon LPs--the first one in particular.  Now this is the sort of ultra-confessional, I-just-jotted-down-what-I-thought-over-coffee, sort of lyrical album that (let's hope) puts the proverbial nail in the coffin of that egregious thing:  SINCERE MUSIC.  Art is artifice, Mark--and for you to (in the most baldly, anti-poetic way) set your bleeding journal to arpeggiated dreadnoughts is crude, cowboyish, the hilt of bad art.  Lauded for its honesty, this record should be pilloried as a travesty--a high school binder put on a plinth (for plinth read:  Pitchfork's 9.2 creamy encominum).  It's bad art in the way the Kristen Stewart's poem in Vogue is bad art.  It's just nowhere-to-turn embarrassing that Kozelek, a very talented, beyond lugubrious sad-sack, would, in his never-had-a-job existence (sorry 'bout that), think this worth inflicting (the word is not too strong) on people.  the song about the Zep film is about the most hypnotically indulgent thing I have ever heard.  At least Neil Young, K's avatar and patron saint, is going into that good night blazing his tweed amp away.  There's nothing here but sophomoric navel gazing (yeah I know that's redundant).  and this when there are good, melodic guitar bands that get very little recognition:  cf, the black watch, "the end of when";  the new LP by Jeff Martin of Idaho  ("You Were a Dick"), and Radiohead.  (Kidding re: Radiohead).  Only rubes and the utter untutored will think this SO BRILLIANT because Mr Kozelek (who knows he's been a total jerk for many years--reviled by many many who have worked with him, for him, near him) tries to make aural amends via a trite, jejune, sad LP that's going to hoodwink a lotta people.  But Pitchfork followers are ripe for/ rife with that already.  buy the aforementioned LPs and the new MBV instead.

I'll try one more Poco which would be one of their greatest hits but I totally disagree with this band being "The band that CSN wish they were".  For me, there's no comparison.  I like country rock but I did not like this one at all.  Even the overhyped "Bonus track" was "blah". reviewText: Remember the part in the John Cusack movie <I>High Fidelity<I> where Cusack puts on that `Beta Band' CD to a head-bobbing reaction from the customers? Well if you got the point of that scene, then you'll hate the new Built to Spill CD, like most who enjoy quality music should. But if you're in that majority who actually thought the scene showcased a great tune, then you'll love this recording, and you have our sympathy. Glam-rock band Built to Spill's latest CD `Ancient Melodies of the Future' represents what happens all too often in the music industry: a band starts off at an independent record label, gains a fan base then sell-out to a big record label, proceed to write five songs in a couple months and use five B-sides to make up a forty-minute record, release it, sell a million copies but it turns out to be amazingly bad, but who cares as long as the band and the record label make money, right? But getting back to the actual album, Built to Spill's latest offering has virtually nothing at all that's enjoyable, or even thought provoking. Every song on the CD sounds the same as the previous one, making it feel like its just one overlong tune, not one song on the whole CD sounds original at all. The enormously dull "You are" shows this extremely well with its lyrics "Everybody/Everybody/Everybody Knows/Everybody Knows/Everybody Knows That/Everybody Knows That" which just drags on and on for four minutes.  The band steals from great groups like Radiohead and Oasis, trying to recreate their tunes, but only accomplish falling flat on their face and failing miserably. However, the album is redeemed with "Fly Around My Pretty Little Miss" which goes back to their original glam-rock roots that made them so great in the beginning, and showcases what they could've been. This is where we say farewell to the great independent band named Built to Spill, and welcome in the tedious, repetitive sell-out band by the same name.

reviewText: KISS died when they released "Unmasked" in 1980, and with due to the cowardice on the part of Gene and Paul with "The Elder" (1981) the band was done and buried as soon as Ace was thrown out. The removal of the makeup, the constant revolving door of band members as fast and as disposable as the groupies they met on the road, were only desperate gasps for air for a corporate machine that was on its last legs - and should have been given it a dignified death. The mid 90's reunion tours with Ace and Peter were only feeble and pitiful parodies of a band that once was Great. For when the same songs from the 1970s are repeated over and over in every concert, in every tour, it can only mean that the material from any post classic-KISS lineup absolutely stinks and is not accepted by the fans. What is even more obscene is the amount of money earned by the 4 original members but was unfairly distributed against the 2 goys. This album, whose content is subpar to even 1980s releases, is the work of a parody band whose bag of good ideas has been empty for quite some time now. No amount of studio trickery and over-amplified guitar sounds can mask the emptiness that lies beneath this pathetic album. I borrowed it from my local library as I did not want to risk enriching the SS duo any further. And after 2 listens - one in the car, the second in my home stereo - from end to end, I can definitely conclude the clown makeup should come off as well as the 2 hired hands pretending to be part of a band whose dues they never paid. I entered this album already biased against the band, but did listen to it twice to search for a hook, some thing that would neutralize the bias, but found only additional fuel with which to condemn this piece of garbage. If you must have this album, download it for free or copy it from your local library. Let's not fuel Gene Simmons' ego anymore, shall we?

reviewText:
An Avoidable Disaster, What a "Mother"

I loved the Dixy Chicks.  I loved Natalie Maines.  But, honestly, that little adventure she had with George "Lil Baby" Bush, which set every Rush Limberger Nut against her, where, oh my, they found it a crime against god and country that a girl would not like the idea of War, well, all the effects and repercussions were apparently too much for her, and yes, not without sufficient cause, for  even to this day, the Dixie Chicks, or any member thereof worries of Life and Limb when crossing the Mason Dixon Line.  You know, they don't call those "Nuts"  Nuts for Nothing.  "Praise God for the Second Amendment and the Right for any American to shoot to death anybody they don't politically agree with"... I hope you know that is my being sarcastic, but that is exactly the Nut mentality America has to deal with.  So, yes, she had Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome.  Her friends from the Dixie Chicks, Emily Robinson and Martie Maguire, tried to stand behind her and did, in so far as they put out that one extremely brilliant but angry CD, "Taking the Long Way" - a work of Art stuck in time and one particular situation - the songs are all wasted by being cemented in the momentary particulars of a drab history... really, they need to be re-done but instead of fuming and fulminating against Lil Baby Bush, they need to be set in the context of , well, maybe Angry and Disappointed love.

Well, Emily Robinson and Martie Maquire  moved on, with a very good CD, as the Court Yard Hounds.  Beautiful work, and hope they come up with more.

But Natalie, what did she do?  How many years has it been since "Taking the Long Way"?  I suppose she was hungry and felt she needed to put something, anything out. And that is what she did.  Where was her Manager!?  Where were the Record Companies!?  For her producer she found this guy,  Ben Harper... well Google Ben Harper and find what you find.  Some scrambling nobody.  A Club Player for a bunch of tone def pool players with not a single Hit.

We all know what made the Dixie Chicks, and that was with an attention getting Hit Song, "Wide Open Spaces"... and if Natalie had been paying attention she would have known that, to keep up the level of her career, she would have to come forward with another Popular Hit.  Well, She didn't.  Not even close.  The entire CD is worse than elevator music.  Yes, she has her voice, but she is no Stevie Nicks, and there is nothing in her just more than adequate voice that could save lame and vapid material.

Now, it's not really her fault.  She, after all, is only the `talent'.  Where were the Agents and the Record Companies?  After all, Natalie Maines was still a recognizable `property'... why would they just throw her away like that... to let her do a dozen sleepy stupid vapid songs under the power of some silly mid-level manipulator Producer like Ben Harper, the Producer of Nothing Good, who wouldn't know a popular hit if it were to come up an bite him in his Harper.

And, really, what was so hard?  The CD was mostly all covers... it was not like she  buried herself in her own filth, insisting on writing her own songs, ... no, she buried herself in other people's filth.  Why not go back and look into Musical History and redo some Hits?  Wasn't there anybody there to suggest that?  Well, no, that was the Producer's Job, and we already determined that he was probably the thickest idiot on the Music Scene today.  Dear God, I hope it wasn't that Natalie found him `cute'.  Well, it wouldn't be the first Music Career thrown away because of the funny tastes female artists develop for career contacts of the opposite sex - Emmy Lou Harris married a performer and did a duet CD with him that, well, decisively breaks the trend of her work getting better and better and better... and we remember how Marilyn McCoo, perhaps the best female popular voice of the 20th Century simply disappeared after she linked up with nobody "sore throat"  Billy Davis Jr.

Anyway, this may be the end of Natalie Maines.  Everyone who had been waiting for her, lovingly, went out and bought what she had to sell, and, listening to it, well, they certainly will never do that again.  Once for Charity, but never again unless the Radio raises her up to a Top 10 Goddess and there is no avoiding her.  So, for now, maybe she should get a Day Job.  I honestly think the Music Business has abandoned her, and she herself, depending entirely on her own resources, doesn't have another hit song in her, no... she should have really clung to her dear friends Emily Robinson and Martie Mcguire - THEY know what a hit is and we will hear from them again.

I am a big fan of Wilson Phillips, but if you're hoping to recapture the group's magic by buying Chynna Phillips' solo effort 'Naked and Sacred', there is a high chance (I'm not saying for sure, but there's a high chance) that you'll be disappointed.

Hardcore Chynna fans may scream at me for saying this - but most of her vocals are mildly pleasing at best, reed-thin and mediocre at worst. The songwriting also leaves much to be desired.

If you, however, can see the originality and poetry in lines like "If I could win your heart/If you'd let me in your heart/I'd be so happy baby/Just for these arms to be/Holding you close to me", then go ahead and disagree with me. But to me, those lines could have been written by an infatuated 11-year old. Apart from bland lyrics, the rhythms and melodies are mostly nothing to shout about either.

"Jewel in my Crown" sounded interesting at first, until I realised that it sounds like a watered-down version of Celine Dion's "Because You Loved Me".

There is just one track which moves me and has some of that magic one would expect from a Wilson Phillips member, and that's "Remember Me". The vocals are heartfelt and quite strong and the song is pretty well-written. It's about the stain in the heart from a love lost, even when one has found someone new and "moved on".

I like the lines "I'm the doorway flooded with tears/The doorways were flooded".

Unfortunately, this one decent track doesn't save the album from a one-star rating for me. I hear that Wilson Phillips has re-united and that is really the best thing, cos the magic and chemistry they had as a group is really irreplaceable by any solo effort.

reviewText:
It is remarkable how other previous reviewers seem to care nothing for Leibowitz's willful alterations to the score (I thought we had long ago passed that nonsense about Schumann's own poor ability to orchestrate which permitted, if not required, others to come in and touch up the scores as it suited them) - as Leibowitz does here - not to mention the intrusively agogic tempi that even Bernstein doesn't attempt. - If you love the "Rhenish", stick to Sawallisch, Szell, or Zinman.

Now I love the engineering of Ken Wilkinson and Charles Gerhardt in whatever capacity, but this is one of the LEAST impressive of their Readers Digest recordings (released by David Chesky). In fact, ironically it is in only the one non-German piece, Liszt's "The Mephisto Waltz," that we get the kind of great sound they were famous for.

Add to all this, a frightfully undistiguished Tannhuser (by the way, the umlaut comes over the second "a", not the first - as the CD liner notes and titles would have it here) bettered by countless other conductors, and you've got a CD for Leibowitz completists only.

The 5.1 mix of Dr. Jimmy is an exception. It sort of lays flat in the speakers which doesn't fit the otherwise dynamic performance. I might have been less critical if the 5.1 "E.P." had at least included the best song on the whole album - "I'm One". Well, at least we get Keith's great "Sea and Sand" drums mixed in 5.1.
 I do like the demos even with the modern added drums on 4 or 5 tracks. If you want the original unadulterated demos in excellent quality, you can get them on bootlegs. For my money, the added drums on some tracks makes them more listenable. In fact, I would have preferred it if Pete took off his sloppy drums on the other demo tracks and replaced them with the professional drums. (Yes, I also prefer colorized movies -- throw stones now)
 I go along with other reviewers who are dissappointed that no Who outtakes are included. I think the book is fairly good with Pete's discussion. Some words from "Roj" would have been welcome as this material has been a good part of his bread and butter in recent years and the way he sings "Love Reign Over Me" is one of if not THE great thrusts of the album. The new stereo mix of is not significantly different from the 90's remix. I do like the 90's mix, and this one, better than the original as they lopped off a good amount of the excessive reverb that was part of the original mix (compare original and new versions of "I'm One" for the most evident example). I also would like to have seen vinyl in this set as we got in the "Aqualung", "Smile" and "Station to Station" super deluxe sets.

reviewText:
I'm quite an admirer of Kate Bush: in the late 70s and early 80s she was an astounding talent whose lyrics exhibited a well-read and truly artistic mind. So it's disappointing to find her releasing an album consisting almost entirely of monotonous piano pieces which sound like they're trying to imitate the Tori Amos of 'Under the Pink'. (And falling far, far short.)

Take, for example, the title track. Where to begin with this? Actor Stephen Fry takes time off from tweeting about being stuck in an elevator or (more recently) on a grounded passenger jet to deliver yet another sequence of staccato inanities. The chorus requires Kate to interrupt his snow-lexicon with the lyrics "Come on man, you've got 44 to go ...". It doesn't pass the cringe test. And unfortunately the famous notion that the Eskimos have fifty words for snow has long been exposed as a myth: Anthony Woodbury identified 15 such words and demonstrated that they all have analogues in English such as sleet, drift, blizzard, and - appropriately for this track - slush. So that was a waste of an idea.

The CD has the feel of a concept album in that it's 65 minutes in length but features just seven tracks. Thus I had the niggling suspicion when I bought it that each tune might wind up taking its time. And how! It's fine for an album to *begin* with a slow, meditative piano piece; but as the hour drifts by and it becomes apparent that the album consists of *nothing but* ponderous keyboard-tinkling, the listener's patience wears thin. It's like being stuck in an elevator. With Stephen Fry.

I do worry about the artistic pedigree of the company Kate Bush is keeping: there's no way I would have bought this album if I knew that at one point Elton John's voice would come crooning through the speakers like an intruder at a Karaoke party. I admire the fact that after all these years Kate Bush is 'still going' (she very much belongs on today's music scene) - but it's a bad move for her to duet with singers who should be long gone.

The verdict? If you find yourself past the midway point of an album and you're still waiting for it to start, you know you've been had. This is a weak effort from someone who can do way better.

reviewText: Lo and behold, William Carragan has unearthed a hot-off-the presses First Symphony from 1866 when most of us hitherto had been thinking that the 1877 Linz edition was synonymous with the premiere. This is praiseworthy. Even so, rewrites by Bruckner can go either way. Simpson argues that the composer progressively ruined his Third Symphony. On the other hand, who can doubt that the Fourth and Eighth symphonies benefited greatly by the wholescale revisions if not recomposition? So what of this original version of the First Symphony? Does it supplant the existing 1877 First? To my mind, the answer is no. Indeed, a Charybdis has roared into being to accompany the Scylla that is the 1890 Vienna edition of the First. I detest both of them. True, there are minimal changes to the first three movements. Most of the amendments come in the finale and to my ears, they are fussy and jejune. Listen to the Tintner at 4'57" which to my mind is where Bruckner becomes Bruckner. In the hands of a Karajan or a Barenboim (with the Berliners), it is also a textbook model of how to build and sustain momentum in a symphony. With Tintner, the argument is far more diffuse - and that's being polite. Bruckner was damned right to rework it in 1877 (and in passing, I urge you to avoid Wand in this symphony as he uses the 1890 version wherein a nervous Bruckner purged the youthful exuberance from the work: it is a travesty). As always with Tintner, this is a Bruckner who does not smile. His Adagio is devoid of radiance. Credit-wise, the RSNO plays masterfully and the Naxos recording is superb. While I have yet to hear the Young, the Karajan has commanded the high ground since the early 1980s and its longevity is no accident Bruckner: 9 Symphonies [Box Set]. There is also much to be said for the Barenboim which is one of the few highlights of his near-dismal cycle with the Berliners (Bruckner: Symphony No. 1 in C Minor (Linz version); 'Helgoland' (Symphonic Chorus For Male Voices And Orchestra)). Either of them will provide you with a better appreciation of this masterwork.

reviewText:
Boston must be the shortest lived success story in the history of popular music.  After the debut Boston album was released in 1976, Tom Scholz and the gang were among the biggest names in the music business, everybody loved this band.  Who would have predicted their rapid rise and fall in popularity?  I'm not old enough to remember Boston, but I have checked their record sales, and it turns out that Tom Scholz released four new albums after the debut came out, and all four of them bombed!

Don't Look Back (1978)

Third Stage (1986)

Walk On (1994)

Corporate America (2002)

All those albums combined don't even come close to equalling the record sales of the debut.  Boston's popularity was so short lived that even The Backstreet Boys had longer music careers than they did.  Boston's mega platinum record sales dropped faster than a brick thrown out of 100th story window, and when the sophmore album was released, it flopped so bad that Tom fired everybody but Brad Delp, and all the band members besides them had to go back to their day jobs to make a living.

But I still admire Boston for breaking the world record in the "Biggest Has Beens Ever" category.  I mean just look at that mountain of unsold Boston records they left behind!  All that plastic could probably be recycled and used for all kinds of useful things!  Maybe we could melt them all down and use it as a construction material!  There's probably enough unsold Boston LPs to rebuild New Orleans!  LOL!  Boston----the ultimate has been band! :-)

- These songs were remixed from the 2nd generation tapes. Not the master tapes.

- Most of the songs are snippets, not entire versions. Often the beginnings and endings are not represented.

- Normally this wouldn't bother me (see my appreciation for The Velvet Underground's Quinn Tapes and MC5's Ready To Testify boxset) but the mixing job on this cd is FUBAR. Imagine being jet-lagged for 18 hours, eating Cap'n Crunch with no milk, and wearing ear muffs (the big puffy types) while listening to Bill O'Reily choke on his vibrator. You will have a near experience.

- Bomp! Records is soley responsible for this release. Tisk tisk on them for this batch of hoaxary. If you visit thier website you will know the importance of this label. Then you will up-chuck a little in your mouth.
